# Pietro Galatino’s Work on the Secrets of Catholic Truth.

->That is,<-

**A most complete commentary on all the difficult passages of the Old Tes-**
tament, drawn from the Talmud and other<gloss>and</gloss> Hebrew books, written both before the birth of CHRIST and afterwards, against the stubborn unbelief <note>original: "perfidiam". In the 16th century, this term was a standard theological label for "unbelief" or the refusal to accept Christian dogma, rather than "treachery" in the modern sense.</note> of the Jews.

->In addition to these,<-

Three books on the <insert>Kabalistic Art</insert> by <insert>Johann Reuchlin</insert> of Pforzheim,
Doctor of Laws, full of all kinds of learning.
<note>The names "Johann Reuchlin" and the phrase "Kabalistic Art" were heavily obscured with thick black ink by a contemporary censor. Reuchlin was a famous scholar whose defense of Jewish books led to a massive controversy, and his writings were often placed on the "Index of Prohibited Books."</note>

->Furthermore,<-

**WE HAVE ADDED** a twofold Index: the first contains the subjects themselves, the other encompasses the obscure passages of Scripture that have been explained.

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page is the beginning of the preface "Ad Lectorem" (To the Reader) of Pietro Galatino's work. It follows the title page (represented by the bleed-through on the previous page). The tone is polemical, typical of 16th-century religious scholarship, aiming to defend Catholic orthodoxy against both Protestant "heresies" and Jewish critiques.</meta>

# To the Reader.

**N**OT SURPRISING is it that in our age—one as unjust as it is polluted by unspeakable crimes—all those heresies, which were once put to rest and condemned by the Catholic Church (in which alone the writings of the New and Old Testaments are held in high esteem), are now rightly sprouting up again. This occurs because almost everyone is permitted to propose to others whatever they have dreamed at night or thought during the day, following Satanic suggestions. And this is astonishing: heresies always find followers and supporters who are so bold, so frivolous, and so shameless that they dare to thrust whatever comes into their mouths as a Divine oracle upon the simple-minded, who are prone to being led astray. The unwary are deceived and are beautifully persuaded by the allure of words, so that they think everything these people babble was brought forth as if from the tripod of Apollo <note>original: "ex tripode Apollinis". A reference to the seat of the Oracle at Delphi; the author is saying these people treat their own ideas as divine prophecies.</note>, or spoken by CHRIST himself, the Son of God. 

Therefore, we are not warned in vain by CHRIST himself not to believe all those who say, "Look, here is CHRIST, look, there he is." They are deceived, and they deceive others, so that they do not seem to wander alone. However, this is the consolation of the Church: that God always raises up some from the elect who oppose these impious seducers, refute the false dogmas spread abroad, and bring forth the Truth from the <term>panoply</term> <note>original: "panoplia" – a full suit of armor. The author views the Bible as a complete set of spiritual weapons.</note> of the divine Scriptures, so that there is no escape for false prophets to either respond or defend their own claims. Professors of Theology ought to diligently drag this company of impious men out of their hiding places through sound doctrine. 

Did not the Satanic offspring of Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) taught that Jesus was a created being, a view condemned as heresy at the Council of Nicaea.</note> cause much trouble for the pious, and was finally destroyed through the word of CHRIST? Did not Paul of Samosata <note>original: "Samosatenus". A 3rd-century bishop whose views on the nature of Christ were condemned.</note> destroy himself with his own knife <note>A metaphorical way of saying he was undone by his own arguments.</note>? Have not also the Anabaptists, Stork <note>Nikolaus Storch (d. 1525), a radical reformer and associate of the Zwickau prophets.</note>, Servetus <note>Michael Servetus (1511–1553), a Spanish theologian executed for his non-trinitarian views.</note>, and countless others been exposed to the mockery of the whole world because of their devised madness without the authority of God's word? The same happens to all heretics. 

When, however, PIETRO GALATINO <note>The author, an Italian Franciscan friar (c. 1460–1540).</note> noticed the arrogance, pride, and insolence of the Jews toward the Christian religion, he considered it his duty—since he had made no small progress in Hebrew letters—to finally bring something forward into the public eye. He successfully set his hand to the task and wrote these Twelve Books, filled with all kinds of erudition and doctrine, for the benefit of the Church of CHRIST, which is tossing about in various opinions. He wrote against that treacherous crowd which not only denies both the divinity and humanity of CHRIST, even when convinced by the Scriptures, but also [denies] all the Scriptures themselves, especially those of Moses and the Prophets...

<summary>This preface introduces Pietro Galatino's defense of Christian doctrine against contemporary heresies and Jewish critiques, framing his work as a divine tool to restore truth in a chaotic era. The author lists historical heretics like Arius and Servetus as examples of those defeated by sound theology.</summary>

<keywords>Pietro Galatino, preface, heresy, Arius, Paul of Samosata, Anabaptists, Michael Servetus, Hebrew scholarship, Catholic defense, counter-reformation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory epistle to the reader. It transitions from a general discussion of heresy to a specific defense of the author, Pietro Galatino, and his use of Jewish sources (the Talmud and Rabbis) to prove Christian truths.</meta>

# EPISTLE

...overturn the truth and devise false interpretations, as much against the genuine sense of Scripture as against the Rabbis, whom he holds in the highest esteem. Indeed, these Rabbis described the times of **CHRIST** so clearly that, among men of sound mind, the testimonies which the Talmudists provide concerning the Kingdom of **CHRIST**, His Passion, and Resurrection are irrefutable.

**GALATINUS**, certainly a prudent man and absolutely learned in Hebrew, Chaldaic, Greek, and Latin literature, aims his writings at a single goal (leaving the life of the Jews—devoted as it is to avarice, deception, and contaminated by various crimes—to God the judge). Nor could anyone more clearly set forth the promises made to the Fathers concerning **CHRIST**—namely those given to Adam, Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses, the Prophets, David, and countless other faithful servants of God. In addition, he describes the times in which the scepter was taken from the Jews, and their Judges (whom they called the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the Jewish people during the Roman period.</note>) were either driven out or killed. They lost the practice of Sacrifices; they are without a Priesthood, without the assembly of Levites, and without a King, ever since the temple was destroyed and all things were reduced to desolation. The miracles that once occurred both within and without the Temple have vanished, and those wretched people have been cast into every corner of the earth. These are certain signs that the **CHRIST** whom the holy Fathers awaited has come and has purged the world of sins. 

Furthermore, their own Rabbis—whom they do not dare to disown—described those final times with such beautiful words that they might easily grasp the Truth, were they not driven to madness against the religion of **CHRIST**. Yet this blinded nation continues with an obstinate mind—even as their own conscience rebels—to defend and devise false interpretations, imagining an external Kingdom of **CHRIST** and the most splendid pomp with which their Messiah is supposed to arrive. 

I tell you, kind Reader, our Author treats all these matters so skillfully in the form of a dialogue that you could desire nothing more in this regard. Anyone who reads this book with an attentive mind will find it of great use when they wish to study the Bible; the Author has focused all his efforts especially on obscure passages known to few, so that the reader may proceed through the Old Testament without hesitation. Everything is divided into chapters. Scriptural references are noted throughout, so that the Reader’s mind does not waver while searching for the cited passages. 

Moreover, he brings forward whatever has been said of **CHRIST** anywhere, providing interpretations gathered not from common sources <note>original: "non ex triuio collecta" — literally "not collected from the crossroads," meaning information that is not trivial or of low quality.</note>, but from the Jewish Rabbis who wrote about the Messiah’s kingdom before the birth of **CHRIST**, as well as from Christian Doctors. You have here (to put much into few words) a commentary on all the difficult passages of the entire Old Testament. Is this not a great treasure being offered, which a student of Theology cannot do without, except to his own great detriment? Furthermore, the diligence which **Mr. Francis Stancarus** <note>Francesco Stancari (1501–1574), an Italian scholar of Hebrew and a theologian who edited this work.</note>, a man most skilled in Hebrew literature...

<meta>catchword: mus,</meta>

<summary>The author praises Pietro Galatino's scholarship, arguing that ancient Jewish texts and the cessation of Temple sacrifices prove that Jesus is the Messiah. He highlights the book's usefulness as a theological commentary that uses Rabbinic sources to clarify obscure Old Testament passages.</summary>

<keywords>Pietro Galatino, Messiah, Talmud, Rabbinic literature, Old Testament commentary, Sanhedrin, Francesco Stancari, Christian Hebraism</keywords>

# TO THE READER.

The honest reader will easily perceive the great effort applied to correcting these books if he compares the old edition with this new one. No one would believe how easily even well-transcribed copies can become corrupted. Also added here are the <term>kabbalistic</term> <note>Referring to the Jewish mystical tradition known as Kabbalah, which some Renaissance scholars sought to harmonize with Christianity.</note> writings of <term>Capnio</term> <note>The Greek-style pseudonym of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and pioneer of Hebrew studies among Christians.</note>, a subject well-suited to this work. In these writings, much mention is made of the ancient Fathers who awaited **CHRIST** the Redeemer with the greatest longing and knew perfectly well that the salvation they had lost would be recovered through the wood <note>The "wood" refers to the wood of the Cross.</note>. Truly, "good wine needs no ivy-wreath hung above the door" <note>original: "uino uendibili non opus est suspensa hedera." This is an ancient proverb meaning that a high-quality product needs no advertisement; its excellence is its own recommendation.</note>. All these things, however, aim toward this goal: that the Church founded by the Apostles may be rebuilt, once we have set aside the sects and conflicting opinions which have never failed to bring in a sea of troubles, and which have either altered or utterly overthrown every well-ordered state. The Jews serve as a daily example to us, lest we fall into the wrath 
->of God through lack of repentance, after<-
->the Truth has been recognized. Farewell.<-

<summary>This page introduces the new edition's improvements and the inclusion of Johann Reuchlin's kabbalistic works, which the author uses to argue for the historical and mystical anticipation of Christ. It concludes with a call for Church unity and a warning against religious division.</summary>
<keywords>Johann Reuchlin, Kabbalah, Church reform, Christian Hebraism, edition corrections, apostolic foundation, repentance</keywords>

# ¶ Epigram of Moses Aaron the Hebrew, in praise of the Author and the Book.

<note>This poem is an acrostic; the first letter of each line spells out "GALATINUS" (ג-ל-ט-י-נ-י-ו-ס) in Hebrew.</note>

**G** — Galatinus is his name, a memorial for generations | bridge toward him and call out: "Who are his sayings?"
**A** — His heart is alive, made to see books | his will is placed there, in the <term>Messiah</term> and his secrets.
**L** — His goodness is... <note>The OCR text here is fragmented.</note> Augustartus <note>Another reference to Hoogstraten, the author's academic rival.</note> and teachers | whose names are... without a sun for their makers.
**A** — He shall explain the words of the study and the scribes | he numbered them also in the writing of his books.
**T** — He gave them as a free gift to those who are crowned <note>Likely referring to scholars or the spiritually "separated."</note> | his words awaken them concerning their faith.
**I** — Verses of his words are illuminating | for he spoke them in truth regarding all his past.
**N** — And... and teachers thus from complete wise men | is it not he who... look toward all his companions?
**US** — ...for from complete wise men.

---

# ¶ Verses of Isaac the Spanish Hebrew, a physician, in praise of the Author and the Work.

<note>This poem forms an acrostic spelling "I AM GALATINUS, MY NAME IS..." (אני גלטיניוס שמי). This was a common way for authors or their editors to "sign" their work in Hebrew poetry.</note>

**I** — I am a child of a book | full of beautiful sayings | with cypress or a trumpet | a mention of honorable things.
**A** — Builders and wise men | youths and old men | great and small | and boys also and girls.
**M** — Sing a new song | and let the pure heart be sanctified | to praise God in holiness | to sing and to give thanks.
**G** — Give thanks to the Lord | His mercy has helped me | the writing of His hand | to save the Laws <note>The author refers to "saving the Torahs," likely meaning the physical preservation of Hebrew books from the inquisitorial bonfires.</note>.
**A** — He strengthened those who were despised | the foundation of Gushtartus | who sought to destroy | and to uproot the testimonies.
**L** — My people, [ask] "What is it?" <note>A play on the word "Manna."</note> | and go about to gather it | go out and see it | in the beloved <term>Messiah</term>.
**A** — Exalted in might | who melts all... | Galatinus to see | row by row.
**T** — Included in me are wisdoms | Greek and also Christian | and logical ideas | in a multitude of languages.
**I** — Also the faithful religion | given to the congregation of God | and in me the <term>Talmud</term> is built | in the holiness of the languages.
**N** — For the people of the breach | from strength and from might | soldiers and a companion | to set straight the oppressed.
**U** — Sublime joys | to Him who rides the clouds | to the Cause of causes | and the Cause of all lights.
**S** — From Him comes understanding | from Him comes a buckler | and a shield for the faith | and corners and stakes.
**M** — May His name be magnified | and may it be sanctified with Him | through the Shepherd of His flock | seeking the lost sheep.

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the introductory Hebrew commendatory verses seen on the previous page to the formal Latin dedication of the work. The author, Pietro Galatino, addresses Emperor Maximilian I, framing his defense of Johann Reuchlin (Capnio) as a matter of imperial honor and religious orthodoxy.</meta>

# To the most invincible Maximilian
## Caesar, Emperor of the Romans, forever August,
## The Letter of Pietro Galatino of the Order of Friars Minor.

**FOR A LONG TIME NOW, I HAVE BEEN TROUBLED** by no small anxiety of mind, **MAXIMILIAN** Caesar Augustus, when I saw the multifaceted and exceptional learning of <note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous humanist scholar who went by the Grecized name "Capnio."</note> Capnio being so unworthily torn apart by the pestilential and poisonous bites of the envious: so much so that some dared to falsely slander many of his sayings, which are most consistent with the <note>original: "Orthodoxae fidei," referring to the established Catholic Church doctrines.</note> Orthodox faith, with the mark of heresy. And although I noticed this was being done as a bad, or rather the worst, example to all learned men—if such unfair gratitude were returned for so many exhausted labors and vigils—I nevertheless did not dare to write anything, nor even to open my mouth, to attempt to defend a man so learned and outstanding in every kind of virtue against the rash ignorance of the wicked. I feared lest the fault of rashness and arrogance be attributed to me: if I, endowed with scarcely mediocre talent and not sufficiently equipped with much erudition, should wish of my own accord and unbidden to act as patron to a man so skilled and excellent in the <note>The Renaissance ideal of mastery in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.</note> triple learning of languages, and therefore more suitable than can be said to defend himself along with the truth itself.

But truly, when my most reverend lord, Lord L. Pucci <note>Lorenzo Pucci (1458–1531), an influential Italian cardinal and supporter of Reuchlin.</note>, Cardinal of the Four Holy [Crowned Martyrs], a most sharp investigator of the Christian faith and (as he ought to be) most observant of your Majesty, had more sharply urged me to undertake this kind of defense with a ready mind—because he thought that your Majesty’s honor was also at stake in this, if even a suspicion of the charged crime should touch his own counselor <note>Reuchlin served as a legal and political advisor to the imperial government.</note>—he compelled me to necessarily undergo the heavy burden of this task, which is unequal to my shoulders. There was added, moreover, the will of the most Holy Pope Leo X, which most especially impelled me to this. Since I was not unaware that the Pope himself, as a unique worshiper of truth and wisdom, greatly desired both that Capnio be freed from such slanders, and that your Majesty should be complied with in this all the more, the more vehemently he wished for his desires to be satisfied.

When I was uniquely intent on this matter, and was sweating with all my might (according to my strength) in unearthing the secrets found in the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, which was the focus of intense legal and theological debate during this period.</note>, which are wonderfully effective both for the confirmation of the Catholic faith and for protecting Capnio’s cause, thereupon your Majesty’s letters arrived. These most kindly urged me to complete this work as quickly as possible, together with several others addressed to the Supreme Pontiff. Re... <margin>Regarding...</margin>

<summary>Pietro Galatino introduces his defense of the scholar Johann Reuchlin (Capnio), addressing Emperor Maximilian I and noting the support of Cardinal Lorenzo Pucci and Pope Leo X. He explains his intention to use the Talmud to prove Christian truths and vindicate Reuchlin against charges of heresy.</summary>
<keywords>Maximilian I, Pietro Galatino, Johann Reuchlin, Capnio, Lorenzo Pucci, Pope Leo X, Talmud, Christian Hebraism, heresy defense</keywords>

->TO C. MAXIMILIAN<-
<meta>The "C." likely stands for Caesar. The Google watermark and bleed-through mentioned in the OCR are noted but do not affect the translation of the text itself.</meta>

and the Catholic King <note>original: "Regemque Catholicum," likely referring to Ferdinand II of Aragon, who held this title.</note>, and several Cardinal Fathers of the Christian aristocracy, having most kindly written in my commendation. Moved by this extraordinary and almost incredible kindness, I began to urge my begun nightly labors <note>original: "uigilias," referring to the scholarly "vigils" or late-night study sessions required to produce the book.</note> not only more pressingly but more ardently, so that they might hasten to a conclusion; but I also decided to consecrate whatever they might become to your majesty, so that they might come forth into the light more auspiciously and, having shaken off the darkness of errors, might reveal the light of Truth much more confidently. For it was not fitting that a Work **ON THE SECRETS OF CATHOLIC TRUTH**, to be completed for the benefit of the Christian Commonwealth <note>original: "Reipublicæ," referring to the collective body of the Christian world rather than a specific political republic.</note>, be dedicated to any other than to the best preserver, defender, and enlarger of both Catholic Truth itself and the entire Christian Commonwealth. Which dedication of mine, if it shall by no means equal the highness of Your Majesty: because you will nevertheless be able to understand that it proceeded from a most devoted mind, you will deign to interpret it favorably and receive it with a calm countenance (as you are always accustomed).

->Receive it therefore now, Most Sacred Emperor:<-
->and me, laboring assiduously in the vineyard of the Lord <note>A common biblical metaphor for serving the Church.</note>,<-
->among the least of Your Majesty’s servants (though<-
->unworthy), according to your mercy,<-
->receive, protect, and cherish.<-

<insert>FORTUNE FAVORS THE BOLD</insert>

# Pietro Galatino’s Work on the Secrets of Catholic Truth.

->*Speakers of the entire work,*<-
->**GALATINO, CAPNIO, HOOGSTRATEN.**<-

---

->**GALATINO,**<-

**A**s much as I am able to perceive from those things which have been said back and forth by you in my presence until now: there is a significant dispute between you regarding the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, which became a focal point of intense Christian debate in the early 16th century.</note>, from which your entire controversy takes its origin. For one of you indeed attempts to condemn the Talmud as entirely evil and utterly repugnant to the Christian religion; and he strives to prove this by many articles framed against the other’s little book, titled the **EYE-GLASS** <note>original: "Oculare Speculum," referring to Johannes Reuchlin’s *Augenspiegel* (1511), a defense of Jewish books against the Cologne inquisitors.</note>. The other, however, strives with the greatest zeal to defend the Talmud itself as being good in many respects, and extremely profitable, convenient, and necessary for the Catholic truth in order to crush the most stubborn neck of the Jews. Since, therefore, both of you seem to seek nothing else but the truth—nor indeed (as I myself believe) did you both meet with me for any other reason than for the sake of searching out that Truth—and since I too intend to say nothing except what savors of the Christian truth for the purpose of defining the articles to be discussed, I judge that I shall perform a worthwhile service for the Christian Commonwealth if, before we come to the articles themselves, I do not neglect to unlock the secrets of the Catholic faith itself lying hidden in the Talmud, both for the foundation of your dispute and for the understanding of the Truth to be investigated. For through these <term>Talmudic</term> <note>Galatino argues that ancient Jewish writings actually contain evidence for Christian doctrines, a common theme in Christian Kabbalah.</note> writings of the ancient Jews, not only are all the <term>cavillations</term> <note>Deceptive or distracting arguments; here, Galatino refers to the interpretations used by Jewish contemporaries to reject Christian claims.</note> of the more recent ones—who strive with every effort to pervert the prophecies of the Prophets—completely refuted, but the Truth of the Orthodox dogma also shines forth most clearly.

# PREFACE

**CAPNIO,** You will indeed do very well, my Galatino. For in this way, the errors of the Jews of our age will be most effectively refuted, and the most powerful testimonies will be brought against them from their own scriptures in support of the Christian truth, which they never cease to attack. But so that they might be less able to resist such great truth, it is necessary that you report the very oracles of the holy prophets or the sayings of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars and rabbis of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>—which you are about to bring against the Jews themselves—exactly as they were written: namely, in <term>Chaldaic</term> <note>original: "Chaldaicè," referring to Aramaic, the language of much of the Talmud and Jewish commentary.</note> and in Hebrew.

**GALATINO,** I will certainly do so most willingly, my Capnio, as you urge: both for the reasons you have stated, and especially so that when the Jews see themselves defeated by their own weapons, they may be forced to acknowledge the truth which they never cease to deny. Thus, having acknowledged it, they may not neglect to both confess and preserve it, if they wish to look out for themselves—lest at last, cast out from the Heavenly kingdom into the outer darkness, they suffer eternal evils. But since it would be both extremely difficult and unpleasant to maintain this in every instance, I shall take care to recount in either Hebrew or Chaldaic (as they themselves have them) only those passages which, above all others, express and attest to the truth against them. 

Truly, all things which I shall need to bring forward from their Scriptures, I will strive to translate into our own language as faithfully as the Latin tongue allows, so that they will neither be able to deny the truth, nor dare to say that it is not so among them. Therefore, in translating the words of the Sacred Page itself, wherever I find that our own codices have deviated from the Hebrew, I will follow neither the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> nor any other translator; instead, I shall turn them into our own speech exactly as the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>original: "Hebraica ueritas," a scholarly concept popularized by St. Jerome asserting the primacy and accuracy of the original Hebrew text of the Bible over later translations.</note> holds. 

For by this means, every path of escape will be blocked for the false-speaking Jews; and many—nearly infinite—passages of Holy Scripture, which are found to be tainted and corrupted among both the Latins and the Greeks (partly due to the length of time and partly due to the fault of scribes), will be truly and excellently corrected for the sake of our faith. In these passages, the Christian truth shines far more clearly and far more perfectly among the Hebrews than in our own Latin or Greek editions. On account of this, I have no doubt that I shall be criticized by many—especially by those who are accustomed to find fault with whatever they have not done themselves, and who disparage everything they do not know. 

To be sure, Truth has many enemies, and rivals have never been lacking for those who constantly profess it. For among the Greeks, Athanasius and Chrysostom suffered them; and among the Latins, Augustine and Jerome; and finally, all those who have uniquely embraced Truth itself. Against them, I invoke nothing other than Truth itself, which I hope (with Divine help favoring me) will be my shield on every side. For I submit myself and all my writings to the determination of the most holy **LEO** the Tenth, Supreme Pontiff, the finest cultivator of Truth itself, and of the Most Holy Roman Church, which is the mistress and teacher of all Churches...

**HOGOSTRATUS,** <note>Jacob van Hoogstraaten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican Inquisitor who was a fierce opponent of Reuchlin in the "Battle of the Books" regarding the Talmud.</note> Because I see you are about to say marvelous and unheard-of things to reveal the Truth, I would wish—so that we might more quickly and easily obtain that Truth which we seek so greatly (with you as our guide)—that you would satisfy my inquiry if any doubt should enter my mind, provided it is not a burden to you.

**GALATINO,** That will indeed be very pleasant to me, and not in the least bit unwelcome. For that reason, I would first of all ask this of both you—who are so powerful in your skill in both Divine and human Philosophy <note>Referring to Scholastic theology and Aristotelian dialectics.</note>—and of Capnio himself, who is not only exceptionally endowed with every kind of literature, but is also the most eloquent interpreter of the <term>three languages</term> <note>Latin, Greek, and Hebrew; the hallmark of a Renaissance "Trilingual" scholar.</note> through which the Divine secrets are opened: That whatever doubts may occur, let them by no means pass by undiscussed; rather, let them be brought forward to be examined by us in turn. For I also, according to the capacity of my own small talent, do not think I should remain silent about whatever my opinion may be regarding those same doubts. 

But because it is very difficult, and almost impossible, for a weak man such as I know myself to be to walk confidently along that path where even some of the strongest have been known to stumble—for I confess that I must necessarily undertake many things far beyond my strength and much greater than myself to track down Truth of this kind—I have therefore decided that I must first implore Divine aid. Thus, while prayer itself to God shall be my staff, and His word a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths <note>A reference to Psalm 119:105.</note>, I may walk secure and safe among the ranks of enemies. By defeating them with their own weapons, I may be able to take away from them—as if from unjust possessors—the truth which they have in their possession but do not know, which they neglect, and which they attack. 

At last, once the truth itself is found in the <term>Talmudic Books</term>, it may be established clearer than light what ought to be rightly thought concerning the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, which was the subject of intense controversy and censorship during this period.</note> itself, about which there is a war between you. So that this may be done more rightly and better, it will be necessary for our entire discourse to revolve around twelve principal themes. Concerning these, twelve specific

# Index of Books.

## IN THE FIRST BOOK IS TREATED
¶ Concerning the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and Gemara.</note>, and concerning those things pertaining to it.

## IN THE SECOND
Concerning the Trinity of divine persons, concerning the unity of the divine essence, and concerning the divine names, through which both the divine Trinity itself with the indivisible unity of nature, and its perfections, are most excellently suggested.

## IN THE THIRD
Concerning the incarnation of the Son of God, concerning the divinity of the Messiah, and his names designating his own divine nature, and concerning the fellowship, participation, and equalization of God and man.

## IN THE FOURTH
Concerning the first coming of the Messiah.

## IN THE FIFTH
Concerning the refutation of the arguments of the Jews of our time, who strive to prove that the Messiah has not yet come.

## IN THE SIXTH
Concerning the redemption and salvation of the human race, for the sake of which the Messiah was to come.

## IN THE SEVENTH
Concerning the most holy mother of the Messiah.

## IN THE EIGHTH
Concerning the mysteries of the Messiah, all of which were completely fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ.

## IN THE NINTH
Concerning the eternal rejection of the Jews, and concerning the calling and salvation of the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>Non-Jewish people.</note>.

## IN THE TENTH
Concerning the institution of the new divine law, which was to be established by the Messiah.

## IN THE ELEVENTH
Concerning the cessation of the old divine law at the coming of the New.

## IN THE TWELFTH
Concerning the second coming of the Messiah, and concerning the things to come in that time.

**N**ow the Index of Chapters will immediately show all these things in detail. However, each individual Chapter will contain many secrets of Catholic truth: just as they have offered themselves to be plucked from <note>original: "carpenda"</note> the Hebrew volumes throughout our proposal; together with texts of Holy Scripture of the <term>Old Instrument</term> <note>A common Latin term for the Old Testament.</note>, which will occur to us to be corrected and explained according to the <note>original: "Hebraicam ueritatem"</note> Hebrew truth <note>A scholarly term referring to the original Hebrew text of the Bible as a standard for correction.</note>, for the confirmation of the Orthodox faith.

The fifth reason, by which it is shown that the time of the first coming of the Messiah has already passed, taken from the punishment of the Israelite people: and that at the coming of the Messiah, the Jews were to be punished with a manifold penalty because of the death they would inflict upon him.

Concerning the sins of the Jews committed during the time of the first and last temple, and concerning the death of the prophets Zechariah and Isaiah: and what the cause of this most recent captivity of theirs might be; and concerning the "hatred without a cause" <note>original: *odio gratis*; a reference to Psalm 69:4 and John 15:25</note> with which they pursued Christ.
**XXIII**
Confirmation of the preceding points, from the selling and the buying of the Messiah <note>Referring to the betrayal of Jesus for thirty pieces of silver</note>.
**Chapter XXIIII**
The sixth reason, showing that the time of the first coming of the Messiah has already passed, based upon the subjection of the Roman Empire: and first, that the Messiah was to subject the Empire of the Romans to himself.
**XXV**
That the Messiah was to rule over the entire world, and concerning the universal kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ.
**XXVI**
That Christ truly subjected the Roman Empire to himself, and concerning the universal dominion of the Roman <term>Pontiff</term> <note>The Pope</note> and the Emperor.
**XXVII**
A refutation of the Jewish opposition.
**XXVIII**
The seventh reason, by which it is demonstrated that the time of the first coming of the Messiah has passed, is taken from the cessation of idolatrous worship; and that at the coming of the Messiah, idolatry was to cease entirely.
**XXIX**

# First book concerning the Talmud.
## Concerning the ancient and authentic scriptures of the Jews. Chapter One.

->GALATINUS,<-

**T**o expose the faithlessness <note>original: *perfidiam*; in Renaissance Christian polemic, this term specifically refers to the refusal to accept the Christian Gospel as the fulfillment of Jewish law</note> of the Jews through their own Talmudic writings, it is necessary above all else to know that there are two kinds of teachings among them, upon which their Synagogue has never ceased to rely, both now and in the past. One of these they call <term>Torah she-bi-khtav: the Written Law</term> <note>original Hebrew: תורה שבכתב</note>, which is the law that is in writing, or which was handed down in writing. The other they call <term>Torah she-be'al peh: the Oral Law</term> <note>original Hebrew: תורה שבעל פה</note>, that is, the law which is in the mouth, or which was handed down by word of mouth. Indeed, they say this is nothing other than an explanation of the Law itself, which they assert was handed down to Moses together with the [Written] Law. For as the ancient Talmudists <term>Talmudists: scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</term> testify in the first chapter of that book which is called *Berachoth* <note>original: ברכות; meaning "Blessings," the first tractate of the Talmud</note>, Moses received both the Law and the exposition of the Law itself on Mount Sinai by the same spirit. This explanation of the Law tends toward a twofold sense: the literal and the spiritual or mystical. They affirm that Moses wrote neither of these, but handed both down by the spoken word. And they say this Law is that of which it is read thus in the *Chapters of the Fathers* <note>original: בפרקי אבות (*Pirkei Avot*); a compilation of ethical teachings and maxims from the Rabbis of the Mishnaic period</note>: "Moses received the Law <note>original: *tora*</note> from Sinai and handed it to Joshua; and Joshua to the Elders; and the Elders to the Prophets; and the Prophets handed it to the Men of the Great Assembly" <note>original Hebrew: משה קבל תורה מסיני ומסרה ליהושע ויהושע לזקנים וזקנים לנביאים ונביאים מסרוה לאנשי כנסת הגדולה</note>. 

This kind of tradition (as gathered from various volumes of the Talmudists, and as reported by Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Rabbi Moses the Egyptian: Maimonides (1138–1204), one of the most influential Torah scholars and philosophers of the Middle Ages</note> at the beginning of his *Deuteronomy* <note>Maimonides' major code of Jewish law, the *Mishneh Torah*, was often referred to by Christian scholars as *Deuteronomium* (the Second Law)</note>) happened to take place in this order: For when Joshua had received this exposition of the Law from Moses, he handed it to Phinehas the son of Eleazar, who was the grandson of Aaron; and who is called by us, by a corrupted name, Phinees. Phinehas handed it to Eli the priest. Eli to Samuel the prophet and priest. Samuel to King David. David to Ahijah the prophet. Ahijah to Elijah the prophet. Elijah to Elisha the prophet. Up to this point, we do not read that the Jews possessed any other scripture besides the Bible, which they call *Macdefciya* <note>original: מקדשיא *Macdefciya*; likely a transliteration of the Hebrew *Mikdash-yah*, meaning "Sanctuary of the Lord" or "Holy Thing of God"</note>, that is, the holy thing of God; for until those times, it is found that no one had committed anything regarding the exposition of the law to writing.

**GAL.** The Jews (as you yourself know) also call the Bible *Arbaa uesrim* <note>original: ארבעה ועשרים *Arba’ah Ve-esrim*</note>, that is, "Twenty-Four," because it contains that many books. For they divide it into four parts. The first of these, which <margin>The Humash.</margin> they call the *Torah* <note>original: תורה; Law</note>, or *Humas* <note>original: חומש *Humash*; meaning "The Fivefold"</note>, and which the Greeks call the Pentateuch, contains five books. They name these after their opening words. For the book of Genesis <margin>Bereshith.</margin> they call *Berescith* <note>original: בראשית *Bereshith*</note>, which is the same as "In the beginning." Exodus they call *Veelle scemoth* <note>original: ואלה שמות *Ve-elleh Shemot*</note>, that is, "And these are the names." Leviticus they call *Vaicra* <note>original: ויקרא *Vayikra*</note>, that is, "And he called." Numbers they call *Bemidbar Sinai* <note>original: במדבר סיני *Be-midbar Sinai*</note>, that is, "In the desert of Sinai." Deuteronomy they call *Elle hadeuarim* <note>original: אלה הדברים *Elleh ha-devarim*</note>, that is, "These are the words."

<margin>Second part.</margin> The second part comprises four books, which they call *Neuiim rissonim* <note>original: נביאים ראשונים *Nevi’im Rishonim*</note>, that is, the "Former Prophets." These are: *Iehofuas*, who is called Joshua among us; *Sophtim* <note>original: שופטים *Shophtim*</note>, that is, "Judges"; *Semuel*, which among us contains the first and second books of Kings <note>In the older Christian tradition, the books of Samuel were often called 1 and 2 Kings</note>; and *Melachim* <note>original: מלכים *Melakhim*</note>, that is, "Kings," which among us includes the third and fourth books of Kings.

<margin>Third part.</margin> The third part also contains four books, which they call *Neuiim Aharonim* <note>original: נביאים אחרונים *Nevi’im Akharonim*</note>, that is, the "Latter Prophets." These are: Isaiah, Jeremiah, *Iehezkel* (whom we call Ezekiel), and the book of the Twelve Prophets, whom we call the "Minor Prophets."

<margin>Fourth part.</margin> Finally, the fourth part, which they call *Chetuuim* <note>original: כתובים *Ketuvim*; meaning "Writings"</note>, or the Hagiographa <note>a Greek term meaning "Holy Writings"</note>, contains eleven books. The first of these is titled *Dibre haiamim* <note>original: דברי הימים *Divrei ha-yamim*</note>, that is, "Words of the Days," which we call by the Greek word *Paralipomenon* <note>commonly known as Chronicles</note>. The second is *Tehilloth* or *Tehillim*, or by contraction *Tillim*, that is, "Hymns"; although *tillim* also signifies "heaps," the singular of which is *tel*, meaning a "heap." This is not irrelevant to the purpose, since the Psalms are, as it were, certain heaps of wise sayings. This book we call by the Greek word "Psalter." The third is *Misle Scelomo* <note>original: משלי שלמה *Mishlei Shelomo*</note>, that is, the "Proverbs," or rather the "Parables of Solomon." The fourth is *Iiob*, whom we call by the corrupted name "Job." The fifth is Ruth. The sixth is *Coheleth* <note>original: קהלת</note>, that is, the "Assembly" or "Preacher," which we call "Ecclesiastes." The seventh is *Echa* <note>original: איכה *Eikhah*</note>, that is, "How," which is called by us "Lamentations" or "Dirges"...

...the book is titled. The eighth is שיר השירים *Scir hascirim* <note>original: *Shir HaShirim*; Song of Songs</note>, that is, the Song of Songs. The ninth is אסתר *Ester* <note>Esther</note>. The tenth is דניאל *Daniel*. Finally, the eleventh is עזרא *Ezras* <note>Ezra</note>, which they count as one book with Nehemiah. These twenty-four books that we have just enumerated are the only ones the Jews hold as sacred and divine. For although they possess the book of Joshua Son of Sirach <note>also known as Ecclesiasticus, not to be confused with the biblical Book of Joshua</note>, and Judith, and Tobit, and the first of the Maccabees, they do not count them among the twenty-four. As for the third and fourth books of Ezra <note>apocryphal books often titled 1 and 2 Esdras in English Bibles</note>, I myself have not yet seen them in Hebrew; however, some among them say they were recently found and discovered in Constantinople. Truly, the second book of the Maccabees and the book of Philo the Hebrew, which is called the Wisdom of Solomon, I have nowhere found among the Hebrews, but have only seen them in Greek. Furthermore, the Song of the Three Youths, and the histories of Susanna and of Bel and the Dragon—which we include within the Book of Daniel—they do not have at all. I have mentioned these things so that we may know which books the Jews approve as authentic.

Therefore, it is certain that besides the aforementioned twenty-four books, no other scripture existed among the Jews until the time of Ezra. For the commentaries on the law itself—both the literal and the spiritual or mystical—were expanded from the time of Moses the lawgiver himself until the Babylonian exile through a successive order (as has been said) among the prophets and sages. But after the Babylonian captivity, when Ezra himself rewrote the Law—which had been burned during the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the Temple—the other sages began to write down the exposition of that same Law. They did this lest, if another destruction of the city should happen to occur in which all the sages might perish, the explanation of the Law itself should perish along with them.

Indeed, it followed that all those sages who lived from the Babylonian exile until the first writing of the Talmudic codex (who are also called in the פרקי אבות *pirke auoth* <note>original: *Pirkei Avot*; translates to "Chapters of the Fathers," a famous ethical tractate of the Mishna</note>, that is, the Chapters of the Fathers, the "Men of the Great Synagogue") and who are known to have taught the Law, handed down the exposition of that same Law to their students both by word of mouth and in writing. The authority of these men is so great among the Jews that their writings, from which the Talmud was afterwards compiled, hold the first place after the prophets. And this is not without merit, since their doctrine was immediately handed down to them by the prophets themselves, whose disciples and successors they were. Therefore, it is no wonder if those who preceded the coming of Christ, in explaining the Law and the Prophets, handed down in writing almost infinite and truly wondrous things concerning Christ and the truths of the Christian faith, all of which are inserted scatteredly throughout the Talmudic books.

This is that Jaddua who, when he heard that Alexander the Macedonian had set out toward Jerusalem after the capture of Gaza, began to be seized by no small dread and fear. When they had done this, as soon as Alexander saw the high priest himself adorned in a hyacinth-blue <note>a violet-blue or purple color</note> and golden robe, wearing on his head both the miter <note>the *kidaris*, a specific priestly headdress</note> and the golden plate on which the four-lettered name of God <note>original: *tetragrammaton* (τετραγράμματον); the name YHWH</note> was written, he immediately approached him alone, worshipped the name of God, and was the first to venerate the High Priest. He warned me not to hesitate at all but to cross over confidently; and he promised that he would lead my army there and deliver the power of the Persians to me. Therefore, I prostrated myself and worshipped him. For from that time, I believe I have been guided by divine help, have defeated Darius, and have broken the power of the Persians. Because of this, I trust that all things which turn in my heart and all that I hope for will come to pass."

### CHAPTER <note>The text likely means to continue the previous chapter's flow or introduces a specific point from Maimonides</note>

Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>original: *Rabbi Moses Ægyptius*; known today as Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> reports in the beginning of his commentary on Deuteronomy <note>specifically referring to the introduction to the *Mishneh Torah*</note> that until the time of Rabbi Judah, son of Simeon <note>Judah ha-Nasi, the compiler of the Mishnah</note>, who lived one hundred and twenty years after the burning of the second Temple, no one had handed down anything in writing regarding the clarification of the law. Instead, he claims that among the succeeding sages, the law was revealed only by word of mouth.

**GALATINUS:** It is indeed true that Rabbi Moses the Egyptian asserts this. However, it must be thought that he did so for two primary reasons. First, so that the secrets of the Messiah—which had been uncovered in the expositions of the law and the prophets before the birth of Christ—might remain hidden from Christians. Second, so that the writings of later rabbis might be rendered more authoritative by this claim. But it can be clearly seen that he spoke falsely from the fact that many writings concerning the exposition of both the law and the prophets are found to have been written before the birth of Christ, as appears plainly in many places of the Talmud itself.

<margin>Joshua ben Sirach</margin>
Joshua ben Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Sirach or Ecclesiasticus</note>, who flourished in the times of Ptolemy Euergetes I <note>A King of Ptolemaic Egypt; Sirach’s grandson translated the work into Greek during his reign</note>, also clearly testifies to this. In the prologue of his book, which is titled *Ecclesiasticus* among us, but *Mishle* (that is, Proverbs) among the Hebrews, he says among other things: "Much and great wisdom has been demonstrated to us through the Law, and the Prophets, and others who followed them, in which things Israel ought to be praised for the sake of doctrine and wisdom. For it is necessary not only that those who speak be experts, but even that outsiders be able, both by learning and writing, to become most learned." And after a few words: "But," he says, "the Law itself, and the Prophets, and the rest of the other books, have no small difference when they are spoken among themselves. For in the thirty-eighth year, in the times of King Ptolemy Euergetes, after I arrived in Egypt and had been there a long time, I found books left there of no small or contemptible learning." From these words, it is openly gathered that besides the Law and the Prophets, other books also were written among the Hebrews long before the coming of Christ. For Ptolemy Euergetes I himself, in whose times this Joshua reports he found books of this kind in Egypt, met his end nearly two hundred and nine years before the birth of Christ.

That many others were also able to do this at that time is clear from this fact: if only six elders were chosen from each tribe, it is certainly reasonable that there were many other men of the same kind among the Hebrews then who could have handed down expositions of the Law and the Prophets in writing. <margin>Rabbi Judah the Holy</margin>
After him, **Rabbi Judah the Holy** <note>original: *Rabbenus haccados*; known as Judah ha-Nasi, the late 2nd-century rabbi who compiled the Mishnah.</note>, which is translated from the Hebrew as "Our Holy Teacher," wrote a book which he called <term>The Revealer of Secrets</term> <note>original: *Gale razeya*</note>. He was certainly not called a holy doctor without reason, since, inspired by the Holy Spirit, he so clearly opened all the mysteries of our Lord Jesus Christ in that book that he seems not to have predicted the future, but to have narrated events as an Evangelist.

<margin>Rabbi Nehuniah ben HaKanah</margin>
A little later, **Rabbi Nehuniah ben HaKanah** followed him. He not only most clearly revealed those things which had been secretly handed down by the prophets concerning the Messiah, but also asserted that he was only fifty years away from his advent. Therefore, to his son Hakanah—whom he both hoped and rejoiced would see the Messiah himself—to inform him of the mysteries of the Messiah, he wrote a letter which he wished to be called <term>The Epistle of Secrets</term> <note>original: *Igghereth hassodoth*</note>.

<margin>Jonathan ben Uzziel</margin>
Around that same time (about forty-two years before the birth of Christ), **Jonathan ben Uzziel**, a student of Hillel and a classmate of Simeon the Just (who received the infant Christ in his arms), translated the whole **Old Testament** <note>original: *Instrumentum*; a term used by some scholars like Erasmus to refer to the Bible.</note> into the **Aramaic** <note>original: *Chaldaean*; in this period, the Aramaic language was commonly called Chaldean.</note> language and explained it. He translated sense for sense and explained every obscure word in such a way that whatever had been written about the Messiah in a doubtful or hidden manner, he rendered certain and most clear. Indeed, his edition seems not so much a translation as a commentary and exposition,

<margin>What a Targum is</margin>
which the Hebrews call a <term>Targum</term>, that is, a "translation." It is of such great authority among them that not only does no one dare to contradict it, but everyone everywhere accords it no less faith than the text itself—both because of the holiness and skill of the man, and especially because of the truth of the interpretation and exposition itself. Therefore, whenever they find anything ambiguous or difficult to understand in the text of the sacred books, they always recur to that same translation and clarification. For this reason, the Masters said concerning this same Jonathan (as is read in the <term>Bava Batra</term> <note>A tractate of the Babylonian Talmud.</note>), that in the hour when he was occupied with that edition and exposition, if a fly or any winged thing flew over him or over the paper, it was immediately consumed by fire from heaven without any harm to him or the paper.

# FIRST BOOK

The edition of the Psalter <note>The Book of Psalms</note>, which the Jews now more frequently have at hand and which the Bishop of Nebbio <note>Agostino Giustiniani (1470–1536), who published a polyglot Psalter in 1516.</note> included in his Polyglot Psalters, many of them attribute to Rabbi Joseph the Blind. From this they infer that Jonathan did not translate the entire Bible into Aramaic. **GALATINUS.** Without doubt, Jonathan translated the entire Bible into Aramaic (as I said before, and I think it is not unknown to you). But his translation of the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible (Torah).</note> is extremely rare; for that reason, it is denied by those who have not seen it. I, however, have seen it once. It begins thus:
"From the beginning the Lord created the heavens and the earth!" <note>original Aramaic: *Min avla bra Yeya yat shamaya vayat ar'a*</note>. That version which belongs to Onkelos, however, begins thus:
"In the beginning the Lord created the heavens and the earth!" <note>original Aramaic: *Be-kadmin bra Yeya yat shamaya vayat ar'a*</note>. Here also, Onkelos turned and explained the whole Bible in Aramaic. His edition and exposition, although it is now hardly found anywhere (except in the Pentateuch), is nevertheless of no less value among the Jews than that version of Jonathan which we just mentioned. They also call it the <term>Targum</term> <note>An Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, because it is also in the Aramaic language, just like the other; even if both were written with Hebrew characters. Jonathan’s own edition of the Psalter is in the possession of very few people. Those who have it hide it as much as they can, because of the mysteries of the Christian faith which it contains.

Finally, Simeon, the son of Hillel—whom the Talmudists, on account of his preeminent holiness, <margin>Simeon the Just.</margin> surname *Tzaddik* <note>original: *צדיק*, meaning "The Just."</note>, and in whom (as it is said in the *Pirkei Avot* <note>original: *פרקי אבות*, "The Chapters of the Fathers," a collection of ethical teachings in the Mishna.</note>, that is, the *Chapters of the Fathers*) the scepter of the Academy of the Great Synagogue failed—said many things about the Messiah. And at last, when in his extreme old age he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death until his eyes had seen the Messiah, the Son of God, he took Christ himself in his arms; he then confirmed in His presence the things he had taught about Him, having been instructed by the Holy Spirit <note>Galatinus identifies the Rabbi Simeon with the biblical Simeon from the Gospel of Luke (2:25–35) who performed the Nunc Dimittis.</note>. His outstanding sayings are found scattered throughout the books of the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and Gemara.</note>. Therefore, from the sayings of all these men, and also many others who, writing upon the Law and the Prophets in those same times, openly showed that our Lord Jesus Christ would be both the unique Son of Almighty God and the true Messiah, almost the entire Talmud is composed.

### *Concerning the Jewish writers who happened to live a little after the passion of Christ, and what they thought of Him. Chapter IV.*

->HOGOSTRATVS<-

Since all these men whom you have enumerated preceded the coming of Christ, and most of them were inspired by the Holy Spirit, no one would think it should be denied that, by explaining the Law and the Prophets, they wrote correctly concerning the Messiah. But concerning those who happened to write after the passion of Christ, and who remained in Judaism with obstinate minds, it is certainly clear that no one ever correctly explained either the Law or the Prophets speaking of the Messiah, but rather twisted them toward a false sense according to their own perfidy. **GALATINUS.** Although that may be rightly said of the Jews of our own time—who are the most filthy dregs of all their race—it does not hold true universally for the ancient ones. Among them, some indeed interpreted the prophecies concerning Christ according to the true sense...

-> BOOK <-

<margin>Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews.</margin>
Those speaking of Christ seem to explain the matter correctly: for many indeed have thought well of the Lord Jesus himself and of the Christians, as is clearly evident in the writings of both. And to say nothing of the others for now, I will bring forward as examples just two whose authority carries the most weight among the Jews: Philo, born of a priestly lineage, and Josephus, the son of Matthias. In their books, they not only confess our Lord Jesus Christ, but they also adorn him with wonderful and divine praises, and treat his followers with the highest regard. For Philo, in that book which he wrote *On the Life of Our Own*—that is, concerning the <term>Apostolic men</term><note>The author is referring to Philo’s work *On the Contemplative Life*. Early Christian writers like Eusebius believed the "Therapeutae" described by Philo were actually the first Christian monks under St. Mark.</note>—describing the first Church at Alexandria under Mark the Evangelist, honored the followers of Christ in a wonderful manner, mentioning that they existed not only there but in many provinces, and calling their dwellings "monasteries."

<margin>The book which is titled the Wisdom of Solomon.</margin>
Furthermore, he published that extraordinary and certainly divine volume which he called the book of the *Wisdom of Solomon*. **HOG.** <note>Hogostratus, the challenger in this dialogue.</note> For what reason did he want this book to be inscribed with such a title? **GAL.** <note>Galatinus, the narrator/author.</note> Certainly not without reason. For what Solomon predicted in the book of Proverbs—enigmatically, parabolically, and as if in a general sense—concerning the Son of God, who is the Wisdom of the Father, Philo now teaches in this book as having been fulfilled, using those same arts of obscurity and concealment. And even if he often does not remain in generalities (as Solomon does), he approaches the very specificity he intends, being unable (as I think) to restrain himself from revealing the truth he pursues. This is shown most clearly, among other examples, by the fact that Solomon warns we must be on guard when he says: *My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not.* Then it follows: *If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood,* along with the rest that follows. What else is all of this but what Philo reports as having happened in his own time, saying: *The ungodly said, reasoning with themselves, but not aright,* with the rest that follows? And descending even further into specificity, he says: *Let us put wood into his bread.* <note>original: "Mittamus lignum in panem eius." This is a famous typological reference to Jeremiah 11:19, interpreted by early Christians as a prophecy of the Cross.</note> Here, by "wood," he designated the cross; and by "bread," he meant our Lord Jesus himself. He took the <term>parable</term> of the bread from the parable then spread (as I believe) from the mouth of the Lord himself, saying: *The bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world.* From this, through the words of the same Lord, he teaches that what Solomon had said would one day happen concerning the same Lord was now fulfilled. Therefore, since the subject matter is the same for both, and the art of obscurity and concealment is the same, and no difference occurs other than that of future and past time, for these reasons this book by Philo is rightly called the *Wisdom of Solomon*. Especially since in it he most excellently suggests the divinity, innocence, and passion of Christ himself, who is both the Wisdom of the Father and is called the Prince of Peace. Hence, to rebuke the ingratitude and impiety of the Jews, he says in Greek, speaking in the person of those whom he calls "the ungodly": "Let us lie in wait for the righteous man, because he is inconvenient to us, and he sets himself against our doings; he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education. He professeth to have the knowledge of God: and he calleth himself the child of the Lord." <note>original Greek: ἐνεδρεύσωμεν τὸν δίκαιον... παῖδα κυρίου ἑαυτὸν ὀνομάζει. This is a quote from the Wisdom of Solomon 2:12-13, a passage Christians traditionally viewed as a prophecy of the trial and death of Jesus.</note>

<margin>Josephus.</margin>
As for Josephus (to omit those things which he narrates with great praise concerning John the Baptist and James the Apostle, nicknamed "the Just"), in the eighteenth book of his <term>Antiquities</term><note>The *Jewish Antiquities*, a 20-volume history of the Jewish people written by Flavius Josephus around 93 AD.</note>, describing the times of Tiberius Caesar under whom Christ suffered, he reports these things about Christ himself in Greek: **At this time there was Jesus, a wise man—if indeed it is right to call him a man, for he was a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of those men who receive the truth with pleasure, and he drew to himself many Jews and many of the Greek race; he was the Christ. Therefore, if these most excellent men, Philo and Josephus—who, even if they wrote in Greek, were both Jews and most fierce emulators of their ancestral traditions—had not correctly understood what had been foretold by the prophets concerning the Messiah, they would neither have thought so well of Christ, nor would they have reported what they said of him so truthfully. For this reason, there is no doubt that if they wrote these things about him in Greek, they also wrote many more things in Hebrew, explaining the Law and the prophets. For both were most highly skilled in both languages, and were initiated into the sacred letters from their very cradles. From this, it is also reasonable to believe that many others besides them existed at that same time who both thought correctly about the Lord Jesus Christ and, explaining the prophecies of the prophets, wrote the truth about him.

<margin>Rabbi Haccanas.</margin>

<margin>The third kind of Jews.</margin>
Finally, others of the Jews, wishing to adhere to Christ neither in faith nor in work, chose like blind men to remain stubbornly in their perfidy. Yet even they (see how great is the power of truth!) were not able to deny the truth entirely. For while explaining the law and the prophets, compelled by truth alone, they were unable to remain completely silent about it in many places. It must not be thought that this happened without divine arrangement—so that we might have testimonies of the truth itself from its very enemies, against those who oppose and deny it. Nor does it prejudice the truth that they themselves did not believe; rather, it adds more to the testimony, because even as unbelievers and against their will, they did not deny it. From the sayings and writings of these men, and of all the others who handed down anything in writing after the Babylonian captivity, the <term>Talmudic code</term><note>The Talmud.</note> was amassed and compiled.

### *Who the author of the Talmud was, when it was published, into how many parts it is divided, and what matters it chiefly treats.*
### Chapter V.

Since I have found various opinions regarding the author of the <term>Talmud</term><note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note> itself and the time in which it was published. Now, the Talmud is that which comprises doctrine, or discipline, all the previous commentaries, statutes, and certain histories of the times—a work truly full on every side with divine and natural, as well as political and legal wisdom.

Each of these parts is divided into several <term>Masechtot</term> <note>original: "massachtoth"</note>, which are treatises or books; and each <term>Masechet</term> <note>original: "massechoth"</note>, that is, each book, is further divided into several <term>Perakim</term>, that is, distinctions or chapters. For the first part is divided into eleven books.

<margin>The first part of the Talmud is called the Order of Seeds.</margin>
The first of these, which is called <term>Masechet Berachot</term> <note>original: "massechoth berachoth"</note>, that is, the treatise of blessings, has nine chapters, in which it treats principally of blessings, of giving thanks to God, of prayers, and divine praises. The second, which is named <term>Masechet Pe’ah</term> <note>original: "massecheth pea"</note>, that is, the treatise of the corner, contains ten chapters, in which the corner portion of harvests or crops that ought to be left for the poor is discussed. The third, designated <term>Masechet Demai</term> <note>original: "massecheth demai"</note>, that is, the treatise of doubt, is divided into ten chapters, in which it deals with the giving of tithes on doubtful things. The fourth, called <term>Masechet Terumot</term> <note>original: "massecheth terumoth"</note>, that is, the treatise of "two out of a hundred," is divided into eleven chapters, in which it discusses the separation of two from every hundred parts of produce, which were to be given to the priests. The fifth, called <term>Masechet Shevi'it</term> <note>original: "massecheth sceuiith"</note>, that is, the treatise of the seventh, is partitioned into ten chapters, in which it treats the seventh year, in which nothing at all was to be sown, nor the land cultivated. At this time, both the fruits of trees and whatever the earth brought forth of its own accord were common to all. The sixth, named <term>Masechet Kilayim</term> <note>original: "massecheth chelaim"</note>, that is, the treatise of mixtures, has nine chapters, in which all types of things that were forbidden to be mixed are discussed. The seventh, called <term>Masechet Ma'aser Rishon</term> <note>original: "massecheth maascer risson"</note>, that is, the treatise of the first tithing, contains nine chapters, in which it deals with the first tithes that were owed to the Levites, from which the Levites themselves were bound to provide tithes to the Priests. The eighth, designated <term>Masechet Ma'aser Sheni</term> <note>original: "massecheth maascer sceni"</note>, that is, the treatise of the second tithing, is divided into five chapters, in which it treats the second tithes, which were to be set aside after the tithes given to the Levites, and were to be eaten and consumed in Jerusalem. The ninth, called <term>Masechet Challah</term> <note>original: "massecheth halla"</note>, that is, the treatise of the cake, is divided into four chapters, in which it deals with the cake of bread, or a twist or roll, which was always to be taken from the dough and given to the Priests. The tenth, called <term>Masechet Orlah</term> <note>original: "massecheth orla"</note>, that is, the treatise of the enclosure, is divided into three chapters, in which it treats the "enclosure" of trees that occurred while they were planted, as a sign that for three years no one was permitted to eat of their fruit. The eleventh, called <term>Masechet Bikkurim</term> <note>original: "massecheth biccurim"</note>, that is, the treatise of the first fruits, has four chapters, in which it deals with the first fruits to be offered in the temple, which [consisted] of only seven...

<margin>What a shekel is.</margin>
Now, although a <term>Shekel</term> <note>original: "siculus"</note> is properly a certain measure of weight, according to that passage in Leviticus 27: "a <term>shekel</term> <note>Hebrew: "seckel"</note> has twenty obols," since it is derived from the Hebrew word <term>shakal</term> <note>Hebrew: "sacal"</note>, which means "to weigh." In this context, however, it is a type of coin weighing twenty obols. For every person, after he had reached the twentieth year of his age, was bound to pay half a shekel each year according to the weight measure of the Temple, for the purpose of buying the two aforementioned lambs, to be offered in the perpetual sacrifice for the redemption of souls.

The fifth, which is denominated <term>Masechet Sotah</term> <note>original: "massecheth sota"</note>, that is, the treatise of the wayward woman, has nine chapters, in which they deal with the straying which a wife makes from her husband by adhering to another. The twelfth, which is called <term>Massecheth Okatzin</term> <note>original: "מסכת עוקצין"; the treatise of the stalks of fruits</note>, has three chapters: in which it is declared when the stalks to which apples and other fruits adhere were said to be contaminated by contact with unclean fruits. Therefore, of the whole Talmud (as stands from the preceding points), there are indeed six primary parts, sixty books, and five hundred thirty-two chapters. In which are found, scattered about, many and almost infinite <term>Ghemara</term> <note>original: "גמרות" (Ghemaroth); concluded traditions or determined conclusions</note>, containing nearly innumerable secrets concerning the Messiah and very much in agreement with our faith; these were handed down and written by the ancient Jews through many courses of years, long before the Talmud was completed. For it happens that scarcely any <term>Ghemara</term> <note>original: "גמרא"; a tradition or conclusion</note> is found in the Talmud itself—handed down, concluded, and determined by those ancient fathers—which does not express some secret of the Catholic truth <note>The author uses 'catholicae veritatis' to mean the universal or orthodox Christian truth.</note>, either explicitly and openly, or implicitly and through figures.

<header>BOOK</header>

### *That the Talmudists, for the purpose of investigating the secrets of the Law, followed the allegorical sense most especially; but the Kabbalists followed the anagogical sense; and what the Kabbalah is, and why our ancestors did not make mention of the Kabbalah.*

### Chapter VI.

->HOGOSTRATUS,<-

**I**f the Jews understand everything only literally—for they do not (as it is often said) consider anything but the "rind" <note>The "rind" or "shell" (cortex) is a common medieval metaphor for the literal meaning of a text, which hides the "fruit" or spiritual truth inside.</note> of scripture—how can it be true that the <term>Talmudists</term> followed the spiritual and mystical sense? GALATINUS: That can indeed be rightly said of the Jews of our own time, who, in order to escape the truth, occupy themselves with nothing but the literal "rind" of the law, utterly rejecting all allegories and figures. For the entire assembly of more recent teachers and younger Talmudists, as if blinded in spirit and completely neglecting the light of the mind, embrace only the historical and literal sense of the divine utterances. The ancients, however, were accustomed to seek out the secrets of the law only through the spiritual and mystical sense. Indeed, the Talmudists very often show how much the spiritual sense exceeds the literal for the purpose of investigating the secrets of the law. <margin>Spiritual and literal sense.</margin> They say that the literal sense is a **דבר קטן** <note>original: "Dauar catan"</note>, that is, a "small matter," but the spiritual or mystical sense is a **דבר גדול** <note>original: "Dauar gadol"</note>, that is, a "great matter." And they call the literal sense a **משל** <note>original: "Mashal"</note>, that is, an "example" or "parable," as <term>Rabbi Moses</term> <note>Referring to Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> reports in the first treatise of the book <term>More</term> <note>original: "Moreh Nevukhim" or "The Guide for the Perplexed."</note>. Furthermore, they compare the literal sense itself to a candle, which is bought for the smallest fraction of a coin. But the allegorical or figurative sense, which they call **בוריה שלתורה** <note>original: "Buria sheltora," likely a corruption of "Be'ur shel Torah" or "the clarity/explanation of the Law."</note>, that is, the "certainty of the law," they liken to a pearl lying hidden in a dark house, which is eventually found by seekers by means of such a candle—that is, through the literal sense or parable. The same Rabbi Moses also explains this most excellently and beautifully near the beginning of that same book, saying: "Know that the key to understanding everything the Prophets said is to understand parables, metaphors, likenesses, and enigmas." For you know it was said in Hosea, chapter 12: **וביד הנביאים אדמה** <note>Hosea 12:10</note>, which is: "In the hand of the prophets I will use likenesses." And again in Ezekiel, chapter 17: **בן אדם חוד חידה ומשול משל אל בית ישראל** <note>Ezekiel 17:2</note>, that is: "Son of man, pose a riddle and speak a parable to the house of Israel." [Specifically regarding] the "great eagle with wings." And a little later: **אמור נא לבית המרי הלא ידעתם מה אלה אמור הנה בא מלך בבל ירושלם ויקח את מלכה** <note>Ezekiel 17:12</note>, which is: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say now to the rebellious house, 'Do you not know what these things mean?' Say: 'Behold, the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and took its king...'"

And so forth. <note>This refers to Ezekiel 17:12, where the prophet explains an allegory about a vine and an eagle.</note> You know, moreover, what the wise man said in Proverbs, chapter 25: <note>original Hebrew: תפוחי זהב במשכיות כסף דבר דבר על אפניו (Tappuhei zahav be-maskiyyot kesef davar davur al afnayv)</note> "Like golden apples in silver carvings is a word spoken according to its two faces." <note>Usually translated as "a word fitly spoken," but here interpreted as having dual meanings: literal and spiritual.</note> Hear, I pray you, the explanation of this sentence. The silver carvings are silver lattices, in which the openings are very tiny, yet penetrable to the sight. Therefore, the meaning is this: a word spoken according to its "two faces"—that is, according to its interior and exterior sense—is like an apple in a silver lattice. It is as if he were saying it is necessary for the exterior sense to be precious and good, like silver. But the interior sense is much better, like gold, so that the exterior is to the interior as silver is compared to gold. It is also necessary that there be something in the exterior sense that leads and draws the observer toward the interior. Just as a golden apple covered by a silver lattice, when viewed from a distance or without much scrutiny, seems entirely silver. But when one who has sharp sight, provoked by the value and beauty of the silver, approaches, he will certainly see the golden apple hiding inside. Such, then, are the words of the prophets. For frequently those things which are on the outside are wisdom useful for many things, such as the shaping of morals and the state of human society. This is evident on the surface of the Proverbs of Solomon. However, those things which are within are wisdom most useful for believing according to the truth. These are the words of that <term>Rabbi Moses the Egyptian</term> <note>Better known as Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note>. From these things, therefore, it is clear that the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> only considered the secrets of the law through the spiritual and mystical sense. But this will be much more evident in what follows. I pass over the Kabbalists and those versed in the Kabbalah itself, who consider the secrets of the law only through the <term>anagogical</term> <note>The "anagogical" sense refers to interpretations that deal with the afterlife, the soul, or the final spiritual destiny of humanity.</note> understanding.

**H O G.**
This name "Kabbalah" is found nowhere among the Holy Fathers, nor among the Doctors of the Church, nor among our masters. For this reason, such a name is rendered highly suspect.

**G A L.**
<margin>What the Kabbalah is, and why our ancient [fathers] did not mention it.</margin>
In ancient times, it was forbidden to hand down this discipline which they call <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>From the Hebrew root meaning "to receive"; it refers to the received mystical tradition of Judaism.</note> to anyone except the most learned and those of advanced age. For this reason, it was not permitted to commit even a small part of it to writing. Hence, besides those things which are said to have been handed down by Rabbi Simeon son of Yohai, few or no other writings by the ancients are found. For as it says in the book <gloss>Haghiga</gloss> <note>Tractate Hagigah in the Talmud, which discusses festive offerings and includes a famous chapter on mystical topics.</note>—that is, of the Solemnity—in the chapter <gloss>En dorsin</gloss> <note>The Hebrew chapter title "Ein Dorsin," meaning "They do not expound."</note> (that is, "They are not preached"), it was permitted to no one to write anything down concerning the Kabbalah, but they handed it down by word of mouth only. Therefore, not ineptly, they called it "Kabbalah," which is interpreted as "Reception" in Latin. However, the teachers of the more recent Jews, lest that paternal teaching should vanish, published something concerning this discipline in writing—though scattered and obscured by several "veils." By this it indeed happens that very few are able to grasp a correct understanding of it. If any, however, think they have obtained something from it, they soon [keep] it in their heart, as a secret to be revealed to no one...

Therefore, it is no wonder if this name "Kabbalah," or the faculty designated by that name, has rarely been on the lips of the saints and other wise men until now, and if our ancestors did not mention it. Even the famous <term>Ægidius</term> <note>Giles of Viterbo (1469–1532), a Cardinal and influential scholar of Hebrew and mysticism.</note> of Viterbo—a man certainly most eloquent and skilled, and excellently learned in every kind of literature, whom the current Pope Leo recently elevated to the dignity of the Cardinalate because of his manifold virtues and merits—having begun the matter from the start, laid the miraculous foundations of this divine wisdom in a small book on the "Sacred Letters," written in a most elegant style. He did this to show openly that many more and much higher things than all others have written on this subject so far were soon to be produced, which would bring the clearest light to such an obscure matter. Finally, I myself, like one gathering grapes after the vintage, have decided to intersperse only those things about this Kabbalistic wisdom within what I am about to say—wherever it is necessary—which seem essential for conveying the secrets of Catholic truth.

And as to the first point, I confess that many absurdities are placed there; however, not everything that *seems* absurd is truly absurd. For those <term>Ancient Talmudists</term> <note>The rabbis of the early centuries CE whose discussions form the Talmud.</note> handed down nearly infinite secrets.

<margin>The ancient Talmudists handed down the secrets of the law under figures and enigmas.</margin>
