While they are ignorant of the ancient manner of theologizing and philosophizing, they turn many secrets of the Talmudic work into mockery and blasphemies. Hence, many of our own people, while they are unable to understand mysteries of this kind, presume to revile and condemn them. 

From this—to say nothing of others—a certain man endowed with no small skill in divine and human letters, writing against the Jews, records many things of this same kind; because he understood them poorly, he calls them follies and inconsistencies. And among other things which he says are found written in the Talmud against divine perfection, he especially reports this: That when God established the firmament, being unable to finish it, He left a certain hole in it on the northern side. He says the Jews assert that He did this (as the Doctor himself says) so that if anyone should ever arise wanting to make himself equal to God, God—pointing out the completion of that hole—might say to him: "If you are God, just as I am, close that place which I left open, if you can." 

But how obvious a lie this is surely escapes no one. For we see the highest axis of the northern pole always above us, never hidden, and we see it all as whole, integral, and perfect. From this, the foolishness of this error is clearly evident. All these things are the opinion of that Doctor. Although he said these and all other things with a good mind and zeal for the Christian faith, he was nevertheless (to tell the truth) not a little deceived. Nor does God, who is the highest truth, need our lie for the exaltation of His faith. 

And especially since most of those things which he rejects as entirely erroneous, if they are understood correctly (as is proper), are more profitable to us for the truth of the Catholic faith against the Jews than if they were judged to be spoken (as he says) as things utterly foreign to truth and reason. For to let other matters pass, this example of the hole of the firmament left in the northern part—which he brings forward as the greatest inconsistency—if he understands it correctly, will be seen not only as no inconsistency, but also as most consistent with our faith. Therefore, so that the truth of the Catholic faith itself may appear more clearly for the confounding of the <term>perfidy of the Jews</term> <note>A common, though prejudiced, historical term used in medieval and Renaissance Christian polemics to describe Jewish refusal to accept Christ.</note>, I will first report the words of that same example in <term>Hebrew</term> <note>original: "Hebraice"</note> exactly as they are written in the Talmud. For as the Talmudic histories relate in the chapter <term>Helec</term> <note>A chapter in the tractate Sanhedrin of the Talmud dealing with the afterlife and history.</note>: while the Second Temple was standing, during the reign of <term>Hyrcanus the Maccabee</term> <note>John Hyrcanus I, a Hasmonean ruler of Judea, late 2nd century BCE.</note>, son of Simon the Maccabee, a certain <term>Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachiah</term> <note>A leader of the Pharisees in the 2nd century BCE.</note>,

on that journey by which he was returning from Alexandria to Jerusalem, entered an inn together with his disciples. Looking at the house, he said, "How beautiful it is." Having said this, he immediately cast him out from his company and the company of his fellows with a ban of excommunication. Therefore, this Jesus, seeing himself treated with such contempt and reproach, set up a stone and bowed down to worship it; he led many of the Jews into the cult of that same idol. He was also a sorcerer, and was eventually hanged for his crimes. Hence, one reads of him in the chapter *Sotah*: **ולא ברבי יהושע בן פרחיה שהיה דוחה ישו הנצרי בשתי ידים** <note>original: "Not like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachiah, who pushed away Jesus the Nazarene with both hands."</note>
This means: "Not like Rabbi Yehoshua, who pushed away Jesus the Nazarene with both hands." Therefore, because in various places of the Talmud itself this Jesus the Nazarene—born of an adulteress and a polluted woman, an idolater, a sorcerer, a subverter of the law, and finally hanged—is mentioned with great contempt, many people (indeed, nearly innumerable ones) are deceived, perhaps by the wickedness of more recent Rabbis or through ignorance of history. They think all those shameful things are said about our most glorious Savior Jesus. But the falsity of this error can be most clearly proven by this fact: as also appears in the Talmudic histories, that Hyrcanus the Maccabee, under whom lived this Jesus the Nazarene (of whom all those shameful things are related), reigned approximately 110 years before Pontius Pilate, under whom Jesus Christ suffered.

<header>ONE</header>

Indeed, no one—unless they were completely out of their mind—would despise the Law and the Prophets simply because of certain things he might find within them. Likewise, no one except a person lacking reason would disregard a precious stone <note>Refers to the "toadstone" or "draconite," gems which folklore claimed were found inside the heads of these animals and possessed magical or medicinal properties.</note> just because it was found in the head of a dragon or a toad. Nor would anyone but a fool or a madman think that honey should be rejected because it is the "spit" of bees, or because it comes from animals that possess a poisonous sting—provided, of course, that he knew how to convert that honey to his own useful purposes and was not ignorant of how to avoid the harm of the sting. 

Therefore, traditions of this kind are by no means to be rejected. This is partly because they could have reached those who wrote them down in an unbroken line of succession from Moses, the prophets, and the other fathers. Indeed, we can hardly imagine that these traditions came from anywhere else but from those same prophets and holy fathers. Furthermore, nothing more powerful can be found to refute the impudence of the Jews, and nothing more effective can be found to convict them of their wickedness. Finally, what is more pleasing to a Christian than to seize the sword from the hands of the enemy and—following the example of David—to cut off the head of the unfaithful with their own blade, or like Judith, to sever it with their own dagger? 

<margin>The Constitution of Clement V.</margin>
For this reason, it was surely by divine providence that Pope Clement V, with the approval of the most holy Council <note>The Council of Vienne, held in 1311–1312.</note>, decreed that the Talmudic books of the Jews should be translated into the Latin language by faithful men skilled in the Hebrew tongue, and that they should be read publicly by Christians. This is found in the <term>Clementines</term> <note>A collection of canon law decrees issued by Pope Clement V.</note> under the section "On Teachers" (*De magistris*). There, among other things, it is stated: "With the approval of this holy council, we have provided for the establishment of schools for the following types of languages wherever the Roman Curia may happen to reside, as well as in the studies of Paris, Oxford, Bologna, and Salamanca. We decree that in each of these places, Catholic men shall be maintained who have sufficient knowledge of the Hebrew, Greek, Arabic, and <term>Chaldaic</term> <note>Usually referring to Aramaic, the language of the Babylonian Talmud.</note> languages—specifically, two experts for each language—who shall manage the schools there. By faithfully translating books from those languages into Latin, they shall diligently teach these languages to others and pass on their expertise through studious instruction. Thus, being sufficiently trained and taught in these languages, they may, by God's authority, produce the hoped-for fruit by healthfully propagating the faith among the infidel peoples themselves." 

Thus far the decree. When it speaks of translating and publicly reading the books of the Jews, this is not to be understood as referring to the Bible, since it has already been translated so many times; nor do the Scriptures belong solely to the Jews, but rather they are ours, or at least shared. Instead, it must be understood to refer to other Jewish books, and especially the Talmudic ones, in which so many Catholic truths are contained, as will be shown most extensively in the following pages. From all these points that have been discussed, it is clearer than the midday sun that the Talmud itself should be accepted by Christians—though not in its entirety, but only in those parts that are good. 

The ancient Talmudists themselves admit this, as is clearly seen in the book <term>Haghigha</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning festival offerings and, in some sections, the transmission of esoteric knowledge.</note>. There, among other things, one reads: "What is the meaning of what is written in Malachi 2: 'For the lips of a priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord'?" <note>original: "Quia labia sacerdotis seruant scientiam, et legem requirunt ex ore eius, quoniam angelus Domini..."</note>

Very much in agreement with the Christian faith are those things which the ancient Jews strove with all their zeal to hide from the Gentiles. For this reason, the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> (to speak of them first), as the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, containing law and tradition.</note> testifies, omitted many things when translating for King Ptolemy, and changed many others. This was done lest the divine secrets happen to become known to the Gentiles, who were then considered unworthy. For this reason also, the <term>Sophrim</term> <note>original: "סופרים"; Hebrew for "Scribes."</note> themselves—that is, the scribes or wise men—erased many things from the divine scriptures as if they were absurd, or as if they were things that would be a crime even to dream of among the nations of the Gentiles. They did this as men who did not yet fully weigh the height of the divine counsel regarding the salvation of the human race. Either they feared the divine scriptures would be mocked by their own people and other infidels because of such things, or they suspected that a scandal of impious belief might be generated among ignorant and simple Jews from such passages. Therefore, it is certain that they did not make those changes—by which the Holy Scripture happened to be corrupted—for the sake of hiding the truth, or from any other evil intent. Since both in these and in almost infinite other places, they did not fail to reveal the truth to one another, as clearly appears in the Talmudic books. 

But it is clear that they acted most wickedly in this, because they dared to act against the command of God, who spoke thus through Moses in Deuteronomy chapter 4: <note>original: "לא תוסיפו על הדבר אשר אנכי מצוה אתכם ולא תגרעו"</note> **You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor shall you diminish from it.** And again, it is said through Solomon in the 30th chapter of Proverbs: <note>original: "אל תוסף על דבריו פן יוכיח בך ונכזבת"</note> **Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and you be found a liar.** For that reason, Jeremiah, speaking in the prophetic manner of the future as if it were the past, rebukes the bold crime of these scribes who were to commit such things with these words in the 8th chapter: <note>original: "איכה תאמרו חכמים אנחנו ותורת יהוה אתנו אכן הנה לשקר עשה עט שקר סופרים"</note> **How do you say, "We are wise, and the law of God is with us"? But behold, the false pen of the scribes <note>original: "Sophrim"</note> has worked for a lie.** 

What kind of lie, or what kind of falsehood the lying pen or reed of the scribes was going to commit, the same prophet expresses in the 23rd chapter, saying: <note>original: "והפכתם את דברי אלהים חיים יהוה צבאות אלהינו"</note> **And you have perverted the words of the living Gods, of the Lord of hosts our God.** And again in the 9th chapter he says: <note>original: "ואמת לא dig לא ידברו למרו לשונם דבר שקר העוה נלאו"</note> **And they will not speak the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak a lie; in acting iniquitously, they have worn themselves out.**

->FIRST<-
c 3

"what worthlessness, and you have made him to expire, or you have afflicted him," says the Lord of hosts. For in that place, <note>original: "אתי והפחתם"</note> *and you have afflicted me* was originally written. However, they wrote <note>original: "אותו והפחתם"</note> *and you have afflicted him*. For the word <note>original: "אתי"</note> *me* which was there, signifies myself; but the word <note>original: "אותו"</note> *him* which they substituted—changing the letter *yod* into a *vav*—designates "him." Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> clearly confirms this in his commentary, saying: *And you made him expire, or you afflicted him.* This is one of the fifteen expressions known as <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term> <note>Hebrew: "תקון סופרים"; literally "Correction of the Scribes." These are traditional changes made to the biblical text by early scribes to avoid anthropomorphisms or perceived irreverence toward God.</note>, that is, a "correction of the scribes." This is because <note>original: "אתי והפחתם"</note> *and you have made me expire*, or *you have afflicted me*, or *you have vexed me*, was originally written. Yet the writing of the scribes placed <note>original: "אותו"</note> *him* instead of <note>original: "אתי"</note> *me*. Furthermore, the word *vehippachtem* signifies an affliction of the soul, just as in Job chapter 11: <note>original: "והפחת נפש"</note> *and their hope is the affliction of the soul.* These are the words of Rabbi Solomon.

That this word *vehippachtem* signifies expiration, affliction, or vexation, Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, or Radak (1160–1235), a famous grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> demonstrates most excellently when he says: "That which is read in Job chapter 31, 'And the soul of its lords <note>original: "והפחתי"</note> *I have afflicted*.' Likewise, in Malachi chapter 1, *vehippachtem* signifies labor and vexation, or the affliction and vexation of the soul. For he who suffers affliction or vexation of the soul is just as if his soul were expiring and departing from him." Thus Kimhi.

From these points, it is clear that the passage in Malachi chapter 1, which our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the Catholic Church at the time.</note> renders as: "Behold, of labor. And you have blown it away, says the Lord of hosts," is entirely corrupted. Therefore, according to the Hebrew truth, it ought to be corrected thus: **Behold, what worthlessness, and you have afflicted me (or made me to expire), says the Lord of hosts.**

Rabbi Rahmon <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Nachman or a similar authority cited in Midrashic literature.</note> posits many other examples of this kind when he says: "That which is written in the third chapter of the Lamentations of Jeremiah, 'In remembering you will remember, and my soul will sink within me'; it was originally written as *your soul upon you*. For that which is now written, 'my soul upon me,' is one of the many <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term> (corrections of the scribes) which you will find in the *Bereshit Rabba* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Genesis.</note>." Thus he says. From this it is evident that what our edition has in Lamentations 3—"Remembering I will remember, and my soul shall languish in me"—has been altered both among the Hebrews and among us. According to this Talmudic tradition, it should be corrected to: **Remembering you will remember, and your soul shall languish upon you.**

Furthermore, Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Moses ha-Darshan (11th century), an influential scholar of Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note> says the following regarding Genesis chapter 15: "And Abraham still stood before God." In many other places he states: "And this is a <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term> (correction of the scribes). For there it was written: 'And God still stood before Abraham.'" This is also what the masters said in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>The Midrash on the Psalms.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Psalter—regarding Psalm 18: "And you shall give me the shield of your salvation." For it is said there: <note>original Hebrew: "ו' א' ותתן לי מגן ישעך מדבר מאבות אבינו ע"ה שהיה אברהם יושב והשכינה עומדת לו ב' ר' ב'יה בשם ר' לוי אמר בקש אברהם לעמוד אמר לו הקדוש ברוך הוא שב ואתה סימן לבניך שיהיו יושבין ואני עומד שנאמר אלהים נצב בעדת אל"</note> "And you gave me the shield of your salvation: this speaks of our father Abraham (peace be upon him). When Abraham was sitting and the Divine Presence <note>The *Shekhinah*.</note> was standing before him, Rabbi Levi said: Abraham sought to stand up, but the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: 'Sit, and you shall be a sign for your children, that they shall be sitting and I shall be standing,' as it is said: *God stands in the congregation of God*." <note>Quoting Psalm 82:1 to show that God honors the assemblies of the righteous by standing while they sit.</note>

That is, another discourse: *And you will give me the shield of your salvation.* <note>original: "Et dabis mihi clypeum salutem tuam"; Psalm 18:35</note> This speaks of our father Abraham, of whom it is written, *And Abraham was sitting, and the Divinity was standing by him.* Rabbi Berachias said in the name of Rabbi Levi: Our father Abraham sought to stand up. It is evident that this was fulfilled when the Apostles—who were the children of Abraham according to the flesh, and the assembly and congregation of God—were sitting, and Christ, the true God, stood before them, washing their feet and wiping them with the towel with which he was girded.

Then (to return to the Talmudic tradition), the aforementioned *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A Jewish homiletic commentary on the Psalms.</note> continues in the same place, saying: **Rabbi Samuel son of Hiya and Rabbi Jodan in the name of Rabbi Hanina said that Rabbi Simon said, this is a <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term> <note>Hebrew: "תקון סופרים"; "Correction of the Scribes." This is in accordance with Psalm 18: *And your humility, or your gentleness, shall strengthen me.*

Then the same Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Rabbi Moses Hadarsan (11th century), a famous scholar of Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note> continues there, saying: Similar to this is what is written in Numbers 11: *If I have found grace in your eyes, let me not see my misfortune.* <note>Numbers 11:15</note> This is a <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term>, that is, a correction of the scribes. For *your misfortune* <note>The original text likely implied the "evil" or "misfortune" brought by God, which scribes changed to "my misfortune" to avoid attributing evil to the Divine.</note> was originally written there. And likewise in Job chapter 7: *What shall I do to you, O guardian of men? Why have you set me against you, so that I am a burden to myself?* <note>Job 7:20</note> For what is written there, *to myself*, is one of the <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term>, that is, the corrections of the wise men. For previously, *to you* was written. So also in Job 32: *And they shall condemn God, or act impiously toward God.* In place of "God," they put "Job." <note>Job 32:3; the scribes changed the text to say the friends condemned Job, rather than saying they had effectively condemned God by failing to answer Job's arguments.</note>

And also that passage in Ezekiel 8: *Is it a light thing for the house of Judah to have committed the abominations they have done here? For they have filled the land with iniquity, and they return to provoke me, and they are putting the stench to their nose.* <note>Ezekiel 8:17</note> This is a <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term>, that is, a correction of the scribes. For where the text has **אל אפם** *el apam*, that is, *to their nose*, it was originally written as **אל אפי** *el api*, that is, *to my nose*. Furthermore, in Hosea 4: *As their number increased, so they sinned against me; I will change their glory into shame.* <note>Hosea 4:7</note> This is also a <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term>, or correction of the scribes. Finally, in Jeremiah 2: *And my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit.* <note>Jeremiah 2:11</note> This too is a <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term>, a correction of the scribes. For there, **כבודי** *cheuodi*, that is, *my glory*, was originally written, and not **כבודו** *cheuodo*, that is, *his glory*. These and many other things of this kind are found in the <term>Bereshit Rabba</term> <note>Genesis Rabbah; an ancient midrashic collection on the book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the Great Exposition of Genesis. It is found in the book *Yevamot* <note>The Talmudic tractate regarding Levirate marriage.</note>, that is, the book of brothers-in-law, at the conclusion of the chapter *The Uncircumcised* <note>original: "חרל ha-erel"</note>, where Rabbi Yohanan spoke in the name of Rabbi Simeon: "It is better that you remove one letter from the Law, so that the name of Heaven may be sanctified in public." The first instance is that of Genesis 18, which among us is read as: *Abraham, however, still stood before the Lord.* It ought to be corrected thus: *God, however, still stood before Abraham.* 

Then, that which is in Psalm 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 18:35.</note>, which our edition has as: *And you have given me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand has supported me, and your discipline has corrected me to the end, and your discipline itself shall teach me.* This also ought to be corrected to: *And you shall give me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand shall strengthen me, and your humility*—or your poverty, or your gentleness—*shall multiply me,* or nourish me. 

Furthermore, that which is read among us in Numbers 11: *And let me find grace in your eyes, lest I be afflicted by such great evils.* This ought to be corrected as: *If I have found grace before your eyes, let me not see Your evil* <note>The author suggests the original referred to "God's evil" (meaning His punishment), which scribes changed to "my evil" to avoid attributing "evil" to God.</note>.

Likewise, that which is read among us in Job 32: *But they had only condemned Job.* Thus it is correctly to be read: *And they shall condemn God,* or they shall act impiously toward God. 

Additionally, that which is found in Ezekiel 8: *Is this a light thing to the house of Judah, that they should commit these abominations which they have done here? For filling the land with iniquity, they have turned to provoke me: and behold, they apply the branch to my nose.* It is to be corrected: *Is it a light thing to the house of Judah to have done the abominations which they have done here? For they have filled the land with iniquity, and they shall repeat their provocation of me, and they shall be the ones sending a stench to My nose.* 

Moreover, that which is in Hosea 4: *According to their multitude, so have they sinned against me; I will change their glory into ignominy.* It is to be corrected: *As is their multitude, so they have sinned against me; I will change My glory into ignominy.* 

Finally, that which our edition has in Jeremiah 2: *My people, however, has changed its glory for an idol.* It should be corrected exactly as: *My people, however, has changed My glory for that which shall not profit.* 

<margin>The second mode of the depravity of sacred scripture.</margin> The second mode of <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term> <note>Hebrew: "Correction of the Scribes."</note>, that is, the method of scribal correction (as found in certain places of sacred scripture), occurs where the Prophets had written something, but the scribes, setting that aside, did not change the letters themselves, but presumed to add vowel points differently than the writing naturally required. For the Hebrews do not have vowel letters, but use certain points in place of vowels. Therefore, by varying those points, the text is read far differently than it was written, and a far different sense is rendered.

**GAL.** Moses (as you yourself know best) did not provide the punctuation <note>The author is referring to the "niqqud," the system of vowel points and accents used in Hebrew, rather than modern punctuation like commas or periods.</note> for the Law. This is why the scrolls that the Jews keep with veneration in their Synagogues are written without points. Nor did any of the prophets point their own books. Rather, later scholars pointed the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa <note>The "Holy Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible (Ketuvim).</note>. Some, therefore, say that Ezra was the first to point the sacred volumes. Others, however, say it was not Ezra, but two others who lived after Ezra, one called ben Naphtali and the other ben Asher, who first applied points to the sacred letters. This latter opinion is the more common. **CAP.** Now, pray, relate some of those instances which the <term>Sophrim</term>—that is, the Scribes—corrupted in the sacred letters by such a change of points.

<margin>2 Samuel 16 <note>original: "2 Reg. 16." In the Latin Vulgate, 1 and 2 Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note></margin>
**GAL.** One of these is found in the second book of Samuel, chapter 16. For there, it was originally written among them in this way: "Perhaps the Lord will look upon **his** humility"—or his affliction, his poverty, or his gentleness—"and the Lord will return good to me for his curse." <note>This refers to David’s response to Shimei’s cursing; the Hebrew text usually reads "my eye" or "my affliction."</note> But the <term>Sophrim</term> (the Scribes), wishing to "correct" this, took the word <term>be-eno</term> <note>original: בעניי. Meaning "in his humility/affliction."</note>, which naturally ought to have been pointed in a way that signifies "his humility" (or affliction, poverty, or gentleness), and instead pointed it as <term>be-eni</term> <note>original: בעיי. Note: The transcription has בעיי, likely a typo for בעני.</note>, which means "in my eye." Hence, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> explains this word—"in my eye"—as "into the tears of my eye."

<margin>Micah 1</margin>
To this, that passage in the first chapter of Micah is very similar: *I will lay all its idols in desolation,* or destruction. And a little later: *Over this I will wail and lament. I will go stripped and naked.* And shortly after: *For its wound is painful and desperate. For it has come even to Judah, it has reached even to the gates of my people, even into Jerusalem. In Gath, do not announce it; in weeping, do not weep.* In the house of dust, I have <term>hithpallashti</term> <note>original: התפלשתי. Meaning "I rolled myself."</note>—that is, I am involved, or surrounded, or I have rolled or surrounded myself—in the dust of the dust. This is how it is and was written. But the Scribes, wishing to correct it, pointed it thus: <term>hithpallashi</term> <note>original: התפלשי. Meaning "roll yourself."</note>, which is the feminine gender, "roll yourself," addressed to someone else. From these words of Micah, it is clearly held that God was to be involved in the ground or dust. This is not hindered by the fact that the Prophet used the past tense <term>hithpallashti</term> ("I rolled myself"), according to the custom of the prophets, who very often use the past for the future to suggest the greater certainty of a future event.

<margin>Isaiah 42</margin>
Hence, upon that passage of Isaiah 42, *I have done these things for them,* Rabbi Solomon says in his gloss: "I have done for them," that is, "I will do for them." For the entire prophetic language speaks of the future as if it were already done. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon.

<margin>Genesis 18</margin>
Furthermore, it should not be ignored here that Abraham also used this word <term>aphar</term> <note>original: עפר. Usually meaning "dust" or "dry earth."</note>, which is ground or moistened dust, when he spoke with the Lord, wishing to express the condition and vileness of the human body, saying in Genesis 18: *Behold, I pray, I have ventured to speak to the Lord, I who am* <term>aphar</term>—that is, ground or moistened dust—*and* <term>ve-epher</term> <note>original: ואפר. Meaning "and ashes."</note>—that is, and ashes. He said "ground and ashes," as if in the ground, or in

# FIRST.

...or in the moistened dust He might express the material principle of man, and in ash his final dissolution. What, therefore, does this saying of the Lord in Micah mean, when it says: "In the house toward the ground—or from the ground of moistened dust—I have enveloped myself"? <note>Micah 1:10. Galatinus is arguing for a Christological reading of a difficult Hebrew phrase, suggesting it refers to God "enveloping" Himself in human flesh.</note> It means nothing else than that He was enveloped in the earthly or fleshy body of the one Virgin; using "I have enveloped myself" in place of "I shall envelop myself," that is, "I shall clothe myself." From these things which have been said regarding this second method of <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term> <note>Hebrew: "Correction of the Scribes."</note>—that is, the correction of the scribes—two texts in particular are corrected, which are held to be corrupt both among us and among the Hebrews. The first is found in 2 Samuel, chapter 16, in our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate, where 2 Samuel is titled 2 Kings.</note> as follows: "If perchance the Lord may look upon my affliction, and the Lord may render me good for this day’s cursing." This text, however, must be entirely corrected thus: "Perhaps the Lord will look upon **his** affliction—or upon his humility, his poverty, or his gentleness—and the Lord will return good to me for his curse." The second text is from Micah chapter 1, which reads among us: "In the house of dust, sprinkle yourselves with dust." This text should also be thoroughly corrected to: "In the house toward the ground—or from the ground of dust—I have enveloped myself, or I have surrounded myself."

<margin>The third way of corrupting the scripture.</margin>
Finally, the third method of <term>Ticcun Sophrim</term> (the correction of the scribes) by which it happened that the sacred scripture was altered, is when the Scribes, leaving what Moses and the Prophets wrote in the text, placed something else on the outside in the margin, which they call <term>Qere</term> <note>Hebrew: "read."</note>, meaning "to be read." And what is inside the text they call <term>Ketiv</term> <note>Hebrew: "written."</note>, meaning "to be written." This is clearly gathered from the words of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> regarding that passage in Deuteronomy 28: "You shall betroth a wife, and another man shall ravish her." For there, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "<note>original: ישגלנה isgalenna</note> is a word for the coitus of a concubine. And the <term>Targum</term> <note>An ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, for the sake of courtliness, put in its place <note>original: ישכבנה Iscauenna</note>, that is, 'he shall lie with her.' And this is a scribal correction." Thus says Rabbi Solomon. Likewise, the same Rabbi says regarding that passage in Isaiah 36: "And <term>Rabshakeh</term> <note>The chief messenger or general of the Assyrian king Sennacherib.</note> said: Has my master sent me to your master and to you to speak these words? Is it not rather to the men sitting on the wall, to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?" The gloss of Rabbi Solomon says there: "<note>original: חריהם Horehem</note>, that is, their dung, which is the filth coming out of the hole that is below; but the <term>Sophrim</term> (the scribes) corrected this into beautiful and courtly language, and they wished that <note>original: צואתם czoatham</note>, that is, 'their egestion,' should be read." For the masters decreed that the scriptures written uncourteously to their shame should be read courtly and politely. Just like that passage in Deuteronomy chapter 28: what is written as <note>original: בעפולים baapolim</note>, that is, "with tenesmus" <note>A distressing or painful sensation of needing to pass stool, often associated with tumors.</note>, they placed outside in the margin to be read as <note>original: בטחורים battehorim</note>, that is, "with hemorrhoids" or dysentery. Likewise, in the same place where Moses wrote <note>original: ישגלנה isgalenna</note>, that is, "he shall ravish her," they placed on the outside <note>original: ישכבנה Iscauenna</note>, that is, "he shall lie" or "he shall sleep with her." Furthermore, in Isaiah chapter 36, where it is written <note>original: חריהם Horehem</note>...

### BOOK

They placed *Horehem* <note>Hebrew: "their excrement"</note>, that is, their dung, outside [the main text], and in its place they put *czoatham* <note>Hebrew: "their bowel movement"</note>, that is, their egestion. In the same place also, where the Prophet put *sethnehem* <note>Hebrew: "their urine"</note>, that is, "their urine," the scribes placed *meme raglehem* <note>Hebrew: "the waters of their feet"</note>, that is, "the waters of their feet." And many other things are similar to these. All these things are according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator</note>. Also, in the prophet Hosea, chapter 9, it is written: *For also woe to them, my incarnation is from them.* <note>Hosea 9:12. The author is interpreting the Hebrew phrase "besari mehem" Christologically.</note> However, the scribes, concerning the word *beshari*, that is "my incarnation" or "my flesh," pointed the vowels <note>Vowel points (nikkud) were added to the Hebrew text later; changing them can completely change a word's meaning</note> against the natural sense of the word as *besuri*, which means "in my departing" or "when I withdraw." I said "against the natural sense of the word" because *besuri*, which is inside the text, is written with the letter *shin* <note>The Hebrew letter ש</note>, just as the prophet Hosea had written it. Therefore, *beshari*, that is "my incarnation" or "my flesh," should have been pointed with an *a* sound, so that it comes from *basar*, meaning "flesh." But the word *besuri*, which they placed on the outside <note>i.e., in the margin as a "Keri" or reading instruction</note> and which means "in my departing," is written with the letter *samech* <note>The Hebrew letter ס. Both letters can make an 's' sound, allowing the scribes to swap them to change the word's meaning.</note>. Whence Rabbi Solomon, explaining this passage, says: "For also woe to them—namely, the fathers—*besuri* is like *besuri* [written with a samech], that is, 'in my departing' from them." And it is one of those cases in which *shin* is written, but *samech* is read.

<margin>Rabbi David Kimchi in the *Book of Roots*</margin>
Rabbi Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, also known as Radak (1160–1235), a famous grammarian</note> also says in the *Book of Roots* <note>The *Sefer HaShorashim*, a Hebrew dictionary and grammar</note> that the phrase "For also woe to them, *besuri*" is written with the letter *shin* but read with the letter *samech*. All these things are from Rabbi Solomon. From these things which we have said here regarding the third method of <term>ticcun Sophrim</term> <note>Hebrew: "Correction of the Scribes." This refers to tradition-sanctioned changes to the biblical text.</note>, that is, the "correction of the scribes," three texts among others are corrected. The first of these is found in Deuteronomy, chapter 28, which in our version is: "You shall take a wife, and another shall sleep with her." But this text, according to the Hebrew truth, must be corrected thus: "You shall betroth a wife, and another man shall ravish her." The second text is from Isaiah, chapter 36, which in our version reads: "And Rabshakeh said: Has my master sent me to your master and to you to speak all these words, and not rather to the men who sit on the wall, that they may eat their own dung and drink the urine of their feet with you?" This text should also be corrected thus: "And Rabshakeh said: Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you to speak these words? Is it not rather to the men sitting upon the wall, to eat their own excrement and to drink their own urine?" The third and final text is from Hosea, chapter 9, which the author of our edition [the Vulgate], following the error of the <term>ticcun Sophrim</term> (the correction of the scribes), translated thus: "But also woe to them when I depart from them." However, this text must be corrected entirely to: "For also woe to them, my incarnation—or my flesh—is from them."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Ticcun Sopherim" (Scribal Corrections), moving from specific word substitutions to a broader list of traditional examples found in rabbinic literature like the Sifre. It focuses on instances where the original text seemed to speak "against the height" (an idiom for speaking disrespectfully of God) and was thus modified by the scribes for the sake of piety.</meta>

-># BOOK ONE<-

...to seek. Thus, in the book *Sifre* <note>An ancient rabbinic commentary (Midrash) on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy</note>, which is considered highly authentic among them, it is held among other things regarding that passage in Numbers chapter 10:

> Arise, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee.

Does He who spoke and the world was made have those who hate Him? Rather, the Scripture announces and teaches that everyone who hates Israel is just as if he hated Him who founded the world by His word. And thus He Himself says in Zechariah chapter 2:

> For he who touches you, touches the apple of his eye.

Where Rabbi Judah <note>Rabbi Judah bar Ilai, a famous teacher from the 2nd century</note> says: "The apple of *his* eye" was not what was said, but "the apple of *my* eye." <note>This is a classic Scribal Correction; the original "my eye" was changed to "his eye" to avoid the suggestion that God’s own eye could be injured by humans.</note> Since it is written this way in the Law, it can be said: the Scripture was speaking "against the height" (that is, against God), but the revised Scripture used a substitute word—that is, it said something else in place of what had been written. This is much like that passage in Job chapter 7:

> Why have you set me as a target against you? and I shall be a burden to you?

Since it is written in the Law, it can be said that the Scripture spoke "against the height" (that is, against God), but the revised Scripture used a substitute word—it named something else in place of what was written. There is also something similar to this in Ezekiel chapter 8:

> And they shall be putting a stench to my nose. <note>The Hebrew text traditionally refers to "their nose," but the author cites a tradition where it originally referred to God's nose in a way deemed offensive.</note>

Since it is written in the Law, it can be said—something similar to this is also found in Habakkuk chapter 1:

> Are you not from of old, O Lord my God, my Holy One? You shall not die.

Since it is written in the Law, it can be said: the Scripture speaks against God, but in place of it, the revised Scripture said "we shall die." <note>The Hebrew tradition notes that the text originally read "Thou [God] shalt not die," but was changed to "We shall not die" (or "You shall not die" referring to the people) to avoid even mentioning the possibility of God's death.</note> Similar to this is Psalm 106:

> And they changed my glory.

But in place of it, the revised Scripture said "their glory." Still similar is that passage in Numbers chapter 11:

> And if you deal thus with me, kill me, I pray you, with death. If I have found grace in your eyes, that I may not see your evil. <note>Modern translations usually read "my wretchedness." The author suggests the original referred to God's "evil" (punishment).</note>

Since it is written in the Law, it can be said: the Scripture spoke "against the height," but the revised Scripture said something else in its place. Moreover, similar to this is Numbers chapter 12:

> ...who is as one dead in his coming out from our mother's womb, and half of our flesh is consumed.

Since it is written in the Law, it can be said that the Scripture spoke "against the height," but the revised Scripture used a substitute word—which the scribes corrected—by putting "his mother" and "his flesh" instead. All these things are from the book *Sifre*.

Many things of this kind are also found in many other books, and especially in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan of Narbonne, an 11th-century scholar known for his Midrashic compilations</note> on Genesis, regarding that passage in Genesis chapter 18:

> And Abraham was still standing before God. <note>Tradition suggests the original read "And God was still standing before Abraham," but was reversed because a superior (God) should not "stand before" an inferior (Abraham).</note>

And in *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that passage of Psalm 18:

> And you have given me the shield of your salvation.

And at the end of the book of Ben Asher, which is called <term>Dikduk</term> <note>Hebrew for "Grammar"; refers to the Masoretic notes on the Hebrew Bible</note>. And in very many other places. In these, both the things we have recounted and not a few others of this kind are set down, though in various ways, according to how they occurred to the Jewish Doctors to be explained.

But omitting others, I shall bring forward a few of those things which are placed in the aforementioned commentaries of the same Rabbi Moses the Preacher in the place previously noted, besides those which have already been brought from there. For there, among other things, is placed that passage of Psalm 21 <note>Psalm 22 in modern numbering</note>:

> Dogs have surrounded me, the synagogue or assembly of the wicked have besieged me, <note>original: "כארו caru"</note>, that is, *they have pierced my hands and my feet.*

They removed from there <note>original: "כארו caru"</note>, which signified "they pierced"...

### Chapter IX: How one should proceed against the Jews by means of their own writings.

->CAPNIO,<-

**S**ince we have deserved to approach you—who, inspired by divine power, are able to uncover these secrets so wonderful and divine lying hidden in the <term>Talmudic</term> <note>Referring to the Talmud, the vast collection of Jewish civil and ceremonial law and legend</note> books of the Jews—we ask you with all earnestness that you do not think any of them should be hidden from us. # Concerning the divine Trinity and the divine names, through which the Trinity of God itself is best introduced, along with the indivisible unity of essence and His perfections.

### *That God is Three and One. Chapter 1.*

->CAPNIO<-
<note>Capnio is the Greek-style pseudonym for the famous Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522).</note>

If, among other things, the more recent Jews especially object to us, that when they hear us confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, they say we worship three gods and posit a plurality of gods. This is an idea which, in truth, we abhor far more than they do. For that reason, it is necessary for you first to prove that God is three and one, using the sayings of the Prophets and the testimonies of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note>. GALATINUS. The Christian religion believes that God is indeed one in the simplicity of substance and nature. But it confesses three persons—who are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whose properties are <term>paternity</term> <note>The quality of being the Father</note>, <term>generation</term> <note>The act by which the Son is produced from the Father</note>, and <term>procession</term> <note>The act by which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son</note>. It confesses that these are not three in essence or nature, but purely one. God is therefore three in persons, but one in essence. Moreover, there is no need to prove with many words that God is one, nor to linger any longer on proving it. Since the very unity of God is so firm and so fixed a conception of the mind that naturally there can be none but one God. And the Jews also, and whoever believes in the Law, all confess and proclaim this. CAPNIO. It is enough here, then, if the error of the younger Jews concerning the <term>sacrament</term> <note>Here used in the sense of a "sacred mystery"</note> of the divine Trinity is refuted by the opinions of the ancient Jews. G A L. <note>Pietro Galatino, the author, defending the use of Jewish sources to prove Christian doctrine.</note>: I confess indeed that it is so. For thus also the Greek text, which ours follows in almost everything, holds. For it says thus: *Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord* <note>Original Greek: ἄκουε ἰσραὴλ, κύριος ὁ θεὸς σου κύριος εἷς ἐστί.</note>. But it is certainly clear that the Hebrew text expresses the truth against the Jews themselves far better than our version, whether Greek or Latin. Moreover, the reason why—where our edition, both Greek and Latin, has "Lord" in this place—I have translated it as "God," is because the Hebrew text in that same place has <term>יהוה</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, often transliterated as Yahweh.</note>, which is that <term>tetragrammaton</term> name of God, which designates God not by His effect, but by His essence. But since the divine essence, according to His proper being, can in no way be grasped by the mind, it is therefore considered a sin among the Jews for the name itself to be pronounced with the mouth as the letters themselves sound from which it is composed. 

Therefore, wherever they find this name, they by no means dare to utter it, but in its place they utter this name <term>אדני</term> *Adonai*, which is the same as "Lord"; yet the letters of the name itself do not signify "Lord," but "God" through His essence. Therefore, the author of both the Greek and Latin editions translated the name according to the meaning of its pronunciation, but omitted the meaning of the scripture, which is more important. 

I, however—to whose heart it is of the greatest importance to reveal the truth which the Jews deny through their own scriptures—have translated it according to its own proper meaning, so that I might more clearly show that God, both three and one, is designated in the aforementioned words. For that great Moses did not place the name of God there three times for any other reason than to distinctly suggest the Trinity of the divine persons. Furthermore, in the word "one," which he immediately added, he suggests that the three divine persons are not three Gods, but one God. This is (as Damascenus <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and Church Father.</note> says) *one essence, one nature, one deity* <note>Original Greek: μία οὐσία, μία φύσις, μία θεότης.</note>. Therefore, the Trinity of persons in no way detracts from the unity of the divine nature. 

Moreover, that in these same words the three divine persons—namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are designated through the tripled name of God, the Jews can by no means deny, since Rabbi Simeon ben Jochai, in the book which is called the <term>zohar</term> <note>The foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah (mysticism).</note>, says the following regarding this text:

### CHAPTER: Why God did not wish the mystery of the Trinity to be handed down so explicitly in the Old Instrument, just as he reserved it to be revealed in the future through the Messiah. GALATINUS.

<margin>Why the mystery of the Trinity was not explicitly handed down under the Old Law.</margin>
<margin>The mystery of the Trinity was to be explicitly revealed through the Messiah.</margin>
The Jewish people (as I do not doubt you know) were extremely prone to idolatry; the entire Old Law was established to avoid this. Therefore, lest they fall into the error of those who worshiped many gods, it was carefully brought about by divine providence that the secret of the divine Trinity itself should be handed down to them not explicitly, but implicitly <note>Meaning the truth was present but "folded in" or hidden rather than stated clearly.</note>. But because idolatry was to be utterly exploded by the Messiah, and the entire world was to be brought back to the worship of one God, therefore that sacrament of the Trinity was reserved to be explicitly and openly revealed in the days of the Messiah. This is also clearly testified by the entire school of the Cabalists, asserting that the secrets of the divine Trinity itself ought to remain hidden and concealed only until the time of the Messiah. At that time, however, when all suspicion of idolatrous error was to be removed, the secrets of the divine Trinity themselves were also to be openly uncovered.

However, in the fact that "Our" is added only in the second place, it was suggested that only the Son would be ours through the assumption of our nature. Nor would they say that He is in different places successively <note>Moving from one place to the next over time.</note>. For then He would be changeable according to location, which they entirely deny, since change can in no way befit God. Since He is eternal, immense, and supremely simple, He cannot be changed according to time, place, or form. Therefore, they—just as we do—assert that He is altogether immutable. For God Himself says in Malachi, chapter 3: **I am the Lord, I do not change.** <note>original Hebrew: אני יהוה לא שניתי</note> 

For that reason, they must admit: God (even if He is one) is, with the truth of His unity, entirely in different places at once. Therefore, it is necessary that they also concede that the divinity itself (even if it exists as only one in number) can be entirely and simultaneously in several persons. For if they concede the first point, why do they deny the second, since one is no more difficult to grant than the other? 

But they certainly cannot deny this, since not only the ancient Talmudists and <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>Followers of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note> (as has already been shown) confess it everywhere, but the divine utterances also bear witness to it. # BOOK [II]
## Page 44

almost always in the same place, the unity of the divine substance is also explained. This is done so that the trinity of persons is not excluded from the divine nature because of the unity of the singular God, nor are multiple Gods believed to exist because of the trinity of persons. Rather, in one sense, those three divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>From the Greek 'hypostasis', referring to the distinct persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) as individual realities within the one divine essence.</note> are believed to be distinct from one another without confusion, while in another sense, the unity of God Himself is entirely preserved.

This is clearly evident in the Song of Moses as well. In that passage where our version has: **See that I am alone, and there is no God besides me**, <margin>Deut. 32. <note>original Hebrew: עמדי ('immadi'), meaning "with me" or "beside me".</note></margin> the Hebrew text reads: **See now that I, I, He, and there are no gods with me.** <note>original Hebrew: ראו עתה כי אני אני הוא ואין אלהים ("Re’u attah ki ani ani hu ve-ein elohim")</note> That is: **See now, because I, I, [am] He: and there are no Gods with me.** 

Where the Hebrews use these three names, which are divine names among them: *Ani, Ani, Hu*. These are interpreted among us as *I, I, He*. What, then, is designated there by these three divine names, if not the plurality and distinction of the three divine persons? And what is signaled by that which is immediately added in the same place, **And there are no Gods with me**, if not that those three divine hypostases, designated by those three divine names, are not three Gods, but one God? 

For even if the entire divine essence is in the Father, the whole in the Son, and the whole in the Holy Spirit: since the Father is true and perfect God, **from whom** all things [exist]; and the Son is true and perfect God, **through whom** all things [exist]; and the Holy Spirit is true and perfect God, **in whom** all things [exist]; yet because that divine nature is entirely one in the three, therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three Gods, but one God, who made all things, and from whom, through whom, and in whom all things proceed, subsist, and are given life, and to whom at last all things are led back. 

For as that <term>Gregory Nazianzen</term>, <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers," highly influential in defining Trinitarian theology.</note> easily the prince of Greek theologians, says: <note>original Greek: εἷς ἐστὶν ὁ θεὸς, ὁ πατὴρ ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα καὶ ὁ υἱὸς δι' οὗ τὰ πάντα, καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐν ᾧ τὰ πάντα...</note> **One is God: the Father from whom are all things, and the Son through whom are all things, and the Holy Spirit in whom are all things. For these prepositions—"from whom," "through whom," and "in whom"—do not indeed divide the nature, but they characterize the properties of the one and unconfused nature.** 

How these things come to be is shown by <term>John of Damascus</term>, <note>An 8th-century Syrian monk and scholar, famous for his systematic defense of Christian doctrine.</note> who attempted to explain this mystery no less elegantly than subtly in that book which he titled *On the Divine Tradition*. Thus in chapter 49, saying among other things: <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς θεότητος μίαν φύσιν ὁμολογοῦμεν, τρεῖς δὲ ὑποστάσεις κατὰ ἀλήθειαν φαμὲν...</note> **In the divinity we confess one nature, but we say there are three hypostases in truth; and all things that are natural and essential, we say are simple; but the difference of the hypostases is in only three properties: the uncaused and paternal; the caused and filial; and the caused and proceeding. We say they are inseparable and indistinct from one another, united and yet without confusion in each other (for they are three, even where they are united), yet divided without distance. For each one subsists by itself, that is, it is a perfect hypostasis, and possesses its own property, that is, a different mode of existence; yet they are united in essence and in natural properties, and they do not stand apart nor depart from the paternal hypostasis, and they both are and are called one God.** 

That is: In the divinity we confess one nature, but we say there are three hypostases according to the truth. And all things indeed [that are] natural and essential, [we say are] simple...

Indeed, the difference of the <term>Hypostases</term> <note>From the Greek 'hypostasis', referring to the distinct persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) as individual realities within the one divine essence.</note> in only three properties—namely, in the unproduced and paternal, the produced and filial, and the produced and proceeding—we have come to know. ## *On the distinction of the divine persons. And on God sending, and God sent. Chapter III.*

### CAPNIO, <note>The Latinized name for Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist and one of the speakers in this dialogue.</note>

For that this person whom He says is to be sent to prophesy is God, He shows evidently by what He says immediately in His person: *And I will place my divinity in your midst. And you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to prophesy to you.* This same point is also openly manifested by the fact that in the aforementioned prophecy, that "sent God" who must be the Messiah is called by that most holy name of God, the **Tetragrammaton** יהוה <note>The four-letter divine name, Yahweh, which was considered too sacred to pronounce.</note>, which belongs to God alone.

To prove also that the Messiah is the "sent God," we bring forward the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>original Hebrew: מדרש שיר השירים</note>, that is, the exposition of the **Song of Songs** by the ancient masters. There it is read word-for-word: *We will exult and rejoice in you.* <note>Song of Solomon 1:4</note> Rabbi Aben explained what was said in the Psalm, *This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.* <note>Psalm 118:24</note> Rabbi Aben said: They did not know in what they should rejoice—whether in the "day" or in "God"—until Solomon came and explained, saying, *We will exult and rejoice in you.* In *you*, that is, in the holy and blessed God. In *you*, that is, in your salvation. 

Now, this is similar to a certain noblewoman whose husband the King, along with her sons and sons-in-law, had set out for a city across the sea. Messengers came and said to her, "Your sons have come." She said, "What is that to me? Or what use is it to me? Let my daughters-in-law rejoice." Again they said to her, "Your sons-in-law have come." She said, "What is that to me? Let my daughters rejoice." But when they said to her, "Your husband the King has come," she said, "**Behold, surely this is for me sufficient and perfect joy.**" 

So it was to be that the Prophets would come and say to Jerusalem, *Your sons shall come from afar* <note>Isaiah 60:4</note>. And she said to them, "What is that to me? *Let the daughters of Judah exult*" <note>Psalm 97:8</note>. And *your daughters shall be nursed or cherished at your side* <note>Isaiah 60:4</note>. But she said, "What is that to me? *Let Mount Zion rejoice*" <note>Psalm 97:8</note>. But when they said to her: *Behold, your King comes to you, righteous and bringing salvation* <note>Zechariah 9:9</note>; just as it is written in Zechariah 2: *Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord.* And *many nations shall be gathered to the Lord in that day, and they shall be my people, and I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you.* In that hour she said: *I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God* <note>Isaiah 61:10</note>. And this is the meaning of: *We will exult and rejoice in you* from the first chapter of the Song of Songs. 

Thus far the tradition, in which their own faithful antiquity has most elegantly and evidently handed down to the faithless Jews of our time that the Messiah is God. ...are subjected; the ancient Talmudists clearly handed down to the wise and those knowledgeable in Holy Scripture that the Messiah is God. In this, both God sending and God being sent are excellently expressed. These two are not indeed two Gods, but only one God. For even if they are two in <term>middoth</term> <note>Hebrew: מדות, literally "measures," used here to mean "properties" or "persons" of the Trinity.</note>—that is, in properties or persons, namely God sending and God sent—they are nevertheless only one in <term>haiuya</term> <note>Hebrew: הויה, a term for "essence" or "being," derived from the root meaning "to be."</note>, that is, in essence. Therefore, the Father and the Son, or God and His Word, are not two gods, but one God.

That the Father is the "God sending" and His Word (or the Son of God) is the "God sent" is openly gathered from the words of Rabbi Simeon ben Jochai <note>A 2nd-century sage traditionally credited with the authorship of the Zohar.</note>. In the beginning of the book <term>Tahanith</term> <note>Hebrew: תענית, the Talmudic tractate "Ta'anit" concerning fast days.</note>, that is, of the Jerusalemites concerning fasting, he says: "Israel migrated to Babylon, and the <term>Shekhinah</term> <note>Hebrew: שכינה, the "Divine Presence" or indwelling of God on earth.</note>—that is, the presence of God—migrated with them." The proof of this is from what Isaiah says in chapter 43: *For your sake I was sent to Babylon.* <note>Isaiah 43:14. Galatinus interprets the passive "I was sent" as referring to the Divine Presence.</note> So too it is said in Psalm 107: *He will send his word and heal them, and rescue them from their miseries* (or corruptions, or dispersions). And in Hosea 1 it is read: *And I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in God (the Tetragrammaton).* <note>Hosea 1:7. The Tetragrammaton refers to the four-letter holy name of God, YHWH.</note> Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, to whom the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets is attributed.</note> translated this into Aramaic as follows:

> <term>And I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the Word of the Lord their God.</term> <note>original Aramaic: ועל דבית יהודה ארחם ואפרקינון במימרא דיי</note>

That passage from Daniel is also by no means foreign to our purpose, when in chapter 9 he says: <term>And now hear</term>

> <term>our God, the prayer of your servant and his supplications, and cause your face to shine upon your sanctuary which is desolate, for the sake of the Lord.</term> <note>original Hebrew: ועתה שמע אלהינו אל תפלת עבדך ואל תחנוניו והאר פניך על מקדשך השמם למען יהוה</note>

That is: *And now hear, our God, the prayer of your servant, and show your face over your desolate sanctuary, for the sake of the Lord.* Here an argument is held: that the Messiah is <term>Adonai</term> <note>Hebrew: אדני, "Lord."</note>, that is, the Lord. Finally, that which is read in Isaiah chapter 48 is especially to be noted: <term>Come near to me, hear this: I have not spoken in secret from the beginning;</term>

This means: *Draw near to me, hear this. I have not spoken in secret from the head—that is, from the beginning. From the time, or from the hour of its being, there I was. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit.*

In these words, not only are the "God sending" and "God sent" shown, but the entire Trinity is also openly and distinctly hinted at.

Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, or Rashi (1040–1105), whose commentary is a cornerstone of Jewish study.</note> also affirms this, regarding that passage in Malachi chapter 1: *The burden of the word of the Lord by the hand of Malachi:* saying thus, that this had already been delivered into his hands many days before. From this, our masters declared in the <term>Mechilta</term> <note>Hebrew: מכילתא, an ancient rabbinic commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Exodus.</note>—a collection of additional traditions—that all the prophets stood on Mount Sinai when the law of Moses was given, and there their prophecies were delivered to them. The author is arguing against the idea that the prophet Isaiah is speaking about his own presence at Sinai.</note> Therefore, so that the wickedness of this Rabbi and the other later teachers following him may be confounded, it is necessary that you refute this childish fiction using the sayings of the ancient Talmudists themselves.

**GALATINUS:** Let Rabbi Solomon and his followers hear, among other things, what is written in the book <term>Mechilta</term>, which they consider a sin to contradict.

<margin>Refutation of the aforementioned heretical exposition.</margin>

When concerning that passage in Exodus chapter 19: *And they came into the desert of Sinai, and they rested, and they encamped in the desert,* it is said in this manner: The law was given publicly, in an open place. For if the law had been given in the land of Israel, the Jews would have said to the nations of the world, "You have no part in it." But it was given in a traversable desert, publicly, and in an open place, so that whoever wished to receive it might come and receive it. Can it be said that it was given at night? The text teaches it was not, in that which is said in Exodus 19: *And it happened on the third day, when morning came.* Can it also be said that it was given in silence? It teaches not, because it is said in the same place: *And there were voices and lightnings,* and so forth. Can it still be said that they did not hear the voice? What should be said to this is suggested by that Psalm: *The voice of the Lord in strength, the voice of the Lord in magnificence, the voice of the Lord breaking the cedars of Lebanon,* and the rest. <note>Psalm 29:4–5.</note> Rabbi Jose said: "And behold, the holy and blessed God himself says to Isaiah in chapter 48: *Not from the beginning have I spoken in secret; from the time it came to be, there I was.*" Likewise, in the same book regarding that passage in Exodus 20: *I am the Lord your God,* Rabbi Nathan said: "If you say the word of God was in secret, does He not Himself say in Isaiah: *Not from the beginning have I spoken in hiding. From the time it came to be, there I was*?"

Behold how clearly these two of the ancient Jewish Doctors assert that those aforementioned words—*From the time it came to be, there I was*—were spoken by God. Therefore, Isaiah did not utter them about himself, as Rabbi Solomon falsely asserted. From these traditions it is also openly clear that it is an absurd and entirely false fiction that all the Prophets were present on Mount Sinai when the law of Moses was given. The absurdity and falsehood of this fiction is especially clear from the fact that neither Moses nor any of the prophets can be found to have ever openly mentioned this. Nor can they cloak their madness even if they say the souls of the prophets were present at the giving of the law without their bodies (a view which seems to smack of the error of those who say all souls were created at the same time); for this openly conflicts with both Holy Scripture and the judgment of their own ancient Doctors. Indeed, in the <term>Bereshith Rabbah</term> <note>Hebrew: בראשית רבה, the "Great Genesis," a major midrashic commentary on the first book of the Bible.</note> in that place where Genesis 5 says, *This is the book of the generations of Adam,* it is read thus: "It is written in Isaiah 57: *Because I will not contend forever with Adam...*"

<margin>The Catholic exposition of the same words of Isaiah.</margin>
Draw near, or approach me, and hear this. *I have not spoken in secret from the beginning. From the time it came to be, I was there.* The meaning is: Draw near to me through faith, and hear what I say. For when I first spoke to Adam, and said to him, <note>Genesis 2:17</note> *But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat,* I did not speak in secret, nor obscurely. However, some—not only from among the Hebrews, but even from our own people—interpret this phrase *from the beginning* as the time when God gave the Law to Moses. That this is false is clear not only from what has already been said, but especially from the fact that God did not then first speak to the human race, but rather when he commanded Adam not to sin. It follows: *From the time it came to be, I was there:* that is, when Adam was made in time, I was there. *There,* meaning in Adam himself, according to the substance of human flesh. <term>HOG.</term> <note>Likely referring to the *Glossa Ordinaria* or Hugh of Saint Cher, a 13th-century biblical commentator.</note> Our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> in this place has it thus: *From the time before they were made, I was there.* <term>GAL.</term> <note>Galatinus, the author, speaking in his own voice.</note> The author of our edition understood this entire speech as referring to the divinity of Christ. For that reason, he directed the whole passage to his divinity. We, however, following the <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>original Latin: "Hebraicā ueritatem" — a common term for the original Hebrew text of the Bible as opposed to translations.</note>, understand it partly as referring to his divinity and partly to his humanity, of which Christ consists. This is more consistent with the truth, both because the Hebrew text does not say *before*, but *from the time of its being* <note>original Hebrew: מאותה היותה (*me-otah heyotah*)</note>, using a feminine demonstration, as is clear to those who know the Hebrew letters. Therefore, the text should be explained thus: *From the hour of its being*, that is, from the hour of the creation of my mother’s flesh within the formation of Adam’s body. Therefore, "there" refers not to the divinity, but to the humanity of the Messiah. For if it spoke of the divinity, it would have said *before it was made.*

<margin>The Kabbalists on the name of God, the Tetragrammaton and Elohim.</margin>
Furthermore, according to the <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>Jewish mystics who sought hidden meanings in the Torah.</note>, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God (YHWH), often translated as "LORD."</note> name of God—<note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note>—in place of which they pronounce *Adonai* <note>original Hebrew: אדני — meaning "My Lord."</note> (which we translate as Lord), properly signifies the Father. This is because that name properly implies the divine essence, and the Father is the principle and origin of the entire divinity. Meanwhile, *Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים</note>, which is translated as God, properly designates the Son. Now, the text says: *And now the Lord God* <note>original Hebrew: יהוה אלהים (YHWH Elohim)</note> *has sent me, and his Spirit*—which is the Holy Spirit.

<margin>What it means to be "sent" in divine matters.</margin>
It is shown most evidently that the discourse here is not about the divinity of the Messiah, but about his humanity. For according to the doctrine of the theologians, and especially what the <term>Subtle Doctor</term> <note>Johannes Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Franciscan theologian.</note> says in the 15th distinction of the first book, and <term>Bonaventure</term> <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), a key scholastic theologian and Doctor of the Church.</note> in the same distinction, question 2: to be "sent" in divine matters is nothing other than to be manifested as proceeding, and to be known as being from another, and it implies a certain "sub-authority." Consequently, the Son, according to his divinity, can be sent neither by himself nor by the Holy Spirit, but only by the Father—since he has his being neither from himself nor from the Holy Spirit, but only from the Father. Therefore, it is necessary to say—according to both the Hebrew Kabbalists and our own theologians—that the saying *From the time of its being* (that is, when it was made in time) is to be understood not regarding the Messiah's divinity, but his humanity.

Therefore, when it says, *And now the Lord God,* or *God God has sent me, and his Spirit,* the words are to be explained according to the Kabbalists as Lord or God

# BOOK TWO.
<page-num>45</page-num>
<sig>c 2</sig>

<note>original: "יהוה"</note> the Tetragrammaton, that is the Father; God, that is the Son; and his Spirit, that is the Holy Spirit, sent me, so that I might be the Redeemer of Israel. In this, three things must be noted. First, indeed, that which the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of Cabala, a traditional system of Jewish mysticism and spiritual interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> maintain: that the name of God, the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, יהוה, often rendered as Yahweh or Jehovah.</note>, represents God’s mercy, while <note>original: "אלהים"</note> *Elohim*, which is also God, represents God’s justice. Therefore, when it says here, "the Lord God" or "the Tetragrammaton God," no conjunction is used, in order to show that in the mission of the Messiah’s humanity, God’s mercy and justice were to be united for the redemption of the human race. This is according to that verse in **Psalm 85: Mercy and truth have met each other; justice and peace have kissed.** The second point is that he does not say "their spirit," meaning the spirit of the Father and the Son, but rather "his spirit." This is to denote that the Father and the Son, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, are not two breathers, but that both are only one single breather of the Holy Spirit itself, a single principle for it. The third and final point is that he does not say "They sent me," but "He sent me." This was to suggest the unity of the divine essence, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are **one God.**

### *Concerning the distinction and number of the divine persons through their properties. Chapter IV.*

-> CAPNIO, <-

**I** think it will be no small benefit, both for a clearer manifestation of the truth and for the greater confusion of the more recent Jews, if you would show that the distinction and number of the divine persons, through their specific properties, is also held among them. To teach that by these three names the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, corresponding to the three attributes by which the world was created, and these are Wisdom, Knowledge, and Understanding. Whence is "Wisdom"? As it is said: "The Lord by wisdom founded the earth." And "Knowledge"? As it is said: "By His knowledge the depths were broken up." And "Understanding"? As it is said: "Establishing the heavens by understanding." And so He says: "For I am the LORD your God, a jealous God." Here are the three attributes by which the world was created. And so the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben say: "The God of gods, the LORD; the God of gods, the LORD, He knows." And what did they see to say it twice: "The God of gods, the LORD"? One for the world being created; "The God of gods, the LORD" for the giving of the Law. One might think they are separate; no, but both were created together. And so He says: "My hand founded the earth, and my right hand spanned the heavens."* This means: **Why does it mention the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, three times? So that you might be taught that by these three names the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world...**

...instructions, warnings, and corrections by which among men a father strives to make his son wise and prudent, he compares the Son of God himself to a father, adapting such instructions, warnings, and corrections to His wisdom as far as possible. Therefore, in the words spoken a little earlier, some refer to the divine nature of the Son of God, and some to the human nature He was to assume. The words themselves clearly indicate both of these. For when he says, *Hear, children, the discipline of a father, and attend to know prudence. Because I have given you a good doctrine or document, that is, a good law,* <note>Proverbs 4:1-2</note> it cannot be understood to refer to Solomon at all. For if Solomon had spoken here of his own wisdom, he would have said "I will give" <note>original: tribuam</note>, not "I have given" <note>original: tribui</note>, especially since he said, *Hear, children, the discipline of a father.* It is necessary, therefore, that this speech was made in the name of Him who previously gave the law to the Hebrews. This, however, is God alone. Therefore, that speech is not to be referred to Solomon, but to God.

And also that which immediately follows, namely, *Do not forsake my law, because I was a son to my father, tender, alone, or the unique one among the sons of my mother.* <note>Proverbs 4:2-3</note> For since this word "because" <note>original: quia</note> is causal, it must provide the reason for the preceding clause. It is as if he were saying openly: This is the reason why you ought not to forsake my law—because I was a son to my father. But if the speech were about Solomon, no reason would be given for not forsaking his law. For people would not have been obliged to follow his law simply because he was the son of David. Indeed, if he had said, "do not forsake my law because I received it from my father David," then he would certainly have given a reason for not forsaking his law; but it would have had to be self-evident that everything handed down by David himself was right and to be observed. However, this was not manifest. It is clear, therefore, that Solomon here was not speaking of himself, but in the person of the Son of God, whose law was to be kept for the reason that he was the Son of God. 

<margin>Why the Son of God is called tender.</margin>

He also calls himself "tender" <note>original: tener</note> for this reason: not only to suggest the tenderness of his immense piety, but also to hint at the capacity of his infinite wisdom. For according to the *saying of Aristotle in the second book on the Soul, text commentary 49* <note>Aristotle’s *De Anima* (421a). In medieval science, it was believed that people with "soft" or "tender" flesh possessed more refined senses and a superior intellect.</note>, *those with hard flesh are inept in respect to the intellect, while the soft, that is, the tender, are well-suited.* Therefore, to show this excellent disposition of his for receiving the documents of the father, he said that he was tender—that is, easily teachable, and rightly and most capable of infinite wisdom. But "tender" to whom? *To my father,* he says. It is necessary, therefore, that he speaks of such a father who can teach nothing but what is right. This, however, is God alone. Thus, the words are to be explained: *Do not forsake my law, because I was a son to my father, tender.* This means: because I received those things from my father, who cannot err in teaching, nor could I err in learning, because I was tender—that is, of the best and infinite capacity for receiving it. *And the alone or unique one among the sons of my mother,* that is, of the Synagogue, as we explained above.
