of my mother, you interpreted as *In the presence of my mother*, as our text has it:
Which certain others have translated as *before my mother*. GALATINUS. The word **לבני** <note>original: *libne*</note>, which is placed here and is written with the letter **ב** <note>the Hebrew letter Beth</note>, signifies neither "in the presence of" nor "before," but properly means the same as "to the sons" or "of the sons." For "before" and "in the presence of" are signified by the word **לפני** <note>original: *liphne*</note>, written with the letter **פ** <note>the Hebrew letter Pe</note>. From this it clearly appears that those who in this place translated it as *in the presence of my mother* or *before my mother* were deceived by the similarity of the words and read *liphne* instead of *libne*. As for what follows, *And he himself taught me, along with the others: Christ made mention of himself*, when in the 8th chapter of John he says, *As the father taught me, I speak these things* <note>John 8:28</note>. And again, He says, *I always do the things that are pleasing to him* <note>John 8:29</note>. And he says certain other things in the same place which agree with almost the same sentiment. In these passages, he clearly shows both that he was taught by the father and that he received from him the mandates of those things which he was to do in the world. What is also said here, *Keep my commandments*, he reported that he himself had fulfilled, saying in John 15, *I have kept my father’s commandments and I remain in his love* <note>John 15:10</note>. That which is finally added, *And live*, he himself explained concerning himself when he says, *As the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself* <note>John 5:26</note>. "Live," therefore, he says, that is: have life in your power. Hence he himself says, *I have the power to lay down my soul, and I have the power to take it up again* <note>John 10:18</note>.

->CAPNIO,<-

<margin>*How the Holy Spirit is named by the Hebrews.*</margin>
**S**ince you have said enough in the preceding sections about the Father and the Son, evidently proving that God is called Father in the Holy Scripture and His begotten Wisdom is called the Son, it now remains for you to discuss something regarding the Holy Spirit in detail. And I find that He proceeds from the Father and the Son as from a single principle, and that He produced the world together with the Father and the Son, and spoke through the Prophets, and was to come upon the Messiah and remain there perfectly. For concerning the goodness of God or His good will, it is held in Psalm 143, where David, pouring out prayers to the Lord, says: **למדני לעשות רצונך כי אתה אלהי רוחך טובה תנחני בארץ מישור** <note>original Hebrew: *Lamedni la’asot retzonecha ki atah Elohai, ruchacha tovah tanchani b’eretz mishor*</note>. That is: *Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and with a noble spirit, or a spirit of nobility, support, or sustain, or confirm me.* This Holy Spirit also, equally with the Father and

# BOOK TWO

We are taught that the Spirit was the author of the world and the maker of men from the Book of Job, chapter 33, where it was said by Elihu: *The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life* <note>original Hebrew: *ruach el asatani venishmat shaddai techayyeni*</note>. And in the words of the Psalmist in Psalm 103: *You will send forth your spirit, and they shall be created, and you will renew the face of the earth* <note>Psalm 104:30 in modern numbering</note>. And again in Psalm 33: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the spirit of his mouth, all their host.* Among the Hebrews, the "host of heaven" refers to the Sun, Moon, Stars, and all the powers and angels that dwell there. Therefore, it was not without reason that Saint Job said in chapter 26: *By his spirit he adorned the heavens.*

<margin>The Holy Spirit to come upon the Messiah</margin>

Furthermore, Isaiah shows most clearly that this Holy Spirit was to come upon the Messiah and find perfect rest there, when he says in chapter 11: *A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots, and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, or the spirit who is God* <note>original Hebrew: *ve-nachah alav ruach adonai*</note>, that is, the spirit who is God Himself. These words are interpreted by the Hebrews literally as referring only to the Messiah, as is clearly evident in countless places in the <term>Talmud|The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara</term> itself, and especially in the *Bereishit Rabbah* and *Zuta* <note>The "Greater" and "Lesser" Great Genesis; classic collections of midrashic or interpretive commentaries on the first book of the Bible</note>, that is, in the greater and lesser exposition of Genesis. There, regarding that passage in Genesis chapter 1, *The earth was formless and empty*, the following is read literally:

<margin>Hebrew exposition of the 4 kingdoms</margin>

Rabbi Simeon explained this scripture as referring to the four kingdoms, saying: *The earth was formless.* This is the Kingdom of Babylon, of which it is said in Jeremiah chapter 4, *I looked at the earth, and behold, it was formless and empty.* *And void:* this is the Kingdom of the Medes, as it is said in Esther chapter 6, *They hurried to bring Haman, and there was darkness.* This refers to the Kingdom of the Greeks, which darkened the eyes of the Jews with its decrees. *Upon the face of the abyss:* This is the wicked kingdom, namely the Roman Empire. For just as the abyss is inscrutable and lacks a bottom, so that wicked kingdom is unsearchable and has no base. *And the spirit of Elohim* <note>original: *Elohim*, the Hebrew name for God, here used in a plural form that the author interprets as indicating the Trinity</note>, that is, of the Gods, *was hovering over the waters.* This is the spirit of the Messiah, of whom it was said in Isaiah chapter 11, *And the spirit of God shall rest upon him.* And because of his merit, the spirit shall serve, and shall come hovering over the face of the waters. This is on account of the merit of repentance, which is compared to water. As it is said in Lamentations chapter 2: *Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord.* All of this is tradition.

To these things it seems necessary to add what Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> said when explaining that passage in Exodus chapter 15: *And by the spirit of your nostrils the waters were gathered.* Here, he says, "by the spirit of your nostrils" means the spirit proceeding from the nostrils of your nose. And the scripture spoke of the *Shekhinah* <note>original: *Sechina*, the divine presence or indwelling of God</note>, that is, of the divinity. So also Job says in chapter 4: *And by the spirit of his nostrils they are consumed.* Thus says Rabbi Solomon. It also seems fitting to connect what was previously mentioned with what is said in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient homiletic commentary on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the gloss of the Psalms, regarding that passage in Psalm 18: *Then the channels of waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were uncovered at your rebuke, O Lord, at the blast of the breath of your nostrils.* That is, *And the rushes appeared...*

The golden support was his precious soul. The purple or scarlet seat or chair was his flesh, all reddened by that precious blood. But its center—namely his heart—was <term>raczuph|Hebrew for 'paved,' 'inlaid,' or 'fitted together'</term>, that is, "laid out"—or according to another meaning, "ignited," as if with coals of affection or love. It is just as if the Messiah had said: "Because God anointed me, he sent me to announce [the gospel] to the poor or the humble." 

From this, it is clear that the Holy Spirit is called "love" or "charity," not only because he proceeds from the Father and the Son by way of the will, but also because he is the love with which the Father and the Son love one another. Wherefore, as gathered from what has been said, those ancient and old fathers of the Jews understood nothing else by the <margin>What the Holy Spirit is according to the ancient Hebrews</margin> Holy Spirit than the third person in the Divine, produced from eternity by the Father and the Son in a single breathing by way of the will—really distinct from them, but essentially the same as them. ### Chapter VII. That the three divine persons are one essence, and that each of them is in the other through mutual indwelling <term>circumincessio|The theological concept (also known as perichoresis) describing how the three persons of the Trinity exist within one another without blurring their distinctions</term>.

->CAPNIO<-

**I** would wish, for a clearer expression of this Catholic truth and for the greater confusion of the younger Jews, that you would prove through one of their own teachers that the three divine persons are one essence, one nature, and that one is in the other through mutual indwelling.

**GAL.** Although I could produce many witnesses from among them to prove this, lest I become tedious, let it suffice to bring forward one out of them all whom the more recent Jews can by no means contradict: namely, Rabbi Isaac ben Schola <note>Isaac ben Solomon ibn Sahula, a 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist and author</note>, a man of great authority among them. In his commentaries on the Psalms <note>original: "Psalterium"</note>, he frequently asserts this very thing, especially regarding that verse of Psalm 111:
*This is it:* "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; a good understanding have all they that do them: his praise endureth for ever." <note>original Hebrew: ראשית חכמה יראת יהוה שכל טוב לכל עושיהם תהלתו עומדת לעד</note>
When he speaks thus: The Wisdom <term>Chokhmah|The second of the ten Sephirot or divine emanations, representing the primordial point of creation or "Wisdom"</term> hinted at by God in this verse is that Wisdom which is found out of nothingness. It is sealed within the word "In the beginning" <note>original Hebrew: בראשית (Bereshit)</note>, meaning in the letter *Bet* <note>The first letter of the Bible. Its shape is closed on three sides and open on one, often interpreted mystically</note>. And they said, "Do not read it as *Beit* <gloss>the letter B</gloss> but as *Bayit* <gloss>a house</gloss>," for it is said: "With wisdom a house is built." This measure is hidden and concealed under the seal of transcendence and is hidden in the matter of which it is said: "It is hid from the eyes of all living, and kept close from the fowls of the air." And it says: "God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof," meaning that no one else besides Him knows the paths engraved within it. In every place where the Sages numbered the "desirable things," they numbered Wisdom among them; it is the first, for it is drawn from the Source of Life, and it is the start of the numbering. 

They also numbered the "Inner Measure," which is the source and the spring hinted at in the phrase "Surely there is a vein for the silver." And he said: "For wisdom is a defense, and money is a defense." The masters of Wisdom understand this "Inner Measure" by many names. Among them are those who call it "The Chosen," because all the divine attributes <term>Middot|The divine qualities or emanations through which God interacts with the world</term> are chosen in it, and it is in them. Others call it by the term "Nothingness" <term>Ayin|The Kabbalistic concept of the 'Nothingness' from which all being emerges, representing the infinite nature of God</term>, for no thought can grasp it. They rely on this language from the scripture which says, "From whence <note>original Hebrew: מאין (m'ayin), which can be read as 'from Nothingness'</note> shall wisdom come?" If you are worthy of this saying, you will further know the secret of life; you will be made like it, you will be preserved, and you will be made perfect. 

Truly, all the other names directed toward this "Measure" are directed in this way. There is an explanation that in this verse there is a hint to this measure in the word "Beginning" <note>original Hebrew: ראשית (Reshit)</note>, which includes Wisdom. Our Rabbis of blessed memory said: "All the prophets prophesied through a glass that is not clear, but our teacher Moses (peace be upon him) looked through a single clear glass <term>Aspaklaria|From the Latin 'specularia,' referring to a lens or mirror through which the divine light is filtered</term>," as it is said, "and they saw the beginning for him." He further added to this verse, "The fear of the Lord," which is the light directed toward the "Beginning," just as "God has made it so that men should fear before Him." 

Since the three measures we have mentioned are called "Faces," they are included one within the other. Thus it says: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." And the wise man said: "The grace of the fear of the Lord is wisdom." And he said: "Get wisdom, get understanding." Thus you have learned that these three crowns are chosen in the crown of perfect unity <term>Keter|The 'Crown,' the highest of the Sephirot, representing the Divine Will or the Absolute Unity of God</term>. They are three "Mothers" matching the world, and the branches that rise after them see by their hands. They are the seven pure sayings, the important seven paths in one branch, full and good. Because they are a knot, firm and strong, they are all together in the faith of "a good understanding for all who do them," meaning those who direct their hearts toward them. It is he who said, "For God made them living," and he said "His praise endures forever" regarding the Inner Measure we mentioned. So also he says, "The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring forever." And he said, "He walked...

[The text continues from the previous page:] ...wisdom which comes forth from *me-ayin* <note>original Hebrew: מאין; literally "from nothing"</note> (that is, from the supreme and most abstract intellect of God) and is found in the word *Bereshit* <note>original Hebrew: בראשית; "In the beginning"</note> (that is, in the letter *beth*). And for this reason they said: Do not call it *beth* <note>The name of the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note>, but *bayit* <note>original Hebrew: בית; meaning "house"</note>. As it is said: "By wisdom a house shall be built." And this property is covered and hidden, and sealed with the seal of secrets. As it is said: "It is covered and hidden from the eyes of all living things, and concealed from the birds of the heavens." <note>Job 28:21</note> And it says: "God understands its ways, and He Himself knows its place." <note>Job 28:23</note> It is as if he were to say that no one besides Him knows the paths which are carved into it. 

And wherever the wise men enumerated the properties <term>Sefirot|The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself and interacts with the universe</term> of God, they placed Wisdom as the prince, since it is drawn from the fountain of life and is the beginning of every number. And they called that intrinsic property the most exuberant vein of brass (which the common folk call a mine), and a fountain or emanation is discovered in it, since there are also flowing veins of silver. And it is said that just as the shadow of wisdom is, such is the shadow of silver. 

Moreover, the authors of wisdom have named this intrinsic property with many names. For some have called it the Crown <term>Keter|The highest of the Sefirot, representing the Divine Will or the "Nothingness" from which all existence emerges</term>, because the individual properties are crowned by it, and it is crowned by the individual ones. But others have named it *Ayin* <note>original Hebrew: אין; "Nothing"</note>, because there is no one who can grasp it with the imagination. (For it is attainable only by the intellect.) And to this alludes what was said: *Me-ayin* <note>original Hebrew: מאין</note>, that is, "from whence shall my help come?" <note>Psalm 121:1. The author is playing on the word "Ayin" to suggest help comes from the Divine "Nothingness."</note> (For *Me-ayin* indeed seems to signify something incorporeal, abstract, secret, and intellectual.) 

And if you are fortunate in my words, you will know the secrets of the highest mountains, since this property is like the light by which all other properties are crowned in the way of light. Therefore, in this text, observe this property in the word "Beginning," in which Wisdom is contained. Thus the doctors said: "All the prophets prophesied in a vision that was not bright; but Moses prophesied in a vision that was bright and clear." <note>A traditional Jewish distinction between the "opaque mirror" of other prophets and the "clear mirror" of Moses's direct revelation.</note> As it is said: "And the beginning appeared to him." <note>Deuteronomy 33:21</note> 

Furthermore, "Fear of God" follows. And this, moreover, is explanatory of the Beginning. As it is said: "God has acted so that I should fear before his face." <note>Ecclesiastes 3:14</note> And these three properties are called "faces" <term>Partzufim|Divine configurations or "visages" in Kabbalistic thought that represent the harmonious interaction of various Sefirot</term>, and they are contained within one another. And for this reason it is said: "Beginning, Wisdom, Fear of God." And the wise man says: "Truly the fear of God is wisdom." <note>Job 28:28</note> It is also said: "Acquire wisdom, acquire understanding." <note>Proverbs 4:5</note> 

Behold, you have learned that these three crowns are one crown, united by a most perfect unity. And they are something most choice, and the three equal foundations of the world (that is, those things by which the world is established). And they are the ascending lights, surpassing all that remains, so much so that by their light all things are illuminated. And they are the words of God, pure and precious words, the meaning of the seven ears of grain on one stalk <note>An allusion to Pharaoh’s dream in Genesis 41, interpreted here as a symbol of unity in diversity</note>, which are full and excellent. And because they are one strong and inseparable bond, they are all gathered into one. As it is said: "A good understanding have all they that do them" <gloss>that is, those who direct their minds to them</gloss>. As is also said elsewhere: "Certainly God has made it today." intrinsic property, which we have mentioned. And he also says: *The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever.* <note>Psalm 19:9; original Latin: "Timor dei mundus permanet iugiter"</note> And he said: *He is your praise, and He is your God.* <note>Deuteronomy 10:21; original Latin: "Ipse laus tua, & ipse Deus tuus"</note> And understand this. From these words, they hold many excellent things which are very much in agreement with our faith against the Jews of our time, and specifically seven points.

**And the first** is that the three properties by which the three divine persons are distinguished, he says (using the words of the Psalmist) are the *beginning*, *wisdom*, and the *fear of God*. And rightly so. For by the **beginning** he understands the Father, both because the Father is the first person in the Trinity, and also because he is the beginning and origin of the entire divinity. Through **wisdom** he suggests the Son, who is the wisdom of the Father. Through the **fear of God**, however, he implies the Holy Spirit, who is not incongruously called the "fear of God" by his effect. For when he glides into the hearts of the faithful, he instills the fear of God, so that they might not be separated by sin from Him to whom they are joined by grace, and so they might not lose God Himself through sin, whom they possess dwelling within them through grace. This he also proves through that saying: *God has made it so that they should fear before him.* <note>Ecclesiastes 3:14; original Latin: "Deus fecit ut timerēt à facie eius"</note>

**The second** is that he says this wisdom proceeds *from nothing* <note>original Hebrew: מאין (me-ayin); in Kabbalistic thought, this refers to the *Ayin* or the primordial Nothingness/Infinite from which Wisdom emanates</note>, that is, from the supreme and most abstract intellect, which is God. For this Hebrew word *me-ayin* carries all these meanings. By this, he wishes to show that the Son in divine matters is produced from the divine intellect. For the "second memory" (which is nothing other than the intellect having a present object—namely, the divine essence) produces the Word, that is, the Son, who is the begotten knowledge and wisdom of the Father.

**The third** is that he says this wisdom is a most abundant vein of brass <note>or "ore"</note>, in which a fountain or emanation is discovered. By this, he wishes to openly imply that the Son of God is the "Art" <note>the blueprint or creative power</note> of the Father, and the Word through which all things were made.

**The fourth** is that he says this wisdom is like a light by which all other properties are crowned in the way of light. By this, he plainly suggests that the Son is *Light from Light*, or the *Light of the World*, as the Son himself says in John 8. *Which enlightens every man coming into this world*, John 1.

**The fifth** is that he says these three properties are called **faces** <note>original Latin: "facies"</note>, that is, **persons**, certainly after the manner of the Greeks, who call persons *prosopa* <note>original Greek: πρόσωπα; literally "faces" or "masks"</note>, that is, faces.

**The sixth** is that he says these three persons are contained within one another in turn. Demonstrating that the Father is in the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the Son is in the Father and the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son through **mutual indwelling** <term>Circumincession|The theological concept of the reciprocal existence of each person of the Trinity in the others</term>, which the Greeks call *perichoresis* <note>original Greek: περιχώρησις</note>.

**The seventh** is that he says these three crowns are one crown, a unity perfected by unity. By this, he clearly shows that the three divine persons are altogether one essence and one nature. He also expressly affirms this in the exposition of the following Psalm, while commenting on that passage of Psalm 112: *The wicked shall see, and shall be angry; he shall gnash with his teeth, and pine away; the desire of the wicked shall perish.* Among other things, he says: *This verse is like the attribute of divine wrath on high, for the wicked person kicks against sufferings and gnashes his teeth without understanding. The proof of this is: "the desire of the wicked shall perish." And concerning such as this it is said: "For the Lord your God is a consuming fire" [Deuteronomy 4:24], and it says: "A fire shall devour before Him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about Him" [Psalm 50:3]. Behold, there in a hint is what he began in the first Psalm, to make known that everything is one, despite these severities.* <note>Galatinus is quoting the Hebrew commentary to show that even "wrath" or "severity" (the attribute of Gevurah) is part of the divine unity.</note>

**GALATINUS:** They certainly cannot deny that the Holy Trinity of God, and His indivisible unity, made man in His image and likeness. For the text itself is clear, which says in the first part of Genesis: *And God said, Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness* <note>Genesis 1:26</note>. **CAPITO:** Why did he first use the word that signifies "to make," saying "let us make man," and then use the word signifying "creation," saying "And *Elohim*—that is, the Gods—created man," along with the other things that follow? 

**GALATINUS:** Because the bodies of Adam and Eve were composed from matter, but their souls were created from nothing. Therefore, he first used the word for "making" [forming from existing material], and then used the word for "creation" [bringing into being from nothing]. Thus, the faithlessness of the Jews of our age can by no means deny that man was made in the image of God, since their ancient teachers everywhere confess it. For to bring forward the first testimony of Abraham himself, it is read in the *Midrash Tehillim* <term>Midrash Tehillim|An ancient Jewish homiletic commentary on the Book of Psalms.</term> upon that verse of Psalm 37: *Do not fret because of evildoers, nor be envious of the workers of iniquity*. This is: "Do not associate with the malignant, or do not be angry, or do not be indignant on account of the malignant. Neither be envious of or imitate those who work iniquity." 

Our father Abraham said to Melchizedek—who was Shem, the son of Noah, who was called the priest of the most high God because he offered sacrifice—"By what method, or for what reason, did you depart from the ark?" He replied: "On account of *Tzedakah* <term>Tzedakah|Hebrew for righteousness or charity.</term>, that is, the alms-giving which we did there." Abraham said to him, "And what kind of alms-giving could you do there, since there was no one there except Noah and his sons? To whom then did you give alms?" He replied to him, "To the wild beasts, the cattle, and the birds. For we did not sleep the whole night, but gave food now to this one, now to that one." 

Therefore Abraham said, "If these men who gave alms to wild beasts, cattle, and birds received a reward, how much more shall I receive a reward, and be delivered from those who oppose me, if I give alms to the sons of Adam who are in the image of the holy and blessed God?" ## *On the Name of God* אלהים *Elohim, and how the Divine Trinity is hinted at through it. Chapter IX.*

<margin>CAPNIO</margin>
**S**ince nothing is more suitable or powerful for proving the mystery of the divine Trinity against the more recent Jews than an explanation of the divine names, it is now necessary for you to prove this same mystery by explaining the names of God themselves. And first, you ought to do this through אלהים *Elohim* <note>The Hebrew name for God used in the creation account of Genesis 1</note>, which is more common than the others.

GALATINUS: אלהים *Elohim* (as you yourself know) is a plural noun, and it signifies what "Gods" means to us. Its singular form is אל *El*, that is, "God," or rather אלוה *Eloha*, which is also the same as "God." Therefore, even if this name אלהים *Elohim* designates plurality, it is nevertheless usually joined with a verb in the singular number whenever it is used in Holy Scripture for the true God. As in that passage at the beginning of the book of Genesis: בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ <note>original Hebrew: *Bereshit bara Elohim et ha-shamayim ve-et ha-aretz*</note>. This is: "In the beginning, Gods created the heaven and the earth." <note>Note that the Hebrew verb *bara* (created) is singular, while the subject *Elohim* is grammatically plural.</note> Where our Greek and Latin editions have "God" [singular], the "Hebrew Truth" <note>A common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text of the Bible</note> says "Gods" [plural]. This was certainly not done without a great mystery. For because—according to the opinion of St. Augustine—the works of the Trinity are undivided in their outward actions, the great Moses, in order to hint that all three divine persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) concurred together in the creation of the world, used אלהים *Elohim* (that is, "Gods" in the plural) and not אלוה *Eloha* or אל *El* (that is, "God" in the singular). However, to show that those three persons are not essentially distinct but are entirely the same—meaning one God and not three Gods—he used ברא *bara* (that is, "created" in the singular) and not בראו *bareu* (that is, "they created" in the plural). It is established, therefore, that through the name אלהים *Elohim* joined with a singular verb, both the Trinity of persons and the unity of the divine essence are perfectly designated.

<margin>The false explanation of the more recent Jews.</margin>
The more recent Jews, however, since they can by no means deny this text, attempt to pervert it with a certain false explanation. For they say that even if this name אלהים *Elohim* is plural, it is nevertheless used indifferently as both singular and plural, and when it refers to the true God, it is always held to be singular and not plural. And so they say it is used here when it is said: "In the beginning *Elohim* created." From this they conclude that since אלהים *Elohim* in this place is held as a singular and not a plural, we can by no means infer from it that the Trinity of persons is being suggested.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
But perhaps they could say these things to those ignorant of Hebrew letters, but not to those who are not entirely lacking in knowledge of them. We, therefore, who are not entirely inexperienced in such matters, will prove through the Hebrew texts of Holy Scripture and through their own Teachers that they explain this text falsely. For in the *Bereshit Rabbah Ketanna* <note>original: רבא ketāna; the "Lesser Midrash on Genesis," a collection of Jewish homiletic teachings</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of Genesis regarding this text, it is read that Rabbi חנא *Huna* said this: "Unless this word had been written, it would not have been permitted to say: And *Elohim* (Gods) created heaven and earth." Also regarding that passage in Genesis 1: ויברא אלהים את האדם בצלמו בצלם אלהים ברא אתו <note>original Hebrew: *Va-yivra Elohim et ha-adam be-tzalmo, be-tzelem Elohim bara oto*</note>, that is, "And Gods created Adam in his image, in the image of Gods he created him." It is read thus written: The heretics questioned Rabbi Semlai,

For it is not written "In the beginning Gods created [plural]" but "In the beginning Gods created [singular]." **Rabbi Simlai** said: "In every place where you find an objection used by the heretics, you also find its remedy right beside it." Similar to this is what is found in the book <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with legal procedures and the high court</note>, in the chapter beginning with *Ehad dine mamonoth* <note>original Hebrew: אחד דיני ממונות; "One procedure for monetary cases"</note>, that is, "one of the judgments of wealth," near the end, where it is said that **Rabbi Johanan** spoke thus: "Every place from which the <term>Epicureans</term> <note>A term used in rabbinic literature to refer to heretics or those who deny divine providence</note> became heretics has its response right beside it." For where it is said, "Let us make man in our image" <note>Genesis 1:26</note>, there is also added, "And <term>Elohim</term> <note>original Hebrew: אלהים; literally 'Gods'</note>—that is, Gods—created man in his [singular] image." Likewise in the same place: "And let us arise and go up to the house of God, and I will make there an altar to God who heard [singular] me in the day of my tribulation." Thus far the tradition.

Many other places besides these are found in the sacred writings in which both the name אלהים **Elohim** and certain other names spoken of God are placed in the plural. Indeed, no interpreter has translated this way of speaking about God, since it seemed greatly incongruous. However, in my opinion, the ancient Scripture allowed that phrasing so that the impiety of the more recent Jews, who deny the plurality of divine persons, might be more strongly refuted. They insert some of these points in the exposition of **Genesis** which is ascribed to **Rabbi Moses Hadarshan**. Where, upon that passage, "In the beginning <term>Elohim</term> [Gods] created the heaven and the earth," it is said word-for-word: The heretics asked **Rabbi Simlai**, saying: "How many Gods created the world?" Furthermore, they also said to him: "Behold, it is written in Jeremiah chapter 23: <note>Jeremiah 23:36</note> 'And you have perverted the words of the living Gods' <note>original Hebrew: *Elohim hayyim*. In Hebrew, both the noun "God" and the adjective "living" are in the plural form here.</note>." He said to them: "Read the end of the sentence. For it is not written 'of the Lords of hosts,' but 'of the Lord of hosts our God' <note>original Hebrew: *Yahweh tsevaot eloheinu*</note>." This is the tradition: where this name <term>Elohim</term> <note>The standard Hebrew word for God, which is grammatically plural</note> is accepted as referring to the true God, it is nevertheless joined with an adjective of the plural number. This would by no means happen if that name (as they claim), when taken for the true God, were always held to be singular.

Moreover, similar to this way of speaking about God is what we read written in Hosea chapter 11: <note>Hosea 11:12 in the Christian Bible, or 12:1 in Hebrew</note> "Ephraim has surrounded me with denial, or lies, and the house of Israel with deceit. But Judah shall still be ruling with God, and with the faithful holy ones." Where the gloss of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> says: "'With the faithful holy ones' means with the holy and blessed God." 

Nor do I think we should overlook what is read in the <term>Midrash Kohelet</term> <note>A rabbinic commentary (midrash) on the Book of Ecclesiastes</note>, that is, in the exposition of Ecclesiastes, regarding that passage in chapter 5: "If you see the oppression of the poor, and the snatching away of judgment and justice in a province, do not wonder at such a matter. For one high official watches over another high official, and there are higher ones over them." <note>Ecclesiastes 5:8</note> For it is said there: "If you see the oppressors of the poor and needy, and justice—that is, the righteous one living forever—multiplying goodness and peace for himself, you should fear the judgment of Gehenna. Because 'one high official watches over another high official'—these are the angels. And 'there are higher ones over them'—this is the Holy and Blessed God."

Furthermore, in very many places, we find this name <term>Elohim</term>, when it is used for the true God, joined with a verb in the plural number. This would not happen at all if, when accepted for the true God, it were always held to be singular. And to pass over almost infinite other examples of that kind, I will bring forward one that most especially serves our purpose. For thus it is written in the first chapter of Genesis: "And <term>Elohim</term> said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." <note>Genesis 1:26</note> That is, and "Gods" said, "Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness." 

If, therefore, in this place <term>Elohim</term> were understood as singular, He would not have said "Let us make," but "I will make." Nor would He have uttered "in our image, after our likeness," but would have said "in my image, after my likeness." Yet He said, "in our image, after our likeness," and not "in our images, after our likenesses," so that He might indicate the identity of the persons and the unity of the divine essence. For even if the three divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>From the Greek *hypostasis*, referring to the distinct persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) as individual realities</note> are personally distinguished from one another—since the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another—they are nonetheless not essentially distinguished, but are altogether the same. Since, therefore, this name <term>Elohim</term> is accepted here for the true God, and is joined with the verb "let us make" which is uttered in the plural, it is certainly clear...

it is established that this name is taken here for the true God, not in a singular sense, but plurally, to suggest the plurality of divine persons.

<margin>False interpretations of the later Jews.</margin>
However, the later Jews attempt to pervert the truth of this text with certain irrational, not to mention false, distortions. For some say that the reason God spoke in the plural when he was about to create man was because he consulted his heavenly family <note>The "heavenly family" or "heavenly host" refers to the angels.</note>.

<margin>Refutations.</margin>
Their statement is certainly empty and void, which is most evident from the fact that all heavenly things serve God, and he does not stand in need of their counsel. Others truly, such as <term>Rabbi David</term> <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as Radak, a prominent medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note> and <term>Rabbi Moses of Gerona</term> <note>Also known as Nachmanides or Ramban (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note>, say in this place that God used this way of speaking because he was then speaking with the earth, for the reason that the man he was about to make had to consist of both divine and earthly substance. But this statement is surely so foolish and ridiculous that it does not require refutation. Indeed, it is a ridiculous absurdity to say that God called upon the earth to be his helper in the creation of man. Finally, some say that, speaking grammatically, in this place this name **אלהים** <gloss>Elohim</gloss> is not joined with the plural verb "Let us make," but with the verb "He said," which is singular. For the text says, **ויאמר אלהים** <gloss>And Elohim said (singular)</gloss>. and afterward follows, "Let us make man." This also amounts to nothing. For even if *Elohim* is not immediately connected with the verb "let us make," it is nonetheless connected mediately, which is exactly the same thing. For it is nothing other than **אלהים אמר נעשה** <gloss>Elohim said: Let us make man</gloss>. Although here this name **אלהים** <gloss>Elohim</gloss>, taken for the true God, is not joined immediately but mediately with a verb of plural number, it is nevertheless joined immediately in many other places, as is easily evident to those reading the Bible written in Hebrew characters. These people, and all others who strive to corrupt the meaning of this text, are easily convicted by what is found in <term>Midrash Koheleth</term> <note>A traditional Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Ecclesiastes.</note>, that is, in the exposition of Ecclesiastes, regarding that which is found in the second chapter: **כי מה האדם שיבוא אחרי המלך את אשר כבר עשוהו** <gloss>For who is the man who may come or enter after the King, whom they have already made him?</gloss> <note>Ecclesiastes 2:12. The author highlights that the Hebrew verb for "made" here is plural (*asuhu*).</note> For it is said there: "After the King," namely the King of other Kings, the holy and blessed God—will you not be able to stand? Moreover, he teaches through this that it must be said that it is not written "who made him" (singular), but "who made him" (plural). Since this is written in the Law, it can be said that the holy and blessed God and his house of judgment made him. If, however, you say from this, "Therefore there are two principles <note>Meaning two gods or two primary powers.</note>," it does not follow. For was it not already said in Deuteronomy chapter 32: "He made you, and fashioned, or prepared, or adorned you"? <note>Deuteronomy 32:6. Here the verb is singular.</note> Thus far the tradition. In which three things are placed that are quite worthy of note and very fitting to the proposed matter. The first is that the verb of plural number "they made" is joined with the name of singular number "King" in the creation of man, because God, when he created man, spoke plurally, saying: "Let us make man in our image." Hence the <term>Psalmodist</term> <note>Referring to the author of the Psalms, King David.</note> said:

# BOOK TWO

->66<-

"Let Israel rejoice in his makers, and the children of Zion exult in their king." <note>A reference to Psalm 149:2. The Latin "factoribus" (makers) is plural, mirroring the Hebrew grammatical structure Galatino is highlighting.</note> From this also Isaiah says in chapter 54: <term>כי בעליך עשיך יהוה צבאות שמו</term> <note>Isaiah 54:5</note>. That is, "For your husbands are your makers; the Lord of hosts is his name." <note>Galatino translates the Hebrew plural "Ba'alayikh" (husbands/lords) and "Osayikh" (makers) literally to emphasize a plurality of persons within the one God.</note>

The second point is when it is said in this tradition that "The holy and blessed God and his House of Judgment made man." Where by "the holy and blessed God," the unity of the divine nature is shown; but by "his House of Judgment," the Trinity of persons is hinted at. For a <term>House of Judgment</term> <note>In Hebrew, a *Beit Din*. This is a traditional Jewish rabbinical court.</note> was spoken of among the Jews when at least three people together brought forward a judgment; and while it could consist of more, it could never be fewer, provided they were always an odd number. Therefore, the House of Judgment of God is nothing other than the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 

For this reason, in the <term>Bereshit Rabbah</term> <note>An ancient collection of rabbinic interpretations on the Book of Genesis.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis—concerning that which is said in chapter 19: <term>ויהוה המטיר על סדם ועל עמורה גפרית ואש</term> <note>Genesis 19:24</note>. This is: "And the Lord rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah sulfur and fire." Rabbi Elazar said: "In every place where the name <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God, YHVH.</note> is placed in Scripture, it always understands Him and his House of Judgment." This same Rabbi also affirms this in the <term>Midrash Shir ha-Shirim</term> <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Song of Solomon.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs—concerning that which is in chapter 1: <term>לססתי ברכבי פרעה דמיתיך רעיתי</term> <note>Song of Solomon 1:9</note>. That is: "To my mare in the chariots (or in the cavalcade) of Pharaoh have I compared you, my friend." 

The third point, however, is when it is further inferred in the same tradition that God and his House of Judgment are not two principles of all created things, but only one principle. From this it is clear that the ancient Doctors of the Jews did not deny the mystery of the divine Trinity, but only denied multiple principles or multiple gods—which the Christian religion detests no less. Since these things are so, it stands clearer than light that through the name **<term>אלהים</term>** <gloss>Elohim</gloss>, the three divine persons ought to be understood, who together concurred as a single principle for the production of all things.

Regarding the City of Rome and the significance of its name, he has uncovered many truly wonderful things. These words are related by Rabbi Nehunia ben Ha-Kana <note>A 1st-century sage and prominent figure in early Jewish mysticism</note> in the *Epistle of Secrets* written to his son Haccana, which the Hebrews call **אגרת הסודות** (*Iggereth Ha-Sodoth*), saying thus:

> Once Antoninus <note>A Roman figure, often identified in Jewish tradition as a friend of Rabbi Judah the Prince</note> asked regarding the truth of the likeness of the four-letter name, the twelve-letter name, and the forty-two letter name. The response: Because you asked to be taught of the truth—that is, the meaning of the name of four letters, the name of twelve letters, and the name of forty-two letters—I am making known to you those living secrets of God, whose existence ought to be hidden from every person. But because I recognize that you are distinguished among the blessed students, and it is consistent with reason to reveal these things to them—since for people of that standing <note>meaning scholars or those of high character</note> such things should not be hidden—I inform you that God has no name that we can fully grasp. This is because His essence is His name, and His name is His essence. And just as we cannot grasp any understanding of His essence (since with such knowledge we would be equal to Him—God forbid!), so we cannot grasp the knowledge of His name. Nevertheless, all His names have a specific meaning. Because the four-letter name is more essential to His actions and demonstrates a more perfect and essential knowledge as far as we are capable of receiving it, all His other names are joined from this one. For this reason, this name is called the **שם המפורש** <term>Shem Ha-Mephorash</term> <note>The "Explicit Name" or "Distinct Name," referring to the Tetragrammaton, YHVH.</note>, not because it is His essential name, but because we say it is as much as our faculty can comprehend, and we cannot ascend any higher. You should also know regarding the twelve-letter name and the forty-two letter name that they are not names where a single word is made of twelve or forty-two letters, but rather, in whatever name it might be, there are many different words that have one single meaning.

This means: Once Antoninus, Consul of the City of Rome, asked Rabbenu Ha-Kadosh <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</note> to instruct him concerning the truth—specifically, what is signified by the name of four letters, the name of twelve letters, and the name of forty-two letters. The response: Because you seek to be informed of the truth, namely what the name of four, the name of twelve, and the name of forty-two letters demonstrate, I make it known to you that these are divine secrets which ought to be hidden from all men. Nevertheless, because I know you to be well-deserving among the scholarly, it is consistent with reason to uncover such things to them; for to men of this kind, such matters should by no means be concealed.

<margin>God properly has no name.</margin>
Therefore, I make it known to you that God has no name of which we can have [complete] knowledge, since His substance is His name, and vice versa. And just as we can have no knowledge of His substance—because if it were known, we would be made equal to Him—so we cannot have knowledge of His name. Nonetheless, all His names are attributive. And because the name of four letters is more peculiar to His operations, and shows a more perfect knowledge of Him and is more suited to Him (as far as it is possible for us to grasp), and since all His names proceed from this name, this name is therefore called **שם המפורש** (*Shem Ha-Mephorash*). This is not because it is His substantial name, but we call it so because it is as much as our faculty can comprehend, and we cannot ascend higher. You ought to note, however, that the name of twelve and the name of forty-two letters are not names of which each is a single word... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

# BOOK

->76<-

...whether the word consists of twelve letters or forty-two, each of them are distinct words pointing to one thing. Thus spoke that author <note>Referring back to Rabbi Nehunia ben Ha-Kana from the previous page</note>. 

However, Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the most influential medieval Jewish philosopher, often called "the Egyptian" because he served the Sultan’s court in Cairo</note> in the book *The Guide* <note>original: "More," referring to *Moreh Nevukhim* or *The Guide for the Perplexed*</note>, in the sixtieth chapter of the first part, says word-for-word: 

"All the names of the Creator found in all the books are derived from His effects <note>Meaning they describe God's actions or how He is perceived by humans, rather than His essence</note>, except for one name, which is YHWH <note>original: "יהוה", the Tetragrammaton</note>. And it is the name specifically assigned to the most high Creator. For this reason, it is called *Shem HaMephorash* <note>original: "שם המפורש"</note>, that is, the 'Explicit Name' or 'Explicated Name.' He means to say that this name signifies and demonstrates the Creator's substance and His 'whatness' <note>A philosophical term for essence or quiddity</note> with a perfect and manifest demonstration and significance. In this name, there is no equivocation <note>ambiguity</note> nor any mixture; that is, there is nothing that is shared between God and His creatures in this name.

However, His other glorious names signify equivocally and with mixture, because they are derived from works similar to those found in us. Thus, even that name which is spoken in place of the four-letter YHWH—which is *Adonai* <note>original: "אדני"</note>—is derived from the word *Adon* <note>original: "אדון"</note>, which means 'Lord.' It is for this reason that an angel is also called *Adonai* <note>Lord</note>, as is said in Genesis chapter 18: 'My Lord <note>Adonai</note>, if I have found favor in your eyes.' <note>Genesis 18:3; Maimonides argues that here the word refers to the excellence of the guest, though others interpret it as addressing God</note>. 

I have made this known to you regarding the word *Adonai*, by which the name of the Creator is pronounced. It is more specifically assigned to God the most high than all other names that identify the Creator. Others, truly—such as *Dayyan* <note>original: "דיין"</note>, meaning 'Judge'; and *Tzadik* <note>original: "צדיק"</note>, meaning 'Just'; and *Hannun* <note>original: "חנון"</note>, meaning 'Gracious,' or 'Pious' and 'Merciful'—it is manifest that these are common and derived titles. 

But as for the name written with four letters, YHWH, no known derivation is discovered for it, nor does it share its meaning with anything else. There is no doubt that this glorious name—which is not uttered, nor pronounced, nor spoken except in the Sanctuary by the sanctified priests of the Lord, and only in the Priestly Blessing, and even then only by the High Priest on the day of the fast of glorious sanctification <note>Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement</note>—is that name in which there is no shared participation between the Creator and anything else. 

Briefly, I say that the height and excellence of this name is considered so great, and such great and terrible caution is taken so that no one speaks it, because it signifies the substance and essence of the Creator. Thus, no creature communicates with Him in that significance. As our masters assert, speaking in the person of God: 'My name is unique,' or 'assigned to Me alone.' All other names of God signify qualities and other attributes. 

And when these types of names for the Creator (derived from His works) were multiplied, it caused the hearts of many sons of Adam to believe that He has many qualities, according to the multitude of works from which those names are derived. For that reason, He promised to give men understanding which would remove this kind of error from them. For it says in Zechariah chapter 14: 'In that day the Lord shall be one, and His name one.' He means to say that just as the Lord Himself is one, so then...

He shall be called by one name only, which signifies His substance or essence without being derived from any action. But when you consider God's essence stripped of every operation, He will have no derivative name at all, but only one, to designate His essence. 

Now, there is no name among us that is not derivative, except for the *Tetragrammaton* <note>original Greek: "τετραγραµµατον", the "four-letter name"</note> YHWH <note>original: "יהוה"</note>. ->78<-

They do not dare to speak it as it is written; instead, they utter in its place **Adonai** <note>Hebrew: "אדני", meaning "My Lord"</note>, which means the same as "Lord." However, those who contend that the name sounds like "Jova" <note>original: "Ioua"</note> in our letters attempt to prove it primarily from what the Hebrew grammarians say: when a <term>sheva</term> <note>a Hebrew vowel sign indicating a very short "e" or no vowel at all</note> follows one of the guttural letters, often both the sheva and the guttural letter itself are removed together through <term>syncope</term> <note>the contraction or dropping of sounds from the middle of a word</note>. 

For example, **Iehuda** <note>Hebrew: "יהודה", Judah</note> is sometimes both written and pronounced as **Iuda** <note>Hebrew: "יודה"</note>; **Iehoshua** <note>Hebrew: "יהושע", Joshua</note> as **Ioshua** <note>Hebrew: "יושע"</note>; **Iehoiachin** <note>Hebrew: "יהויכין"</note> as **Ioiachin** <note>Hebrew: "יויכין"</note>; and **tehilim** <note>Hebrew: "תהלים", Psalms</note> as **tillim** <note>Hebrew: "תלים"</note>. There are many other examples of this kind. They wish for something similar to happen in this great name of God. From this, they infer that it should sound like "Jova" among us, since the sheva precedes the guttural letter *He*. 

But if this were true, the name would not be written as **YHWH** <note>Hebrew: "יהוה"</note>, but as **YWH** <note>Hebrew: "יוה"</note> without the sheva and the letter *He*. In that case, it would not be a <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>a "four-letter name"</note>, but only a three-letter name. This is unthinkable. For it is a sacrilege <note>Latin: "Nefas"</note> to either add or subtract anything from that name. It must be written and pronounced exactly as God Himself commanded Moses to write it (if, indeed, it is to be pronounced at all). Therefore, the rule of the Hebrew grammarians they cite has no place here; moreover, that rule is almost never observed in the twenty-four sacred books <note>the books of the Hebrew Bible</note>, but perhaps only in other volumes, and especially among the authors of the <term>Talmud</term> <note>the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note>. 

Therefore, it is necessary that the four-letter name of God be written and pronounced with the sheva and the letter *He* (which has a gentle breathing sound). Let those who affirm it sounds like "Jova" be careful. For it is not "Jova," nor "Ieova," but it must be pronounced **Jehovah** <note>original: "Iehoua"</note> with a gentle aspiration, just as it is written.

Rabbi Abina objected, saying: "It is written: *This is my name.* And it is written again in the same place: *This is my memorial.*" The Holy and Blessed God said: "I am not read as I am written. For I am written with *Yod, He, Vav, He* (**יהוה**), which is the four-letter name. But I am read with *Aleph, Daleth, Nun, Yod* (**אדני**), which forms **Adonai**, meaning 'Lord'." For this reason, the masters commanded that "Adonai" ought to be read in its place. 

So it is written there. Furthermore, as one reads in the book **Sanhedrin** in the chapter **Helec**: "Abba Saul said: 'He who pronounces the four-letter name itself, according to how its letters sound, shall have no portion in the world to come.'" For that...

Taught by that great man Moses, in order to designate this ineffability of the divine trinity and unity, they established that this name should not be uttered at all. <margin>Three divine names composed from the letters of this name.</margin>

For the first is composed of the first and second letters, namely from *Yod* and *He*, in this manner: יה <gloss>Yah</gloss> <note>The OCR reads יאח, likely a transcription error for יה (Yah), as the text specifies it consists of the first two letters of the Tetragrammaton, Yod and He.</note>, which is the same as "God," and it designates the Father, who is the fountain of the entire divinity. The second name, however, consists of the second and third letters, thus: חו <gloss>Hu</gloss> <note>He/Himself</note>, which is interpreted as "He Himself," and signifies the Son. For He is surely the one whom the prophets foretold would come for the salvation of the human race, and who would one day be pointed out with a finger, according to that passage in Isaiah, chapter 35: "God himself will come and save you" <gloss>original: אלחים הוא יבא ויושעכם</gloss>. Finally, the third name is constituted from the third and fourth letters, namely from *Vav* and *He*, thus: והו <gloss>Ve-hu</gloss>, and the whole of it sounds like "and He Himself," and it denotes the Holy Spirit. For He also was to be sent visibly after the Son, though not in the same manner. For the Son was to be sent in a human nature <term>hypostatically</term> <note>A theological term meaning "personally" united; in the Incarnation, the divine and human natures are joined in one person (hypostasis).</note> united to Himself. But the Holy Spirit was sent in the form of a dove, and in tongues of fire, not hypostatically united to Himself, but as if under a sign.

In this, moreover, the second name descends from the first, and the third from the second. For the letter ה <gloss>He</gloss> is common to the first and second names, and ו <gloss>Vav</gloss> is common to the second and third; it is clearly shown that the Son is <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Of the same substance or essence; a core Christian doctrine that the Father, Son, and Spirit are the same "stuff."</note> with the Father, from whom He is begotten, and the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Son, who is consubstantial with the Father. Thus it is openly clear both that the Son is in the Father, and the Father in the Son, and the Holy Spirit in both.

**CAP.** I also judge that it was not done without a great mystery that all the letters of this name are those same ones from which the three tenses—namely the past, present, and future—of the indicative <term>substantive verb</term> <note>The verb "to be" (sum, esse).</note> are formed among the Hebrews.

**GAL.** It is exactly as you say. For in this, two secrets are revealed. The first is: because only the substantive verb signifies substance—from which it is called "substantive"—while all others signify accidents, which is why they are called "adjectives." Therefore, only the indicative substantive verb designates stability, while the others designate changeability. In this, therefore—that all the letters of this name are taken from the indicative substantive verb—the absolute and everlasting stability of the divine persons is denoted. 

The second secret is that this name consists of the same letters from which the three tenses of the same verb are composed, which are the past, present, and future. Among them, they sound like this: היה <gloss>hayah</gloss>, that is, "He was"; הוה <gloss>hoveh</gloss>, which means "He is"; and יהיה <gloss>yiheyeh</gloss>, that is, "He will be." Thus, from this, the eternity of the same persons is most clearly evident: namely, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit always have been, are, and will be.

**CAP.** Why is this name called among the Hebrews <term>Shem ha-Mephorash</term> <gloss>שם המפורש</gloss>, which among us is the same as "Explained" or "Declared"?

**GAL.**...

It is clear to me, according to my own strong opinion, that it was not one single name, but two or three names joined together, whose letters totaled twelve. For they taught that to no one who knew it, except their own sons and disciples who were such that they deserved to know it, and this only once in a week <note>Maimonides actually refers here to a seven-year cycle (a sabbatical week), though the Latin *hebdomada* can mean a seven-day week.</note>. But when schismatic and insolent men multiplied in the world and learned the name of twelve letters, they corrupted the faith with it. Just as happens to one who is imperfect when he perceives a thing not to be as it seemed to him at first. For this reason, those fathers hid that name of twelve letters and taught it to no one further, except to the honest and modest who were in the priesthood, so that they might bless the people in the sanctuary with it, after they had prohibited the mention of the "Exposed Name" <note>The *Shem Ha-Mephorash*, the explicitly pronounced name of God.</note> in the sanctuary because of the malice of the sons of Adam. All these things says Rabbi Moses the Egyptian, son of Maimon. <margin>The name of twelve letters.</margin>

Moreover, their own letters provide proof of this wonderful explanation to the Jews. For if these names are written in Hebrew letters, thus: אב <gloss>Ab</gloss>, that is, Father; בן <gloss>Ben</gloss>, that is, Son; ורוח הקדש <gloss>ve-Ruah Ha-Kodesh</gloss>, that is, and the Holy Spirit. ## *Concerning the name of God of forty-two letters, through which the ancient Jews most clearly explained the mystery of the divine trinity and unity.*

### Chapter XII.

->**CAPNIO,**<-
<note>Capnio is the Greek-style pen name of the humanist scholar Johannes Reuchlin.</note>

**N**ow it remains for you to say what the name of God of forty-two letters is, and how the Tetragrammaton was explained by the ancient Jews through it. 

**GALATINUS.** Through the name of God of forty-two letters, the ancient Hebrews explained the name of twelve letters. Therefore, just as they asserted the name of twelve letters was derived from the name of four letters, so they said the name of forty-two letters emanated from the name of twelve letters. So that I might say nothing of myself regarding this name (as I have done with the others), but only report those things which they themselves assert, first hear what Rabbi Moses, son of Maimon <note>The famous Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204).</note>, says in the book *The Guide* <note>The *Moreh Nevukhim* or *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>, in the sixty-second chapter of the first part. For he says thus:

> Rabbi Tarfon said: "Once I went up with my mother’s father to the platform <note>The *duchan*, where priests blessed the congregation.</note> and I inclined my ear toward the Priest, and I heard that he swallowed the Name <note>Meaning he mumbled or spoke it softly so it was obscured by the singing.</note> amid the pleasant singing of his fellow priests." And they also had a name of forty-two letters. It is known to every person of understanding that it is impossible in any way for forty-two letters to be a single word; rather, these were many words whose total letters were forty-two. There is no doubt that all of these indicate matters in the science of those subjects which approach the truth of the perception of God Himself (blessed be He) in the ways we have mentioned. Indeed, these many words were called "a name" because they indicate one single matter, unlike other specific names. Truly, these words were many for the sake of understanding the matter, because a single concept cannot be understood except through many words.

As it says in Matthew chapter 28:
> All power (he said) is given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.

In this formula, therefore, in which he commanded those who had been instructed to be baptized, when he set down "Father," "Son," and "Holy Spirit," he clearly signaled that he had already thoroughly taught his disciples the secret of the Trinity and divine unity. For these three names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—express the Trinity of the divine persons. Furthermore, in that he said "in the **name**," and not "in the **names**," he clearly showed that there is one essence and nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And this is undoubtedly the truest and most distinct exposition of the four-letter name of God, which was explicitly contained both in the Name of Twelve Letters and in the Name of Forty-Two Letters. With these names, namely the twelve and forty-two letters, our Lord Jesus Christ most perfectly explained the Tetragrammaton name of God to his disciples. For this reason, addressing the Father (as found in John chapter 17), he said:
> Father, I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me.

And again he said:
> These have known that you sent me, and I have made known your name to them.

Indeed, following the doctrine of Christ’s disciples, Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius, to whom the Athanasian Creed—a statement of Trinitarian faith—was traditionally attributed.</note> excellently and perfectly explained the Tetragrammaton name of God itself, first through the name of twelve letters, which is (as was clear a little earlier): Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Then through the name of forty-two letters, saying:
> God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, and yet there are not three gods, but one God.

From which it clearly appears that the faith of the ancient Hebrews and our own was one and the same.

...why this name יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH.</note>, which we mentioned a little while ago, is called <term>Arba’ Otiyot</term> <note>Hebrew: *Arba' Otiyot*, meaning "Four Letters."</note>, that is, "of four letters" or the <term>Tetragrammaton</term>? **GALATINUS.** Because the letters of no other name so distinctly indicate the internal secrets of the divinity. For there is no doubt that this name, יהוה, which we said a little earlier is proper to God alone and signifies the divine nature more distinctly than the others, also designates the secrets of the divine Trinity and Unity above all others. Other names of God, however, since they are not proper to God alone but are derived from works similar to those found in us <note>Galatinus is referring to "communicable" attributes like "Justice" or "Mercy" which humans can also possess, unlike the unique essence of YHWH.</note>, do not so distinctly suggest the mysteries of the divine Trinity and Unity as that name does. Therefore, that name alone is called the Tetragrammaton by way of excellence among the others, even if certain other names of God are found among the Hebrews to be written with four letters. **CAPITO.** For a greater expression of Catholic truth, therefore, I would wish that you say something about each of those names which I have brought forward as examples. And first, indeed, in what way is the Trinity of divine persons suggested through the name אדני <term>Adonai</term>, which they speak in place of the Name of Four Letters? <note>Jewish tradition forbids the vocalization of YHWH, substituting it with 'Adonai' (Lord) during prayer or reading.</note> **GALATINUS.** Certainly, the Trinity of divine persons is designated, albeit somewhat obscurely, through this name אדני, *Adonai*, which is interpreted as "Lord." For just as the name אלהים <term>Elohim</term> implies plurality (as we showed above), so also אדני, *Adonai*, is a plural name. For from this name אדן <term>Adon</term>, which is singular and signifies "Lord," comes this plural אדנים <term>Adonim</term>, which is the same as "Lords." From the singular name *Adon*, however, comes *Adoni* <note>original: "Adoni"</note>, which is interpreted as "my Lord." But from the plural *Adonim* comes אדני, *Adonai*, which is a divine name and properly signifies the same thing as "my Lords." Therefore, those ancient fathers, having been taught by Moses, ordained that God be called "Lords" in the plural number, so that from this it might be openly shown that the universal lordship over all things is common to the three divine persons. For the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord. However, so that it might be suggested that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three Lords, but one Lord, it was decreed that the name itself, אדני, *Adonai*, even if it be plural, should only be joined with a verb in the singular number, or likewise with an adjective in the singular number.

***

Here, therefore, is placed the name of God, <term>Ehie</term> <note>אהיה - Ehyeh</note>, which encompasses the differences of the three tenses of the indicative substantive verb: namely, the past, the present, and the future, which are "I was," "I am," and "I shall be." Therefore, the name itself, <term>Ehie</term>, is interpreted as "I was, I am, and I shall be." For the second and third letters of this name, namely <term>He</term> [ה] and <term>Yod</term> [י], designate the first person (which is the third among them <note>In Hebrew grammar, the "root" or dictionary form is the 3rd person singular, unlike Latin or English which often prioritize the 1st person.</note>) of the past tense of the same verb, which is <term>haithi</term> <note>הייתי - "I was"</note>, that is, "I was." But the fourth letter of that name, namely <term>He</term> [ה], indicates the first person of the present tense, which is <term>houe</term> <note>הוה - "is" or "being"</note>, that is, "I am." Moreover, the first letter, namely <term>Aleph</term> [א], which is usually placed at the beginning of the first person of the future tense of any verb, denotes the first person of the future tense of that same verb. Although the first person for us is the third for them, and the third for us is the first for them, since they begin to decline verbs from the third person. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that this name <term>Ehie</term> contains within itself the distinctions of the three tenses of the indicative mood of the substantive verb. Wherefore it is most aptly interpreted as "I was, I am, and I shall be," to suggest the supreme, all-encompassing, and everlasting stability of God, who always was, is, and shall be. ### *Regarding the name of God <term>Agla</term><note>A famous Kabbalistic acronym frequently used in both Jewish prayer and medieval Christian protective charms.</note>, through which the infinite power of the divine trinity is expressed. Chapter 15.*

->GALATINO,<-

**I** shall say a few very brief things regarding the name of God Agla to satisfy your request. I would have you know that the name of God itself, Agla (as its letters suggest), denotes nothing other than the eternal and infinite power of God, which He possesses in respect to creation, whether yet to be produced or already brought forth. For its first letter, namely א (*aleph*), stands for *Atta*, which means "You." The second, namely ג (*ghimel*), stands for *Ghibor*, which is interpreted as "Mighty." The third, namely ל (*lamech*), stands for *Leholam*, which is the same as "forever." Finally, the fourth, namely א (*aleph*), stands for *Adonai*, which is translated into our language as "Lord." From this it is clearly evident that the name Agla signifies nothing else than this whole phrase: **אתה גבור לעולם אדני** <note>Transliteration: Atta Ghibor Leolam Adonai.</note> That is: *You are mighty forever, O Lord.* From these things, therefore, it is plain that this same name Agla openly expresses the very omnipotence of the divine trinity.

Would they not have stolen their sufficiency?" <note>Obadiah 1:5. original: אם גנבים באו לך אם שודדי לילה איך נדמיתה הלא יגנבו דים (Im gannabim bau lach... halo yignebu dayam).</note> That is, their *dayam*, which means "their sufficiency." Then he adds: Therefore, He who is absolutely and in truth wealthy and sufficient unto Himself is He who needs no other. And this is God alone. Of all others, truly, this is said figuratively, or according to a specific sense. Thus far **Algazel**. Since therefore God alone, three and one, is sufficient unto Himself, for that reason the name <term>שדי</term> **Sadai** <note>Shaddai; the author derives this name from the Hebrew words 'She' (who) and 'Dai' (enough/sufficient).</note> rightly carries and signifies the sufficiency of the divine trinity, by which God is sufficient unto Himself.

---

### *Regarding the seventy-two names of God, through which the perfections of the divine trinity and unity are most aptly suggested.*
### Chapter XVII.

->CAPNIO,<-

<margin>GALATINO</margin>
**C**oncerning the seventy-two names of God, although many men have said many things—and some indeed empty and worthy of laughter—for that reason, for a greater knowledge of the divine names, I would finally wish to hear your opinion about them. <note>Speaker changes to Capnio</note> So that I may say regarding these things only those which I have received from the <term>Kabbalistic</term> <note>Kabbalah refers to the tradition of Jewish mysticism; Reuchlin/Capnio was a pioneer in bringing these studies to a Christian audience.</note> books: first, I will bring forward the texts from which the names themselves are formed, from the fourteenth chapter of **Exodus**, where it is said in Hebrew thus:

> And the Angel of God, who went before the camp of **Israel**, moved and went behind them; and the pillar of cloud moved from before their face and stood behind them.
> And it came between the camp of the **Egyptians** and the camp of **Israel**; and it was a cloud and darkness, yet it gave light by night, so that the one came not near the other all through the night.
> And **Moses** stretched out his hand over the sea; and God caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. <note>These are verses 19, 20, and 21 of Exodus 14. In the original Hebrew, each of these three verses contains exactly 72 letters.</note>

->This is, to render it word for word:<-

> And the Angel of the Gods who went before the camp of **Israel** moved himself, and walked after them: and the pillar of the cloud moved from their face, and stood after them.
> And he came between the camp of the **Egyptians**, and between the camp of **Israel**, and it was a cloud and darkness, and it illuminated the night, and one did not approach the other the whole night.
> And **Moses** turned over the sea, and God took away the sea by a strong south wind the whole night, and turned the sea into dry ground, and the waters were divided.

This series of words is distinguished among the Hebrews into three <term>פסוקים</term> <gloss>verses</gloss> <note>original: "pasukhim"</note>, that is, texts or verses. Each of which consists of seventy-two letters. From which the Kabbalists, in a certain wondrous way,

<page-num>97</page-num>
<header>SECOND [BOOK]</header>

...they extracted the seventy-two <term>Divine Names</term> <note>Original: "Deinomina," a Latin compound for "Names of God."</note>. And indeed, they accomplished this in ten ways.

<margin>Rule for the names of the first method</margin>
Of these, the first is as follows: first, the first letter of the first verse is taken, which is **ו** <note>Vau</note>. Next, the last letter of the second verse is taken, which is **ה** <note>He</note>. Finally, the first letter of the third verse is taken, which is **ו** <note>Vau</note>. From these three letters, the first name of the first method results, which is **והו** <note>Vahu</note>. After this, they take the second letter of the first verse, which is **י** <note>Iod</note>; then the second-to-last of the second verse, which is **ל** <note>Lamed</note>; and finally the second letter of the last verse, which is **י** <note>Iod</note>. Thus they constitute the second name, which is **ילי** <note>Yeli</note>. Following this order, they proceed continuously until the entire number of letters is exhausted. This is easily apparent to anyone looking at the names of the first method themselves.

<margin>Rule for the names of the second method.</margin>
However, the names of the second method are formed from the same letters according to their system in this way. First, take the first letter of the first verse or text, which is **ו** <note>Vau</note>; then the first of the second, which is also **ו** <note>Vau</note>; and the first of the third, which is likewise **ו** <note>Vau</note>. Thus you will form the first name of the second method, which is **ווו** <note>Vvv</note>. Then, if you take the second letter of the first text, which is **י** <note>Iod</note>; the second of the second, which is similarly **י** <note>Iod</note>; and the second of the third, which is also **י** <note>Iod</note>; you will constitute the second name of the second method, which is **ייי** <note>Yyy</note>. Likewise, from the third letter of the first text, which is **ס** <note>Samach</note>; the third of the second, which is **ב** <note>Beth</note>; and the third of the third, which is **ט** <note>Teth</note>; the third name of the second method is produced, which is **סבט** <note>Sabat</note>. By proceeding in this order until all the letters of the same texts are exhausted, the seventy-two names of the second method are created. This can be seen by observing the names of the second method themselves. As for the names of the remaining eight methods and how they are composed from these same letters: to avoid being overly long-winded, I do not provide the rules now, but leave them to be investigated by the studious. For I believe everyone will judge that I have done enough, seeing as I have provided the rules for making the names of the first and second methods, and have recorded all the names of the ten methods (just as I found them in the books of the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Kabbalists; practitioners of Jewish mysticism.</note>).

<meta>This page continues the systematic presentation of the 72 Divine Names, known as the Shem HaMephorash. While the preceding page established the first five methods of arrangement, this page lists modes six through ten. These tables represent a sophisticated "combinatorial theology" where the names of God are permuted to reveal different cosmic influences. Renaissance scholars believed that by meditating on or invoking these specific letter combinations, one could access the angelic hierarchies governing the physical and spiritual worlds.</meta>
