--- Page 125 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnio (the scholar Reuchlin) and Galatinus regarding the 72 Divine Names. Having previously established the methods of arranging the letters, they now move to the controversial issue of their "punctuation" (vowel points) and their specific theological meanings, bridging Hebrew mysticism with Christian doctrine.</meta>

->BOOK<-

**CAPNIO.** Some of our people say that the names of the first and second modes, punctuated as you have set them down, are not truly Hebrew, because they are punctuated contrary to the usual custom of Hebrew scripture. <note>He is referring to the "niqqud," or Hebrew vowel points. Traditional Hebrew is written without vowels, and the specific vocalization of the 72 names was a point of intense scholarly debate in the Renaissance.</note> **GALATINUS.** Perhaps those who say this are of that class of men who, failing to rightly measure themselves or their own abilities, imagine they know everything to such an extent that they believe what they themselves do not know, no one else can know. You, however, would by no means say such a thing, both because you have always loathed the manners of such men, and also because in the Cabalistic books you have—I believe—frequently read these same names punctuated in this way, especially those of the first mode. I too have found them punctuated exactly so in many places: particularly in Rome in the library of the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Vatican Library</note>, in the place where the books of Flamineus—a man once most skilled in the three languages <note>The "three languages" refer to the sacred triad of Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. "Flamineus" likely refers to the scholar and convert Flavius Mithridates, who taught several prominent Renaissance humanists.</note>—are kept in safekeeping. Therefore, let those who deny that these names so punctuated are Hebrew search there among the Hebrew codices, and they will find the names of the first mode punctuated in this way. And even if they have been somewhat corrupted there by the fault of the scribes, I have nevertheless taken care to report them more accurately according to the norms of the Cabalists.

<margin>Why the names of the first and second modes are punctuated in this way.</margin>
**CAPNIO.** Not without reason, therefore, some desire to know why these names are punctuated with points of this kind. **GALATINUS.** Although that is a great secret among the Cabalists—even to the point that they command it must by no means be written down, but only revealed by word of mouth and only to the very few and the worthy—lest it happen that divine names become known to the unworthy and the base, like pearls cast before swine—I, however, whose greatest heart's desire is to hide the truth from no one, but rather to reveal it to all, shall speak. These names are punctuated in this way because the letters from which they are composed are found so punctuated in the aforementioned texts. For indeed the letters found punctuated in those texts, together with the points themselves, concur in the formation of these names. Those letters which are not found punctuated in the same texts—such as those placed at the end of words, which for the most part do not receive points—are punctuated in these names with the points that their pronunciation naturally requires. This is clear to anyone looking at the names themselves. Nor did the Cabalists wish them to be punctuated so without a great mystery. Since from this kind of punctuation, a trinity of syllables results in each of these names, which distinctly designates the trinity of divine persons in one divine essence. <note>This is a core argument of Christian Cabala: that the very grammar and phonetics of Hebrew mysticism "prove" the Christian concept of the Trinity.</note> **CAPNIO.** How are these names interpreted? **GALATINUS.** Some of our people have interpreted the names of the first mode in this way:

The Exalter, The Helper, Hope, Salvation, The Sought, The Proclaimed, The Patient, The Adorable, The Memorable, Thou, To Be Exalted, The Timely; The Much-Celebrated, The Uplifter, Being, The Advocate, The Ruler, Justice, He who Hears, The Rescuer, The Strong, The Right Hand, The Guardian, The Awaited; The Wonderful, To Be Invoked, The Savior, The Swift, The Healer, From Youth, The Only, The Upright, The Pensive, Expectation, Supplication, Glory; The Countenance, The Refuge, The Helper, The Defender, The Liberator, The Guardian, Of the Morning, The Teacher, The Compassionate, The Worker, The Magnificent, The Revealer; The Greatest, The Merciful, The Rejoicing, The Most High.

<summary>In this passage, Galatinus defends the specific Hebrew vocalization (vowel points) of the 72 names, citing ancient manuscripts in the Vatican Library. He further argues that the three-syllable structure of these names provides mystical evidence for the Christian Trinity.</summary>
<keywords>Christian Cabala, Hebrew vowel points, niqqud, Vatican Library, Trinity, Divine Names, 72 names of God, Flamineus, grammar as theology</keywords>

--- Page 126 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 100, moving from the technical discussion of Hebrew vowel points and manuscript history to the specific list of the Seventy-Two Divine Names and their corresponding biblical proofs. This list is a cornerstone of Renaissance Cabalistic practice, linking the mystical names derived from the Book of Exodus to the Book of Psalms.</meta>

<page-num>101</page-num>
->## BOOK TWO<-

True, Ruler, Eternal, Builder, Protector, Mind, Rising, Just, Blessed, Lovable, Praiseworthy, Pitiful, Entreatable, Assistant, Giver, Good, Reward, God, Abundant, Rest.

Now these seventy-two names, so interpreted, are applied to the seventy-two verses of the Psalms written below. Namely:

<note>The "Seventy-Two Names" (Shem HaMephorash) are derived by medieval and Renaissance Cabalists from three verses in Exodus 14:19-21. Here, the author provides a Latin attribute for each name and a corresponding verse from the Psalms that "proves" or activates the power of that name.</note>

*The Exalter*. And you, God, are a shield about me, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head. *The Helper*. And you, O God, be not far away; my strength, hasten to my aid. *Hope*. Saying, God is my hope and my strength, my God, in whom I will trust. *Salvation*. Return, O God, deliver my soul; save me for your mercy’s sake. *The Sought*. I sought God, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my troubles. *The Proclaimed*. Sing to God, who dwells in Zion; declare his thoughts among the peoples. *The Patient*. The Lord is gracious and merciful, patient and of great mercy. *The Worshipful*. Come, let us worship and fall down, and let us kneel before the face of God our maker. *The Mindful*. Remember your mercies, O God, and your kindnesses, for they have been from of old. *You*. Let your mercy, O God, be upon us, according as we have hoped in you. *The One to be Exalted*. God lives, and blessed be my God, and the God of my salvation shall be exalted. *The Timely*. Why, O God, do you stand far off, looking away in the time of trouble? *The Sung*. Shout for joy to God, all the earth; shout aloud and sing. *The Lifter*. And God will be a height for the oppressed, a timely height in trouble.

*The Being*. And God will be a refreshment for me, and my God for the help of my hope. <note>original: *Ens* — this refers to God as pure existence or "He Who Is."</note> *The Advocate*. O God, the God of my salvation, I have cried by day and in the night before you. *The Ruler*. O God our Ruler, how great is your name in all the earth. *Justice*. Judge me according to my justice, O my God, and let them not triumph over me. *The Hearer*. In waiting I have waited for God, and he leaned toward me and heard my cry.

*The Rescuer*. And I will call upon the name of God; I beseech you, O God, deliver my soul. *The Strong*. And I have hoped in you, O God; I said, you are my God.

*The Right-Handed*. May God keep you; the Lord is your protection over your right hand. <note>In this context, "Dexter" implies being favorable or protective, like a shield on the right side.</note> *The Guardian*. May God guard your going out and your coming in, from this time forth and even forevermore. *The One to be Awaited*. God is pleased with those who fear him, and those who wait for his mercy. *The Wonderful*. I confess to God with my whole heart; I will tell of all your wonders. *The One to be Invoked*. I have cried with my whole heart; hear me, O God, I will keep your precepts. *The Savior*. Rescue me, O God, from the evil man; save me from wicked men. *The Swift*. O God, be not far from me; O my God, hasten to my aid. *The Healer*. O God, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you. *From Youth*. Because you are my expectation, O God; O God, my confidence from my youth. *The Only*. I will enter into the strength of God; O God, I will remember your justice alone. *The Upright*. Because the word of the Lord is right...

--- Page 127 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalogue of the seventy-two Divine Names, providing the Latin attributes (titles) and the specific scriptural verses—primarily from the Book of Psalms—associated with each. This sequence is a central component of Renaissance Cabalistic practice, intended to link the mystical names of God with the liturgical power of the Bible.</meta>

To these seventy-two aforementioned verses, which are taken from various Psalms, they apply the seventy-two interpretations mentioned before. They say these belong to those seventy-two names of God, which are formed in the first manner from the letters of the three previously mentioned texts <note>This refers to the three verses of Exodus 14:19-21, each containing 72 letters, used to derive the Shem HaMephorash.</note>. But they are certainly very much mistaken. Indeed, these interpretations are clearly recognized as belonging not to the names themselves, but rather to the verses to which they are applied. For the Jews, following the meaning of these seventy-two verses, devised these seventy-two interpretations to serve as markers for those seventy-two names of God, as if they were indexes of those same verses. This is clearly shown by the fact that these interpretations correspond to the verses to which they are applied, not to the names of God themselves. 

For this name *Exalter* <note>original: "Exaltator"</note> has no connection with this name יהו <note>Yod-He-Vav, the 7th name of the 72</note>, but only fits the verse to which it is applied: namely, "But you, O God, are a shield around me, my glory, and the lifter of my head." <note>Psalm 3:3</note> Similarly, *Helper* <note>original: "Auxiliator"</note> in no way agrees with this name יהי <note>Yod-He-Yod, the 8th name of the 72</note>, but only with this verse to which it is applied: "But you, O God, be not far off; O my strength, hasten to help me." <note>Psalm 22:19</note> You will find the same thing in all the others if you look closely.

However, this one thing in them (which especially supports our purpose against the Jews of our time) is particularly to be noted: that each of those names

# Book Three.

## On the divinity of the Messiah and on his divine names designating his divine nature.

### That the Son of God was to be incarnated, by taking a body from a woman. Chapter 1.

->CAPNIO,<-
<note>Capnio is the scholar-name of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous humanist and pioneer of Hebrew studies among Christians.</note>

Since you have sufficiently proved through the Jewish scriptures that God is three and one, it is now fitting for you to say something about those things contained in their books concerning the incarnation of the Son of God. GALATINUS: It is certainly necessary, not just fitting; for we must speak most especially about those things which concern the Messiah against their <term>perfidiam</term> <note>Latin: "unbelief" or "lack of faith." In this historical context, it was a standard term used by Christian polemicists to describe Jewish rejection of Christ.</note>. While they deny that he would be God and man, they are by no means willing to believe in the work of the divine incarnation. Concerning their unbelief, the prophet Habakkuk prophesied well in the first chapter, saying: <term>For I am working a work in your days which you will not believe when it is told.</term> <note>Hebrew: "Ki po'el po'al bi-ymeikhem lo ta'aminu ki yesuppar." Original Hebrew phrase: כי פועל פועל בימיכם לא תאמינו כי יסופר</note> This means: "Because a work will be done in your days, which you will not believe when it is told." Here it is certain that the prophet spoke of the work of the divine incarnation, which the greater part of the Jews, due to their obstinacy, was by no means going to believe. HOOGSTRATEN: Our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the Catholic Church at the time.</note> has it differently in this place. For it says: "Because a work *has been* done in your days, which no one will believe when it is told." GALATINUS: The <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>Latin: "Hebraica veritas." A term used by scholars to argue that the original Hebrew text was more accurate than the Latin or Greek translations.</note> which I myself have translated here, is far better than what the author of our edition translated. For whether this work is to be understood literally concerning Nebuchadnezzar, or mystically concerning the incarnation of the Messiah: in any event, if we wish to emphasize the force of the word, neither our Latin nor the Greek edition—when it says "No one will believe the truth"—seems consistent. First, if it is understood as being about Nebuchadnezzar, all the Jews believe it. But second, when it is explained as being about the incarnation of Christ, both countless gentiles and very many Jews have believed. Therefore, our translation, by not following the sense of the Hebrew truth in this, receives a <term>calumniam</term> <note>A "calumny" or "falsehood," here referring to a textual error that forces a scholar into a convoluted or false explanation.</note> of this kind: "No one," meaning "hardly anyone," will believe; it forces us to explain it away. But the Hebrew letter admits no such error here; rather (which is very pleasant to us)...

"I have guarded it for you," I have learned: "Whoever guards this, the kingdom is established for him." From where do we know this? From Boaz, as it is written: "As the Lord lives, lie down until the morning," for he was subduing his inclination <note>A reference to Boaz resisting the temptation to lie with Ruth before the legal redemption was settled.</note> until he swore an oath to the Lord to guard this covenant for His sake. **What does he mean by, "From my flesh"? For it would have been more appropriate to say, "From my substance." Yet he said, "From my own flesh."** <note>Job 19:26. Galatinus is arguing that Job’s use of the word "flesh" refers specifically to the human body of the Messiah.</note> This is what is written: **The holy flesh shall pass from you.** <note>Jeremiah 11:15.</note> And furthermore it is written: **And my covenant shall be in your flesh.** <note>Genesis 17:13, referring to circumcision.</note> This signifies the sign that was given to us. For whenever a man is marked with this sign which proceeds from Him, he shall see God himself, and his holy soul shall become one with Him. But whenever he does not keep this <term>covenant</term> <note>original: "foedus," referring to the religious and physical bond of circumcision.</note>, it is written of him: **They shall perish by the breath of God.** If indeed this sign is of God, and they do not observe it. But if you have been worthy of that sign and have guarded it, the divinity shall by no means depart from you; in time you shall be bound to holiness and ascend into the prepared place. 

But what is the reason for what we read above concerning the union of the holy soul—that is, of God—to man? It is certainly none other than that one male and one female shall be joined into one, which shall be called by one name, just as justice proceeding from heavenly mercy shall rest upon them. In this word is the rest of the clarity or the splendor of the male. And what is mercy? I say mercy which shall come from the highest wisdom, and shall be crowned by the word, and for that reason shall be incorporated into the female. <note>In Kabbalah, the union of the Sefirot (Divine attributes) is often described in gendered terms; Galatinus applies this to the Incarnation of Christ (the Word) through the Virgin Mary.</note> And so it has been handed down to us: **God, behold God the strong illuminator.** The masculine letter *Vav* and *Daleth* and the feminine letter *He* are joined into one, which is called **God**. <note>Galatinus is performing a mystical analysis of the Hebrew letters in the name of God to show the union of masculine and feminine principles.</note> And his most holy soul is placed in this spot, though not bound within it. And for this reason it is written: **And from my flesh I shall see God.** Since this happiness is considered universal. 

It follows: **And from my flesh**, as if he were to say: **From this very flesh of my own.** Because of this, those of the people of Israel—at least the holy ones—who say that this is God shall be worthy; they shall be worthy both in this world and in the world to come. And for the sake of this matter it is written: **He who guards this covenant.** And from this we have learned that he who guards this pact, God will guard him. But what is the proof of this? This is clear in Boaz, who said to the Moabite woman <note>Ruth.</note>: **As God lives, lie down until morning.** And though he was enticed by lust, yet he guarded this covenant. Therefore he merited that from him should come forth Kings most powerful among all other Kings, and moreover the King Messiah, who is called by the name of the Holy and Blessed God.

## Chapter II. What is signified by the name Messiah, and concerning the two natures and one person of the Messiah.

->CAPNIO,<-

**H**is is one thing among others that you must strive hardest to prove against the more recent Jews through their ancient scriptures: namely, that the Messiah was to be true God, as well as true man. GALATINUS: I will try to do that according to my strength, and indeed more effectively because they deny it so obstinately. HOOGSTRATEN: In order that what you are about to say concerning the divinity of the Messiah may be better understood, it is first necessary that you explain what is signified by the name Messiah. GALATINUS: Just as there are (as has been said) three persons in the divinity, which, although they are distinguished from one another without separation, are nevertheless united to each other without confusion through a mutual indwelling which the Greeks call <term>perichoresis</term> <note>original: περιχώρησιν; a theological term describing the mutual indwelling of the three persons of the Trinity.</note>. In the same way, in the one Christ, we confess there to be three substances: namely, the divinity, the rational soul, and the human body. These are united without confusion in such a way that they are inseparably distinguished. And just as the three divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: "hypostases," meaning the distinct persons or "realities" of the Trinity.</note> are one God, so these three—divinity, soul, and body—constitute the one Messiah promised in the Law, who is nothing other than these three. For he is both perfect God and perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and human flesh. However, we do not say he is composed of these as a man is composed of soul and body, or as a body is composed of the four elements. For that which is "composed" is indeed something different from the parts out of which it is composed. Christ, however, or the Messiah, is neither something other than those parts from which he consists, nor anything else but those very things which are united in him. For as John of Damascus says in the forty-seventh chapter of his book *On the Tradition of the Orthodox Faith*: **We confess the same one to be, and to be called, perfect God from divinity and perfect man from humanity, both out of two natures and in two natures.** <note>original: "ἐκ θεότητος καὶ ἀνθρωπότητος θεὸν τέλειον, καὶ ἄνθρωπον τέλειον τὸν αὐτὸν, καὶ ἓν καὶ ἐκ δύο τε καὶ ἐν δυοὶ φύσεσιν ὁμολογοῦμεν."</note> This same one, therefore, who is both perfect God and perfect man, can be called in Hebrew <term>Massiah</term> <note>original: משיח</note>, in Chaldaic <term>Meshicha</term> <note>original: משיחא</note>, in Greek <term>Christos</term> <note>original: χριστὸς</note>, and in Latin *Unctus* [Anointed]. The same John of Damascus proves this most beautifully in the same place, saying: **We say the name "Christ" refers to the person, not signifying one aspect alone, but signifying the two natures. For he anointed himself; anointing as God—who anointed the body with his own divinity—and being anointed as man. For he is both this and that, and the divinity is the anointing of the humanity.** <note>original: "τὸ χριστὸς ὄνομα τῆς ὑποστάσεως λέγομεν, οὐ μονοτρόπως μὲν ἀλλὰ τῶν δύο φύσεων ὑπάρχον σημαντικὸν, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἑαυτὸν ἔχρισεν. χρίων μὲν ὡς θεὸς, ὃς ἔχρισε τὸ σῶμα τῇ θεότητι αὐτοῦ, χριόμενος δὲ ὡς ἄνθρωπος, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐστὶ ὅπερ κἀκεῖνο, χρίσις δὲ ἡ θεότης τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος."</note> This means we call "Christ" the name of the individual subject, existing as significant of the two natures, not just one. For he himself anointed himself: anointing indeed as God, who anointed the body with his divinity; yet being anointed as man, for he is both this and that. Moreover, the anointing of the humanity is the divinity. CAPNIO: These things are indeed beautiful. But because the Jews now...

In his words, not only is this name "Messiah"—which is the same as "Anointed"—clearly expressed (for indeed, he is called Messiah or Christ from the act of anointing), but it is shown that regarding his humanity, he was to be anointed both as King and as Priest with the oil of gladness—that is, the anointing of divinity—above his participants or associates, meaning above all other men who participate with him in the condition of one and the same human nature. Furthermore, the two natures, namely the divine and the human, which were to be <term>hypostatically</term> <note>original: "hypostatice"; a theological term meaning the union of two natures in one individual person or "hypostasis."</note> united in him, are most openly suggested. For when he says, *Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, a scepter of equity is the scepter of your Kingdom,* he certainly implies that the one he addresses is God, and thus he openly confesses his divinity. But when he immediately says to the same person: *You have loved justice and hated impiety, therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your participants or associates,* he undoubtedly confesses the same person to be man as well, openly manifesting his humanity. For since there is only one God, it would certainly be a crime to say that He has either a God or an associate. But if the more recent Jews do not believe that this prophet said these things concerning this name "Messiah" and concerning the dual nature—divine and human—implied by it, let them hear the sayings of their ancient Teachers, who spoke more openly about the two natures and the single person of the Messiah. ### BOOK THREE

Jacob took three stones, and said: "If God unites his name over me, just as he united it over my fathers, let them all become one." He stood, and found that all had been made one. As it is said in Genesis, chapter twenty-eight: *And he took the stone.* <note>Genesis 28:11. In the biblical text, Jacob takes stones (plural) for his pillow, but later the text says "he took the stone" (singular), leading to a Midrashic interpretation that the stones merged into one.</note> Indeed, by this word he teaches that they were all made one. But the Masters <note>Referring to the Rabbis of the Talmudic or Midrashic tradition.</note> said less, that there were two stones. This is from the Midrash. Whether he took three stones or two, or perhaps first three and later two, in either case the union of the Messiah is excellently signified. For the union of two stones signified the union of two natures in Christ, namely the divinity and the humanity. The union of three stones, however, designated the union of three substances in the one person of Christ: namely the Word, the soul, and the body.

This union is also excellently attested by what is said in the book of the Sanhedrin, in the chapter titled *Helec* <note>The 11th chapter of Tractate Sanhedrin in the Babylonian Talmud, which discusses the afterlife and the Messiah.</note>, regarding that passage from Isaiah, chapter twenty-three: *And it shall come to pass in that day, that Tyre <note>original Hebrew: צור, Czor</note> shall be forgotten seventy years, like the days <gloss>or: like the days of the King</gloss> of one.* <note>Isaiah 23:15. The Latin "unitionis" or "uniti" here interprets the Hebrew "echad" (one) as "united."</note> Who is this "united King"? It is said that this is the King Messiah. But the Rabbi <note>Referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi), the primary redactor of the Mishnah, often called simply "Rabbi."</note> said: "This <note>original: זה, Ze</note> is two (namely natures) and three generations (that is, substances)." As it is said in the seventy-first Psalm: *They shall fear you with the sun and before the moon, for a generation and generations.* <note>Psalm 72:5 in modern numbering; 71 in the Vulgate.</note>

**The Gloss of Rabbi Solomon.** <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> It is as if he says: O Messiah, concerning whom it is written "Before the sun *Yinnon* <note>original: ינון, yinnon; a name for the Messiah derived from Psalm 72:17, meaning "he shall sprout" or "continue."</note> is his name" (that is, the son or the begotten), the Israelites shall fear you; and "before the moon," that is, before the Kingdom of the house of David, which is likened to the moon, as it is written in Psalm eighty-eight: *Like the moon it shall be established forever.* <note>Psalm 89:37 in modern numbering.</note> Likewise, another gloss of the same man on that passage of Isaiah: *Like the days of the united King.* He says: "The days of David were seventy years, and I do not know what this sign means that is given here."

Since these things are so, it must be carefully noted how the Talmud, in this aforementioned tradition, says that the Messiah is a "united King." Then, what is more wonderful is how this Rabbi (who is called "Rabbi" by excellence <note>original: antonomasice; referring to his title as the supreme teacher.</note> and is alone held holy) insinuates what he had received from the fathers: the matter and form of the union of the Messiah. For he says that *Ze* <note>original: זה, Ze; meaning "this" or "this one."</note>—that is, this one, namely the Messiah about whom the preceding discourse was made—or *Ze* (meaning that which refers to the union of the King Messiah) is "two": namely God and man, or the two natures united in the Messiah, the divine and the human. And "three generations" are the three substances of these natures: namely the Word of God, the rational soul, and the human body.

He proves this through the prophet, who, addressing the Messiah in the spirit, says in Psalm seventy-one: *They shall fear you* (namely the Israelites, as they explain it, or whoever else) *with the sun*—namely that sun of which it is said in Psalm eighty-three: *The Lord God is a sun and a shield, he will give grace and glory.* <note>Psalm 84:11; original Hebrew: שמש ומגן יהוה אלהים חן וכבוד יתן, Shemesh u-magen Yehovah Elohim chen ve-khavod yitten.</note> In this phrase where he says "They shall fear you with the sun," he insinuates the conjunction of the divinity and humanity of the Messiah. But what he adds, *And before the moon*, that is, before the Kingdom...

**BOOK [THREE]**

David (as Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "Rabbi Selomo," referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> explains) refers to the Church, which is compared to the moon, according to what is written in the sixth chapter of the Song of Songs: *Who is she that looks forth as the morning, or Venus: fair as the moon, clear as the sun?* <note>Song of Songs 6:10. The author uses "Venus" to translate "aurora" or the morning star.</note> Then, let them see our Teacher the Holy One <note>original: "Rabbenum Haccados," referring to Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note> openly discussing this same matter. In the book which he titled *Gale Razeya* <note>original Hebrew: גלי רזיא, meaning "The Revealer of Secrets." This was a mystical work often cited by Christian Hebraists of the Renaissance.</note>, regarding that passage in the ninth chapter of Isaiah, *Of the increase of his government,* <note>Isaiah 9:7. The Hebrew word "le-marbeh" (למרבה) is written with a "closed" letter Mem, which was interpreted by mystics as a sign of a hidden mystery.</note> he says among other things: Just as the letter *He* (ה) is composed of a *Daleth* (ד) and a *Vav* (ו), so the King Messiah is composed of divinity and humanity. And just as these two *He*s are two *Daleth*s, and from these proceed two *Vav*s, like two sons who arise from them; so in the substance of the King Messiah two sonships are found, one of which is of divinity, by which he is the Son of God; the other will be of humanity, by which he will be the son of the prophetess, of whom Isaiah spoke in the eighth chapter: *And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.* <note>Isaiah 8:3.</note> And just as each of these letters, *Daleth* and *Vav*, which make up the *He*, is distinct from the other, even though both are one letter; so in the Messiah, the substance of divinity will be distinct from the substance of humanity, and vice versa. These two joined together are the Messiah. These are the words of him whom the Jews call "our holy master." From what has been said, therefore, it is manifest that this name "Messiah" signifies two natures, namely the divine and the human, and encompasses three things in one person: namely, a human body, a rational soul, and the Word of God.

### *What the Word of God is according to the Hebrews, and that the Word of God is of the same substance <term>consubstantial (original Greek: ὁμοούσιον)</term> with God. Chapter III.*

->CAPNIO,<- <note>"Capnio" is the Greek-derived nickname (meaning "smoky") for the famous humanist scholar Johannes Reuchlin, who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

<margin>The triple Word.</margin> To prove the divinity of the Messiah, it is necessary above all to say what the ancient Jews thought about this "Word of God." GALATINUS: It must therefore be noted that just as man has a triple word—that which is written on paper, that which is uttered by the mouth, and that which lies hidden in the mind—it is this last one that more truly deserves the name "word," since it is the cause and principle of the others. For no actions of men would exist unless they were first spoken in the mind. Therefore, the saying of a certain Arabic poet is not to be entirely despised when he says: *The word is indeed in the heart, but the tongue was made to be the heart's interpreter.* In the same way, according to the Hebrews, God himself—in whose image man was made—is said to have a triple word. For he has the word written in the books of the prophets; he also has the word which is uttered by the mouths of the holy ones and the teachers, concerning which he himself says in the first chapter of Jeremiah: *Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.* <note>Jeremiah 1:9.</note> He also has a word within himself, from himself, and not from elsewhere. Concerning this, the Psalmist speaks in Psalm 33:

For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his work is done in faithfulness. He loves righteousness and justice; the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host. <note>Psalm 33:4–6.</note> *That is, Because the word of God is upright, and all his works are in faith, loving justice and judgment, the earth is full of the mercy of God. By the word of God the heavens were made, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host.* This word of God, therefore, through which not only the four elements but even the heavens themselves were made, is nothing other than that **Beginning** <term>Rescith: Hebrew for "beginning" or "first principle"</term>, of which it is written in *the first chapter of Genesis:* **In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.** <note>Genesis 1:1.</note> That is, in the beginning God created heaven and earth. For it is established that this "beginning" is nothing other than the begotten wisdom of God. This is stated in the persona of the divine wisdom itself in *the eighth chapter of Proverbs:* **The Lord possessed me as the beginning of his way, before his works of old.** <note>Proverbs 8:22.</note>

> *That is, God possessed me as the beginning of his way, before his works, from then, or before then.*

From this it is clear that they are entirely the same thing in reality, though they differ in name: the "beginning" by which the world was created, and the "wisdom" which God possessed. Since what is here called the "beginning of his way" (that is, of his creation) becomes that very Word of God by which (as was said) the heavens were made. Concerning this, the 104th Psalm—embracing all the works of God (which Holy Scripture divides by various names in different places) into one title of power—says: **How manifold are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all.** <note>Psalm 104:24.</note> That is, *How multiplied are your works, O God; you have made them all in wisdom, or through wisdom.* You see, therefore, that whether you say "the beginning," or "the word," or "the hand," or "the arm of God," or anything else of this kind, these do not indicate a diversity of things, but only the one power and wisdom of God, by which he made all things. It must also be carefully noted that when it is said in the words mentioned a little earlier, *Because the word of God is upright, and all his works are in faith,* it is immediately added concerning the same word, *Loving justice and judgment.* This is to openly suggest that the Word we are dealing with here is a rational substance and <term>consubstantial: of the same essence (Greek: ὁμοούσιον)</term> with God. Indeed, to love justice and judgment is a property of a rational and intellectual substance. For that reason, the Word of God itself is frequently called the "eye" or "eyes" of God. For where the Lord speaks concerning the Jews in *the 7th chapter of Ezekiel:* **My eye will not spare you.** <note>Ezekiel 7:9.</note> *That is, And my eye shall not take pity upon you.* So Jonathan in the <term>Chaldean translation: The Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</term> says: **And my Word will not have mercy upon him.** <note>The Aramaic "Memri" (My Word) is used here as a personified divine intermediary.</note> That is, *And my word will not have mercy upon you.* Behold, where the prophet, speaking in the person of God, placed "my eye," there the Chaldean translator said "my word." Moreover, in saying, *And my word had mercy upon them,* it is clearly shown that the Word of God has life, since having mercy is a property of a living thing. And this is what is said in *the 1st chapter of John: What was made, in him was life.* Also that which is written in *the 24th chapter of Jeremiah:* **And I will set my eyes upon them for good.** <note>Jeremiah 24:6.</note> *This*

### BOOK III ###

<center>114</center>

it is written: **And I will set my eyes upon them for good.** <note>Jeremiah 24:6.</note> In the same way, Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic paraphrases of the Prophets known as the Targum.</note> translated this into Chaldaic <term>Chaldaic: an older term for Aramaic, the language spoken by Jews after the Babylonian exile</term> as: **And I will set my word upon them for good.** <note>original: ואשוי מימרי עליהון לטבתא</note> That is, "And I will set my word upon them for good." Also, regarding the opposite, which the Lord says against them in *Amos, chapter 9:* **And I will set my eyes upon them for evil, and not for good.** <note>Amos 9:4.</note> Thus Jonathan himself explained it in Chaldaic: **And I will set my word upon them for evil, and not for good.** <note>original: ואשוי מימרי אליהון לבישא ולא לטבא</note>

<margin>How often the Word of God is mentioned.</margin>
That is, "And I will set my word upon them for evil, and not for good." To further suggest the consubstantiality <term>consubstantiality: the theological doctrine that the Word/Son shares the same divine essence or "substance" as God the Father</term> of this Word with God, the Word of God itself is sometimes called in the Holy Scriptures the **face of God**, sometimes the **mouth of God**, and sometimes the **hand of God**. Indeed, it is called the "face of God" in *Jeremiah, chapter five*, where it is said: **Will you not tremble before my face, I who have placed the sand as a bound for the sea, an eternal decree which it shall not pass?** <note>Jeremiah 5:22.</note> <note>original: אם מפני לא תחילו אשר שמתי חול גבול לים חק עולם ולא יעברונהו</note> That is, "If you will not dread my face, I who have set the sand as the limit for the sea, an eternal precept that shall not pass away." Jonathan himself translated this into Chaldaic as: **Will you not tremble before my word, I who have placed the sand as a bound for the sea.** 

As for it being called the "mouth of God," this is held from what Isaiah produced in the voice of God in *chapter 48*, saying: **The former things I declared from that time, and they went out from my mouth.** <note>Isaiah 48:3.</note> <note>original: הראשונות מאז הגדתי ומפי יצאו</note> That is, "The prior things I announced from then, and they went out from my mouth." Jonathan turned this into Chaldaic thus: **The ancient things from then I showed, and from my word they went forth.** <note>original: קדמיתא מבבין הויתי וממימרי נפקא</note> That is, "The ancient things from then I announced, and from my word they proceeded." Similar to this is what is read in *Jeremiah 15*: **Therefore thus says the Lord: If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me; and if you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth.** <note>Jeremiah 15:19.</note> <note>original: לכן כה אמר יהוה אם תשוב ואשיבך לפני תעמוד ואם תוציא יקר מזולל בפי תהיה</note> That is, "On account of this, thus says God: If you are converted, I will convert you (or, I will make you rest), you shall stand before my face (or, you shall stand in my presence). And if you lead forth (or extract) the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth." Jonathan also translated this into Chaldaic: **Therefore thus says the Lord: If you return, I will bring you back, and you shall minister before me; and if you return the wicked so that they become righteous, you shall fulfill the pleasure of my word.** <note>original: בגין בדן אמר יהוה אם תתוב ואת יבינך קדמי תשמש ואם תתיב רשיעיא למהוי צדיקיא רעות מימרי תקיים</note> That is, "On account of this, thus says God: If you are converted, I will convert you, you shall minister before me; and if you convert the impious so that they become just, you shall fulfill the good pleasure of my word." Where the prophet put "precious" and "vile," the translator here explained "just" and "impious." And where the prophet said "mouth of God," the translator rendered it as His "word." 

Finally, that the Word of God is called the "hand of God" is most clearly evident from what is read in *Isaiah, chapter forty-eight*: **My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens with a span.** <note>Isaiah 48:13.</note> <note>original: אף ידי יסרה ארץ וימיני טפחה שמים</note> For Jonathan explains this in the Targum thus: **By my word also I founded the earth, and by my power (or my strength) I measured the heavens.** <note>original: אנא במימרי שכלליתא ארעא ובגבורתי תלית שמיא</note> Again, in the same prophet, *chapter forty-five*, it is said: **I made the earth, and created man upon it; my hands stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host.** <note>Isaiah 45:12.</note> <note>original: אנכי עשיתי ארץ ואדם עליה בראתי אני ידי נטו שמים וכל צבאם צויתי</note> That is, "I made the earth, and I created Adam upon it. My hands extended the heavens, and I commanded all their host." The same translator explained it thus in Chaldaic: **I by my word made the earth, and man upon it I created; I by my power extended...** <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the end of the page.</note>

"I stretched out the heavens and all their host by my word." <note>original: תלית שמיא וכל חיליהון במימרי</note> That is, "I made the earth by my word, or through my word, and I created humans upon it. I, in my strength, stretched out the heavens, and I established all their powers." From all these things that have now been said, it is clearly evident that the **Word of God**—which is the same as the **Wisdom of God**, through which He created and perfected the world from nothing—is of exactly the same substance as God Himself.

<margin>The heretical exposition of the more recent Jews.</margin>

**CAPNIO:** <note>Capnio is the scholarly nickname for Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist of the Renaissance. In this dialogue, he represents the inquiring scholar.</note> Regarding that passage in *Proverbs, chapter 8: The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his way.* You have explained this as referring to the uncreated Wisdom of God, which is the Word through which God made all things. However, the more recent Jews assert that this "Wisdom" is the Mosaic Law. They say that the Law itself speaks there, saying: *I love those who love me.* Since this is entirely contrary to Catholic truth and is heretical, you ought to refute it using their own authentic scriptures.

**GALATINUS:** <note>Pietro Galatino, the author of this work, who argues that Christian truths are hidden within Jewish mystical and legal texts.</note> This is indeed of such great absurdity that it does not even need refutation. For if the Law of Moses is capable of neither love nor hate—except as other inanimate things of this kind that are written on parchment—how can they say that it says of itself, *I love those who love me*? To love is a property of a rational nature. Furthermore, if the Law of Moses itself began at the time when it took its beginning of existence on Mount Sinai, in what way could it have been with God before the start of all things? How could it say of itself, *The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his way, before he did anything,* along with the rest of the passage?

Likewise, they say regarding this place that this word <term>קנך (Kanan): a Hebrew root meaning to acquire, create, or possess</term> *Kanan* is ambiguous; sometimes it means *to buy*, and sometimes *to possess*. They say it means *to possess* in the place where Melchizedek, blessing Abraham, said in *Genesis 14*: "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth." <note>original Hebrew: ברוך אברם לאל עליון קונה שמים וארץ</note> But here, they say the word <term>קנך (kanan)</term> is the same as *to buy*. Therefore, they must be asked: If God "bought" the heaven and the earth and the Law itself, who was the seller of these things? Certainly, they can name no one.

Therefore, it is shameful even to dream of such things, let alone say them. Let them cease even thinking such things and, according to the ancient traditions of their own Doctors, believe: that Solomon in this place was not mindful of the Mosaic Law, but of that very Wisdom of God through which God fashioned the world. Let them now read what is written in the book <term>Sanhedrin: a major section of the Talmud dealing with law and the high court</term> in the chapter <term>Dine Mamonoth: "Monetary Laws," a specific section of the Talmud</term> regarding that passage in *Proverbs, chapter 9*:

"Wisdom has built her house, she has hewn out her seven columns; she has sacrificed her victim, she has mixed her wine; she has even set her table; she has sent out her maidens to call from the heights of the city." <note>original Hebrew: חכמות בנתה ביתה חצבה עמודיה שבעה : טבחה טבחה מסכה יינה : אף ערכה שלחנה : שלחה נערותיה יה תקרא על גפי מרומי קרת</note>

For there they explain these things thus: "Wisdom has built her house." This is <term>מדתו (Middatho): His attribute or property</term> the property of the Holy and Blessed God Himself, who created the entire world in wisdom, or through wisdom. Just as it is said in *Psalm 103*: "How multiplied are your works, O God, you have made all things in wisdom." She has hewn out...

## *That God is the Word, and the Word of God is God himself.*
### Chapter 4.
### CAPNIO,

**E**ven if in the preceding matters you have sufficiently and abundantly proven that the Word of God is of the same substance as God, from which it necessarily follows both that God is the Word and that the Word of God is God Himself; nevertheless, so that the very stiff necks of the younger Jews may be further crushed, I beg you: would you be willing now to show more clearly that God is the Word, and the Word of God is God? 

<margin>GAL.</margin> That God is indeed the Word is evident most especially from this: where Isaiah in chapter 45 says, *Israel shall be saved in the Lord <note>The text uses "tetragrammaton" to refer to the four-letter divine name, YHWH.</note> with an everlasting salvation*, or an eternal one. <note>original Hebrew: ישׂראל נושע ביהוה תשועת עולמים</note> Thus the Targum of Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the prophetic books of the Bible.</note> says: *Israel shall be delivered in the Word <term>Memra: The Aramaic word for "Word," used in the Targums to refer to God’s presence or agency without implying a physical form.</term>, or through the Word of the Lord, with an eternal deliverance.* <note>original Aramaic: ישׂראל אתפריק במימרא דיי פורקן עלמיא</note> Where Isaiah said "In the Lord"—a name attributed to none but God—the Aramaic interpreter translated it as "in the Word of God." By this, he openly shows that God is the Word. 

Likewise, where it is said in Hosea, chapter 1: *And I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Lord their God.* <note>original Hebrew: ואת בית יהודה ארחם והושעתים ביהוה אלהיהם</note> So the same interpreter turned it into Aramaic: *And upon the house of Judah I will have mercy, and I will deliver them in the Word of the Lord their God.* <note>original Aramaic: ועל דבית יהודה ארחם ואפריקינון במימרא דיי אלההון</note> This is also seen in what Isaiah says in chapter 8: *And the Lord added to speak to me still.* <note>original Hebrew: ויוסף יהוה דבר אלי עוד</note> Jonathan himself translated this into Aramaic as: *And the Word of the Lord added to speak with me still.* <note>original Aramaic: ואוסיף מימרא דיי למלל לי עוד</note> 

Likewise, what the same prophet said in chapter 41: *Fear not, for I am with you.* <note>original Hebrew: אל תירא כי עמך אני</note> Thus he translated it: *Fear not, for my Word is for your help.* Also, what is said in the same place: *Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel; I have helped you, says the Lord, and your redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.* <note>original Hebrew: אל־תירא תולעת יעקב מתי ישׂראל אני עזרתיך נאם יהוה וגאלך קדוש ישׂראל</note> This is:

It is clearly follows that God Himself is the Word, and the Word of God is God. This was the point to be proven.

### CAPNIO,

"Now, through what will they be healed, or in what shall we believe?" He said to him, "He shall heal them and deliver them from their destructions, and with these wonders we shall believe in him and honor him." He said to him, "Why did he not say, 'He shall send his word and heal *you*,' but rather 'heal *them*'?" Because it appears to me that he was speaking of specific individuals. He answered him, "You have spoken the truth; for the Word came to heal everyone, but none received it except the individuals who were the life of the miracle <note>Likely referring to the spiritual life or the 'remnant' of Israel.</note> from among the masses: the fishermen, the servants of the sea." This is: *He will send his word and heal them, and snatch them from their plagues* <note>Psalm 107:20</note>. <term>Rabbi Samuel the Levite</term> says: "The Word of God is His messenger." Regarding which it is written: *Truly, my word is like fire, says God.* And this is what was said: *Let your word come, and we will honor you.* <note>A paraphrase often attributed in these polemics to the people's response to a prophet.</note> Certainly when the Word of God comes, which is His messenger, then we shall honor him. <term>Rabbi Saul</term> said: "Did not the prophets come, and we killed them and shed their blood? How then shall we now receive His word? He answered: "This is (as I feel) because he was speaking of a part, and of certain people only, and not of everyone; which is signaled according to the property of the <term>Hebrew language</term> <note>original: "Hebraei sermonis"</note> in the word *Them*." He said to him: "You certainly speak the truth. For His word came to heal everyone in general, not just some in part. But it was not received except by certain individuals who were considered among everyone else to be of a coarser wit: men who were fishermen and those who work upon the sea." And this is what was said: *Those embarking upon the sea in ships, doing work in great waters, they have seen the work of God.* <note>Psalm 107:23</note> Those men indeed, if you consider it rightly, did not seem fit to be able to admit anything intellectual—or pertaining to the intellect—on account of the rudeness of their senses. Those men, I say, received the truth of the prophecy and the vision, because they believed in His word. And this is what is written: *He believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.* <note>Genesis 15:6</note> From these things it is clear that God was going to send His word, that is, His son, the true <term>Messiah</term>, so that He might heal the whole human race. Yet not everyone was to be healed, but only those who would receive Him and believe in Him; and especially common men and fishermen, as the <term>Apostles</term> were.

<header>BOOK THREE</header>

# That Jesus the Nazarene, the true Messiah, is the Word of God, sent by the eternal Father for the salvation of mankind.

## Chapter VI.

### CAPNIO

I would like you to prove this conclusion: namely, that our Lord Jesus the Nazarene was the true **Word of God**, and consequently the true Messiah, sent into the world by the eternal Father for the salvation of men. **GALATINUS:** So that I say nothing myself in this place, hear the words of **Libertatus** (for such is the man’s name) **Cominetus**, a Spaniard recently converted from Judaism to the faith. He is a man not only exceptionally learned in the divine scriptures but also skilled in fourteen languages. In explaining that passage of the **147th Psalm**, *He sends his word and melts them* <note>original: ישלח דברו וימסם — Psalm 147:18. Note that the Latin text mistakenly cites the healing of "them" (eas/eos) which appears in Psalm 107, but the Hebrew text provided here specifically quotes Psalm 147:18 regarding the melting of ice/snow.</note>, *his spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow*, he says the following:

<margin>"He shall melt"</margin>
*He sends his word and melts them.* He should have said, "He shall speak," and so on, and not "He shall send his word." For "speaking" is more appropriate to a word than "sending." As it is said: *And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light.* He did not say, "And God sent his word to make or create the light," because the language of "sending" does not apply unless there is a **messenger** <term>Shaliach: A sent one or agent; the Hebrew implies a physical manifestation or representative</term>. As it says: *Behold, I send to you Elijah the prophet.* This means that God used to send the prophets to announce His word and show His wonders. We see this also in the **Bronze Serpent** which God commanded to be made by the hand of Moses His prophet in order to heal Israel when they looked upon it. For it would have been more appropriate in those times to heal them by a word alone, so that the people would see His wonders and believe in Him, rather than with that serpent, which placed a doubt in the hearts of the people that it might be a work of sorcery—what are today called "magicians" <note>original: מוגיצי - likely a transliteration of the Latin "magici"</note>. Truly, if He had healed them by a word alone, He would have removed all doubts from their hearts. But what appears to me from this verse is that David prophesied the coming of **Jesus, the Messiah of our Righteousness**, by saying "His Word." For the truth is that He would be His Word and the announcer of His words. And just as speech is not a thing separate from one's essence, so He is not separate from God. And this is why it says, "He shall come, heal, and [bring] His health." For it should have said, "The word and its health shall come," but instead it shows that He, the Exalted, and the Word are one thing. Those who honor the Word, honor Him; and those who honor Him, honor the connection, for they are inseparable in their essence. And this is the Word which was prophesied to come to heal the sick and revive the dead by a word. The Word itself lived, as we see in Jesus, the Messiah of our Righteousness, who healed the sick and revived **Lazarus** <note>original: אלעזר (Eleazar)</note> four days after his death. These things are not appropriate for anyone except God. And immediately following this, it says: *His spirit shall blow and the waters shall flow.* It seems there is no connection at all between the healing of bodies and the flowing of waters. But understand how David prophesied the truth by saying "shall blow" <note>or "return/rest"</note> and did not say "He shall cause to return." This means that God would cause His Holy Spirit to rest with Him and at His right hand. After this, "waters shall flow," meaning that the **Holy Waters** <term>Mayim HaKedoshim: Here referring to the waters of Baptism</term> would remain to save His people, and they are the cause of our salvation. As it is said: *And you shall draw water with joy from the wells of salvation.* Through these, God is attached to us, as it is said: *When you pass through the waters, I am with you.* He did not say "through the seas," but "through the waters," meaning the

<margin>"He shall melt them"</margin>
**Holy Waters**. This is: *He sends his word and heals them.* It seems it should have been said: "He shall speak His word," but not "He shall send His word." For it is more fitting for a word to be pronounced and brought forth than to be sent, which seems to be the role of a messenger. And the Scripture agrees with this matter, saying:

God said, *Let there be light: and there was light.* <note>original: "Sit lux: & fuit lux" — Genesis 1:3</note> However, he did not say, "God sent his word to create the light," because a "sending" cannot be fulfilled without a **messenger** <term>Shaliach: In Jewish law, a person authorized to act on behalf of another; here applied to the Word as an agent of God</term>. For this reason it was said: *Behold, I send to you Elijah the prophet* <note>original: "Ecce mitto ad uos Eliam prophetam" — Malachi 4:5</note>; indicating that God sends prophets to announce his word and to make manifest his wonders. Furthermore, the **bronze serpent** <note>In Numbers 21:8-9, Moses was commanded to make a bronze serpent on a pole; those bitten by snakes who looked at it were healed. The text argues this physical object was used instead of a direct "word" to prevent the people from confusing God's power with magic.</note> increases the doubt—that serpent which God commanded to be made by the hand of his prophet Moses, so that the people of Israel might be healed when they looked upon it. For it appears more reasonable and fitting, especially in those times, that God ought to have healed the people by a word rather than by the sight of a serpent—a thing which could have led to a suspicion of incantation and **magic**. And yet, even then, he did not heal by a word.

How then does it fit, what the prophet says: *He shall send his word, and heal them*? <note>original: "Mittet uerbum suum, & sanabit eos" — Psalm 107:20</note> But it is resolved. For as far as I myself perceive: David in this place prophesied the coming of Jesus the Messiah, our Just One. He is rightly called His **Word**. But the truth is: Jesus is the Word of God, and he is the messenger of the words of God. And just as the Word of God is not something distinct from the essence of God, so also the Messiah is not entirely distinct from the divine substance. And this is what is written: *Your word shall come, and we shall honor you.* <note>original: "Veniet uerbum tuum, & honorificabimus te"</note> If the Word were entirely divided from Him, it would have said: "And we shall honor *it*." By these words it is clearly shown that God and the Word of God are one and the same, since they are held as the same: to honor both God and the Word of God, as being in no way distinct in essence.

And this is the Word about which it was prophesied that he would come to heal the sick and to raise the dead by a word. And indeed, he was to perform all these things by a word. Nevertheless, he was the Word itself. All these things were fulfilled in **Jesus the Messiah**, our Just One; by whose works almost innumerable sick people were healed, and **Lazarus** was raised from the dead, even after the fourth day of his death. And these things belong to God alone.

What follows immediately is consistent with our exposition: *His spirit shall blow* <note>original: "Sedebit spiritus eius" — The Latin text uses "sedebit" (shall sit), but the Hebrew root in Psalm 147:18 is "yashev," which in this context means "to cause to blow." The translator is likely playing on the double meaning of "dwelling/sitting" and "blowing."</note>, *and the waters shall flow.* For even if they seem to have no connection—namely, healing the sick and the flowing of waters—it is nevertheless the truest sense of the prophet. He also did not speak without a **mystery** <term>Mysterium: A hidden spiritual meaning or sacrament</term> when he said, *His spirit shall sit* (or blow); he did not say, "His spirit shall return," demonstrating that God ought to make his Holy Spirit "sit" or dwell with Him. And he added: *And the waters shall flow*, signifying that the holy waters were to remain for the salvation of his people. These waters, indeed, are the causes of our salvation. Just as it is written: *You shall draw waters from the fountain of salvation.* <note>original: "Haurietis aquas de fonte salutis" — Isaiah 12:3</note> For through the intervention of the holy waters, God is joined with us. As it is written: *When you pass through those waters, I am with you.* <note>original: "Cum transieris per aquas illas, ego tecum sum" — Isaiah 43:2</note> And he did not say "through waters" only, but "through *those* waters." He was demonstrating that he spoke not of just any waters, but of the holy waters, which are the waters of **baptism**.

All these things were said by the aforementioned Teacher, most learned of the Hebrews, recently converted to the truth of the Christian faith. By these things he excellently proves that Jesus the Nazarene [is the Messiah]...

### *That the Messiah is the Son of God, and also concerning the word* <note>Hebrew: בר</note> bar: *and what the Firstborn is, according to the Hebrews themselves. Chapter VI.*

## CAPNIO,

**A**lthough from what you have said, it follows that the Messiah is the Son of God. For if the Messiah himself is the Word of God, he must also undoubtedly be the Son of God. However, so that the faithlessness of the Jews of our age may be more and more overcome by their own weapons, you ought to demonstrate more expressly through their scriptures that the Messiah himself is the Son of God.

**GAL.** First, let that Psalm be brought against them which begins, *Why do the nations rage?* <note>original: "Quare fremuerunt gentes" — Psalm 2:1</note> This is interpreted by the ancient Jews as referring to the Messiah, as **Rabbi Selomone** <note>Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> bears witness, who says of it: "Our masters have interpreted this Psalm concerning the Messiah." Therefore, at the end of the same Psalm, it reads: <note>original Hebrew: נשקו בר פן יאנף ותאבדו דרך כי יבער כמעט אפו. אשרי כל חוסי בו</note> *Kiss the son, lest he be angry, and you perish from the way. When his wrath is kindled but a little, blessed are all they that put their trust in him.* <note>Psalm 2:12</note> David was therefore warning the judges of the earth to receive this "kiss" of the Son of God. This is shown by **Rabbi Abraham Auen Azra** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish rabbi, philosopher, and biblical commentator.</note>, who, explaining this, says: <note>original Hebrew: נשקו בר</note> *Nasfecu bar*, that is, "kiss the son." Behold, serve the Lord—this is in contrast to what he had said above, namely, [those who stood] *against his Messiah.* The explanation of this word <term>Bar: An Aramaic word for "son," often used in the Hebrew Bible in poetic or specific contexts, whereas "Ben" is the standard Hebrew term.</term> *Bar* is the same as that found in Proverbs, chapter thirty-one, where it is said: <note>original Hebrew: מה ברי ומה בר בטני ומה בר נדרי</note> *What, my son? and what, the son of my womb? and what, the son of my vows?* <note>Proverbs 31:2</note> And so it is written in this same Psalm: <note>original Hebrew: בני אתה</note> *You are my son.* <note>Psalm 2:7</note> These are the words of the same Rabbi Abraham. In the **Midras tillim** <note>Midrash Tehillim: A homiletic commentary (midrash) on the Book of Psalms, also known as Midrash Shocher Tov.</note> as well, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, it is said concerning these same words: <note>original Hebrew: נשקו בר הוא מה דכתיב. חסד ואמת נפגשו צדק ושלום נשקו . אמר רב משל למלך שכעס על בני המדינה והלכו בני המדינה ופייסו את בן המלך שיפייס את המלך והלך את הבן ופייס את אביו כיון שנתפייסו לבנו הלכו בני המדינה לומר הימנון למלך אמר להם לי אתם הימנון לכו ואמרוהו לבני שאלמלא הוא כבר אבדתי את המדינה חיי נשקו בר</note> That is: This is what is written in Psalm 85: *Mercy and truth have met together; righteousness and peace have kissed.* <note>Psalm 85:10</note> The Rabbi said: This is like a King who was angry with the citizens of a city. The citizens went and pleaded with the King's son to appease the King. The son went and appeased his father. Once the King had been appeased through his son, the citizens went to give thanks to the King. But the King said to them: "To me you [give] thanks?

...do you give thanks? Go and give thanks to my son. For if he had not been there, I would have already destroyed the city. And this is what was said: *Kiss the son* <note>Psalm 2:12</note>. Thus far the tradition. **HOG.** Our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible, the standard version used by the Church at the time.</note> translates this as: *Lay hold of instruction*. **GAL.** The author of our edition, deceived by the ambiguity of words, translated many things quite differently than the Hebrew truth contains. For although this word <term>בר</term> *Bar* <note>The Hebrew word "Bar" is indeed ambiguous; in Aramaic it means "son," but in Hebrew it can also mean "pure," "grain," or "instruction."</note> sometimes signifies "son," sometimes "discipline" or "doctrine," sometimes "grain," sometimes "pure" or "clean," and sometimes "chosen." As Saint **Jerome** <note>Hieronymus (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Vulgate.</note> also seems to believe, when he wrote to Pammachius in his apology against Rufinus: "*Bar* among the Hebrews has various meanings. For it is called *Bar* as "son," such as *Bar-Jona*, that is, son of a dove; and *Bartholomew*, that is, son of Ptolemy; and *Barnabas*, that is, son of the prophet; and *Barchineus*, and *Barchiseus*, and *Barabbas*. It also means wheat, and a bundle of thorns, and the chosen one, and the pure." These are the words of Jerome. 

Nevertheless, in this place, *Bar* is not understood as anything but "son," just as the aforementioned **Rabbi Abraham** <note>Likely Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a major Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> understands it in his exposition of this text. And although the Chaldean interpreter <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> whom the Jews now frequently have in hand—whether it be the blind Rabbi Joseph, as some prefer, or Rabbi Aquila, as others wish—has taken *bar* in this place for "doctrine," saying: <term>קבילו אולפנא</term> <note>Aramaic: *Kabilu Ulpana*</note> that is, *Receive instruction*. Yet it is more correctly and fittingly understood here as "son" (as we have said). For in this way it both favors our faith more (as has been seen) and agrees more with the exposition of the ancients (as was evident in the traditions mentioned above), and it better suits the literal truth of the letter. 

For what follows—*Lest he be angry*—along with the rest, cannot apply to anyone but the Son of God alone. From this it is also clear that the interpretation of those who, in order to escape the truth and deny the divinity of the Messiah, interpret these same words <term>נשקו בר</term> *nashiku bar* as "worship purely," is not true. Moreover, that "kiss" by which the Church of the ancients, by kissing the Son of God, asked to be kissed by him in return, was nothing other than the learning and doctrine to be brought forth from the very mouth of God, who had given them the law through the hand of Moses. For this reason (as the ancient Talmudists explained), in the first chapter of the Song of Songs, it said: <term>ישקני מנשיקות פיהו</term> <note>Song of Songs 1:2</note> That is, *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth*. This means: *Let the Messiah, the Son of God, kiss me with the kiss of his mouth*: that is, let him instruct and teach me with his own mouth, and let him not despise the touch of my mouth when I ask him about the way of salvation. 

Let him no longer send Moses, who had a heavy tongue <note>A reference to Exodus 4:10, where Moses describes his speech impediment.</note>. Not Isaiah, who said he was of polluted lips <note>Isaiah 6:5.</note>. Not Jeremiah, who said he did not know how to speak because he was a child <note>Jeremiah 1:6.</note>. But let the Son of God himself, who is the wisdom and power of the Father, come and teach me with his own mouth. By this it is also proved that the Messiah is the Son of God, because God himself says of him in Psalm 89: <term>הוא יקראני אבי אתה אלי וצור ישועתי אף אני בכור אתנהו עליון למלכי ארץ :</term> <note>Psalm 89:26-27</note> That is, *He shall call me, Thou art my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation; also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth.*

For this Name is nothing else than the Son of God, or the Word <note>The author is identifying the "Name of God" with the "Logos" or the "Word" described in the Gospel of John</note>, by which, or through which, God Himself established the world from nothing. 

This is expressed more clearly in the Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> translation of **Rabbi Jonathan** <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note>. For he explained those same words of Isaiah in Chaldaic thus: **I am the Lord who makes all things; I stretched out the heavens by my word; I established the earth by my power.** <note>original: "אנא יהוה עביד כולא תלית שמיא במימרי שכלילית ארעא בגבורתי"</note> That the Name of God is said to be the Messiah is shown most clearly in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Psalms</note>, when it comments on Psalm 18: **He magnifies the salvations of his King, and shows mercy to his Messiah, to David.** <note>original: "מגדיל ישועות מלכו ועשה חסד למשיחו לדוד"</note>

Just as it is said in Jeremiah, chapter 31: **From afar the Lord (the tetragrammaton) appeared to me.** <note>Jeremiah 31:3</note> Thus far the tradition. 

To this also pertains what is read in the book of the **Sanhedrin** <note>A major section of the Talmud dealing with law and the Messiah</note> in the chapter *Helec*, in this manner: **Rabbi Yohanan** <note>A prominent 3rd-century Jewish sage in the Land of Israel</note> said, "If you see a generation making itself small and fading away, expect the Messiah." As it is said in Psalm 18: **For you will save the humble people, and will bring down high eyes.** <note>Psalm 18:27 (numbered as Psalm 17 in the author's text)</note> Rabbi Yohanan also said: "If you see a generation upon which many tribulations are coming, expect the Messiah, of whom it is said in Isaiah, chapter 59: **And they shall fear the name of the Lord (the tetragrammaton) from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun. For he shall come like a distressing river.**" Then it follows: **And there shall come to Zion a Redeemer** <note>original: "גואל" (Goel)</note>, **and to those who turn from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord.** <note>Isaiah 59:19-20</note> All this is tradition. Since, therefore, there is no redeemer but God.

### Chapter IX. That the Messiah was to be called by the four-letter name of God, the Tetragrammaton.

->CAPNIO,<- <note>Capnio is the Latinized name of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist, who acts as a character in this dialogue.</note>

<margin>GAL.</margin> <note>Galatinus, the author, speaking.</note>
**H**ere I would like you to prove that the Messiah was to be called by the four-letter name of God, the <term>Tetragrammaton (YHWH)</term> <note>The sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew, often rendered as "the LORD" in English Bibles.</note>, by which the divine essence itself is designated. To prove this, therefore, I will first bring forward the words of Jeremiah, speaking thus in the twenty-third chapter: *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch, and a King shall reign, and be wise, and execute judgment and justice in the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell in safety. And this is his name by which they shall call him: **The Lord (Tetragrammaton) our Righteousness.*** <note>original: "הנה ימים באים נאם יהוה והקימותי לדוד צמח צדיק ומלך מלך והשכיל ועשה משפט וצדקה בארץ : בימיו תושע יהודה וישראל ישכון לבטח : וזה שמו אשר יקראו יהוה צדקנו"</note> That this prophecy is understood to be about the Messiah, the Jews cannot deny. First, because the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>The ancient Jewish sages who compiled the Talmud.</note> explain it as being about the Messiah. Secondly, because of the Chaldaic translation <note>The Aramaic Targum.</note>, which speaks openly about the Messiah. In this prophecy, not only is the double nature of the Messiah—divine and human—expressed, but it is also clearly shown that the Messiah himself was to be called by the name of the Tetragrammaton, when it is said: *And this is his name, by which they shall call him, **The Lord (Tetragrammaton) our Righteousness.*** CAP. The Jews of our time say that Jeremiah did not say "they shall call" here, as we have it, but "he shall call." For this reason, they claim the sense of these words is this: *This is his name, [namely] of him who shall call him (that is, the Messiah), **The Lord our Righteousness.***

<margin>GAL.</margin>
They are plainly lying. By falsely adding vowel points, they strive to corrupt the text. For from *yikre'u* <note>original: "יקראו"</note>, which means "they shall call," they want to make *yikra* <note>original: "יקרא"</note>, which is the same as "he shall call." But it is most clearly evident through almost all the writings of their ancestors that they are manifest forgers. And first, through the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translators, who translated this passage exactly as our edition has it. Then, through the <term>Targum</term> of Rabbi Jonathan, who turned those same words into Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> thus: *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish for David a Messiah of righteousness...* <note>original: "הא יומין אתן אמר יהוה ואקים לדוד משיח דצדקא"</note> and afterward he adds: *And this is his name which they shall call him: **The Lord (Tetragrammaton) our Righteousness.*** <note>original: "וזה שמו אשר יקראו יהוה צדקנו"</note> That same prophet refutes their falsehood in no small way when he says again in the thirty-third chapter: *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will perform the...*

**CAP.** <note>Capnio (Johannes Reuchlin)</note> To what, then, does that feminine pronoun **her** <note>Hebrew: "lah" (לה)</note> refer, which is placed there? For it is said: *And this is he who shall call her, God our just one.* 

**GAL.** <note>Galatinus</note> It refers to that which precedes in the same words—namely, to the house of Judah and to the house of Israel; that is, to the Jewish nation, to whom the Messiah was first to be sent. Finally, the same point is clear through other ancient teachers of the Jews. Just as it is written in the last chapter of Ezekiel: *And the name of the city from that day shall be: The LORD (the Tetragrammaton) is there.* And the name of its king is like the name of its God. As it was said: *And this is his name, by which they shall call him, God our just one.*

**CAP.** <note>The "Capio" or Jewish interlocutor in this dialogue.</note> The Jews of our age attempt to make this conclusion void, saying that not only the Messiah, but truly also Moses, and Israel, and the city of Jerusalem are found to be called by the Name of God, as the very traditions now brought forward by you openly show. **GAL.** <note>Galatinus, the author/defender of the Christian interpretation.</note> They do not wish to pay proper attention (they only desire to deceive) to the fact that, as appears in those same traditions, neither Moses nor Israel were called by this name of God—the Tetragrammaton—by which only God and the Messiah alone are called. For when this name is spoken of the Messiah, it is spoken with a <term>toar</term> <note>Hebrew: תואר, meaning an adjective or a descriptive title.</note>—that is, it is spoken with the adjective "Just"—and in that way and form which it is most frequently spoken of God. However, when it is said of the heavenly Jerusalem, it is not with a <term>toar</term> (adjective), but with a local adverb <term>samma</term> <note>Hebrew: שם (*sham*), meaning "there."</note>, that is, "there"; by which it is clearly demonstrated that the city itself is not God, but that God himself exists in it through glorification. And so it is then clear that the name is consonant with the thing. Indeed, this way of speaking is customary among those who are used to naming their sons "God-gave," "God-save," and others of this kind. Yet no one would be so insane as to call his son "God" with a <term>toar</term> (adjective), such as "God the Just," or "Holy God," or "his God," and other things of this sort. For through this manner, he would clearly be considered to be God himself. No one doubts that this would be exceedingly impious. Since, therefore, God called the Messiah by His own name in this way, and decreed he should be so named—as has already been proven—it necessarily follows that the Messiah is undoubtedly God. Otherwise, since names must be consonant with things, He would have commanded him to be called by His own proper name falsely. Which is most wicked to think about God, let alone to say.

What then did the Holy and Blessed God do? He mixed the names by which both had called that place, and called it Jerusalem.* Thus far the tradition. From which the proposition is clear.
