From the fact that there are three letters in this name <note>The Tetragrammaton, יהוה (YHWH).</note>, which differ from one another first in sound and then in shape—namely **י** (*yod*), **ה** (*he*), and **ו** (*vau*)—and then one of them, specifically **ה** (*he*), is placed again at the end of the name to complete and perfect it, it is clearly suggested that when this name is spoken of the Messiah, there are three substances within him that differ from one another: namely, a human body, a rational soul, and divinity itself. These are so joined and united to one another that although the first two are united to the third, there are not two persons in the Messiah—God and man—but only one; nor are there two Messiahs, but only one. For just as the three different letters mentioned above produce one glorious name of God, so these three—body, soul, and the Word of God—make one Messiah or Christ.

For even if there are two natures in Christ—one of which is divine, by which he is <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Of the same essence or substance. original: "cosubstantialis"</note> with the Father, co-eternal, and equal in all things except in being begotten; the other of which is human, by which he is consubstantial with his mother and entirely similar in nature—nevertheless, there is only one person in him, which is divine and sustains both natures. <term>Psellus</term> <note>Michael Psellos (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine monk, philosopher, and politician known for his vast writings on theology and science.</note> both testifies to and explains this best in his book *On Different Questions*, saying in chapter 3:

> The holy catholic and apostolic Church dogmatizes one <term>hypostasis</term> <note>A theological term for "person" or "individual reality."</note> and two natures in our Lord Jesus Christ: the incarnate Son as the hypostasis, and divinity and humanity as the natures. Therefore, it does not call the animated and intellectual body which he assumed a "hypostasis," lest it be found saying there are two hypostases (the nonsense babbled by the heretic <term>Nestorius</term> <note>Nestorius (c. 386–450) was a bishop whose teachings led to the belief that Christ was two separate persons, one human and one divine, rather than one person with two natures.</note>), but instead calls it <term>enypostaton</term> <note>A technical term meaning "having existence within a person." It suggests the human nature doesn't have its own separate personality but exists within the person of the Son of God.</note>, as it receives its being within the hypostasis of the Son. For the Son of God himself, being one hypostasis of the Holy Trinity, also became the hypostasis for the body he assumed. Wherefore the body of the Lord is indeed *enypostaton*, but it is not a *hypostasis* of itself. <note>The author provides the original Greek of Psellos followed by a word-for-word Latin translation. Both have been consolidated here into a single English passage for readability.</note>

according to Our Holy Rabbi <note>original: "Rabbenū Haccados"; referring to Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah, though here cited in a Kabbalistic context</note>: **Father God, Son God, the Holy Spirit God, three in one and one in three** <note>original Hebrew: אב אלהים בן אלהים הקדוש אלהים שלשה באחד אחד</note>. That is: Just as the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Messiah. 

Indeed, these letters in Hebrew exist as forty-two. For **as** <note>Hebrew: באשר, *caasser*</note> is written with four letters; **the soul** <note>Hebrew: הנפש, *hannephes*</note> likewise with four; **rational** <note>Hebrew: המשכלת, *hammascaleth*</note> with six; **and the flesh** <note>Hebrew: והבשר, *uechabasar*</note> with five; **man** <note>Hebrew: אדם, *Adam*</note> with three; **one** <note>Hebrew: אחד, *ehad*</note> likewise with three; **so** <note>Hebrew: כך, *cach*</note> with two; **God** <note>Hebrew: האל, *hael*</note> with three; **and man** <note>Hebrew: והאדם, *uehaadam*</note> with five; **Messiah** <note>Hebrew: משיח, *Massiah*</note> with four; **one** <note>Hebrew: אחד, *ehad*</note> with three. When all these are joined together, there are forty-two letters. Through these, the trinity of substances that exists in Christ, along with the unity of his person, is excellently explained. This is according to that saying of Athanasius <note>Referring to the Athanasian Creed, a Christian statement of belief focusing on Trinitarian doctrine and Christology</note>: *Just as the rational soul and the flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.* From all of this, it is clearly concluded that the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH</note> name of God, when spoken of the Messiah, most aptly fits him according to the whole of his being.

Now, that this prophecy speaks of the Messiah, is proven by...

Just as it is said in Malachi, chapter 3:

Therefore, the younger Jews <note>The author refers to his contemporaries to argue that their own tradition supports the Christian view of John the Baptist and Jesus</note> cannot at all deny that the aforementioned words of Malachi were spoken regarding the Messiah. This messenger, of whom the prophet first speaks, was John the Baptist, who was sent by God to prepare the way for the face of God—that is, the Messiah. Furthermore, that the Messiah is the "Face of God" is held by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century preacher from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations</note> regarding that passage in Genesis, chapter 22, "On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes," when he says: This is what is written in Hosea, chapter 6:
> **He will revive us after two days, and on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live before his face.**

And we shall know, that we may follow, to acknowledge God. Afterward he adds: "He will revive us after two days, and we shall live before his face"—which is the King Messiah. Just as it is said in Psalm 79 <note>Psalm 80 in modern numbering</note>:
> **Lord God of hosts, convert us, and show us thy face—that is, thy Messiah—and we shall be saved.**

And this is the meaning of "on the third day he will revive us." This is the tradition. Moreover, concerning this "Face of God," it is said in the **Small Genesis** <note>original: "Beressith ketanna"; likely referring to a specific midrashic collection</note>, where, regarding that passage in Genesis, chapter 3:
> **And the Lord God sent him out of the garden, or paradise of pleasure.**

> **I, in justice, or through justice, shall contemplate thy face—that is, thy Messiah; I shall be satisfied when thy form—that is, thy figure, or thine image, or thy likeness—shall arise.** <note>original Hebrew: "Temunathecha"</note>

The Holy and Blessed God said: "In that hour I will justify him—namely Adam—from that sentence." David said to the Holy and Blessed God: "And in that hour in which he who is in thy likeness shall awake or rise, I shall be satisfied, and in justice I shall contemplate thy face—that is, thy Messiah."
The Gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the most famous medieval commentator</note> on "I shall contemplate thy face" says: Just as it is said in the fifty-second chapter of Isaiah:
> **For they shall see eye to eye, when God dwells in Zion.**

Which Jonathan translated into Aramaic <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets</note> as: **For with their eyes they shall see the power, or the strength, which God shall perform when his divinity shall sit or dwell in Zion.** <note>original Aramaic: "Ari be-enehon yehezun gevuran di-yaabid YHWH kad yatib shekhinteh le-Tsiyon"</note>

From these things, therefore, it is manifest that the Messiah is both called and is the **Face of God**. And this is only because of his divinity, on account of which all names that are spoken concerning God apply most fittingly to him.

# That the Messiah is Light or Brilliance, which is God.

->CAPNIO,<-

## *That the name of God Shaddai properly belongs to the Messiah.*
### Chapter 14.

->CAPNIO,<- <note>Capnio is the scholar-protagonist, representing Johannes Reuchlin</note>

Reuchlin interprets this name etymologically as "He who is sufficient" (She-dai)</note> belongs to God alone. And although I do not doubt in the least that all the names spoken of God are likewise most aptly spoken of the Messiah according to his divinity, I would nevertheless wish, for a greater manifestation of the Messiah's divinity, that you would provide the reason why this name Shaddai properly suits the Messiah himself, and that you would prove it properly belongs to him through Hebrew testimonies.

He says "The soul of Shaddai," that is, of him who suffices, or who is sufficiency. Since, therefore, neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit has a soul, but only the Son of God—who is the power and wisdom of the Father—he who possesses that soul is the one he united to himself in the Messiah. It follows clearly that Job was speaking of the Son of God alone when he said: *And the soul of Shaddai has given life*—or rather, "will give life"—*to me*. Namely, the soul of him who alone is enough for the redemption and salvation of the human race. For he alone is in the form of God, who, by assuming human nature, was destined to come, not to be served,

## That the name of the Messiah *Yinnon* belongs to him according to his divinity. Chapter 15.

For since *Yinnon* (as we said) is interpreted as "son" or "born" or "begotten," it cannot belong to the Father in the Godhead, nor to the Holy Spirit. These things neither existed before the foundation of the world, nor was there anyone present to whom such commands could be assigned. Moreover, how can they say that penance, which naturally follows sin, preceded sin itself and sinners? <margin>IIII.</margin> And by what reason do they assert that Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna, a historical valley in Jerusalem used as a metaphor for a place of fiery purification or punishment, often translated as Hell</note> was created before the world was founded, when they have their own Talmud openly contradicting them, even in the very book they cite for their own side? Let them therefore read from that same book, *Pesahim* <note>original Hebrew: פסח (*Pesah*), the Talmudic tractate concerning Passover</note>, in the chapter which begins *Macom* <note>original Hebrew: מקום (*Macom*), meaning 'The Place'</note>. For there, Rabbi Jose is reported to have said: "The fire which God, holy and blessed, created on the second day of the week—that is, Monday—shall not be extinguished forever." As it is said in the last chapter of Isaiah: *And they shall go forth and see the carcasses of the men who have rebelled against me; for their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh.* <note>Isaiah 66:24</note> There is also a tradition that Rabbi Baba <note>original Hebrew: בבא (*Bava*)</note> said: "Why was it not said on the second day of the week, 'And God saw that it was good'?" <note>Referring to the account of Creation in Genesis, where the phrase "it was good" is missing from the second day</note> "Because on that day the fire of Gehenna was created." All this is found there. Here we have two witnesses of the greatest authority among them, stating that the fire of Gehenna was created on the second day of the world's creation. Therefore, since it is written in the nineteenth chapter of Deuteronomy: **על פי שנים עדים או על פי שלשה עדים יקום דבר** <note>original: "By the mouth of two witnesses, or by the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established."</note>, they must concede that these masters spoke the truth. From the truth of this matter, it clearly follows that it is entirely false that the fire of Gehenna was produced before the creation of the world. <margin>V.</margin> Furthermore, the Temple, which was made by hand and built from created things—how could it exist before the very materials of which it consisted? <margin>VI.</margin> Finally, how could he who was born from the seed of Adam be created before Adam? What greater madness can there be than to believe such things, let alone speak them? They grope for the wall like the blind, according to that passage in the fifty-ninth chapter of Isaiah, speaking in their person: **נגששה כעורים קיר וכאין עינים נגששה** <note>original: "We grope for the wall like the blind, and we grope as if we had no eyes."</note>. Therefore, the name of the Messiah is not said to be "before the ages" to suggest it was created then—since before the ages nothing at all was created—but so that the Messiah himself might be shown to be begotten of the Father from eternity according to his divinity. And for this reason the prophet said: "Before the sun, **ינון** *Yinnon* <note>Hebrew name for the Messiah</note> was his name." For *Yinnon* (as we said before) signifies both "the one born" and "the one who causes to be born." Thus, two things are hinted at in one word: namely, the eternal birth of the Messiah, by which he was eternally born of the Father; and the resurrection of the dead, whom he himself will raise at the end of the world, making them, as it were, to be born anew.

<summary>The author argues against the literal interpretation that the Law, Gehenna, and the Temple existed before the world, using Rabbinic texts to prove Gehenna was created on the second day. He concludes that the Messiah's name existing "before the sun" refers to his eternal divinity and his power to raise the dead.</summary>

### That the Messiah in sacred scripture is for the most part called the Sprout, to designate that it was more fitting for the Son to be incarnated than the Father or the Holy Spirit. Chapter XVI.

->CAPNIO,<-

Among the other names of the Messiah, I find that he is very often called "the Sprout," <note>original Latin: *Germen*. This term is frequently translated in English Bibles as "The Branch," but the author emphasizes its sense of growing or budding forth.</note> and especially in Zechariah, where he says in the sixth chapter, **Behold the man whose name is the Sprout.** <note>original Hebrew: *hinneh ish tsemach shemo* (Zechariah 6:12)</note> I would therefore like to hear the reason why the prophets thought he should be called by this name? **GAL.** Not without reason, indeed, was the Messiah called the Sprout. For in this it is clearly shown that the divine incarnation and the assumption of human nature were fitting for the person of the Son of God, and not for the person of the Father or the Holy Spirit. This was so that he would not be a son to Adam, Abraham, and David in his humanity unless that **attribute** <term>midda: a Hebrew word meaning "measure" or "quality," used here to refer to a specific person or property within the Trinity</term>—that is, the person or property which was the "Son" in the divinity—were the same as the "Son" in the humanity; thus he would not be one Son in humanity and another in divinity. That this was indeed to be fulfilled in the single person of the Messiah is most evidently suggested by Isaiah and Jeremiah according to the Targum <note>term: Targum, ancient Aramaic paraphrases and translations of the Hebrew Bible used to clarify the meaning of the text</note>, that is, according to the Chaldean <note>term: Chaldean, a historical name for the Aramaic language</note> translation. For Isaiah says in the fourth chapter: **In that day the Sprout of God shall be for beauty, or joy, and for glory, or honor; and the fruit of the earth for loftiness, or nobility, and for an ornament to the remnant of Israel.** <note>original Hebrew: *ba-yom ha-hu yihyeh tsemach Adonai...* (Isaiah 4:2)</note> Where the Targum says: **In that time the Messiah of the Lord shall be for joy and honor.** <note>original Aramaic: *be-idana ha-hi yehe mashiacha d’Y...*</note> Furthermore, Jeremiah says: **In those days and at that time, I will cause a Sprout of righteousness to sprout for David.** <note>original Hebrew: *ba-yamim ha-hem u-va-et ha-hi atsmiah le-David tsemach tsedaka* (Jeremiah 33:15)</note> Where the Targum also says: **In those days and at that time, I will raise up for David the Messiah of righteousness.** <note>original Aramaic: *be-yomaya inun...*</note> Since, therefore, wherever each prophet says "Sprout," the Targum places "Messiah," it is clearly given to all to understand—at least those who do not have the eyes of their heart blinded by the darkness of error—that just as the Messiah was truly the Sprout of God, that is, the Son of God according to his divinity, as Isaiah says; so he was to be the Sprout for David, that is, the Son of David according to his humanity, as Jeremiah says. From these two sources, it clearly results that the Messiah, in the unity of his person, is both the Son of God and the Son of David at the same time, though in different ways. For he is the Son of God before all time, but in time he is the Son of David. He is also the Son of God immediately and without a mother; but he is the Son of David after many intermediate generations of both the just and the unjust, from a mother alone without a father. This is indicated clearly enough by Jeremiah through the name "Sprout" and the verb "to sprout." Isaiah also shows this same thing in the aforementioned words, when he first mentions the Sprout of God and immediately joins to it the "fruit of the earth." We find no man who is also a prophet, whose birth was prophesied before the birth of his father and mother, except only for our righteous Messiah; and for this reason it says,

> From the womb, before the morning star, is the dew of your birth. <note>Psalm 110:3 (Vulgate 109:3). The author uses this to argue for the Messiah's pre-existence.</note>

This means: your birth was prophesied before the womb of your mother was created. And with this agrees that saying,

> His name was begotten before the sun, or "Son" is his name. <note>A variation of Psalm 72:17. The Latin *Ante solem genitus* emphasizes the Messiah's existence before creation.</note>

The meaning of which is: That before the sun was created, the name of our Messiah was subsisting and firm, and he sat at the right hand of God. And this is what [the scripture] says,

> Sit at my right hand. <note>Psalm 110:1.</note>

And elsewhere,

> Mercy shall prepare the throne, and he shall sit upon it in truth. <note>Isaiah 16:5.</note>

Thus says that author. Moreover, we shall prove that the "dew" proceeding from the womb of the morning in this place is the Messiah, through what is written in the commentaries of <term>Moses Hadarsan</term> <note>Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan (11th century), a famous preacher from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note> on the book of Genesis. For there, regarding that passage in Genesis, "And Reuben said to them," it is said thus:

> The Redeemer whom I am about to raise up from among you shall be without a father.

And it is added a little later: Concerning him David also says in Psalm 110,

> From the womb of the morning is the dew of your birth.

Therefore, the Messiah is not inappropriately called "dew." First, indeed, because of the similarity of his descent. For dew descends from on high, and its descent is hidden from our sight. For it descends at night, and especially in the time of spring, and it refreshes and makes the earth fruitful. In the same way, the divine power made the most blessed Virgin fruitful in the nighttime. For just as the **oyster** <note>A common medieval and Renaissance belief was that pearls were formed when oysters rose to the surface at night to catch the morning dew.</note> receiving the dew at night and in the springtime generates a most precious pearl-gem in its interior: so the glorious Virgin, when the Holy Spirit came upon her and she conceived the Son of God, generated the Messiah, the precious pearl.

Just as the dew, gently spreading itself over the surface of the herbs, grants greenness and vigor to the herbs and plants—and that which the heat of the day had caused to wither by drying and consuming it, the nightly dew moistens, nourishes, and raises up.

So our true Messiah grants greenness and vigor to those believing in him and persevering in good, and he rules them and raises them up to eternal life.

Furthermore, just as the dew collects itself on the tips of the herbs and seeks again its own origin: so the Messiah our redeemer raised himself up on the height of the cross, and from there returned to his glory.

For these reasons, the Messiah was not unsuitably called "dew" by the ancient fathers. From this, the hidden and incomprehensible incarnation and birth of the Son of God was designated. Wherefore, not without reason, Isaiah said in the 45th chapter,

> <note>original Hebrew: הרעיפו שמים ממעל ושיחקים יזלו צדק תפתח ארץ ויפרו ישע וצדקה תצמיח יחד אני יהוה בראתיו</note>
> Drop down, or drip, O heavens from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, and they shall bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together. I, God, have created him. <note>Isaiah 45:8.</note>

Where by "heavens" are understood the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Concerning whom <term>Lucifer</term> <note>The fallen angel, often identified with the King of Babylon in Isaiah 14.</note>, when he was in the empyrean heaven, is read to have spoken thus in the 14th chapter of Isaiah,

> <note>original Hebrew: השמים אעלה ממעל לככבי אל ארים כסאי</note>
> I will ascend to the heavens, above the stars of God I will exalt my throne.

With the rest up to that point,

> And I will be like the Most High. <note>Isaiah 14:13-14.</note>

But the "clouds" were the prophets, and the "earth" was the blessed Virgin opening her consent. And thus they brought forth the fruit of the Holy Spirit.

### That the Messiah was to be called Emmanuel. And that this name belongs to the Messiah alone. Chapter XVIII.

-> CAPNIO, <- <note>The pseudonym for the famous Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin in this dialogue.</note>

**C**um Isaiah said the Messiah was to be called Emmanuel. For thus he says in the seventh chapter, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she herself shall call his name Emmanuel." <note>Isaiah 7:14. The Hebrew quoted is: *Hineh ha-almah harah ve-yoledet ben ve-karat shemo Immanuel*.</note> Pray tell me, by what reasoning does this name belong to the Messiah himself? **GAL.** <note>Pietro Galatino, the author's persona who defends the Christian interpretation of Hebrew texts.</note> Emmanuel (as you know very well) is translated as "God with us" in Latin. Therefore, the most blessed Virgin herself, forewarned and instructed by the angel Gabriel, was going to call the Messiah himself Emmanuel. So that from this, the union and conjunction of the divine and human natures in the one person of the Messiah might be clearly demonstrated. For the Messiah was going to be both God and man. Wherefore to him alone this name Emmanuel—which sounds like "God with us" in Latin—rightly belongs. **HOG.** <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, the Dominican inquisitor portrayed here as the skeptical questioner.</note> "And his name *shall be called* Emmanuel," our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate bible, which uses the passive "vocabitur" rather than the active "vocabit".</note> has it. **GAL.** Indeed it is so. But the Hebrew letter says exactly thus (as I myself have translated): "And she shall call." Which agrees far better with the truth of our faith. For from this, that "she herself shall call his name Emmanuel," the prophet showed that the Messiah would not have a human father who would impose a name upon him. For among the Hebrews, fathers almost always, and not mothers, were accustomed to give names to their sons. This appears in many places in the Old Testament, and is clearly gathered from the birth of John the Baptist. Therefore, from the fact that the prophet referred the giving of the name—which belonged to the father—to the mother alone, he clearly wished to hint that the Messiah would not have had a father on earth who could give him a name. This the angel also seems to have suggested, in that he said to Mary, "You shall call his name Jesus." <note>Luke 1:31.</note> "You shall call," he said therefore, and not "He shall be called": so that he might openly show that he agreed with the prophet. Or it can also be said in another way, and not ineptly indeed: that when the prophet said, "And she herself shall call his name Emmanuel," which is "God with us," through this he clearly hinted that she alone was to know with certainty that the Messiah, her son, was God and man, since she alone was to call him Emmanuel. For although he was to be called by another name <note>Referring to the name Jesus (Yeshua).</note>, she nonetheless alone could have spoken of him with certainty as "Emmanuel," that is, "God with us." For which reason he said not without cause, "And she herself shall call his name Emmanuel." As if he were saying openly: "And she shall call him 'God with us' within herself." Because she alone could have said this with certainty. Which Luke also seems to suggest when he says: "But Mary kept all these words," <note>Luke 2:19.</note>

### THIRD BOOK

...[pondering] these things in her heart. <note>original: "hæc, conferens in corde ſuo" — a reference to Luke 2:19, describing the Virgin Mary's reflection on the events of Christ's birth.</note> Therefore also in her heart, that is, within herself, she was going to call him Emmanuel. This is also confirmed by what she said to the ministers at the wedding: "Whatever he says to you, do it." <note>John 2:5</note> It is as if she were keeping the secret within herself that her son was God, who was able to produce wine from any source. From these things, therefore, it is clear that for the sake of our faith, the Hebrew text is more accurate than our own [Latin] version.

<margin>A false objection.</margin>
**CAPNIO.** These things are indeed very well said. For from these, one can easily respond to the wickedness of the Jews of our time, who say that the Messiah, the Son of God, was by no means called Emmanuel by his mother, but **Yeshua** <note>original Hebrew: ישוע</note>, that is, Jesus. For this reason (as they assert), it happened that he was afterwards called Jesus by all Christians. Therefore, I would like you to use their own scriptures to convict them of their faithlessness. They attribute these words—*Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and she herself shall call his name Emmanuel*—to the wife of Isaiah and his son, saying that he was called Emmanuel by his mother or by the Holy Spirit. This they prove by the testimony of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, who explains this passage thus: "Behold the **ha-almah** <note>original: העלמה; <term>almah</term>: A Hebrew word meaning a young woman of marriageable age. In Christian tradition, it is translated as "virgin," while in Jewish tradition, it often refers to a young woman, here identified by Rashi as Isaiah's wife.</note>, that is, my wife, shall conceive this year, which is the fourth year of King Ahaz. And she shall bear a son, and she herself—namely the *almah* or the Holy Spirit—shall call [him]. (For 'Spirit' among the Hebrews is of the feminine gender) <note>In Hebrew, the word for Spirit, "Ruach," is grammatically feminine, which the text uses to explain why a feminine verb for "naming" is used.</note> who shall be or shall descend upon her, [naming] him Emmanuel." As if to say, "Because our Creator will be with us."

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
**These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. GALATINO.** Let us grant them that this exposition is true and good, with this one exception: that he says Isaiah here used the word **almah** for his own wife, and consequently that it was Isaiah's son who was to be called Emmanuel. However, that **almah** here must be understood not as Isaiah's wife but as the mother of the Messiah, we shall prove most extensively in the following sections when we discuss the virginity of that same mother. For now, let it be enough for us to show that this Emmanuel was not, nor could have been, the son of Isaiah and his wife. This is first evident from what is said by the same prophet in the eighth chapter: **"And therefore, behold, the Lord will cause the strong and many waters of the river to rise over them—the King of Assyria and all his glory."** <note>Isaiah 8:7</note> And the rest, up to: **"And the extension of his wings shall be the filling of the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel."** <note>Isaiah 8:8</note> This, however, can in no way apply to the son of Isaiah, because he was a private citizen and never had any land subjected to his own rule.

<margin>Another objection.</margin>
For this reason, certain others, explaining this prophecy as referring to Hezekiah, the son of King Ahaz, say that he was the one called Emmanuel. This opinion is first refuted by **Rabbi Solomon** himself, who, in explaining this passage, says: "And she herself shall call his name Emmanuel. There are some who explain this as being said of Hezekiah."

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
But this is not possible. For if you count his years, you will find that he was [born] nine years before his father's reign...

...to have been born. This is the opinion of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a premier medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, whose assertion can indeed be proved in this way. For Ahaz his father reigned sixteen years, as is held in 3 Kings, chapter 16 <note>In older Bibles, 1 and 2 Kings were called 3 and 4 Kings; this is 2 Kings 16:2.</note>. Hezekiah himself, his son, succeeded him in the Kingdom when he was twenty-five years of age, as is gathered from 4 Kings, chapter 18 <note>2 Kings 18:2.</note>. From this it is clear that in the first year of the reign of his father Ahaz, Hezekiah himself was already nine years old. Since therefore this prophecy (as Rabbi Solomon says) was made in the fourth year of the reign of that same Ahaz, it is clear that Hezekiah was then thirteen years old. From these facts, therefore, it is manifestly evident that this prophecy cannot be explained as referring to anyone but the Messiah, since he alone is truly Emmanuel <note>Meaning "God with us." The argument is that since Hezekiah was already a teenager when the prophecy "a virgin shall conceive" was spoken, it could not refer to his birth.</note>.

**CAPNIO.** Your Christ (the Jews say) was called Jesus, and not Emmanuel. Therefore you cannot say that he was that Emmanuel of whom the prophet speaks.

**GALATINUS.** A name of nature is one thing, a name of <term>imposition</term> <note>A name "imposed" or given by society/parents, as opposed to a name that describes the inherent essence of a thing.</note> is another. For it is established that nature itself, which gives the form to a thing, also gives a name to that same thing. Just as it gives both humanity and a name—which is "man"—to a human being. For someone is not called a man except because of the nature of man, of which he is a partaker. In this same way, our Messiah was called "Emmanuel"—which is interpreted as "God with us," that is, God and man—by the Holy Spirit and by his mother. And he is both believed to be and called such by all Christians, since he partakes of two natures, namely the divine and the human. In this manner, he was called by the Holy Spirit through the prophets by many and diverse names, signifying his divine nature, his human nature, or both at once. Therefore, "Emmanuel" is a name of nature, designating the union of both natures which was to occur in the virgin's womb. "Jesus," however, is a name of imposition, which is interpreted as Savior, or Health, or Salvation.

**CAPNIO.** The Jews still insist on this point, because immediately afterward the prophet added: *Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil and choose the good.* <note>original Hebrew: חמאה ודבש יאכל לדעתו מאוס ברע ובחור בטוב; Isaiah 7:15</note> This (they say) least of all fits your Christ according to your own teaching, since you say he possessed the fullness of knowledge from the very instant of his conception. From this they infer that he is not this Emmanuel whom the prophet mentions.

**GALATINUS.** They can by no means deny that in Holy Scripture spiritual things are frequently signified by bodily things. Therefore, the prophet predicted that our Emmanuel would eat butter and honey so that he might hint that he would possess within himself not only the nature and truth of humanity, but also of divinity. For butter, which is made from the milk of animals, suitably designates humanity. But honey—because of its supreme sweetness and because it often comes down invisibly like dew from the heavens—quite appropriately signifies divinity. Concerning both of these, Isaac said to Esau, when he was urgently asking to be blessed by him, in Genesis 27: *Behold, your dwelling shall be from the fatness of the earth and from the dew of heaven from above.* <note>original Hebrew: הנה משמני הארץ יהיה מושבך ומטל השמים מעל; Genesis 27:39</note> It is as if he were to say: "From humanity and divinity..."

->of the Messiah<-

...of the coming Messiah. **CAPNIO.** The Jews object again, because of what follows regarding that same Emmanuel in the same place in Isaiah: **For before the boy knows** <note>original Hebrew: *ki betérem yedá ha-ná’ar ma’ós ba-ra u-vakhór ba-tov té’azev ha-adamáh*</note> **how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land shall be forsaken.** Along with the rest that follows. They say, therefore: "If your Christ was that Emmanuel, you are not able to excuse him from ignorance. Since you assert that there was no ignorance in him, you cannot possibly say that he was this Emmanuel."

**GALATINUS.** This saying of Isaiah must be understood concerning the human knowledge of Christ. For although there was no ignorance in him, yet because he was made man in time, he also possessed human knowledge in time. And before he possessed that knowledge, the liberation of that land and people foretold by Isaiah was completed. Thus, the prophet’s saying is to be explained in this way: "Before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land shall be forsaken," and so on. That is: Before he becomes man, or before he is conceived and born of the aforementioned virgin, the land shall be forsaken. 

In the same way, one must answer regarding what is said of the same boy in the following chapter: **For before the boy knows** <note>original Hebrew: *ki betérem yedá ha-ná’ar qeró aví ve-immí*</note> **how to call, or to say: 'My father' and 'my mother'.** That is: Before he becomes man, or before he arises as a man.

That this boy of whom Isaiah speaks is both God and man—and consequently truly to be called Emmanuel—appears most clearly from what Isaiah sets down in the same place, saying: **And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself a large scroll, and write upon it with a man’s pen: To the quick spoil, hasten to the prey.** <note>original Hebrew: *wayyómer Adonái elái qakh-lekhá gillayón gadól u-khetóv aláv be-khéret enósh le-mahér shalál khash baz*</note> 

These words are explained by **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi</note> as follows: "Take for yourself a large volume," that is, a roll of paper or a writing tablet. "And write upon it with a man’s pen," that is, in such a script and in such a manner that every man might be able to run through it, whoever reads it, even if he is not a wise man. Moreover, **Jonathan** <note>The Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> translated it this way: "Write," he said, <term>mephoras</term> <note>Hebrew: *mep̄ōrāš*</note>, that is, explicitly or clearly. 

And why did he say "Large," when he commanded nothing to be written in it except these four names? There are some who explain that the substance of the writing consisted of those four; but many more things were written in that volume. These are the words of **Rabbi Solomon**. However, **Rabbi Khimchi** <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a prominent medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> says these same things with a greater explanation regarding the word <term>Heret</term> <note>Hebrew: *ḥereṭ*, meaning a stylus, engraving tool, or pen.</note>. 

Therefore, many more things than these four words were written in that volume concerning this boy who was to be called Emmanuel, as **Rabbi Solomon** says. These four, however, are like the titles of what follows: namely, "To the Quick Spoil, the Hastening Preayer." These words fit the Messiah perfectly. For he himself was to be the "quick despoiler" of Hell, and a "swift plunderer." Many other things which Isaiah wrote about him in that same volume relate partly to his divinity, and partly to his humanity and divinity together. From these, he openly hinted that he was rightly to be called Emmanuel. For he wrote...

->THIRD.<-

the prophets, in order to instill the truth of his two natures, sometimes call him God by the name of the <term>tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, considered too sacred to pronounce.</note>, or by another divine name, and sometimes call him man, or by other names designating a human nature.

<margin>JESUS.</margin>
But because the salvation of the human race could not be achieved except through God <term>hypostatically united</term> <note>A theological term meaning the union of divine and human natures in the one person of Christ.</note> to humanity, therefore this name **Jesus**, which is interpreted as "Savior," is more proper and more fitting to him than the other names attributed to the Messiah. For it does not only signify both natures—namely the divine and the human—which were to be hypostatically united in the Messiah himself, but it also most clearly suggests that very salvation of the human race which he was to bring about. Indeed, this name was imposed upon him from eternity through eternal predestination by the eternal Father, and was later revealed by him to the prophets. Whence **Habakkuk**, as if giving thanks to God, said in chapter 3: *But I will rejoice in God, I will exult in God my Jesus.* <note>Habakkuk 3:18. The original Hebrew "ישעי" (yish’i) means "my salvation," but Galatinus interprets this as the proper name "Jesus."</note> **Ezras**, moreover, speaking in the person of God the Father in the third chapter of the third book <note>Often referred to today as 4 Esdras or the Apocalypse of Ezra.</note>, spoke thus: *My son Jesus shall be revealed with those who shall rejoice with him.* And again in the same place he says: *My son Jesus shall die, and the world shall be turned back to me.* Even <term>Rabbenus Haccados</term> <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century compiler of the Mishnah.</note>, who lived in the time of the Roman Consuls, says these things among others concerning the name itself in the book **Gale Razeya** <note>Hebrew: "The Revealer of Secrets."</note> when addressing Consul Antoninus: "Because the Messiah shall save men, he shall be called *Yeshuah* <note>original: "ישוע"</note> (Jesus). However, the peoples of other nations who follow his faith shall call him **Jesus**." And for that reason, you will find this name Jesus designated in the text of Genesis chapter 49: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah...* in the first letters of these words: *Iauo Shilo Velo* <note>Genesis 49:10: "Until Shiloh comes, and to him [shall be the gathering of the people]." The Hebrew "יבא שילה ולו" begins with the letters Y-S-V, forming the name "Jesu."</note>. For if you take the first letters of these words, they will form the same letters **Jesu**. Thus speaks that great Rabbi, whom the Jews call "our holy master." Therefore, since the Gentiles also who were to believe in him had to be saved through him, this name was revealed not only to the prophets and the ancient Jews, but also to certain of the Gentiles for a clearer expression of the truth. For the **Erythraean Sibyl** (to say nothing of others) composed certain verses about the end of the world, from the first letters of which, if read correctly, these words result: *Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior, Cross.* <note>A reference to the famous acrostic cited by Saint Augustine in "The City of God." original Greek: "ιησȣς χριστος θεȣ υιος, σωτηρ, σταυρος."</note>

**CAP.** Since the prophets also predicted that the Messiah should be called by other names, for that reason the more recent Jews utterly deny that the proper name of the Messiah ought to be "Jesus."

**GAL.** They certainly cannot deny it. Firstly because, as we have shown, not only the prophets but also their own ancient teachers assert this. Secondly, because it is also proven by reason. For if the human race was only to be saved through the Messiah, and the name **Jesus** is interpreted as "Savior," it follows plainly that this name can properly suit no one other than the Messiah. Wherefore it is necessary that they concede that this alone ought to have been his proper name...

the name of the Messiah himself. Other names by which he was called even by the prophets themselves are derived—as we have said—from the effect of salvation itself, since they concern only the beginning, the middle, or the end of our salvation. But this name **Jesus** sufficiently contains the whole process of our salvation: namely, the beginning, the middle, and the end. Wherefore it also includes all other names within itself. For this reason, he ought to have been named by this name more than any other. 

**CAP.** <note>Capnio is the pseudonym of the famous Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin.</note> This, therefore, seems to me to be that name of which **Isaiah** speaks in chapter 61 <note>The quote is actually from Isaiah 62:2.</note>, saying: *And you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name.* <note>original Hebrew: "וקרא לך שם חדש אשר פי יהוה יקבנו"</note> Why then did he say it would be "new"?

**GAL.** Because it was to be given to no one before the Messiah. For one reads in the Sacred Scriptures of no one ever having existed who was called by this name. This was done primarily so that it would be openly shown that it could rightly and properly belong to no one except the Messiah, the true Savior.

**HOG.** On the contrary, we read in the Sacred Scripture of three others who were called by this name.

**GAL.** And who are they, I pray?

**HOG.** **Joshua son of Nun**, **Jesus son of Sirach**, and **Jeshua son of Jozadak**. <note>In the Latin Vulgate, "Joshua" and "Jeshua" are both rendered as "Iesus."</note> Our Doctors say that these were a <term>figure</term> <note>A "figure" or "type" is a historical person believed to foreshadow the life of Christ.</note> of the true Jesus. For just as **Joshua son of Nun**, a most brave man, having conquered the enemies, led the children of Israel into the promised land; and **Jesus son of Sirach**, a most wise teacher, renewed wisdom in his times (as it is read); and **Jeshua son of Jozadak**, a most holy priest, built the temple for the Lord; so Christ, the true Jesus, having overcome the enemies of the human race by his own strength, led his faithful into the heavenly fatherland. By his own wisdom and truthful doctrine, he illuminated the world, purging it of errors. By his own holiness, being himself a priest forever, he constructed a spiritual temple—that is, the Church of the faithful—out of living and chosen stones.

**GAL.** I concede that they bore the "figures" of the true Jesus, but I entirely deny that they were called by the name "Jesus." In this (to tell the truth), very many of our people are greatly mistaken, thinking that they were called by this name. It is certain that this has arisen from ignorance of the Hebrew letters. For every one of those whom they assert were called by this name "Jesus" was not called **Yeshua** <note>Hebrew: ישוע</note>—that is, Jesus—but **Yehoshua** <note>Hebrew: יהושע</note>. This is not the same name as **Yeshua** (Jesus), but is quite different from it and signifies something else. For **Yeshua**, or Jesus, is the same as "Savior," or "health," or "salvation" <note>Hebrew: ישועה, Yeshuah</note>. **Yehoshua**, however, is interpreted as "God will save." This was so that it might be clearly manifest from the name itself that to save was not the business of any of those men, but of God alone. He, who was to be <term>hypostatically united</term> to human nature, would be the true **Yeshua** (Jesus) of the human race—that is, the Savior. Therefore, they themselves were not called **Yeshuoth** <note>Hebrew: ישועות, meaning "salvations"</note> or Jesus—that is, Saviors or Salvations—but **Yehoshua**, that is, "God will save." Thus, it was openly hinted that only one Savior was to come, who would be both God and man. And indeed God, so that he might save

...so that he could save. But he became man so that, by undergoing death for the salvation of the human race, he might satisfy divine justice, which required that the one making satisfaction be of the same nature as the transgressor.

**HOG.** Therefore, it is not without reason that some of our people say this name **Jesus** is nothing other than the very name of God, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often rendered as Yahweh or Jehovah.</note>. For it is established (as you have excellently explained) that the principal letters of the Tetragrammaton itself are three: namely, *iod*, *he*, and *vau*. Since the fourth letter is nothing but the second, which is placed twice in the same name—specifically, in the second and fourth positions <note>The letters are Y-H-V-H; thus only three unique letters exist.</note>. These three letters seem to correspond to our own letters: *i*, *h*, and *u*. When joined together in this way—**ihu**—they form this blessed name. Moreover, a title <note>original: "titulus" — referring to a superscript mark or abbreviation stroke used in medieval manuscripts.</note> is placed above it, so that the cross through which we are saved may be signified. From this, it is manifest that this name **Jesus** is nothing other than the name of God, the Tetragrammaton.

**GAL.** That would indeed be beautiful if it could be verified in every language. For those three letters of the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, seem to have this conformity only when the name **Jesus** is written in Latin letters <note>In medieval Latin, Jesus was often abbreviated as "Ihu" with a bar above it, which the speaker interprets as a cross.</note>. For in Hebrew letters it is written thus: יהושע <note>original Hebrew: "Yehoshua"</note>; in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> thus: י⸱ח⸱ו⸱ע <note>original: "Yeshua"</note>; and in Greek thus: ιησῦς <note>original Greek: "Iesous"</note>. In all of these, except for the first letter, no other letter is used from those which compose the Tetragrammaton. Therefore, since this similarity of letters is not preserved in the Hebrew language (to say nothing of the others)—where it ought most of all to be preserved, since both names are Hebrew—it seems it should by no means be said that this name **Jesus** is the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, entirely. For even if Christ should be called properly and directly by the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, as true God (as we have shown above), yet that name suits him only according to his divine nature, whereas this name **Jesus** belongs to him according to both natures, both divine and human. It follows without doubt that this name is not that one, nor is the meaning of both the same, as has been shown sufficiently and abundantly (I believe) in the preceding sections. Furthermore, many mysteries of this most holy name **Jesus** would need to be revealed, which are reserved to be spoken of more opportunely in another place. Now, however, let it suffice that, as far as our purpose is concerned, we say something about those names of the Messiah which are spoken of him in the Sacred Page metaphorically or by <term>antonomasia</term> <note>Antonomasia is a rhetorical term for using a title or epithet instead of a proper name, such as calling a king "His Majesty."</note>.

"I will pluck a tender one." <note>original: "Tenerum carpam," a reference to Ezekiel 17:22.</note> For there is no way to have mercy except through the tender one, who is growing, uniting, and bound together. For this Hebrew word **Hu** <note>original: הוא</note>, which in Latin means "He" or "Himself," is a divine name among the Hebrews and properly signifies God. This is clearly evident in Isaiah, chapter 42, where God himself says: "I am the Lord, *Hu* is my name." <note>original Hebrew: אני יהוה הוא שמי. In English: "I am the LORD: that is my name." Galatinus treats the pronoun "Hu" as a formal name of God.</note> Therefore, when Zechariah said, "Your King comes to you, just and a savior *himself* (Hu)," what else did he wish to express than that which Isaiah clearly expressed in chapter 35, saying: "God *himself* (Hu) will come and save you." <note>original Hebrew: אלהים הוא יבא וישעכם.</note> To save...

For [mercy] properly belongs to God alone. The other things, however, which are added in the same prophecy of Zechariah, explain the humanity of the Messiah. According to this humanity, he was to be poor, and finally, as his passion approached, sitting upon a donkey and upon her colt, he would seek Jerusalem for the sake of saving the human race. From this, the false opinion of the Jews is especially refuted, who think the Messiah will reign temporally over the whole world. For since a temporal worldly kingdom and poverty do not agree at all, nor can they exist together, it must necessarily be conceded that the Messiah's Kingdom—according to the prophecy of this prophet—was to be not temporal, but spiritual. Therefore he himself said, *My kingdom is not of this world.*

<margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin>
CHAPTER. The more recent Jews, since they are most obstinate, in order to deny the divinity of the Messiah expressed through this prophet, say that in the Hebrew text it is written <term>נושע</term> <note>original: "nosa" (nosha)</note>, which is interpreted as "saved," and not "savior." This, they argue, can by no means apply to God. For even if it is proper for God to save, being saved can in no way befit Him. From this they conclude that since the Messiah in this prophecy is called "saved" and not "savior," we cannot infer from it that he is God. Therefore, they say this prophet called the Messiah "just and saved" because the Messiah himself, on account of his justice, is to be saved from the sword of **Gog and Magog** <note>In biblical and apocalyptic tradition, these represent the ultimate enemies of God's people who are defeated in the end times.</note>. GALATINUS. We shall not respond to them with anything other than what the ancient Talmudists say. For this reason, I will bring forward the words of *Rabbi Berachiah*, which *Rabbi Menahem Recanati* <note>A 13th-14th century Italian rabbi and Kabbalist known for his mystical commentaries.</note> records regarding the 3rd chapter of Genesis, saying: "The salvation of Israel is the salvation of God, holy and blessed. As Rabbi Berachiah the priest said: Because it is written in Zechariah chapter 9, 'Just and saved,' and not 'Just savior himself.'" Where this old priest tries to show that God, by saving Israel (that is, the faithful), is said to be "saved," because this prophet says "Just and saved." For by "the Just One" (as his words clearly sound), he understands God. And the reason upon which his saying seems to be founded is this: Just as the perfection of a work is accustomed to redound upon the worker, so the salvation of the human race in some way reflects back upon God. Therefore, according to the exposition of this good Talmudist, the prophet called the Messiah "saved" because, since he himself as God was to save the human race, the salvation of the human race itself was to redound upon him as the author of salvation. For this reason, the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> not ineptly followed the sense more than the words in this place, translating it as <term>δίκαιος καὶ σωτήρ</term> <note>original: "dikaios kai soter," meaning "just and savior."</note>. The author of our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate translation.</note>, imitating them, rightly translated it "Just and savior." It is also proved by this that the Messiah is called "The Just" by antonomasia <note>The use of a title or epithet in place of a proper name.</note> and by way of excellence, because in the book <term>יומא</term> <note>original: "Ioma" (Yoma), a volume of the Talmud concerning the Day of Atonement.</note> in the chapter <term>אמר להם</term> <note>original: "Amar lahem," meaning "He said to them."</note>,

<margin>Note-worthy points.</margin>
it is read in this way: *Rabbi Eliezer* said, "The world was created even for the sake of one just man. Just as it is said in Genesis chapter 1, 'And God saw the light, that it was good.'" *That the Messiah is called a "Man of War" (just as God is called by that name) because of the victory he was to obtain against the devil.*

Among the other names which are spoken of the Messiah either by antonomasia or metaphorically, none so expressly suggests his divinity as this name, "Man of War," which properly belongs to God alone. And for this reason, David said in 1 Samuel 17 <note>The Latin text cites 1 Kings 17, following the Vulgate numbering where 1 & 2 Samuel are called 1 & 2 Kings.</note>: "You come to me with spear, and sword, and shield. But I come in the name of God, or with the name of the God of hosts." All this is tradition. From which three most worthy points are gathered. First indeed is that God was going to sanctify or prepare His name among the Jews in such a way that He would be not only a man, but would also be a "man of war" Himself. Second truly is that God was going to do this for the purpose of sanctifying them from their guilt or sin, or cleansing them. Third, however, is that for God to become a "man of war" belongs to none of the attributes of God, but only to the property of His name. Fourthly and finally, it can be added to the aforementioned that it is quite difficult for unbelieving Jews to believe such things. For since God fills heaven and earth, as is proved here through Jeremiah—nay, what is greater, since as Solomon testifies, the heavens and the heavens of heavens cannot contain Him (as said in 2 Chronicles 2)—how would it be credible, unless God had said that God Himself could become a man? But surely he is far too foolish and impious who suspects that those things which God Himself asserts are impossible, or seeks another author for them.

From these things, therefore, which have been said in this tradition, it is concluded: that this name "Man of War" belongs to God alone by reason of the property of His name, the Tetragrammaton. It remains now for us to show that the Messiah is a "man of war." Wherefore, those things which Rabbi Yochanan said in the chapter <term>Helek</term> <note>A famous chapter in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin (folio 90a onward) discussing the world to come and the Messiah.</note> concerning that saying of Zechariah, chapter 1, are greatly to be noted: <gloss>original: "I saw by night, and behold, a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were red, speckled, and white horses."</gloss> This means: "I saw the night. And behold, a man riding upon a red, or blood-colored, horse. And he was standing among the myrtles, which were in the valley. And after him were red, varied, and white horses." There, therefore, the same Rabbi says: " 'I saw,' he says, 'the night.' For the Holy and Blessed God wished to turn the whole world into night. 'And behold, a man riding upon a red horse.' This man is none other than the Holy and Blessed God. 'And he was standing among the myrtles.' The myrtles are none other than the righteous. Just as it is said in Esther, chapter 2: 'And he was the foster-father of <term>Hadassah</term>,' <note>original: *hadassa* (הדסה)</note> who is Esther; for *Hadas* <note>original: הדס</note> in Hebrew is called *myrtus* in Latin [myrtle in English]." Thus ends the tradition.

For the understanding of this, it should be noted that in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>The "Midrash on the Psalms," an ancient Jewish commentary.</note> on Psalm 20, it is read in this way: "The Holy and Blessed God calls the Messiah by His own name." Just as it is said in Exodus, chapter 15: "The Lord is a man of war; <term>Yahweh</term> [the Tetragrammaton] is His name." Since, therefore, in the aforementioned tradition held in the chapter *Helek* of the book <term>Sanhedrin</term>, it is said that God, a man of war (as said in Exodus 15), is the Holy and Blessed God, riding upon a red horse; and in the other preceding tradition which is found in *Midrash Tehillim*, it is said that God calls the Messiah by His own name, the Tetragrammaton, and that the God-Man of War is the Messiah himself, whose name is <term>Yahweh</term> (the Tetragrammaton of God)—it is consequently necessary that the Messiah Himself is God. The red horse, however, upon which the prophet saw the Holy and Blessed God riding, is nothing other than the body of the Messiah, made red by his own most precious blood in the battle of his passion, by which he was to conquer the devil. Truly the variegated horses, who are more rightly called the doctors and preachers, who are endowed with various documents of doctrine and virtues, run about like horses, now here, now there, by writing and teaching. Moreover, the white horses are none other than the virgins, both men and women, who are adorned with the brightness of snowy virginity. All of these, not without reason, are designated by horses, since horses are more suited for battle than other animals. And indeed, the martyrs conquer the world; the doctors or preachers, however, conquer the devil; and the virgins conquer their own flesh by fighting. Thus it happens that these alone, above other kinds of men, are gifted in the [heavenly] fatherland with the <term>aureola</term> <note>A "golden crown" or special reward in medieval theology given to martyrs, virgins, and teachers for their specific spiritual victories.</note> as the prize of victory.

To prove this point, I cite what is written in **Psalm 17** <note>original: "Psalmo 17." Therefore, it is rightly said in the aforementioned Psalm: *I have sworn to David my servant,* meaning the Messiah. What he swore to him, however, is shown when he immediately adds: *Forever I will establish,* or prepare, *your seed.* That is, your disciples and others believing in you. For disciples and others instructed by someone are rightly called both "children" and "seed" of the one by whom they were taught (as we shall show elsewhere). It follows: *And I will build up your throne to generation and generation* (namely, the Jewish and the Gentile) *Sela,* that is, perpetually or always. 

Since the Hebrew word **Sela** <note>original: סלה</note> used there signifies neither interruption nor end, it can therefore be translated as "into eternity," or "unto ages of ages," or "always," or "perpetually," or "eternally." It is certainly clear that the statement: *And I will build up your throne to generation and generation, Sela,* that is, perpetually or eternally, can apply neither to David the former King, nor to any of his sons, but only to the Lord **Jesus**, the true Messiah. His throne is the Christian people, established by divine power from the two "generations"—that is, the Jews and the Gentiles. For more than one thousand four hundred years have now passed since the throne of David itself, or the kingdom of the Jews, was utterly destroyed and wiped out.

## *That the Messiah is frequently called Solomon in the sacred scriptures, to suggest the incarnation of the Son of God, which was to proceed from the seed of David.* Chapter XXVI.

->CAPNIO,<-

**I**t remains for you to explain how this Messiah is, not without reason, called Solomon in the Jewish writings. GAL. In many places where the Messiah's divinity, incarnation, and redemption are expressed, it often happens that he is called Solomon. First, therefore, hear what is said in the *Midrash* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary or homiletic interpretation.</note> on <term>Shir ha-Shirim</term> <note>original: "Sir hassirim." The Hebrew title for the biblical book "Song of Songs."</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs, regarding the third chapter of that same book: *Go forth and see, O daughters of Zion, King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him.* <note>Song of Songs 3:11</note> For there it is said literally: "Go forth and see, O daughters of Zion," that is, the sons marked for me with the tonsure <note>Likely referring to the tonsure or specific hair-cutting rituals, though here allegorically applied to the Jewish people.</note>, and circumcision, and fringes <note>The "tzitzit" or ritual tassels worn on garments.</note>. "King Solomon," that is, the *Perfecting King*, who created all his creatures in <term>shelemuth</term> <note>original: "selemoth." Hebrew for "perfection" or "completeness," a wordplay on the name Solomon (Shelomo).</note>, which means perfect. For he created the sun and the moon in their fullness. Adam and Eve were also created as if they were children of twenty years. Likewise, in another way, "King Solomon" means the King whose peace is peace. Again, in another way, "King Solomon" means the peaceful King, who made peace with his creatures through his works. Just as he pacified the fire for our father Abraham, and for the three youths: Shadrach <note>original: "Sidrach."</note>, Meshach <note>original: "Meiach."</note>, and Abednego <note>original: "Aued nego."</note>. He also pacified the sword for Isaac. Furthermore, he pacified the angel for Jacob. Yet again, in another way, "King Solomon" means the King who made peace among his creatures. From this Rabbi Yohanan said: It is written in Job 25: *He makes peace in his high places.* For the firmament is made of water, and the stars of fire, yet they do not destroy one another.

<margin>The Synagogue, the mother of God.</margin>
There follows in the Song: *With the crown with which his mother crowned him.* Rabbi Yohanan said that Rabbi Simon questioned Rabbi Elazar, the son of Rabbi Jose, and said to him: "Is it possible that you have heard from your father what is meant by the phrase, 'With the crown with which his mother crowned him'?" He answered him, "Yes." He said to him, "In what way?" He told him, "In the beginning, the Holy and Blessed God loved Israel and called them <term>Bitti</term> <note>original: "Bitti." Hebrew for "my daughter."</note>, that is, my daughter. And this is what is written in Psalm 45: *Hear, O daughter, and see.* But he did not cease to love them until he called them <term>Ahothi</term> <note>original: "Ahothi." Hebrew for "my sister."</note>, that is, my sister. As it is said in the fifth chapter of the Song: *Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one.* Again, he did not cease to love until he called them <term>Immi</term> <note>original: "immi." Hebrew for "my mother."</note>, that is, my mother. As it is said in the 51st chapter of Isaiah: *Attend to me, my people, and my mother, give ear to me.* For it was not <term>Ammi</term> <note>original: "Vmmi" (meaning 'my people' in a common sense).</note>, that is, my people, written there, but <term>Immi</term> <note>original: "immi."</note>, that is, my mother." Rabbi Simon rose and kissed him on the head, and said: "If I had come for no other reason than to hear this word from your mouth, it would have been <term>Dai</term> <note>original: "Dai." Hebrew for "enough" or "sufficient."</note>, that is, enough for me."

This was done so that it might be openly shown that the incarnation of God was to come from the Jews. Why then is it said, 'born to you' <note>original: "נולד לך Nolad lach"</note>? 'To you' means for your care or for your medicine—that is, for the medicine of your sins which are within you. All of this is from the tradition. From this it clearly appears that when the scripture says, "A son is born to you," along with the other things that follow, all these are to be understood as referring to the Messiah under the veil of the name "Solomon," even though on the surface they seem to be spoken of King Solomon. For the things stated in this exposition—namely, that a son was to be born to David to provide medicine and healing for his sins—can in no way apply to Solomon his actual son. Solomon was entirely unable to provide medicine for his own sins or to heal his own offenses, if one considers his deeds even briefly.

Hence the Jews object to us that these words ought to be understood literally as referring to Solomon, who constructed the temple for God, and not to the Messiah. GALATINUS: Just as the "house of Israel" and the "house of David" and similar phrases in many places of Holy Scripture do not refer to a pile of stones and wood, but to the congregation of people itself; so also here, the "House of God" to be built by the spiritual Solomon (that is, by the Messiah) should be understood not as a material structure, but a spiritual one which in Greek is called the <term>ekklesia</term> <note>The "assembly" or "church."</note>. Therefore, although the material Solomon built a material house for God, the spiritual Solomon—the Messiah—was to build for Him a spiritual house. This spiritual house is far more excellent and far more perfect, built of "living and chosen stones"—that is, of the Jews and Gentiles who would believe in him. Just as the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Jewish scholars who compiled the Talmud, a central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> interpreted "Solomon" here mystically as the Messiah, so too the material house of God which was to be built by the material Solomon must be understood as the assembly of the faithful which was to be gathered by the Messiah. All these things become more manifest if the preceding words are rightly inspected. When David thought to construct a house for the Lord, the prophet Nathan spoke to him in the person of the Lord, as is found in the seventeenth chapter of the first book of Chronicles, where it is said in Hebrew:

> <note>original Hebrew: "והיה כי מלאו ימיך ללכת עם אבותיך והקימותי את זרעך אחריך אשר יהיה מבניך והכינותי את מלכותו : הוא יבנה לי בית וכננתי את כסאו עד עולם אני אהיה לו לאב והוא יהיה לי לבן וחסדי לא אטיר מעמו כאשר הסירותי מאשר היה לפניך והעמדתהו בביתי ובמלכותי עד העולם וכסאו יהיה נכון עד עולם :"</note>
> "And it shall come to pass, when your days are fulfilled that you must go to be with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, who shall be of your sons; and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son; and I will not take my mercy away from him, as I took it from him who was before you. But I will settle him in my house and in my kingdom forever; and his throne shall be established forever."

That is to say, when you have finished your days to go to your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall be of your sons. And I will establish his Kingdom. He himself shall build me a house, and I will firm up his throne forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me. -> *On the fellowship of divinity and humanity. And on God's equality and* <-
-> *participation with man. Chapter XXVII.* <-

### CAPNIO,

**O** Galatinus, since you have spoken quite abundantly in the preceding sections concerning the names of the Messiah—by which both the incarnation of the Son of God and the twin nature of the Messiah itself (namely, the divine and the human) are best suggested—it is now necessary for you to say something regarding those things which express that same incarnation of the Son of God. Therefore, first show the fellowship of divinity and humanity, and that there was to be an equality and participation of God with man. **GALATINUS:** Concerning the fellowship, participation, and equalization of God with man—through which the firmness of our faith is greatly strengthened, and the depravity of the Jews of our time (who deny the incarnation of the Son of God) is countered in many ways—many things are certainly found said in their books by their own ancient writers. ->THIRD BOOK<-

Therefore, we must listen to what Isaiah says in chapter 35 with these words: <note>original: "גמול אלהים הוא יבא יושיעכם"</note> "The retribution of God, or the retribution—whether it be the reward or the prize—God Himself will come and save you." <note>Isaiah 35:4</note> Rabbi Jonathan, in the <term>Targum</term> <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, explained it in this way: <note>original: "יהוה אגריתן אלהים הוא יתגli ויפרוק לחון"</note> "The God of retributions, God Himself will reveal Himself and save you." Whereby, from the fact that Rabbi Jonathan explained "God Himself will reveal Himself" where the prophet said "God Himself will come," 

<margin>The coming of God.</margin>

it is clearly demonstrated that the "coming" of God is nothing other than Him revealing Himself, according to the interpretation of the ancient Jews. For since God is present everywhere by His own immensity and is contained by no place, it is plainly established that the Son of God was not to come according to His divine nature, but according to this: that by assuming human flesh and being made visible, He was destined to appear as a man. For if He were to come only as God, He would not have "come" to those who were unable to see Him. Therefore, such a God was to come to us as we were able to see. Unless, therefore, He was to assume the form of a visible nature, He would by no means have been said to "come" to us. 

Those ancient fathers understood this perfectly, as noted regarding what is said in Isaiah chapter 25: <note>original: "ואמר ביום ההוא הנה אלהינו זה קוינו לו ויושיענו זה יהוה קוינו לו נגילה ונשמחה בישועתו"</note> "And they will say in that day: Behold, this is our God, we have waited for Him (or we have expected Him), and He will save us. This is the Lord, we have waited for Him (or we have expected Him), and we shall rejoice and be glad in His salvation." <note>Isaiah 25:9</note> Indeed, these words are to be explained no differently than how 

<margin>Talmudic interpretation.</margin>

the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> themselves explained them. Through these words, they taught that there would eventually be a time when the world would see God with its eyes, and the peoples would point Him out to one another with a finger. For in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>A Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Psalms.</note> concerning that verse in Psalm 39, <note>original: "קוה קויתי"</note> "In waiting, I waited for my expectation (or my cry)," it is said: This is what is written in Isaiah chapter 25: "And they will say in that day: Behold, this is our God, we have expected Him, and He will save us." And it is also said in Lamentations chapter 3: "The Lord is good to those who wait for Him." <note>Lamentations 3:25</note> For this reason, because the nations of the world do not cease to say, "Where is their God?" it is destined to happen that the Holy and Blessed God will sit in the midst of the righteous, and they shall point Him out with a finger. Just as it is said in Psalm 48: <note>original: "כי זה אלהים אלהינו עולם ועד הוא ינהגנו על מות"</note> "Because this is God, our God forever and beyond; He will lead (or govern) us even unto death." And again, he says in Psalm 4: <note>Galatinus cites Psalm 4, though the quote "Be strengthened and let your heart be comforted" is found in Psalms 27 and 31.</note> "Be strengthened, and let your heart be encouraged, all you who hope in the Lord." This is the tradition. 

Likewise, in the <term>Beressith Ketanna</term> <note>The "Lesser Genesis," likely referring to a specific section of the Midrash Rabbah or a similar homiletic collection.</note>—that is, in the minor exposition of Genesis—concerning that passage in Genesis chapter 18, "And the Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre, and he was sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day," it is read word-for-word: It is written in Job chapter 19: "And again (or afterward) I shall be clothed round about with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God." <note>Job 19:26</note> Thus far the tradition. Behold in what an admirable way the ancient Jews, joining these two testimonies of Holy Scripture in this place, taught the mystery of the divine Incarnation.

<margin>Response.</margin>Just so, among all wise men, according to the nature of divinity, it is impossible for God the creator—and altogether incongruous—to be able to be corrupted <note>In this philosophical context, "corrupted" refers to undergoing any physical change, decay, or movement that implies a lack of perfection</note>. For this is said to be characteristic of a creature having a body and feet. Furthermore, God is in every place, although not in a localized way, and he fills the whole world. As is gathered from Jeremiah, who says: "Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord" <note>Jeremiah 23:24</note>. Since God is therefore everywhere, and is essentially absent nowhere, it follows that he cannot leave one place and go to another, which is what walking about means. For that is entirely contrary to the nature of divinity. **GAL.** Therefore, regarding the fulfillment of God’s promise, who said in *Leviticus chapter 26*, "I will walk in your midst," as we have just related, and for the truth of the sacred scripture, which asserts many things of this kind about God, as well as for the confirmation of the aforementioned traditions, which seem to explain scriptures of this kind for the truth of our faith, we say as briefly as possible: That God spoke through the prophets in this way to openly suggest that he was one day going to unite man to himself in such a true and such a powerful union, that upon seeing the man united to him, He himself would be said to be seen. And with that man walking among other men, God himself could truly be said to walk; and pointing out that same man with a finger, we could truly say: "This is our God." Which Baruch also excellently affirms, when in chapter 3 he says: <note>original Hebrew: זה אלהינו ולא יחשב אחר לפניו זה מצא כל דרך חכמה ונתנה ליעקב נערו ולישראל חמודו ואחרי זה בארץ נראה ובאנשים הירגיל</note> "This is our God, and no other shall be esteemed in his sight. He found out every way of wisdom, and delivered it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved. After these things he was seen upon the earth, and conversed with men" <note>Baruch 3:36–38. This deuterocanonical passage was frequently cited by early Christian authors as a prophecy of the Incarnation</note>. What can be said clearer than these words? What more plain? What more evident? What more manifest? For if it is certain that God, according to his divinity, can neither be seen by eyes nor converse with men—since only colors <note>original: "chromata." In Aristotelian philosophy, color is the primary object of sight</note> are seen, and conversation properly occurs between those <term>of the same substance</term> <note>original: "homousios," from the Greek "homoousios," meaning sharing the same essence</note>—the Jews must necessarily concede that it was intended that God would eventually become man, so that according to his humanity he could be perceived by eyes and would converse with men. On which account he is frequently called the "brother of Israel" and his "kinsman" in the sacred scriptures.

> *that God, through the assumption of our nature, ought to become*
> *our brother.*
