This is primarily evident in the book <term>Mekhilta</term><note>A collection of ancient Jewish legal and narrative commentary on the Book of Exodus.</note>, that is, in the exposition of Exodus, where it is easily seen. Regarding what is said in Exodus chapter 14, "Why do you cry out to me?", we read the following: Rabbi Halcusi said: Does not the scripture already say in Proverbs chapter 17: **A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity**? <note>original: "בכל עת אהב הרע ואח לצרה יולד"</note> This refers to the Holy and Blessed God, who said, "I will be a brother to Israel in the hour of their trouble or distress." This is just as it was said in Psalm 122: **For the sake of my brothers and my friends, I will now speak peace within you.** <note>original: "למען אחי ורעי אדברה נא שלום בך"</note> That is to say: For the sake of my brothers, and my friends, or my kinsmen, or my companions, I will now speak peace in you. Thus far the tradition. From this, it is clearly held that God is called the friend and brother of Israel, He who was destined to be born for adversity according to His humanity.

Furthermore, regarding the truth of the aforementioned tradition, what is written in <term>Midrash Tehillim</term><note>A classic rabbinic commentary on the Book of Psalms, also known as Midrash Shocher Tov.</note> (that is, in the exposition of the Psalms) is particularly helpful, concerning that verse in Psalm 4: "Hear me when I call, O God of my righteousness." There, it is read literally as follows: <term>Rabbi Iodan</term> said: Whoever turns to, or runs after, "flesh and blood" <note>A common Semitic idiom meaning "mortal human beings."</note> has a patron. But when the time of distress or trouble arrives, he does not immediately enter that patron's presence. For he comes and stands before the patron's door, and calls out to his servant, and the servant indeed says: "Behold, he is waiting at the door." But the Holy and Blessed God does not act this way. For when the time of trouble or distress comes upon Israel, he will not call upon Michael, or Gabriel, but will invoke God Himself, and He Himself will hear him. And this is what is written in Joel chapter 3: **And it shall come to pass, that everyone who calls on the name of God (the Tetragrammaton) shall be delivered.** <note>original: "והיה כל אשר יקרא בשם יהוה ימלט". The Tetragrammaton refers to the four-letter holy name of God, YHWH.</note>

And further down, <term>Rabbi Symeon</term> said: Flesh and blood has a **karob** <note>Hebrew for "relative" or "near one."</note>, that is, a kinsman or neighbor, and if that person is wealthy, the patron will acknowledge him. But the Holy and Blessed God does not act this way. For when Israel is in a state of humility, it is then that He calls them brothers and kinsmen. Just as it was said in Psalm 122: "For the sake of my brothers and my kinsmen, I will now speak peace in you."

Likewise, further down, Rabbi Aben said in the name of **Rabbi Aha**: Flesh and blood, having a **karob** (that is, a kinsman) who is a captive or plundered, is ashamed to confess that the man is his relative. But the Holy and Blessed God caused the captive and plundered Israel to be led out, and yet He expressly calls them **kerouim** <note>The plural of "karob," meaning relatives or neighbors.</note>, that is, kinsmen or relatives. As it is said in Psalm 148: **For the children of Israel, a people near to him (his kinsman), Praise the Lord.** <note>original: "לבני ישראל עם קרובו הללויה"</note>

And again further down, the Holy and Blessed God said (Isaiah 65): "And it shall be, before they call, I will answer, and I will hear." However, even though this is so, it is nonetheless necessary that their invocation be made in truth. As it is said in Psalm 145: **God is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth.** <note>original: "קרוב יהוה לכל קראיו לכל אשר יקראהו באמת"</note> Is it possible that He is near to everyone who calls upon Him? The scripture teaches what should be said to this in the words that follow: "To all who call upon Him in truth." Thus far the tradition. From which it is manifest...

It is also very much worth noting that the aforementioned tradition, explaining that passage in Deuteronomy 32, *Consider the years of generation and generation* <note>Deuteronomy 32:7.</note>, speaks in this way: "This is the generation of the Messiah,

in whom there are three generations." In this, it should be understood that nothing else is being said except that the generation of the Messiah is "generation and generation" (doubled), and yet in Him there are nonetheless three generations. This "twin" generation of the Messiah refers to the divine, by which He was begotten of the Father before the ages, and the human, by which He was born of His mother in time. And consequently, it follows that there are three generations in Him—namely, three substances: body, soul, and divinity. And again, these two and three are the one Messiah.

### That God was to be made equal to the church, and that the Messiah was to be the head of the church. Chapter 30.

### CAPNIO <note>The scholar Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneer of Hebrew studies among Christians, who appears here as a character in the dialogue.</note>,

To suggest even this incarnation of the Son of God (as I judge), God Himself called the church His sister and companion. Thus in chapter 5 of the Song of Songs, saying: *Open to me, my sister, my companion, my dove, my perfect one.* <note>original Hebrew: פתחי לי אחתי רעיתי יונתי תמתי (Song of Solomon 5:2).</note>

<margin>GALATINUS <note>Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540), the author of this work and the primary speaker explaining these mysteries.</note></margin> It is certainly as you say. But another greater mystery lies hidden in these words, which is most relevant to our purpose. For where it is now written *tammathi* <note>original Hebrew: תמתי</note>, that is, "my perfect one," Solomon actually wrote *teumathi* <note>original Hebrew: תאומתי</note>, that is, "my twin." For the ancient Talmudists testify that it was written thus. For we read in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>A traditional rabbinic commentary on the Song of Songs.</note>, in the exposition of the Song of Songs upon this text, that Rabbi Immai said that *teumathi*—"my twin"—was written. From which it can be said: it is written in the law. Rabbi Judah said there in the name of Rabbi Levi: "my twin" (*teumathi*) was said by God because just as it happens with twins of this kind, if the body of one feels something, the companion is immediately disturbed and troubled. Thus, since it is said in the law, it can be stated: because God said in Psalm 91: *I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him, and honor him, and show him my salvation.* <note>original Latin: "Cum ipso sum ego in tribulatione..." (Psalm 91:15).</note> This is the tradition. From which it is clearly shown that God and the church were to be like two twins. And then God, existing and dwelling together with man, would honor him and rescue him from tribulation. This cannot be understood except as the incarnation. From which it is plainly inferred that the Messiah was to have a dual nature: namely, divine and human. So that in the one He would be true and perfect God, and in the other, true and perfect man.

<margin>CAPNIO</margin> According to which nature ought the Messiah to be the head of the church? Namely, according to the divine nature, or according to the human nature, or according to both together?

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> According to both together, I say, although far more according to the human than according to the divine.

...divine nature. For according to that nature, he ought to be the head of the church more properly in the sense that it was more fitting for the church itself to be his mystical body. But according to his human nature, it is much more fitting for the universal church of Christ to be his mystical body than according to his divine nature, since he properly possesses "members" <note>In Christian theology, the "members" are the individual believers who make up the "Body of Christ."</note> according to his human nature, and not according to his divine nature. ### In order that the stubbornness <note>original: *perfidia*. This term was historically used in Christian polemics to describe Jewish refusal to accept Christian doctrine; here it reflects the confrontational tone of 16th-century debates.</note> of the Jews may be more fully refuted, it must be proved in this place that the Messiah was to be the head of the entire church, which was to be gathered from both Jews and Gentiles. GALATINUS.
<margin>The Messiah was to be the head of the Church.</margin>

First, therefore, I shall bring forward Hosea, who speaks clearly about this "head" and "body" in his first chapter: *And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head, and they shall go up from the land, for great shall be the day of Jezreel.* <note>original Hebrew: ונקבצו בני יהודה ובני ישראל יחדו ושמו להם ראש אחד ועלו מן הארץ כי גדול יום יזרעאל (Hosea 1:11).</note> These words are interpreted thus: "And the children of Judah and the children of Israel will be gathered together, and they will set for themselves one head. And they will ascend from the earth. Because great is the day of Jezreel." Regarding this, the commentary of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), known as Rashi, the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: "And they shall appoint for themselves one head: this is David their King. For great shall be the day of Jezreel: that is, the day of the gathering of their seed." Thus far Rabbi Solomon. 

All of this was fulfilled when the apostles and the rest of Christ's disciples (some of whom were from the tribe of Judah, such as James, John, the other James, and his brothers, and others from each of the other tribes) were gathered together into the one faith of Christ along with converts from the Gentiles, and they appointed for themselves one head, David their King—that is, the Messiah. That "David" is understood to mean the Messiah has been made abundantly clear in the preceding pages. Where, among other things, it was said that whether the Messiah be among the living or the dead, his name is David. 

The prophecy continues: *And he shall ascend from the earth*, that is, from earthly perception and way of life, and from the humility of the literal sense, to the height of spiritual understanding. *For great is the day of Jezreel*, which in Latin sounds like "what God will sow" <note>Jezreel (*Yizreel*) literally means 'God sows' or 'God will sow' in Hebrew.</note>. # Book Four.
## Concerning the first advent of the Messiah.

->*That the coming of the Messiah is twofold: one with humility, for the redemption of the human race; the other with glory and majesty, for the judgment of the entire world.*<-
->*Chapter I.*<-

<note>The following section begins with a decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a male figure, likely a scholar or prophet, seated with a book.</note>

->**CAPNIO**<- <note>Capnio is the Greek-inspired pseudonym of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian humanist and scholar of Hebrew.</note>

Because there are two things in particular that the Jews of our age deny regarding the Messiah: namely, his divinity, and that he has already come. For they assert that he is a mere man, and they still wait for him to come in the future. Therefore, just as you have abundantly proven through their own scriptures that the Messiah was to be both God and man, you must also show that he has already come. Thus, when they recognize through their own scriptures—which speak most clearly on this matter—that the very same person they still wait for with such great longing has already arrived, they may be forced to confess that our Lord Jesus Christ was the true Messiah and Savior of the world. 

**GALATINUS** <note>Pietro Galatino, the author of this work, acting as the lead speaker in the dialogue.</note>: I will certainly show this. But first, one thing must be clarified which none of you has asked about. 

**HOGSTRATUS** <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, a Dominican theologian who was often a rival of Reuchlin, here acting as a participant in the discussion.</note>: What is that? 

**GALATINUS**: I will tell you immediately. Since it should be our intention not only to overcome their disbelief <note>original: *perfidiam*. In Renaissance theological Latin, this often refers specifically to the rejection of the Christian faith rather than "treachery" in the modern sense.</note> with the truth, but also to strive with all our might to bring them back to the recognition of the truth, we must certainly explain where they find the occasion for such a great error—that they never cease waiting for the one who has clearly already come. Once the cause of this error is removed, its effect—that is, the unbelief itself which arises from this error—may also be removed, unless they wish to remain stubborn in the blindness of their disbelief. It is therefore necessary to know that the coming of the Messiah is twofold, as the prophets have spoken of it everywhere. One coming is indeed with humility, for the purpose of redeeming or saving. The other, however, is with glory and majesty, for the purpose of judging. Nevertheless, the more recent Jews, as if altogether blinded and not knowing how to distinguish this twin coming of the Messiah, confuse the predictions of the prophets. They entangle themselves in various errors and compose almost infinite lies concerning the mysteries of the Messiah. For some expect that the Messiah himself will appear in his coming immediately with such great power and authority.

Others still—both because of what the prophets predicted concerning the humility and passion the Messiah would undergo in his first advent, and because of what the prophets themselves foretold concerning the manifestation of his majesty and glory in his second advent—affirm that there will be two coming Messiahs. But if they were willing to rightly understand the sayings of the prophets and the expositions of the ancient **Talmudists** <note>The scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law and legend.</note>, they would not only avoid falling into so many errors, but they could also easily recognize the truth itself. For to speak first of the prophets, if they would notice the various manners of coming which they assign to the Messiah himself, they would find that these cannot be fulfilled in one and the same advent. Rather, they themselves would concede from the different modes of coming that there are two advents of the Messiah. If they did this, they could easily reach the recognition of the truth.

**CAPNIO**: I have indeed read these very often.

**GALATINUS**: It is certain, therefore, that both prophets spoke of one and the same Messiah in these places; yet they attribute to him vastly different modes of coming...

Then the Holy One, blessed be He, will say to him: "You ask for life from me? Even before you spoke, your father David already prophesied this concerning you." These things are from the **Talmud**. Indeed, they contain nothing that is contrary to our Lord Jesus Christ. For regarding what follows—that the Messiah, the son of David, was not to die—it can be appropriately said: even if the Lord Jesus suffered and died according to his humanity as a man, nevertheless He himself "asked for life," and "length of days forever and ever" was given to Him when God raised Him up on the third day after His death, never to die again. 

Furthermore, from this tradition, many other points are held against the Jews. First, indeed, that the Messiah, the son of David, was to redeem them "quickly." Consequently, it means that in "their days"—that is, while they were still lords and powerful in their own land—the Messiah, the son of David himself, was meant to come. For the "days" of any nation or king are said to be those in which they rule and flourish. Next, that Psalm 2 speaks of the Messiah. From this it follows that the Messiah is the Son of God, because it is said in that same Psalm: *God said to me, you are my son.* And He is not merely an adopted son, because of what is immediately added: *Today I have begotten you.* To Him, as a true son, He gave the nations as an inheritance and the entire world as a possession—which is clearly fulfilled in the Christians. Finally, that Psalm 21 <note>In the Vulgate numbering used here, Psalm 21 begins "O Lord, in thy strength the king shall rejoice," corresponding to Psalm 21 in the KJV.</note> is understood entirely to be about the Messiah.

For this is what is written concerning him in Zechariah chapter 12: *And they shall look upon me, whom they have pierced.* <note>original Hebrew: *Ve-hibitu elay et asher dakaru*</note>

Thus far the tradition. From which a very strong argument against the Jews is taken. For since he who says the following in the same prophet, immediately before the aforesaid words, must be God: *And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of prayers.* <note>original Hebrew: *Ve-shafakhti al beit David ve-al yoshev Yerushalayim ruach chen ve-tachanunim*</note> For doing this belongs to God alone. And since that same speaker immediately adds what was just said, namely: *And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced.* The Jewish Masters explained that this was spoken concerning the killing of the Messiah son of Joseph, as is clearly evident in this tradition. It certainly follows, therefore, that the Messiah son of Joseph must be both God and man. Inasmuch as he is God, he would be able to pour out the spirit of grace and prayers upon those who believe in him; and inasmuch as he is man, he could be pierced with nails on the cross. 

From these traditions, therefore, because they are not correctly understood, the irrational folly of the Jews of our age expects two Messiahs to come: one the son of David, the other the son of Joseph. But that they are most shamefully deceived is evident in two ways. First, through Holy Scripture. For even if Saul, David, and certain others are called "Messiahs" <note>literally "Anointed Ones"</note>, it can nowhere be shown in all twenty-four books of the Holy Page <note>The 24 books of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)</note> that any scripture mentions more than one single Messiah who is to come for salvation. Secondly, this is also most clearly demonstrated through their own ancient traditions. For among the ancient Jews, both the Messiah son of Joseph and the Messiah son of David were considered to be one and the same. 

### CHAPTER

Listen then to the first thing said in **Bereshith Rabbah** <note>A classic Midrashic commentary on the book of Genesis</note>. For there it is said regarding Genesis chapter 28: *And Jacob went out from Beersheba*—that is, from the "well of the seven." Thus it is read literally. This is what is written in Psalm 120 <note>In the Vulgate/Hebrew numbering; modern Bibles usually list this as Psalm 121</note>: *I will lift up my eyes to the mountains, from whence my help shall come.* "Who are you, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel?" This great mountain is the Messiah, the son of David. 

And a little later it is added: "Grace to it"—this was said because he himself will be the one giving grace and prayers to Israel. Just as it is said in Zechariah 12: *And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of prayers.* All these things are the tradition. At the end of which it is said that the Messiah son of David was to give grace and prayers to Israel. To prove this, the authority of Zechariah is brought forward: *And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of prayers.* Yet this same authority was brought forward in the preceding tradition concerning the Messiah son of Joseph. From which it is manifest beyond doubt that the Messiah son of Joseph and the Messiah son of David are altogether [the same...]

**CAP.** Indeed, they even resist us in this way quite often. For since this prophecy does not speak openly of Christ under the name of "Messiah," but obscurely under the name **Shiloh** <note>Hebrew: שִׁילֹה (Shiloh); a cryptic term in Genesis 49:10 traditionally interpreted by Christians as referring to Christ</note>. For where our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> has, *Until he comes who is to be sent*, the Hebrew text (as has been seen) says, *Until Shiloh comes*. This word is certainly ambiguous among the Hebrews. For **Shiloh** <note>שילה</note> can be the proper name of a certain place so called, and it can signify a "mission" or "one who is sent," derived from the verb **Shalach** <note>Hebrew: שָׁלַח (shalach), meaning "to send"</note>. For that reason, some of the more recent Jews, attempting to subvert the true sense of this prophecy and taking "Shiloh" as a place, say that it should be understood not as the Messiah, but as **Saul**. They claim that Saul, having been elected as King, came to be anointed in Shiloh, where the Ark of the Lord was, in which the anointing oil was kept. And then they say the "scepter"—which is understood here as a kind of primacy and had until then been in the tribe of Judah—was removed from that tribe and transferred to the tribe of **Benjamin**, from which Saul himself came.

**GAL.** This exposition of theirs is entirely false. Firstly, because before the election of Saul, the Ark of the Lord (in which the anointing oil was kept) had already been transported from Shiloh to **Kiriath-Jearim**, as is clear from the seventh chapter of the first book of Kings <note>Known in modern Bibles as 1 Samuel 7</note>. Consequently, Saul was anointed not in Shiloh, but in Kiriath-Jearim. Secondly, because immediately after Saul—indeed, while Saul himself was still reigning—**David**, who was the first to reign from the tribe of Judah, was instituted as King and anointed by the priest **Samuel**. Therefore, it seems not at all likely that the scepter was taken away from the tribe of Judah at that time, when...

-># BOOK FOUR<-

...so the people of the Jews were governed. For **Zerubbabel**, who stood as the Prince of the people during their return from that same captivity, was of the tribe of **Judah**, as we read in Zechariah, chapter 4, and in Haggai, chapter 1. Similarly, all others who held the leadership of the people until the time of the **Maccabees** were of the tribe of Judah. Even the **Talmudists** <note>scholars of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> themselves pass down this tradition. Furthermore, the **Maccabees**, who subsequently held the principality of the Jews until **Herod the Ascalonite** <note>Herod the Great, whose father was from Ascalon</note>, were reckoned as being of the tribe of Judah because the royal tribe and the priestly tribe had intermingled. This is evident from the fourth book of Kings, chapter 11 <note>original: "libri 4. Reg. ca. 11"; in modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 11</note>. Thus, even the Maccabees themselves were descended from the tribe of Judah through their maternal line. 

<margin><unclear>was</unclear></margin> All of these things are excellently confirmed in the book of the **Sanhedrin** <note>a tractate of the Talmud concerning the high court and legal procedures</note> in the chapter titled ***Dine mamonoth*** <note>Hebrew: דיני ממונות; "Judgments of Property" or "Monetary Laws"</note>. For there it is said: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah*. These are the "Heads of the Exile" who ruled Israel with rod and scepter. *And the scribe from between his feet*. These are the sons of the sons of **Hillel** <note>a famous Jewish sage whose descendants headed the Sanhedrin for generations</note>. On this, the gloss <note>interpretive commentary</note> says: The "Heads of the Exile" in Babylon were **Zerubbabel** and his kin, and the Prince who was in the land of Israel. This was **Mattathias** and his kin, namely the ***Hasmonai*** <note>Hebrew: חשמונאי; the Hasmoneans</note>, that is, the **Maccabees**, and the others 

<margin><unclear>Hasmoneans</unclear></margin> descending from them. The "sons of the sons of Hillel" were the **Sanhedrin**, that is, the aforementioned judges taught by the disciples of Hillel; for this reason, they are called his "sons' sons" on account of his doctrine. From this it is manifest that until the times of Herod the Ascalonite himself, the scepter had not departed from the tribe of Judah.

Thirdly, this is most clearly shown through the **Targum**, that is, the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> translation of **Rabbi Onkelos**. In this place, it says: *The ruler or maker of power and royal dominion shall not pass away from the house of Judah, nor the scribe from his children's children forever, until the Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs. And the peoples, or the gathered nations of the gentiles, shall obey him.* <note>original Aramaic: "לא יעדיון עביד שולטן מדבית יהודה וספרא מבני בנוהי עד עלמא עד דייתי משיחא דדי ליה היא מלכותא וליה ישתמעון עממיא"</note> If this Chaldean translation and exposition is examined diligently, many things are found that support our proposal. 

The first of these is that through the Hebrew word ***sceuet*** <note>Hebrew: שבט; "scepter" or "rod"</note>, which is interpreted as a rod or scepter, a certain royal act and dominion is understood. This agrees with Psalm 45: *The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom* <note>original Hebrew: "שבט מישור שבט מלכותך"</note>. The second is that through the word ***Mehokec*** <note>Hebrew: מחוקק; "lawgiver"</note>, which is the same as "scribe," a great legislator ought to be understood. Hence, in Deuteronomy chapter 33, in the blessing of Gad, where the Latin says "Teacher," the Hebrew has ***Mehokec***. Onkelos explained this in Chaldean concerning **Moses**: *In his possession, Moses the great scribe of Israel was buried* <note>original Aramaic: "באחסנתיה משה ספרא רבא דישראל קביר"</note>. This means the great legislator was buried there. Also, in what we find in Isaiah 33, *The Lord is our lawgiver*, the Hebrew uses this same word ***Mehokec*** <note>Hebrew: יהוה מחוקקנו; "The Lord is our Lawgiver"</note>. # BOOK FOUR

In the ancient *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>original: "Berefith Rabba"; a 5th-century collection of Jewish interpretations of the Book of Genesis</note> this is also excellently proven, where it is said regarding this passage, *Until **Silo** <note>Hebrew: שילה; typically rendered as Shiloh in English</note> comes*: "Until Silo comes. This is the Messiah. And to him the nations shall gather themselves. For he himself shall judge the entire world." And this is what was said in Micah, chapter 4: *And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many peoples.* And again in Isaiah, chapter 11: *And he shall judge the poor in justice, and shall rebuke with equity for the mild of the earth. And he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked.* All these things are found there. To these is connected quite fittingly what is read in **Echa Rabbathi** <note>Hebrew: איכה רבתי; an ancient commentary on the Book of Lamentations</note>, that is, in the exposition of the lamentations of Jeremiah. While commenting on that passage in Lamentations, chapter 1: *Because the comforter, who restores my soul, is far from me*, it is said: "What is the name of the Messiah? Those who were of the house of Rabbi Sela said, '**Silo**' is his name. Just as it is said in Genesis, chapter 49: *Until Silo comes*, that is, the Messiah."

<margin>Why the Messiah is called Silo.</margin>
CAPITO: If, therefore, in this prophecy "Silo" can be understood as nothing other than the Messiah, why did the prophet not say, "Until the Messiah comes," but rather "Until Silo comes"? 

GALATINUS: It was certainly not without reason that he spoke thus. For in this he wished to openly suggest that the Messiah was to be born from a mother without a father, or rather, was to be conceived from the mother's matter without the seed of a man. This is clearly testified by Rabbi Kimhi in the *Book of Roots* <note>original: "Serassim," referring to David Kimhi’s *Sefer Shorashim*, a famous 12th-century Hebrew dictionary</note>, while he says the following about him: "The Messiah is called Prince and Ruler. For it is the custom of a Ruler to have a rod in his hand. And because the rod of the people's discipline shall be in his hand, he is therefore also called **Mehokec** <note>Hebrew: מחוקק; 'Mechokek,' often translated as 'lawgiver' or 'commander'</note>, which signifies a scribe."

<margin>Silo, its etymology and interpretation.</margin>
Furthermore, *Until Silo comes* is explained as "his son born of a woman." And it is a prophecy concerning the Messiah. The name **Silo** is derived from the word **Silya** <note>Hebrew: שילא; 'Shilya,' referring to the fetal membrane or placenta</note>, which is a certain little sac in which the infant remains in the mother's womb, and which is sometimes used in scripture for the embryo in the matrix. All these things are from Rabbi Kimhi. From these it is most aptly clear that "Silo" in the aforementioned prophecy is the same as "the son of a woman." From this it is evident why the prophet said, "Until Silo comes," namely to show that the Messiah himself was to be born of a mother without a father. From all of which it is clearly evident, against the faithlessness <note>original: "perfidiam"; a term common in the 16th century to describe the refusal of Jews to accept Christian doctrine</note> of the Jews of our time, that according to the expositions of the ancient Talmudists, the previous prophecy can be correctly understood of no one else but the Messiah. And consequently, according to the sayings of the ancients, it is concluded that at the coming of the Messiah himself, the scepter of the Jewish Kingdom was bound to fail completely.

Instead, the House of Judgment <note>the Sanhedrin</note> of seventy-one judges sat in the Chamber of **Gazith**, which means "hewn stone." Other houses of judgment of twenty-three judges sat in various locations: one sat at the gate of the Temple Mount, another at the gate of the Temple courtyard, and the remaining houses of judgment of twenty-three judges sat in the individual cities of Israel. 

When a matter needed to be decided by the house of judgment in one’s own city, the question was asked. If the judges had heard the tradition, they spoke it. If not, the parties went to the court in the nearest city. If those judges had heard the tradition, they spoke it to them. If not, they went to the court at the gate of the Temple Mount. There they would say: "Thus I have expounded, and thus my colleagues have expounded; thus I have taught, and thus my colleagues have taught." If those judges had heard the tradition, they spoke <note>original: "picebant", likely a printer's error for "dicebant"</note> it to them. If not, they went to the court at the gate of the Temple courtyard. Again they would say: "Thus I have expounded, and thus my colleagues have expounded; thus I have taught, and thus my colleagues have taught." If they had heard the tradition, they spoke it. But if they had not, then both groups went to the Chamber of **Gazith**—that is, the hewn or polished stone—where the Great Sanhedrin sat from morning until evening. On Sabbaths and festival days, however, they sat on the wall. But from the time the disciples of **Shammai** and **Hillel** <note>the two most famous competing schools of Jewish thought in the 1st century BCE</note> multiplied—those who did not serve as was fitting—schisms increased in Israel, and the Law became like two separate Laws.

<margin>The lineage of Herod the Ascalonite.</margin> Therefore, Herod the Ascalonite was the first foreigner to obtain the kingdom of the Jews through trickery. He received the kingdom of the Jews from the Romans so that he might oversee the tributes and obey the Roman Empire. He took as his wife the granddaughter of **Hyrcanus**, the High Priest and Prince of the Jews (who was the son of **Alexandra**, Queen of the Jews, and descended from the **Maccabees**). He circumcised himself and became a **proselyte** <note>a convert to Judaism</note> out of love for the kingdom and for her. 

Eventually, he killed the same Hyrcanus by trickery, because Hyrcanus claimed the kingdom was owed to him. For although Herod had received Judea—which was in no way his—from **Augustus** and the Senate while the High Priest Hyrcanus was held captive by the **Parthians**, Herod later killed Hyrcanus when he returned from Parthian captivity. He also killed **Antigonus**, Hyrcanus's son, who had succeeded his father in the High Priesthood and the kingdom. He likewise slaughtered as many as were of the royal line, because of that scripture in Deuteronomy 17: *From the midst of your brothers you shall set a king over you.* 

He ordered all the books containing the genealogies of the kings to be burned, lest he or his sons be judged as foreigners to the kingdom. Among other cruel acts he committed, he also killed the husband of his sister **Salome**; and when he had given her to another in marriage, he killed him as well. He also murdered the **Scribes** and teachers of the Divine Law with similar wickedness, so that he might strip the Jews of any means or hope of recovering the kingdom. Therefore, it was at this time that the scepter of the kingdom was properly and truly taken away from the tribe of **Judah**, since it was believed that no one of the royal line remained. At that time also, judicial power was removed from them, when Herod himself ordered all the members of the **Sanhedrin** to be killed. 

The **Talmudists** recount all these events. ### CHAPTER.
If a Jew were to object that the scepter of Judah did not depart in the time of Herod, since the aforementioned **Baba ben Bota**—a survivor from the Sanhedrin itself—could still have established other Sanhedrin members, what should the response be?

**GALATINUS.** That is entirely false. For it is neither found written elsewhere that he did so, nor could he have done so by right. This can easily be seen from what is written in the book of the Sanhedrin in the chapter **Dine mamonoth** <gloss>Judgments of Wealth/Civil Law</gloss>. For there it is said, among other things: "Rabbi <note>original: *Rabba*</note> son of Rab Ashi said that the confirmation or appointment of the aforementioned judges was done either by hand or by name only. For they would either lay a hand upon his head and confirm him, or they would appoint him by name, calling him **Rabbi**. But one person alone did not make an appointment." Thus says he. And the reason why one person could not appoint a judge is (as it says in the same place) because such an appointment through the laying on of hands <note>The rite of *Semikhah* or ordination</note> could not be done except by three people, as **Rabbi Ishmael** said, or by five, as **Rabbi Judah** said. For that many were necessary.

Moreover, although with Herod’s permission other judges of this kind of college were later appointed who were under the King himself—just as they had existed before under others—nevertheless, because they were not true judges, they had no power to judge in serious or criminal matters. Thus it is clearly shown that under Herod this authority to judge, along with the scepter of dominion, utterly failed among the Jews. For this reason, when our Lord Jesus Christ spoke concerning these judges who were chosen in that time from the scribes and Pharisees, [he said]: "Upon the chair..." <note>A reference to Matthew 23:2, "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat"</note>

From all this it is manifest when, how, and why the **scepter** of the Jews utterly failed.

-> *Conclusion of the argument that the Messiah has already come. Chapter VII.* <-

### CAPNIO,

Now that all these points have been deduced, the argument itself must be formed, and it must be concluded that the Messiah came at that time. **GALATINUS.** If, therefore, the Messiah was absolutely meant to come at that time when these two things—the power of ruling and the authority of judging—were utterly failing among the Jews; and if it has been proven through their own scriptures that these things were entirely taken away from the Jews in the time of Herod of Ascalon, under whom Christ was born; it is certain, therefore, that the time for the Messiah’s arrival has already passed, and the Messiah himself has already come. The major premise of this argument is clearly evident from what has been said. For when **Jacob**, through the Holy Spirit in the blessing of **Judah**, spoke—and **Moses**, full of the same Spirit, wrote in the Law—that the "scepter" and the "scribe" would not depart from Judah until **Shiloh** came. And the "scepter" and "scribe," according to the expositions of the ancient Talmudists, refer to the college of the Sanhedrin—that is, the seventy-one judges—and the consistory of **Gazith** itself—that is, "hewn," <note>original: *dolatum*, referring to the Chamber of Hewn Stone</note> constructed from polished and corner stones. Furthermore, "Shiloh" is nothing other than the Messiah, as has already been proven through their own scriptures. And since the college of the Sanhedrin and the power of judging were lost nearly forty years before the destruction of the second Temple (as has been shown), it follows necessarily for all who are not entirely ignorant of logical consequences that either the Messiah came around that time, or Jacob and Moses were completely lying. But since the latter...

### *That when the scepter of the Jews failed, the miracles of the temple likewise ceased.* Chapter VIII.

But from then on, it was sometimes strong and sometimes not, and yet the priests never stopped adding wood all day long. A blessing was still sent upon the omer <note>The sheaf offering of the first grain</note>, and upon the two loaves, and upon the showbread; so that whatever priest received a portion the size of an olive, he ate and was satisfied, and there were some for whom leftovers remained. But from that time, a curse was sent upon the omer, the two loaves, and the showbread, and all the priests received from them only a portion the size of a bean."

Never did a serpent or scorpion cause harm in Jerusalem. Nor did a man ever say to his neighbor: "The place where I stay in Jerusalem is too narrow for me." ->*The second reason taken from the failure of the second temple. That the time of the first coming*<-
->*of the Messiah has already passed. Because the Messiah himself was to come before the*<-

### CAPNIO,

**N**ow bring forward the second reason, by which it is proved that the time of the first coming of the Messiah has already passed. GALEATUS. ->### BOOK FOUR###<-

"...is mine, and the gold is mine, says the Lord of hosts. The glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the first, says the Lord of hosts. And in this place I will give peace, says the Lord of hosts." <note>original: "est aurum, dixit Deus exercituum..." citing Haggai 2:8-9</note>. This prophecy, like others that clearly foretold the designated time of the Messiah's coming, more recent Jewish scholars <note>the "recentiores," likely referring to medieval commentators like Rashi or Kimhi</note> strive to corrupt in many ways, wishing to show that it is not to be understood as referring to the Messiah at all. But their false claims are easily refuted by the interpretations of the **Talmudists** <note>scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note>, who expressly say that this discourse is about the Messiah. For in the book **Sanhedrin**, in the chapter *Helek* <note>a famous section of the Talmud discussing the afterlife and the messianic age</note>, it is said exactly thus: "Rabbi Akiba interpreted: 'Yet once more, in a little while, and I will shake the heavens and the earth, and I will bring the desire of all nations.' This refers to the days of the Messiah, and the King Messiah, and the time that was after the destruction of the first House." Another interpretation says: "Yet once more, a little while." This "little while" refers to the coming Kingdom of Israel after the destruction of the first House. And after that Kingdom, "Behold, I will shake the heaven, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land, and all nations. And afterward the Messiah shall come." All these things are found there.

In this place, through these two interpretations by the ancient Talmudists, it is openly shown that this prophecy ought to be understood as referring to the Messiah. This is exactly how we ourselves maintain it should be understood. Nor is this surprising; for if our faith is none other than that of the prophets, it was certainly necessary for the ancient <term>Hebræorum Doctores</term> <note>Teachers of the Hebrews; the early Sages</note>, who wished to correctly explain the prophecies speaking of the Messiah, to agree with us in their interpretations. And even if these interpretations are disapproved of by **Rabbi Solomon** <note>original: "Rabbi Selomone," referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator</note>, both are nevertheless true. For the Messiah himself came after that "little while" of the <term>Machabæorum</term> <note>Maccabees; the Hasmonean dynasty that ruled Judea</note> kingdom, in the time of **Herod of Ascalon** <note>Herod the Great</note>, as was made most clear in the previous argument.

<margin>Arguments.</margin>
Setting aside, therefore, the false claims of the younger Jewish scholars, and explaining this prophecy according to the opinion of the ancients, we shall prove that the time of the Messiah’s coming has already passed through three main points placed within it. And first, indeed, because it says, "Yet once more, it is a little while," which is to say, according to the <term>glossa</term> <note>explanatory note or commentary</note> of **Rabbi Akiba**: "A little time remains until the revelation of the Messiah." If, therefore, according to the error of the Jews of our own age, the first coming of the Messiah were still to be expected, it would surely follow that the Prophet suggested something false. For he said that from that time, only a little time remained until the Messiah’s coming. Yet from the time this prophecy was uttered, more than two thousand years have passed. Therefore, from the first part of this prophecy, it is necessarily inferred that the time of the Messiah's first coming has already passed. This is further shown by what follows, when he says, "And I will fill this house with glory." For no one doubts that the prophet spoke of the **second house of God** <note>the Second Temple</note>, which was to be built after the return from the **Babylonian captivity**; and this house was to be filled with the glory of the Messiah’s presence.

-># BOOK [FOUR] #<-

...while that [house] was still standing, the Messiah was to come. But since that house was utterly destroyed in the year 42 after the passion of Christ <note>The author uses a traditional dating system where the destruction of the Temple by Titus in 70 AD is calculated as 42 years after the Crucifixion.</note> by **Titus**, the leader of the Roman army, it is certainly established that the time of the Messiah's coming has already passed. This very thing finally becomes more clearly evident through those things which are added in the same prophecy. For when he says, "The glory of this latter house shall be greater than the first," the prophet was speaking about the second house of God (as has been said), to the building of which he wished to lead the people. For God, seeing those who were occupied with the structure of that same temple proceeding so sluggishly that they either did not dare to begin the work or wished to desist from what they had started, sent to them the prophet **Haggai**. He, in order to lead them to the beginning and completion of the work, foretold to them the Mystery to be consummated in that same temple. And among other things, he prophesied,

<margin>The glory of the second house.</margin>
that the last house of God which was to be built would have greater glory than that first one which had been erected by **Solomon**. Let the Jews therefore say: in what did the greatness of this glory, which this last house was to have, consist? **Rabbi Selomo** <note>This refers to Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note> responds that, according to some, the greatness of this glory consisted in the physical size of the building, while according to others,

<margin>The duration of the 1st and 2nd temples.</margin>
it consisted in the duration of its existence. He himself, however, asserts that it consisted in both. For no building similar to the one by **Herod** (who restored that last temple) was ever seen, and the second temple itself lasted ten years longer than the first. For the first stood for four hundred and ten years, while the second (as he says) persisted for four hundred and uiginti <note>original: "quadringentis & uiginti," meaning 420 years.</note> years. But this latter point is surely of no importance, as appears especially from these reasons: First, because if the second temple (as he says) had surpassed the first by only ten years, it would seem very absurd for the prophet to have mentioned such a short span of time, especially since the words he used seem to imply great excellence. Second, because even if it had remained for many more than ten years, since it was nevertheless violated many times, that greater duration of time would have turned out not to its honor and glory,

<margin>How many times the temple was profaned.</margin>
but rather to its disgrace. For first, it was profaned by **Antiochus**, who both plundered the vessels of God that were in service and placed an image of Olympian Jupiter in the same temple. Then indeed by **Pompey**, who, coming to Jerusalem while **Hyrcanus** and **Aristobulus** (the sons of **Alexandra**, Queen of the Jews) were fighting over the throne, captured the city, and having unsealed that same temple, went even into the **Holy of Holies**. Furthermore, **Cassius**, in the seventh year of **Cleopatra**, having captured Judea, despoiled the temple itself. Therefore, that duration of time by which the second temple is said to have exceeded the first should be attributed to it not as glory, but rather as a reproach. Nor can the saying of Rabbi Selomo regarding the magnitude or beauty of the building be verified, since there could be no comparison between the first and second temple. For concerning the first indeed, it is written thus in the second book of **Chronicles** <term>Paralipomenon</term> <note>Paralipomenon is the Greek-derived name for the Books of Chronicles, meaning "things omitted" [from the Books of Kings].</note>, chapter 3: "And the great house..." <note>original Hebrew: ואת הבית הגדול (v'et ha-bayit ha-gadol)</note>

But when the gentiles entered the temple, the trees—namely the golden ones—became dry, as it is said in the first chapter of Nahum: 'And the flower or sprout of Lebanon has languished or withered.'" 

Even if these things were said metaphorically, they are nevertheless highly relevant to the purpose. From these accounts, therefore, it can be gathered how great the glory of the first temple was. For this reason, as is read in the fourth chapter of the book of **Ezra** <note>This refers to Ezra 3:12 in modern Bibles</note>, when the work of the second temple was completed, many of the priests and others who had seen the first temple wept while the others were exulting, because that second temple, in comparison to the first, was almost nothing. 

Also, almost all the vessels which had been gold in the first temple were made of bronze in the second, as the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars and compilers of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> relate. Nor does the truth of the statement of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi</note> hold regarding the construction of **Herod**, even though it was immense (as **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> says). For **Herod** was unable to be compared with **Solomon** in riches, nor in power, nor in any other thing. 

Nor can it be said that the greatness of glory, by which the second house of God was meant to exceed the first, was the holiness of the place itself. For as the <term>Talmudists</term> say, among other marks of holiness of the first temple which were lacking in the second: neither the fire which descended from heaven in the first temple to consume the burnt offerings was ever seen to descend in the second; nor did the glory of God <note>The Shekhinah</note>, which used to appear in the first temple in the Holy of Holies between the **Cherubim**, ever appear in the second; nor was the Holy Spirit, which very often came to speak with the prophets in the first temple, accustomed to come in the second. All these things are best proven through the <term>Talmud</term>. <margin>Five things were missing in the second temple.</margin>

...captives, thus it is said: Rabbi Samuel says, "Five things were missing in the last temple which were present in the first." And from where is this proven? From that which is said in the first chapter of Haggai: <note>original Hebrew: עלו ההר והבאתם עץ ובנו הבית וארצה בו ואכבד אמר יהוה</note> This is, "Go up to the mountain, and bring wood, and build the house, and I will be pleased with it, and I will be honored, said God." The word <term>Veeccabda</term> <note>Hebrew: ואכבד, meaning "and I will be honored"</note>, that is, "and I will be honored," or "I will honor it," is written in a diminished form, without the letter <term>He</term> <note>ה</note>, which designates the number five. This signifies the five things in which the last sanctuary was diminished compared to the first. Namely: the fire, the ark, the <term>Urim and Thummim</term> <note>Lumina and Simplicities, the oracular devices on the High Priest’s breastplate used to determine God's will</note>—that is, the "Rationale of Judgment"—the anointing oil, and the Holy Spirit. 

Furthermore, the <term>Gloss</term> <note>A commentary or marginal explanation</note> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the famous medieval commentator</note> on the word *Veeccabda*—that is, "and I will honor it"—says this: "The letter *He* is missing here, which signifies five, on account of the five things which were missing in the second temple but were present in the first. Namely: the <term>Urim and Thummim</term>, which are the lights and perfections, that is, the rationale of judgment; and the ark; and the fire; and the <term>Divinity</term> <note>The manifest presence of God</note>; and the Spirit." 

Likewise, in the book <term>Yoma</term> <note>A volume of the Talmud; the word means "The Day," referring to the Day of Atonement</note>, it is read: Rabbi Aha said, "What is the reason that in the word *Veeccabda* the letter *He* is missing? Because through it are designated the five things which were in the first temple and were missing in the last. These are the ark with the mercy seat, the <term>Cherub</term> <note>The angelic figures atop the Ark</note>, the fire, the <term>Shekhinah</term> <note>Hebrew: שכינה, the indwelling presence or glory of God</note>, the Holy Spirit, and the Urim and Thummim." 

In the <term>Midrash</term> <note>An ancient commentary on Hebrew scripture</note> on <term>Shir HaShirim</term> <note>The Song of Songs</note>, regarding that verse in the eighth chapter: <note>original Hebrew: אחות לנו קטנה ושדים אין לה</note> That is, "We have a little sister, and she has no breasts." It is said thus: "We have a sister"—these were the ones ascending from captivity. "Little"—because they were poor in numbers. "And she has no breasts"—these are the five things in which the last house was diminished compared to the first. 

Furthermore, in the book *Yoma* it is said: In the second sanctuary there was no ark. For there is a tradition that from the time the ark was removed, there were removed with it the jar of manna, the flask of anointing oil, Aaron’s rod with its almonds and flowers, and the coffer which the Philistines sent as a gift to the God of Israel. Just as it is said in 1 Samuel 6: "And all the vessels which you have returned to Him for a trespass offering, put in a coffer by its side." 

Therefore, since the prophet Haggai said that the glory of the last house of God would be greater than that of the first, and since the first house shone with such an abundance of glory that the second house could not be compared to it in even a single thing, it must necessarily be said: This "greater glory" which the last house of God was to have over the first was nothing other than the presence of the Messiah, by which that last house was to be honored more than the first. For if this greatness of glory cannot be understood as referring to duration of time, nor to excellence of workmanship, nor to riches, nor to holiness (as has been proven), it must be understood as the presence of the Messiah. Since no other reason can be assigned, one of two things must be granted: either the Messiah [was present in] the temple...

## Refutation of the Jews' objection, and a universal explanation of the prophecy of Haggai himself, according to their own glosses. And the confirmation of the aforementioned reasoning through Jeremiah. Chapter X.

### CAPNIO,

<margin><unclear>illegible note</unclear></margin>
**O**ur Jews of this time, being of the stiffest neck and the most obstinate of all, opposing the things you have said, say: Since the prophet says, "Yet once, a little while, and I will shake all nations" <note>original Latin: "Adhuc unum modicum est, & ego commouebo omnes gentes"</note>. And later he adds the words by which you have tried to show that the Messiah's coming has already passed. From the words of the same prophet, it appears clearly enough that all these shakings were either to precede the Messiah's coming, or were destined to occur around his birth. But since it is known that shakings of this kind have not yet happened, it clearly follows that neither has this prophecy been fulfilled, nor has the Messiah himself yet arrived. Therefore, show that they are entirely speakers of falsehood in this matter by their own scriptures. 

**GALATINUS:** We will prove, therefore, that all these shakings of which the prophet speaks did indeed happen around the birth of Jesus of Nazareth, even according to them. For if we wish to explain this prophecy according to their own expositions, we will find that it was entirely fulfilled in the time of our Lord Jesus Christ. For which reason it should be noted that when Haggai himself had said these things, among others, to Zerubbabel the prince of the Jews, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak the High Priest: "And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says God; be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the Great Priest." Afterwards, as if giving a reason, he added the words of this prophecy, saying: "My spirit shall be standing in your midst" <note>original Latin: "Spiritus meus erit stans in medio uestri"</note>, that is, according to the <term>gloss</term> <note>A commentary or explanatory note</note> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note>, "I will place, or I will cause my spirit to descend upon you." "Yet once, a little while"—that is, according to the explanation of Rabbi Akiba, whom they call <term>עקיבא</term> <gloss>Akiva</gloss>—"Yet a short time remains until the coming of the Messiah. And I will shake the heaven and the earth, the sea and the dry land, and I will shake all nations." Rabbi Solomon and Rabbi David <note>Likely David Kimhi, known as Radak, a medieval grammarian and exegete</note>, although they strive to twist this prophecy from its true sense by whatever means they can, to show that it is not to be understood as being about the Messiah...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous chapter regarding the fulfillment of Haggai’s prophecy. <header>BOOK</header>

Yet they could not remain entirely silent about the truth. For Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "Rabbi Selomo." This refers to Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> said that heaven and earth and the rest were to be moved by miracles, so that everyone would understand that God himself was present in that second temple. However, although Rabbi David <note>original: "R. uero Dauid." This refers to David Kimchi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, a famous rabbi, philosopher, and grammarian.</note> says those shakings are to be understood metaphorically, the falsehood of this is most evident because the prophet, in this entire prophecy, speaks in plain language and not in metaphors or parables. Nevertheless, he says he found it written in the book of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian who chronicled the history of the Jews and the war with Rome.</note> that a massive earthquake occurred in Judea during the time of Herod of Ascalon. He says the nations were also "shaken" in this sense: that God moved their hearts so they would leave their homes and come to see the glory of this temple, and certainly not with empty hands, but with their precious things. All of these things should not be thought entirely alien to the truth, as will soon be seen in our own explanation.

We say, therefore, that heaven and earth were shaken by miracles and wonders (as Rabbi Solomon explains) around the birth of Christ, as many great miracles were seen both in heaven and on earth. In heaven—to say nothing of the three suns that appeared simultaneously in Rome around the time of Augustus <note>Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus (63 BC–14 AD), the first Roman Emperor.</note> (under whom Christ was born) and gradually merged into the same orb—soon after 

<margin>Portents occurring around the birth of Christ.</margin> 

Christ was born, that new and wondrous star appeared, which provided guidance to the three Kings from the furthest regions to his birthplace. Regarding this, Chalcidius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and translator of Plato.</note> says in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*: "That star," he says, "did not announce disease or death, but the arrival of a venerable God." When certain men of the Chaldeans <note>Commonly referred to as the Magi or Wise Men from the East.</note>—who were truly excellent and highly experienced in the science of celestial matters—had observed it, they are said to have sought out the birth of the newly arrived God. 

The earth was also shaken then, not only by portents—which occurred throughout the world at almost the same time, such as oxen speaking, serpents flying through the air, infants crying out certain words from their mothers’ wombs, and women being changed into the male sex—but also in Rome on the same day Christ was born, a fountain of oil flowed abundantly from the earth. Furthermore, in Judea, of whose land the prophet specifically speaks, a massive earthquake occurred. This was also due to the victory that the Romans obtained everywhere on earth. Then, therefore, the land and the sea (that is, the islands of the sea) and all the nations were shaken. This occurred when, at Christ's birth, an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the entire world should be registered, and everyone set out for their own city. Next, the prophet adds: *And they shall come with the desire of all nations*, which is to say, according to Rabbi David’s gloss: *And they shall come to worship with their precious things.* This is never recorded as having happened in the second temple. It must therefore be understood as referring to those three Kings who came from the East to worship Christ with gifts. Just as Isaiah had foretold in his 60th chapter, saying: *All they from Sheba shall come: they shall bring gold and incense; and they shall show forth the praises of the Lord.* <note>original Hebrew: "כלם משבא יבאו זהב ולבונה ישאו ותהלות יהוה יבשרו"</note>

->FOURTH<-
<note>Likely referring to the fourth book or section of a larger treatise.</note>

...of which we will speak more broadly elsewhere. After this follows in the prophecy: **"And I will fill this house with glory"** <note>Haggai 2:7</note>. As Rabbi Akiba <note>Akiva ben Joseph (c. 50–135 AD), a foundational figure in Rabbinic Judaism.</note> explains this, it is understood to refer to the Messiah, by whose presence the Second Temple was to be made illustrious. Malachi also predicted this more clearly at that same time, when he spoke as follows in Hebrew in his third chapter:

> <note>original Hebrew: הנני שולח מלאכי ופנה דרך לפני ופתאום יבא אל היכלו האדון אשר אתם מבקשים ומלאך הברית אשר אתם חפצים הנה בא אמר יהוה צבאות</note>
> **Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before my face. And suddenly the Lord, whom you seek, shall come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire. Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts.**

That is: *Behold I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face. And immediately the Lord, whom you seek, shall come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant, whom you want. Behold, he comes, says the God of hosts.* Where Malachi also spoke concerning the Second Temple. Therefore, through the three points he makes, he signaled that the coming of the Messiah was then only a short time away. In saying **"Behold,"** he shows the matter as if it were present. In saying **"immediately"** <note>original Latin: "statim," often translated as "suddenly" in biblical contexts.</note>, he hints that the time is very near. And finally, in repeating **"Behold, he comes,"** he assigned the shortest possible time for his arrival. 

Furthermore, he said **"to his temple,"** so that he might show two things at once which the Jews were going to deny. For in this phrase he both suggested his divinity—for unless the Messiah were to be God, he would have said he was coming to his temple in vain—and he also fixed the time of his arrival, since he predicted he would arrive while that temple was still standing. By this, the error of the Jews of our own time is refuted, who assert that when the Messiah comes, he will find the temple desolated and the people dispersed in captivity. 

But let us return to Haggai. Lest they believe he was speaking of the worldly <term>temporal glory</term> <note>glory relating to time, material wealth, or earthly power, as opposed to eternal or spiritual glory</note> which that Second Temple was to have, he added this: **"The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, says the Lord of hosts"** <note>Haggai 2:8</note>. It is as if he were saying: "Do not think that I consider an abundance of silver and gold to be glory, since these things, wherever they may be, are mine." Therefore, the prophet was not speaking of temporal glory, but of spiritual glory, with which that temple was to be filled because of the presence of the Messiah himself. 

For this reason he also added: **"The glory of this last house shall be great, more so than the first"** <note>Haggai 2:9</note>. This must be understood regarding the miracles which the Messiah, by his divine power, was to perform in that Second Temple, not to mention his own presence. For in this, it is most established that the glory of the Second Temple was far greater than that of the first: that God spoke to the people in the first temple through prophets, but in the second he spoke through himself; through himself he taught the crowds, and through himself he performed miracles. 

And he notably said **"of this last house"** <note>original Latin: "domus huius nouissimæ"</note> and not "of the second." This was so that it would be openly known from that phrasing that a third temple was not to be built, and that the temple which was to be constructed through the Messiah was not a material one (contrary to the error of the younger Jews), but was to be a spiritual one. Finally, regarding what he added at the end: **"And in this place I will give peace"**—this cannot be understood as temporal peace, since from the beginning of that temple until its end, the Jews were always afflicted by various hardships of war from other nations. Therefore, it concerns spiritual [peace]...

This is also necessarily drawn from what is read in Jeremiah chapter 30, if the **Targum**—that is, the Chaldaic translation <note>The Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible, often reflecting ancient Jewish interpretation.</note> which is found in that place—is diligently inspected. And out of them shall proceed thanksgiving and the voice of those who make merry; and I will multiply them, and they shall not be diminished; I will also glorify them, and they shall not be small. And his children shall be as of old, and his congregation shall be established before me, and I will punish all that oppress him. And his noble shall be of himself, and his governor shall proceed from the midst of him; and I will cause him to draw near, and he shall approach unto me; for who is this that engaged his heart to approach unto me? says the Lord.**

That is: *Behold, I turn the conversion, or the rest of the tabernacles of **Jacob*** (which was fulfilled under **Zerubbabel** <note>The governor of the Persian province of Judah who led the first group of captives back from Babylon.</note>) *and I will have mercy on his tabernacles. And the city shall be built upon its high place, or upon its mound. And the "armon," that is, the basilica or temple, shall sit according to its judgment. And from them shall go forth praise, or confession, and the voice of those playing. And I will multiply them, and they shall not be diminished. And his sons shall be as they were of old, and his assembly shall remain before me. And I will visit [punishment] upon all his oppressors. And his Leader shall be from him, and his ruler shall come forth from his midst. And I will bring him near, or apply him, and he will approach, or cling, or be joined to me. For who is that one pledging his heart so that he might cling or be joined to me, said God?* The same prophet says all these things. Moreover, those words, *And his Leader shall be from him, and his ruler shall come forth from his midst,* Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, traditionally the author of the Targum on the Prophets.</note> translates thus into the Chaldaic:

That is: *And their King shall nourish himself, or be anointed from them, and their Messiah shall reveal himself from their midst.* From the aforementioned words of Jeremiah, therefore, if anyone pays diligent attention, it is openly given to be understood: that when the status of the children of the Jews—who were to return from the Babylonian captivity and build the temple and the city—had become as it had been of old (which occurred in the time of the Maccabees <note>A Jewish rebel group that established the Hasmonean dynasty in the 2nd century BC.</note>), then the **Messiah** was to be born and revealed. The **Targum** clearly shows this when it says: *And their Messiah shall reveal himself from their midst.* Indeed, the prophet manifests that this was to happen after the union of the divine and human natures, which ought to occur in the Messiah, when he says in the person of God: *And I will bring him near, and he shall cling, or join himself to me.* From which it is certain that the time of his coming has already passed.

# Refutation of the Jews' opposition and a rebuke of their madness. Concerning those who admit the Messiah was born long ago, but say he has not yet come. Chapter XII.

## CAPNIO

**R**ecent Jews, convinced by these authorities, admit indeed that the Messiah was born long ago, because the Talmudic testimonies now brought forward by you assert that he was born on that very day the Temple was destroyed. But they say he has not yet come. They attempt to show that this madness of theirs is true even through those words of Isaiah, by which you best proved that the Messiah was born before the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the Temple. And they do this especially from what is read in **Bereshit Rabbah**—that is, in the Great Exposition on the book of **Genesis** <note>A collection of ancient Jewish homilies and interpretations of the Book of Genesis, compiled around the 5th century AD.</note>—concerning that which is said in the thirtieth chapter of Genesis: *In every heat of the sheep* <note>Refers to Genesis 30:41, describing Jacob’s breeding of the flocks.</note>. There it is read that **Rabbi Samuel** said: "From where do you prove that the Messiah was born on the very day that the house of the sanctuary was destroyed? From that which is said in the sixty-sixth chapter of **Isaiah**: *Before she travailed, she brought forth; before her pain came, she was delivered of a male child. Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things?* <note>Isaiah 66:7–8.</note>" For in the hour when the house of the sanctuary was destroyed, Israel cried out like a woman in labor. And therefore, through this authority of Isaiah and the Talmudic traditions which you brought forward in the preceding chapter, the younger Jews strive to prove that the Messiah was born on that day the Temple was overturned by **Titus**, the son of Vespasian <note>Titus was the Roman general who besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note>. From this they infer that we can by no means show through those same scriptures that our Lord **Jesus Christ** was the Messiah, since he was not born on that same day the Temple collapsed, but long before.

**GAL.** In responding to these things, we first indeed concede that the Messiah is called a "male" in the aforementioned words of Isaiah because of his absolute perfection. And we concede that the Jewish people brought him forth, since he was born from the tribe of **Judah** according to the flesh. But we entirely deny that he was born on the day the Temple collapsed, since he was born approximately seventy-five years before. For that word <term>terem</term> <note>original: טרם</note> placed in the words of Isaiah, does not mean "not yet," as the more recent Jews understand it, but "before." From which it is clear that since the Jewish people were "not yet" in labor—that is, grieving over the destruction of the Temple—the Messiah was born; he was born *before* they travailed. <margin>Three reasons.</margin> This is established by a threefold reason. The first of these is the wonder of the prophet himself, who says: *Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things?* For if she had brought forth while in labor, nothing wonderful would have occurred, since all women bring forth while they are in labor. Therefore, so that the prophet's wonder is not in vain, nor the comparison inappropriate, the Jews must concede that the Messiah was born before the destruction of the Temple itself. The second reason is that this Hebrew word <term>terem</term> <note>original: טרם</note>, just as in those same...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Galatino refutes the Jewish claim that the Messiah was born on the exact day of the Second Temple's destruction. He focuses on the philological analysis of the Hebrew word 'terem' to prove the birth happened before the catastrophe.</meta>

->BOOK<-
GAL
<meta>Catchword: ba, id</meta>

<margin>Isaiah 66</margin>
...in the words of Isaiah, as in almost all other places, the word **terem** <note>Hebrew: טרם, meaning "before" or "not yet."</note> is always used for **kodem** <note>Hebrew: קודם, meaning "prior to."</note>, which signifies "before." This is best shown by **Rabbi Kimhi** <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as Radak, a preeminent medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator.</note>, the most excellent expositor of words among them. For in his *Book of Roots* <note>The original text says "Seraphim," likely a printer's error for "Shorashim" (Roots), the title of Kimhi’s famous Hebrew dictionary.</note> he says: "Before she travailed, she brought forth." For the sense of this word **terem** is **kodem**, that is, "before." Just as in the book of Samuel—that is, the third chapter of the First Book of Kings <note>In the Vulgate and some older traditions, 1 & 2 Samuel were called 1 & 2 Kings.</note>: **Before he knew the Lord, and before the word of the Lord was revealed to him.** <note>1 Samuel 3:7. Original Hebrew: טרם ידע את יהוה וטרם יגלה אליו דבר יהוה.</note> There, **terem** is used for **kodem**, which is the same as "before." Rabbi Kimhi brings forward many other authorities in which this word **terem** is placed, and at the end of each he says that *terem* signifies nothing other than *kodem*, which is entirely the same as "before."

Finally, the third reason, the strongest of all, is that both the Hebrew commentary of **Rabbi Moses Haddarsan** <note>Moses ha-Darshan, an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic interpretations.</note> and the **Targum** <note>The Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>—that is, the Chaldean translation—take this word **terem** not as "while," but as "before" (as was seen above). From these things it follows that the Messiah was born not on the day of the Temple's destruction, as the Jews deliriously claim, but before it (as the Christians assert).

Furthermore, regarding the traditions of the **Talmudists** <note>The scholars and authors of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> who say the Messiah was born on the day the Temple was destroyed, we say that the word "day" is usually understood in three ways. First, for the time the sun is above the horizon, which astronomers call the **artificial day**. Second, it is taken for a space of 24 hours, which they call the **natural day**. Finally, third, for any **indeterminate time**. And in this sense, it is placed only in the feminine gender <note>Referring to grammatical usage in Hebrew where "day" (yom) can occasionally take feminine constructs or refer to broader eras.</note>. Indeed, we find it used this way very often in Holy Scripture. And especially in Isaiah, in almost innumerable places, saying: **In that day** <note>Hebrew: ביום ההוא (be-yom ha-hu).</note>, which means "in that time." It is certain that this can only be understood as a certain course of years.

And it is in this sense of "day" that the Talmudists speak when they say the Messiah was born on the day the Temple fell. For even if that Temple, as far as the physical structure is concerned, remained for 42 years after the suffering of Christ, nevertheless, as far as its **sanctity** is concerned, it was destroyed at the very hour in which He suffered. For then (as we have said elsewhere) it lost all its holiness. Therefore, at the moment of Christ’s death, as a sign of this, its **veil was torn** from top to bottom. The cessation of miracles was also a primary proof of this fact. For as we have shown elsewhere through their own writings, the miracles that used to occur in the Temple utterly failed forty years before its actual ruin.

From these sayings it is clear that the Messiah was not born on the same day the Temple was overturned (as the Jews of our time falsely claim), but before the Temple's overturning, as we have already proved.

### CHAPTER [XIII]
**If the Messiah was born in Bethlehem on the same day the Temple was destroyed (as they say), and yet he has appeared nowhere since then, where do they say he has been hiding for so long?**

## CAPNIO
**P**lease listen to the ridiculous fables they tell. For in **Bereshit Rabba** <note>A collection of ancient Jewish homilies on the Book of Genesis.</note>, that is...
