...is, in the great exposition of the book of Genesis <note>The Bereshit Rabbah, a central collection of ancient Jewish interpretations of the book of Genesis.</note>, concerning the passage in the thirtieth chapter, "And it happened in every heat of the sheep," it is read word for word thus: Rabbi Samuel said that once, when Elijah of blessed memory <note>The prophet Elijah is a central figure in Jewish folklore, often depicted as wandering the earth to help the righteous or announce the Messiah.</note> was traveling on the way, on the very day that the house of the sanctuary <note>The Second Temple in Jerusalem, destroyed by the Romans in 70 AD.</note> was destroyed, he heard a daughter of a voice <note>A *Bath Kol*, a divine echo or heavenly voice that provides guidance or judgment.</note>, that is, a voice crying out from the heavens and saying, "The house of the holy sanctuary goes to its destruction." When Elijah of blessed memory heard this, he thought the whole world was to be destroyed. He went along and found men plowing and sowing, and he said to them, "The holy and blessed God is angry at his world, and he wishes to destroy his house and take his children captive among the nations of the age. And yet you care for and are anxious about this temporal life?" But the daughter of a voice came forth—that is, the heavenly voice—and said to him, **Leave them alone, for a savior has already been born to Israel.** <note>original: הנח להם שכבר נולד לישראל מושיע</note> Elijah said, "And where is he?" The voice said, **In Bethlehem of Judah.** <note>original: בבית לחם יהודה</note> He went, therefore, and found a certain woman who was sitting at the entrance of her house, and her son, stained with blood, was lying before her. He said to her, "My daughter, have you given birth to a son?" She said, "Yes." He asked her, "What does it mean that he lies there so stained with blood?" And she said, "It is a very great evil, for on the very day he was born, the house of the sanctuary was destroyed." He said to her, "My daughter, be constant and take care of him. For the salvation of Israel shall be great through his hand." And soon she was encouraged and took care of him. Elijah then left her and went away. 

But after the fifth year, he said, "I will go and see the savior of Israel, whether he is being nurtured in the manner of Kings or in the manner of the angels who minister to God." He went, therefore, and found the woman standing at the entrance of her house. He said to her, "My daughter, in what state is that boy?" She, answering, said, "Rabbi, did I not tell you that it was an evil thing to nurture him? For on the day he was born, the house of the sanctuary was destroyed. And not only this, but he has feet and does not walk; he has eyes and does not see; he has ears and does not hear; he has a mouth and speaks not at all. And behold, he lies there like a stone." While Elijah was still speaking, winds blew upon him from the four corners of the world and carried him away to the Great Sea <note>The Mediterranean Sea.</note>. Elijah then tore his garments, pulled out his hair, and cried out, saying, "Alas, the salvation of Israel is lost!" And the daughter of a voice came forth—that is, a revelation—and said to him, "Elijah, it is not as you say. But for four hundred years he shall remain in the Great Sea; eighty years in the ascent of the smoke among the sons of Korah <note>A reference to a group mentioned in the Psalms and Numbers; in legend, they were swallowed by the earth but continued to live in a subterranean place.</note>; eighty years at the gate of Rome; and for the remainder of the years he shall return upon all the great cities, until the end of time." All these things are found there. 

Also in the book of the Sanhedrin <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing primarily with law and courts.</note>, in the chapter *Helek*, it is likewise written: Rabbi Joshua son of Levi found Elijah and Rabbi Simeon standing in the garden of pleasure—that is, in Paradise—and said to them: "Have we come to the world to come..."

...them? They said to him, "Yes, if this master wishes." He said to them, "I saw two and heard the voice of three." The gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> says: "The Divinity (he says) was with them." He also said to them, "When will the Messiah come?" They said to him, "Go and ask him himself." He said to them, "Where does he stay?" They said to him, "At the gate of Rome." <note>This tradition suggests the Messiah waits in the heart of the enemy empire, identifying with the suffering of the exile.</note> "And what is his sign?" "He sits among the poor who suffer from infirmities." The gloss of Rabbi Solomon explains this as "among the lepers." For he himself is also a leper, according to what is written in the fifty-third chapter of Isaiah: *And he was struck for our sins.* And again: *Truly he has borne our infirmities, and he has carried our sorrows. And we esteemed him as a leper.* <note>original: "Et nos reputauimus eum leprosum." While standard Christian Bibles often translate this as "stricken by God," the Hebrew word *nagu'a* was interpreted in the Talmud to mean "afflicted with leprosy," leading to the title "The Leper Scholar."</note> The lepers undo one wound and tie another. He, however, unties one wound and reties another, for he does not wish to do otherwise lest he be delayed. The gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "The Messiah unties and wipes one wound, then immediately ties it back. He does this with the others and does not untie them all at once. For he fears he might be delayed in tying all his wounds if he were called upon to liberate Israel." Therefore he went to him (that is, Rabbi Joshua <note>Rabbi Joshua ben Levi, a famous 3rd-century scholar often featured in mystical legends.</note> went to the Messiah) and said to him, "Peace be upon you, my Rabbi and my Lord." He said to him, "Peace be upon you also, son of Levi." Then he said to him, "When will you come, Lord?" He answered him, "Today." He then came to Elijah and said to him, "The Messiah lied. For he told me he would come today." Elijah answered him, "**Today**, that is, **if you will hear his voice**." <note>A reference to Psalm 95:7, implying the Messiah's coming is conditional on the people's repentance.</note> All these things are found there. Although they may not be literally true—unless perhaps understood metaphorically and spiritually—they are nonetheless excellent for arguing against the Jews. For by these stories they can be convinced both that the Messiah was born long ago and that he was once in Rome. Also, those words of Isaiah: *Behold, my servant shall understand*, along with the rest until the end of the fifty-third chapter, were understood by Rabbi Solomon to refer to the Messiah—although elsewhere he tried to twist them to refer to the Jewish people. And according to the word of Elijah, that verse from Psalm 95 should also be understood as referring to the Messiah:

> For he is our God | and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand. Today, if you will hear his voice, do not harden 
> your hearts. <note>original: "כי הוא אלהינו | ואנחנו עם מרעיתו וצאן ידו היום אם בקולו תשמעו אל תקשו לבבכם"</note>

This is, to render it word for word: *Because he himself is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. Today if you will hear his voice, Do not harden your hearts.* This is a most clear testimony that the Messiah is God. And that the wretched Jews would have the Messiah today—namely our Lord Jesus Christ—if they were willing to hear his voice through obedience and belief, and if they did not harden their hearts.

...that his time has already passed, can it be proven? GALATINUS. It certainly can. For Micah, whom (as was seen a little while ago) the ancient Talmudists follow, foretold that he would be born in Bethlehem, when he says in chapter five: *And you, Bethlehem Ephratah, though you are small among the thousands of Judah, out of you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel; and his goings forth are from of old, from the days of eternity.* <note>original Hebrew: "ואתה בית לחם אפרתה צעיר להיות באלפי יהודה ממך לי יצא להיות מושל בישראל ומוצאותיו מקדם מימי עולם" (Micah 5:2).</note> These words sound thus in English: "And you, Bethlehem Ephratha, you are a little one among the thousands of Judah. From you shall come forth to me he who is to be ruler in Israel. And his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of the age," that is, according to the exposition of Rabbenu Hakkadosh <note>Literally "Our Holy Rabbi," usually referring to Judah ha-Nasi, the redactor of the Mishnah.</note>, from eternity, and from the days of the age. This prophecy cannot be understood as referring to anyone but the Messiah. This is true both because of the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Rabbi Jonathan, which explains those words, "From you shall come forth to me one who is to be ruler," in Aramaic as: *From you, before me or from my part, the Messiah shall go forth.* <note>original Aramaic: "מנך קדמי יפוק משיחא"</note> It is also clear because of the gloss <gloss>interpretive commentary</gloss> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, which explains this prophecy thus: "And you, Bethlehem Ephratha, from which David went forth. As it is said in the first book of Kings, chapter seventeen: *The son of that servant of yours, Jesse the Bethlehemite.* Bethlehem was also called Ephratha. As it is said in Genesis, chapter forty-eight: *On the way to Ephrata, which is Bethlehem.* You are a little one among the thousands of Judah. On account of the humble status of Ruth the Moabite, who was in you. From you the Messiah, son of David, shall come forth for me. As he himself says: *The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.*" Jonathan, however, translated it thus: "From you for me—that is, from my part—the Messiah shall go forth. And his going forth is before the days of the age." As it is said in Psalm seventy-one <note>Psalm 72 in modern numbering.</note>: "Before the sun, *Yinnon* <term>Yinnon (ינון)</term> — that is, born, or begotten, or 'son' is his name." But this scripture is mystical. Thus says Rabbi Solomon. He [Rashi] has explained these words about the Messiah well enough and faithfully (to tell the truth)—which he does very rarely—except for this one thing: where it is said of the Messiah, "And his going forth is from of old, from the days of the age," or "from eternity and the days of the age," he seems to want this to be understood regarding the Messiah's name alone, when he says: "And his name was spoken before the days of the age." We, however, departing in no way from the truth of the text, do not deny that the name of the Messiah, *Yinnon*, existed before the sun and before the days of the age. This is nothing else than that the Messiah existed from eternity as the Son of God. For *Yinnon* (as we have said elsewhere) means entirely the same in English as "born" or "begotten" or "son." Since, therefore, that prophecy speaks of the Messiah, it is surely clear according to it that the Messiah himself...

...we shall refute [his] explanation. We, therefore, explain it thus: "And you, Bethlehem Ephratah, although you are the least among the thousands of Judah. Yet because the first King of Judah, that is David, arose from you, the Messiah, who will be the last, shall also come forth from you for me." And he says "shall come forth" <note>original Latin: *egredietur*</note> rightly, in order to show that he ought not to be generated from human seed alone. In this, he also suggested his twofold nature—namely the divine and the human—with wonderful brevity. For when he said, "from you," he demonstrated his humanity. But when he said, "for me," he hinted at his divinity. "For me," he says, as if he were saying: "That man who shall come forth from you will be worthy to be united to me—that is, to my divinity." This he then expressed more clearly, saying: "And his goings forth are from eternity and from the days of old." For "goings forth" <note>original Latin: *egressus*; the author notes that this word is plural in both Hebrew (*motsa’ot*) and Latin to signify two distinct origins.</note> in this place, in the Hebrew language just as in Latin, is in the plural number. Therefore the meaning is: the goings forth—that is, the proceedures of this ruler or Messiah—are two. One is from eternity, by which he proceeded from the Father according to his divinity. The other is from the days of old, by which he came forth from a mother according to his humanity. This certainly agrees perfectly with that saying of Athanasius <note>Referring to the Athanasian Creed, an early Christian statement of faith defining the Trinity and the nature of Christ.</note>:

> God is begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages, and man is born from the substance of his mother in time.

Nevertheless, Athanasius says "in time" <note>Latin: *in seculo*</note> because he received birth itself; but the Prophet says "from the days of old" because when the matter of Adam was formed, the matter of the glorious Virgin was soon after sewn <note>Latin: *insuit*, implying a grafting or weaving of the lineage into the very beginning of human history.</note> into that same matter, and the humanity of the blessed Christ was sewn into the most precious blood of that same Virgin. All of these things the Jews of our time can by no means deny. For almost the very same things are said by Rabbenu HaKadosh <note>meaning "Our Holy Teacher," a title for Rabbi Judah the Prince; here the author cites a work attributed to him to support Christian doctrine.</note>, when in the book <term>Gale Razeya: *גלי רזיא*, "The Revealer of Secrets," a work of Jewish mysticism or a polemical text used to find Christian truths in Jewish tradition.</term> explaining the same prophecy, he says: "And his goings forth are from eternity and from the days of old." The prophet says "goings forth" in the plural number because there are two goings forth of the Messiah. One of divinity, which is eternal, and therefore he says "from eternity." The other of humanity, which exists in the substance of his mother, which was created from the hour of the world's creation. And for that reason he says, "from the days of old." For as the same author says a little earlier in the same place, the mother of the King Messiah was created by God so that the Messiah himself might sit within her, to show the glory of his majesty to all mortals. Therefore she is shown to be the first creature of God in the human race. These are the words of that Rabbenu HaKadosh, whom they call "our holy master." 

From these things which have been said, therefore, the perversity of Rabbi David <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (Radak), a famous 12th-13th century Jewish commentator who interpreted this verse as referring to the Messiah's ancient Davidic lineage rather than divinity.</note> is easily disproven. For to say that the goings forth of the Messiah—which the prophet asserts were from eternity and from the days of old—were only from the days of King David (as Rabbi David himself wishes) is both distorted and impious. For even if the prophet meant "from the beginning" (as Rabbi David himself falsely explains) and not "from eternity," that time which he says passed between David and the Messiah was by no means "from the beginning" or "from the days of old." Indeed, the authorities that he adduces in the name of the Christians (see how great is his blindness!) show this distortion even more clearly. For one authority affirms that the Messiah is God, while the other affirms that his going forth according to his humanity was together with the world's...

To put it briefly, I say that here all expositors, both Christian and Hebrew, agree on the manner of interpreting the weeks. They take a "week" here to mean a span of seven years, just as we do. For the final position this "week" holds demonstrates it is the last of all, and its midpoint was to abolish the bloody heap of sacrifices.

From this it necessarily follows that these weeks are not indeed of jubilees, nor centuries, nor decades, nor any other number, but are spans of years only; otherwise, they would by no means have been completed at that time. ## BOOK FOUR

Indeed, one way a "week" is understood is as a span of seven days, as is clear from Leviticus chapter 23. There it is said that seven weeks are to be counted from the feast of Passover, which makes 49 days, and the fiftieth day is the feast of <term>Pentecost</term> <note>Derived from the Greek word for 'fiftieth,' this harvest festival occurs fifty days after Passover.</note>. In another way, however, a week is taken for a cycle of seven years. This is as stated in Leviticus chapter 25: "You shall count seven weeks of years," which makes 49 years. And the fiftieth year immediately following is commanded to be a <term>Jubilee</term> <note>A year of "remission" or release in the Jewish tradition, where debts were forgiven and enslaved people were freed.</note>, which among the Jews was the year of remission. Therefore, since no other way can be found in the Holy Scriptures for a week to be understood, and since a week in the aforementioned words of Daniel cannot be understood as a span of seven days (because if so, the entire prophecy of Daniel would have been completed within a year and a half), it follows by necessity that it must be understood as a cycle of seven years.

<margin>What is called in Hebrew: our venerable master Saadia.</margin> This is then proved by Rabbi Abraham <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish rabbi, philosopher, and biblical commentator.</note>, a great glossator and doctor among them, in this manner, when he says: Our venerable master <term>Saadia</term> <note>original: "סעדיא" (Seadia). Saadia Gaon was a prominent 10th-century Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> said that these are seventy weeks of years. A witness to this matter is what is said in Daniel chapter 10: "After this, I Daniel was mourning for three weeks of days; I ate no pleasant bread." And so on, until the completion of three weeks of days. However, he did not count days with the seventy weeks. For the previously mentioned "middle of the week" consists of one thousand, two hundred, and twenty days, as I shall prove with sufficient evidence. Furthermore, it is possible that the "middle" is not a perfect middle, having neither more nor less, like that in Numbers 32: "And a half to the tribe of Manasseh," and many things of this sort. Know, however, that in the Holy Scripture, "days" are always days and not years. Nevertheless, it is possible that when "days" are mentioned, a "day" may be a perfect year, the year returning in the repetition of days, as when it is said in Exodus 13: <term>From year to year</term> <note>original: "מימים ימימה" (mi-yamim yamimah). While the literal Hebrew is "from days to days," it is idiomatic for "annually."</note>, that is, from year to year, which is a perfect year. However, when "days" are mentioned with a number, such as two days or three, the days cannot be years, but must be days exactly as they are called. And because of this, it is said in Leviticus 24: "And you shall count for yourself seven weeks of years." And for that reason I said that one thousand, two hundred and ninety days are the half or middle of the aforementioned week. And this is that from Daniel 12: <term>Blessed is he who waits and reaches the one thousand, three hundred, thirty-five days.</term> <note>original: "אשרי המחכה ויגיע לימים אלף שלש מאות שלשים וחמשה" (Ashrei ha-m'chakkeh...).</note> For if here "days" were said to be "years," how could it be true that a man might "wait and reach" them, especially since it is written in Psalm 89 <note>Psalm 90 in the modern English numbering.</note>: "The days of our years in them are seventy years." These are the words of Rabbi Abraham regarding Daniel. From these, three arguments are taken.

The first is that the aforementioned weeks of Daniel are entirely composed of years. The second is against the Jews of our time, who more frequently say that the 1,335 days mentioned in Daniel 12 are years, at which time they ought to be visited and have their Messiah...

# BOOK FOUR

Indeed, they calculate these years from the destruction of the last temple, which is clearly false based on the explanation of Rabbi Abraham <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a major Jewish scholar whose commentaries were often studied by Christian Hebraists.</note> provided earlier. From all of this, it is clear that in this week of Daniel’s prophecy, it is understood only as a span of seven years. Therefore, those seventy weeks contain four hundred and ninety years. 

**HOG.** <note>Likely Jacob van Hoogstraten, the inquisitor who acts as the challenger in this dialogue.</note> How are the years of these weeks to be understood? 

<margin>Whether the years of these weeks are solar or lunar.</margin> 
For Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), an English monk and scholar famous for his works on history and chronology.</note> and certain others among our people say they are lunar, moved primarily by two reasons. First, because in the text these weeks are said to be "abbreviated." Since lunar years are eleven days shorter than solar years—for a solar year contains 365 days, a quarter, and 5 minutes, while a lunar year consists of 354 days—it clearly follows that the years of these weeks ought to be lunar, not solar. Second, because when the angel spoke to Daniel, who was a Hebrew, and the Hebrews calculated by lunar years, it is reasonable to believe he was not speaking of solar but of lunar years. 

**GAL.** <note>Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540), the author, defending the use of Hebrew sources to support Christian theology.</note> Those who say this err not a little. For (to respond to their reasons) the text itself does not call these weeks "abbreviated." Where our <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The standard Latin Bible used by the Western Church.</note> edition has "abbreviated," the Hebrew text says <term>Nehtach</term> <note>original: "נחתך" (Nehtach). This term appears in Daniel 9:24.</note>, which is the same as "cut off." This comes from the Hebrew verb *Hatach* <note>original: "חתך" (Hatach).</note>, which properly signifies to cut in, or to cut off, as well as to determine and establish. For this reason, according to the "Hebrew Truth" <note>A term used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Old Testament.</note>, these weeks should not be called abbreviated, but rather cut off, predefined, or predestined. 

They are called this because they were predestined seventy years before they were announced to Daniel by the angel Gabriel. This is best shown in the book called <term>Seder Olam</term> <note>original: "סדר עולם" (Seder Olam), meaning "The Order of the World." An ancient Hebrew chronological work.</note>, where it is written at the end of the book that Rabbi Jose said: "What is the meaning of the phrase, 'seventy weeks are cut off'? By this it is taught that they were cut off by decree seventy years beforehand." 

Furthermore, if the Jews had a year eleven days shorter than the solar year, then according to their Law they are bound to celebrate <term>Passover</term> <note>The spring festival commemorating the Exodus from Egypt.</note> on the 14th day of the first month of any given year. It would certainly follow that in celebrating Passover, they would always anticipate the celebration of the next year’s Passover by eleven days. If that were the case, within a short time they would celebrate their Passover in every month of the year, nor would they agree with us on the timing of the celebration. That this is false is clearly evident from their practice, since they always celebrate the Passover at almost the same time. Therefore, it is manifest that they calculate time by solar years just as we do. For even if they have lunar months, every third year among them has thirteen months or lunations, while each of the others contains only twelve months. Thus, through <term>intercalations</term> <note>original: "embolysmos." The practice of inserting a leap month into the lunar calendar to keep it aligned with the solar year and the seasons.</note>...

**CAP.** <note>Capnio, the persona of Johannes Reuchlin.</note> As far as I can see, no Christian ought to despise these numbers, reinforced as they are by both the testimonies of the Holy Scripture and the traditions of the <term>Talmud</term><note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note>. Indeed, one should embrace and love them above gold, topaz, and every precious stone. For nothing more concise, nothing more effective, and nothing more necessary can be found to demonstrate against the Jews that these seventy weeks of Daniel were completed in the death of Christ. ### Against the obstinate recklessness and madness of Rabbi Solomon, Rabbi Levi, and other more recent scholars, who most shamelessly attempt to pervert the words of Daniel. Chapter XVII.

# CAPNIO,

Although, because of the things that have been said, the more recent Jews—defeated by their own scriptures as if by their own weapons—are in no way able to deny that the Messiah has already come, and that he was our Lord Jesus himself. Yet they are blinded by such a great desire for misrepresentation and contradiction that they do not notice in the least how absurd, how impossible, and how inconsistent with divine scripture are the things they babble in various ways against this prophecy of Daniel. They attempt with all their might to show that what Gabriel said to Daniel about the Messiah should be understood not as the true Messiah promised in the Law and the Prophets, but as some other person. 

For some say that the first "Messiah" expressed in Gabriel’s speech, when it is said, *unto Messiah the Prince*, was Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great, the Persian king who issued the decree for the Jews to return from exile.</note>. Among these is Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "Rabbi Selomo," referring to Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac, 1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> in the commentary he produced on Daniel. But others <margin>Diverse errors of the Jews regarding the meaning of "Messiah."</margin> say that this Messiah was Nehemiah <note>The governor of Judea who oversaw the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.</note> himself. Among these is Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "R. Abraham Auen Ezra," a 12th-century Spanish-Jewish polymath.</note>, as his commentary on Daniel shows. Still others assert that the Messiah was Joshua the High Priest <note>Joshua son of Jozadak, the first High Priest of the Second Temple period.</note> himself. Among these is Rabbi Levi <note>original: "Rabbi Leui," referring to Gersonides (1288–1344).</note>, as his writings on Daniel indicate. 

Furthermore, others affirm that the Messiah was Zerubbabel <note>The governor of the Persian province of Judah and a descendant of David.</note> himself; many today follow their opinion. Again, others explain that the "Messiah" mentioned in the second instance—namely where it is said, *And after sixty-two weeks the Messiah shall be cut off*—was Agrippa <note>Agrippa II, the last ruler of the Herodian dynasty, who lived during the destruction of the Second Temple.</note> himself. Rabbi Solomon also followed these people. Therefore, so that their madness might be more apparent, I would like you to refute the delusions of each one with a truthful response. 

GAL. You rightly <margin>Refutation.</margin> judge them to be insane in this, as in all other matters. For what else does such an absurd diversity of opinions show in contradicting such clear testimony from Gabriel, than that the mournful omen of Moses has befallen them? It was prophesied of them in Deuteronomy, chapter 28: *The Lord shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart: And thou shalt grope at noonday, as the blind gropeth in darkness, and thou shalt not prosper in thy ways.* <note>original Hebrew: "יככה יהוה בשגעון ובעורון ובתמהון לבב וחיית ממשש בצהרים כאשר ימשש העור באפלה ולא תצליח את דרביד" (Deuteronomy 28:28-29). The author provides the Latin translation immediately after the Hebrew.</note> 

Therefore, where it was said by the angel to Daniel, *Unto Messiah the Prince, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks*, it is manifest that whoever asserts that "Messiah" there is anyone other than the true Messiah promised in the Law and the Prophets has incurred both madness and the other curses mentioned just before. For no one is ever found in Holy Scripture called "Messiah" <note>The term "Messiah" (Mashiach) literally means "Anointed One."</note> who was not anointed either with that sacred physical oil with which Kings and Priests were anointed, or with the spiritual oil—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit (which Saint David in Psalm 45 calls the *oil of gladness*). [The Rabbi] affirms that the weeks were to be fulfilled after the destruction of the temple. This is manifestly false. The second error is when he says that the angel’s phrase, **To consume transgression and to finish sin**, should be understood in this way: that in the captivity in which they [the Jews] currently reside, the Jews' transgression is to be consumed, and their sin will have an end through the mediation of their persecutions. For those most serious and unbearable sins committed by the Jews during the time of the First Temple—namely **idolatry**, the murders of so many prophets, and so many unspeakable crimes—were wiped away by a Babylonian captivity of only seventy years, a captivity in which He even conferred many benefits upon them, such as prophets, miracles, and other honors. Yet the sins committed during the time of the Second Temple, which were light in comparison to those others, He has not yet wiped away despite such a long captivity and so many calamities; nor has He ever granted them any of the benefits in this current captivity which He had granted them in the Babylonian one. Therefore, it must necessarily be concluded that the angel spoke to Daniel about a different transgression and a different sin than those which this treacherous Rabbi has mentioned.

Now consider that phrase: **Know therefore, and understand, from the going forth of the word**. For this reason, he strove many times, now by himself and now through others, to persuade the Jews not to choose to be the cause of that place’s destruction.

<margin>**The false interpretation of Rabbi Levi.**</margin>
I will first relay his words, which are as follows: **"Seventy weeks," (he says) "are decreed <note>Original Latin: *praecisum*, meaning 'cut off' or 'determined'.</note>, that is, it is established that it shall be upon your people,"** and so forth. It is conceivable that the angel said these things to Daniel because Daniel himself was thinking of adapting his prayers and petitions to this end: that the return of Israel from exile would be of such a nature that the temple would never be destroyed again. For he thought this could lawfully happen because their sins had been erased by the punishments they had already endured. ...it will be desolating, until Israel, which will be desolated by the final desolation, is laid waste. These are the things which that untrustworthy <note>Original Latin: *perfidus*. This reflects the harsh polemical tone common in Renaissance-era Christian-Jewish debates, where "faithless" or "treacherous" was a standard epithet for those whose interpretations differed from Church doctrine.</note> Rabbi Levi says regarding this vision of Daniel. If these things are examined correctly, two main points are found against him. 

<margin>Refutation of the aforementioned exposition.</margin>

The first point is that among the other vain talk he asserts regarding the angel and Daniel, he accidentally concludes the very understanding of the prophecy (or vision) that he believes he is fleeing from, quite contrary to his own intention. The second point is that while he approves of something inconsistent because he is striving to avoid a different conclusion, he falls into many other inconsistencies. 

Therefore, when he says that the mysteries contained in the angel's first proposition were to be fulfilled within the time of seventy weeks, he seems to have clung to the truth. But when he saw that this contradicted his own false purpose, he refused to descend into a clear explanation of those mysteries with a perverse caution; and for the sake of satisfying the common people, he abandoned his first explanation and came to a second. In this second view, he agrees with Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, with only a few things removed. For he assigns that phrase, *to bring in everlasting righteousness*, to the true and proper Messiah. He says this mystery was prefigured in the dream of Nebuchadnezzar as interpreted by Daniel. 

From this, it necessarily follows that the "Fifth Kingdom" of the Messiah was meant to arise within the time of these seventy weeks. For if all the mysteries contained here were to be completed within that time, and "everlasting righteousness" is understood as the Fifth Kingdom of the Messiah (as he himself says), then it follows without a doubt from his own words that the Messiah was to come within that time. 

However, when he says that the angel did not care about an abundance of extra years in the division of the weeks, provided that the mysteries were verified, it is undoubtedly ridiculous. For why would the angel have divided that time into parts and distinguished the mysteries to be completed in each part from one another, if all things could happen in any indeterminate time without regard for the chronological choice? 

Furthermore, when he says that by "Messiah the Prince," one should understand the High Priest, he himself does not sufficiently understand his own reasoning. For these two dignities—the royal and the priestly—are usually attributed to no one in Holy Scripture except the Messiah. For both that saying of David in Psalm 110: **"You are a priest forever"** <note>Original Hebrew: *Atah kohen l'olam*.</note>, and that written in Isaiah 55: **"Behold, I have given him as a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the nations"** <note>Original Hebrew: *Hen ed le'umim netativ, nagid u-metzaveh le'ummim*.</note> are spoken of the Messiah. 

Therefore, it can by no means be said that the angel was speaking of Joshua <note>Specifically Joshua the son of Jozadak, the High Priest during the return from Babylonian exile.</note> the High Priest (as he asserts). This is especially true since we never read that he held both of these dignities. Finally, that which he says regarding the clause, *The Messiah shall be killed and shall have nothing*, comes directly against him. For he wants that phrase to speak of the cutting off and end of the Kingdom. From this, it necessarily follows that the priestly office then had its end, since he understands the "High Priest" by "Messiah the Prince." He also confirms this through the last part of the prophecy, when he says the Jewish people were to be desolated by the final desolation by Titus <note>The Roman Emperor who, as a general in 70 AD, destroyed the Second Temple in Jerusalem.</note>. <margin>The word *Naghid*.</margin> At that time—that is, from the fourth year of King Zedekiah and the twelfth of Nebuchadnezzar—according to the angelic instruction, the calculation of these weeks was to begin, and they were to terminate at the time of the Messiah. Therefore, he added: *until the Messiah the Naghid* <note>original: "נגיד Naghid"</note>, that is, the Leader, or Prince, or Principal One, or the one made manifest. For this Hebrew word *Naghid* (as Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), also known as the Radak, a preeminent medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator.</note> says in the book *Shorashim* <note>original: "Serassìm," referring to Sefer Shorashim (The Book of Roots), a famous Hebrew dictionary.</note>) is derived from *neghed* <note>original: "נגד neghed"</note>, which properly signifies "before" or "in the presence of." And from this it is said in the sixteenth chapter of the First Book of Kings <note>1 Samuel 16 in modern bibles.</note>: *Is not His Messiah before [neghed] the Lord?* <note>original: "נגד neghed, id est coràm Domino Messias eius"</note> And for this reason a Prince is called *Naghid*, according to what is said in the fifth chapter of the Second Book of Kings <note>2 Samuel 5:2.</note>: *And you shall be for a leader* <note>original: "ואתה תהיה לנגיד", literally "and you shall be for a Naghid."</note>—this means, "And you shall be a prince or one made manifest." From this also noble and precious things are called *Neghidim* <note>original: "נגידים Neghidìm"</note>, that is, principal things, as in that passage of Proverbs chapter 8: *Hear, for I will speak of principal things.* <note>original: "שמעו כי נגידים אדבר"</note> From this also it is said in Isaiah chapter 58: *And announce to my people their wickedness* <note>original: "והגד לעמי פשעם", where "announce" (ha-ghed) shares the same root as Naghid.</note>—which means, "make their crime manifest before my people." These are the words of Rabbi Kimhi. From which it is clear that *Naghid* is the same as Leader, Prince, Principal, one made manifest, and one announcing. 

Afterward, the angel divides these weeks into three parts: namely, into seven weeks, into sixty-two, and into one which remains at the end, on account of the special works that were to be done in each of these parts, saying: *Seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks.* For the first seven weeks make forty-nine years. The sixty-two that follow return four hundred thirty-four years; if the first seven are added to these, they constitute four hundred eighty-three years. Indeed, the entire seventy weeks contain four hundred ninety years (as we have said elsewhere). Then, wishing to suggest those things that were to happen in the first seven weeks, he says: *She herself shall return, and the street shall be built*—that is, the city of Jerusalem, which he called a "street" <note>original: "platea," often meaning a wide square or open space.</note> on account of its size—*and the wall* <note>original: "fossatum," literally a ditch or trench, but interpreted here as a defensive wall.</note>—meaning its fortification. So Rabbi Selomo <note>Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> and Rabbi Levi <note>Gersonides (Levi ben Gershon), a 14th-century philosopher and commentator.</note> and nearly all others explain it. *But in a narrowness of times* <note>original: "in angustia temporum," often translated as "troublous times."</note> he says, namely on account of the neighboring nations by whom the Jews were to be harassed by constant wars, as Ezra and Nehemiah testify. 

It follows in the prophecy: *And after sixty-two weeks, the Messiah shall be slain.* <note>Daniel 9:26.</note>

Therefore (as they say) the text in this place does not say "the Messiah shall be killed," but "the Messiah shall be cut off." 

**Galatinus:** Although the word *iccareth* in its primary institution signifies "to cut off," it is nevertheless frequently used in Holy Scripture for "to kill." As in that passage of Genesis 9: *And I will establish my covenant with you, and all flesh shall no longer be "iccareth"* <note>Genesis 9:11.</note>—that is, all flesh shall not be killed any further by the waters of the flood. Likewise in Ezekiel chapter 21: *And I will "iccareth" from you the righteous and the wicked* <note>Ezekiel 21:3.</note>—that is, "And I will kill from among you the righteous and the impious." # FOURTH.

In the third book of Kings <note>Known as 1 Kings 18:4 in modern Bibles.</note>, chapter 18, it is read as follows: **And it came to pass, when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord.** <note>original Hebrew: ויהי בהכרית איזבל את נביאי יהוה</note> Now, that this word is used in this sense <note>meaning "to kill" or "execute"</note> in that passage is clearly evident by what is immediately added; for there follows: **Has it not been told to my lord what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of the Lord?** <note>original Hebrew: הלא הגד לאדני את אשר עשיתי בהרג איזבל את נביאי יהוה; this refers to the account of Obadiah hiding the prophets.</note> From these examples, it is clear that this word **shall be cut off** <note>original Hebrew: יכרת, iccareth</note> is accepted in this place to mean "he shall be killed."

<margin>The Jews are going to kill the Messiah.</margin>
That they themselves were to kill the Messiah will be made very widely apparent in the following sections—where the death of the Messiah is discussed—through their own ancient Teachers. For now, among other things, it is enough to relate the words of Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai in the book **The Investigation of Pieties** <note>original: מחקר חסדות, Mehkar hassodoth. Simeon bar Yochai is the traditional author of the Zohar; "Mehkar Hassodoth" is a title often cited in Christian Hebraist works to find Christian truths in Jewish mysticism.</note>, which the Rabbi heard. For there, Hosea <note>The prophet Hosea.</note> said weeping: "Woe to them, woe to them, woe to them, the impious, unjust murderers of Israel! Out of love for them, so that He might forgive their sin, God will send His holy son, and he shall clothe himself in human flesh. Woe to them, because on account of their depraved actions, they will be rebellious against this Messiah; they will not look upon the commands by which he shall order them to be cleansed with the water of purification to expiate their sins. They will not walk in the ways pleasing to God, nor do His will, but moved by a great wrath, they will kill him."

Immediately after the angel said "the Messiah shall be killed," he added: **and not for him.** <note>original Hebrew: ואין לו, Veen lo; from Daniel 9:26.</note> The author of our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translated this as: *And the people who shall deny him shall not be his.* However, the text says: **and not for him** <note>original: ואין לו, ueen lo</note>, that is, **and nothing for him.** This means that what the faithless Jews will suppose—namely, that he lies dead after being crucified and will not rise again—shall not be for him. Rather, although the Messiah is killed, he shall nevertheless rise on the third day, ascend to the heavens, and send the Holy Spirit upon the believers.

Next, the angel continues: *And the city* (meaning Jerusalem) *and the sanctuary shall the people of the Prince who is to come destroy*—that is, the people of Titus, the son of Vespasian. *And its end shall be with a flood* (or a violent snatching away), namely, by the Roman people. This did not happen within those specific weeks, but forty years after they had elapsed. But the angel added it immediately after speaking of the death of the Messiah to show that this would happen to the Jews as a punishment for the death of the Messiah. Moreover, he said the **people** of the Prince who is to come, and not the **Prince himself**, would destroy the city and the sanctuary. This was to openly suggest—according to the gloss of Rabbi Levi—that Titus would participate in this not willingly, but reluctantly. For he himself (as Josephus says in the book *The Jewish War*) used the greatest effort, first with the Jews and finally with the soldiers, to prevent the destruction of the city and the temple. However, he was not able to obtain this, since that devastation was destined to follow because of the murder of Christ. And until the end of the cut-off war—that is, the determined or predestined war of Gog and Magog, namely, of the Antichrist—desolations (understood) shall endure. After these things, the angel returns to the final week, to reveal what ought to happen in it, saying: *But he* (namely the Messiah) *shall confirm a covenant...*

Concerning this law, it was predicted in this way in Jeremiah 31: <note>Jeremiah 31:31-32 in modern Bibles.</note> **"Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah; not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant which they broke, though I was a husband to them."** <note>original Hebrew: הנה ימים באים נאם יהוה וכרתי את בית ישראל ואת בית יהודה ברית חדשה לא כברית אשר כרתי את אבותם ביום החזיקי בידם להוציאם מארץ מצרים אשר המה הפרו את בריתי ואנכי בעלתי בם</note> These words are translated into Latin <note>and here into English</note> as follows: **Behold the days shall come, says God, and I will cut a new covenant—that is, a new law—with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. Not according to the covenant which I cut with their fathers—that is, not like the law which I gave their fathers—on the day in which I strengthened their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they disturbed** <margin>The word Berith.</margin> **my covenant, and I rejected, or neglected, or abandoned them.** Therefore, when it is said here, **"But he shall confirm the covenant with many in one week,"** the "covenant" is understood to mean the Law. For although <term>Berith<gloss>covenant or treaty</gloss></term> means a league or a pact, or even a firmament, it is nevertheless accepted in many places of Holy Scripture to mean "Law." This is clearly evident in the aforementioned words of Jeremiah. This is also openly proven in the book <term>Mechilta<gloss>An early Jewish legal commentary on Exodus</gloss></term> regarding the statement in Exodus 12, **"In the tenth of this month,"** where it is said: **"It is not a covenant [Berith] except for the Torah [the Law], just as it is written in these words: These are the words of the covenant which the Lord commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which he made with them in Horeb."** <note>original Hebrew: אינו ברית אלא תורה כמו שכתוב באלה הדברים אלה דברי הברית אשר צוה יהוה את משה לכרות את בני ישראל בארץ מואב מלבד הברית אשר כרת אותם בחורב; quoting Deuteronomy 29:1.</note> Thus far the quote.

<margin>The Messiah was to teach for three and a half years.</margin>
From these things it is clearly evident that "covenant" is understood as "law." Furthermore, that the Messiah ought to teach with His own mouth for three and a half years is made clear by the Talmudists. For it is read in <term>Midrash Tehillim<gloss>A rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</gloss></term> (that is, in the exposition of the Psalms), that Rabbi Johanan said: **"For three years and a half the Shekhinah [the Divine Presence] stood and proclaimed on the Mount of Olives: 'Seek the Lord while he may be found, call upon him while he is near.'"** <note>original Hebrew: שלשה שנים ומחצה היתה שכינה עומדת ומכרזת בהר חזיתים דרשו את יהוה בהמצאו קראהו בהיותו קרוב; the citation is a mix of Midrashic tradition and Isaiah 55:6.</note> This is also confirmed in **Bereshit Rabbah** (that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis). Where <term>Rabbi Moses Hadarshan<gloss>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne often cited by Christian Hebraists</gloss></term> says as follows: "What did Solomon wish to say in the Song of Songs when he says, 'We will exult and rejoice in thee'?" **"When do we rejoice? When the feet of the Shekhinah [the Divine Presence] stood upon the Mount of Olives."** <note>original Hebrew: אימתי אנו שמחים כשעמדו רגלי שכינה על הר חזיתים</note> And these are the words of Rabbi Johanan son of Zakkai. From these things it manifestly appears that these three and a half years are those in which, according to the word of the angel, the Messiah was to confirm His law through Himself by deed, word, and miracles. # FOURTH BOOK

[He] received baptism, and from then until His passion, nearly three and a half years passed. In those years, He traveled through Galilee and Judea, frequently staying and teaching upon the Mount of Olives, confirming His law by deed and word. Rightly, therefore, the angel placed this "week"—in which these and many other divine works were to occur—at the very end, as the completion <note>original: complementum</note> of all things. And because, by divine decree, the Messiah was to die in the middle of this final week, through which all the sacrifices of the Old Law were to reach their end, for they had merely prefigured that true sacrifice which the Messiah Himself was to make—offering His most holy body on the altar of the cross for the remission of the sins of the human race. For this reason, the angel added: *And in the middle of the week he shall cause the sacrifice* <note>original: decollationem, literally "the slaughtering" or "cutting off"</note> *to fail* (that is, of animal sacrifices) *and the offering* (that is, of all other things offered in the temple), all of which were meant to cease in terms of their spiritual significance at the death of the Messiah. As a sign of this fact, at the very hour of Christ’s death, the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom, and all the miracles that used to occur in the temple came to an end, as we have discussed abundantly above. And finally concluding, the angel says: *And upon the abominations*, that is, because of the abominations committed against the Messiah, *there shall be desolation*. And it shall persist until the consummation and the preordained end; namely, desolation upon desolation. From this it is clear that the Jews will never return to Jerusalem from this most recent captivity, unless perhaps after the war of the Antichrist, when they have received the faith of Christ.

<margin>Conclusion of the argument.</margin>
Therefore, reducing all that we have said most extensively over the five preceding chapters regarding this prophecy of Daniel into the form of a logical argument, we conclude as follows: Since the angel Gabriel told Daniel that from the going out of the word regarding the people’s return until the Messiah appeared as the leader, there would be 7 and 62 weeks, and since this number was completed 40 years before the burning of the second Temple; and since no one besides the Lord Jesus, either then or since, has appeared until now who possessed the signs of the leader and true Messiah (as is even conceded by our adversaries); and since <note>original: Quique, likely intended as "and who"</note> after those 7 and 62 weeks, by both teaching and performing works possible only for God, He was made manifest and then killed—it is a necessary consequence, for all who are not devoid of reason, that He was indeed the leader and the true Messiah.

...that the time has now passed, and has been fulfilled in our Lord Jesus, just as you have now most effectively shown through Daniel. **GALATINUS.** That is also excellently proved through Isaiah. And first indeed from this, that in the 9th chapter, having listed eight names for the Messiah—which are: Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father, Eternal, Prince, Peace—at the end of them all where it says, **of the increase of the government** <note>Hebrew: *lemarbe hamisrah*</note>, that is, for the multiplying of his princedom; in the middle of the word **to increase** <note>Hebrew: *lemarbe*</note>, contrary to the nature of writing and against the rules of grammar, a "closed mem" is placed, where an "open" one should have been positioned. **HOGOSTRAT.** Unless you explain these things, I cannot understand them. **GALATINUS.** The Hebrews have two forms of the letter *mem* <note>The Hebrew letter equivalent to 'M'</note>. One is "open," which looks like this **מ**, and is never used at the end of a word, but always at the beginning and in the middle. The other is "closed," which they shape like this **ם**, and they are only accustomed to write it at the end of a word. In this word **to increase** <note>original: *lemarbe*</note>, therefore, since the letter is in the middle of the word, it should not be closed but open; yet a closed one is placed there contrary to custom. This is found nowhere else in the text. Therefore, it is by no means to be believed that this was done without a mystery. For as it is said in the book **Sabbath** <note>The Talmudic tractate *Shabbat*</note>, in the chapter **The Builder** <note>original: *Habbone*</note>, it is stated: **A closed Mem signifies a closed word** <note>original: *Mem stumah davar satum*</note>, or a closed matter—that is, a hidden thing. For Isaiah himself wanted this to be understood by the wise, but to be hidden from the impious. For that reason, in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter **All Israel** <note>original: *Col Israel*</note>, it is related: When Rabbi Tanhum asked what the reason was—that since every *mem* placed in the middle of a word is open, this one alone is found closed—immediately in that hour there went forth a "daughter of the voice" <note>original: *filia vocis*, referring to a *Bat Kol*, a heavenly voice or divine revelation</note>, saying: **My secret is mine, my secret is mine** <note>original: *Razi li, razi li*</note>. Explaining this, Rabbi Shlomo <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century Jewish commentator</note> says that God said, "This secret concerning the coming of the Messiah is mine." Nevertheless, as the ancient Jews illuminated by the Holy Spirit said, many secrets are designated by the "closed mem" in this place; and especially, as we shall prove elsewhere, that the Messiah himself was to be born from a "closed virgin" <note>An allusion to the Virgin Mary and the concept of *virgo clausa*, suggesting her womb remained sealed or pure</note> who was to be called Mary, beyond the common way of birth and beyond the natural order. Now, however, we shall show that through this same closed *mem*, the fixed time of the Messiah's arrival is signified. For because this type of closed *mem* designates the number six hundred <note>In Hebrew gematria, the final or closed *mem* has the numerical value of 600</note> among the Jews, it is shown without doubt that from the time of this prophecy until the birth of the Messiah there would be six hundred years. This event was afterward proved by the reality of the matter. This is proved thus: for that prophecy came from the mouth of Isaiah at the same time as when the same prophet prophesied, saying: *Behold, a virgin shall conceive*, along with the rest. For both of these prophecies are in one and the same context. Therefore, this prophecy was made in the 4th year of the reign of King Ahaz, as Rabbi Shlomo says. He proves this in this way regarding the Second Book of Kings, chapter 15: when it is written (he says) in the 20th year of Jotham son of Uzziah, it should have been said in the year...

4. **Ahaz**. For behold, all the days of King *Jotham* are sixteen years. For just as it is said in 4 Kings 15 <note>In the Latin Vulgate used by the author, 1 & 2 Samuel and 1 & 2 Kings are titled 1–4 Kings. Therefore, 4 Kings refers to what is now commonly called 2 Kings</note>, *Jotham* the son of *Uzziah* King of Judah was 25 years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for sixteen years. But because *Ahaz* was impious, it pleased the Scripture to count four years among the years of *Jotham* while he was in the tomb, rather than among the years of *Ahaz* while he was alive. This is stated in the book called <term>Seder Olam <note>Hebrew: "Order of the World," a 2nd-century CE chronological work</note></term>, that is, the *Order of the World*. Thus says *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, the famous medieval commentator known as Rashi</note>. Moreover, that six hundred years passed from the going out of that same prophecy until the birth of Christ is shown in this way. 

For if *Ahaz* reigned for 16 years, as held in 4 Kings 15, and in the 4th year of his reign this prophecy was made (as *Rabbi Solomon* says), it follows that after that prophecy *Ahaz* himself reigned for 12 years; after whom his son *Hezekiah* reigned for 29 years, as read in 4 Kings 16. *Manasseh* reigned for 55 years, as held in 4 Kings 18. Then *Amon* reigned for two years, as said in 4 Kings chapter 21. *Josiah* for thirty-one years, as is clear in 4 Kings chapter 21. *Jehoahaz* for three months, as is reported in 4 Kings 22. *Jehoiakim* for eleven years, as gathered from 4 Kings chapter 23. *Jehoiachin* for three months, as held in the same place. Finally, *Zedekiah* reigned for eleven years, as is clear in 4 Kings chapter twenty-four. The sum of these years contains 151 and a half years. 

For from the fifth year of the reign of King *Ahaz* until the eleventh of *Zedekiah*, the Kings of the Jews reigned for 151 years <note>The author likely rounds the half-years or months to reach this total</note>. Then from the eleventh year of *Zedekiah*, which was the 19th of *Nebuchadnezzar*, as is clearly gathered from Jeremiah the last chapter and from 4 Kings 25: *Nebuchadnezzar* himself reigned for 26 years. *Evil-merodach* his son reigned for twenty-three years, as shown above, and *Belshazzar* for three years. *Darius* for two. *Cyrus* for thirty. *Ahasuerus* for fourteen. After whom succeeded *Darius*. In the sixth year of his reign the temple was finished and perfected. Adding these to the above-mentioned 151 and a half years in which the Kings reigned, and further the four hundred and twenty years which they say the second temple lasted: there are, from the fourth year of King *Ahaz* until the destruction of the second temple, six hundred and seventy-five and a half years. 

If from these are subtracted forty-two years, which passed from Christ’s passion until the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the temple, and the nearly 33 and a half years in which Christ himself lived among men, there will be, from that time in which *Isaiah* prophesied concerning the conception and birth of the Messiah until the birth of Christ himself, precisely six hundred years, which the aforementioned <term>mem clausa <note>The final form of the Hebrew letter M, which has a numerical value of 600 in the 'Gematria' system of letter-numerals</note></term> designates. 

To prove this, that which is said by the same prophet in the fifty-fourth chapter is very much to the purpose: <note>original: "כי מי נח זאת לי אשר נשבעתי מעבור מי נח עוד על הארץ כן נשבעתי מקצף עליך ומגער בך"</note> "For this is as the waters of Noah to me: as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth; so have I sworn that I would not be angry with you, nor rebuke you." Which indeed *Rabbi Jonathan* <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, traditionally the author of the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets</note> thus turned into Aramaic: "For as the days of Noah this is before me..."

For if, according to his exposition based on the opinion or tradition of Elijah and his disciples, the <term>Messiah</term> was to come at the end of four thousand years of the world, and according to the calculation of the Jews from the beginning of the world until the present year—which is the year of Christ one thousand five hundred and sixteen—five thousand two hundred and seventy-six years have passed (although according to our count many more, as will be proven a little further below), it is certainly concluded of necessity that the arrival of the <term>Messiah</term> has already passed by one thousand two hundred and seventy-two years according to them.

<margin>Bar Cozba, a false Messiah received by the Jews.</margin>

These names are entirely the same. For *Bar* is indeed a Chaldean <note>The author uses "Chaldean" to refer to Aramaic.</note> word and *Ben* is Hebrew; both mean the same as "son" among us. *Cazab* <note>original: **כוזב**</note>, however, is interpreted as "a lie." Therefore, Bar Cozba or Bencozba means exactly the same as "the son of a lie" or "the son of falsehood." This man, thrusting himself forward as the Messiah, was accepted by the Jews. As it is read in the book of the <term>Sanhedrin</term>, in the chapter "Helec." Where, among other things, it is said of him: "Bar Cozba reigned for thirty and a half years. Having left [Judea], Titus returned to Rome. However, on the tenth of July <note>Original: "quinto Idus Iulij." In the Roman calendar, the fifth day before the Ides of July corresponds to July 11th, though historically the Temple was destroyed on the 9th or 10th of the month of Av.</note>, after the city was captured and razed to the ground and the Temple destroyed, and after peace was established with those who remained in Judea, he decreed that no Jew should henceforth observe the Sabbath, nor should any woman observe the laws of separation during her period. <note>This refers to *Niddah*, the Jewish ritual purity laws concerning menstruation.</note> This is fully recorded in the Talmud, in the book called *Megillah* <note>original: "מגילה Meghila"</note>, which means "The Scroll" or "The History."

<margin>Regarding the second false Messiah.</margin> 

After forty-eight and a half years had passed since the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, the Jews established a city named Betar <note>original: "Bitter"</note> as their capital. There they appointed another false Messiah over themselves. In their madness and mental blindness, they failed to notice that he was also called *Bencozba* or *Barcozba* <note>Known historically as Simon bar Kokhba, "Son of a Star." "Bar Cozba" means "Son of a Lie."</note>, just like the one their predecessors had accepted in Jerusalem, for whose sake they had been destroyed. It reached such a point that even Rabbi Akiba—notwithstanding that he had been shamefully deceived by the aforementioned false Messiah in Jerusalem—did not shudder to shamelessly accept this one. Rather, he attempted to persuade the people through the authority of Holy Scripture that this man was the true Messiah.

For as one reads in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the book called *Taanit* <note>original: "תענית Taanich," meaning "On Fasting"</note>, in the chapter beginning with *Shlosha Perakim* <note>original: "בשלשה פרקים Bislosa perakim," meaning "In Three Chapters"</note>, Rabbi Akiba interpreted that scripture written in Numbers 24: "A star shall rise out of Jacob" <note>original: "דרך כוכב מיהקב"</note> in this way: "*Barcozba* shall rise out of Jacob." And when he saw Barcozba himself, he would say: "Behold, here is the King Messiah!" This same account is also clearly found in the commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, which is called *Eicha Rabbah* <note>original: "איכה רבתי Echa rabbethi"</note>, regarding that passage in Lamentations 2: "The Lord has swallowed up without pity." There it is said that Rabbi Judah, son of Ilai, stated that when Rabbi Akiba was explaining the saying "A star shall rise out of Jacob," he said that one should not read it as *Cochab* <note>original: "כוכב"</note>, meaning "star," but as *Cozab* <note>original: "כוזב"</note>, meaning "deceit" or "a lie"—which was the name of his false Messiah.

<margin>The Jews besieged by Hadrian.</margin> 

Therefore, when the Jews rebelled against the Roman Empire under his leadership, Hadrian Caesar crossed the sea and fiercely besieged them and that same false Messiah in the city of Betar, in which there was an innumerable multitude of Jews. For in *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>original: "Beresthith rabba," the Great Commentary on the book of Genesis</note>, in that place where it is said, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau," it reads thus word-for-word: Rabbi Johanan said, "There were eighty thousand pairs of trumpet-blowers in Betar, and each one of them was in command of many armies who were there with Barcozba." He also had two hundred thousand men who had a finger cut off. These men had each cut off one of their own fingers when they were being tested, wishing to show their boldness and courage by this sign. 

Because of this, the sages sent word to Barcozba himself, saying, "How long will you continue to make the sons of Israel into mutilated men?" He replied and said, "And in what other way shall I test them?" They said to him, "Anyone who, while sitting upon his horse, cannot uproot a cedar of Lebanon, shall not be enrolled in your service." Thus he had another two hundred thousand men who were tested in this way. And whenever he went out to battle, he would say: "Lord of the world, do not support us, but do not grant us courage [either]. <note>This is a famous blasphemous prayer attributed to Bar Kokhba, essentially telling God "Just stay out of our way and don't help the enemy, and we will win on our own."</note> For have You not, O God, rejected us?"

**To all the house of Israel:** <note>original: "אל כל בית ישראל" (El kol beit Yisrael). This serves as a heading or proof-text for the following passage from Ezekiel 5.</note> That is: *And you, son of man, take a sharp sword, using it as a barber’s razor to shave your head and your beard. Then take balances for weighing and divide the hair. You shall burn a third part with fire in the midst of the city when the days of the siege are completed. Then you shall take a third and strike it with a sword all around the city. And a third you shall scatter to the wind, and I will unsheathe a sword after them. You shall also take a small number from there and bind them in the hem of your garment. And of these you shall take some again and throw them into the midst of the fire, and burn them in the fire. From there, a fire shall go out into all the house of Israel.* These are the prophet’s words. <note>This is a close paraphrase of Ezekiel 5:1-4. The author uses this symbolic act of the prophet Ezekiel to explain the history of the Jewish diaspora.</note>

Therefore, by the third part which he threw into the fire, we should understand those of that people who were devastated by burning. By the third part which he commanded to be struck with the sword, we understand those who were killed by iron weapons. By the third part which he scattered to the wind, we understand those who were led into captivity. <note>This refers to the "Galut" or the scattering of the Jewish people across the globe.</note> Finally, by the remainder, which he commanded to be tied in the edges of the cloak, he designated those who remain to be converted at the end of time. Concerning these, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> writing to the Romans in the 11th chapter says: *Blindness in part has happened in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel will be saved.* From these premises it is clear that for no other reason were the Jews struck with such manifold and cruel punishment—both by Vespasian and Titus, as well as by Hadrian—except that, having rejected the true Messiah and put him to a cruel death, they received false messiahs.

## The fifth reason showing that the time of the Messiah's first coming has already passed, taken from the punishment of the Israelite people; and that the Jews, at the coming of the Messiah, were to be punished with many penalties because of the death they would inflict upon him. Chapter XXII.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
The falsity of this exposition is clearly apparent from the very flow of the prophecy. For it is gathered from it that the Jews were to suffer innumerable evils through this king; however, through Hezekiah <note>The son of Ahaz; Kimhi argued the "cornerstone" was Hezekiah</note>, as he himself even asserts, it happened not only that they suffered no evils, but they were even liberated from the enemy Sennacherib <note>The Assyrian king who besieged Jerusalem during Hezekiah's reign</note>. For this reason, it can by no means be said that this prophecy speaks of Hezekiah himself. Furthermore, when he says from that clause, *The one who believes will not be in a hurry*, that the prophecy was not to be verified in the near future, he seems to openly contradict himself. For if it was spoken in the days of Ahaz (as he says), whom Hezekiah himself followed immediately, would it not have been fulfilled quickly enough? It is certain, therefore, that this part of the prophecy must necessarily be understood not of Hezekiah, but of the Messiah. This is first clearly evident through the Translation <note>Targum</note> of Rabbi Jonathan, who translated and explained this passage in Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaicé"</note> thus: *The Lord God said, behold I appoint in Zion a Messiah King, a powerful, robust, and strong King.* 

<margin>The exposition of Rabbi Solomon.</margin>
That is: The Lord God said, "Behold, I appoint in Zion the Messiah King, a powerful, robust, and strong King." Next, it is evident through Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the most influential Jewish commentator</note>, who, explaining the prophecy as referring to the Messiah, says: "Behold, it is I who have founded in Zion, that is, in my mind I have decreed to appoint the Messiah as King, who will be a strong stone and the foundation of foundations. So that he who believes this prophecy will come to pass will not be in a hurry, that is, he will not [anxiously] yearn for his arrival." Thus he says. With this exposition standing, we see without doubt that the final destruction of the Jews following the coming of the Messiah was foretold through this prophecy. Therefore, the prophecy cannot be fulfilled in the Messiah whom the Jews falsely expect to come, since they hope to receive infinite blessings from him. However, so that the perversity of Rabbi David and other more recent writers who strive to subvert this prophecy may be seen more clearly, their opinions will be recited and refuted here and there in the true exposition of the prophecy itself, which I shall now undertake.

<margin>The true and Catholic exposition of this prophecy.</margin>
I say, therefore, that through this prophecy, the entire mystery of Jesus Christ was summarized and foretold. For when the prophet was rebuking the wicked works of the Jews living in the times of Ahaz, wishing to predict this mystery to them, he wanted to show them where their successors, following their same way of life, would finally arrive. "Hear," he said, "the word of God, you scoffers, who rule this people who are in Jerusalem. Because you have said: We have struck a covenant with death, and we have made peace with the grave <note>original: "sepulchro," translating the Hebrew *Sheol*</note>." That is,

<summary>The author refutes the Jewish interpretation that the "cornerstone" in Isaiah 28 refers to King Hezekiah, arguing instead that even Jewish sources like the Targum and Rashi support a Messianic interpretation. He concludes that this Messiah must be Jesus Christ, whose coming brought the judgment foretold by the prophet.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s theological argument regarding the "cornerstone" prophecy in Isaiah 28. Having previously dismissed David Kimhi’s interpretation, the author now uses the authority of other Jewish commentators like Rashi and the Targum to argue that the stone represents the Messiah, while simultaneously turning the prophecy into a warning against those who would reject him.</meta>

### FOURTH BOOK

Because you, the leaders, are a greater cause of evil to others, being unwilling to keep God's commands or obey the warnings of his prophets, saying: "We have struck a <term>covenant</term> <note>original: "foedus," a formal treaty or alliance</note> with death, and with the grave we have made peace, so that we care for nothing." Therefore, thus says the Lord God: "Behold, I will lay a stone in Zion," that is, the King Messiah, as Rabbi Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the prophets</note> among the ancients and Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator</note> among the more recent scholars explain. This Messiah will indeed be a cornerstone, precious, and the "foundation of the foundation," that is, the foundation of all foundations. "He who believes shall not hasten," which is to say, according to the gloss of the same Rabbi Solomon, he who believes this prophecy is to come will not "hasten"—he will not desire his coming. That is to say, any of the Jews who believes the Messiah is coming, understanding the evils that are to arise upon them at his arrival, will not desire to hasten his coming; rather, he will ask God to delay it. 

The prophet immediately lists these evils, saying: "And I will lay judgment to the line, and justice to the plummet," along with the other things that follow. He says these things to denote that the limit of their salvation or damnation was to be set then, in such a way that the hope based on lies would deceive them. For at the coming of the Messiah, retribution—either of grace or of punishment—was to be rendered to everyone according to their merits. And since the prophet saw that the majority of them would decline toward the worse, before he came to the description of the evils they were to suffer, he wished to assign the cause of them—which was to be none other than the death of the Messiah—and so he added: "And your covenant with death shall be abolished, and your peace with the grave shall not stand." 

It is as if he were saying: "The covenant I entered into with your fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and their seed, will be abolished and dissolved by the death of the Messiah which will be perpetrated by you. For you, through the death which you will inflict upon the Messiah himself, will make that covenant void. In a similar way, your peace promised by me to you will not stand with the tomb of that same Messiah." For because of that, you are to suffer infinite calamities, and I will wage war against you continuously. 

The truth of this exposition is most strongly confirmed by this: if the prophecy were explained otherwise, it could by no means be fitted so well, and many inconsistencies and contradictions would follow. However, he used this manner of speaking to show that they had, in a sense, prophesied this mystery with their own words. It is as if he said: "Since you have said, 'We have struck a covenant with death, and with the grave we have made peace,' and the rest, therefore I say that you have spoken correctly. For thus says the Lord God: 'Behold, I will lay a stone in Zion,' that is, I will establish the Messiah, through whom your words will be proven true. For on his account you will suffer all these evils and the scourges which you said could not come upon you, as well as infinite others." Wherefore he immediately added: "When the overflowing scourge passes through, you will be trodden down by it," with the remaining words that follow. The truth of this interpretation is especially clear from what he says: "Just as on the mountain of divisions <note>Mount Perazim (2 Samuel 5:20), where David defeated the Philistines</note> God shall rise up, and just as in the valley that is in Gibeon he shall be angry, that he may do his work, his strange work..."

That he might perform his work, his work is strange <note>original: "extraneum," referring to Isaiah 28:21, where God's judgment is called a "strange work" because it seems contrary to His nature of mercy</note> and his act is alien. From these words it is clearly gathered, as Rabbi David <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (1160–1235), known as the Radak, a major medieval biblical commentator</note> testifies from his father's opinion, that the work he was to perform against Israel is called strange and alien to God because God himself, by his own will, ought not to have come to it; for his purpose tended mostly toward this: that he might found that stone for their good, and not for their harm. But if the contrary effect followed, the cause is to be ascribed not to God, but to themselves. It is as if he were saying openly: "Do not mock or laugh at my words to your greater punishment. For I confess to you and promise that I have heard from God that this is the cause of your final ruin, not only in Jerusalem or in Judea alone, but also in the whole earth." For the lashes will never allow you to rest while you are dispersed throughout the whole circle of the earth. This agrees with that saying of Moses in Deuteronomy 28: *And among those nations you will find no ease, nor shall there be rest for the sole of your foot.* <note>original Hebrew: ובגוים ההם לא תרגיע ולא יהיה מנוח לכף רגלך</note> Through this prophecy, therefore, it is clear—both from those things explained according to the <term>glosses</term> <note>interpretive comments or explanations added to a text</note> of the Hebrews, and from the rest which are inserted up to the end of chapter 28 <note>the text says 29, but refers to the context of the preceding prophecy</note>—that the Jews, because of the death they were to inflict upon the Messiah, were to be struck with manifold punishment and dispersed throughout the world in a final destruction.
