<header>BOOK 3</header>

For these things says God, the King of Israel and his redeemer, the Lord of Hosts is his name: **I am the first, and I am the last.** <note>original: Isaiah 44:6</note> **I will kill, and I will make alive.** <note>original: Deuteronomy 32:39</note> This was indeed said after the manna was given to them for the resurrection of the dead. **I will kill, and I will make alive.** **Let my soul die the death of the righteous.** <note>original: Numbers 23:10</note> **Let Reuben live and not die.** <note>original: Deuteronomy 33:6</note> **He will bring us to life on the day of days.** <note>original Latin: "Viuificabit nos in die dierum." This refers to Hosea 6:2, often interpreted by theologians as the resurrection on the third day.</note> Another discourse: **I will kill, and I will make alive.** Can I understand from this that death is in one person and life in another? Not at all. For it is said: **I will inflict the wound, and I will heal.** Thus, death and life are in one and the same person. **And there is no one who can rescue from my hand.** Fathers will not save sons; Abraham will not save Ishmael, nor Isaac save Esau. From this, it is held that fathers will not save sons. But how is it proved that brothers will not save brothers? From what is said: **A brother does not redeem, will a man redeem?** <note>original: Psalm 49:7. The author argues that no mere human relative can pay the spiritual price for another's soul.</note> For Isaac will not save Ishmael, nor will Jacob save Esau. And even if they gave all the riches of the world for their ransom, they are not sufficient to save them, nor are they a worthy price for their souls. And this is what is written: **A brother does not redeem, will a man redeem? And he will not give to God his price.** From the aforesaid things, therefore, it is most clearly evident that only God was to be the savior and redeemer of Israel, and that He Himself would give Himself as the price for human redemption.

### That this Savior and Redeemer had to be the Messiah. Chapter 11.

-> CAPNIO, <-

Now it must be proved that this future savior and redeemer was none other than the Messiah. GALATINUS: In many places this is manifest. First, therefore, I will bring forward those things written in the *Bereshith Rabba* <note>A significant collection of ancient Jewish interpretations (Midrash) on the book of Genesis.</note> of <term>Moses Hadarsan</term> <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note> regarding that passage in Genesis 24: **And Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother.** <note>The OCR says chapter 23, but the verse is Genesis 24:67.</note> These things are written for our purpose. For thus it is said there: "This is the King Messiah, who was in the generation of the wicked." Just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 53: <note>original Hebrew: ובחברתו נרפא לנו</note> **And in his wound we are healed.** And because of this, God preserves him, so that he may save Israel and exult with them in the resurrection of the dead. According to what is said in Deuteronomy chapter 33: <note>original Hebrew: אשריך ישראל מי כמוך עם נושע ביהוה מגן עזרך</note> that is: **Blessed are you, Israel. Who is like you, a people saved in the LORD, or through the LORD, the shield of your salvation?** Whence it is also said in Isaiah 45: <note>original Hebrew: ישראל נושע ביהוה תשועת עולמים לא תבשו ולא תכלמו עד עולמי עד</note> that is: **Israel shall be saved in the LORD, or through the LORD, with a salvation of ages or eternal. You shall not be ashamed, nor shall you be confounded unto the ages of eternity.** Moreover, <term>Rabbi Jonathan son of Uzziel</term> <note>The traditional author of the Targum (Aramaic translation/paraphrase) of the Prophets.</note> thus translated and explained those things in <term>Chaldean</term> <note>The term used by Renaissance scholars for Aramaic.</note>: <note>original Aramaic: ישראל אתפריקו במימריה דיהוה פורקן עלמיא</note> that is: **Israel shall be saved by the Word of God, or through the Word of God, with a salvation of ages.** Since, however, it was proved in the third book that the Messiah is the Word of God,

-># BOOK SIX<-

It follows that God intended this salvation of the ages, or eternal salvation, to be performed through the <term>Messiah</term>. This is also confirmed by <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a premier medieval Jewish commentator.</note> who, explaining that phrase in <term>Daniel</term>, **"And the sanctuary shall be justified,"** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-nizdak kodesh* (Daniel 8:14).</note> says as follows: "The sin of <term>Israel</term> shall be pardoned, and they shall be redeemed with eternal salvation through the King <term>Messiah</term>. Just as it is said in <term>Isaiah, chapter 45</term>: **Israel** shall be saved in **God** (or through **God**) with the salvation of the ages." These are the words of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term>.

Therefore, since in the traditions which we brought forward in the previous chapter from many books considered authentic among them, it is proved by those same oft-mentioned words of <term>Isaiah</term>—namely, "Israel shall be saved in <term>God</term> (or through <term>God</term>) with everlasting salvation"—that this savior is none other than <term>God</term>. And now, in this present tradition, by those very same words, this eternal salvation is attributed to the <term>Messiah</term>. The glossator <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> does the same, and through the <term>Chaldean</term> translation <note>The Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible used in Jewish liturgy and study.</note> this same salvation is attributed to the Word of <term>God</term>.

For this reason, it necessarily follows that this savior <term>God</term>, who was to save the human race with eternal salvation, is none other than the <term>Messiah</term>, the Word of <term>God</term> and the Son of <term>God</term>. For if <term>God</term> alone was to be the savior with the salvation of the ages or eternal salvation (as was proved in the preceding chapter through the testimonies of the prophets and the traditions of the ancients), and if now, with the same testimonies in their own traditions, the savior with the salvation of the ages or eternal salvation is called the <term>Messiah</term> (as has now been shown), then it necessarily follows for all who are not ignorant of logical consequences—and whom the devil has not blinded as their sins deserve—that the <term>Messiah</term> is beyond doubt not only man, but also <term>God</term>.

If, however, you wish to see something even greater than what has been concluded here against the faithlessness of the <term>Jews</term> of our time, hear what is written in <term>Hosea</term>, the first chapter: **"I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, for I will utterly forget them (or, in taking them away, I will take them away). But I will have mercy on the house of Judah (that is, the house of confession), and I will save them in the Lord their God (or through the Lord their God)."** <note>original Hebrew: *lo osif od arakhem et beit Yisrael... ve-et beit Yehudah arakhem ve-hoshatim bi-YHWH Eloheihem* (Hosea 1:6-7).</note>

<term>Rabbi Jonathan</term>, <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Targum of the Prophets.</note> translating this into <term>Chaldean</term>, explained it thus: **"I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel; however, if they repent, I will surely forgive them. But I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Word of the Lord their God."** <note>original Aramaic: *lo osif od lerakhama al beit Yisrael... ve-al d'beit Yehudah arakhem ve-afrekinun be-Memra de-YHWH Elohehon*.</note>

Since, therefore, the <term>Targum</term> (that is, the <term>Chaldean</term> translation) has placed "the Word of <term>God</term>" where the prophet placed the name of <term>God</term>, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> which is <term>YHWH</term> (which is the same as the Lord <term>God</term>), it is openly suggested that the Word of <term>God</term> is <term>God</term>. Consequently, it clearly shows the <term>Messiah</term> to be the Word of <term>God</term> and the Lord <term>God</term>, in whom and through whom this eternal salvation was to be accomplished. Hence, and not without reason, he was called <term>Yeshua</term>—that is, <term>Jesus</term>—as we have proved elsewhere, which is interpreted as "Savior" or "Salvation."

### Chapter III. That the redeemer, in order to be a perfect redeemer, had to be both God and man.

->CAPNIO,<-

**F**rom these things you have said, it has become clearly evident that the redeemer of the human race was to be both God and man. GALATINUS: Precisely so; otherwise he could not have sufficiently satisfied for the sin of the human race. CAPNIO: I would therefore like you—in order to further confound the faithlessness of the younger Jews who utterly deny this—to prove it more clearly through the testimonies of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>The ancient Jewish rabbinic authorities whose traditions are recorded in the Talmud.</note>. GALATINUS: I shall certainly do so. But first I will report what is read on this matter in the commentaries of <term>Rabbi Abraham Picus</term> <note>Likely referring to the author of the *Sefer ha-Tagin*, an esoteric work on the decorative flourishes on Hebrew letters.</note>, which are titled *On the Significance of the Crowns* <note>original Latin: *de significatione apicum*</note>, which are written above the letters of the book of the Law, and which the Hebrews call <term>taghin</term> <note>Hebrew: *taghin* (crowns/flourishes). In Jewish tradition, these small strokes on certain letters are believed to hold deep mystical secrets.</note>. For there, among other things, they have this: <note>original Hebrew: "Solomon, peace be upon him, handed down: 'I saw all the living who move under the sun with the second child who shall stand in his place' (Ecclesiastes 4:15). It is certain that it is characteristic of man to be born a boy, and a youth, and to progress daily, and to take increase until he comes to perfection. And this is what he says... with the second child, that is, the second who is understood by the eye of the mind... and this is enough for the wise..."</note> That is: Solomon (peace be upon him) handed down this saying, **"I saw all the living, who travel under the sun, with the second youth, who shall remain in his place."** (Ecclesiastes 4:15). It is certain that it is characteristic of man to be born a child, and a youth, and to progress daily and receive increase, until he comes to perfection. And this is what he means: "All the living traveling," that is, progressing "under the sun, with the second youth." And the sense of this word, according to my teaching (by which I command you to perceive with the intellect), is that the "second youth" is the **first intelligence**, that is, God. Nor is it permitted to disclose and reveal these things except to him alone who understands them by himself. And this is what is found in <term>Job, chapter 33</term>: namely, that a remission was made by God on two occasions. But the third, man performed. And he soon adds: **"That he might redeem souls from hell, and give them another shining body, that it might shine in life."** And by "life," eternal life is understood. Thus it is there. From these words it is clearly evident that the redeemer was to be both God and man. Next, to prove it more clearly, I will bring forward what is said in <term>Echa Rabbathi</term> <note>A Midrash (homiletic commentary) on the biblical Book of Lamentations.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the lamentation of Jeremiah. For there, upon that passage of <term>Lamentations chapter one</term>, it is said: **"And they went without strength before the pursuer."** Thus it is read that <term>Rabbi Aha</term> said: "Just as Israel was not taken captive except through a **full pursuer** <note>original: *Rodeph male*</note>, so they will not be redeemed except through a **full redeemer** <note>original: *Goel male*</note>, or a perfect one, as it is written in Isaiah..."

->*That the salvation and redemption to be made through the Messiah was to be spiritual in nature.*<-

## Chapter IV.

->CAPNIO,<-

Although from these things you have said, it is clearly suggested that the eternal salvation or the most potent redemption, which was to be made through the Messiah, was not to be temporal nor bodily (as the Jews of our age fabricate <note>The author, Galatinus, frequently argues against contemporary Jewish interpretations of his time, which often looked for a political Messiah to liberate them from Roman or later exile, by contrasting them with what he claims are "ancient" traditions.</note>), but was to be spiritual. Nevertheless, to further convince their stubborn disbelief, you must prove this more clearly to me through their own scriptures. GALATINUS. First, I bring against them that which is already read in Psalm 72—which is entirely explained as concerning the Messiah by the ancient Hebrews—in this way: **"He shall spare the poor and the needy: and shall save the souls of the poor. He shall redeem their soul from fraud and iniquity: and their blood shall be precious,"** or honored, **"in his sight."** <note>original Hebrew: יחס על דל ואביון ונפשות אביונים יושיע מתוך ומהמס יגאל נפשם ויקר דמם בעיניו</note> <margin>Reasons of the Talmudists.</margin> Through the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars and teachers of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> as well, this same point is proved. And first, indeed, from what they say: that belief in this redemption is necessary for salvation. This certainly would not be the case if the most potent redemption were temporal. Furthermore, it is the opinion of many ancients that the reward for good works is not to be expected in this world, as is held in <term>Bereshit Rabbah</term> <note>An ancient Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis, regarding that saying of Deuteronomy: **"Which I command you today to do them."** <note>original Hebrew: אשר אנכי מצוך היום לעשותם</note> For it is said there: **"Today to do them, but not to give their reward today."** <note>original Hebrew: היום לעשותם ולא לתן שכרם היום</note> Where almost all the Talmudists understand the word "today" as the present age. Wherefore they also say elsewhere: **"The reward of a commandment is not in this world."** <note>original Hebrew: שכר מצוה בהאי עלמא ליכא</note> Since, therefore, by the consensus of all, the redemption of the Messiah is not to be expected except through repentance and the works of virtues—by the merit of which the salvation of redemption is hoped for—and no salvation of this world is to be hoped for as a merit of good works, it surely follows that the redemption or salvation which the Messiah was to perform (which is numbered by them among the articles of faith, which they call "the roots of faith") must not be believed to be temporal or of this world. ...that the redemption was to be not temporal, but spiritual. This is also confirmed by Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets.</note>, who almost everywhere, and especially in the Psalter, when there is a discussion concerning salvation or redemption, always expressly explains it as spiritual. There is also that saying of Isaiah 12: **"You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of salvation."** <note>original Hebrew: ושאבתם מים בששון ממעיני הישועה</note> This is understood to refer to the Messiah according to the opinion of all the Hebrews, and he himself interprets it in the Chaldaic <note>Aramaic, often referred to as Chaldaic in this period.</note> as: **"And they shall learn a new doctrine from the chosen of the righteous."** <note>original Aramaic: וילפון אולפן חדש מבחירי צדיקיא; this interpretation suggests that the "water" drawn from the Messiah is actually divine knowledge.</note> 

The ancient Talmudists also understand spiritual salvation by the "land of promise," and by "Jerusalem" or "Zion." In the book of the Sanhedrin <note>The Talmudic tractate dealing with law and the afterlife.</note>, at the beginning of the chapter *Helec*, it is said: **"All Israel has a portion in the world to come."** <note>original Hebrew: כל ישראל יש להם חלק לעולם הבא</note> As it is said in Isaiah: **"And your people shall all be righteous, they shall inherit the land forever."** There they understand the "land" to mean the spiritual world, which they call the "world to come."

Furthermore, Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), one of the most influential Jewish philosophers.</note> in the <term>hilchoth tessuba</term> <note>Hebrew: Hilkhot Teshuvah, or "The Laws of Repentance."</note>, that is, in the eighth treatise on repentance, says: **"Eternal life is designated by the prophets with different similes, such as these: the mountain of God, His holy place, the way of holiness, the courts of God, the sweetness of God, the tabernacle of God, the temple of God, the gate of God."** 

Having seen these things, who will doubt that "Israel"—that is, the congregation of the righteous—and the "rebuilding of the temple" also require a spiritual sense? <margin>Conclusion.</margin> Rabbi Solomon <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> expressly affirms this regarding the temple described by Ezekiel in the chapter *Helec*. From all these things it is clearly evident that the "salvation of the ages," or the eternal and most perfect redemption which was to be achieved through the Messiah, was not to be temporal nor of bodies (as the Jews of our time deliriously maintain), but was to be of the spirit and of souls. 

By this redemption, the Messiah himself was to save and redeem the human race from original sin, from all other sins, and from the devilish servitude which men had incurred because of the sin of our first parents; and he was to lead them back to the heavenly and eternal blessedness which they had lost because of that same sin.

This is most clearly expressed and confessed by Rabbi Nehumias, son of Ha-Kana <note>Nehunia ben ha-Kana, a first-century sage to whom many mystical works were attributed by later scholars.</note>, a most esteemed man whose authority is great among the Hebrews. He says thus at the beginning of the <term>Ighereth hassodoth</term> <note>Hebrew: Iggeret ha-Sodot, or "The Epistle of Secrets."</note>, that is, the "Epistle of Secrets," which he wrote to his son Ha-Kana: 

"When I considered the end and perfection of the human race, for which our soul is greedy, I found it to be blessedness and happiness: namely, that the soul itself be bound in the **'bundle of life'** <note>A common Jewish liturgical and biblical phrase (1 Samuel 25:29) referring to the eternal resting place of souls with God.</note> with the Lord our God. This, however, consists in the coming of our Messiah, without whom we can in no way reach that immense and inestimable perfection, which cannot be compared to dyed colors, nor to the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire."

<summary>This page argues that the Messiah's redemption is spiritual and eternal rather than physical, citing ancient Jewish authorities like Maimonides and Rashi to support a non-literal interpretation of the "Land of Israel" and the "Temple." It emphasizes that the Messiah's true purpose is to liberate humanity from original sin and the devil's power.</summary>

# **On original sin, by which, on account of the sin of our first parents, the entire human race was corrupted. And what original sin is according to the Hebrews, and by what name they call it.** Chapter 5.

## CAPNIO.

**S**o that, therefore, the very stiff neck of the Jews might be further subdued, and so that eternal salvation itself—and the most powerful and perfect redemption which was to be achieved through the Messiah—might appear more clearly to be spiritual and of the soul, we must now discuss original sin itself, on account of which the entire human race was corrupted. Tell me, therefore, I pray, what original sin is according to the Hebrews, and by what name they call it.

<margin>What original sin is.</margin>
**GAL.** Although that initial sin, properly speaking, is the lack of initial or original justice owed to us but lost in our first parents—which flows from the actual fault of the first parents to all descendants coming after them by natural propagation (who have not been prevented by the privilege of special grace)—it binds them to a double death, namely spiritual and corporal, and to the other punishments that follow such a lack. 

<margin>The kindling or concupiscence of sin.</margin>
Sometimes, however, among us, original sin itself is called by its effect: the "kindling of sin" <term>fomes peccati; literally "tinder" or "fuel," referring to an innate tendency or "spark" that incites one to sin</term>, namely concupiscence <note>The internal pull toward worldly or bodily desires instead of God.</note>. This concupiscence of sin is sometimes called the "law of the members," sometimes the "law of the flesh," sometimes the "languor of nature," and sometimes the "tyrant who is in our members." For there is in us (as Augustine says) a concupiscence which must not be allowed to reign. There are also its desires, which are actual concupiscences—the weapons of the devil which come from the languor of nature. This languor is the tyrant who moves evil desires. If, therefore, you wish to be a victor over the tyrant and find your enemy the devil unarmed, do not obey evil concupiscence. These are the sentiments of Augustine in his book *On the Baptism of Infants*. 

<margin>How original sin is named by the Hebrews.</margin>
In the same way, among the Hebrews, initial sin is called by many names. For they call it original sin, or the "kindling," the evil inclination <gloss>yeczer hara</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: יצר הרע; in Jewish thought, this is the innate drive toward physical pleasure or selfishness which, if unchecked, leads to sin.</note>, which is the same as a "formation" or an "evil device." Wherefore Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic (interpretative) commentaries.</note> says regarding that passage in the eighth chapter of Genesis: **The inclination of the heart of man is evil from his youth** <note>original Hebrew: יצר לב האדם רע מנעוריו</note>—this means from his adolescence, or from his childhood, or from his "shaking out," that is, from the time he was shaken out from his mother's womb. Thus he says: This is what is written in Psalm 103: **For he knows our inclination; he remembers that we are dust.** <note>original Hebrew: כי הוא ידע יצרנו זכור כי עפר אנחנו</note> Rabbi Joses <note>Likely the 2nd-century sage Rabbi Yose ben Halafta.</note> said: It is a sad or dark leaven, against which the one who created it bears witness that it is evil. Moreover, the Masters said: It is a sad plant, against which its planter bears witness that it is evil, according to what is said in Jeremiah chapter 11: **And the Lord of hosts who planted you has spoken evil against you.** <note>original Hebrew: ויהוה צבאות הנוטע אותך דבר עליך</note> This means: And the God of armies...

<summary>This page explores the concept of original sin, defining it through Christian scholasticism (as a loss of original justice) and connecting it to the Jewish concept of the "Yetzer Hara" or evil inclination. The author uses both St. Augustine and Rabbinic commentators like Moses Hadarsan to argue that human nature is fundamentally corrupted from birth.</summary>

...who planted you, spoke evil against you, or concerning you. He replied to him, "From the hour in which he is formed." All these things are recorded by that Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his Midrashic compilations.</note>. In the **Midrash on Ecclesiastes** <gloss>original: *Midras coheleth*</gloss>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes, those words from the fourth chapter of that same book are explained: **Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king, who no longer knows how to take heed.** <note>Ecclesiastes 4:13</note> 

The "poor and wise youth" refers to the **good inclination** <note>original: *figmentum bonum*</note>, or the good affection, or good reason, or good intellect. And why is he called a "youth"? Because he is not joined to a man until after his thirteenth year and beyond <note>Refers to the age of Bar Mitzvah, when a person is traditionally considered responsible for their moral choices.</note>. And why does it call him "poor"? Because not everyone obeys him. <margin>Wisdom.</margin> But why "wise"? Because he teaches creatures and instructs them in the right way.

The text continues: **Than an old and foolish king.** This is the **evil inclination** <gloss>original: *yeczer hara*</gloss>, that is, the evil formation, or original sin, or the kindling of sin. And why does it call him a "king"? Because almost everyone obeys him. And for what reason does it call him "old"? Because he is coupled and joined to a man from his infancy until his old age. But why does it call him "foolish"? Because he shows man a way that he does not know. 

<margin>Midrash Tehillim on Psalm 9.</margin> The same is also found in the **Midrash Tehillim**, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that verse of Psalm 9: **I will praise the Lord with my whole heart.** <note>Psalm 9:1</note> This is explained there as follows: that is, with both the good and the evil inclination, so that there is no schism <note>A division or conflict.</note> in my heart. This is also what is written in Ecclesiastes 4: **Better is a poor and wise youth,** along with the rest. The "poor and wise youth" is the good inclination, that is, good reason or good intellect. And why call him a "youth"? Because he is joined to a man from the 13th year and beyond. Why "poor"? Because not all the people obey him. But why "wise"? Because he directs the creature to the good way. 

The text continues: **Than an old and foolish king.** This is the evil inclination, or the kindling of sin <term>fomes; literally "tinder," referring to the innate tendency toward sin</term>. Why call him a "king"? Because all the members of the body comply with him. And why "old"? Because he is joined to a man from his infancy until his old age. 

<margin>R. Rabbi Joshua said: This "enemy" is the "evil formation" or inclination. For according to the ways of the world, if a man is nurtured with a companion for two or three years, he becomes bound to him by love. But the **evil inclination** <gloss>original: *yeczer hara*</gloss>, that is, the evil formation or kindling of sin, grows and is nurtured with a man until old age; and nevertheless, if it finds an opportunity in the middle of seventy years, or in the middle of eighty, it will cast him down to ruin. 

In the **Midrash Tehillim** also, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that verse of Psalm 34: **The Lord redeems the soul...**

### Chapter VI. That all the fathers of the Old Testament, however holy they were, were guilty and blameworthy before God on account of original sin until the coming of the Messiah.

->CAPNIO<-
<note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist and one of the dialogue's characters.</note>

GALATINUS: From almost innumerable places, both in Holy Scripture and in the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> itself, this is clearly shown. **David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: "Master of the Universe, even though I was a king, I have made You King over me." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: "I do not acknowledge your goodness; my goodness is not above you. For whom then do I acknowledge goodness? For the holy ones who are in the earth." For the Holy One, blessed be He, does not call the righteous "holy" until they are placed in the earth until the day of their death; for the evil inclination <note>Hebrew: *yeczer hara*</note> troubles man in this world, and God does not believe in them until the day of their death.** And so Solomon said: **"For there is no righteous man on earth."** <note>Ecclesiastes 7:20</note> Therefore, he is not called "holy" until he is placed in the earth. At the time when He said to Moses: **"Go and gather the elders of Israel,"** <note>Exodus 3:16</note> and he [Moses] said to God: **"Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants."** <note>Exodus 32:13</note> Rabbi Phineas said: "Even if the Patriarchs had sought to have their dwelling-place above, they would have been able; and nonetheless they were not called holy until they were placed in the earth." <meta>This page continues the discussion of the "evil inclination" (yetzer hara) and its relationship to sin and human nature. # THE SIXTH BOOK #

**He drew the mighty with his power** <note>original Hebrew: *mashaḥ abbirim be-koḥo* from Job 24:22</note>; this refers to the **evil inclination** <gloss>Hebrew: *yetzer hara*</gloss> which draws the mighty with its power, such as the generation of Enosh, the generation of the Flood, the generation of the Division <note>Referring to the building of the Tower of Babel</note>, and the Sodomites. **And their sorrows were multiplied** <note>Psalm 16:4</note>, just as it is written: **In sorrow you shall eat [of the ground]** <note>Genesis 3:17</note>, and it says: **I will greatly multiply your sorrow** <note>Genesis 3:16</note>; He has indeed given many sorrows to the nations of the world. And lest they might lose anything because of them, it says: **I will not pour out their drink offerings of blood.** <note>Psalm 16:4</note>

That is to say, David spoke before the **Holy and Blessed God** <note>A standard Jewish title for God: *HaKadosh Baruch Hu*</note>: "Lord of the world, although I was king, yet I appointed you as king over me." The Holy and Blessed God said to him, "I do not confirm good for you at all. My goodness is not upon you." And for whom do I confirm good? "For the saints who are in the earth, and the wonderful ones, all my will is in them." For the Holy and Blessed God does not call the righteous "holy" until they are committed to the earth, that is, until the day of their death. And why?

<margin>No one is called holy except after death.</margin>

Because the **evil inclination** <gloss>Hebrew: *yetzer hara*</gloss>, that is, the "evil formation," which is the <term>fomes</term> <note>A theological term meaning "tinder" or "kindling," referring to the internal impulse toward sin</note>, or evil desire, is formed, fashioned, or renewed in a person in this world, and one is not secure from it until the day of their death. Therefore Solomon said in the eighth chapter of Ecclesiastes: **There is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin.** This means there is no just person on earth who does good without sinning. For even the Patriarchs were not called "holy" until they were committed to the earth. Therefore it was said in the twenty-fifth chapter of Job: **Behold, he does not trust in his holy ones.** When, therefore, does he trust in them? In that hour when he said to Moses in the thirty-second chapter of Exodus: "Go, go down to the elders of Israel." Moses responded and said: "Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants."

Rabbi Pinhas said: "If the fathers of the world <note>The Patriarchs</note> had sought to have their dwelling place above [in heaven while alive], they would have obtained it. Yet they were not called 'holy' because of this until they were committed to the earth, and until their faces were veiled by the shroud." Rabbi Abba, the son of Papa, said: "What is it that is written in the 24th chapter of Job, **And he drew the mighty with his power**? This is the **evil inclination** <gloss>Hebrew: *yetzer hara*</gloss>, that is, the evil formation, which is **original sin**. For it drew the mighty with its power—that is, the generation of Enosh, the generation of the Flood, the generation of the division of languages at the Tower of Babel, and the people of Sodom." Just as it is written of it in the 3rd chapter of Genesis: **In sorrow you shall eat of it**, that is, in affliction, or in pain, or in labor you shall eat it. And again, in the same place: **I will greatly multiply your sorrows.** This means: "O Eve, you have multiplied labors for the fathers of the world." As it was said in the sixteenth Psalm: **Their sorrows, or their burdens, shall be multiplied; they have endowed or betrothed another.** That is because Adam and Eve endowed another besides God—namely the devil—by handing themselves over to him through their consent. And did they perhaps lose anything from this? He teaches what should be said in the part that follows: **I will not pour out their drink offerings of blood**, that is, "I will not offer their libations, or I will not gather their congregations of blood." All of this is tradition. ...I was born in sin, and in guilt my mother warmed, or conceived me. <note>original Latin: *peccato genitus sum, & in culpa calefecit, uel concepit me mater mea*. This is a citation of Psalm 51:5, often used in Christian theology to discuss Original Sin.</note> Thus he said, which is as if he had said: "Behold, on account of the **concupiscence** <term>concupiscence: an intense desire or lust, often specifically referring to the human tendency toward sin</term> planted in the heart of Adam, it is as if I were born in sin." And the meaning is that at the hour of birth, this very **evil inclination** <gloss>Latin: *figmentum malum*; Hebrew: *yetzer hara*</gloss> is planted in the heart. As for what he says—*And in guilt my mother warmed me*—this is a foreign way of speaking, as if he were to say "she was made warm by me." And there are those who say that by this it is hinted that Eve did not give birth until after she had sinned.

There follows in the same Psalm: **Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right, or stable, or fit spirit within me.** <note>original Hebrew: *Lev tahor bera li Elohim, ve-ruach nachon chadesh be-kirbi* from Psalm 51:10</note> And he said this for this reason: because he had remembered that he was born with sin. And the sense is that the planted concupiscence led him to guilt, and therefore he prays to God to help him against the **evil inclination** <gloss>Latin: *figmentum malum*</gloss>, that is, his **tinder of sin** <term>fomentum/fomes: literally 'tinder' or 'kindling,' used here to describe the internal spark or inclination that ignites sinful actions</term>, so that he does not commit this kind of sin again. As for his saying "a clean heart" and "a right spirit," along with the rest, it is a repetition of the same idea. Thus says Rabbi Abraham. <note>Likely referring to Abraham ibn Ezra, a medieval Spanish rabbi and philosopher.</note>

In the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Rabbi Moses Hadarshan, an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne</note> on the book of Genesis, that saying in the 4th chapter of the same book is explained thus: **Will you not, if you do well, receive? But if you do not do well, sin will be lying at the door.** <note>Genesis 4:7</note> This means: "Will you not, if you do well, receive a blessing? And if you do not do well, you will receive a curse." Alternatively: "Will you not, if you do well, receive pardon from me? But if you do not do well, it will be lying heaped up at the door." The word *rouezeth* <gloss>Hebrew: *rovetzet*</gloss>—that is, "crouching" or "lying" in the feminine gender—is not written, but rather *rouez* <gloss>Hebrew: *rovetz*</gloss> in the masculine. This is because in the beginning, the **tinder of sin** <gloss>fomes</gloss> is weak, like a woman, but afterwards it becomes strong, like a man.

Rabbi Akiba said: The **evil inclination** <gloss>Hebrew: *yetzer hara*</gloss>—that is, the "evil formation" or "tinder"—is in the beginning like a silk thread, but in the end it becomes like a ship’s rope, which is commonly called a mooring line. As it is written in the fifth chapter of Isaiah: **Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords.** <note>Isaiah 5:18</note>

Rabbi Isaac said: The **evil inclination** <gloss>fomes</gloss> is in the beginning a stranger, or a newcomer; then it becomes a traveler; and finally it becomes the Lord. As it is written in the second book of Kings, chapter 12: **And a traveler came to the rich man.** <note>2 Samuel 12:4</note>

Rabbi Abba said: And of this the scripture says in Job, chapter 21: **The clods of the valley—or the banks of the stream—were sweet to him. And he draws every man after him, and before him they are without number.** <note>Job 21:33</note> This is similar to a certain solitary robber who, sitting at a crossroad, said to every passerby: "Give me what you have on you." And when a certain wise man passed by and saw that he had neither a sword nor anything in which he could place his hope, he began to crush him. So too, the **evil inclination** has destroyed many generations, and many strong and vigorous men. For it cast down the generation of Enosh, the generation of the Flood, and the generation of Discord <note>The builders of the Tower of Babel</note>, as well as Samson, David, and Solomon. When...

For indeed Abraham said, *Whereby shall I know that I shall possess it?* in Genesis 15. Isaac indeed loved Esau, my enemy. And so concerning the rest. Thus says Rabbi Solomon. There are also those who explain these words of Isaiah differently, saying, *Your first father sinned.* This is the first **Adam**. *And your wordy or talkative ones.* These are those two themselves, namely **Adam and Eve**, on account of what was said in Genesis chapter 3: *And Adam said, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me from the tree, and I ate."* So also it is written in the same place: *And the woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."* It follows: *They were guilty against me.* This refers to what was said in Genesis 3: *And she took of its fruit, and gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.* It follows: *And I excommunicated, or excluded*, the **Gloss of Rabbi Solomon** says, namely on account of your sins. *The princes of the sanctuary, or of holiness*, that is, the **Fathers**. *And I gave Jacob to a curse or prohibition*, these are the **prophets**. *And Israel to reproaches or shames*, these are all the **righteous**. That is to say, *Behold you were angry, and we have sinned in them* **holam**, *that is, always, and we shall be saved. And we were all like an unclean thing, and like a cloth of wounds, or of menstruation, or of spoils, were all our righteous acts. And we fell like a leaf, and our sins like the wind carry us away. You have hidden your face from us, and have loosened, or permitted us to waste away or fluctuate in the hand of our sins.*

Where the gloss of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> says: *And there is no one who calls upon your name raising himself,* that is, prevailing over the "evil inclination" <term>figmentum malum: the yetzer hara, or the innate human tendency toward evil</term>, or his own "kindling of sin" <term>fomitem: a theological term for the "tinder" or inclination toward sin remaining even after baptism</term>.

<margin>Catholic exposition.</margin>
namely God—says the prophet in the person of the whole human race—"were angry," namely at our first parents, and not only at them, but also at all of us, their children. And because "we sinned in them," namely in our first parents—not only as an example, but also in regards to our very nature—**holam**, that is, "always," or "from the age," meaning from the beginning of the world when Adam sinned. For this reason, we are all born as sinners, just as we are born mortal and children of God’s wrath, except for the Messiah and his mother. Hence, the prophet well says in this place, "And we all sinned in them **holam**," that is, always. For all (as **Paul** says) have sinned in Adam, and lack the grace of God, so that they may be saved. For this reason, the prophet adds, "And we shall be saved." It is as if he were saying: Although this is the case, we shall nevertheless be saved by the merit of the Messiah’s passion. Just as the same prophet more expressly suggests elsewhere in chapter 53, saying:

Where he has spoken abundantly about the future healing of us all through the passion of the Messiah, as will be more fully evident in the eighth book. It follows: "And there is no one who calls upon your name raising himself." That is: No one among those calling on your name is sufficient to lift himself up, or to rise by himself, or (according to Rabbi Solomon’s exposition) who is sufficient to prevail against his own "kindling," that is, against the guilt of original sin. While the previous page established the universal state of sin, this section provides a detailed taxonomy of the "Lower World" according to Jewish tradition and clarifies that no human merit—not even that of the patriarchs—could save a soul from these depths.</meta>

<page-num>454</page-num>
-> BOOK <-
<meta>catchword: Gloss</meta>

<margin>Names of hell.</margin> ...son of Levi. There are seven names for Gehenna <note>a term for hell or a place of purification, often associated with a valley near Jerusalem where fire was used</note>. And these are: **Sheol** <note>original Hebrew: שאול</note>, which is the underworld; **Abaddon** <note>original Hebrew: אבדון</note>, which is destruction; **Bor Shachath** <note>original Hebrew: בור שחת</note>, which is the pit or lake of corruption; **Bor Seon** <note>original Hebrew: בור שאון</note>, which is the pit of tumult or moaning; **Tit Hayaven** <note>original Hebrew: טיט היון</note>, which is the miry clay; **Tzalmaveth** <note>original Hebrew: צלמות</note>, which is the shadow of death; and **Eretz Tachtith** <note>original Hebrew: ארץ תחתית</note>, which is the land of crushing, or terror, or the lower land. Indeed, it is called **Sheol**, the underworld, as it is said in Psalm 15 <note>Psalm 16:10 in modern numbering</note>: **For you will not leave my soul in Sheol** <note>original Hebrew: כי לא תעזוב נפשי לשאול</note>. Truly, it is called **Abaddon**, which is destruction, as it is written in Psalm 88: **Shall your mercy be declared in the grave, and your faithfulness in destruction?** <note>original Hebrew: היסופר בקבר חסדך אמונתך באבדון</note>. Moreover, it is called **Bor Shachath**, that is, the pit or lake of corruption, as it is written in Psalm 55: **And you, O God, shall bring them down into the pit of corruption** <note>original Hebrew: ואתה אלהים תורידם לבאר שחת</note>; likewise **Bor Seon**, the pit of tumult or moaning, and **Tit Hayaven**, the miry clay, as it is written in Psalm 40: **And he brought me up out of the pit of tumult, and out of the miry clay** <note>original Hebrew: ויעלני מבור שאון מטיט היון</note>. Also **Tzalmaveth**, which is the shadow of death, as it is written in Psalm 106: **Those sitting or dwelling in darkness and the shadow of death** <note>original Hebrew: ישבי חשך וצלמות</note>. All these things are found there. Furthermore, among them the underworld is called by the proper name **Gehinnom** <note>original Hebrew: גהינם</note>, which means a deep valley. 

Likewise, that **Sheol** is the underworld, and that all men descend into the underworld, and that none of them could satisfy the price of redemption, is held in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>a traditional Jewish commentary or 'explanation' on the Book of Psalms</note> regarding that verse of Psalm 48: **Both the sons of Adam and the sons of man, rich and poor alike** <note>original Hebrew: גם בני אדם גם בני איש יחד עשיר ואביון</note>. Where it is said: *Sons of Adam*. This <term>Adam</term> is the first Adam. Although others say this is Abraham, who is called "the great man among the giants" in Joshua, chapter 14. It follows: *Also the sons of man*. These are the sons of Noah, who was called a "just man." There are, however, those who say these are the seventy nations, all of whom descend into Gehenna. It follows: *Rich and poor alike*. That is, rich in the Law <note>the Torah</note> and poor in the Law; all descend into Gehenna, even if they were heads or Princes, that is, the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>the supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation</note>, which are the ordinary judges whom Moses ordained. It follows below: **They who trust in their strength and boast in the multitude of their riches.** What can they do? For their riches will not remain with them. As it is said in Zephaniah, chapter 1: **Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them** <note>original Hebrew: גם בספם גם זהבם לא יוכל להצילם</note>. Let no man say, "my father was rich," namely in the multitude of merits, "and therefore I shall be delivered through his merit." Or, "my brother was righteous, and therefore I shall be delivered through him." For Abraham will not deliver his son Ishmael, nor Isaac his brother Esau. And this is what it says: **No man can by any means redeem his brother** <note>original Hebrew: אח לא פרה יפרה איש</note>. That is, a brother does not redeem; will a man, or anyone else, redeem?

<summary>This page explores the various Hebrew names for the underworld (Sheol/Gehenna) and cites Jewish commentaries to argue that every human, regardless of their status, wealth, or even the merits of their ancestors like Abraham, must descend there because no human can pay the price of spiritual redemption.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Psalm 49 and other biblical texts to illustrate the Jewish conception of the afterlife and the insufficiency of human merit for redemption. It specifically engages with the commentaries of Rashi (Rabbi Solomon) and the Midrash to explain the permanence of Sheol (the underworld) for those without divine aid.</meta>

**R**abbi Solomon’s gloss <note>referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> says: *A brother shall not be able to redeem a brother.* And why is the word **ach** <note>original: "אח"</note> used? It means "brother," or "alas," as if the righteous say regarding that day: "Alas, how heavy it is!" Why is it also said, *He shall not give to God his ransom* <note>original: "לא יתן לאלהים כפרו"</note>? This means: he shall not give to God his satisfaction or his atonement. This is because of what follows: *And the redemption of their souls is precious* <note>original: "ויקר פדיון נפשם"</note>. And what also is *And it ceases forever* <note>original: "וחדל לעולם"</note>? It means that he who is excluded on that day will be excluded forever. It follows: *And he shall yet live forever, he shall not see corruption.* And where do they go? The sons of Korah said: To the underworld. As it is said, *Like sheep they are placed in the underworld* <note>original: "כצאן לשאול שת"</note>. Rabbi Solomon’s gloss: "Just as sheep," he says, "are gathered into a fold, so they are plunged into **Sheol** <note>original: "אל שאול"</note>, that is, into the underworld." It follows: *Death shall feed on them.* Rabbi Solomon’s gloss: "The angel of death shall devour them." Do not wonder at this kind of phrasing. For we find something similar in another place, namely in Job, chapter 18: *The firstborn of death shall eat his branches* <note>original: "יאכל בדיו בכור מות", referring to the extensions of a person’s life or offspring</note>, or his limbs. And what does it mean when it says, *And the upright shall descend into them in the morning*? It teaches that the righteous visit them every morning, speaking to the sons of Korah. What do the righteous do? In that hour, they say to them those words from Psalm 46: *God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.* **T**hey also say that verse from Nahum, chapter one: *The Lord is good as a stronghold in the day of trouble.* And what is "in the day of trouble," except that in whatever tribulation approaches us, He is found for us? As He Himself says in the ninety-first Psalm: *He shall call upon me, and I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will deliver him and glorify* <note>or honor</note> *him.*

**A**ll these things are the **Midrash** <note>a form of Jewish biblical exegesis or storytelling that explains the deeper meaning of the text</note>, that is, the explanation mentioned above, excluding the glosses of Rabbi Solomon. Also in the **Midrash Koheleth**, that is, in the explanation of **Ecclesiastes**, that saying from the first chapter is explained thus: *All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full.* This means that all the dead enter nowhere but **Sheol**, that is, the underworld, and the underworld is never filled. As it is said in Proverbs 27: **Sheol and Abaddon** <note>that is, the underworld and destruction</note> **are never satisfied.** Concerning this also, in the commentaries on **Genesis**, **Rabbi Moses the Preacher** <note>Rabbi Moses Hadarshan, an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne</note> says regarding that which is written in the first chapter: *Fill the waters in the seas.* It is understood in this way: "Seas" here signify nothing but **Gehenna** <note>the place of punishment or purification</note>. For just as this sea is deep, according to what is said in Genesis chapter 1: *And the gathering together of the waters He called seas*, so Gehenna is called "the depths." As it is said in Proverbs, chapter 9: *In the depths of Sheol are her invited guests.* Concerning this matter, moreover, the Psalmist speaks so beautifully:

*For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to the underworld. I am counted with those who go down into the pit; I have become like a man without strength, free among the dead. Like the slain sleeping in the grave, whom you remember no more.* <note>original: "כי שבעה ברעות נפשי... אשר לא זכרתם עוד"</note> This means: "Since my soul is saturated with evils, and my life has approached the underworld. Concerning this, Job also says in chapter 10: <margin>This means,</margin> *Who will grant that you might hide me in the underworld, and conceal me until your wrath turns away, and set a limit for me, and remember me?* <note>original: "מי יתן בשאול תצפינני... ותזכרני"</note> Furthermore, David, speaking in the person of the holy fathers—who had by no means committed any actual sin for which they should go into the underworld, or if by chance they had, they had already made satisfaction—says this in Psalm 44: *Our heart is not turned back, nor has our step declined from your path; though you have crushed us in the place of dragons, and covered us with the shadow of death.* <note>original: "לא נסוג אחור לבנו... ובצלמות"</note> This means: "Our heart has not turned back, nor has our step turned aside from your path. Since you have crushed, or cast down, or humbled us in the place of dragons <note>The "place of dragons" often refers to a desolate wilderness or the abyss of the underworld</note>, and you have covered us in the shadow—or with the shadow—of death." From the preceding points, it is clear that everyone, on account of original sin, descended to the underworld until the arrival of the Messiah.

### *That the Patriarchs as well as the Prophets and the rest of the saints of the Old Testament, all descended to the underworld until the death of the Messiah. Chapter VIII.*

->CAPNIO,<-
<note>"Capnio" is the Greek-derived pseudonym for Johannes Reuchlin, the famous humanist and Hebraist who is a character in this dialogue.</note>

Therefore, so that it might be more firmly established that no one was exempted from this divine decree, it would not be improper to prove here that the Patriarchs also, and the prophets, and the rest of the saints of the Old Testament all descended to the underworld until the death of the Messiah. GALATINO: I shall therefore first show that this was true regarding the Patriarchs. And concerning Abraham indeed, it is gathered from where it was said to him by God in Genesis 15: *And you shall go to your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age.* <note>original: "ואתה תבוא אל אבתיך בשלום תקבר בשיבה טובה"</note> This means: "And you shall go, or enter, unto your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age." Regarding this, **Rabbi Nahmon** <note>likely referring to Nachmanides, also known as Ramban</note> says: "You shall go to your fathers," who were idolaters, just as it is said in the 24th chapter of Joshua: "Thus said the Lord God of Israel: Your fathers dwelt across the river from ancient times." For **Terah**, the father of Abraham and the father of **Nachor**, worshipped foreign gods. If, therefore, it was said to Abraham, "You shall go to your fathers," and since his fathers were idolaters, there is no doubt that they were in the underworld. For which reason, it is certain that Abraham himself was to descend to the underworld. Nevertheless, since Abraham was most faithful...

# THE SIXTH BOOK.
### 457

A worshiper of God, and just, was neither to be infested by the fire of hell, nor by demons. Therefore, it was said of him that he would go to his fathers in peace. Regarding Jacob, however, it is held from that which is written in Genesis 37: *And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted; and he said, "For I will go down to my son mourning into the underworld." Thus his father wept for him.* <note>original Hebrew: "ויקומו כל בניו... ויבך אתו אביו"</note> That is to say: And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him. And he refused to be comforted, and said, "Because I shall descend to my son mourning into the underworld." And his father wept for him. The <term>Gloss</term> <note>A "gloss" is a scholarly explanation or commentary on a text.</note> of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>original: "R. Selomonis" refers to Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: "Into the underworld," he says, means into the grave according to the literal surface of the text, but according to the **Midrash** <note>original: "Midras"; a method of biblical interpretation providing deeper homiletic meaning.</note>—that is, according to the inner commentary—it means into <term>Gehenna</term> <note>A place of spiritual punishment or purification, often translated as hell.</note>. Moreover, in the **Bereshith Rabba** <note>An ancient collection of rabbinic interpretations on the Book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis, regarding this passage, it is said: Why is it said "all his daughters," when he had only one daughter, namely Dinah? Because it is not forbidden for a man to call his son-in-law his "son," and his daughter-in-law his "daughter." It follows: *And his father wept for him*, which means that **Isaac** <note>original: "Ishac"</note> wept with him. However, when he departed from him, he would wash himself and anoint himself, and eat and drink. And why did he not reveal to him (that is, Isaac to Jacob himself) that Joseph was alive, since he knew this through a prophetic spirit? Because Isaac said, "God has not revealed it to him, so shall I reveal it?" So it is written there.

### CHAPTER.

The Jews of our age, not knowing how to set aside their wickedness in perverting the scriptures, <margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin> say that in this place, the word **Sheol** <note>original: "שאול"</note> does not mean the underworld, but a pit or a grave.

**GALATINUS:** <margin>Refutation.</margin> Reason does not allow their assertion to remain hidden as a falsehood. For Jacob did not believe that his son’s body had been buried, but rather devoured by a most evil beast. Whence he said in Genesis 38: *An evil beast has eaten him; Joseph is surely torn in pieces.* <note>original Hebrew: "חיה רעה אכלתהו..."</note> That is: A bad beast has eaten him; Joseph was snatched away by a plundering. From this it is clear beyond doubt that he was speaking neither of himself nor of his son in regards to the body, but in regards to the soul; nor was he speaking of a tomb, but of the underworld, where he believed his son’s soul had already preceded him, and thus he brought forth those words. 

**Rabbi Solomon**, noticing this, did not seize upon this particular falsehood, but another, saying: <margin>False exposition of Rabbi Solomon.</margin> That when it says *el beni* <note>original: "אל בני"</note>, that is "to my son," the word *el* <note>original: "אל"</note> here signifies not "to" or "towards," but "on account of." Whence he says the sense is: "I shall descend on account of my son, mourning into the grave." The falsehood of this, and of those following him, is evidently shown by **Rabbi Onkelos** <note>original: "Rabbi Ankelos," the famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic (the Targum Onkelos).</note> the Chaldean interpreter, who translated these Hebrew words *el beni* (to my son) into Chaldean <note>The author uses "Chaldean" to refer to Aramaic.</note> as *leuath beri* <note>original: "לות ברי"</note>, which means "with my son" or "at my son." From this it is openly clear that *el* in this place does not signify "on account of," but "to," "towards," or "with." And so wherever this word *el* is placed in the **Pentateuch** <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note> among the Hebrews, he himself interpreted it in Chaldean as *leuath*, which is the same as "with," "to," or "towards." For that which is written in the book of Genesis in Hebrew as: *And Esau went "el" Ishmael*—that is, *to* Ishmael—he himself translated into Chaldean as: *to* or *towards* or *at* Ishmael <note>original: "לות ישמעאל"</note>. Also, that which is said in Hebrew in Genesis 18: *And Abraham ran "el" the herd* <note>original: "ואל הבקר רץ אברהם"</note>—that is, *to* the cattle—he likewise translated into Chaldean as...

translated it, **"Abraham ran toward the cattle."** <note>original Aramaic: "Vluath tore rahat Abraham." The author is comparing Hebrew and Aramaic prepositions to clarify Jacob's meaning.</note> If, therefore, in the aforementioned words of Jacob, this word **"to"** <note>Hebrew: "el"</note> had meant "because of," the translator would not have placed there the word **"toward"** <note>Aramaic: "Leuath"</note> which means "near," "at," or "toward," but would have used **"on account of."** <note>Aramaic: "Bedil"</note> For properly, **"on account of"** <note>Bedil</note> in <term>Chaldaic</term> <note>A language closely related to Hebrew, now commonly called Aramaic, used in the Jewish Targums (translations of the Bible).</note> is the same as "propter" in Latin. Building on the previous discussion of Jacob, the author now turns to the biblical account of the spirit of Samuel being summoned for King Saul to prove that even Samuel resided in the "infernum" (the lower regions or underworld).</meta>

<meta>Catchword: into the lower regions</meta>

# SIXTH BOOK

The woman did what she did, and she made him <note>Samuel</note> ascend, just as it is said in the first book of Kings, chapter 28 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 28.</note>: *And the woman saw Samuel, and she cried out: "Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul."* And how did she recognize him? Our Masters <note>A traditional way of referring to the Jewish Rabbis and their commentaries.</note> said that a dead man does not ascend in the same way for a King as he does for others. For when he ascends for a king, he has his face upward and his feet downward. But for a commoner <note>original: "rustico," literally a rustic or peasant, used here to mean a non-royal.</note>, he has his face downward and his feet upward. The king said to her, "Do not be afraid; what did you see?" And the woman said: **Elohim** <note>original Hebrew: אלהים. This word can mean "God," "gods," "angels," or "judges."</note>, that is, "I saw **gods** or **judges** ascending from the earth." She said **Elohim** (gods or judges) because there were two of them. And who were they? Moses and Samuel. When Saul heard this, he was afraid, because he had called for one, but two had ascended. For so it is said in that place: *Ascending from the earth* <note>The Latin text notes the plural "ascendentes" to justify the idea of two spirits appearing.</note>. And he said to her, "What is his form?"—meaning the form of Samuel. She said, "An old man is ascending, and he is wrapped in a cloak." And Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me, or made me tremble, by making me ascend?"

Behold the words in which there is an argument from the "greater and the lesser" <note>A logical principle where if something is true for a significant case, it is even more true for a lesser one.</note>. For if the most excellent of all prophets, namely Samuel, feared judgment, how much more should all others? And what is it that he added to him? *And tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.* "With me," that is, in my peace. And when Saul heard this, he hurried and fell to the earth according to the fullness of his stature. Abner and Amasa said to him, "What did he say to you?" He said to them, "You will go to battle and you will fall, and your sons will be reckoned as Princes." Rabbi Simeon said: Then the Holy and Blessed God called the ministering angels and said to them, "Come and see what sort of creature I have created in this world. For in the life of this world, a man who goes to a banquet does not make his sons go with him, lest they be afflicted by the evil eye. Yet behold, this man descends into battle and knows he is to be killed, and nevertheless he takes his sons with him, rejoicing and applauding the divine justice, which he was not ignorant was hanging over him."

<margin>The sins of Saul on account of which he was killed.</margin>The Masters have handed down that he was justly killed on account of five sins, as it is said in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 10: *And Saul died because of his transgression, by which he transgressed against the Lord, namely because he did not keep the word of the Lord regarding them.* And because he killed Nob, the city of priests, as read in 1 Chronicles 10. And because he did not obey Samuel, who had said to him, "You shall wait seven days." And the rest, but he did not do so, but offered a sacrifice. And because he spared Agag <note>The King of the Amalekites, whom Saul was commanded to destroy.</note>, as is held in 1 Samuel 15. And because he consulted a medium <note>original: "phitonissam," referring to the Witch of Endor.</note> and not the Lord. Therefore He killed him. All these things are from the aforementioned **Midrash** <note>A type of ancient Jewish commentary or storytelling that explains biblical texts.</note>. 

Nothing can be more effective or stronger than these points to prove against the Jews of our time that all men, both good and evil, descended to the underworld <note>original: "infernum." In this context, the author refers to the "Limbo of the Patriarchs," where the righteous were believed to wait until Christ's resurrection.</note> until the coming of the Messiah, and were detained there by divine permission. For if Moses and Samuel, the chiefs of the prophets and the holiest of all (about whom God Himself, bearing witness in Jeremiah 15, says: **If Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people** <note>original Hebrew: אם יעמוד משה ושמואל לפני אין נפשי לעם הזה</note>) were in the underworld—

### BOOK III

were held in the underworld <note>original: "inferno," referring here to the "Limbo of the Fathers" rather than the place of eternal punishment</note> on account of original sin, as has been shown from this tradition. How much more must it be judged that all others—who were neither like them, nor endowed with such holiness or dignity—descended there and were held there until the redemption of the Messiah?

<margin>Objection.</margin>
**CAP.** <note>The speaker is Capnio, the pseudonym of the scholar Johannes Reuchlin.</note> Some say, and indeed piously, that it was not Samuel whom the medium <note>original: "phitonissa," referring to the Witch of Endor</note> caused to ascend, but the enemy of the human race himself <note>Satan</note>, who, in order to deceive Saul,

<margin>First reason.</margin>
lied by claiming to be Samuel. For as it is said in the Decretals <note>A collection of Church laws; specifically referring to the Decretum Gratiani, 26.q.5.c.</note>, "It is no wonder." How could it happen that Samuel, who was holy by birth and righteous in the works of his life, could be pulled away by magic arts? But if he was not pulled away, he must have consented, and to believe either of these things about a righteous man is contrary to reason. For righteousness has no support for such things.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Whether he was pulled away or came voluntarily, he would have lost the spiritual merit which he sought while living in the flesh. Furthermore, if Samuel had truly appeared to Saul, that righteous man would by no means have allowed himself to be worshipped <note>original: "adorari"</note> by him, for he had preached that God alone is to be worshipped.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
How, moreover, could a man of God, who was in a "place of refreshment" <note>original: "refrigerio," a common term for the rest of the righteous in the afterlife</note> with Abraham, say to a man of pestilence, worthy of the fire of Gehenna <note>The place of punishment/Hell</note>, "tomorrow you will be with me"? Therefore, that malignant spirit betrayed the subtlety of his own deception by these two titles. Because, under the clothing and name of Samuel, he allowed himself to be worshipped against the law; and he lied that a man weighed down by a burden of sins would be with the most righteous Samuel in the future (even though there is a great distance between sinners and the righteous).

<margin>Response.</margin>
**GAL.** <note>The speaker is Galatinus, representing the author's defense of the text.</note> These men wonder in what way a malignant spirit could have stirred the soul of a righteous man so that he might be seen and speak with Saul. Is it not even more wonderful that Satan took the Lord himself, and placed him upon the pinnacle of the temple, and transported him to a high mountain? For it is not absurd, my dear Capnio, to believe that some things were permitted by divine dispensation. In this way, not by the dominance of magic art, but by the hidden arrangement of God (which was concealed from both the medium and Saul), the spirit of the righteous man showed himself to the sight of the king, so that he might be struck by the divine sentence.

<margin>Another objection.</margin>
**CAP.** For what reason, then, did Samuel allow himself to be worshipped by Saul, when the cult of worship should be exhibited to God alone, according to what is said in Deuteronomy, chapter 6: *You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.*

<margin>Response.</margin>
**GAL.** First, one should notice what the scripture says in this place, in the first book of Kings, chapter 28 <note>In modern Bibles, 1 Samuel 28</note>. For it says this: **wayyiqqōḏ 'appayim 'arṣā wayyištaḥu** <note>original Hebrew: ויקד אפים ארצה וישתחו</note>. That is, "And he bowed his face to the earth, and worshipped <note>or "prostrated himself"</note>." It does not say, therefore, that Saul worshipped Samuel, but only that he "worshipped." For this reason, it can be said without incongruity that he worshipped God then, and not Samuel. For whatever is doubtful, kindness must always interpret for the better. Furthermore, even if he did worship Samuel, Samuel himself should not be said to have acted against the law by allowing himself to be worshipped. For this word **wayyištaḥu** <note>original Hebrew: וישתחו</note>, which means "to worship," is taken in two ways among the Hebrews (as you yourself know), just as *adorare* (to adore), *colere* (to cherish), *venerari* (to venerate), and *revereri* (to revere) are used among the Latins—namely, for the worship of **latria** <note>A technical theological term for the supreme worship due to God alone</note>,

However, the Hebrews assert that Saul was saved, and after death was received into the place of the righteous. For he was not ignorant that he would no longer be able to fight, nor live much longer except in contempt of God and as a mockery to himself. Indeed, they say it is no sin, but rather a merit, for a man to destroy himself when he sees that he would live only to the creator's dishonor. For this reason they say Samson killed himself. For this reason they also affirm that that venerable man laid hands upon himself, concerning whom it is read in 2 Maccabees, chapter 14: "When he was now being captured, he struck himself with a sword, choosing to die nobly rather than become subject to sinners and be treated with unworthy injuries contrary to his noble birth." Since, therefore, Saul was to be justified both on account of the penance he was about to perform and on account of the martyrdom he was to undergo by waging the war of the Lord, they say Samuel could rightly say to him, "Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me."

Therefore, the aforementioned objections notwithstanding, I say—saving the definition of the Holy Roman Church, to which I always submit myself in all things—that it was then truly Samuel himself, and not a devil, who appeared to Saul. For although certain things said in the preceding history could be attributed to the vision of the medium (who said she saw gods) and to the understanding of Saul (who understood the one ascending to be Samuel), and not to the logic of truth; nevertheless, on account of three things reported there, if the soul of Samuel had not truly been present then, it would not seem...

the writer of this sacred history could not be excused from a lie, nor would he be considered a speaker of truth—which is certainly an absurd thing to say. This is especially true since, through the truth of this matter, the magnitude of the loss from original sin is shown to us, and the necessity of the coming, mercy, and grace of the Redeemer is demonstrated. Finally, it more effectively refutes the impudence of the more recent Jews who deny that the righteous and ancient fathers descended to limbo.

### CAPNIO,

### BOOK VI

<margin>Two dwellings for souls, according to the ancient Hebrews.</margin> From this it is clearly evident that there were once two dwellings for souls among the Hebrews, one for the good and another for the evil. Both, however, were called "hell" <note>original Latin: "infernus." In this context, it refers to the general realm of the dead, rather than exclusively a place of punishment.</note>. But the place of the ungodly was called the **lowest hell** <term>seol tahtith</term>, while the place of the righteous was called the "upper hell." This can be gathered from what is written in <term>Deuteronomy chapter 32</term>, when it says: **For a fire is kindled in my anger, and shall burn even unto the lowest hell.** <note>original Hebrew: "ki esh qadehah be-appi... ve-tiqad ad sheol tahtith."</note> The commentary in the book <term>Tanhuma</term> <note>A collection of ancient Jewish homilies and teachings.</note> says: "In my anger," that is, in the midst of Gehenna <note>Gehenna is a term often used in Jewish tradition for the place of purification or punishment for the wicked.</note>. This follows from the phrase: "And it shall burn even unto the lowest hell." Likewise, in the fifteenth chapter of Proverbs: **The path of life leads upward for the wise, that he may turn away from hell below.** <note>original Hebrew: "orach hayyim le-ma'alah le-maskil..."</note> 

This tradition is also found in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>An ancient rabbinic commentary on the Book of Psalms.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that verse in the eighty-fifth Psalm: **For your mercy is great toward me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell.** <note>original Hebrew: "ki hasdekha gadol alay..." In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 86:13.</note> It is read that Rabbi <term>Ioden</term> <note>Rabbi Yudan, a well-known scholar from the Talmudic period.</note> spoke thus: "The path of the adulterers is given into the depths of hell." And this is why it says: "For your mercy is great toward me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell." Here, the commentary of Rabbi <term>Selomon</term> <note>Refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: "The path of the adulterers is such that they are in the depths of hell, and you have freed me from there," referring to when Nathan the prophet said to David, "The Lord also has put away your sin." These are the words of Rabbi Selomon. Therefore, since a "lower" place is only named in relation to a "higher" place—for "upper" and "lower" are relative terms which depend on one another to exist, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval texts. Here, the author cites his work "Categories" (Prædicamentis).</note> says—it is surely manifest that because David mentions the lower hell, he necessarily hinted that there is an upper hell. 

This is also clearly shown through their own expositions. <term>Hezekiah</term> called this upper hell the "gates of hell" when he spoke in the thirty-eight chapter of Isaiah: **I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of hell.** <note>original Hebrew: "ani amarti bi-demi yamai..."</note> That is to say: "I shall go to Limbo." Since this is, as it were, at the beginning of hell, it is not inaptly called the "gate of hell." And Christ despoiled this hell when he led the souls of the holy fathers out from there.

<margin>What the Hebrews called the Limbo of the Fathers.</margin> For what we call "Limbo"—that is, the place of rest or "Abraham’s Bosom"—the ancient Hebrews called a **bundle** <term>czeror</term> (meaning a binding place or conservatory), or a **treasury** <term>oczar</term> (meaning a storehouse or cellar), or the "gates of hell," or the "upper hell." From this it is clear that their faith and ours were entirely one and the same.

The author uses Hebrew scriptures and rabbinic commentaries to prove that the Christian concept of Limbo is identical to these ancient Jewish beliefs.</summary>

## That the souls of the elect could not, and should not, be freed from hell except by the Messiah, God and man. Chapter X.

### CAPNIO,

**I**t is now right for you to show that the souls of the righteous—who were held thrust down into hell as if in a prison because of Adam's sin—were to be freed from there by God alone. **GAL.** To prove this, I first bring forward what is read in the <term>Midrash Shir HaShirim</term> <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Song of Songs.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs. For there, regarding that saying in the 2nd chapter, **"I am the narcissus of Sharon, the rose of the most fertile field, the lily of the deeps or the valleys,"** <note>original Hebrew: "Ani khavatzelet ha-sharon, shoshanat ha-amaqim."</note> it is said: This is what is written in Psalm 130, **"Out of the depths I have called to you, O Lord."** <note>original Hebrew: "Mi-ma’amaqim qeratika Yahweh."</note> Moreover, the Masters said that the assembly of Israel spoke this. She says, "I am the one beloved by God. I will indeed be given into the depths of Gehenna <note>A term for the underworld or place of purification.</note>, so that the Holy One, blessed be He, may redeem me from there." This is also what was said in Psalm 89 <note>Modern Bibles place this verse in Psalm 40:2.</note>, "And he made me come up out of the pit of tumult, and from the dregs of the pit," that is, from hell. Rabbi Ruben said: "Unless the scripture in Isaiah chapter 66 had said it, it would not be permitted to say it; but since it is written, it can be said: **For in fire the Lord was judged.**" <note>original Hebrew: "Ki be-esh Yahweh nishpat."</note> For it is not written *sophet* <note>original: "שופט"</note>, that is, "judging," but *nishpat* <note>original: "ננשפט"</note>, that is, "was judged." And this is the very thing that David said through the Holy Spirit in Psalm 23: **"Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death,"** that is, of hell, **"I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod,"** that is, your torments, **"and your staff,"** that is, your Law, **"they shall comfort me."** Will this be possible without torments? He teaches what should be said to this when he says in the same place, **"Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me."** And is this possible in this age? He teaches what must be said in what follows: **"All the days of my life."** And why? **"Because I will dwell in the house of the Lord for a length of days."** All this is from tradition. 

Furthermore, that Adam, and also his children, were thrust into the prison of hell until the arrival of the Redeemer because of his own sin, and that they could be restored by no one other than God Himself, is excellently suggested in the <term>Midrash Koheleth</term> <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes.</note>, that is, in the exposition of Ecclesiastes. There, regarding that saying in the 7th chapter of the same book: **"Behold the work of God. For who can repair that which he has twisted or made crooked?"** <note>original Hebrew: "Re’eh et ma’aseh ha-Elohim..." (Eccl 7:13).</note> So it is read literally. Rabbi Azdrias said: In the hour when the Holy One, blessed be He, created the first Adam, He took him and led him, and led him back, through all the trees of Paradise, and said to him: "See my works, how beautiful and how praiseworthy they are, and whatever I have created, I created for your sake. Pay attention..."
