In this brief and fitting likeness, it was clearly shown to the Jews by their ancient Teachers that the whole human race was once, because of the sin of Eve and Adam, justly detained in the prison of the King of the whole world. For if Moses, the greatest of all prophets among them—according to that passage in the last chapter of Deuteronomy: **"And there has not arisen since in Israel a prophet like Moses, whom God knew face to face."** <note>original Hebrew: "Velo qam navi od be-Yisrael ke-Mosheh asher yedao Yahweh panim el panim."</note> That is, as Rabbi <term>Onkelos</term> <note>A famous 1st-century scholar who translated the Torah into Aramaic.</note> says in the <term>Targum</term> <note>The Aramaic translation and explanation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>: **"To whom the face [of God] was revealed face to face."** <note>original Aramaic: "De-itgali leh appin be-appin."</note>—if even he could not be removed from detention in the prison of the heavenly King, as the preceding parable clearly shows, how much less was anyone else able to be removed from there. In that which the aforementioned tradition relates—that God said to Adam that if by sinning he should in some way corrupt or destroy his world, there would be no one after him who could repair it—it is openly suggested that the universe, corrupted in a way because of Adam’s sin, could not be repaired except by God.

<margin>A human being could not repair the human race.</margin>
For when Adam sinned, he infected and corrupted the whole human race with his sin, binding himself and his descendants to a double death and to the infernal prison. Therefore the whole universe, which had been created for the sake of man, as the aforementioned tradition testifies, since it was frustrated of its purpose, was in a certain way corrupted and destroyed. For this reason, for the restoration of the universe itself, someone was necessary who, after Adam, would not be [inferior] in power, time, dignity, virtue, or holiness, but in all these ways, and even in eternity, would be before him. Since therefore Adam preceded all men, no mere man could have restored the human race itself, nor consequently the universe.

<margin>An angel ought not to have restored human nature.</margin>
And although the angels preceded Adam himself both in time and in dignity according to nature, nevertheless man ought not to have had an angel as his restorer and redeemer. Partly because perhaps for such a great undertaking no power except the divine was sufficient; and partly because if an angel had freed man from eternal damnation, man would seem bound to his service and slavery. ...dignity, which he would have possessed had he not sinned, he would by no means have been restored. For if man himself—who was intended to be a servant of God alone and, through grace, equal to the angels—were to become the servant of one who was neither God nor one whose servants were angels, <note>The author argues that if a mere angel or creature redeemed humanity, humans would owe their primary allegiance to that creature rather than God, upsetting the natural order where humans are second only to God.</note> he would not truly be restored. Therefore, it is concluded that man, ruined in the manner described above, had to be repaired and liberated from eternal damnation not by a mere creature, but by God Himself. Indeed, God alone was sufficient for this through His omnipotence, wise through His infinite wisdom, and willing through His immense clemency.

However, He ought not to restore the human race without the satisfaction of His justice, since mercy cannot in any way act to the prejudice of justice. <note>This is a central point of medieval and Renaissance theology: God’s love (mercy) and His fairness (justice) must both be satisfied simultaneously.</note> Hence it is that in the Holy Scriptures, just as He is very often proclaimed as merciful, so too is He frequently called just. For although there is in God a clemency or mercy that surpasses every offense, there is also in Him a justice that permits no sin to remain unpunished. For if He did not punish sin through justice, but always forgave it through mercy alone, God would certainly conduct Himself in the same way toward the sinner as toward the non-sinner, and the wicked and the righteous would be equal in His sight. That this can in no way befit God is clearly shown by the words of Holy Scripture.

For the <term>Psalmographer</term> <note>A traditional term for King David as the author of the Psalms.</note> says in Psalm 11: **"The Lord tests the righteous; but the wicked and the one who loves violence His soul hates."** <note>original Hebrew: "Yahweh tzaddiq yivchan ve-rasha ve-ohev chamas saneah nafsho."</note> The Wise Man also says in Proverbs chapter 10: **"The expectation of the righteous is joy, but the hope of the wicked shall perish."** <note>original Hebrew: "Tochelet tzaddiqim simchah ve-tiqvat reshaim toved."</note> Likewise, Isaiah in chapter 3: **"Tell the righteous it is well, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds. Woe to the wicked! For the reward of his hands shall be given to him."** <note>original Hebrew: "Imru tzaddiq ki tov ki peri maalelehem yokhelu: oi la-rasha ra ki gemul yadav yeaseh lo."</note> And to omit other passages of this kind, I will finally bring forward the words of David in Psalm 61, speaking thus: **"And to You, O Lord, belongs mercy, for You render to each according to his work."** <note>original Hebrew: "Velekha Adonai chased ki atah teshalem le-ish ke-maasehu."</note>

Therefore, although God—to whom alone the restoration of the human race belonged—could have forgiven the sin of our first parents through mercy alone, His justice nevertheless demanded a satisfaction. This justice required that both the transgressor and the one making satisfaction be of the same nature. For this reason, it was necessary for the one who was to repair the human race to be both God and man. This person could be none other than the Messiah, who was to be God and man.

<margin>No mere creature was sufficient to restore the human race.</margin>
That no mere creature would be sufficient for the healing, restoration, and redemption of the human race can be seen most especially from what is read in the <term>Echa Rabbethi</term> <note>Also known as Lamentations Rabbah, a classical Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Lamentations.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Lamentations of Jeremiah—regarding what is said in the second chapter of that book: **"What shall I testify to you? What shall I liken to you, O captive daughter of Jerusalem? What shall I equal to you, that I may comfort you, O virgin daughter of Zion? The last two letters of this word are **Yod** and **He** <note>original: יה</note>. So much for that. Furthermore, that the son of Perez, through whom all things must be perfected and completed (as the preceding tradition says), is the Messiah himself, is found in **The Great Commentary on 'And These are the Names'** <note>original: ואלה שמות רבה (Ve-elleh Shemot Rabbah); the Midrash on the Book of Exodus</note>, in the exposition on chapter 21 of that same book, regarding the statement: *And these are the judgments.* There it says: "You find all the 'generations' recorded in Scripture are diminished <note>written "defectively," missing a letter</note>, except for these two: namely, 'These are the generations of the heavens and the earth' in Genesis 2, and 'These are the generations of Perez' in the last chapter of Ruth." This truly carries a profound meaning. For why is it that when it says, "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth," the word for "generations" is written in full—that is, it does not lack the letter **Vau** <note>original: ו; the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note>—unlike the others? It is because God created His world and the Angel of Death was not yet in it. For this reason, the aforementioned word **toldoth** <note>original: תולדות; meaning "generations" or "births"</note> is written **male** <note>original: מלא; meaning "full" or "plene"</note>, that is, completely. But when Adam and Eve had sinned, God diminished the **toldoth**, that is, the generations that appear in Scripture. However, when Perez arose, the **toldoth** became **male** again; they were written in full. For the **Vau** is not missing there. This is because the Messiah will rise from him, and in his days the Holy and Blessed God will swallow up or destroy death. As it is said in the twenty-fifth chapter of Isaiah: **"He will swallow up death forever."** <note>original: בלע המות לנצח (Bila ha-mavet la-netzach)</note> This means: He has swallowed or destroyed death for eternity. Therefore, the **generations** of Perez are written **full**. This is the tradition. This same point is also confirmed in the **Midrash Ruth** <note>an ancient commentary on the Book of Ruth</note>, regarding those same words: *These are the generations of Perez.* It says there: "Wherever it is said in the Law, **toldoth** (generations), it is diminished—that is, one letter called 'Vau' is missing there—except for these two instances: 'These are the generations of the heavens and the earth' (Gen. 2) and 'These are the generations of Perez' (Ruth 4)." And as to why this was done, the same reason is eventually given in both places as was given in the preceding tradition. From these things it is clear that at the coming of the Messiah, the whole universe, which had almost collapsed because of Adam's sin, was to be restored, and death itself was to be destroyed.

That is: He—namely David—said to the people of Israel concerning Psalm 89: "Since I have said, the world shall be built in mercy, you [God] shall restore, or set right, or prepare the heavens." Moreover, this is like a parable of a throne or a seat having four legs, one of which had moved. Someone therefore took a clod of earth, or a fragment of stone, and propped it up. So the heavenly throne (as can be said from what is written in the Law) had been moved, or shaken, or diminished, until the Holy and Blessed God propped it up. And with what did He prop it up? With mercy. And this is what was said: "The world shall be built in mercy; you shall restore, or renew, the heavens." 

And so David says in Psalm 136: "To Him who made the heavens with prudence." And by whose hands are they standing? Upon mercy. As is said consequently: "For His mercy endures into the age, or forever." He extended the earth. And by whose hand? "For His mercy endures forever." Because of this, Psalm 63 says: "Because your mercy is better than life." All these things are from the aforementioned Midrash. Here it is very fitting to place that saying from Isaiah 16, which was introduced in the previous tradition: <margin>Isaiah 16</margin> <term>והוכן בחסד כסא וישב עליו באמת באהל דוד שפט ודורש משפט ומהר צדק</term> <note>original: Ve-hukan be-chesed kisse ve-yashav alav be-emet be-ohel David shofet ve-doresh mishpat u-mehir tzedek</note> That is: "And the throne or seat shall be prepared in mercy. And he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and expediting or hastening justice."

Moreover, Rabbi Jonathan <note>Rabbi Jonathan ben Uzziel, to whom the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets is traditionally attributed.</note> translates these things into Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldæū"</note> as follows: *Then the Messiah of Israel shall establish his throne in goodness, and shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, seeking judgment and doing truth.* <note>original Aramaic: בכין משיחא דישראל יתקין בטוב כורסוהי ויתיב עלוהי בקשוט במשכנא דדוד ותבע דין ועביד קשיט</note>
That is: *In this or because of this the Messiah of Israel shall set, or shall fit in goodness his throne. And he shall sit upon it within the city of David, and he shall judge judgment, and shall do truth.* Since, therefore, it was proven in the preceding tradition through these words of Isaiah that God was to confirm and restore the supernal throne with mercy—by applying a clod or a fragment of stone to its diminishing and its shaking or commotion—and here it is openly shown through the Aramaic translation that these same words of Isaiah speak of the Messiah, it follows necessarily and clearly that the Messiah himself is God, the restorer of the supernal throne. For no one can be understood to have placed the fragment of the aforementioned stone more rightly than the Messiah, the restorer of both heavenly and earthly things. He who, by his immense mercy and passion, healing sinful men by the bruising of his passion (as Isaiah witnesses <note>A reference to Isaiah 53:5, "by his stripes we are healed."</note>) and leading them into the supernal Jerusalem, became the support for the angelic ruin. And thus, by joining justified men to the angels, he restored and supported the supernal throne—that is, the choir of the angels, which had been diminished because of the fall of the demons. And it is called the "supernal throne" because God sits upon it in a certain way, according to what the Psalmist said in Psalm 79 <note>Psalm 80:1 in modern Bibles.</note>: *He who sits upon the Cherubim.* <note>original Hebrew: ישב על הכרובים</note> And again in Psalm 98 <note>Psalm 99:1 in modern Bibles.</note>: *He sits [above] the Cherubim, let the earth be moved.* <note>original Hebrew: ישב הכרובים תנוט הארץ</note> From these things it is clear that through the Messiah, not only was the universe (which had been corrupted in a certain way because of the sin of our first parents) to be repaired and death itself destroyed, as was shown in the preceding points, but the angelic ruin was also to be restored (as has now been proven).

But other books have there the word *lo* (**לא**), written with the letter *aleph*, which signifies the negative "Not." In that case, the same words are translated: "There is no arbiter between us." Hence our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> has: "There is none who is able to argue against both, and to lay his hand upon both." Both readings, however, are good and return to the same meaning. 

For according to the first reading, which the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> provides, the holy <term>Job</term>—thinking upon how perversely and ruinously the first man had sinned, and how inexorably the Creator of men had been angered—was searching for the <term>Messiah</term> as a mediator of God and man. He sought one who would "lay his hand on both," which is to say, one who would embrace and bear both natures simultaneously: the divine and our own. He would be the only one among men to appear and be truly innocent, and yet would proceed toward the punishment for sin voluntarily and without fault of his own. Thus, by word and example, he would rebuke man so that he might not sin, and by enduring an ignominious punishment on behalf of man while being innocent himself, he would withstand the severity of divine justice so that it might not strike. 

According to the other reading, however, the same holy <term>Job</term>, by the foresight of the Holy Spirit, saw that no one before the <term>Messiah</term>, nor anyone coming after him, would be able to undergo the guilt of others' sins without being weighed down by his own. Seeing that no one else was able to satisfy the severity of divine justice, he deplored the far too long delay of the <term>Messiah’s</term> coming, saying: "There is no arbiter between us"—that is, between God and man—who can argue with equity, since all are guilty until he comes who (as has been said) may "lay his hand upon us" and alone argue with equity for the humble of the earth—that is, for the salvation of humble men. <term>Isaiah</term> also sought this arbiter with burning desire in his 64th chapter, saying: **לוא קרעת שמים וירדת** <note>original Hebrew: "Lu qara’ta shamayim ve-yaradta"</note> which is: "Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend."

### *That not only the Jews, but the Gentiles also were to be redeemed and saved through the Messiah. Yet not all, whether Jews or Gentiles, but only those from both groups who were destined to receive and confess Him.*

## Chapter 14.

# CAPNIO,

Although from all these things which you have said so abundantly and truthfully from the fourth chapter until now, it is clearly gathered that eternal salvation and the perfect redemption which was owed to faith through the Messiah was to be not physical (as the more foolish among the younger Jews <note>A common polemical reference in Renaissance texts to contemporary Jewish scholars who disagreed with Christian interpretations of the Old Testament.</note> assert) but spiritual. By which the Redeemer himself, both God and man, was to redeem and save the human race from hell and from eternal death, into which all men had fallen because of the sin of our first parents. Yet because many of the Jews say that this redemption or salvation was to belong to Israel alone, and not to the nations, therefore, so that their lack of faith may be further refuted, you ought to prove through their ancient scriptures that not only the Jews who were to receive the Messiah, but also the Gentiles, were to believe in the Messiah himself, and be redeemed and saved by him. <margin>GAL.</margin> This is clearly held from many places. And first indeed from those things read in *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>original: "Baresfith rabba"; a classic collection of ancient Jewish interpretations (Midrash) on the Book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis, upon that word in the 41st chapter of the same book: "And Pharaoh said to Joseph: I am Pharaoh, and without you no man (or anyone) shall lift up his hand" <note>original: "ויאמר פרעה אל יוסף אני פרעה ובלעדיך לא ירים איש את ידו"</note>. Far from it; rather, he will save and liberate all who confess him with their mouth, with their deeds, and with their heart." <meta>This page continues the argument that the Messiah’s salvation is universal, extending beyond the Jewish people to all who believe. It concludes a tradition (traditio) regarding the confession of faith and begins a systematic breakdown of why terms like "Judah" and "Israel" should be understood spiritually to include the Gentiles.</meta>

-># SIXTH BOOK<-

...they will confess You in their heart, they will confess You with their mouth, they will confess You with their works, and they will confess You equally by all these things. As it is said in Zephaniah, chapter 3: <note>Zephaniah 3:9</note> *For then I will restore to the peoples a chosen lip <note>original: "labium electum"; usually translated as "pure speech" or "pure language."</note>, so that they may all call upon the name of the Lord and serve Him with one shoulder <note>A Hebrew idiom meaning "with one accord" or "unanimously."</note>.* This means: "Because then I will turn toward the nations a chosen lip, that they may all invoke the name of God and serve Him with one shoulder." However, the "name of God" is not mentioned in this place except to mean the King Messiah, of whom it is said in Isaiah, chapter 30: *Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar.* The same is taught regarding the Holy and Blessed God, as said in Jeremiah, chapter 23: *Am I a God nearby, says the Lord, and not a God from afar?* And why should they "serve Him with one shoulder"? Because the government was placed upon his shoulder. As it is said in Isaiah, chapter 9: *And the government was upon his shoulder.* <note>The Hebrew text provided in the manuscript here actually reads "And Israel shall dwell in safety" from Jeremiah 23, but the author translates it using the famous "government on his shoulder" phrase from Isaiah 9:6.</note> Thus far the tradition. 

In this tradition, many things must be noted that are most worthy of attention. First, indeed, is that the Redeemer was not to be a respecter of persons <note>meaning he does not show favoritism based on ethnicity</note>, but the Savior of all who confess Him. Therefore, it is necessary that this Redeemer is the Messiah, because of those words of Jeremiah introduced there: *In his days Judah shall be saved.* These words are explained as referring to the Messiah in the Hebrew scriptures and in the Chaldean translation <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, as was proven in the previous sections. 

Second, in the aforementioned words of Jeremiah, "Judah" does not refer to the Jews themselves—as they often argue against us—but to all those, both from the Gentiles and the Jews, who were destined to confess the Messiah in heart, mouth, and deed. 

Third, the Messiah was to be given as a light to the nations and a salvation even to the ends of the earth. 

Fourth, "Messiah" is the name of God, whom the peoples—that is, the Gentiles—were meant to serve with a chosen lip. 

Fifth, He Himself was to come "from afar," which is to say, from the Holy and Blessed God. This is proven there by that passage in Jeremiah: *Am I a God nearby, and not a God from afar?* Therefore, it follows that the Messiah is God. 

Sixth, those words written in Isaiah, chapter 9—*A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and the government shall be upon his shoulder*—are understood to refer to the Messiah. This stands against the delusions of the younger Jews. 

It must be noted further that, just as in the aforementioned tradition regarding those words of Jeremiah, *In his days Judah shall be saved*, "Judah" does not mean the Jews themselves but all who confess the Messiah; so too in the same words when it immediately follows: <margin>How "Israel" is interpreted.</margin> *And Israel shall dwell in confidence.* By "Israel"—which is interpreted as "a man seeing God"—one should not, by the same reasoning, understand those of the Israelite people alone. Rather, it means all who see God; that is, all from the Israelite nation as well as from the other nations who were destined to see the Messiah Himself, the true God and man, through faith and works. Such were the apostles and the rest, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, who were converted to Christ; for in seeing Christ, they saw the true God. And this is the literal exposition. For "Israel" was not the proper name of Jacob himself, but was bestowed upon him in a vision of angels. Since therefore...

<margin>Who are the true Israelites.</margin>
The Messiah, as has been shown most extensively in the preceding pages, is greater than the angels, since he is the true God. Those who have seen and do see the Messiah himself are the "true Israelites." To this tradition should also be added what is written in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The *Midrash Tehillim* is a traditional Jewish commentary on the Book of Psalms, compiled over many centuries.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Psalms—regarding that verse of Psalm 66 <note>Modern Bibles usually number this as Psalm 67:2.</note>: *That your way may be known upon earth, your salvation among all nations.* <note>original Hebrew: "Lada’at ba’aretz darkecha."</note> There it is said: "The Holy and Blessed God will not save Israel because of their own works, but to make his power known, and to make his name known to the nations." For Asaph <note>A levite singer and traditional author of several Psalms.</note> says in Psalm 76: *God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel.* And again he says in Psalm 77: *You are the God who does wonders; you have made your power known among the peoples.* Could the Jews say to the Gentiles that the Redeemer is a "respecter of faces"—that is, a respecter of persons <note>A biblical term meaning someone who shows partiality or favoritism based on status or ethnicity.</note>? By no means; rather, he belongs to those who confess him. As it is said in Psalm 67: *The peoples shall confess you, O God; all the peoples shall confess you,* and so on. This is also what Isaiah says in chapter 61: *For as the earth brings forth its sprout, and as a garden makes its seeds spring up, so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all nations.* <note>original Hebrew: "Ki ka’aretz totzi tzimchah..."</note> Thus far the Talmud <note>The author uses "Talmud" here loosely to refer to Jewish traditional literature, specifically the Midrash just cited.</note>. Likewise, in the same *Midrash Tehillim* regarding that verse of Psalm 100: *A Psalm for confession: Shout to the Lord, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness; come before him with singing.* <note>original Hebrew: "Mizmor l’todah..."</note> It is written there: "Rabbi Jacob said, it was said by Rabbi Abhu in the name of Rabbi Aha: 'A Psalm for confession. All the nations shall confess me, and I will receive them.'" As it is said in Isaiah 65 <note>The author likely means Isaiah 45:23.</note>: *Since every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall swear, and I will receive them.* From these things which have been said, it is clearly demonstrated that not only the Jews, but the Gentiles also were to be redeemed and saved through the Messiah. Yet, not all Jews nor all Gentiles were to be saved at the time of the Messiah, but only those from both groups who would receive the Messiah himself and confess him with their heart, mouth, and works.

The King Messiah, however, comes from the descendants of their descendants. And this is what Zophar said to Job in the eleventh chapter, saying: "Can you find the deep things of God? Zophar said to him: "Yet these judgments came before the Holy and Blessed God. For Lot slept with his daughters, and Judah with his daughter-in-law. And yet the Holy and Blessed God took from both instances and established from them kings in this world, and the Redeemer in the world to come. And this is the King Messiah." This is the tradition.

Likewise, in the same book, it is read that Rabbi Hanina said the following: "What is the meaning of the text of Genesis, chapter nineteen, where the daughters of Lot said, 'That we may preserve seed from our father'?" Because they said "seed" and not "sons," it seems that the secret of the Messiah's coming was revealed to them—that the Messiah was to come from the seed of Adam through them. They were hinting at that "seed" of the Messiah of whom Adam said, "The Lord has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel," <note>Genesis 4:25, traditionally interpreted by some commentators as referring to the Messianic line.</note> suggesting that he would proceed from them. Therefore, they wished to sleep with their father to preserve this kind of seed, led not by any malice or indecency, but because they believed no other man existed in the world besides their father, due to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. Therefore, lest the coming of the Messiah be prevented, each of them lay with their father for one night. Having become pregnant, they gave birth to two sons: one was Ammon, the other Moab. From them, two great nations emerged, which are called Ammon and Moab.

From Moab, moreover, came Ruth the Moabite, who took Boaz as her husband. From his line came King David, as is clear from his genealogy. King Solomon, among his other wives, had Naamah the Ammonite, and from her was born Rehoboam, King of Judah. David, among his other sons, had Solomon and Nathan. From Nathan descended the Most Blessed Virgin, according to the genealogy in Luke. From Solomon and his son Rehoboam, however, comes Joseph, the spouse of the same Virgin, as we shall say more extensively in the following book. Since the daughters of Lot did not know from which of them the Messiah would come, and each thought he would proceed from herself, they said: "That we may preserve seed from our father," which they did without any evil intent.

### Chapter XVII.

->CAPNIO,<-

**H**ow then was the world, or the human race, to be saved through the Messiah? For you ought to show this as well through their own scriptures. GALATINUS: The ancient scriptures show that the world itself, or the human race, was to be saved in the time of the Messiah through a general <term>remission of sins</term> <note>The theological concept of God's pardon or forgiveness for transgressions.</note>. (He says, "they will be absolving," in the plural, because of the trinity of divine persons in one essence, who were to concur together for the remission of sins). Then it is added in the same tradition: "Just as it is said in the fourteenth chapter of Hosea: I will heal their backsliding [or their turning away], I will love them freely [or spontaneously]. Because my anger is turned away from him" <note>original Hebrew: "Arpa meshuvatam ahavam nedava ki shav api mimenu." Hosea 14:4.</note>—that is, because of him. This is the tradition. Jonathan also explains these words in Chaldaic: **They shall be gathered from the children of their captivities; they shall dwell or sit in the shadow of their Messiah; the dead shall be revived, and good shall be multiplied in the land. With these things established, the Jews must be asked a question. Since it is said here by the prophet, "Those sitting or dwelling in his shadow shall return," to which of the preceding things does this pronoun "his"—which they call a <term>Chinnui</term> <note>A Hebrew grammatical term for a pronominal suffix, such as "his" or "their."</note>—refer? For the nature of such <term>Chinnuim</term> (that is, pronouns) is to refer back to things previously mentioned, specifically the closer ones, as can be seen from countless places in Holy Scripture. For instance, when it is said in Exodus chapter 15: **The Lord is a man of war; the Lord is his name** <note>original Hebrew: "Adonai ish milchamah, Adonai shemo"</note>, this pronoun "his" refers back to the other things mentioned: either to God, or to the man, or to both. Thus also here, when it says, "Those dwelling or sitting in his shadow," this pronoun "his," once the circumstances of the preceding words are diligently inspected, must refer either to that one of whom it was said a little before that God was going to absolve the whole world because of his penance, or to the "dew," which the Chaldaic translation...

*That the salvation of the world or the human race was to be accomplished through the wood of the cross. And concerning the mysteries and excellence of the cross itself. Chapter XV.*

->CAPNIO,<-

What then was this penance which the Messiah was to perform for the remission of the sins of the whole world? <margin>GALATINUS</margin> The passion of the Cross, which he had to undergo for us. For that reason, the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of Cabala, a Jewish mystical tradition that seeks to understand the hidden divine nature of reality and the scriptures.</note> extol it with the highest praises. For from the Cabalistic fragments, that verse of Psalm 139—**Thou hast fashioned me behind and before, and laid thy hand upon me** <note>original Hebrew: "Achore v'kedem tzartani v'tashet alai kappechah."</note>—is explained in this way: **"And hear all that I speak to you: know that the Creator (blessed be He) created the lower men in the image of the upper men, and created man with two faces, front and back, as it says, 'Behind and before you formed me.' And so there are found in him the Good Inclination and the Evil Inclination, and these are two angels, even though one is a prince and the other an angel; for everyone whom God brought into existence is called an 'angel.' Concerning this, the sages of blessed memory said: there is a good angel and an evil angel. The good angel is the one who leads man to do good in his life; and if he does the opposite, he turns into himself, and that is Gehenna (Hell). Therefore he is called 'half total, half wagon'—half good and half evil—and this is the secret of 'front and back.' From him comes forth nourishment and life and death, and from him flows good or everything..."** <note>This Hebrew passage is a mystical commentary on the dual nature of humanity, balancing the "Yetzer Tov" (Good Inclination) and "Yetzer Hara" (Evil Inclination).</note>

### BOOK SIX

The wise men likewise said: Indeed, that which is superior among the lower things proceeds from the second hidden intellect which governs all of existence, as we have said. Because of this, two inclinations are poured out from it, along with the power of the "warp and the woof" <note>original Hebrew: ha-shetī ve-ha-erev. This is a technical term for weaving that Cabalists used as a cipher for the Cross.</note>—Hosts, Hosts <note>original Hebrew: Tzevaot Tzevaot</note>, without right or left. And the Name served him by His blessed name, and said: "His name shall not be called [as others], for My name is within him." Therefore they called him "Beings" <note>original Hebrew: Ishim, referring to the tenth rank of angels who are closest to human intellect.</note>, for he makes himself heard to all beings, and because evil is found within him alongside the good.

That is: "Now, pay attention to all that I speak to you. I want you to know that God the Creator created the lower man in the image of the superior beings; and He created man having two faces, namely a front and a back. As it is said: **You have formed me behind and before.** <note>Psalm 139:5</note> And there is found in him a good inclination and an evil inclination, and these are two angels: though one of them is a devil, and the other an angel. Yet the intellect that gave them being is God, and it is called an angel. And therefore it is said by the wise: 'A good angel and an evil angel.' The good angel is he who directs man toward the good in his life. And if man does the opposite, he turns himself against him, and it becomes a hell for the man. And for this reason, he is called 'the middle,' signifying that half of the sphere is good, and half is evil. And this is the secret contained in that which is said: **Before and behind**, and the rest.

"Moreover, from him proceeds the essence providing life and providing death; and from him, furthermore, is the good nature and the contrary nature, that is, the evil one. And they said that the work of the lower things belongs to the second hidden intellect, which is set over the whole universe and directs it, just as we have said before. And therefore we were made by him as having two desires, the secret of which is the cross, and it hints at 'Sebaoth Sebaoth' <note>Sebaoth means 'Hosts,' as in the 'Lord of Hosts.'</note>, signifying right and left. And the Name—that is, God—bestowed a crown upon it, which is His most high name. And He said to it: 'Let your name be called by my name.' And this is what was said: **My name is in it.** <note>Exodus 23:21</note> And for this reason, he called it 'man,' because it flows down upon all men. And it is found that the evil formation, or the evil desire, or original sin, is its opposite. Since it is itself the highest good." All these things are from that source.

Where, among other wondrous mysteries of the cross, it is said that the cross hints at *Sebaoth Sebaoth*, signifying right and left. This is undoubtedly said because for those calculating by the method of <term>arithmetic ratio</term> <note>This refers to Gematria, a Jewish system of assigning numerical values to letters to find hidden meanings between words with the same total.</note>, the letters that signify the "cross" and the letters by which "Sebaoth" is written twice result in precisely the same number from each calculation. For they call the cross **the warp and the woof** <note>original Hebrew: ha-shetī ve-ha-erev (השתי והערב)</note>. Its letters, by arithmetic ratio, yield 998 among them. For the letter **He** (ה) yields 5; **Shin** (ש) 300; **Tau** (ת) 400; **Iod** (י) 10; **Vau** (ו) 6; **He** (ה) 5; **Ain** (ע) 70; **Res** (ר) 200; **Beth** (ב) 2. When these are joined together, the predicted number results, namely 998.

And precisely the same number results from the letters by which **Sebaoth** (צבאות) is written twice. For the letter **Tzadi** (צ) carries 90; **Beth** (ב) 2; **Aleph** (א) 1; **Vau** (ו) 6; **Tau** (ת) 400. From these joined together, 499 is made. # Seventh Book.

## Concerning the most holy mother of the Messiah.

### That the mother of the Messiah was foreseen by God from eternity as the one who would conceive His son and give birth to the Messiah, true God and man. Chapter 1.

->CAPNIO,<-

**S**ince you have said so many and such great things in the preceding sections concerning the Messiah, it is now fitting that you say something about his most holy mother. Therefore, first show from the ancient scriptures of the Jews that she herself was foreseen by God from eternity, destined to conceive the son of God himself, and to give birth to the true Messiah, both God and man. **GAL.** If indeed (as we shall discuss more extensively in the following chapter) according to the opinion of <term>Rabbeni Haccados</term> <note>Hebrew: "Our Holy Rabbi," a title typically referring to Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century compiler of the Mishnah.</note>, God created the world for this reason: because he had seen that the "stone without hands" <note>A reference to the prophecy in Daniel 2:34, interpreted here as the miraculous birth of Christ.</note> was to be hewn out of Israel, which is the primary rock—that is, the most blessed Virgin, from whom the Messiah was to come forth. It is certainly a consequence, according to the opinion of the ancients, that the mother of the Messiah was foreseen by God before the foundation of the world, as the one who would conceive and give birth to the Messiah himself. For God, who foresees all things before they happen and gazes upon future things as if they were present, knew before he created the world that Adam would sin, and that the entire human race would be condemned on account of his sin. Being the best of physicians, he willed to prepare the best and most effective medicine for the whole human race. Indeed, he thought no remedy more effective, nor any cure better for such a great wound, than the incarnation and passion of his own son, so that through this he might show the immensity of his love toward the human race. Therefore, before he brought forth the world, he foresaw the glorious Virgin who would conceive his son and become the mother of the Messiah. And thus she was already created in his mind, according to that saying of the wise man <note>King Solomon</note> speaking in the person of the mother of the Messiah herself in the eighth chapter of <term>Proverbs</term>, saying in Hebrew: *The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was. When there were no depths, I was brought forth.* <note>original Hebrew: "יהוה קנני ראשית דרכו קדם מפעליו מאז : מעולם נסכתי מראש מקדמי ארץ : באין תהומות חוללתי"</note> This means: God possessed me as the beginning of his way, the start of his works from that time. From eternity I was ordained from the head, and from the ancient times of the earth; before the abysses existed, I was brought forth. <margin>The false opinion of the Jews, who say the Law was established before the production of the world.</margin>
They say that the aforementioned things were said not of the mother of the Messiah, but of the Law of God, which they claim was created before the foundation of the world; they say it was written in letters of black fire on a background of white fire, and that it preceded the world by two thousand years. <margin>Refutation.</margin> <margin>The first reason.</margin> To these people we respond that they are telling most vain dreams. First, indeed, because they cannot calculate any number of years before the establishment of the world. This is proved by a double reason. The first of which is that God is not subject to time. The second is because time follows the motion of the celestial orbs and is joined to it. For a planet makes the hour, governing one hour. And the motion of the sun makes the day, which lingers for twenty-four hours from the time it rises until it begins to rise again in the east. Moreover, the seven planets make the week, of which each one governs one day; for the sun governs the Lord’s day <note>Sunday</note>. Hence some have wished the Lord’s day to be named from the dominion of the sun, which is the king of the planets. The moon itself governs the day of the moon <note>Monday</note>. Mars governs the day of Mars <note>Tuesday</note>, and so on for the others. The course of the moon completes the lunar month. The course of the [Zodiac] signs completes the solar month, because each sign of the zodiac dominates its own month. The sun completes the year, which in a full year traverses the twelve signs of the zodiac. For this reason, if the heavens were not created, there was no time. Therefore, since time did not exist, "two thousand years before the creation of the world" is falsely cited by the Jews. It is also clear that their opinion is heretical from this: that fire is one of the four elements. However, the elements were not created except in the creation of the world. If, therefore, their opinion were true, <margin>The second reason.</margin> two inconveniences against their own law would follow. The first, indeed, that the world would have been eternal, since fire already existed. The second, indeed, that God did not create the world out of nothing, but made it out of something. Both of these are the greatest heresy, even according to them, since it is against that which is said in Genesis chapter 1: <note>original Hebrew: בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ</note> "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." And the rest. Therefore, the aforementioned words of the Wise Man <note>Refers to the author of the Book of Wisdom or Ecclesiasticus</note> can by no means be understood as referring to the Law. Therefore, they must be understood as referring to the Virgin mother of the Messiah. Nor do I think their opinion should be approved who affirm that those same words are said not of the most blessed Virgin, but only of Divine Wisdom. Which (if I may say so with their permission) is entirely false. For even if the preceding words of Proverbs, "The Lord possessed me," <note>Proverbs 8:22</note> along with the rest, are rightly said of Divine Wisdom which was begotten from eternity—as we ourselves explained concerning that same Wisdom in the third book—nevertheless those words of Ecclesiasticus, "From the beginning and before the ages I was created," <note>Ecclesiasticus 24:9</note> can by no means suit that same Divine Wisdom. The reason for this is: because according to the opinion of sacred theologians, there is nothing in God which is not God Himself. This the ancient Talmudists also felt, as is clear through <term>Rabbenum Haccados</term> <note>Hebrew: "Our Holy Rabbi," usually referring to Judah the Prince</note> in the first petition of the book *Gale Razeya* <note>Hebrew: "The Revealer of Secrets," a kabbalistic/theological work often cited by Galatinus</note>, saying thus: <note>original Hebrew: לא נמצא שום דבר באל אשר לא יהיה אל</note> That is, "Nothing is found in God which is not God." Therefore, it is a necessary consequence that the Wisdom which is in God is God. Wherefore it must also be uncreated. Therefore, those words, "From..."

### *That God created the world out of love for the mother of the Messiah the King, and for her son. Because He saw that they would be immune to the sin of Adam. Chapter 11.*

It is because of this secret that it was said in Jeremiah 33:25: <note>Hebrew: "Im lo beriti yomam va-laylah huqqot shamayim va-arets lo samti"</note> 'Unless my covenant were day and night, I would not have appointed the laws of heaven and earth.'" Thus spoke that Holy Teacher.

As it is said in Micah, chapter 5: *And his goings forth are from of old, from the days of eternity.* <note>original Hebrew: ומוצאתיו מקדם מימי עולם (v’motza’otav mi-kedem mi-yemei olam). They held that the glorious mother of the Messiah stood out as the principal one, since (as was said) the world was created for the love of her. 

For when God fashioned Adam, He made a kind of mass <note>Latin: *massa*, referring to the raw material or "dough" of humanity.</note>, from whose nobler part He took the matter of the undefiled mother of the Messiah; from the remainder and the surplus He formed Adam. From the matter of the immaculate mother of the Messiah, a power <term>virtus | a spiritual or essential force</term> was made, which was preserved in the nobler place and member of Adam’s body. This power afterwards emanated to Seth, then to Enos, then in succeeding order to the rest, even to the holy Iehoiakim. <note>Galatinus uses the Hebrew-influenced form "Iehoiakim" for Joachim, the father of the Virgin Mary.</note> From this power at last the most blessed mother of the Messiah was formed. And for that reason Zechariah, in the 4th chapter of his prophecy, rightly called her *the primary stone*. <note>original Hebrew: את האבן הראשה (et ha-even ha-roshah). Usually translated as "the capstone" or "top stone."</note> From this stone, as the ancient Jews explained, the Messiah was to be hewn out. And this was not without reason, since she was primary in time, rank, and excellence. From this opinion it is clearly concluded that the flesh of the glorious mother of the Messiah was not infected by original sin, but was preserved as most pure by divine providence. Wherefore her soul was not to contract sin of this kind in its conception either.

...preserved [a portion of flesh] in Adam as corrupted but not infected, through which human nature could be saved. And they hold that this same portion was passed down without any infection to the blessed Virgin, and from it the body of Christ was formed. However, this is considered erroneous for two reasons. First, because according to this position, Christ would not truly be the son of the Virgin, nor truly born from the lineage of any person except Adam alone. For that part, because it remained uncorrupted in human nature, would have been like something foreign to all others descended from Adam, and natural to Adam alone according to his first state <note>This refers to the "state of innocence" before the Fall of Man.</note>. Second, because the proper order of satisfaction <note>In theology, "satisfaction" refers to the making of amends for sin, specifically Christ's atonement for humanity's sins.</note> is taken away. For just as it was not fitting for someone who was not of that race to make satisfaction for Adam and his corrupted descendants, it would also not have been fitting for the Son of God to heal the infected nature by making satisfaction unless he assumed that very thing which was previously infected. And therefore, it must be said that the flesh of Christ, as it existed in his ancestors and even in the blessed Virgin herself, was infected by sin before he assumed it. But in the act of assumption itself, it was purged of all infection of sin, so that insofar as it is actually the flesh of Christ, no stain is found in it. These are the words of the blessed Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher.</note>. From these words, it clearly appears that the flesh of the most blessed Virgin was infected by the sin of Adam.

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> Since by these same arguments that Saint Thomas makes, it could be proven that the unstained Virgin was not the daughter of the blessed Joachim, nor that she came from the tribe of Judah and the royal lineage. If we wish to follow the opinion of those ancient Jews, they say that a certain small portion of flesh in Adam was preserved most pure from every stain, and that it descended from generation to generation down to the immaculate Virgin herself. For that reason, we shall prove this opinion to be true by the testimonies of both the Holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, and of the ancient Hebrew Doctors. For from the Old Testament, we bring forward that saying from Genesis, chapter 4: *And she called his name Seth, saying: "For God has appointed for me another seed."* <note>original Hebrew: ותקרא את שמו שת כי שת לי אלהים זרע אחר (vattikra et shemo Shet ki shat li Elohim zera acher).</note> For Adam, seeing that all souls were going to be lost on account of his sin, and therefore according to the edition of the 70 interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, he abstained from relations with his wife for 130 years after he fathered Abel, lest he should beget children who would be damned. Nevertheless, after he prophesied the coming of the Messiah, through whom the world was to be saved, he knew his wife and fathered Seth. And because he knew that power was in him from which the mother of the Messiah was to be produced—in whose most precious blood the Messiah himself was present—he therefore called the name of his son <term>Seth<gloss>derived from the verb "shath," meaning "to appoint" or "to place."</gloss></term>, saying, "Because the Lord has appointed for me another seed." The sense is: "In me is found a foreign seed, and a certain power from which the Messiah is to be born." Furthermore, from the New Testament, we have among others the testimony of John the Baptist, who says in the first chapter of John: *In the midst of you stands one whom you do not know. He is the one who is to come after me, who was made before me.* And again in the same place: *Behold* (he says) *the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins [of the world].*

For Aristotle indeed, in the eighteenth book of *On the History of Animals*, says: "In Socrates, there is a power <note>The Latin 'virtus' here refers to a biological or generative force or essence.</note> proper to Socrates, and also of his parents, and of his grandfathers, and of the rest of his predecessors, both paternal and maternal, and this goes all the way to the last." And there is also in him the power of a "human," and then the power of an "animal." Therefore, when the power of Socrates is strong, a male is generated; when it is weak, a female is generated. If, however, the proper power of Socrates prevails, the child resembles Socrates, whether it be male or female. If, however, the power of Socrates' father prevails, a son is generated resembling not the father of Socrates, but the grandfather. And so on, ascending. And if the power of the lineage fails, a human is generated who resembles no one in the family. But if the power of "human" fails, where the movement of all [traits] fails, there remains only the power of generation [producing] a monster—

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
And so it also proceeds from the mother's side. The same philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> in the seventh book of the *History of Animals*, says as follows: "Some children are also generated similar to their parents, or to their grandparents and ancestors. Others show no similarity at all; as in the case of the woman in Sicily who committed adultery with an Ethiopian: her daughter did not reflect the color of the Ethiopian father, but the son born from that daughter did. He, however, brought back the likeness of his Ethiopian grandfather. For the most part, females resemble the mother and males resemble the father. But it also happens the other way around, so that females are created similar to the father and males similar to the mother." These are his words. From these things it is clearly evident that whether a son is similar to his parents or not, and whether the birth is perfect or monstrous, the offspring is always the child of the one generating it. Since, as has been said, Ethiopians have generated white children. Therefore, the untainted Virgin, although she was not like her progenitors in the fault <note>referring to the "fault" or "stain" of original sin</note>, is not for this reason to be called anything other than their daughter. And thus the response is given to the first argument of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian who famously questioned the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception</note>. To the second argument, indeed, we say: That just as (witnessed by the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note>) the human race flowed forth more strongly because the matter of the untainted mother of the Messiah was together with the matter of Adam, and she herself stood in the first cause of the same Adam: in the same way we also say, for that reason, the order of satisfaction <note>the theological process of making amends for sin</note> was more fitting. For since the body of Christ was within the most precious blood of the most blessed Virgin, it was fitting that he should come to purge sin. For just as when some boy perhaps soils a house, we call his mother to wipe away the child's filth and clean the house, so also it was fitting that to wash away the impurities which Adam had made, the humanity of Christ should come. Therefore, notwithstanding the arguments of the Holy Doctor <note>Aquinas</note>, the truth of the conclusion of the ancient Talmudists regarding the immaculate conception of the most blessed mother of the Messiah remains in its full strength.

### To the second objection of Hogostratus. And that the opinion concerning the immaculate conception of the glorious virgin is most ancient. Chapter 5.

#### HOGOSTRATUS,

<margin>Authors of the sacred pages of the Old Testament.</margin>
<margin>Objection of the more recent Jews.</margin>
**T**his opinion concerning the conception of the Virgin Mother of God, which now seems to prevail, is quite recent. Those who had exited Egypt, and those they had sent to explore the land, only those remained who had been born in the desert, all of whom were just. And because of them (as they say), this text says: *You are altogether beautiful, my love,* along with the rest.

<margin>Their objection. Response.</margin>
**GAL.** It is clear that this reasoning of theirs is false from the fact that the text says: *And there is no stain in you.* <note>original: "Et macula non est in te," quoting Song of Songs 4:7.</note> This least of all suits them, since they were not immune to original sin. **CAP.** To this they themselves respond: that circumcision cleansed them from original sin, and sufficiently opened the gate of paradise to them. **GAL.** That also is false. For even if circumcision were a remedy against original sin, it was nonetheless not enough to open the gate of heaven. This is especially evident from the fact that Moses, and Samuel, and all the greatest of the prophets, along with all others, descended to the underworld <note>original: "ad inferos." In this context, it refers to the "Limbo of the Fathers" (Limbus Patrum), where the righteous of the Old Testament were believed to wait until the Resurrection of Christ.</note> (as was shown in the preceding book). If, therefore, circumcision had unlocked the gate of the heavenly Kingdom for them, they certainly would have emigrated to heaven, not to the underworld.

<margin>Hogastratus's objection. Refutation.</margin>
**HOG.** But I say that this text, according to the exposition of some, speaks not of the undefiled Virgin, but of the Church of God. **GAL.** This also (if I may say so with their permission) is entirely false. Firstly, because all things which Mother Church sings were instituted by the Holy Spirit, whom it is impossible to be a liar. Since the Holy Church attributes this saying of the Wise Man <note>referring to Solomon, the traditional author of the Song of Songs.</note> to the Mother of God, it must necessarily be said that it speaks of her. Secondly, because the praises of that most glorious Virgin are immense and incomprehensible. If we, therefore, wishing to praise her, attributed to her the praises of another, we would undoubtedly show that those praises were not in her, but were borrowed from another. This, however, is completely false, since she herself lends of her own praises to others, and does not receive them from others, being most worthy of all praise. From these points, therefore, it is manifest that this text can appropriately be understood of no one else than the Mother of the Messiah. This is also shown openly in many other places. For in the same book, the Wise Man himself in the first chapter says also: <note>original: נאוו לחייך בתורים (Na’vu le-khayayikh ba-torim)</note> *Your cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove.* <note>Song of Songs 1:10. Traditional translations often use "with ornaments" for the Hebrew *ba-torim*, but Galatinus follows a tradition linking the word to *tor* (turtledove).</note> Where he compares the Mother of the Messiah to a turtledove for this reason: to show that just as the turtledove lacks gall <note>Galatinus relies on ancient natural history, which claimed doves and turtledoves lacked a gallbladder, making them symbols of purity and freedom from bitterness or "gall" (sin).</note> and was created from the beginning without it, so neither original, nor actual, nor even mental sin was to be attributed to the Mother of the Messiah. Therefore, in the second chapter of the same book, he also likened her to a dove, which also lacks gall, saying: <note>original: קומי לכי רעיתי יפתי ולכי לך יונתי בחגוי הסלע בסתר המדרגה הראיני את מראיך (Kumi lakh ra'yati yafati u-lekhi lakh... yonati be-khagvei ha-sela...)</note> That is: *Arise, hurry, my love, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall, show me your face.* <note>Song of Songs 2:13-14.</note> From which it is gathered that the Mother of the Messiah is not only compared to a dove for the reason mentioned above, but even her foundation and beginning were to be without original sin. And because a rock is the beginning and foundation upon which a building is sustained, therefore he says, *in the clefts of the rock*; that is, in the embryo, where she was conceived, in which there is a "cleft" where she was built—there she was a dove, cleansed from the gall of original sin...

...integrity and innocence. Nevertheless, the author of our edition <note>Referring to Saint Jerome, the translator of the Latin Vulgate</note>, flattering the Jews so that they might not be able to criticize him, translated it as "of salvation" and not "of Jesus" <note>In Hebrew, the word for "salvation" (Yeshuah) shares the same root as the name "Jesus" (Yeshua)</note>. He does this in almost infinite other places; for wherever the meaning is twofold, he almost always chooses the one that favors them. For he could have said here, and rightly so: "Because he clothed me with the garments of Jesus." Just as in the third chapter of Habakkuk it is said, **But I will rejoice in the Lord, and I will exult in God my Jesus.** <note>Habakkuk 3:18. From these things it is therefore clear that the ancient authors of Holy Scripture firmly held that the immaculate mother of the Messiah was to be conceived without original sin.

<margin>Authors of the Holy Scripture of the New Testament.</margin>
The writers of the New Testament held this same view. For we read in the eleventh chapter of the Gospel of Matthew that our Savior said this concerning John the Baptist:
> Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist.

Since, therefore, Saint John the Baptist was not greater than Christ himself (who was also born of a woman), and the text says, "arisen"—which cannot be said except of someone who first fell and afterwards rises—we are necessarily compelled to interpret this saying of the Savior in this way: "Among those born of women," that is, among those who were conceived in original sin, "there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist." But Christ did not fall into sin, therefore John is not greater than Him. Since the most blessed Virgin is also greater than the same John the Baptist, it follows necessarily that she did not fall into original sin. If this were not granted, it would plainly follow that John the Baptist stood as greater than her, which is entirely false. From the Gospel, therefore, and by the judgment of our Savior, it is necessarily concluded that she was conceived without original sin.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
**HOG.** That would indeed be true if the Gospel said "among those born as men and women." Since it says only "among those born" <note>The Latin *natos* is masculine</note>, it clearly shows that the saying of our Savior is to be understood not concerning women, but concerning men alone. Therefore, it cannot be inferred from this that the most blessed Virgin did not fall into original sin.

<margin>Response.</margin>
**GAL.** Your objection is worthless, since according to the grammarians the masculine gender encompasses the feminine. Therefore, when He said "among those born," He meant both men and women. The apostles also held this opinion regarding the immaculate conception of the Virgin, as is clearly evident from the words of the blessed Apostle Andrew. When he was explaining the mystery of the cross to the Proconsul Aegeas, he said among other things:
> And since the first man had been made from immaculate earth, who through the tree of transgression brought death into the world, it was necessary that the perfect man <note>Jesus</note> should be born of an immaculate virgin, in whom the Son of God, who had made the first man, might restore eternal life, which men had lost through Adam.

The blessed Dominic, founder and leader of the Order of Preachers, later followed this same opinion, saying in his treatise on the Body of Christ:
> Just as the first Adam was formed from virgin earth that was never cursed, so it was fitting for it to happen in the second Adam <note>Christ</note>.

<margin>Ancient Doctors of the church.</margin>
And indeed the Greeks, such as Gregory Nazianzen, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, John Chrysostom, and all the others, as is clearly evident to those reading their books. # To the third objection of Hoogstraten. Wherein it is proved by natural reasons that the mother of the Messiah was to be conceived without original sin.

## Chapter VI.

->HOOGSTRATEN,<-

**I**f this were true, the word of the Apostle Paul would be entirely false, who, writing to the Romans in the 3rd chapter, says: "All have sinned in Adam and lack the grace of God." <note>original: "Omnes in Adam peccauerunt & egent gratia Dei." This is a reference to Romans 3:23, often conflated in the Latin tradition with Romans 5:12 to emphasize that all humanity inherited sin through Adam.</note> Therefore, it must necessarily be said that the glorious Virgin sinned in Adam, and consequently both her matter <note>In the Aristotelian philosophy used here, "matter" refers to the physical substance or "stuff" from which a person is formed.</note> was infected by Adam’s sin, and she herself was conceived in original sin. For he who says "all" excludes no one. GALATINUS. To show that you have spoken (if I may say so with your permission) with less decorum than is fitting, I will do two things. First, I will prove by seven natural reasons both that the matter of the undefiled mother of the Messiah ought to have been preserved clean and immaculate in Adam, and consequently that the mother of the Messiah herself was conceived without initial sin. Then, I will respond to the authority of the Apostle Paul.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
For the foundation of the first reason, I shall put forward two principles. The first is that in every subject four causes must be found: namely, the material, efficient, formal, and final. <term>Four causes</term> <note>Galatinus is using Aristotle’s framework: the Material (what it's made of), Efficient (who made it), Formal (its shape/essence), and Final (its purpose).</note> Of these, the final cause is more sublime and excellent than the others. The second principle is that the final cause and the intent of nature always remain, and they never cease to provide perfection and form to their subject and individual, provided they find matter suitable for receiving a form of this kind. Therefore, it is necessary for every agent—whether natural, voluntary, or artistic—to prepare the most capable matter possible for any subject, so that its particular "end" or purpose may come to it, according to the design and goal intended by the agent. For example, the pepper, whose end is heat and dryness, naturally performs the operation of fire. On the contrary, the violet, which nature disposes toward the quality of water, is a thing suited to coolness, which is its own particular end. By the same reasoning, the sapphire, the diamond, and other precious stones, which nature and the final cause dispose toward a certain sublime, bright, and transparent matter from the four elements, so that they may receive their own peculiar form. This is despite the fact that they consist of the earthly element, which is dark and obscure. Since this is the case in natural things, it certainly follows that the glorious Virgin—since she was the subject in which the Son of God was to be incarnated—was disposed more perfectly and sublimely than any human creature, indeed, than any created being. Just as the particular end for which she was created was more perfect and sublime than all others, since she alone was created so that the Son of God might be born from her. But if her matter had been unclean, and she herself conceived in original sin, she would by no means have been disposed more perfectly and sublimely than every created being. Therefore, it was necessary that her matter be preserved pure and immaculate, and that she herself be conceived without original sin.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Likewise, to each...

Galatinus argues that because the Virgin Mary's "final cause" (purpose) was to bear God, nature must have prepared her physical "matter" to be more perfect and pure than any other creation.</summary>

Galatinus is currently presenting a series of "natural reasons"—philosophical arguments based on the order of nature and Aristotelian logic—to prove that it was more fitting for the mother of the Messiah to be preserved from original sin from the moment of her conception.</meta>

<page-num>503</page-num>
<header>SEVENTH [BOOK]</header>

In any being that lacks a certain perfection, there is an implanted natural desire <note>In scholastic philosophy, this "natural appetite" or *appetitus* refers to an innate tendency in things to reach their full potential or a higher state of being.</note> to liken itself to a perfect being, and it shuns things lower than itself. Furthermore, if the disposition of a subject is suitable for receiving, Nature gives it a greater perfection the more capable it is. For this reason, the sapphire, whose matter is from the earth, naturally desires to ascend to the degree of clarity found in the element of air; receiving clarity from that element, it becomes bright and transparent. Likewise, a mineral desires to become a vegetative being <note>The "vegetative soul" was the level of life attributed to plants, involving growth and nutrition.</note>, even if it does not possess a vegetative soul. Nature gives it the perfection of growth when it has matter suited for growing. Truly, the vegetative being desires to become an animal. Therefore, because of the disposition of the matter it possesses, Nature gave the mandrake the figure of a human, even if it lacks a sensing soul <note>The mandrake root was famously thought to resemble the human form, which medieval thinkers saw as nature "striving" toward a higher human shape.</note>. Furthermore, an animal desires to become a human, which is why the monkey has the likeness of a man and mimics those things which a man himself does, even though it lacks a rational soul. Since, therefore, there was a desire in the matter of the mother of the Messiah to be conceived without original sin, and the disposition of that matter was capable of receiving this kind of perfection, it necessarily follows that it is far more reasonable that she was conceived without original sin than that she was purged after conception.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
Likewise, the more perfect the "end" or purpose of the matter, the form, and the efficient cause, the higher they themselves are. Just as the four elements are more sublime when they first obtain a sensing soul <note>The "sensitive soul" refers to the level of life in animals, including senses and movement.</note> than when they possessed only a vegetative soul. Minerals also are more noble when they are first made into precious stones. For the sapphire and the diamond are more noble than jasper and porphyry. Moreover, jasper and porphyry are more excellent than the stones with which houses are built. By this same reasoning, among herbs, grain is more honorable; and among architects, the one who builds a royal palace is more outstanding. By this reasoning, it is more sublime to erect basilicas than to build the palaces of kings. And it is more excellent to serve God out of love than out of necessity. It follows, therefore, that the more sublime the "final cause" <note>The "final cause" is the ultimate purpose for which something exists.</note> is, the more perfections flow from it into the subject, so that it might be more excellent in the future. Since this is so, it was necessary that the undefiled virgin mother of the Messiah—who was to be the subject and the tabernacle in which the Son of God would be incarnated—be conceived at a more sublime level than lesser subjects who are conceived with original sin, so that she might have an excess of perfection over all others. Therefore, she was conceived without original sin.

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
Likewise, it is most well-proven in nature that in any thing where many "ends" are found separate from the first, the second end is more sublime than the first, and the third more than the second. And so on, step by step. By the same reasoning, the matter and form of the second end are more perfect than the matter and form of the first, and the matter and form of the third are more sublime than the second. For example: to be an animal is a more perfect end than to be a vegetative being. To be a human, however, is a more perfect end than to be an animal. Furthermore, when we wish to give the definition of a human insofar as he is only an animal, we say he is a "nourishing, sensing body." But if we define him insofar as he is a human, we say he is...

<summary>Galatinus uses the Aristotelian "Great Chain of Being" and the concept of "final causes" to argue that because Mary’s purpose was the highest possible (bearing God), her physical and spiritual beginnings had to be uniquely perfect and free from sin.</summary>

...to be a rational animal <note>Scholastic philosophers defined a human being as a "rational animal."</note>, which is a higher definition than the first. Since, therefore, the immaculate Virgin was conceived not only that she might be a human being, but that she might also be the Mother of God; and since this end is more excellent and higher than the ultimate end of the rest of the human race, it was fitting that she, in her conception, should possess a perfection of matter and form <note>Galatinus uses the Aristotelian concept of "hylomorphism," where everything is composed of "matter" (the physical stuff) and "form" (the essence or design that makes it what it is).</note> beyond that which merely made her a human. This [perfection] is none other than that she was not infected by original sin. For just as the matter of animals is higher and more perfect than the matter of plants, and the matter of humans is more excellent than the matter of animals, so too is it both reasonable and necessary that the matter of the glorious Virgin was more perfect and higher than the matter of [other] humans, since she ascended to the highest possible degree of humanity.

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
Likewise, nature is said to be "equal" <note>Here meaning "equitable" or "fair."</note> and to act according to its own character when it gives as much perfection to a subject as that subject is capable of receiving. According to this principle, something is not said to happen "against nature" [if it receives its full due]. For a thing would only be called "against nature" if nature itself did not provide the perfection which the subject was capable of receiving. For just as it is against nature to give perfection to one who does not deserve it, so too is it against nature to take perfection away from one who does. Since this is the case, it was necessary that the matter of the glorious Virgin—which was skillful and fit to receive this kind of perfection so that she might be conceived without original sin—should have been produced without any initial stain. 

<margin>Sixth reason.</margin>
Likewise, for the sixth reason I make two propositions. Let the first be this: It is certain that original sin is not the efficient cause <note>In philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the agent or force that actually brings something about. Galatinus is arguing that procreation itself is a natural good, and sin is merely a secondary corruption.</note> of generation. This is clear, because if Adam had not sinned, he certainly would still have generated [children]. Let the second be this, which I prove by example: Suppose a certain king is about to enter a filthy and foul house. I ask: Is it more fitting for that house to be decorated and filled with various scents *before* the king enters, or *after* he has entered? Certainly it befits royal dignity to make it clean, bright, and fragrant before rather than after. So we say of the Queen of Heaven: it was more just and fitting that the matter which was to be the matter of the Mother of God should be cleansed and sanctified while it was still the matter of the parent <note>Original: *dum generantis esset materia*. He refers to the physical substance provided by her parents during her conception.</note>, and that the efficient cause of original sin be removed from it then, rather than afterward when she had already been formed. Otherwise, a defect would be shown in the Queen of Heaven, and it would contradict the text of Holy Scripture which says of her (as we proved above): *You are all beautiful, my love, and there is no spot in you.* <note>Original: "Tota pulchra es amica mea, & macula non est in te." This verse from the Song of Solomon (4:7) was the central scriptural proof-text for the Immaculate Conception.</note> This reason is confirmed: For it is certain that a thing in which no stain or filth ever fell is more perfect and noble than one in which there was first a stain that was afterward purged. This is just as a man who never sinned is more excellent than a reconciled sinner. For if a reconciled sinner were more perfect than a just man who never sinned, or if they were of equal perfection, God would not have confirmed the glorious Virgin in a state of grace. Therefore, it must be confessed that she was conceived without initial sin. 

<margin>Seventh reason.</margin>
Lastly, the closer the beginning and the end are to one another, the more perfect the "middle" must be, and the more the beginning and middle must agree with the end. Just as a greater...

<summary>Galatinus argues through Aristotelian logic and the "King’s House" analogy that Mary’s physical and spiritual substance must have been purified from the moment of conception to be a fitting vessel for God. He asserts that a being who was never stained by sin is naturally more perfect than one who is cleansed after the fact.</summary>
