-># SEVEN<-

[greater] influence comes from the final cause <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "final cause" is the purpose or goal for which a thing exists; it is thought to influence the beginning of a process.</note> in any operation, and the end is much more eagerly desired in the middle and the beginning. Therefore, once it is recognized that the end goal of the conception of the undefiled Virgin was for the sake of the conception of the Son of God, it was necessary that the beginning (which was the Blessed Virgin) and the middle (which was her being conceived without original sin) should agree with the end (which was the incarnation of the Son of God from her). And just as when the Word was first made flesh <note>original: "verbum caro factum fuit," a reference to John 1:14.</note>, He gave the matter of Christ all the perfections it was ever to have, and none were lacking to Him. So also it was necessary that the matter of the most Blessed Virgin, immediately in her own conception, should have been granted all the perfections she was capable of receiving, and the purging of original sin was not to be expected <note>i.e., she did not need to be "cleansed" later because she was never stained.</note>. **HUGO.**

<margin>Objection:</margin>
Since the body of Christ was glorified in his resurrection, it is clear that it did not possess all perfections at the moment of his conception. Therefore, the conclusion you just put forward (if I may say so) is false. **GALATINUS.** <margin>Response:</margin> Since the divinity was united to Christ, and had glorification bound up within itself in a certain way, it did not allow his body to perform the actions of a glorified being during his life, since he was destined to suffer and die. Just as if someone, holding a boy with a strong hand, does not permit him to do what he wishes. But indeed, when necessity compelled it, Christ’s body did perform the works of a glorified body. For in his birth, he came forth from the virginal womb without the mother’s corruption <note>A traditional theological claim that Mary's physical integrity remained intact during childbirth.</note>. For glorified bodies have this special quality: that by their subtlety <term>Subtlety (subtilitate): the theological term for a glorified body's ability to pass through solid matter.</term> they may pass through a wall without it being broken. Also, in his transfiguration, he made use of a glorified body. Furthermore, when the Jews wanted to stone him, he went out of the temple while they could not see him. <margin><unclear>John 8.</unclear></margin> Moreover, it supports the confirmation of our reasoning that no mention is found among the Evangelists of any "glorification" of Christ happening during his resurrection <note>The author argues that Christ was already glorious; the resurrection merely allowed that glory to be visible.</note>. For this reason, it follows that the glorious Virgin, in the instant of her conception, was without the stain of initial sin. Rather, in her conception, her matter possessed all the perfections she was ever to have. Indeed, as soon as her soul was infused into that same matter, it actually attained all the perfections that can be found in a soul, such as knowledge, wisdom, understanding, prophecy, grace, and whatever else can be attributed to a soul. When, moreover, the Son of God came to be incarnated in her, she ascended to the highest degree. <margin><unclear>Luke 1.</unclear></margin> For He left the rule and governance of the entire world to her as His mother, and made her to be the Queen of the heavens and the angels. Now let us respond to the words of Saint Paul. When <margin>Regarding the authority of the Apostle Paul.</margin> he says, therefore, "All have sinned in Adam," <margin><unclear>Romans 5.</unclear></margin> let us explain the word "All" as follows: namely, all those who fall under the rule of Adam alone, and do not obtain a higher rank. These are indeed sinners in Adam, and conceived in original sin. But since the glorious Virgin ascended to a higher rank than Adam, she cannot be said to have fallen into the sin of Adam. For she alone among all other creatures was granted this privilege: that the Son of God should be conceived in her. <margin><unclear>Galatians 4.</unclear></margin> That this was her ultimate purpose, and the purpose of her conception, is most clear from the fact that no other creature besides her was ever conceived for this: that the Son of God should be incarnated in her; because in no other but her, the Son...

...the Son of God was incarnated. Therefore, so that the Son of God might be conceived in her, she herself was conceived. It is concluded, then, that the incarnation of the Son of God stood as the final cause <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "final cause" is the purpose or goal for which something is done.</note> of the conception of the Virgin herself. Wherefore, as is gathered from the previous reasons, it was necessary that the matter and form of the same immaculate Virgin were more perfect and more sublime than any other matter and form in the human race, and produced without the infection of original <note>original: "initialis," referring to the sin contracted at the very beginning of existence.</note> sin.

### *To the fourth objection of Hoogstraaten. Wherein the conclusion regarding the immaculate conception of the Virgin is confirmed by seven theological as well as natural reasons. Chapter VII.*

->HOOGSTRAATEN,<-

<margin><unclear>unreadable</unclear></margin> **I**t is certain that God does not wish to remove the order of nature which He Himself instituted. But if God had preserved the most blessed Virgin immune from original sin, He would certainly have removed, or rather perverted, the order of nature which He established; for on account of Adam's sin, He decreed that all humans descending from him by natural propagation be conceived with original sin. Therefore, it is by no means to be said that the undefiled Virgin herself was preserved from the stain of original sin. **GALATINUS.** You are certainly greatly deceived—forgive me—Hoogstraaten. This I shall prove by seven theological as well as natural reasons, so that at last a response may be given to your objection, which is worth nothing. <margin>First reason.</margin> Let the first reason, then, be this: it is certain that greed and stinginess cannot be attributed to God, since He gives as much perfection to each creature as it is fit to receive. For example: when God created the world, He attributed as much perfection to each kind of thing as its subject <note>In this context, the "subject" refers to the underlying nature or physical substance of a thing.</note> was able to hold. For if the subject of a donkey had been able to receive the perfection of a horse, or a lion, or even a man, He certainly would have given it. But since it was not fit to receive it, He did not give it. Since this is so, it clearly follows that God made the glorious Virgin without original sin, because her nature <note>original: "subiectum"</note> was so fit for it. Otherwise, He Himself would have been greedy and stingy, which is entirely false. Therefore, she was conceived without original sin. <margin>Second reason.</margin> <margin><unclear>unreadable</unclear></margin> Let the second reason be this: it is certain that the starting point of understanding a work is its intended end. Thus it happens that, since the goal of divine knowledge was to have the most blessed Virgin clean and pure from original sin, it was far more fitting to have made her clean and without sin from the start than to have cleansed her afterward. For if it were not so, divine operations would be compared to various and inconsistent human works. But this is false. Therefore, He made her entirely clean and pure from original sin. <margin>Third reason.</margin> Let the third reason be this: a certain desire is implanted by nature in every human being that his mother be more perfect in all the perfections of the world. And this is because he is born from her blood; for if the mother consists of clean and excellent matter, the son also [is born] of the same...

<meta>This page continues the theological argument from page 506, where the author (Galatinus) provides seven reasons why the Virgin Mary must have been conceived without original sin, refuting the objections of Hoogstraaten.</meta>

<page-num>507</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>

...will be fashioned from the same matter. Therefore, a son always desires the perfection of his mother and hates her imperfection. If, therefore, the Son of God—who loves virtues and perfections above all else, but greatly detests vices, sins, and imperfections—had not desired that his mother be nobler and more perfect in goodness, justice, holiness, and other perfections, he would surely have been disordered in his will and appetite. This is because he would have inclined his desire toward base and imperfect things rather than toward more noble and perfect ones. Furthermore, it would follow that he possessed a baser appetite than any pure human creature, since he would have willed his own matter and humanity to be imperfect. This, however, is manifestly false and entirely against reason. Since God is perfect with the highest perfection, and it belongs to a perfect being to love perfect things rather than imperfect ones, he surely ought to have both desired and made his mother perfect with every possible perfection. Wherefore, he caused her to be conceived without original sin.

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
Let the fourth reason be this. It is certain that before the creation of the world, God foreknew both that Adam would sin and that He Himself would be incarnated for the redemption of that sin. From this it follows that if God had decreed to be incarnated in a woman conceived in original sin, then God Himself would have stood as the cause of sin, and Adam would have been forced to sin, his free will having been taken away. If this were the case, Adam would by no means have deserved punishment. From these things, however, many absurdities <note>original: "inconvenientia," a technical term in scholastic logic referring to logical inconsistencies or "unfitting" conclusions that arise from a false premise.</note> would follow. Wherefore, it must necessarily be said that the woman from whom God was to be incarnated was preserved from the stain of initial sin <note>original: "peccati initialis," another term for original sin.</note> from eternity.

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
Let the fifth reason be this. The beginning of the human race was Adam, and its end <note>The "end" (finis) here refers to the ultimate purpose or goal of humanity's existence.</note> was Christ, for whose love the human race was created. So that the beginning, the middle, and the end might agree with one another, it was necessary that—just as Adam, who is the beginning, and Christ, who is the end, were made without original sin—so also the middle, which is the most blessed Virgin, should be conceived without that same sin. Furthermore, it follows that just as Eve was one flesh with Adam and the first "middle" for the preservation of the human race, made without original sin, so also it was necessary that the undefiled Virgin—who is the final "middle" for the salvation of souls and one flesh with Christ, who is the end—be conceived without original sin. Otherwise, the beginning and the first middle would not agree with the last middle and the end, which is very unfitting.

<margin>Sexta ratio.</margin>
Let the sixth reason be this. It is known that any most powerful king, wishing to construct a palace for himself or to erect a basilica to the honor of the best and greatest God, first seeks and prepares whatever things are necessary for the building, of as much perfection and excellence as can be found. We read that King Solomon did just this. <margin>A beautiful figure <note>A "figure" (figura) is a symbolic foreshadowing or a person/event in the Old Testament that prefigures something in the New Testament.</note> concerning the Virgin's conception.</margin> Because of the excellence of the temple which he constructed in God's service, he willed that in the craftsmanship and the cutting of the stones, no hammer or any kind of iron instrument should be used, nor should even the sound of them be heard. <margin>The *Zamir* worm.</margin> Instead, he found a worm named *zamir* <note>original: "zamir." This refers to the Shamir, a legendary creature or substance mentioned in the Talmud and Midrash that had the power to cut through stone, used by Solomon so that no metal tools of war would touch the Temple stones.</note>, which, when placed upon the stones, as it moved across them, immediately [it would]...

<meta>This page continues the sixth argument from page 507 regarding the purity of the Virgin Mary's conception, specifically using the allegory of Solomon’s Temple. It then transitions to the seventh reason, which addresses an objection by the inquisitor Jacob van Hoogstraten.</meta>

<page-num>508</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>

...was breaking. It is clear that this happened as a figure <note>A "figure" or "prefiguration" is an Old Testament event seen as a symbolic prophecy of a New Testament reality.</note>. For in the building of the temple, in which the Son of God was to be incarnated <note>Here, the author treats the physical Temple of Solomon as a symbol for the Virgin Mary, who "housed" God during the Incarnation.</note>, and in the tabernacle in which God was to show his brightness and holiness, there could be no lack of material of such great perfection for its construction. Nor was there any need for any **iron**—which signifies **original sin**—to be used in the hewing of the stones, that is, in the conception of the undefiled Virgin. 

The reason for this matter is that one sin cannot be healed by another, but only by something simple and, in a way, very small: that is, by a "worm." Therefore he found the <term>zamir</term> <note>The *Shamir* (translated here as *zamir*) is a legendary creature or substance from Jewish midrash said to have been used by Solomon to cut the Temple stones, as the use of iron tools was forbidden at the site.</note>, which is to say Christ, who is compared to a worm and is called so by the Psalmist in Psalm 21 [22], when he says: *And I am a worm and not a man* <note>original: "ואנכי תולעת ולא איש" (ve-anokhi tola'at ve-lo ish)</note>. And he fashioned the most blessed Virgin without iron, that is, without any sin. And just as in the building of the temple, not even the sound of iron was heard, so in the building and conception of the immaculate Virgin, not even the "voice" of original sin was found. For if the most holy matter for her conception had been lacking in him, he would have been in a state of great deficiency, and of a lesser degree than King Solomon. This, however, is false; therefore she was conceived without original sin.

<margin>Seventh reason for the response to Hoogstraten's objection.</margin>
Let the seventh reason be this, as a response to the objection of <term>Hoogstraten</term> <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican inquisitor and a leading opponent of Reuchlin and the "Humanists," who argued against certain doctrines regarding the Virgin.</note>, who says that God does not wish to abolish the rule and order of nature which he himself instituted. We confess indeed that this is true, yet it ought not to be understood in every respect as Hoogstraten himself understands it. For when necessity requires it, God has many times acted against the rule and order of nature. 

It is not the rule and order of nature for a cut and dry tree to produce flowers, leaves, and fruit. Yet the **rod of Aaron** brought forth buds, flowers, leaves, and almonds. Nor is it a work of nature for a tree to bring forth all these things in a single night; yet that same rod of Aaron produced them all in one night. Nor is it according to the course of nature that a tree, whether green or dry, should have a sensitive soul; yet the **rod of Moses** was made into a serpent. Nor is it possible by the order of nature for any brute animal to speak and reason; yet **Balaam’s ass** disputed with him. 

According to the course of nature, prophecy cannot be found except in the human race, for no brute animal can prophesy. Yet we read that God spoke with **Jonah’s whale**. Also, according to the order of nature, it is impossible for the wheel of the heavens to cease from its circular motion; yet in the time of **Joshua**, while he was in the battle of Gibeon, the sun set itself in the middle of the sky and stood still for an entire day, that is, remained immobile for twenty-four hours. It is also impossible according to the order of nature for the wheels of heaven, which move from east to west, to go backward; yet in the time of **Hezekiah**, the sun went backward ten degrees from the journey it had made. It is also impossible according to the course of nature for a lion to cease from its ferocity and restrain itself from killing, especially when it is famished; yet when **Daniel** was cast into the lions' den, the lions brought no harm to him. Also, fire, according to the order of nature, always burns and devours; but for **Ananias, Mishael, and Azariah**, when they were placed in a most fiery furnace...

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely referring to the Three Youths in the fiery furnace from the Book of Daniel.</note> ...suffered no harm, nor was a hair of their clothing damaged. Furthermore, after God created Adam and Eve, he established this rule and order of nature: that a human being could not be generated without the seed of a man and a woman. Yet we find that Christ was generated without human seed. From all these examples, it is clearly evident that whenever necessity requires it, God acts outside the order of nature. Therefore it is plainly obvious that although God does not wish to remove the order of nature in general or in every part, he does so occasionally in particular cases. Nor can he be said to break the rule of nature because of this specific exception. Or, if we wish to speak according to the opinion of the Hebrews, that God does this occasionally due to a special condition, it will be said much less that what he does is "against nature."

<margin>The response of the Talmudists:</margin>
For the Talmudists <note>The "Talmudists" are the Jewish sages who compiled the Talmud; here the author cites a Jewish tradition that God made a "contract" with nature at the moment of creation.</note>, seeing all these things which seem to happen against nature and wishing to give a reason why they occur, say that when God created the world, he granted this faculty to nature: that it should work according to the order instituted by him, but he promised that he would not be bound by it if a specific condition arose. This condition was that if necessity required things to be otherwise, he himself could do whatever seemed right to him, even if it were against nature itself. Therefore, when something of this kind happens, they say nature can by no means complain that it is done against her, because God gave her strength only conditionally. Since, therefore, the glorious Virgin alone among all those born of man and woman was conceived without original sin, it cannot be said to have been against nature, but rather one of the exceptions mentioned above. This is especially true since the person <note>original: "subiectum"</note> of the immaculate Virgin, as shown in the preceding chapter, was fit to receive this kind of perfection, so that she might be produced without the initial stain.

### *Response to the fifth objection of Hoogstraten. And that the undefiled mother of the Messiah was generated without lust and concupiscence. Chapter VIII.*

### **HOGOSTRATVS,**

IF the most blessed Virgin had been conceived without original sin, she would have been generated without lust and concupiscence <note>In medieval theology, "concupiscence" refers to the disordered desire or "tinder" of sin that was believed to be passed down through the physical act of procreation.</note>. This is proved because original sin is mixed with lust, concupiscence, and pleasure. Saint Augustine affirms this in his book *On Faith to Peter*, first part, question twenty-four. His saying is also placed in the *Decretals* <note>The Decretals were the primary source of Canon Law in the Catholic Church during this period.</note> in the section *On Consecration*, fourth distinction, in the chapter beginning *Firmissime*. There it is said: *Hold most firmly, and do not doubt at all, that every human who is conceived through the sexual union of a man and a woman is born with original sin, subject to impiety and subject to death.* <note>original Latin: "Firmissime tene, & nullatenus dubites, omnem hominem qui per concubitum uiri & mulieris concipitur, cum peccato originali nasci, impietati subditum, mortiq; subiectū."</note> Therefore, all those generated from the lust and pleasure of sexual intercourse are conceived with original sin. But the glorious Virgin was generated with the lust and pleasure of intercourse, since she was generated from the very true union of Saint Joachim and Saint Anne, just like other humans. Consequently, it follows that she was conceived in original sin. GAL. <note>The abbreviation "GAL." refers to the author, Pietro Galatino, signaling the start of his rebuttal which will follow on the next page.</note>

The author uses a philosophical principle—that a stronger force or sensation can overwhelm and extinguish a weaker one—to explain how Mary could be conceived by her parents, Joachim and Anne, without the "stain" of original sin (often associated in this period with the "lust" or "fomes" of the sexual act).</meta>

### BOOK SEVEN

...it is: the greater deprives the lesser. For we know by experience that the sun deprives the moon and the candle of their brightness. We also see that a greater sense deprives a lesser one. For a man who places his entire thought and imagination intensely upon one thing, either by studying or by meditating, loses his lesser senses for that time. For if anyone were to pass in front of him then, he would not see the person passing; if one spoke to him, he would not hear. I confess, therefore, that Saint Joachim and Saint Anne joined together as a married couple; however, because of the burning devotion and intense contemplation by which they were both held, with one mind intent upon the generation of the most blessed Virgin, the *fomes* <term>fomes: literally "tinder" or "kindling," a theological term for the inclination toward sin or carnal lust</term> was entirely extinguished in 그 act. Therefore, original sin had no place in the conception of the Immaculate Virgin. 

We are confident, moreover, that we can show the things we say to be true. For when her parents had been expelled with a rebuke from the temple by the priests as if they were profane—because they were sterile and, already worn out by old age, had not yet fathered children—they, grieving and suppliant, asked God to grant them offspring to be procreated for his service. Their prayers having been heard, an angel appeared to each of them separately, announcing that they would give birth to a child for the service of God, saying (according to the testimony of Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a Church Father known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note>): "I am the angel of the Lord sent to you to announce that your prayers have been heard, and your alms have ascended into the sight of the Lord. For I have seen your shame and heard of your sterility—a reproach wrongly cast against you. For God is the avenger of sin, not of nature. And therefore, when he closes someone’s womb, he does so that he might later open it more miraculously. So that what is born may be known to be not of lust, but of a divine gift." 

Therefore, according to the angelic command, the two of them met, rejoiced over their mutual vision, and, being secure and certain of the promised offspring, they adored the Lord and returned home, joyfully awaiting the divine promise. And they joined together with such great devotion that, without lust or bodily pleasure, they fathered the glorious Virgin who was to be the Mother of God. For the most intense devotion and delight of the soul extinguished all bodily pleasure, concupiscence, and lust.

<margin>How Joachim and Anne are interpreted.</margin>
For this reason, the names Joachim and Anne were not undeservedly given to them. For "Joachim" is interpreted in Latin as "God will elevate," or "erect," or "raise up," and also "confirm." The name "Anne" truly is derived from the name *Hen* <note>Hebrew: **חן**</note>, which is "grace." Thus, from the names themselves, it should be openly known that through the offspring they were to bear, God, by the grace of his mercy, would elevate the human race from the sin of our first parents, raise them from eternal death, and erect and confirm them in heavenly glory. Since, therefore, the most blessed Virgin was fathered without concupiscence and lust, it is a necessary consequence that she was also conceived without original sin, since lust and concupiscence were the cause of Adam's sin. Indeed, Adam himself, clinging to worldly vices and carnal concupiscences (as is clear through that passage in Genesis, chapter 3: "And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes...") <note>Original Hebrew: **ותרא האשה כי טוב העץ למאכל וכי תאוה הוא לעינים**</note>

# BOOK SEVEN

<margin>M 2</margin>

...that is: "And the woman saw that the tree was good for eating, and delightful to the eyes" [Genesis 3:6]. He filled himself with pride and disobedience, and transgressed God's command. In this way, he infected his flesh so that all who descend from him are conceived with that same pride and disobedience, which is the origin of all sins. Therefore, it is called "original" or "initial" sin. For this reason, children are procreated with lust and unbridled pleasure, and they are inclined toward fulfilling their own will, making them liable to sin and to transgressing God’s command.

This is most evident to our senses. For when a man is in the grip of unbridled lustful desire, the genital organ becomes so "proud" <note>original: *superbit*; here meaning the organ acts defiantly or independently of rational control</note> and proceeds to carry out the desired pleasure, that even if death were standing before him, he would not cease from that act. This is found to be the case in no other limb. For when someone approaches a theft, and before he completes it, he repents of the crime, his feet immediately stop walking and his hands refrain from the robbery according to his will; they are obedient to the mind. 

Nevertheless, as the <term>Master of Sentences</term> <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1164), whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook of medieval theology</note> says in the 19th distinction of his second book: if the first humans had not sinned, they would have come together in carnal union in paradise without any sin or stain. There would have been an immaculate touch and a joining without carnal desire <note>original: *concupiscentia*</note>. They would have commanded their genital organs just as they did the others, so that they would feel no unlawful movement there. And just as we move other parts of the body toward one another without the heat of lust—such as bringing the hand to the head—so they would have used their genital organs without the "itching" of the flesh. For this lethal sickness took hold of human limbs because of sin. They would therefore have fathered children in paradise through immaculate intercourse without corruption.

> Hence <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Church Father</note> writes on Genesis: Why should we not believe (he says) that the first humans before sin could have commanded their genital organs for procreation, just as they use their other limbs for any work without the itching of pleasure? For it is not incredible that God made those bodies such that, if they did not sin, they would command those members just like feet. They would neither sow with heat nor give birth with pain. But after sin, they earned that movement which marriage regulates and continence restrains. And the weakness prone to the ruin of shame is rescued by the honor of marriage, so that what would have been a duty for the healthy is a remedy for the sick.

From this reasoning, therefore, it is gathered that the undefiled Virgin was conceived without <term>original sin</term>. For although it is not naturally possible for anyone to be propagated without sin—since the "matter" of our bodies is prone to sin because of Adam's infection—the glorious Virgin nevertheless achieved this, not by nature, but by grace, so that she might be propagated without sin. 

For it was more reasonable and fitting that God should have cleansed the matter from which his mother was to be made while she was still the potential matter of the "maker" <note>referring to the parents' role in generation</note>, and before she became the actual matter of the "receiver" <note>the child being formed</note>. Therefore, God took away all bodily lust and unbridled pleasure from Saint <term>Joachim</term> and Saint <term>Anne</term> <note>the traditional names of Mary's parents</note>, so that in that way they might generate the immaculate Virgin herself, just as the first parents would have fathered their children in paradise had they not sinned.

<margin>Response to the argument of Hogostratus.</margin>
From these points, the solution to the objection of Hogostratus <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican theologian and inquisitor who famously opposed the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception.</note> is clear. Regarding the saying of the Blessed Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western theology whose views on original sin were debated by both sides of this argument.</note> which he brings forward, we say that it is indeed true insofar as all humans generated through the sexual union of a man and a woman with bodily lust and pleasure are not free from original sin. However, our statement is even truer: that the glorious Virgin herself was propagated without unbridled lust and bodily pleasure. We maintain that this proceeded from divine grace and will, since she was to be the tabernacle of Him from whose most precious blood the body of Christ—God and man—was to be formed. Therefore, it was necessary that she be the most perfect and purest of all creatures. Augustine himself supports this opinion with his own words; thus, in the book *On Heresies against the Manichaeans*, speaking in the person of Christ, he says: <note>original: "Si potuit inquinari mater mea, cum eam facerem, potui inquinari ego, cum ex ea nascerer."</note> "If my mother could have been defiled when I created her, I could have been defiled when I was born of her." And in the book *On Nature and Grace*, he says: <note>original: "Excepta uirgine Maria, de qua propter honorem Domini mei, cum de peccatis agitur, nullā prorsus uolo facere quæstionē."</note> "Excepting the Virgin Mary, about whom I wish to raise no question at all when the subject is sin, for the sake of the honor of my Lord." And in many other places as well, he proclaims her to be immaculate, most pure, and immune from all sin.

->*Regarding the sixth objection of Hogostratus. And that by the merit of Christ’s passion yet to be offered, the glorious Virgin was redeemed from original sin in the most noble manner.*<-

### Caput IX.

->HOGOSTRATUS,<-

**T**he glorious Virgin was redeemed through Christ's passion. Otherwise, she would have been deprived of such a great good, and Christ would not have existed as the universal redeemer, which is highly unfitting. Therefore, He was also the redeemer and savior of the Virgin herself. She herself confesses this in her song <note>The Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55).</note>, saying: "And my spirit has rejoiced in God my savior." But redemption or salvation presupposes a fault. For she cannot be understood as redeemed and saved unless it is from some fault. Since, therefore, she never had any actual fault, it follows plainly that she was redeemed from original sin. For this reason, it follows that she was conceived in original sin. **GAL.** <note>Likely the author's persona, "Galenus," using a medical/philosophical framework to answer theological questions.</note> Your reasoning is void. For he is equally a redeemer and savior who guards a person so they are not taken captive, as he who frees them from captivity.

<margin>What medicine is.</margin>
In the same way, one is called a physician who gives a person a rule and order so that they preserve their health and do not fall into sickness, just as much as one who heals the sick. For this reason, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose Canon of Medicine was the standard text in Europe for centuries.</note> defined medicine as the science by which the dispositions of the human body are known, both from the part by which it is healed (or infirmity is removed from it) and the part by which health, once possessed, is preserved, and if lost, is recovered. By this same reasoning, we say that he should be called a redeemer and savior who prevents someone from falling into sin, just as much as he who lifts a person up out of sin.

<margin>Twofold redemption.</margin>
From these things, we can say that there is a double redemption: the "lifting" kind and the "preservative" kind.

The author argues, using medical analogies from Avicenna, that Christ's redemption of Mary was "preservative," preventing her from ever falling into sin rather than cleansing her after the fact.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument for the Immaculate Conception, specifically focusing on the "Preservative Redemption" theory. While the previous page addressed objections regarding natural procreation, this page explores the hierarchy of how Christ redeems humanity, arguing that preventing sin is a more "perfect" act of divinity than curing it after the fact.</meta>

<page-num>515</page-num>

<header>SEVENTH [BOOK]</header>

Preservative redemption <note>term: *redemptio præseruatiua* — the act of being saved from falling into sin before it occurs, rather than being cleansed of it afterward.</note> is far nobler and more perfect than restorative redemption <note>term: *redemptio subleuatiua* — literally "lifting-up" redemption; the act of being rescued or "lifted" out of a state of sin after one has already fallen.</note>. For just as it is much better to preserve someone from a wound than to apply a remedy to them after the wound has been received, so it is far nobler and more perfect to preserve someone from sin so they do not fall into it, than to liberate them from sin after they have fallen. Therefore, he who is preserved immune from future sin is redeemed in a nobler and more perfect way, and receives a greater benefit, than he who is snatched away from a sin already committed. Consequently, preservative redemption is much more excellent and perfect than restorative redemption. All other human beings were redeemed from sin by restorative redemption. However, the glorious Virgin alone, among those propagated from a man and a woman, was redeemed by preservative redemption. In this same way, the good angels were redeemed from sin so that they would not fall with Lucifer, as John Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> most excellently perceives. Regarding the immaculate Virgin herself, Anselm <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher; the work cited, *Cur Deus Homo* (Why God Became Man), is a landmark text on the theology of the Atonement.</note> says in the second book of *Why God Became Man*, chapter 10: "The blessed Virgin," he says, "stood in need of redemption and the passion of Christ, not because of sin that was in her, but because of the sin that *would have been* in her, unless He himself had preserved her through a special privilege." Furthermore, the very perfection of human redemption necessarily required this.

<margin>Six modes of redemption.</margin>
There are, indeed, six modes of this redemption. The first is when someone is redeemed from **actual mortal sin** <note>term: *peccatum mortale* — a grave sin committed with full knowledge and consent that "kills" the life of grace in the soul.</note> after they have fallen into it. In this way, sinners who have fallen into mortal sin are redeemed through the Sacrament of Penance. The second mode is when someone is preserved from that same mortal sin. In this way, the Apostles were redeemed; after they received the Holy Spirit, they never committed a mortal sin. The third mode is when someone is redeemed after committing a **venial sin** <note>term: *peccatum ueniale* — a "pardonable" or minor sin that does not destroy the relationship with God but weakens it.</note>. In this way, the just are usually redeemed, for by common law they cannot entirely avoid venial sin. As the saying of the Wise Man goes: *The just man falls seven times a day, and rises again* <note>original: "Septies in die cadat iustus, & resurgat" — a reference to Proverbs 24:16.</note>. This cannot be understood as referring to anything other than venial sin. The fourth mode is when someone is preserved from venial sin itself. In this way, John the Baptist was redeemed, who, as it pleases some to believe, was entirely free from venial sin; for this reason the Church sings of him: *Lest you might be able to stain your life with even a light word* <note>original: "Ne leui saltem maculare uitam, famine posses" — a line from the hymn *Ut queant laxis*, traditionally sung for the Feast of John the Baptist.</note>. The fifth mode is when someone is redeemed from **original sin** <note>term: *peccatum originale* — the state of sin into which all humans are born as a result of the Fall of Adam and Eve.</note> after it has been contracted. In this way, baptized infants are redeemed through the Sacrament of Baptism. Finally, the sixth mode is when someone is preserved unharmed from original sin itself. And in this way, the most blessed Virgin alone among those born of natural propagation was redeemed. Therefore, unless she had been preserved entirely immune from original sin by the merit of the foreseen death of her Son, neither would the human race have been perfectly redeemed, nor would Christ himself have stood as the perfect redeemer of the human race, since he would not have redeemed it in all the ways in which it was meant to be redeemed.

->M 3<-

<margin>What the Tree of Life is.</margin>

The death and passion of Christ were necessary, since divine justice would not spare the human race without them. Therefore, it was necessary for Christ to have a body capable of suffering and mortal. Likewise, since the undefiled Virgin was to give birth to a son capable of suffering and death, who was to be "one flesh" with her; and
<margin>Why the Mother of the Messiah died.</margin>
since a suffering and mortal being cannot naturally proceed from one who is incapable of suffering and immortal, she herself was necessarily mortal as well. For this reason, both the mother and the son died. Nevertheless, the blessed Virgin herself was freed from the incidental evils and punishments resulting from Adam’s sin—those not necessary for Christ’s passion—since she was entirely immune from original sin. This includes giving birth with pain (which was given to Eve as a curse), being defiled by menstruation, and being afflicted by the infirmities arising from sin; the glorious Virgin was entirely free from all of these. And just as the death and passion of Christ and the untouched Virgin were for the redemption of the human race, as has been said, so too Christ’s resurrection—notwithstanding that it was necessary for the confirmation of the Catholic faith—had to occur by necessity, because he was entirely free from original sin. For the same
<margin>The Mother of the Messiah died and soon rose in glory.</margin>
reason, the immaculate Virgin herself rose as soon as she died, and was taken up together with her son into the empyrean heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, thought in medieval cosmology to be the dwelling place of God and the blessed, composed of pure light or fire.</note>, and exalted upon the throne of the heavenly Kingdom; sitting at the right hand of her son, she reigns most gloriously in both soul and body. And therefore the Psalmist <note>original: *Psalmographus* — literally "The Psalm-writer," referring to King David.</note>, speaking in Psalm 132 of the resurrection of the son and the mother, says: **Arise, O Lord, into your rest; you and the ark of your strength.** <note>original Hebrew: *Kūmāh Adonai li-menūḥātekhā, attāh va-arōn ‘uzzekhā*</note> Regarding her sitting at the right hand of her son and the glory of her body, the same says in Psalm 45: **The queen stood at your right hand in a diadem, or golden clothing.** <note>original Hebrew: *Nits’ḇāh sheḡāl li-mīnekha be-kethem Ōp̄īr*</note> Where, by the "golden clothing," is expressed the heavenly and most excellent glory of the body, which is the garment of the soul. CAPITO: And you have indeed rightly said that the glorious Virgin never suffered menstruation, since she had to be most pure, so that (as Augustine says) a most pure son might be born from a most pure mother. Hence also Anselm <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher known for his "Ontological Argument."</note> says: "It was fitting that the Virgin should shine with a purity so great that none greater can be imagined under God." For this reason, she not only had to be most pure from every stain of sin, but no other impurity could be attributed to her. Therefore, since reason itself demands that she be an exception to the rule of women regarding menstruation, I have no doubt that she was never defiled by it.
<margin>The Mother of the Messiah never suffered menstruation</margin>
I would, however, like you to prove this with reasons. GALATINUS: To satisfy your singular devotion toward her, I will prove what you ask with a three-fold reason. First, because she was so well-proportioned and of such a balanced temperament <note>term: *complexionata* — refers to the "complexion" or the balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) which medieval medicine believed determined health and personality.</note> that she completely lacked menstruation. Since Avicenna <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a primary textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> and other natural philosophers write that the cause of menstruation in a woman is an excess of matter. Therefore nature, to expel this kind of excess, found the path of menstruation. However, the glorious Virgin, since...

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
...because of the excellent <term>complexion</term><note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determine a person's health and temperament.</note> she possessed, she had no superfluity of matter within herself. For this reason, menstruation had no place in her. Furthermore, because when a woman suffers her period, she is sickly and in pain all over. Since all such illnesses proceed from the sin of our first parents, and since the untainted Virgin was not at all a partaker in their sin, it clearly follows that she never suffered menstruation. Hence we also do not read

<margin>The third reason.</margin>
that she was ever sick, or labored under any pain. Finally, because a menstruating woman is said to be "polluted" or "unclean," according to what is said in the eighteenth chapter of Leviticus: **And to a woman in the uncleanness of her menstruation you shall not approach.** <note>original Hebrew: ואל אשה בנדת טמאתה לא תקרב (*Ve-el isha be-niddat tumatah lo tikrav*)</note> Therefore, if we were to say the most blessed Virgin suffered menstruation, it would surely follow that she was polluted. If that were so, that word of the Wise Man in the fourth chapter of the Song of Songs, spoken of her in the person of God, would be entirely false: *Thou art all fair, my love; and there is no spot in thee.*

<margin>Objection.</margin>
**HOG.** If the most blessed Virgin had died before the passion of her son, tell me where her soul would have gone? To the lower regions, or into the celestial paradise? For if you say to the celestial paradise, that could in no way have been, since the gates of heaven were not yet open. Therefore, you would have to say she would have descended to the lower regions—specifically to the higher hell, which we call <term>limbo</term><note>Limbus Patrum: the "Limbo of the Fathers," believed to be the place where the righteous who died before Christ's resurrection waited for heaven to be opened.</note>, where the holy fathers descended before the death of Christ. But the holy fathers went there for no other reason than because of original sin. Therefore, she too would have gone there because of original sin. Consequently, it follows that she was also conceived in original sin.

<margin>The first response.</margin>
**GAL.** I give you two responses. For first I say: she would have entered neither place, but would have gone to another most holy place in the heavens.

<margin>The second response.</margin>
Secondly, I say that your premise about her death before the passion of her son is utterly false, since it was impossible for her to have died before the passion of her son.

<margin>It was impossible for the mother of the Messiah to have died before the passion of the Son.</margin>
This is proved by a triple reason. The first is because it had been so pre-ordained by God that she should see the passion of her son. Therefore, it could not have happened otherwise. The second is because it was necessary that she also should intervene for the remission of sin, since all things that had intervened in the perpetration of Adam's sin ought to intervene in its release. Just as that sin was committed by means of a woman, so also by means of a woman it was to be remitted. So that just as a sinful woman brought death into the world, so a most holy and immaculate woman might bring life. According to that saying of Saint Augustine: *Eve was the author of sin, Mary the author of merit. Eve by killing was a hindrance, Mary by bringing life was a help. The former struck, the latter healed.* <note>original: "Auctrix peccati Heua, auctrix meriti Maria..."</note> Finally, the third reason is because God makes no one die before the appointed time, except for two reasons: either on account of their crimes, for which they deserve death, or on account of their goodness and virtues, lest they lose them by sinning. For when God knows someone is about to fall back into sin...

### CAPNIO,

**F**rom what you have said, I judge that the Israelite people were called the special people of God because of the love which God had from eternity toward the mother of the Messiah. GALATINUS: You judge quite correctly. For so great and so immense from eternity was God’s love for the mother of the Messiah, that on her account He made the Israelite people His own special people, because she was to come forth from them. This was most clearly suggested by that Rabbi whose authority among the Hebrews is so great that they call him <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term><note>Hebrew: *Rabbeinu HaKadosh*, "Our Holy Master." This is the traditional title for Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, that is, "Our Holy Master." For in the book called <term>Gale Razeya</term><note>Hebrew: *Galei Razia*, "The Revealer of Secrets." An influential work of Jewish mysticism.</note>, that is, "The Revealer of Secrets," in response to the sixth petition of the Consul Antoninus, he said among other things: "Regarding what you asked: as to why Israel was called the special people of God, I will tell you what I found written by Rabbi Simeon son of Yohai in the book entitled <term>Mechkar Hassodoth</term><note>Hebrew: *Mechkar HaSodot*, "The Investigation of Secrets."</note>, that is, 'The Investigator of Mysteries,' speaking thus: Rabbi Isaiah began his discourse and said: 'Woe to you, Moab; you are lost, O people of Chemosh! He has given his sons into flight and his daughters into captivity.' <note>A reference to Numbers 21:29.</note> Woe to them, woe to them, who are called the fathers of the whole world and of the human race, and moreover, the special people of God." And after a few words: "God, seeing," he says, "that out of Israel was to be cut the stone without hands, which is the primary rock from which the Messiah is to come, who shall extend His mercies over the whole world, therefore He willed Israel to be called the father of the whole world and His special people." Thus far that author. However, Rabbi Nehumias, son of Hakkanah, in <term>Beigereth Hassodoth</term><note>Hebrew: *Iggeret HaSodot*, "The Epistle of Secrets."</note>, that is, in "The Epistle of Mysteries," explaining the aforementioned words, says thus: "This primary rock is the mother of the King Messiah." Therefore, for their clarification, I say that that ancient Doctor felt that Israel was called the special people of God for no other reason than on account of a certain property of theirs hidden from us. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Galatinus and Capnio (Johannes Reuchlin). Galatinus is explaining that things act upon the world in three ways: by quantity, by quality, or by a "hidden property." He uses this philosophical framework to argue that God chose the people of Israel not for their size or their own merit, but for the "hidden property" of being the lineage that would produce the Virgin Mary.</meta>

<page-num>518</page-num>
<header>BOOK II</header>

[nature], or by a certain property innate to itself. That which acts by **quantity** is, for example, food; if someone takes it beyond measure, he falls into stomach pain, but if he takes less than is due, he falls into a wasting disease <note>original: "ethicam," referring to a consumption or "hectic" fever where the body wastes away</note>. That which acts by **quality** is like fire, which heats, and snow, which cools. One of these is hot by the quality of heat, the other cold by the quality of cold. Heat and cold are qualities. Finally, that which acts by a **hidden property** is like the magnet <note>the lodestone</note>, which draws iron to itself; or the little stone that the common people call "turquoise" <note>original: "turchinam"</note>, which, if someone wears it and falls from a high place, the stone is broken if the person's limbs were meant to be broken, but the wearer remains unhurt. Or like the amethyst, which, while it is worn, prevents drunkenness. Or like other little stones and gems having various properties. Regarding these, if anyone asks: "Why do they perform such operations?" the jewelers respond that these things proceed from their hidden property. However, they say the reason for this thing is unknown to them.

But I say that even if such properties are hidden from us, they are nevertheless known to God, who created the world from nothing and instilled a specific power into every single thing. Therefore, He Himself knows best why the magnet draws iron. And so it is with each individual thing. These things having been established, let us ask the Jews: By which of these operations did God choose the Israelite people, so that they might be an elected and peculiar people for Him above all nations: namely, by quantity, or by quality, or by property?

If they say by **quantity**, namely because of their great number, it is entirely false, since it is written in Deuteronomy, chapter 7: *The Lord your God has chosen you to be a peculiar people to Himself out of all the peoples who are upon the earth. Not because you surpassed all nations in number was the Lord joined to you and chose you, since you are fewer than all of them.*

If, however, they respond by **quality**, that is, because of their holy works, this is likewise false, since it is also written in Deuteronomy, chapter 9: *Not because of your righteousness and the uprightness of your heart shall you enter to possess their lands.*

It must therefore be granted that God chose the Israelite people for no other cause than a **hidden property** that was innate to them, which was the immaculate mother of the Messiah who was to proceed from them. Just as that ancient Teacher of theirs asserted, whom we mentioned is called by them <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term> <note>Hebrew: "Our Holy Master," the title of Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century compiler of the Mishnah</note>, that is, our holy Master.

### SEVENTH BOOK

... it is. From which tribe, then, and from which family did the ancient Jews assert she was to come forth? 

**GAL.** From the tribe of Judah, and from the house or family of David. For if it is most abundantly clear, both through the Holy Scripture and through the Talmudic books, that the Messiah was to be born from the tribe of Judah and the house of David, and the ancient Jews themselves handed down the tradition that the Messiah himself was to be generated from a woman without a man (as will be abundantly proven in what follows), it certainly follows that they were by no means ignorant that his mother would also, without a doubt, be from the tribe of Judah and the Davidic line. And to omit others who happened to live before her, that ancient Doctor of theirs, whom they call <term>Our Holy Master</term> <note>original: "Rabbenu Haccados," referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</note>, in that book which he named <term>The Revealer of Secrets</term> <note>original: "Gale Razeya," a mystical work often cited in medieval Christian-Jewish polemics</note>, responding to the third petition of Antoninus, a Consul of the city of Rome, and reporting those things which he had received from Elijah (who appeared to him while he was praying in a cave) among other matters, says this: "Regarding what you asked—whose daughter she would be (that is, the mother of the Messiah, of whom they were speaking) and from which tribe—you should notice that her father will have a double name: one **Eli**, the other **Jehoiakim**. **Eli**, which is a derivative name, shows that he will ascend to a sublime rank. **Jehoiakim**, however, which is a compound name, signifies that God will raise up in his hand the greatest salvation of Israel. Moreover, the tribe of Judah descends from the house of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel. Just as it is written in the fourth chapter of Zechariah: 'Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel, he shall bring forth the primary rock into a plain.' <note>A paraphrase of Zechariah 4:7</note> This primary rock is the mother of the King Messiah." Thus says that *Rabbenu Haccados*. 

**CAP.** Even if certain ancient Jews who lived before the mother of the Messiah predicted that she would be from the tribe of Judah and the house of David, as is clearly shown from these things you have now brought forward, nevertheless, their younger descendants confess indeed that the Messiah will be born from the tribe of Judah and the Davidic line. Consequently, they could not deny this regarding his mother either, if they were willing to concede according to their scriptures that the Messiah himself was to be conceived of a virgin without male seed. <margin>The argumentation of the younger Jews.</margin> But they deny that the glorious Virgin Mary herself, the mother of our Messiah, was descended from the tribe of Judah and the Davidic progeny, since this is not established from the Gospel. For they say: "If Mary, the mother of your Christ, was born from the tribe of Judah and the royal lineage of David, why did the Evangelists, when writing the genealogy of your Christ, make no mention of this? For neither does Luke report it, who traces the genealogy of your Christ from Joseph all the way back to Adam; nor does Matthew attest to this, who, tracing it from Abraham down to Joseph, finally says: 'And Jacob begat Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.' <note>Matthew 1:16</note> Therefore, you must concede one of two things: either your Christ had Joseph as a father, or he himself was not descended from the tribe of Judah and the Davidic line." <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Galatinus and Capnio regarding the lineage of the Virgin Mary. Having established in the previous page that the Messiah’s mother must be from the tribe of Judah, Galatinus now addresses specific genealogical objections and provides his own interpretation of the lineage of Mary versus Joseph.</meta>

->BOOK<-

... let their deceitful lips be silenced <note>original: "fiant eorum labia dolosa"; a reference to Psalm 31:18, often used in polemics to wish for the silencing of opponents</note>. I would like you to prove through their own scriptures that our Holy Virgin Mary descended in a direct line from the Davidic progeny. **GAL.** The impious cunning of the Jews has invented slanders from every side to attack the truth. But it certainly labors in vain, since the very light of truth <margin>Response of some of our people.</margin> cannot remain hidden in the darkness. Therefore, some of our own people, wishing to remove this difficulty, say that Mary and Joseph were from the same tribe. For this reason, Joseph was compelled by the Law to marry her. They say the order of Christ’s generation is traced down to Joseph because it is not the custom of the Scriptures to weave a series of generations through the female line. But while these men indeed speak the truth, they do not at all remove the difficulty that the Jews present to us. For they do not prove that the most blessed Mary herself descended from the tribe of Judah and the house of David, nor consequently that she and Joseph were from one tribe. 

<margin>Another response of some of our people.</margin> Therefore, some others, wishing to prove this, say that Levi—who (as Luke reports) descends in a direct line from the chain of Nathan, the son of David—begot Melchi and Panthera <note>Panthera is a name that appears in early Christian and Jewish traditions; some Christian traditions identified him as an ancestor of Mary, while hostile Jewish traditions used the name "Ben Pantera" as a slur</note>. Then Panthera begot Barpanthera (so called), and Barpanthera begot Jehoiakim. Then Jehoiakim begot the mother of God herself. <margin>Refutation of the aforementioned response.</margin> But these men surely depart far from the truth, and they in no way solve the objection made to us by the Jews. Since it is by no means true (if I may say so with their permission) that Levi begot Melchi and Panthera. On the contrary, Melchi begot Levi himself. As appears clearly enough from Luke, who, following the generation of Christ from the sons back to the fathers, says: *And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, who was of Eli, who was of Matthat, who was of Levi, who was of Melchi.* From this it is clearly evident that Melchi was not the son of Levi, as those men assert, but the father. Even if it were as they say, they still do not prove it to be so through the Gospel or through the scriptures held as authentic by the Jews. Thus, it follows that they by no means satisfy their argument. 

What then shall we say? I will say whatever I myself feel on this matter, yet saving a better judgment and the determination of the Holy Church, <margin>Galatinus’s true response.</margin> to which I always submit myself in all things. We read that David, among others, had two sons: namely, **Solomon** and **Nathan**. Through the line of Solomon descended Joseph, the spouse of the glorious Virgin. But through the line of Nathan descended the most blessed Virgin herself, the mother of the true Messiah. Matthew, therefore, describes the genealogy of Joseph himself by descending through Solomon's line. Luke, however, expresses the progeny of the mother of God by ascending through the line of Nathan. This is especially suggested by the prophecy of Zechariah, who, when he had seen in the spirit that the most blessed Virgin would come forth from Zerubbabel <note>The governor of Judah who led the first wave of Jewish returnees from the Babylonian exile</note>, son of Shealtiel, from whom the Messiah was to be born, spoke thus in the fourth chapter: *Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain. And he shall bring forth the primary stone, and he shall place grace of grace upon it.* <note>original Hebrew: "מי אתה הר הגדול לפני זרובבל למישור והוציא את האבן הראשה תשואות חן חן לה"; see Zechariah 4:7</note> Here, by "the primary stone," he understood the undefiled Virgin, from whom the Messiah was to proceed, as <term>Our Holy Master</term> <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince</note> explained a little earlier.

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the genealogy of the Virgin Mary, specifically addressing the differences between the lineages provided by the Evangelists Matthew and Luke. Galatinus is explaining how Mary's descent from David is verified through the line of Nathan, as opposed to Joseph's descent through Solomon.</meta>

->SEVENTH [BOOK]<-

explained. For this reason, Rabbi Jonathan son of Uzziel <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel was a famous student of Hillel the Elder, to whom the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets is attributed.</note> explains these words of Zechariah, *And he shall bring forth the primary stone* <note>Zechariah 4:7</note>. He explains it in Aramaic thus: *And from this stone the Messiah shall come forth, and his name is for eternity.* <note>original: "ומינה אבנא יפוק משיחא ושמיה יהי לעלמא"</note> This agrees with what the Evangelist says: *In the beginning was the Word.* Why the glorious Virgin is called the "primary stone" has been discussed in the preceding pages. 

It should be noted, however, that this Zerubbabel <note>A governor of Judah who led the first wave of Jewish exiles back from Babylon; his name appears in two different New Testament genealogies.</note> is the one of whom Luke writes while weaving the genealogy of the Virgin herself through the line of Nathan. He is not the one mentioned by Matthew, who describes Joseph’s genealogy through the line of Solomon. This is because there were two men named Zerubbabel, and two named Shealtiel, who were the fathers of those Zerubbabels. This is especially clear from the fact that the Zerubbabel of whom Matthew writes was born two generations after the Babylonian exile. For he says: *Josiah begat Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the Babylonian exile. Jeconiah begat Shealtiel. Shealtiel begat Zerubbabel.* 

But the Zerubbabel mentioned by Zechariah and Luke lived before the Babylonian exile. This can be clearly seen from the words of the prophet Haggai, who says in the second chapter: *The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the High Priest, and to the remnant of the people, saying: Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory?* From these words, it appears that this Zerubbabel had seen the House of God in its first building <note>Solomon's Temple, before it was destroyed by the Babylonians.</note>, and consequently was born before the Babylonian exile itself. 

Furthermore, the prophecy of Zerubbabel himself took place during the exile; indeed, he led the people out of that same exile, as is held in the second chapter of Ezra. From these things, therefore, it is openly shown that the Zerubbabel written about by Zechariah and Luke was one person, and the one mentioned by Matthew was another. Therefore, in the genealogy described by Matthew, only eleven generations are placed from Zerubbabel to Joseph. However, in the one Luke deals with, many more are found from Joseph to Zerubbabel, because of the greater span of time that intervened. 

From all of this, it is plainly gathered that the glorious Virgin Mary, the mother of our Savior, stood from the tribe of Judah and the royal lineage of David, and proceeded through the direct line of Nathan, the son of David, which Luke describes so well. If anyone should object to what we have said because no mention is made of Saint Joachim, the Virgin’s father, in the series of that genealogy: I say that Heli was Joachim himself, who is placed first in the ascending order. For among the Syrians, "Joachim," "Eli," and "Eliakim" are the same name, as Philo the Jew writes. Hence, the father of the Messiah’s mother was called both Eli and Joachim, just as Rabbi Haccados <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishna, often called "Our Holy Rabbi" (Rabbeinu HaKadosh).</note> had predicted earlier through the revelation of Elijah, as was shown in the premises. This was afterwards excellently testified by Rabbi Haccanas, the son of Rabbi Nehunia.

<margin>Question.</margin>
**CAP.** If Joseph was not his son, but rather the son of Jacob himself, as Matthew records in his genealogy, for what reason does Luke call Joseph himself the son of Eli, saying: *Who was of Eli*, namely, the son?

<margin>Response of some of our people.</margin>
**GAL.** Some of our people say that Jacob and Eli were brothers, and when Eli died without children, his brother Jacob married his wife to raise up seed and a name for him (as the Law commanded), and from her he fathered Joseph himself. For that reason, they say he had one father according to nature and the other according to the Law <note>This refers to the "Levirate marriage," a Jewish custom where a man married his deceased brother's widow to continue the family line.</note>.

<margin>Refutation of the aforementioned response.</margin>
But to tell the truth, they are greatly mistaken. First, because although Jacob and Eli were from the same tribe and issued from the Davidic stock, they could not have been brothers. Since one descended through the line of Solomon and the other through the line of Nathan, they were quite distantly related. Furthermore, when someone married the wife of a deceased brother, they would give the name of the deceased brother to the son they had from her, according to the ancient institution. This was so that he might raise up both seed and name for his brother, as the Law commanded both to be raised. Therefore, if Jacob (as they say) had taken the wife of his deceased brother Eli, he would have given Joseph the name not of Joseph, but of Eli, just as the deceased had been called. I say, therefore, saving better judgment:

<margin>Galatinus's response.</margin>
Because spouses were made "one flesh" through a true marriage, according to 그 passage in Genesis: *They shall be two in one flesh*, therefore the father of one spouse was rightly called the father of the other. This is also confirmed in *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>A significant collection of ancient Jewish interpretations of the Book of Genesis.</note>, upon that passage in Genesis chapter 37, which says: *And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him* <note>original: "ויקומו כל בניו וכל בנותיו לנחמו"</note>, namely Jacob. For it is said there: "Why is it said 'all his daughters,' when Jacob had only one daughter, namely Dinah? Because it is not prohibited for a man to call his son-in-law his son, and his daughter-in-law his daughter." And although carnal intercourse did not occur between the most blessed Virgin and Joseph, there was nonetheless a true marriage between them, and thus they were true spouses. The angel testified to this when he said in the first chapter of Matthew: "Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit." For that reason, Joseph could not inaptly be called the son of

"In the days of the King Messiah, one shall not say to another, 'Teach me knowledge,' because it is written: *And a man or anyone shall no longer teach his brother, for they shall all know me, from the smallest of them to the greatest of them.* <note>original: "In diebus regis Meſſiæ... à paruulis eorum uſque ad maiores eorum." A reference to Jeremiah 31:34.</note> Moreover, in that time the **Ancient of Days** <note>A title for God from the Book of Daniel, used extensively in Kabbalistic literature to refer to the most hidden aspect of the Divine.</note> shall awaken, and the spirit which came forth from the **closed womb** <note>original: "uulua clauſa," referring to the womb of the Messiah's mother remaining sealed/virginal.</note>. Truly, when he himself rises, all spirits shall rise with him. And who are those? These are certainly they who are gifted with the holy crowns of the **Lesser Countenance**." <note>original: "iunioris facierum," likely a translation of the Kabbalistic term *Zeir Anpin*, referring to the manifested attributes of God.</note> Thus he spoke above. Where I do not know what could have been said more clearly regarding the divinity of the Messiah and the virginity of his mother, long before the birth of the virgin herself.

Furthermore, the virginity of the Messiah’s mother was shown and declared beforehand through **figures** <note>In theology, a "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament person or event believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note>. And first indeed through that which is read in Exodus chapter 3: **And he saw, and behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed. And Moses said: I will go near now and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned.** <note>original Hebrew: *Vayar vehineh hasneh boer ba-esh vehasneh einennu ukkal: vayomer Moshe asurah-na ve-ereh et hamareh hagadol hazeh madduah lo yivar hasneh*</note>. It follows: *And God called to him from the midst of the bush.* And shortly after: *And he said to him, I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.*

In this event, the birth of the Son of God from an untouched and incorruptible virgin was miraculously shown to Moses. For by the bush being set on fire and yet not consumed, it was shown that he would come forth from that people while the integrity of his mother remained intact. He, by the fire of his divinity, would take on the nature of human flesh—like the thorns of a bush—and yet preserve the unconsumed substance of humanity within the very flame of divinity.

It is also read in the Book of Judges, chapter 6, that Gideon spoke thus: **If there shall be dew on the fleece only, and dryness upon all the earth, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken.** <note>original Hebrew: *im tal yihyeh al-hagizzah levaddah veal-kol-haaretz horev ve-yadati ki toshia beyadi et-yisrael kaasher dibbarta*</note>. And it was done so. In this, the fleece—which is the garment of a lamb—signifies human nature, which the dew of divinity assumed. The dry earth, truly, is the virgin’s womb, not infused by human seed. However, what is said afterward—that the fleece alone was dry, and all the earth had dew—signifies that the "garment" of Christ was not infused <note>original: "infuſus," suggesting it was not produced by natural human generation</note>, while the whole "earth" of the virginal body was imbued by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The virginity and integrity of the Mother of God was also signified in the **Rod of Aaron**. By the power of God alone, without any external moisture, it flowered, grew leaves, and produced fruit, sweet and useful to both the healthy and the sick. For thus it is read of it in Numbers chapter 17: **And behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi flowered, and brought forth a flower, and sprouted a bud, and perfected the almond.** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-hineh parah matteh-aharon le-veit levi vayotse pherach vayatsits tsits vayigmol sheqedim*</note>. Nor does it hinder us that it is said here that the rod of Aaron flowered for the house of Levi. For the Messiah was to be born not only from the tribe of Judah, but also from the tribe of Levi, and even from the Gentiles. Therefore, against all laws of nature, the rod of Aaron produced what could not be supplied by seed or root. Thus, the rod was able to produce nuts against nature, and the Virgin Mother of God could not...

### Refutation of the recent oppositions of the Jews who attack the virginity of the Messiah’s mother. Chapter XV.

## CAPNIO,

Even though these things are so, our contemporary Jews, desiring to attack the virginity of the Messiah's mother, do not cease to contradict in many ways that wonderful sign concerning the virginal conception and birth given by Isaiah and introduced by you. They consider it impossible that a virgin would conceive and bear a son. Therefore, they assert that these words of Isaiah, when he said, "The *Alma* <note>original: "Alma." A Hebrew word (*'almah*) at the center of a centuries-long debate; Christians translated it as "virgin," while Jewish scholars argued it simply meant "young woman."</note> shall conceive and bear a son," should not be understood as referring to the mother of the Messiah, as their ancestors explained them and as the Catholic faith affirms those same words were predicted concerning the glorious Virgin Mary. On this account, they are accustomed to make many arguments against us. I desire you to respond using their own scriptures so that their barking <note>The author uses "latratus" (barking), a common bit of harsh 16th-century polemical language used to dismiss the arguments of opponents.</note> against the mother of the Messiah may be silenced. First, they argue thus:

<margin>The first argument of the Jews.</margin>
"This sign," they say, "which the prophet gave, was a sign of the future liberation of King Ahaz from the two kings who had come against him. However, your Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz. Therefore, this sign could not have been of his conception from a virgin (as you say)."

GALATINUS. It will be easy for us to respond to this argument if we first <margin>The solution.</margin> note a summary of the history for the understanding of prophetic truth. At the time, therefore, when Ahaz was reigning in Judea, two powerful kings—specifically those of Syria and Israel—had besieged Jerusalem with a massive army, as is written in Isaiah chapter 7 and 2 Kings 16. Then the Lord God sent Isaiah to Ahaz to warn him not to fear the army of those kings. But he, being wicked and unbelieving (for he was a worshiper of idols), refused to believe the prophet's words. For which reason the prophet warned him that, since he did not believe him, he should ask for some sign of his liberation to be performed, saying: "Ask a sign or a miracle for yourself from the Lord your God. Make the request deep, or lift it up high." <note>Quoting Isaiah 7:11.</note> That is: Ask for a sign of your liberation to be made, whether from the depth of hell through the resurrection of some dead person, or from heaven through the standing still of the sun, as was done in the time of Joshua. But he—
