...since he was wicked, and unwilling to ask for a sign from God, he offered an excuse: that to do so would be to tempt God. Whence he said, "I will not ask, and I will not tempt," or "I will not exalt God." For the word <term>נסא (nasa)</term> <note>The author is discussing the Hebrew root used in Isaiah 7:12. While the standard text uses *nasah* (to test/tempt), the author links it to *nasa* (to lift or exalt) to show the king's duplicity.</note>, which is placed there, signifies both to tempt and to exalt. Therefore, when Isaiah realized that Ahaz had spoken this not in good faith, but rather because he had very little fear of God, the prophet judged him unworthy of such a sign. He refused to give the sign to him personally, but instead gave it to the House of David, saying: "Hear then, O House of David. Is it too little for you to weary men, that you must also weary my God? Because of this, the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she herself shall call his name Emmanuel." From these words it is clear that the sign of the virgin’s conception and birth was not given to Ahaz himself, but to the House of David, from whose seed the Messiah was to be born according to the flesh. Therefore, one must reject the argument that says this sign was given specifically to Ahaz. Furthermore, regarding the objection that Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz, and thus his conception from a virgin could not be a sign of the predicted liberation from those two kings: we say that a twofold sign is found in Holy Scripture.

<margin>
A twofold sign: prognostic and memorial.
</margin>

One is <term>prognostic</term> <note>From the Greek *prognostikos*, meaning foretelling or predicting a future event.</note>, the other is <term>memorial</term> <note>Latin: *rememoratiuum*. A sign that serves as proof of a past promise or authority after the event has occurred.</note>. A prognostic sign is indeed in respect to a future outcome. Of this sort was the sign given to Gideon in the fleece (as told in Judges, chapter 6) as an indication of a future victory. But a memorial sign is in respect to the past. Of this sort was the sign the Lord gave to Moses in Exodus, chapter 3, saying: <gloss>And this shall be a sign to you that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: וזה לך האות כי אנכי שלחתיך בהוציאך את העם ממצרים תעבדון את האלהים על ההר הזה</note> That is to say: "You will offer sacrifices upon this mountain, giving thanks to me for this mission which is now imposed upon you." Therefore, the sign concerning the virgin’s conception and birth was memorial, not prognostic. Nor does the great distance of time stand in the way, since a memorial sign looks back to the past across a great distance just as a prognostic sign looks forward to the future. It was certainly fitting for this sign to be given at a great distance, so that Ahaz, who was faithless toward the word of the prophet, might find that sign as far removed from himself as he was far removed in his own mind from believing it. Yet those who were to descend from him were eventually destined to see it. Therefore, this sign was given not to him, but to the House of David.

**CHAPTER.** Next, they object: that where our edition <note>The Vulgate (Latin) translation of the Bible.</note> says, "Behold, a virgin," the Hebrew letter says, "Behold <term>העלמה (ha-alma)</term>."

<margin>
The second Jewish argument.
</margin>

They say that among them, *Alma* does not signify a "virgin," but a "young woman," a term used for both a virgin and one who has been defiled. They say, therefore, that the prophet was speaking not of the conception and birth of a virgin, but of a young woman. For if he had spoken of a virgin's conception, he would not have said "Behold, *alma*" (that is, a young woman), but "Behold <term>בתולה (bethula)</term>," which is the specific word for virgin.

<margin>
The Solution.
</margin>

**GALATINUS.** There are (as you know) three words among the Hebrews that signify almost the same thing: namely, <term>Naara</term>, <term>Bethula</term>, and <term>Alma</term>. For *Naara* refers only to age, meaning a girl...

signifies a girl or a young woman, whether she is a virgin or has been defiled. **Bethula**, however, having regard only to virginity, signifies a "virgin," whether she be a young girl or an old woman. But **Alma**, having regard to both aspects—namely, to youth and to virginity—designates both a young woman and a virgin. Therefore, a woman, whether she be young or aged, as long as she is a virgin, can be called **bethula**. On the other hand, as long as she is a young woman, whether she is a virgin or has been defiled, she is called **naara**. But no woman can be called **alma** unless she is both a young woman and an untouched virgin.

This is also clearly indicated by the interpretation of the word itself. For <term>עלמה</term> (alma) <note>Hebrew: "young woman" or "maiden."</note> is derived from the verb <term>עלם</term> (alam) <note>Hebrew root: "to hide" or "to conceal."</note>, which signifies "to hide" or "to conceal," as Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as Radak, was a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator. The author is citing his work "Sefer Shorashim" (Book of Roots).</note> says in the book *Shorashim*. It is just as it is said in Psalm 90: <term>שת עוֹנֹתינוּ לנגדך עלוּמנוּ למאור פניך</term>, which is: "Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins <note>original: "abścondita nośtra" (our hidden things)</note> in the light of thy countenance." And again in Psalm 44: <term>הוּא יודע תעלמֹת לב</term>, that is: "He knoweth the secrets <note>original: "abścondita" (hidden things)</note> of the heart." And in Job, chapter 28: <term>ותעלמה יוציא אוֹר</term>, that is: "And the thing that is hid <note>original: "abścondita"</note> he bringeth forth to light." Likewise in Genesis, chapter 24: <term>העלמה היֹצאת לשאֹב</term>, that is: "The maiden <note>alma</note> coming out to draw water." All these things (says Rabbi Kimhi) signify hiding and concealment.

For this reason, **alma** signifies among them a young woman hidden, concealed, and kept away from the sight of men, and entirely untouched, concerning whose modesty and integrity there is no doubt—especially when the "article" is prefixed to it, which among the Hebrews is this letter <term>ה</term> (he) <note>The Hebrew definite article, equivalent to "the" in English.</note>. This letter causes a word to signify something specific, and it is often added to things which are either well-known or have been mentioned previously. In the entire Holy Scripture, this word <term>העלמה</term> (**ha-alma**) is not found written with the letter *he* (the article) except in three places. 

The first is indeed in Genesis, chapter 24, when it is said of Rebecca: <term>הנה אנכי נצב על עין המים והיה העלמה היֹצאת לשאֹב ואמרתי אליה השקיני נא מעט מים מכדך</term>, that is: "Behold, I stand by the well of water, and it shall be that **the maiden** <note>ha-alma</note>, that is, the virgin coming out to draw water, and I shall say to her: Give me, I pray thee, a little water to drink from thy pitcher." Now, while she was called **alma**, she was a virgin and untouched, as is clear from the text, which says of her in the same place: <term>בתולה ואיש לא ידעה</term>, that is: "A virgin, and no man had known her." 

Next, it is found in Exodus, chapter 2, when it is written thus of Miriam, the sister of Moses: <term>ותלך העלמה ותקרא את אם הילד</term>, that is: "And **the maiden** <note>ha-alma</note>, that is, the virgin, went and called the child's mother." And she too was then a young virgin. 

Finally, the third is found here in Isaiah, as was shown a little while ago. Excepting only these three places, nowhere else in the entire Holy Page among the Hebrews is this word **ha-alma** found written with the article. If, therefore, the first two women so named were untouched virgins when they were so called, the same must be held regarding this woman of whom Isaiah speaks. For according to the opinion of the wise, concerning things that are entirely similar, the judgment must be entirely the same. For that reason, the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, when they came to this passage, translated **ha-alma** as "the virgin" with the article prefixed, saying: <term>ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος</term> <note>Greek: "Behold, the virgin."</note> and so forth. And that it must be understood in this way...

That it ought to be so is also clear from this: that the sign given by Isaiah for the liberation of the city, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator known as Rashi.</note> says, had to be truly miraculous. For a young girl to conceive and bear a son without her virginity remaining is no miracle, since this happens naturally every day. Therefore, it must necessarily be said that the sign which the prophet gave them—namely, that a virgin would conceive and bear a son—was to be beyond the course of nature and brought about by the miracle of God alone. 

Thus, to respond to the Jewish objection, the woman who was to conceive and bear the Son of God had to be both a young girl or maiden and an entirely untouched virgin. For this reason, so that Isaiah might imply both, he said, "Behold, <term>haalma</term>" <note>Hebrew for "the young woman/virgin."</note> which (as has been said) signifies both youth and virginity. He did not say, "Behold, <term>bethula</term>," <note>Hebrew for "virgin."</note> which designates only one of those aspects. Furthermore, if he had said "Behold, <term>bethula</term>," he would not have prefigured the absolute virginity of the Messiah's mother. For <term>bethula</term>, even if it signifies a virgin, does not always mean one who is entirely untouched. 

Rabbi Solomon clearly shows this when commenting on that passage in Genesis chapter 24 <note>Genesis 24:16, describing Rebecca.</note> where it says <term>Bethula</term> (that is, she was a virgin) and "a man had not known her." Seeking to give the reason for this, he asks: if the text already said she was a <term>Bethula</term> (a virgin), why did it add "and a man had not known her"? He says: <insert>A virgin in the place of virginity, and a man had not known her in an unnatural way; <note>original: "she-lo k-darkhah," a rabbinic phrase referring to non-vaginal intercourse.</note> because the daughters of the nations preserve themselves in the place of virginity, but abandon themselves in another way; therefore the verse testifies of this woman that she was clean in every way.</insert> <note>This is a translation of the Hebrew citation from Rashi's commentary.</note> 

That is to say: she was a virgin, and a man had not known her—specifically through an improper way. For the daughters of the heathens would guard their bodies in the place of virginity, but would prostitute themselves in another place. It is clear from this that she was clean in her entirety, that is, completely unknown and untouched. From these things it is manifest that <term>bethula</term> does not mean someone entirely untouched and unknown by a man, since she could be corrupted against nature and yet still be "known" by men. <term>Alma</term>, however, signifies one who is entirely untouched and completely unknown to either way.

The author argues that "the way of a man in a virgin" refers to the miraculous conception.</note> That is: Three things are separate, or distant from me, or are wonders to me, and a fourth I have not known at all. The way of an eagle in the heavens, the way of a snake upon a rock, the way of a ship in the heart (or in the midst) of the sea, and the way of a man in <term>alma</term> (that is, in a virgin). ...its last way—that is, from his ascension into heaven—he finally arrived at the first, which is his incarnation that was to come from a virgin. Regarding these "ways," let us seek no other interpreter than the one whom they themselves call <term>Rabbenus Haccados</term> <note>Hebrew: "Rabbeinu HaKadosh," meaning "Our Holy Rabbi," the title given to Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, that is, our holy Master. # BOOK SEVEN

...that is, with the definite article placed before it, as if speaking of a well-known person among the prophets, and of whom Solomon had already made mention. 

### CHAPTER. On the perversity of the Jews of our age. 
<margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin> 
The perversity of the Jews of our time, against what has been said concerning the *alma* <note>The Hebrew term *almah*, which Christians translate as "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14, but which Jewish critics often translate as "young woman."</note>, still crying out with mocking and blasphemy, says: "Follow the text you have introduced! Read further what follows in Proverbs, chapter 30. For you will find it written there immediately: <term>Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, 'I have done no wrong.'</term> <note>original Hebrew: *ken derek ishah menafet akelah umachatah piha veamarah lo paalti aven* (Proverbs 30:20).</note>" 

Behold, they say, that *alma* in this place can be nothing but a corrupt woman, because she is compared to an adulterous woman.

<margin>Refutation.</margin> 
To restrain their audacity, it is answered that Solomon’s words in this book are called <term>Misle</term> <note>Hebrew: *Mishlei*, the title of the Book of Proverbs.</note>, that is, Proverbs or parables, because they almost always present one thing on the surface while intending another. Otherwise, a <term>Massal</term> <note>Hebrew: *Mashal*, meaning a parable, proverb, or similitude.</note>—that is, a parable, or a likeness, or an example—will not be a parable if it is understood entirely as it sounds. We ought not, therefore, to take "the way of the adulterous woman" literally here, but rather as the life and most wicked way of acting of someone else who imitates the deeds of an adulterous woman. 

For this reason, certain ancient Jews understood "the way of the adulterous woman" in this place to mean the transgression of our first parent <note>Adam</note>. Wherefore that same man, whom we said is called by them <term>Rabbeno Haccados</term> <note>Hebrew: *Rabbeinu HaKadosh*, "Our Holy Master," referring to Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi.</note>, that is, our Holy Master, explaining this passage in the same place, says: "*Such is the way of an adulterous woman.* Along with the rest, Adam did all this, who excused himself for his sin and refused to confess it, but said: 'The woman whom you gave to be my companion gave to me from the tree, and I ate.' He acted like a harlot who eats and cleans her mouth, contending that she has done nothing wrong. For this reason, it is consistent with reason that the whole world should be struck. And when the time of salvation comes, it is right that God should descend to the lower regions and save them." 

And this is what was said in the second chapter of Jeremiah: <term>Behold, I will enter into judgment with you because you say, "I have not sinned."</term> <note>original Hebrew: *hinni nishpat otak al amrek lo chatati* (Jeremiah 2:35).</note> Likewise in the sixty-sixth chapter of Isaiah: <term>For by fire the Lord will be judged.</term> <note>original Hebrew: *ki va-esh Adonai nishpat* (Isaiah 66:16). While modern translations usually say "the Lord will execute judgment," the author uses the Latin *iudicabitur* (will be judged) to suggest God's personal involvement or the Messiah's suffering.</note> Thus he spoke.

We, however, can say that by "the way of this adulterous woman," the faithlessness of the Jews is also aptly designated. To whom it is said by the Lord
<margin>The Jews are compared to an adulterous woman.</margin>
through Isaiah in the fifty-seventh chapter: <term>But you, come here, sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer and the prostitute.</term> <note>original Hebrew: *ve-atem kirvu hinnah bene anonah zera menaf ve-tizneh* (Isaiah 57:3).</note> Concerning them it is also written in the sixteenth chapter of Ezekiel: "Thus says the Lord God to Jerusalem." And further below: <term>And you were not like a harlot who scorns a fee, but like an adulterous wife who receives strangers instead of her husband</term> <note>or "on behalf of her husband." Original Hebrew: *velo hayit kezona lekalles etnan... ha-ishah ha-menafet tachat isha tikach et zarim* (Ezekiel 16:31-32).</note>. And after some other things in the same place: <term>And I will judge you with the judgments of adulteresses and those who shed blood, and I will give you the blood of fury and jealousy.</term> <note>original Hebrew: *ushfatich mishpete noafot veshofkot dam unetatich dam chemah vekinah* (Ezekiel 16:38).</note> That is, and I will judge you in the judgments...

<summary>The author refutes Jewish claims that the word "alma" in Proverbs 30 refers to a non-virgin by arguing that the book is parabolic. He uses ancient Jewish commentary to link the "adulterous woman" to Adam's sin and the unfaithfulness of Israel rather than the "alma" herself.</summary>

-># BOOK SEVEN<-

<margin>The Jews’ lying is delightful to them.</margin>
...with the judgments of adulteresses and those who shed blood, and I will give you the blood of fury and jealousy <note>original: "iudicijs adulterarum & effundentium fanguinem, & dabo te fanguinẽ furoris & zeli" — a reference to Ezekiel 16:38, comparing Israel's infidelity to adultery.</note>. From these things, therefore, it is clear that the "adulterous woman" in the aforementioned parable of Solomon is the Jewish Synagogue. She eats, and she does not cease to eat, that bread which is most flavorful to her, of which it is written in Proverbs, chapter 20: *Bread of deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel.* <note>original Hebrew: *Arev le-ish lechem shaker ve-achar yimale pihu chatzatz* (Proverbs 20:17).</note> That is to say: the bread of lies is most flavorful to a man, and afterward, or finally, his mouth will be filled with gravel. "Gravel" in this place is nothing other than the eternal punishment of hell. For since gravel is hard, it cannot be chewed, nor consumed, nor swallowed, nor spat out when the whole mouth is full. So the punishment of hell is indeed most hard and durable; it can in no way be escaped, nor ended, nor diminished, nor softened by any moisture of tears. 

That the "bread of lies" is sweet and flavorful to the Jews is shown most of all by what is said of them in Jeremiah, chapter nine: *And they do not speak the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak lies.* <note>original Hebrew: *ve-emet lo yedaberu limedu leshonam dabar shaker* (Jeremiah 9:5).</note> Likewise, in the fifth chapter of the same book: *And though they say, "As the Lord lives," surely they swear falsely.* <note>original Hebrew: *ve-im chai YHWH yomeru lachen lashaker yishabeu* (Jeremiah 5:2).</note>

Just as, therefore, the "way of an eagle in the sky," and the "way of a serpent or snake upon a rock," and the "way of a ship in the heart or middle of the sea," and the "way of a man" or a powerful one—that is, of God into the <term>alma</term> <note>The Hebrew word *almah*, which the author argues refers to the Virgin Mary.</note>, that is, into the virgin—were made wonderful and difficult for Solomon, and stood far beyond his understanding; so too was the most wicked "way" of this adulterous woman quite wonderful to him, and very distant from his reason. 

For how could Solomon’s reason have grasped or contained the immensity of malice, the depth of impiety, and the scale of treachery by which this "adulteress" <note>The Synagogue, in the author's allegory.</note> was going to condemn the just and entirely innocent Messiah to death, while asking for the seditious murderer Barabbas to be released? 

<margin><unclear>Miracles of the Messiah</unclear></margin>
Or how would the intellect of that same wise man have been sufficient to comprehend by what foolishness, by what insanity, by what poverty of mind, or by what diabolical envy she was stimulated—or by what evil demon driven—that she could reject the true Messiah? He who by a word alone gave light to the blind, directed the lame, cured the weak, cleansed the lepers, restored speech to the mute and hearing to the deaf, liberated the demon-possessed, and satisfied several thousand men from a few loaves of bread. 

And yet, she would instead receive two false Messiahs, who had never done any such thing, one after the other, as the true Messiah: namely, <term>Bencozba</term> <note>A derogatory name for the rebel leader Simon bar Kokhba, meaning "Son of a Lie."</note> before the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and <term>Barcozba</term> at Betar <note>The site of the final battle of the Bar Kokhba revolt (135 AD).</note> not long after the burning of that same city. She ought to have held these men in horror and suspicion from their names alone, since both names are interpreted as "son of a lie" or "of falsehood." 

Most excellently, therefore, did Solomon himself, marveling at the height of the mysteries of the Messiah and the ingratitude, impiety, and treachery of this adulterous woman, add these words: *Such is the way of an adulterous woman.*

The author claims this rejection was a "way" so wicked it was beyond Solomon's comprehension.</summary>

# BOOK VII

...and indeed, it is a thing so admirable, and so difficult to understand, and stupendous beyond what can be expressed. She <note>Referring to the "adulterous woman" or the Synagogue from the previous page.</note> both eats and never ceases to eat so greedily the bread of so many lies. And as if wiping her mouth, as if she has done no evil, she does not know how to blush. And this is what is said to her in Jeremiah, chapter 3: <note>original Hebrew: *u-metzach isha zonah hayah lach me'anta hikkalem* (Jeremiah 3:3)</note> *You had the forehead of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed.* Since things are so, notwithstanding the barking of their <note>The Jewish critics.</note> oppositions against the virginity of the mother of the Messiah, the previously mentioned words of Isaiah are to be explained thus: *Behold, the virgin* <note>original Hebrew: *ha-almah* (Isaiah 7:14). Galatinus argues this specific term implies a hidden or pure virgin.</note>, <margin>Exposition of the aforementioned words of Isaiah.</margin> that is, the holy and hidden virgin herself, whom Solomon mentioned long before, will conceive by divine power and bear a son. And the virgin herself—forewarned and instructed by the angel Gabriel, and filled with the Holy Spirit—shall call his name **Emmanuel**, which is the same as "God with us," by which the divine and human natures are clearly demonstrated in the one person of the Messiah. As for the other arguments of the Jews, which they are accustomed to bring against us to pervert the true sense of this prophecy, we have already responded more fully in the third book, where we showed that the Messiah was to be called Emmanuel.

### ->That the mother of the Messiah was to conceive the Son of God through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit. Chapter XVI.<-

### ->REUCHLIN,<-
<note>The character "Capnio" is the scholar Johann Reuchlin.</note>
not without reason I would like to know whether the ancient Jews, just as they foretold that the mother of the Messiah as a virgin would conceive and give birth, also foretold that she ought to conceive from the Holy Spirit. **GALATINUS.** That was indeed foretold by the prophets long ago, and expressly explained by the ancient Jewish teachers. For concerning the prophets, Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Holy Spirit, says in the 8th chapter: <note>original Hebrew: *ve-ekrav el ha-neviah va-tahar va-teled ben* (Isaiah 8:3)</note> *And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.* <margin>The false exposition of the Jews.</margin> **REUCHLIN.** The younger Jews <note>Medieval Jewish commentators, whom Galatinus often contrasts with "ancient" authorities.</note> explain these words as referring to the approach of Isaiah himself through sexual intercourse with his wife. # SEVENTH BOOK

...thus Jonathan <note>Rabbi Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Targum (Aramaic paraphrase) of the Prophets.</note> translated into the Aramaic <note>The text uses the term "Chaldaean," a common historical term for Aramaic.</note>: **And the Lord said to me: Call his name: Swift to the spoiling of the spoil, and quick to the plundering of the prey.** <note>original Aramaic: *Ve-amar YHVH li krei shemeh ochi le-mivaz biza u-le-madi adach*</note> That is, And God said to me, Call his name: Swift to spoil the spoils, and quick to plunder the prey. These things in no way fit the son of Isaiah. Since he was never called by such a name, nor is there any mention made in Holy Scripture of his name, nor of his life, nor of his deeds, nor of his death. Therefore, they do not fit him, but most appropriately fit the Messiah. For He was to be swift to spoil hell <note>Refers to the "Harrowing of Hell," a traditional Christian belief that Christ descended into the underworld to liberate the souls of the righteous.</note>, and quick to plunder—that is, to take away from the devil the prey which he possessed because of the sin of the first man. Our Messiah testified that this was to be fulfilled in himself, when he said in Luke, chapter 11: *When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are in peace. But when one stronger than he assails him and overcomes him, he takes away his entire armor in which he trusted, and distributes his spoils.* But concerning the preceding matters, let us ask two things of the Jews.

<margin>The first question to be asked of the Jews.</margin>
First, for what purpose did the prophet bring in those witnesses? Did he truly have need of witnesses when he approached his wife for intercourse? For it is a foul thing even to think of this, let alone to say it.

<margin>The second question.</margin>
Then, who exactly were these witnesses? Namely, **Uriah** the priest and **Zechariah** son of Jeberechiah <note>The text uses the Latin "Barachiae," which is the equivalent of the Hebrew "Berechiah."</note>. For it is certain that this Uriah was not that worshiper of idols, as some of our own people think, to whom Ahaz (as is read in 2 Kings, chapter 16) <note>original: *4. Regum 16*. In the Latin Vulgate, 1 and 2 Kings are titled 3 and 4 Kings.</note> wrote letters from Damascus. Rather, he is the one whom Jeremiah mentions in chapter 26, saying: *There was a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah the son of Shemaiah, whom King Jehoiakim also killed.* It is also certain that this Zechariah, son of Jeberechiah, was the one who is the eleventh among the number of the twelve [Minor] Prophets. For according to the expositions of the Hebrews, Isaiah is speaking of these men there. However, it happened that these men were born long after Isaiah. From this it is clear that Isaiah himself brought forth those words not in his own person, but in the person of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, this Holy Spirit—before he approached the prophetess, that is, that virgin who was to conceive and give birth to the Savior, so that by his power and cooperation she might conceive and bear the Son of God without the seed of a man—ought to have employed these prophets for himself as witnesses of the future truth. For one of them, namely Uriah the son of Shemaiah, predicted many evils that were to come upon the Jews and their city, which afterwards befell them in the Babylonian captivity. But the other, that is, Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah, prophesied many and very great good things that were to come to them at the arrival of the Messiah. And especially when he said in chapter 2: **Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold I come, and I will dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord.** <note>original Hebrew: *Roni ve-simchi bat Tziyon ki hineni va ve-shachanti ve-tochach neum YHVH*</note> That is, Praise and be glad, daughter of Zion. Because behold I come, and I will dwell in your midst, says God. And again in the ninth chapter: **Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your King comes to you, he is just and having salvation.** <note>original Hebrew: *Gili meod bat Tziyon harii bat Yerushalayim hinneh malkecha yavo lach tzaddik ve-nosha hu*</note> That is, Exult enough, daughter of Zion, shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold your King will come to you, the Just One and the Savior himself. Moreover, that this is so, as we have explained, is seen most clearly through the Targum of Rabbi Jonathan, that is, through the Aramaic translation, which in that place has it thus: **And I took unto me faithful witnesses...** <note>original Aramaic: *Ve-ashid kodami sahadin meimanin yat*</note>

He asserts that the witnesses Uriah and Zechariah prove the prophecy is spiritual and refers to the Virgin Birth, as these men lived long after Isaiah's time.</summary>

# BOOK
<meta>Catchword: Jehoiakim,</meta>

**And I said that I would bring about the prophecy of Uriah the priest, and behold it comes; and also all the comfort that I said I would bring through the prophecy of Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah, I am prepared to bring.** <note>original Aramaic: "ואמרת לאיתהא בנביאת אוריה כהנא והא אתי ואתי כל נחמתא דאמרית לאיתהא בנביאת זכריה וברכיה בן יברכיה אנא עתיד לאיתהא"</note> This is to say: *And I called to witness on my part the evil testimonies which I said would come in the prophecy of Uriah the Priest: behold, it shall also come to pass that all the consolation which I said would come in the prophecy of Zechariah the son of Berechiah, I shall bring to pass.* **And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.** <note>Isaiah 8:3</note> Where it is clearly shown that these words were not Isaiah’s, but those of the Holy Spirit.

<margin>The explanation of Rabbi Solomon.</margin>
That these prophets are the very same ones of whom Isaiah speaks in the person of the Holy Spirit is evident first through **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note>. Explaining this passage, he says: *And I took for myself even in the days of Jehoiakim two faithful witnesses. One of whom is Uriah the Priest, whom Jehoiakim killed.* As it is said in the twenty-sixth chapter of Jeremiah: **There was also a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath-jearim. And he prophesied against this city, and against this land, according to all the words of Jeremiah.** <note>Jeremiah 26:20</note> *And the other is Zechariah the son of Berechiah, who prophesied in the second year of Darius, saying: "Old men and old women shall yet dwell," or sit, "in the streets of Jerusalem."* <note>Zechariah 8:4</note> Therefore, Uriah was a sign for Zechariah. For if you have seen the prophecy of Uriah fulfilled, you should be expectant that the prophecy of Zechariah will also be fulfilled. And this is just as I took witnesses for myself in the matter of Sennacherib. For Amos was a witness to the punishment of the ten tribes, saying in the 7th chapter: **And Israel shall surely be led away captive.** <note>Amos 7:17</note> But Isaiah spoke to encourage Hezekiah, so that he might act with confidence. It follows in the Prophecy: **And she bore a son**, namely that same son whom the prophetess called **Emmanuel**. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon.

Next, the same point is proved through the **Talmud** <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note>. For it is read at the end of the book **Makkot** <term>Makkot; literally "Stripes" or "Floggings," a tractate of the Talmud dealing with legal punishments</term>, that Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Joshua, and Rabbi Akiba, when they had once gone up to Jerusalem after its destruction and had reached the Mount of the Watchmen <note>Mount Scopus</note>, they tore their garments. And when they had made their way to the mountain of the house of the Lord, and saw a fox coming out of the Holy of Holies, they began to weep. But **Rabbi Akiba** was laughing. They said to him, "Why do you laugh?" He replied to them, "And for what reason do you weep?" They said to him, "Because of the place of which it is written in Numbers chapter 3: **And the stranger who comes near shall die.** <note>Numbers 3:10</note> Now in it is fulfilled that which was said in Lamentations chapter 5: **Because of Mount Zion, which is desolate, the foxes walk upon it.** <note>Lamentations 5:18</note> And after these things, shall we not weep?" Rabbi Akiba said to them, "For this reason I laugh. For it is written in Isaiah chapter 8: **And I took to me faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest, and Zechariah the son of Berechiah.** <note>Isaiah 8:2</note> And what is the connection of Uriah with Zechariah? For Uriah lived during the first Temple. As it is said in Jeremiah chapter 26: **There was also a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath-jearim. And he prophesied against this city, and against this land, according to all the words of Jeremiah.** And King Jehoiakim heard..."

### SEVENTH BOOK

->O 4<-

<margin>The marginal notes on this edge are faded.</margin>

**Jehoiakim**, and all his mighty men. And they brought **Uriah** out of Egypt, and led him to King Jehoiakim, and he struck him with the sword. **Zechariah**, however, belonged to the time of the second sanctuary <note>The "second sanctuary" refers to the Second Temple period, following the Babylonian exile.</note>. But Scripture suspends the prophecy of Zechariah within the prophecy of Uriah. For regarding Uriah, it is written in the third chapter of **Micah**: <margin>Micah 3.</margin> *Because of you, Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the holy house shall be as the high places of a forest.* <note>original: "Causa uestri Syion quasi ager arabitur, & Ierusalem aceruus erit. Et mons domus sanctæ bestijs syluæ, uel in excelsa syluæ." See Micah 3:12.</note> But regarding **Zechariah**, it is written in the eighth chapter: <margin>Zech. 8.</margin> *Old men and old women shall yet dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, and every man with his staff in his hand because of the multitude of his days.* <note>Zechariah 8:4.</note> Therefore, when the prophecy of Uriah was fulfilled <note>The destruction of the First Temple.</note>, I rejoiced, because I know that the prophecy of Zechariah will also be fulfilled. Upon hearing this, they said to **Rabbi Akiba** <note>A foundational tannaic sage of the late 1st and early 2nd centuries.</note> these words: *You have comforted us, you have comforted us.* All of this is from the **Talmud**. 

From these things it is clearly evident that these are the very same prophets of whom **Isaiah** spoke in the person of the **Holy Spirit**. Furthermore, it can easily be seen that these prophets were born long after Isaiah. For Uriah was indeed put to death by King Jehoiakim. Isaiah, however, uttered the aforementioned words in the fourth year of **King Ahaz** (as **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi.</note> says). From the fourth year of Ahaz until the time of Jehoiakim, 140 years passed. For all the years in which Ahaz reigned were sixteen. When four are subtracted, twelve remain. At the beginning of those twelve years, the aforementioned prophecy of Isaiah was made. Then his son **Hezekiah** reigned for twenty-nine years. After him, **Manasseh** for fifty-five. Then **Amon** for two years. Afterward, **Josiah** for thirty-one years. After that, **Jehoahaz** for three months. After him, **Jehoiakim**, who killed the aforementioned prophet Uriah, reigned for eleven years. All these years, when taken together, amount to 160 years and three months. 

From this it is quite clearly shown that the first witness, namely Uriah, <margin>1st Witness.</margin> whom Isaiah (or the Holy Spirit) called to himself, was not yet born when he was called. Regarding the second witness, that is Zechariah, no one should doubt this. <margin>2nd Witness.</margin> Since from the fifth year of Ahaz until the second year of **Darius**, in which Zechariah himself prophesied, 250 years passed. Therefore, since these great prophets whom Isaiah—or rather the Holy Spirit through Isaiah—called as witnesses when he spoke of the virgin prophetess and her son **Emmanuel**, were not yet born in the time of Isaiah, it is openly shown to all who have sound use of reason that the prophetess of whom the Holy Spirit spoke through Isaiah, saying: *I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son,* had not yet been born. Consequently, she could not have been Isaiah's wife, as the delirious younger Jews <note>A polemical reference to contemporary or medieval Jewish commentators who argued against the Messianic/Christological interpretation of Isaiah 8.</note> falsely affirm. But rather, she is that **Virgin** who, by the intervention of the Holy Spirit, was to conceive and give birth to the **Son of God**, of whom he had also made mention a little earlier, saying: <margin>Isa. 7.</margin> *Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel.* From these points it is also clear that this "going to the prophetess" was to be a spiritual event. Since these things are so, it is clear that this prophetess was none other than the **Virgin Mary**, who [bore] the Messiah of God...

<summary>The author uses a chronological timeline of Judean kings to prove that the witnesses Uriah and Zechariah lived centuries after Isaiah. This serves to argue that Isaiah’s prophecy of a "prophetess" conceiving a son must refer to the future Virgin Mary rather than Isaiah's own wife.</summary>

# SEVENTH [BOOK]

...[it is wri]tten: *Let the redeemed of the Lord say, whom he has redeemed from the hand of the enemy.* <note>original Hebrew: "יאמרו גאולי יהוה אשר גאלם מיד צר" (Psalm 107:2).</note> That is, let the redeemed of God speak, those whom he has rescued from the hand of the oppressor. For there, among other things written in Hebrew, we read: *Rabbi Judah bar Shalom said: It is beautifully said, "He has redeemed," even though it was yet to happen. For the word of the Holy One, blessed be He, is as if it were an accomplished deed.* <note>original Hebrew: "אמר רבי יהודה בר שלום יפה הוא אומר לפי שנאמרו של הקדוש ברוך הוא מעשה"</note> *Rabbi Huna said in the name of Rabbi Dustai, in the name of Rabbi Samuel bar Nachman: We learn from another place also that the word of the Holy One, blessed be He, is itself an action. And from where do you learn this? From Abraham. What is written? "On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abraham, saying: To your offspring I have given this land."* <note>original Hebrew: "ביום ההוא כרת אברהם ברית לזרעך נתתי"</note> *He does not say "I will give," but "I have given." And yet, up to that time, he had not yet fathered children! But because the word of the Holy One, blessed be He, is an action, the Holy One said: "I have spoken the word, and the deed is done." So here also he says "the redeemed," as if he had already redeemed them.*

That is, Rabbi Judah, the son of Shalom, said: It is elegantly phrased as "He redeemed," even though it was in the future. This is because the speech of the Holy and Blessed God is regarded as a fact. Rabbi Huna said in the name of Rabbi Dustai, in the name of Rabbi Samuel the son of Nachman: We are taught from another place as well that the word of God is as a deed. For what is written concerning Abraham in the book of Genesis, the fifteenth chapter? *On that day the Lord cut a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your seed I have given this land."* <note>original Hebrew: "ביום ההוא כרת יהוה את אברם ברית לאמור לזרעך נתתי את הארץ הזאת"</note> This means: On that day God struck a pact with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I have given this land." He did not say, "I will give," but "I have given." And how could this be, when Abraham had not yet fathered sons? Because the word of God is a deed, he spoke thus. From this we are also taught that the word of God is a deed when it is said, "I the Lord have spoken, and I have done it." And when did he do it? It can only be because the word of God is considered a finished deed. Therefore, it is well said, "He redeemed," even though it was yet to be. This is the tradition.

Furthermore, the gloss of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>This refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> regarding that passage of **Isaiah**, *I have done these words for them*, says this: *"I have done," that is, "I will do." For the entire language of the prophets speaks of the future as if it were already done.* From these things it is entirely clear that the objection of the Jews <note>Referring to contemporary Jewish scholars who argued the "prophetess" in Isaiah 8:3 was Isaiah's wife and the event was past.</note> is of no weight. Since, according to the aforementioned tradition, those words of Isaiah must be understood as: *And I approached*—that is, I will approach—*the prophetess; and she conceived and bore*—that is, she will conceive and will bear—*a son.*

->*That the mother of the Messiah was to be a prophetess, excelling all other prophets.*<-

### Caput XVII.
### CAPNIO,

**F**rom these things it has also been most excellently shown that the glorious Virgin, the mother of the Messiah, was to be a prophetess. Indeed, I am not unaware that she stood out as the most excellent of Seers. This appears clearly, especially in those things which she predicted so miraculously in her Song <note>The Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55).</note>. Among these, she sang of herself: *And my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior. For he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaiden; for behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.* Nevertheless, so that the impious treachery of the younger Jews may be crushed—those who do not fear to attack her with innumerable blasphemies—I would wish that, just as you have demonstrated her in the preceding pages to be free from original sin and a most pure virgin through their own scriptures, [you would now...]

You would also show that the prophetess herself was to come through one of their ancient authors who spoke of this explicitly. GALATINUS: Since many things have been said on this matter previously, and more will be said in the following pages, let it suffice for now to hear only that man of the highest authority among them, whom they call **Rabbeinu HaKadosh** <note>original: **רבנו הקדוש**; "Our Holy Teacher," a title for Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</note>, that is, "our holy Master." For in the third inquiry of that book titled **Galei Razia** <note>original: **גלי רזיא**; "The Revealer of Secrets," a mystical work attributed to Rabbi Judah</note>, that is, *The Revealer of Mysteries*, he was questioned by Antoninus, the consul of the city of Rome, as to who that prophetess is whom Isaiah mentions when he says in the eighth chapter, *And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.* He responded thus: "I have often been suspended and anxious regarding this question. But one day, having entered the cave of the fathers—where Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah are buried—to pray there, I found Elijah, whom I questioned. Therefore, I am making known to you what I received from him: This prophetess is the mother of the King Messiah, whom the Holy and Blessed God promised he would send to Israel. She is called a 'prophetess' because by her own prophetic gift she knows all things from the beginning even to the end, which none of the prophets was ever able to know. For she herself is the mistress and teacher of all the prophets. And she is that *alma* <note>original: *alma*; a Hebrew word for a young woman, often interpreted in Christian tradition specifically as "virgin"</note> of whom Solomon spoke in the 30th chapter of Proverbs: *And the way of a man in an alma,* that is, *And the way of God into a virgin.* Of her also Isaiah says in the 7th chapter: *Behold, the alma shall conceive and bear a son.* Concerning her it is also said in Micah, chapter 5: *And you, Bethlehem Ephratah, though you are small...* and a little later, *Because of this he will give them up until the time when she who is in labor gives birth.* Furthermore, concerning the King Messiah himself, whom this prophetess is to bear, Isaiah said in the 9th chapter: *A child is born to us, a son is given to us. And the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.*" Thus spoke that man, long before this prophetess was even born. The Jews can by no means deny his words, since they call him "our holy Master," and his authority (as was said) is the greatest among them.

## *That the mother of the Messiah was to be the seat of God, upon which the divine majesty ought to sit. Chapter XIX.*

->CAPNIO,<-

<insert>W</insert>hen Jeremiah, in chapter 17, brought forth these words: **A throne of glory, exalted from the beginning, is the place of our sanctuary, the hope of Israel, the Lord.** <note>original Hebrew: **כסא כבוד מרום מראשון מקום מקדשנו מקוה ישראל יהוה**</note> What does he understand there by the "throne of glory"? For I judge that by "throne of glory" in that place is understood the glorious Virgin, the mother of the Messiah. Since she is exalted in heavenly glory above all the angelic choirs, she is rightly called the "throne of glory of the heights"—that is, the seat of the Most High God upon which the divine majesty sits.

It also introduces the concept of the Messiah's mother as the "Throne of Glory" (Solium Gloriae), interpreting Jeremiah 17 as a reference to her exalted status above the angels.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN

->GALATINUS<-: You speak rightly, my dear Capnio <note>Capnio was the Greek-derived nickname for Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist</note>. So that your feelings may be more clearly explained, I shall bring forward the words of Rabbi Moses ben Maimon <note>Maimonides, the influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher</note> from the first part of his book, *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More*; a reference to *Moreh Nevukhim*</note>, chapter nine. Explaining how a "seat" or "throne" is attributed to God, he says among other things: "What a throne signifies is well known. When someone sees one adorned and prepared in the pontifical <note>In this context, 'pontifical' refers to high-ranking or ceremonial splendor, like that of a high priest or bishop</note> manner, they will assume a King or some Emperor is to sit upon it. For the seat itself displays the excellence and majesty of the one who sits. For this reason, the House of God is called the 'Seat of God,' since it shows the dominion and power of Him who reveals His glory and brightness within it. Therefore Jeremiah said: *A throne of glory, set on high from the beginning, is the place of our sanctuary.* By the same reasoning, the heavens are called the 'Seat of God,' insofar as they show the strength of their Creator, the mover and governor of this lower world, and they reveal the influence of His grace. Therefore it is said in Isaiah, chapter 56 <note>The text cites chapter 56, but the quote is actually from Isaiah 66:1</note>: **The heavens are my throne** <note>original Hebrew: **השמים כסאי** (*Ha-shamayim kis’i*)</note>. It is as if He were saying: The heavens continually show my essence, strength, and power. Just as a throne suggests the dominion and majesty of the one worthy to sit upon it. This understanding is necessary for one who believes in God. Not that this seat is a physical body in which God might sit—heaven forbid that we should fall into such an error! For since we have already proved that God is not corporeal, how could we say He requires a physical place or tabernacle? It is certain (as we have said) that any place magnified by God with His glory, such as the Holy House or the heavens, is called His seat. However, when God spoke in a more expansive way in Exodus chapter 17: *Because the hand of the Lord alone, and the war of God will be against Amalek from generation to generation* <note>This refers to a difficult Hebrew phrase in Exodus 17:16 often interpreted as 'A hand upon the throne of the Lord'</note>, this refers to God’s own substance and essence. One must not imagine that this 'throne' is something distinct from Him, or created by God like His other creatures. For it would follow that God existed in time, and was without a throne before He created it. To say or believe this is the greatest heresy, since it is written in Psalm 102: **But you, O God, remain forever; your throne is from generation to generation** <note>original Hebrew: **ואתה יהוה לעולם תשב כסאך לדור ודור** (*Ve-attah Adonai le-olam teshev; kis’aka le-dor va-dor*). Note: The Latin text integrates 'throne' into this verse, which usually reads 'your remembrance' in standard Psalters</note>. This means: just as You, O God, are eternal, so too is Your throne eternal. And by this it is shown that this throne is not something distinct from God. Therefore this throne, and whatever else signifies God’s own essence, are not things distinct from Him." Thus far speaks that Egyptian Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides spent the latter part of his life in Egypt</note>.

<margin>A triple kind of throne.</margin>
From his words, three conclusions are drawn, since he himself introduces three kinds of thrones. Two of these are created, but the third is truly uncreated.

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
The first conclusion is this: regarding the first created throne, although the Doctor <note>Referring to Maimonides</note> himself accepts it as the Holy House [the Temple] and says that in it the majesty of the Sitter is known because of its excellence,

<margin>The first throne is the Mother of the Messiah.</margin>
it is nevertheless more correctly understood as the undefiled Mother of the Messiah. Because of her perfection and excellence, she was to be the "Seat of God," in whom God Himself was to show His glory and brightness—which is the Messiah, the glory, light, and brightness of the whole world. Because of this, it was said...

<summary>Galatinus uses Maimonides' philosophical definition of the "Throne of God" to argue that the Virgin Mother is the ultimate "created throne" through which God's glory enters the world. He distinguishes between the Temple, the Heavens, and God's eternal essence as three distinct types of divine seats.</summary>

### BOOK SEVEN

<margin>Isaiah 9</margin>
It is said in the ninth chapter of Isaiah: **The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of the shadow of death, light has dawned upon them.** <note>original Hebrew: **העם ההולכים בחשך ראו אור גדול יושבי בארץ צלמות אור נגה עליהם** (*Ha-am ha-holechim ba-choshech rau or gadol yoshvei be-eretz tzalmavet or nagah aleihem*)</note> That is: "The people who were walking in darkness saw a great light. Upon those who sat in the land of the shadow of death, a light has arisen." Therefore, the words of Jeremiah, when he says, *A throne of glory, exalted from the beginning* <note>Jeremiah 17:12</note>, are not to be understood as referring to the holy house that was in Jerusalem. For even if God showed His glory in that house, that glory was nothing in comparison to the glory and brightness He was to show in the Mother of the Messiah. Furthermore, we do not find that the holy house existed from the beginning of the world, whereas it has been proven in the preceding sections that the Mother of the Messiah existed <note>Galatinus is referring to the concept of the "pre-existence" of the Messiah's soul or the plan for his birth in the mind of God from the beginning</note>. Moreover, that holy house cannot be called a "throne of glory," since the glorious seat of God must be perennial or perpetual, and not pass away. For whatever God once accepts, He never dismisses. And although the two other seats of God which He Himself asserts—namely the heavens and God’s own essence—are one perpetual and the other eternal, the holy House in Jerusalem passed away and vanished in destruction. Finally, it follows in the text of Jeremiah: *God is the expectation of Israel.* <note>Jeremiah 17:13</note> But the true expectation and hope of Israel was none other than the Messiah, who was to come forth from his most holy mother. For these reasons, it is clearly shown that the aforementioned words of Jeremiah are to be understood not of the holy house (as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides</note> feels, which fell along with Jerusalem), but of the Mother of the Messiah, just as you yourself so excellently perceive they should be understood. For she herself (as Rabbenus Haccados <note>A title for Rabbi Judah the Prince, though the text cited, *Gale Razeya* ("Revealer of Secrets"), is a later mystical work</note> says in the book *Gale Razeya*, in response to the third petition of Antoninus, the consul of the City of Rome) was to be the seat which God constructed, so that the King Messiah might sit upon it, to show the glory of His majesty to all mortals.

<margin>The second and third conclusions.</margin>
The second and third conclusions are that the second seat is created, while the third is truly uncreated.

<margin>The second seat is the humanity of the Messiah.</margin>
These two seats of God are the Messiah himself. For his humanity is indeed created, which by the Word of God was made a seat; but his divinity itself is uncreated. That the humanity of the Messiah is called the seat of God is evident through that saying in Psalm 44 <note>Psalm 45 in modern bibles</note>: **Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.** <note>original Hebrew: **כסאך אלהים עולם ועד שבט מישר שבט מלכותך** (*Kis’aka Elohim olam va-ed shevet mishor shevet malchuteka*)</note> For just as the glory of their designer is shown from the working of the heavens—by this argument: whatever is moved necessarily has a mover and a governor; the heavens are moved, therefore they have a mover and a governor—so from the humanity of the Messiah, on account of his divine works, his "person" <note><term>suppositum</term>: a technical philosophical term meaning the underlying substance or person that acts</note> is shown to be God, the founder and governor of the entire world. For just as the heavens show the glory of their mover and the management of this lower world by means of the influence of His grace, so the humanity of the Messiah shows the magnificence and dominion of the designer and mover of this world, by means of the influence of salvation, which God pours into that humanity.

<margin>The third seat is the divinity.</margin>
He says the third seat is the divinity, which is uncreated. For the Father is uncreated, the Son is uncreated, and the Holy Spirit is uncreated.

<summary>Galatinus argues that the "Throne of Glory" in Jeremiah refers to the Mother of the Messiah rather than the Temple in Jerusalem, and further defines the Messiah's humanity and divinity as the created and uncreated seats of God.</summary>

->### BOOK SEVENTH<-

The meaning of those words which he brings forward—*But you, O Lord, remain forever; your throne from generation to generation* <note>original Latin: "Tu autem Deus in æternum permanes, sedes tua in generationem & generationem," a reference to Lamentations 5:19 or Psalm 102:12</note>—is this: Just as you, O God, are eternal, so your throne, which is your son, is eternal. For the Father is eternal, the Son is eternal, and the Holy Spirit is eternal. Therefore, from the words of Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204)</note> himself, it is clearly shown (as we have proved) that the previously mentioned words of Jeremiah—*A throne of glory, exalted from the beginning, is the place of our sanctification* <note>Jeremiah 17:12</note>—must be understood as referring to the most blessed mother of the Messiah, who is the throne of God Most High. Moreover, he said, "From the beginning," to show that she was conceived without original sin. 

The same point is also very well suggested by what is said in the first chapter of Ezekiel: **And above the firmament that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, in appearance like a sapphire stone: and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it.** <note>original Hebrew: **וממעל לרקיע אשר על ראשם כמראה אבן ספיר דמות כסא ועל דמות הכסא דמות כמראה אדם עליו מלמעלה** (*u-mi-ma’al la-rakia asher al rosham ke-mareh even sappir demut kisse ve-al demut ha-kisse demut ke-mareh adam alav mi-lemalah*)</note> This means: "And above the firmament, which was hanging over their heads, like the appearance of a sapphire stone, was the likeness of a throne, and upon the likeness of the throne was something like the appearance of a man from above." 

In this passage, Ezekiel prophesied about the immaculate mother of the Messiah. For after he had seen the four living creatures and their movement, he said that he saw standing above the heads of the creatures in heaven the likeness of a throne, or a royal seat, which is the glorious mother of the Messiah. And shortly after, upon this likeness, was the appearance of a man, who is the incarnate Son of God, or the Messiah. 

<margin>The Mother of the Messiah is compared to a sapphire.</margin> 

He says that the appearance of this seat is like a sapphire, so as to suggest not only the glory of this undefiled virgin, but also her complete and absolute purity. For just as the sapphire, although it has its origin in the terrestrial element—which is opaque and dark—is nevertheless translucent and clear from its very beginning; so the immaculate mother of the Messiah himself, even if she came from parents subject to sin, was nevertheless from her own beginning most bright and without the stain of original sin. 

Let these things said according to the opinions of the ancient Hebrews concerning the immaculate and most holy mother of the Messiah suffice. Now returning to her son, let us discuss his mysteries.

# Book Eight.

## On the mysteries of the Messiah which were fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ.

### That the Messiah, according to the flesh, was to descend from Jacob and the other patriarchs through a direct line. Chapter 1.

->REUCHLIN,<-
<note>original Latin: "Capnio," the Greek-derived nickname of the humanist scholar Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

Since I am now about to speak concerning the mysteries of the Messiah, by which the treachery of the younger Jews is best refuted—for through these it is clearly shown that our Lord Jesus Christ was the true Messiah, as in him all those very mysteries of the Messiah foretold by the prophets were fulfilled to the letter—you ought first to reveal that the Messiah himself was to descend from Jacob and the other patriarchs through a direct line.

<margin>GALATINUS</margin>
I will therefore bring forward what is written regarding this matter in Numbers, Chapter 24, in this manner: **A star has gone forth from Jacob, and a rod** (or scepter) **has risen out of Israel, and has crushed the corners** (or tops) **of Moab, and destroyed** (or scattered) **all the sons of Seth. And Edom shall be his possession. And Seir shall be a possession for his enemies, while Israel acts valiantly. And he shall rule from Jacob, and shall destroy the remnant** (or remains) **from the city.** <note>original Hebrew: **דרך כוכב מיעקב וקם שבט מישראל ומחץ פאתי מואב וקרקר כל בני שת והיה אדום ירשה והיה ירשה שעיר אויבו וישראל עשה חיל : וירד מיעקב והאביד שריד מעיר** (*darakh kokhav mi-ya’akov ve-kam shevet mi-yisra’el...*)</note> Where the gloss of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> says: "From the city" (he says), meaning the famous city of Edom, which is Rome. But it is said concerning the King Messiah, "And he shall rule from Jacob," along with the rest. For it is said of him in Psalm 72: "And he shall rule from sea to sea." Likewise in Obadiah: "And there shall be no remnant of the house of Esau" <note>The printed Latin text here says "house of Jacob," but the reference to Obadiah 1:18 and the context of destroying enemies suggests Esau/Edom</note>. These are the words of **Rabbi Solomon**. 

Moreover, these words—"A star has gone forth from Jacob, and a rod (or scepter) has risen from Israel"—**Rabbi Onkelos** <note>The 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic</note> translated into Aramaic <note>original Latin: "Chaldaicè," referring to the Aramaic language used in the Targums</note> thus: **A King shall rise from the house of Jacob, and the Messiah shall be anointed** (and magnified) **from Israel.** <note>original Aramaic: **יקום מלכא מיעקכ ויתרבי משיחא מישראל** (*yekum malka mi-ya’akov ve-yitarbi mishiha mi-yisra’el*)</note> From which Aramaic translation two things are gathered. First, that this scripture speaks of the Messiah. Second, that in the same passage, the past tense is used for the future, in the prophetic manner. 

Furthermore, in the commentaries of **Rabbi Moses Hadarshan** <note>An 11th-century Jewish scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic (interpretive) style</note> on the book of Genesis, regarding that which is said in Chapter 49 of the same book, "The scepter shall not depart from Judah," along with the rest, it is said thus: "This is what Balaam says..."

Galatinus uses Jewish sources like Rashi, Targum Onkelos, and Moses Hadarshan to prove that Jewish tradition itself identifies this prophecy as referring to the King Messiah.</summary>

<header>EIGHTH BOOK.</header>

[Ba]laam, **A star has gone forth from Jacob**, and so forth. And when will this prophecy be fulfilled? When Shiloh comes, that is, the Messiah. From these things the proposition is clear. That the Messiah was also to come forth from Judah, and subsequently from Jesse, is held in the *Lesser Genesis* <note>original: *Bere’shith Ketanna*, an exposition or midrash on the Book of Genesis</note>, specifically upon that saying in Genesis chapter 49: **Judah, your brothers shall praise you** <note>original Hebrew: יהודה אתה יודוך אחיך (*Yehuda attah yodukha akheikha*)</note>. Where it is said: Judah was the fourth born among the tribes, and on the fourth day the lights of heaven were created; and of the Messiah it is written in Psalm 88 <note>Psalm 89 in modern Bibles</note>: **And his throne like the sun before me.** And from Judah the Messiah was born, according to that saying of Isaiah chapter 11: **And a rod shall go out from the stem of Jesse, and a plant from his roots shall bear fruit.** This is the tradition. That he was also to be born from David is held in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: *Midras tehilim*, the rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note>, where it discusses the saying of Psalm 17 <note>Psalm 16:9</note>: **Therefore my heart was glad, and my glory rejoiced.** <note>original Hebrew: לכן שמח לבי ויגל כבודי (*Lakhen shamakh libbi va-yagel kevodi*)</note> Thus it is said: **Rabbi Abhu said, "My heart was glad" in the words of the Law, "and my glory rejoiced" in the King Messiah, who was to come forth from me; "for over all the glory shall be a covering"** <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי אבהו שמח לבי בדברי תורה ויגל כבודי במלך המשיח שעתיד לצאת ממני כי על כל כבוד חפה (*Amar Rabbi Abhu shamakh libbi be-divrei Torah...*)</note>. That is, Rabbi Abhu said, "My heart was glad," namely in the words of the Law, "and my glory rejoiced," namely in the King Messiah, who was to come forth from David himself. Because it was said of him in Isaiah chapter 4: **For over all the glory shall be a covering** <note>original Hebrew: כי על כל כבוד חפה (*Ki al kol kavod huppa*)</note>, or a bridal chamber. So it says there. Moreover, Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a prominent medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian</note> said that the word *huppa* <note>original: חפה (*huppah*), a canopy or room for marriage rites</note>, which is placed in the words of Isaiah, is the place in which a bride hides herself with the groom. From these things it clearly appears that the Messiah, according to the flesh, was to proceed from Jacob and the other fathers. But since many things have been said on this matter in the preceding sections, let what we have said now suffice.

### REUCHLIN,

<note>original: "Capnio," the humanist name of Johann Reuchlin</note>

Although in the previous sections you have said much concerning the virginity of the mother of the Messiah, nevertheless, because the more recent Jews assert that the Messiah is to be generated from a man and a woman in the manner of other men—bringing no small blasphemy in this regard both upon the mother and the son—therefore, to repress their false-speaking and impious boldness, prove, I pray you, through their own scriptures, that the Messiah himself was to be born in a new way, that is, from a mother without a father. **GALATINUS.** That the Messiah was to be generated in a new way, and was by no means to have a carnal father, was said in many ways by the ancient fathers. That is, I will tell the precept...

Rabbi Hunna said: "Tribulations were divided into three parts: one was taken by the patriarchs of the world and all generations, one by the generation of the persecution <note>Referring to the Hadrianic persecutions or the Roman wars</note>, and one by the generation of the Messiah." Just as it is said in *Psalm 110*: **From the womb out of the dawn, or from the womb of the dawn, the dew of your birth is yours.** Rabbi Hunna said (or as it is read elsewhere, Rabbi Idi): Tribulations are divided into three divisions. One was borne by the fathers of the world (namely Abraham and the others) and all generations. Another was borne by the generation of destruction (namely those who were destroyed by the Romans). The third, however, is for the generation of the Messiah. And when his hour comes, God, holy and blessed, will say: "It is upon me," that is, it is my concern, "that I should create him as a new creature." And this is what he says: **Today I have begotten you.** Thus far the tradition.

In this tradition, there are two things that clearly enough show that the Messiah was to be conceived and generated not like other men, but in a new way. One is what he says at the end: namely, that God was to create him as a **new creature**. The other is what he said a little before according to the "Hebrew Truth" <note>A common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text of the Bible</note> in that place where we have: *From the womb before the day-star I begat you.* <note>The Vulgate translation of Psalm 110:3</note> **From the womb out of the dawn, or from the womb of the dawn, the dew of your birth is yours.** For the Hebrew text holds this, which harmonizes with the truth of our faith. For since it has been proved through that tradition that these things were said about the Messiah, nothing else can be reasonably and appropriately understood by "the womb of the dawn" than the matrix or womb of his most holy mother, literally. She was to conceive and give birth to him by divine power, without male seed, and with her virginity intact. Just as the dawn receives the sun and brings it forth without corruption. All of this is given to be understood through the "dew of the birth" of the Messiah from the "womb of the dawn."

<margin>What the dawn is.</margin>
For the **dawn** is that part of the sky and earth which appears illuminated in the morning before the sun rises in the place where the sun comes up. As soon as it begins to grow light, it is called dawn; but as soon as the sun rises and is seen, it is no longer called dawn. <margin>What the womb of the dawn is.</margin> The **matrix** or **womb of the dawn**, however, is called that interval between the earth or the sea of our horizontal view, through which the sun brings itself forth and raises itself, and is seen to rise and ascend. <margin>What the dew of birth is.</margin> The **dew of birth** is the first conception of a man in the womb, which is not without reason called "dew." For just as dew is quickly dissolved by the sun, so also the first conceptions of both men and other animals very easily become abortions; <margin>The Catholic exposition.</margin> those of longer duration are aborted with more difficulty. The sense, therefore, is: that just as the pre-existing sun, by itself and without any other bringing it forth, produces itself from the center of the dawn, so the Word of God by itself, without a generating man, ought to receive the first conception of the birth of his humanity from the center of the dawn,

<note>original: "רגליו עד כי יבא שילה"</note> **Until he comes to Shiloh [under] his feet.** This means: **The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a scribe from the midst of his feet, until Shiloh comes,** <note>Genesis 49:10</note> that is, his son—the son of the woman. For Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, also known as Radak (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and exegete.</note> explains this word "son" in his concordance under the entry for "Shiloh," as was shown more extensively in the 4th chapter of the fourth book. To clarify this, it must be noted that the Hebrews make a great distinction in their grammar (as you yourself well know) between masculine and feminine indicators. For if they are to say "his son" or "that [man's] son" using a masculine indicator, they say **Beno** <note>original: "בנו"</note> with the letter *vav* (ו) at the end of the word. If, however, they are to say "her son" or "that [woman's] son" using a feminine indicator, they say **Bena** <note>original: "בנה"</note> with the letter *he* (ה) at the end of the word. 

However, although this word **Shiloh** <note>original: "שילה"</note> is pronounced with a masculine sound, even though it should rightfully be called *Shila* according to the spelling the scribes adapted, it is nonetheless written with the letter *he* (ה), which is a feminine indicator. For it is read as **Shiloh**, which is the same as "the son," specifically the son of the woman. Thus, the text says: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a scribe from the midst of his feet, until the son of that woman comes.* 

In order to understand what "the son of the woman" signifies, one must note the words written in Genesis chapter 15: <note>original: "ודור רביעי ישובו הנה"</note> **And in the fourth generation they shall return here.** <note>Genesis 15:16</note> These words were spoken by God when He announced the Egyptian captivity to Abraham, which prefigured the captivity of souls in the underworld. <margin>False interpretation of the younger Jews.</margin> Truly, however, some of the younger Jews interpret these four generations as having been four hundred years, asserting that each one of them was a hundred years. <margin>Refutation.</margin> Their interpretation is worthless. For they must calculate these years either from the time the prophecy was delivered, or from when the Egyptian captivity itself began. Both are false. For if they calculate from the time the prophecy was delivered, they will find that much more time than four hundred years passed. But if they calculate from the beginning of the captivity itself, the predicted number of years will not be completed, since the captivity itself lasted no longer than two hundred and ten years. <margin>Another of their interpretations.</margin> 

Certain others, and especially Rabbi Solomon, <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105).</note> want these four generations to have been the father, son, grandson, and great-grandson. <margin>Refutation.</margin> Their interpretation is also falser than the first. For these four generations must be counted either from the time of the prophecy or from the start of the captivity. If we count them from the time of the prophecy, we find seven generations, not four: namely, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, and Caleb. But if we calculate them from the beginning of the captivity, as Rabbi Solomon <margin>Rabbi Solomon's interpretation.</margin> does—counting Judah, Perez, Hezron, and Caleb—there will be fewer than four. For Judah and his son Perez were born before they entered Egypt, <margin>Refutation.</margin> as is clear in Genesis chapter 45. Therefore, we must see through a more subtle investigation what these four generations signify. Thus, it is not yet found to be four generations of men. <margin>Fourfold generation of men.</margin> The first was indeed that of Adam, who was created without man or woman. The second was that of Eve, who was from a man without a wo...

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the virgin birth of the Messiah. It applies Aristotelian logic to the four ways a human can be produced to prove the necessity of a child born of a woman without a man.</meta>

<page-num>552</page-num>

-># BOOK EIGHT<-

...woman was produced. Since, therefore, according to the doctrine of Aristotle <term>Aristotelis doctrina</term> <note>Referring to Aristotle’s logical principle that the study of opposites is the same; if one contrary exists, the other must also be possible.</note>, the science of opposites is the same, and once one side of a contradiction is established, the other must also be set forth. For if "black" is found, it is necessary that "white" also be found. If "sweet" is discovered, one must grant that "bitter" is also discovered. Therefore, it is necessary that, having established two modes of generation, the two opposite modes be assigned. Thus, the opposite of the generation of Adam (who was produced without man or woman) is the third generation, by which all people are commonly generated from a man and a woman. But the opposite of the generation of Eve (who was formed from a man without a woman) is the fourth generation, by which the Messiah was to be born of a woman without a man.

<margin>Catholic exposition.</margin>
For this reason, the aforementioned words are to be explained thus: *In the fourth generation they shall return here* <note>Genesis 15:16</note>—that is, with the coming of the Messiah's generation, souls shall be freed from the captivity of hell and shall return to the heavenly homeland from which they had been expelled on account of Adam's sin, with the Messiah himself as their leader. Because of this generation, therefore, Jacob said: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a scribe from the midst of his feet, until the son of that woman comes* <note>Genesis 49:10</note>, that is, the Messiah, who was called the "son of the woman" for this reason: because he was to be born of a woman without a man.

And the nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising.* <note>The author provides the Hebrew text: קומי אורי כי בא אורך... and follows with a Latin translation, here rendered into English.</note> That is, "Arise, be enlightened, because your light has come, and the glory of God has shone upon you, or has arisen. For behold, darkness will cover the earth, and a thick fog the peoples. But over you God will shine, or will arise, and his glory will appear over you. And the nations will go to your light, and Kings to the splendor of your illumination." Moreover, Rabbi Jonathan, translating this into Aramaic <term>Chaldaicè</term> <note>Rabbi Jonathan ben Uzziel is traditionally credited with the Targum (Aramaic translation) of the Prophets.</note>, explained it thus:

*Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because the time of your salvation has approached, and the honor of God has revealed itself over you. For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and a mist the kingdoms. But the divinity of God shall dwell within you, and his honor shall be revealed over you. And the nations shall go to your light, and Kings to receive your splendor.* <note>This is a translation of the Aramaic Targum quoted in the text.</note> This means: Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because the time of your salvation has drawn near, and the honor of God has revealed itself over you. For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and a mist the kingdoms. But over you the divinity of God shall descend, and his honor shall be revealed over you. And the nations shall go to your light, and Kings to receive your splendor. 

That these things were spoken concerning the Messiah is evident from what is held in the *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>A midrashic commentary on the Book of Genesis.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis—regarding that which is said in Genesis chapter 25: *And he sent them away from his son Isaac, while he was still living, to the eastern region.* <note>Genesis 25:6</note> For there it is said: This is what is written in Job chapter 6: *Look upon the paths of Tema, the ways of Sheba, wait for him, or for them.* <note>Job 6:19</note> There is no "Sheba" except the sons of Abraham, as it is said in Genesis chapter 25: *And Jokshan begot Sheba and Dedan.* <note>Genesis 25:3</note> When Solomon was magnified in his kingdom, they said: "Perhaps this is the Messiah," and they immediately came to him. As it is said in 1 Kings chapter 10: *And the Queen of Sheba, having heard of the fame of Solomon in the name of God, came to test him with riddles.* <note>1 Kings 10:1</note> Do not read *Malkat Sheba* <note>original: מלכת שבא</note>—that is, the "Queen of Sheba"—but rather *Malkut Sheba* <note>original: מלכות שבא</note>—that is, the "Kingdom of Sheba." 

And what is meant by the phrase "in the name of God"? There were prophets among them who prophesied to them in the name of the Lord their God words which had been handed down to them, and which had come into their hands in succession from Abraham. And from where is it held that they were to come in the days of the Messiah and serve him? From that which was said in the sixtieth chapter of Isaiah: *A multitude of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All those from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense, and announcing the praises of the Lord.* <note>Isaiah 60:6. The author notes the use of the Tetragrammaton (the four-letter name of God) in the text.</note> For this is the King Messiah. Just as it is said in Jeremiah, chapters 23 and 33: *And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord Our Just One.* <note>Jeremiah 23:6 and 33:16. Again, the author notes the use of the Tetragrammaton (יהוה).</note> This means: And this is the name by which they shall call him, God <note>original: tetragrammaton</note> our righteous one. And thus Isaiah says in the sixtieth chapter: *And over you God <note>original: tetragrammaton</note> shall shine, or shall arise, and his glory shall appear over you. And the nations shall go to your light, and Kings to the splendor...*
