> Do not read "Queen of Sheba," but "Kingdom of Sheba." <note>This refers to the rabbinic interpretive technique known as *Al Tikrei* ("Do not read X, but Y"), used here to argue that a single representative can stand for an entire nation.</note>
Because since a King represents all those existing in his Kingdom, the Queen of Sheba herself, who came to Solomon, represented that entire kingdom. Therefore, since among the Kings who came to worship the newborn Christ, there stood one king of Sheba who represented all those of that same kingdom, it was rightly predicted through Isaiah:
> All they from Sheba shall come; they shall bring gold and incense.
It has also been proven in the preceding pages that in the Sacred Script, "all" is rarely used to mean every single individual, but rather is frequently used to refer to a very small part.

Secondly, it should be noted in the same tradition that it says those from Sheba were to come in the days of the Messiah and would serve him. He shows that this was to happen through the aforementioned words of Isaiah. Thirdly, because it says those of Sheba were sons of Abraham, which he proves through the authority of the Sacred Scripture which he introduces there; and that there was a prophet among them who prophesied words to them in the name of his God, which had been handed down to them, and which had come successively into their hands from Abraham. Fourthly, because in explaining that passage of Isaiah,
> All they from Sheba shall come; they shall bring gold and incense, and they shall announce the praises of God <note>original: "tetragrammaton"</note>.

> And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord <note>original: "Deus (tetragrammaton)"</note> our Just One. <note>Jeremiah 23:6</note>
Which (as has been said in the preceding pages) is a name unique to God and appropriated to him alone, indicating the essence of the Creator himself. Therefore, no pure creature can be called by that name. From which it clearly follows that the Messiah is God. Fifthly, that the Gentiles were to go to the light of this Messiah, called by the name of the God of the four letters. This agrees perfectly with what John the Evangelist says:
> That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world. <note>John 1:9</note>
And also with what the Church sings in the Creed <term>symbolo</term>:
> Light from Light, true God from true God.

->*That the Messiah was to be called back from Egypt, where he was to go after his birth, fleeing Herod. Chapter IV.*<-

### CAPNIO, <note>Capnio is the Greek-style pen name for Johannes Reuchlin, a famous German scholar of Hebrew who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

There is yet another mystery that was to occur after the Messiah was born: namely, his departure into Egypt, and his subsequent return from there into the land of Israel. For as the Evangelist relates, after the departure of the Magi kings, while Herod was preparing the death of the infant Christ, Christ himself was carried in his mother’s bosom at the warning of an angel. Fleeing Herod, he went into Egypt. And later, after Herod had died, he returned to the land of Israel. I would therefore like to hear from you if any of the ancient Jews who preceded the coming of Christ predicted anything concerning this mystery. 

**GALATINUS:** <note>The author, Pietro Galatino, presenting himself as the teacher in this dialogue.</note> Those ancient fathers were certainly not silent about the fact that the Messiah, after his birth, would go away into Egypt while fleeing the persecution of Herod, and would later return by the command of God. For it is written in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century Jewish scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic (interpretive) commentaries.</note> regarding that which is said in the fortieth chapter of Genesis: *And behold, a vine was before me.* <note>The original text provides this in Hebrew: וְהִנֵּה גֶפֶן לְפָנַי (Genesis 40:9, from the Chief Butler's dream).</note> This is interpreted in this way: "This is Israel, just as it is written in the eightieth Psalm: *You shall transfer* (or move) *a vine out of Egypt.*" <note>Hebrew: גֶפֶן מִמִצְרַיִם תַּסִּיעַ (Psalm 80:8/9)</note> Another exposition: "And behold, a vine was before me. This is the King <margin>The Messiah is called a vine.</margin> Messiah, of whom it is said in the eightieth Psalm: *And the vineyard which your right hand has planted...*" <note>Hebrew: וְכַנָּה אֲשֶׁר נָטְעָה יְמִינֶךָ (Psalm 80:15/16)</note>

> *That the Messiah was to perform miracles by his own power. And concerning the miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ and his disciples, from the Talmud. Chapter V.*

### CAPNIO, <note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pseudonym of Johann Reuchlin, the famous 16th-century Hebraist and scholar.</note>

Since our Lord Jesus Christ performed many miracles by his own power, you must show—in order to prove that he was the true Messiah—that the Messiah himself was destined to perform miracles. GAL. <note>Galatinus, the other speaker in this dialogue.</note> Isaiah, among others, clearly foretold this when he said in chapter 25 <note>The quote is actually from Isaiah 35:4–6.</note>: *God’s reward—or God himself as reward—will come and save you. Furthermore, the ancient Jews handed down the tradition that these words of Isaiah must be understood as referring to the Messiah himself. They also publicly foretold that the Pharisees—whom they call **פריצים** <gloss>parecim</gloss>, meaning "the lawless," "corrupt in morals," or "the reckless"—would not believe in the miracles of the Messiah. *Rabbi Natronai asked: What is the meaning of that which is written: "We have not seen our signs; there is no longer a prophet, nor is there anyone with us who knows anything more, or how long"? Rab Aha answered him: This was said concerning the generation of the lawless, who will not believe the signs which our righteous Messiah will perform. Instead, they will say of him that he works them by magic and by names of impurity <note>Referring to the accusation that Jesus used the "Shem HaMephorash" (the forbidden Name of God) or occult arts to perform wonders.</note>, and that the signs he gives were not those signs that the prophets prophesied concerning the Messiah. And even if they were those signs, they were hidden from them, and there was no prophet among them who could tell them they were true...*

...prophet, who could manifest the truth to them. For this reason, it was necessary for him to bring forth proof of his words; otherwise, they would have killed him. And therefore the prophet cries out, saying: *How long, O Lord, shall the adversary reproach? Shall the enemy blaspheme your name forever?* <note>Psalm 74:10</note> It is as if he says to God that He should not endure such words. These things are recorded there. Furthermore, although the more recent Jews cannot deny that Christ performed miracles—since his miracles were most great and manifest—they have nevertheless attempted to defile them with lies and blasphemy. For seeing that these deeds were of such a nature that they exceeded all created power, they dared not attribute them to diabolical power as their fathers had done. Instead, they attributed them to the Divine Name, which they call <term>Shem HaMephorash<note>original: "שם המפורש" — The "Explicit Name" or the Tetragrammaton (YHWH). Wishing to show how he learned that Name, they composed a certain book full of lies and blasphemies <note>This likely refers to the "Toledot Yeshu," a medieval Jewish polemic that offered a satirical life of Jesus.</note>—not from the Talmud, from which we have gathered these secrets of Catholic truth, but from diabolical suggestion. But it can be seen most clearly that they are altogether lying and speaking falsely from the fact that the apostles and his other disciples, after his death, performed miracles not through the *Shem HaMephorash*, but in the name of Jesus the Nazarene himself, as the Talmud testifies.

### CAPNIO
Where in the Talmud is that held?

### GALATINUS
In the Jerusalem Talmud, in the book called <term>Avodah Zarah<note>original: "עבודת זרה" — "Foreign Worship" or "Idolatry," a tractate of the Talmud.</note></term>, that is, "Alien Service." There it is read, word for word, as follows: *Rabbi Johanan said that the grandson of Rabbi Joshua son of Levi had swallowed something deadly, and a spell was cast over him in the name of Jesus son of <term>Panther<note>original: "פנתר" — Panthera; a name used in the Talmud to refer to the father or an ancestor of Jesus, often in a polemical context.</note></term>, and he was healed. But when he had recovered, the boy’s father said to the one who had made him well: "What did you say over him?" He replied to him: "I invoked the name of Jesus the Nazarene." The boy’s father said: "It would have been better for him if he had died and not heard this word."* And so it immediately happened to him <note>meaning the boy died anyway</note>—specifically because of the father's ingratitude.

Rabbi Joses also said: *A certain serpent bit Elazar son of Duma. Therefore, Jacob—that is, James, a certain man from the disciples of Jesus son of Panther—came to him to cure him, and said to him: "I will speak to you in the name of Jesus the Nazarene, and you shall be healed." Rabbi Samuel said to him: "This is not permitted to you, son of Duma." But Elazar said to him: "I will bring proof that it is permitted for me, so that he may cure me." But he did not allow him to bring the proof before he died.* And what proof could he have brought? That which is written in the 18th chapter of Leviticus: <note>Leviticus 18:5</note> <gloss>Which (namely, my commandments) if a man do, he shall live in them.</gloss> <note>original: "אשר יעשה אתם האדם וחי בהם" — Elazar intended to argue that saving a life supersedes religious prohibitions.</note> All these things are in that same book of the Jerusalem Talmud. The same is also held in the <term>Midrash Kohelet<note>original: "מדרש קוהלת" — A rabbinic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes.</note></term>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes, upon that saying in the 1st chapter: <gloss>All things are wearisome; man cannot utter it.</gloss> <note>Ecclesiastes 1:8. The Latin text uses "difficult things/words" for "wearisome."</note> Or: *All difficult matters, or all difficult words, a man cannot express in speech.* Where it is said in this manner: *It happened that a serpent bit Rabbi Elazar son of Duma...*

**CAPNIO.** Why do they call the Lord Jesus "the son of Panther"?

**GALATINUS.** Because he had no father on earth, some called him the son of Panther, who according to certain sources was the great-great-grandfather of his glorious virgin mother, from the line of Nathan son of David. ### *Chapter VI. That the miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ and his disciples can in no way be denied.*

->CAPNIO,<-

**S**ince we have begun a discourse on the miracles of our redeemer and his disciples, in order that the impious boldness of the more recent Jews—who so obstinately either deny or attack them—may be more greatly rebuked, it must be proven that those miracles are so firmly established that they cannot be denied by any wickedness of the adversaries.

**GALATINUS.** That is certainly shown in a three-fold way: namely, through various scriptures, through frequent report, and through necessary reason. By the scripture of the Jews, I mean as has been made clear from what has already been said. However, there is no need to bring forth the scripture of the Christians for this purpose, both because there is no doubt concerning it, and also because the adversaries do not accept it—although they ought to accept it, since it narrates nothing but the truth. <margin>What Muhammad thought about the miracles of Christ.</margin>
Therefore, in the law of the Saracens, which is called the <term>Alchoran<note>The Quran.</note></term>, it is contained among other things that the angel Gabriel was sent by God to the Virgin Mary to announce to her the conception of the Lord Jesus by the power of God alone, without the seed of man. Also, that he impressed his own likeness upon one of his disciples, who of his own will was crucified by the Jews in his place. The miracle of the <term>Seven Sleepers<note>A legend about a group of youths who slept for centuries in a cave to escape religious persecution, recognized in both Christian and Islamic traditions.</note></term>—who were shut up in a certain cave behind a very strong wall by the Emperor Decius for their confession of Christ, and after a sleep lasting two hundred years, woke up in the time of the Emperor Theodosius, bearing witness to the Christian faith and the future resurrection—is also beautifully found in the Quran itself.

<margin>What "frequent report" is.</margin>
Next, the miracles of Christ are established through <term>frequent report<note>original: "crebra fama," a term for mass testimony or widely held public knowledge.</note></term>. This is, according to the opinion of wise men, the narration by many people of something perceptible by the senses, either occurring in the present time or in the successive and uninterrupted past. It is impossible, according to custom, for such a multitude of people to come together in secret to fabricate such a thing. There are two kinds of things (as they say) which possess "frequent report." The first is that those who perform the acts narrate them...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how truth is established through "frequent report" or universal testimony, moving from the testimony of the Saracens (Muslims) to the philosophical requirements for historical certainty.</meta>

<page-num>561</page-num>

<sig>Q 3</sig>

...they create a report <note>original: "famam"</note>, something which they themselves perceived either by sight or by some other sense. However, a narrative of this kind provides true knowledge when two things concur. One of these is that the multitude of narrators reaches such a number that it would be impossible, according to common experience, for that multitude to secretly agree to fashion a lie. For example, if we see men from diverse and distant regions, and of diverse customs and languages, agreeing that there is a city in the world called Rome, it will be established for us as a certainty that this city exists in the world. 

The other requirement is that the thing narrated must be capable of being subject to the senses. For if all the people of the East and the West were to narrate that the world had a beginning, or that it was eternal, or were to say that there existed one or many creators of the world, their narration certainly would not provide certain knowledge, but only faith <note>original: "fidem" — here meaning belief or conviction rather than scientific certainty</note>, since narrated things of this kind cannot be perceived by the senses. If, however, for the sake of example, they narrated that in some region—say, in Flanders—they use sods <note>original: "glebis" — referring to peat or turf used as fuel</note> instead of wood to make fire, their narration would produce certain knowledge, since what they narrate can be apprehended by the senses. 

Whenever, therefore, these two things concur—namely, that the narrators are so many and of such a kind that they could not have secretly agreed to fashion a lie, and that the thing narrated was something perceptible to the senses—then without doubt, according to the opinion of <term>Avicenna<note>An influential Persian physician and philosopher (d. 1037).</note></term>, <term>Al-Ghazali<note>A prominent Persian theologian and jurist (d. 1111).</note></term>, and <term>Ibn al-Khatib<note>original: "Ibnazatib" — likely referring to a commentator on Arabic logic or a corruption of an Arabic name like Ibn al-Tayyib.</note></term>, it provides certain knowledge. And in this way Jacob knew that his son Joseph—whom he believed to be dead—was actually alive.

The second kind of things held through frequent report is when the narrators are as we have described, but they say they have not seen the thing they narrate themselves. Nevertheless, they assert that they have seen and heard such a multitude as we described, which said that they themselves had seen and heard what they now narrate. This kind provides certain knowledge when those two things concur in it which we said concur in the first kind, along with this third requirement: that even if the chain of narrators extends quite far, it is never interrupted nor thinned out, but the end and the middle always correspond in quantity and quality to the beginning. 

In this way, if some spoke regarding the Law of Moses, saying it came down to Ezra and a few certain others. In this same way today people know that Alexander the Great existed; in this way Caesar, in this way Plato, in this way Aristotle, and in this way all the other most excellent men whom ancient antiquity has handed down. In this way also, if you pay attention, it is necessary for the Jews of our time to know that Moses existed, that he performed wonders, and gave the Law; and also that the ancient Jews worshipped the golden calf, killed many prophets, and rejected the Lord Jesus who asserted himself to be the Messiah, and received two false Messiahs in his place. Therefore, Moses directed the Jewish people toward this way of knowing when he said in Deuteronomy chapter 32: <note>original: "זכר ימות עולם בינו שנות דר ודור שאל אביך ויגדך זקניך ויאמרו לך"</note> that is, "Remember the days of old, consider the years of generation and generation. Ask your father, and he will announce it to you; your elders, and they will tell you." This way of knowing, David also...

...He establishes this when he says in Psalm 77 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 78:6-7. The author uses the Vulgate numbering.</note>:

That the last generation might know, the children who would be born, that they should arise and tell their children: that they might set their hope in God and not forget the works of God, and keep His commandments. <note>original Hebrew: "למען ידעו דור אחרון בנים יולדו יקומו ויספרו לבניהם: וישימו באלהים כסלם ולא ישכחו מעללי אל ומצותיו ינצרו:"</note>

That is: 

That the last generation may know; children will be born, they will rise and tell their children. And they will put their trust in God, and will not forget the works of God, and will keep his commandments. 

<margin>An objection.</margin>
CHAPTER. This mode of knowing through frequent report <term>frequent report: a technical term (Latin: fama) referring to knowledge passed down through widespread, consistent testimony over generations</term> seems very weak according to the doctrine of Aristotle. This is because, firstly, regarding specific things perceived by the senses that are far removed from our own senses, there is no direct sensation, and consequently no scientific knowledge. Secondly, we do not become "simply experienced" in matters of faith and belief because of this report. Indeed, it is for this purpose that "probable propositions" exist, which are set forth by Aristotle in his book on the *Greater Rhetoric*. Finally, because according to Aristotle, that which is "famous" or "well-known" is the same as that which is "probable," as is clear in the five modes of probability established by him in the first book of the *Topics*. <note>Aristotle’s *Topics* and *Rhetoric* were the standard textbooks for logic and persuasion; the author is arguing that universal testimony is often dismissed as mere "probability" rather than "certain truth" in these systems.</note>

<margin>The response of Ibnazatib.</margin>
GAL. To this objection, let Ibnazatib <note>likely a Latinization of an Arabic philosopher such as Ibn al-Tayyib</note>, one of the Arabic philosophers listed above, respond, saying among other things: "Know that there has been a controversy among the wise. Does the knowledge held through frequent report constitute 'necessary' knowledge <note>meaning certain and undeniable</note> or 'probable' knowledge?" Regarding this, after many things were said on both sides, the final choice of all is that it is "necessary" knowledge. Indeed, that which is "necessary" is that which we neither wish to, nor are able to, make doubtful to ourselves when we test ourselves. Furthermore, when we have heard all the objections raised against frequent report and then test ourselves, we find our souls judging precisely that—for example—Moses existed, and said that he was a messenger of God sent to the faithful of Israel. We do not find anything in the objections that can pierce through this certainty. The same applies to those things which are necessary truths. Therefore, nothing said against frequent report deserves a response. For a response ought to be "probable" <note>persuasive</note>. But to hold a "necessary" truth alongside a "probable" one leads to circular reasoning and is impossible. These are his words, translated word-for-word from the Arabic.

From these points, it is clear that the arguments made against frequent report do not deserve a response.

<margin>What is "necessary."</margin>
Finally, the miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ are proved to be established by necessary reason—that is, through their effects. For the art of reasoning and demonstration teaches us to best conclude causes from their effects. Indeed, no one who partakes in reason would doubt that strength exists in someone in whom he has clearly seen the acts of the strong. And whoever possesses speed, it is manifest that he is fast. For the nature of each thing does what is proper to itself, and does not mix with the effects of contrary things. Therefore, that our Lord Jesus Christ and his followers visibly performed works in his name which surpass the capacity of all nature—in the miraculous healing of illnesses, in the raising of the dead, in the stupendous transformation of celestial bodies and elements, and what is more wonderful, in the sudden inspiration of human minds—it is clear that unlearned and ignorant men were instantly filled with the Holy Spirit and attained the highest wisdom, understanding of the Scriptures, and the eloquence of various languages. I say that all these things were done by our Lord Jesus Christ, and after him by his followers in his name, as the subsequent effect evidently shows. Namely, that it was not by the violence of arms...

...violence, not by the permission of pleasures or license, but through the unrefined and simple disciples of Christ—who were exceedingly few and poor—against the unheard-of rage and tyranny of the persecutors of the whole world, both Jews and Gentiles. Innumerable crowds, not only of the common and uneducated but also of the wisest men, turned with the greatest affection to the faith of the Lord Jesus himself. They rejected the worship of demons, which previously enticed souls so strongly that even the Jews themselves—despite seeing many astounding miracles through Moses or others—had never been so completely turned away from it. In this faith, they teach things that transcend all human intellect and reason; the pleasures of the body, most desired by mortals, are restrained, and they are commanded to laboriously seek invisible things and to despise all worldly things. That the souls of mortals should assent to these things is both the greatest miracle and a manifest work of divine inspiration. 

Moreover, that this was not done by fortune or chance is most clear from this: that God foretold through the oracles of the prophets many centuries before that He would do this, designating both the time and the manner of its accomplishment. Therefore, this so miraculous conversion of the world to the faith of Christ is the most certain proof of the miracles of the past which are narrated and read in written books. Thus, it is not necessary for those miracles to be repeated further, since they appear most evidently in their effect. Although even in our own times, God does not cease to perform miracles through His saints for the preservation of the Christian faith. 

Wherefore, if the Jews with whom we are in conflict should wish to deny the miracles of Christ to us, this one grand and greatest miracle of all remains for us: that to believe such arduous things, to do such difficult things (contrary to <term>flesh and blood: a biblical idiom referring to human nature and its physical desires</term>), and to hope for such high and hidden things, the world was led away from its errors and vices—by which it had been enticed and absorbed—by so few men, who were ignorant and beggarly according to the standards of the world, and the world believed them without further miracles. <note>This is a famous rhetorical argument: if the apostles converted the world without miracles, that conversion is itself a greater miracle than any they could have performed.</note> Moreover, that the Jews would indeed reject the miracles of Christ while the Gentiles would receive them was announced by the prophets long ago. Therefore, if the Messiah ought to be a prophet, and your Christ was not a prophet, it necessarily follows that he was not the Messiah himself. <margin>Response.</margin> <term>GALATINUS</term>: Let it be answered to them that our Christ was indeed a prophet, and we hold him as a prophet. <margin>Jesus of Nazareth was a true prophet.</margin> For regarding him, Luke says in chapter 24: "Who was a man, a prophet, powerful in work and word." <note>original: "Qui fuit uir propheta, potens in opere & ſermone"</note> For which reason that Samaritan woman (as John reports in chapter 4) said: "Lord, I see that you are a prophet." For concerning himself, there is that passage in Luke chapter 18: "Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things that were written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be delivered to the Gentiles, and will be mocked, and scourged, and spit upon. And after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again." Likewise in Matthew chapter 16: "The Son of Man," he said, "is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels. And then he will reward each one according to his works."

But concerning his disciples, he spoke in Matthew chapter 10: "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and simple as doves. But beware of men. For they will deliver you up to councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues, and you will be led before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and the Gentiles." And so forth.

Finally, he prophesied concerning the Jews when, as Luke says in chapter 19: "Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying, 'If you had known, even you, and indeed in this your day, the things that belong to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For the days will come, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and encircle you, and hem you in on every side, and level you to the ground, and your children who are within you; and they will not leave in you one stone upon another. Because you did not know the time of your visitation.'" He said the same in other places as well. For which reason, there is no doubt that he was a true prophet, and none other than that same one of whom Moses spoke, as we have already shown.

### Chapter VIII. That the Messiah ought to preach repentance. ###

-> CAPNIO <-

**W**e read in the Gospels that our Lord Jesus Christ taught repentance; <note>The Latin "pœnitentia" can be translated as either "repentance" or "penance." In this context of early preaching, "repentance" fits the biblical "metanoia."</note> indeed, when he first began to preach, he put forward these words: "Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven will draw near to you." <note>original: "Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim uobis Regnum cœlorum"</note> It is certain that by preaching repentance, both by himself and through his disciples, he brought the whole world to the worship of the one and true God. For that reason, so that you might be able to show by this mystery also that he was the true Messiah, [show] that the Messiah himself was going to preach repentance, and through repentance [bring] the whole world...

...to lead the entire world to the goal of salvation, you must demonstrate this through the scriptures of the ancient Jews. **GALATINUS.** Regarding repentance, which the Messiah was to preach both by himself and through his disciples, it is written in the Jerusalem book **Maccoth** <note>original: "Maccoth", referring to the Talmudic tractate Makkot, meaning "lashes" or "stripes"</note>, in the chapter that begins **Ellu hen haggolin** <note>original: "Ellu hen haggolin," meaning "These are the exiles"</note>. There it is said word-for-word: *Rabbi Pinhas said, It is written in Psalm 25:* <note>The author uses both Psalm 25 and 24, reflecting differences between the Hebrew and Vulgate numbering.</note> **Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he will teach sinners in the way.** <note>original: "tob ve-yashar Adonai al ken yoreh hata’im ba-derekh"</note> That is to say: God is good and upright, for this reason he will teach those who wander the way, or [instruct them] in the way. Why is he good? Because he is upright. And why is he upright? Because he is good. For this reason, he will teach those who wander the way. Indeed, he will teach the way through which they may perform repentance. 

For Wisdom was asked: what is the condemnation of a sinner? And she said to those who had asked, as it is written in *Proverbs chapter 13:* **Evil pursues sinners.** <note>original: "hata’im teraddef ra’ah"</note> They also asked the prophet: What is the condemnation of a sinner? And he said to them in *Ezekiel chapter 18:* **The soul that sins, it shall die.** <note>original: "ha-nefesh ha-hote’t hi tamut"</note> They also questioned the Law, saying: What is the condemnation of a sinner? And it answered them: Let him offer a sacrifice, and it shall be forgiven him. Just as it is written in *Leviticus chapter 1:* **And it shall be accepted for him, to make atonement for him.** <note>original: "ve-nirtzah lo le-kapper alav"</note> Finally, they asked God, the Holy and Blessed: What is the condemnation of a sinner? And He said to them: Let him perform repentance, and He will forgive him. And this is what is written in *Psalm 25*: "Good and upright is God; therefore he will teach those who wander, or sinners, the way, or [instruct them] in the way." For he himself will show sinners the way of performing repentance. This is the tradition.

In the book **Yoma** <note>original: "Yoma," the Talmudic tractate concerning the Day of Atonement</note> as well, in the chapter that begins **Yom ha-kippurim** <note>meaning "The Day of Atonement"</note>, it is read: Rabbi Isaac said, "Come and see that the way of the Holy and Blessed God is not like the way of flesh and blood." For the way of flesh and blood is that if a man offends his neighbor, sometimes he may appease him with words, and sometimes he cannot appease him with words alone. But the way of the Holy and Blessed God is not so. For a man commits a transgression, and yet he appeases Him with words. Just as it is said in *Hosea chapter 14:* **Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity. Take words with you and return to the Lord.** <note>original: "shuvah Yisrael ad Adonai Elohekha..."</note> This means: return, or perform repentance, Israel, even unto the Lord your God. For you have struck against, or fallen in, your iniquity. Take words with you, and return to God. And not only this, but He also grants him goodness. As is said subsequently: **Say to him, take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously [lit. take good].** <note>original: "yomru elav kol tissa avon ve-kach tob"</note> Not only this, but the scripture regards him as if he were offering calves in sacrifice. As it is then said: **And we will render the calves of our lips.** <note>original: "u-neshallmah parim sefatenu"</note> Perhaps you will say: "The calves of guilt?" He teaches what should be said regarding this in what follows: **I will heal their** <margin>The efficacy of repentance.</margin> **rebellion [or turning away], I will love them freely.** <note>original: "erpa meshubatam ohabem nedabah"</note> This is the tradition.

How great the efficacy and power of repentance still is, appears most clearly from what is written in the **Midrash** <note>A Jewish homiletic commentary</note> **Shir ha-Shirim** <note>original: "Shir ha-shirim," the Song of Songs</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs, upon...

...concerning that saying in the fifth chapter of the same book <note>referring to the Midrash on the Song of Songs</note>, **Open to me, my sister.** For there it is said: Rabbi Jose said, that the Holy and Blessed God said to Israel: "My children, open for me one opening of repentance, even as small as the eye of a needle, and I will open for you openings of mercy, through which wagons and chariots shall enter." Rabbi Levi said, if the children of Israel had performed repentance for even a single day, they would have been redeemed immediately, and the son of David—that is, the Messiah—would have come to them immediately. From where does he prove this? From that which is written in Psalm 94 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 95:7</note>: **Today, if you would hear his voice.** <note>original: "ha-yom im be-qolo tishma’u"</note> This is the tradition. From these words of the Psalm cited last concerning the Messiah, and by the reasoning of the preceding words of the same Psalm, it necessarily follows that the Messiah is God. For in the same Psalm, it is first stated: **Come, let us worship and bow down, let us kneel before the face of the Lord our Maker. For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand.** <note>original: "bo’u nishtahaweh ve-nikra’ah nivrakhah lifne Adonai osenu; ki hu Elohenu ve-anahnu am mar’ito ve-tson yado"</note> And then immediately following is that which was explained concerning the Messiah: "Today, if you would hear his voice." From this it follows certainly that the God who was to teach the way of repentance (as was said at the beginning of this chapter) is none other than the Messiah himself, who was destined to preach repentance.

In confirmation of this matter, it should be further noted what is also said in the *Midrash Shir ha-Shirim* <note>The Rabbinic commentary on the Song of Songs</note> regarding that saying in the seventh chapter of the Song of Songs: **Looking toward Damascus**, or "the face of Damascus." <note>original: "tsofeh pene Damasek"</note> There one reads: Rabbi Johanan said, "In the future, Jerusalem shall reach as far as the gates of Damascus." What is the proof for this? That which is written in Zechariah chapter 9: **The burden or prophecy of the word of God in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be his rest.** <note>original: "massa devar Adonai be-erets Hadrach ve-Damasek menuhato"</note> What is "Hadrach"? Rabbi Judas and Rabbi Nahmias disagree on this. For Rabbi Judas says it is a place near Damascus called Hadrach. But Rabbi Nahmias says that this is the King Messiah, who is **sharp** <note>original: "had," meaning sharp or acute</note> toward the nations of the world, and **tender** <note>original: "rach," meaning soft or tender</note> toward Israel. Another explanation says that **Hadrach** is the King Messiah, who is to come **to lead** <note>original: "lehadrich," meaning to guide or direct</note> or to bring the entire world through repentance to the face of the Holy and Blessed God. It follows: "And Damascus shall be his rest." And when Damascus is his rest, his rest shall be nowhere else but the House of the Sanctuary. Just as it is written in Psalm 132: **This is my rest forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it.** <note>original: "zot menuhati ade ad"</note> All this is tradition.

To understand these things, one must observe that this word "Hadrach" is spoken and pronounced by the Hebrews in two ways. For sometimes it is written with the letter **He** <note>The 5th letter of the Hebrew alphabet: ה</note>, and then it is a single word signifying "to lead along a way." But sometimes it is written with the letter **Heth** <note>The 8th letter: ח</note>, and then it is two words: namely, **sharp** and **tender**. Both of these suit Christ perfectly; he will be sharp to the repenting through justice, and tender through mercy. He was also sharp to Paul while he was a persecutor near the gates of Damascus, and afterwards tender to the same man when he repented.

### That the Messiah ought to be poor and humble. Chapter IX.

->CAPNIO,<-

Among the other things that modern Jews most strongly deny concerning the Messiah is his poverty and humility. For when they hear that the poverty and humility of our Lord Jesus Christ was so great—that he had nowhere to lay his head (as Matthew witnesses), nor the means to pay the <term>didrachma</term> <note>A silver coin worth two drachmas, required for the annual Temple tax.</note>, nor the means (as Luke records) to satisfy the hunger of his poor disciples—they deny that the Messiah himself was to be poor and humble, so that they might not be forced to confess that he was the true Messiah. It is necessary that you show this, in order to convict them of their faithlessness through their own scriptures. GALATINUS: Although Jewish blindness and pride have erred so greatly in this matter—even to the point of deciding that the Lord Jesus was not the Messiah because he was exceedingly poor and humble—nevertheless, they used to read that the Messiah King would be poor. Yet, because of their pride, they did not understand that he would come in such a manner. CAPNIO: This is exactly what I say you must prove. GALATINUS: First, therefore, let them hear Zechariah speaking these things, among others, in the 9th chapter: **Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king comes to you; he is righteous and saved <note>The Latin 'salvatus' and Hebrew 'nosha' are passive, implying one who has received salvation or victory from God, rather than an active conqueror.</note>, he is poor and riding on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.** <note>original Hebrew: "gili me’od bat tsiyon heri’i bat yerushalam hinneh malkekh yavo lakh tsaddiq ve-nosha hu ani ve-rokhev al hamor ve-al ayir ben atonot"</note> And after a few words: **And he shall speak peace to the nations; and his dominion shall be from sea to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth.** <note>original Hebrew: "ve-dibber shalom la-goyim u-mishlo mi-yam ad yam u-mi-nahar ad afse arets"</note> Now, that these words ought to be understood as referring to the Messiah is clear through the <term>gloss</term> <note>An explanatory note or commentary, here referring to the standard medieval Jewish commentary.</note> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105).</note>. Which says thus: **Behold, your king comes to you.** This cannot be explained except regarding the King Messiah. Because it is said here: **And his dominion shall be from sea to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth.** And we do not find that there was any such ruler in the Second House—that is, in the time of the Second Temple. From these things it is clearly evident that the Kingdom of the Messiah must be understood spiritually, since a temporal kingdom and such poverty cannot exist together. To this also pertains what Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>Moshe ha-Darshan of Narbonne, an 11th-century preacher and commentator.</note> says in his exposition of Genesis, concerning that saying in the 49th chapter of the same book: **Binding his foal to the vine.**

Thus it says: "When the Messiah comes to Jerusalem, he himself will be girding his donkey, and will ride, and upon it he will come into Jerusalem, to lead himself in poverty, or humility." As it is written in Zechariah chapter 9: "Poor and humble, riding upon a donkey, or an ass." <note>original: "Pauper & humilis, equitans super asinum, uel asinam."</note> It follows in the same place in the book of Genesis: "And to the vine-shoot, my son, his ass." For when he comes to gather Israel, as it is said in Zechariah 10: <gloss>I will whistle for them and gather them, for I have redeemed them</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: אשרקה להם ואקבצם כי פדיתים (eshreqah lahem ve-akabtzem ki feditim)</note>. This is the tradition.

Likewise, in the *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>A significant collection of ancient Jewish interpretations (midrash) on the Book of Genesis.</note> upon that text of Genesis chapter 49, where it is written, "The scepter shall not depart from Judah," along with the rest, it is read thus: "The scepter shall not depart." This is the King Messiah, the son of David, who is to come to break the kingdoms with a rod, or with a staff. As it is said in Psalm 2: <gloss>You shall break them with a rod of iron; you shall dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: תרועם בשבט ברזל ככלי יוצר תנפצם (teroaem be-shevet barzel ki-khli yotzer tenafzem)</note>. This is also the King Messiah, who is to come to crush the nations with his feet. Just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 26: <gloss>The feet of the poor shall trample it</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: תירמסנה רגלי עני (tirmasnah raglei ani)</note>. This is: "The foot of the feet of the poor man shall trample it." For that poor man is the Messiah, of whom it is said in Zechariah chapter 9: "Poor and riding upon an ass." Thus ends the tradition.

From these things which have been said, therefore, it is quite clearly evident that the Messiah was to be poor and humble, and was to come riding upon an ass for the sake of bringing salvation. Wherefore the Jews will be least able to deny that our Savior was the true Messiah, on the grounds that he was poor and humble.

# *That the Messiah was to undergo many sufferings, and God also was to suffer many things. Chapter X.*

->CAPNIO,<-

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q'</note>
**S**ince the Jews of our time, when they hear that our Redeemer was hungry even after a fast of forty days and nights, and was tempted in many ways by the devil, or was exhausted from his journey while he went about the cities and towns preaching the kingdom of God and leading sinners to repentance, or that he fled like a fearful man from the Jews who wished to stone him, or that at the approaching hour of his passion he began to fear and be weary and to be sorrowful—so that he might show himself to be a true man—they say that he was neither the true Messiah, nor did he exist as God. For that reason, you would not act unsuitably if you would show through their own scriptures that both the Messiah and God himself (for each was to be the same) were to suffer such things, and indeed far more grievous things.

### EIGHTH.

"The God who made you to be born, or who begot you, you shall weaken, or afflict, and you shall forget the wounded God, or the slain, or the afflicted, or your grieving one." <note>This is a highly interpretive translation of Deuteronomy 32:18, which usually reads "You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you." The author is using a variant or polemical reading to suggest divine suffering.</note> Thus far <term>R. Selomo</term> <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, the famous medieval commentator known as Rashi.</note>. Similar to this is what is held in the book **Siphre** <note>original: "ספרי" (Sifre), an ancient Jewish legal commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note>, in the place where the previously mentioned words "The God who begot you, you shall weaken or afflict" are explained along with the rest. There it is said word-for-word:

<margin>Talmudic exposition.</margin>
> The Holy and Blessed God said to Israel: "You have made me as if I were a male wishing to give birth. For if it were a woman in labor, sitting upon her birth-stool, would she not be in distress?" Just as it was said in the 32nd chapter of Isaiah <note>This citation actually corresponds to Isaiah 37:3.</note>, **"The children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to bring forth"** <note>original Hebrew: "באו בנים עד משבר וכח אין ללדת" (ba'u vanim ad mashber ve-koach ayin laledet).</note>. And if there were some woman in pain, and giving birth for the first time, would she not be in even greater distress? As in Jeremiah, chapter 4, **"For I have heard a voice as of a woman in labor, and the anguish as of one bringing forth her first child"** <note>original Hebrew: "קול כחולה שמעתי וצרה כמבכירה" (kol ke-cholah shamati ve-tzarah ke-mavkeirah) from Jeremiah 4:31.</note>. And if there were two in her womb, would she not be in more anguish? As it was said in Genesis, chapter 25, **"And the children struggled together within her"** <note>original Hebrew: "ויתרוצצו הבנים בקרבה" (va-yitrotzatzu ha-banim be-kirbah) from Genesis 25:22.</note>. And if it were a male, who has no way of giving birth, who sought to give birth, would not his anguish be doubled? Just as it was said in Jeremiah, chapter 30, **"Ask now, and see, whether a male gives birth"** <note>original Hebrew: "שאלו נא אם יוליד זכר" (sha'alu na im yolid zachar) from Jeremiah 30:6.</note>.

Another exposition. "The God who begot you, you shall weaken or afflict, and you shall forget the wounded God, or the slain, or the afflicted, or your grieving one." The Holy Blessed God said: "You have forgotten me because of the merit of your fathers." And so He Himself says in Isaiah, chapter 51, **"Look to the rock from which you were hewn"** <note>original Hebrew: "הביטו אל צור חצבתם" (habitu el tzur chatzavtem) from Isaiah 51:1. <margin>Another Talmudic exposition.</margin>
Yet another exposition. "The God who begot you, you shall weaken." The Holy and Blessed God said: "At every time when I sought to do good for you, you weakened my heavenly power." It follows, "And you shall forget the grieving God." <term>R. Meir</term> <note>A famous miracle-working rabbi of the 2nd century.</note> said: "Namely, the God who will be pained for you, or through you. The God, I say, who will be distressed for you, or through you." As it was said in Psalm 47 <note>The author likely means Psalm 48:6.</note>, **"Anguish was there, as of a woman in labor"** <note>original Hebrew: "שם חיל כיולדה" (sham chil ke-yoledah).</note>. All these things are from the book **Siphre**.

It is also read in the book **Sanhedrin** <note>A tractate of the Talmud.</note> in the chapter **Helec** <note>The eleventh chapter of Sanhedrin, which contains many messianic discussions.</note> what <term>R. Is it not because of his passion, or his tribulation?" <note>This refers to the "Birth Pangs of the Messiah," a period of intense global suffering expected before his arrival.</note> For there is a tradition that the disciples of <term>Eliezer</term> asked him, saying: "What shall a man do to be delivered from the passion or tribulation of the Messiah?" So also said **Rabbi Yohanan**, <note>A prominent 3rd-century scholar in the Land of Israel.</note> "Let the Messiah come, but let me not see him." **Resh Lakish** <note>A contemporary of Yohanan, known for his strength and past as a gladiator.</note> said to him, "What is the reason? Is it because of what is written in **Amos, chapter 5**, *As if a man should flee from the face of a lion?*" By no means; rather, it is because of what is written in **Jeremiah, chapter 30**: *Ask now, I pray you, and see if a male gives birth.* For what reason? Or what does this mean? <margin>Why do I see every man with his hands on his loins like a woman in labor, and every face turned pale?</margin> That is: *Because I saw every man, whose hands are upon his loins like one in labor, and all faces turned to paleness* <note>original Latin: "ictericiam," literally jaundice, but here referring to the pale-greenish color of extreme fear.</note>—namely, the faces of the angels and of Israel, according to the gloss of **Rabbi Solomon**. <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> But what does it mean by *I saw every man*? **Rabba** said, "This refers to Him who possesses all virtue and power—God Himself," as the gloss of **Rabbi Solomon** says, "who will Himself be in distress <note>original Latin: "metangustiabit," a rare term for being in narrow straits or extreme labor-like pressure.</note> like one giving birth." And what does it mean, *And all faces turned to paleness*? **Rabbi Yohanan** said, "Even the faces of the family above and the family below." For in the hour when the Holy and Blessed God said, "These are the work of my hands, and those also are the work of my hands; how then shall I destroy these on account of those?" **Rabbi Papa** said, "To this point is what men say: 'The ox ran and fell, and they put a horse in its place in the stable.'" Thus far the tradition. But the gloss of **Rabbi Solomon**, explaining the example introduced at the end, says this: "When a certain man's ox was running, it fell. Therefore, they put a horse in its place in the stable. The owner of the ox and horse would not have done this before, for he loved the ox so much. But after the ox was healed, it was difficult for him to expel the horse from the stable to put the ox back there." <margin><unclear>Genesis Rabbah</unclear></margin> So does the Holy and Blessed God: for when the fall of Israel occurs, God gives their greatness to the nations of the world. But when Israel later returns to repentance, it is hard for God to destroy them—namely, the Gentiles—on account of Israel. This is according to **Rabbi Solomon**. Certainly, several things are to be noted in this tradition. First, that the coming of the Messiah was desired with great affection by all, even by those who, because of the torments he was to suffer, did not wish to see him. Next, that according to that authority of **Jeremiah** which they introduce there, wishing to give the reason why they did not want to see him—namely, *Ask, I pray you, and see if a male gives birth. For what reason? Because I saw every man with his hands on his loins like one in labor*—God Himself, in the time of the Messiah, was to suffer extreme torments. For the wise Talmudists explain "every man" there as being the Holy and Blessed God. Third, finally, that the nations of the world were established by God in the place of the Jews, and the Jews themselves were cast out from their place. <margin><unclear>Genesis Rabbah</unclear></margin> This is also clearly evident, as far as it pertains to our purpose, in the **Bereshith Rabbah Ketanna** <note>The "Smaller Genesis Rabbah," likely a reference to a specific Midrashic compilation.</note> (that is, in the minor exposition of the book of **Genesis**), where it is written upon **Genesis, chapter 36**, *And Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom.* Thus it is said: "This is what is written in **Jeremiah, chapter 30**, *For thus says the Lord: We have heard a voice of terror (or trembling), of dread and not of peace. Ask now, and see if a male gives birth.*"

## That the Messiah was to voluntarily undertake the most bitter torments for the sake of the human race. Chapter XI.

### CAPNIO, <note>The persona of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist, used as a character in this dialogue.</note>

Since we read that Christ suffered voluntarily for the salvation of the human race, I would like to know whether the ancient Jews predicted that the Messiah would undergo torments of his own free will. **GALATINO:** <note>The author, Pietro Galatino, acting as the teacher in the dialogue.</note> Precisely so. For even leaving the prophets aside for now, it is most clearly shown in the exposition of the book of Genesis by **Rabbi Moses Ha-Darshan** <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic (interpretive) compilations.</note> that the Messiah himself was to suffer torments spontaneously and voluntarily out of love for the human race. There, upon that statement in the first chapter of the same book: <term>ויאמר אלהים יהי אור ויהי אור</term>, that is: *God said, "Let there be light," and there was light,* it is read as follows: This is what is written in Psalm 97 <note>The text says Psalm 96, but it refers to 97:11.</note>: <term>אור זרע לצדיק</term>, that is: *Light is sown for the righteous.* **Rabbi Abba** said: It is also written in Daniel, chapter 2: <term>ונהורא עמיה</term>, that is: *And the light dwells with him.* For this is the light of the King Messiah. For thus it was said of him in Psalm 36: <term>כי עמך מקור חיים באורו נראה אור</term>, that is: *For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light.* For that is the light of the King Messiah. Moreover, it teaches that God hid the Messiah and his generation under the Throne of His Glory <note>A concept in Jewish mysticism representing the residence of God and the pre-existent souls.</note>. Then **Satan** said before God: "Lord of the world, this light hidden under the throne of Your glory—to whom does it belong?" He answered him: "To the Messiah and his generation." **Satan** said before Him: "Lord of the world, allow me, and I will oppose the Messiah and his generation." God said to him: "You will not be able to prevail against him." **Satan** spoke again before Him: "Allow me, and I shall be able." The Holy and Blessed God said to him: "If you, Satan, are so eager for this, I will destroy you from the world. However, I will not destroy even one single soul of that generation." And soon the Holy and Blessed God began to speak with the Messiah, and said to him: "Messiah, my righteous one, those who are hidden with you—this will be their condition: it will happen that their sins will lead you into a heavy yoke. For your eyes shall not see light, and your ears shall hear great reproach. Your nose shall smell the stench, and..."

<margin><unclear>...t... / ...os</unclear></margin> “[...] your mouth will taste bitterness, and your tongue will cling to the roof of your mouth, and your skin will stick to your bones, and your strength will be weakened by mourning and groaning. Is it therefore your will to be in these sufferings? For if you take these upon yourself, it will indeed be well. But if not, behold, I will drive them away from now on.” The Messiah responded before him: “Lord of the world, I indeed gladly take up these tribulations, or torments, upon myself, yet on this condition: that in my days you give life to the dead, and to those who from the first Adam until then shall have died. And not only that you save them, but also those who were devoured by wolves and lions, and those who happened to be submerged in seas and rivers. Nor them alone, but even the miscarried. Nor only the miscarried, but truly those also who rose up in your foreknowledge to be created—that you save them in my days.” The Holy and Blessed God said to him, “I grant it.” Immediately, therefore, out of love, the Messiah took upon himself all the torments and tribulations. As it is written in Isaiah chapter 53: <term>He was oppressed, and he was afflicted</term> <note>Hebrew: "niggas ve-hu na'aneh"</note>. That is: He was offered up, and he himself was afflicted. All this is tradition. Wherein five things especially most worthy of note against the Jews of our age are contained. Of which the first indeed is, that the Messiah, before he existed according to his humanity, was light and illumination with God, and in God, and the principle by which God created the world. To which that word of the Lord Jesus himself is very much in agreement, saying in John chapter 8: *Before Abraham was, I am.* Likewise in chapter 7 <note>The original text cites chapter 7, though this quote is more closely associated with John 8:12 or 12:46</note>: *And I, the light, have come into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.* The second truly is, that by divine permission, Satan was to oppose the Messiah and those believing in him, and was to disturb him with every effort. To which that saying of the same Lord in Luke chapter 22 greatly <margin>*</margin> agrees: *Simon, behold, Satan has asked for you, that he might sift you like wheat.* From which it is clear that it detracts nothing from Christ that he was tempted by the devil. The third, moreover, is that the Messiah was to suffer in manifold and most heavy ways on account of the sins of the human race. Which is noted where it is said that God entered into a covenant with the Messiah, and said to him: “My righteous Messiah, those who are stored up with you—namely through predestination—shall be of such a kind that their future sins will lead you into a most heavy yoke.” Whence it is clear that nothing of those things which our Savior suffered prevents him from having been the Messiah. Since it was necessary for the Messiah himself to suffer for the salvation of men, and so that the scriptures might be fulfilled. The fourth also is, that just as through Adam all were dying, so through the Messiah all were to be made alive. This, moreover, is noted where the Messiah is introduced speaking with God and saying: “Lord of the world, I indeed gladly take up these tribulations, or torments, upon myself, on the condition that in my days you make the dead alive,” along with the rest. Finally, the fifth is: That the Messiah was to be tortured and suffer torments not unwillingly, but willingly and voluntarily out of charity, for the sake of the salvation of the human race. From which not only is the proposition clear, but also that the Messiah himself, who was to be affected by torments, is true God.

### That God was to suffer blows, reproaches, insults, and even death. Chapter 12.

**CAPNIO,**

**A**lthough in the preceding sections you have shown sufficiently and abundantly that the Messiah was to be both God and man, and that God Himself was to undergo many torments; nevertheless, so that Jewish unbelief <note>original: "perfidia"</note> may be more and more convinced, you ought still to prove even more expressly from their own scriptures that God Himself was to be affected by blows, reproaches, and even death for the salvation of the human race. **GALATINO.** This is first evident from what is written in <term>Lamentations, chapter 3</term> <note>original: "Tren. 3. cap."</note>: <term>He will sit alone and be silent, because he has taken it upon himself. He will put his mouth in the dust, perhaps there will be hope. He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him, he shall be filled with reproach</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Yishev badad ve-yidom ki natal alav; yiten be-afar pihu ulai yesh tikvah; yiten le-makkehu lechi yisba be-cherpah"</note>. This means: He shall sit alone and hold his peace, because he has carried, or borne, it upon himself. He shall place his mouth in the ground, or in the dust. Perhaps there will be hope. He will offer his cheek to the one who strikes him; he shall be satisfied with reproach, or insult. 

That these things ought to be understood as referring to God is clear in the <term>Midrash Echa</term> <note>a Jewish homiletic commentary on the Book of Lamentations</note>, that is, in the exposition of the lamentations of Jeremiah. Where, upon these same words, it is said word for word: <term>Rabbi Samuel bar Nahmani</term> <note>original: "Rabbi Semuel filius Nahman," a famous 3rd-century scholar</note> said that the Holy and Blessed God called the ministering angels and said to them: "When a human king <note>original: "Rex caro & sanguis," literally "a king of flesh and blood"</note> mourns, what does he do?" They said to him: "He hangs sackcloth over his door." He then said to them: "I also will do thus." Just as it is said in <term>Isaiah</term>, the fiftieth chapter: <term>I will clothe the heavens with darkness, and I will make sackcloth their covering</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Albish shamayim kadrut ve-sak asim kesutam"</note>. 

Again He said to them: "When a human king mourns, what does he do?" They said to him: "He extinguishes the lights." And He said to them: "I also will do thus." And this is what is written in <term>Joel</term>, the third chapter: <term>The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their brightness</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Shemesh ve-yareach kadaru ve-kochavim asfu nogham"</note>, and God shall roar from Zion, and utter His voice from Jerusalem. 

Still He questioned them, saying: "When a human king mourns, what does he do?" They answered him: "He goes barefoot." He said to them: "I also will act thus." And this is what is written in <term>Nahum</term>, the first chapter: <term>God's way is in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet</term> <note>original Hebrew: "YHVH be-sufah u-ve-se'arah darko ve-anan avak raglav"</note>. 

Once more He questioned them, saying: "When a human king mourns, what does he do?" They said to him: "He sits and keeps silence." And He said to them: "I even so will do." And this is what is written in <term>Lamentations</term>, the third chapter: "He shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has carried, or borne, it upon himself; he shall put his mouth in the ground, or in the dust. Perhaps there will be hope. He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him, he shall be filled with reproach." Wherefore the Rabbi, when explaining this scripture and arriving at these <term>verses</term> <note>original: "pasukim"</note>, always wept. All this is tradition. <term>Micah</term> also spoke of the striking of God's cheek in this manner in the fifth chapter: <term>With a rod they shall strike the judge of Israel upon the cheek</term> <note>original Hebrew: "be-shevet yakku al ha-lechi et shofet Yisrael"</note>. This means: They shall strike with a rod...

<meta>catchword: hate (original: odi)</meta>

upon the cheek of the judge of Israel. Who this judge of Israel might be, Isaiah shows when in chapter 33 he says, **The LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us** <note>original Hebrew: "יהוה שפטנו יהוה מחקקנו יהוה מלכנו הוא יושיענו"</note>. That is: God is our judge, God is our lawgiver, God is our King; He Himself will save us. Furthermore, that God was to suffer the gravest insults from the Jews was foretold through the prophet Hosea, speaking in the words of God in chapter 7: **Woe to them, for they have strayed from me; destruction to them, for they have rebelled against me. I would redeem them, but they speak lies against me** <note>original Hebrew: "כי נדדו ממני שד להם כי פשעו בי ואנכי אפדם"</note>. This means: Woe to them, because they have departed—meaning they *will* depart—from me. Destruction for them, because they have been guilty—meaning they *will* be guilty—against me. And I have redeemed—meaning I *will* redeem—them. But they have spoken—meaning they *will* speak—lies against me. 

In these words, God threatened the Jews with two supreme evils: namely, eternal damnation in the world to come, because by denying Him before Pilate <note>Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor who presided over the trial of Jesus</note>, they were to depart from Him. And for this reason He says: *Woe to them because they have departed*, that is, they will depart from me. He also threatened their final devastation and dispersion throughout the world when He says: *Destruction for them, because they have sinned*, that is, they will sin in me—which is to say, against me. And wishing to express the cause, He adds: *And I have redeemed*, that is, I will redeem them. *But they have spoken*, that is, they will speak lies against me. It is as if He had said: "Behold how great their ingratitude shall be. For while I am redeeming them, they themselves will speak lies against me," namely, by falsely accusing me before Pilate and by inflicting the most grievous insults upon me. 

That these things ought to be interpreted exactly as they have been explained is clearly evident through their ancient Teachers <note>Referring to Jewish rabbis and sages</note>, and especially through those things said in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>A Jewish homiletic commentary on the Book of Psalms</note>, in the exposition of the 39th Psalm on the verse: **I said, I will guard my ways, from sinning with my tongue** <note>original Hebrew: "אמרתי אשמרה דרכי מחטוא בלשוני"</note>. For it is said there: This is what is written in Proverbs, chapter 15: **A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger** <note>original Hebrew: "מענה רך ישיב חמה ודבר עצב יעלה אף"</note>. This means: A tender response restrains anger, and a hard word excites fury. For a "bad tongue"—which specifically speaks against God—is more serious than idolatry. For when the children of Israel finally sinned in the desert, the sentence of judgment was not carried out against them until they sinned against God with their mouths. For so the Scripture says: *And God heard their words, and he was angry.* And again, in Numbers chapter 14, He says: *As I live, says God, if I do not do to you just as you have spoken in my ears, so shall I do to you.* 

And likewise Malachi says in chapter 2: **You have wearied the LORD with your words** <note>original Hebrew: "היגעתם יהוה בדבריכם"</note>. That is: You have troubled God with your words. He does not say "in your deeds," but "in your words." And so also Isaiah himself says in chapter 3: **For Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen, because their tongue and their deeds are against the LORD, defying his glorious presence** <note>original Hebrew: "כשלה ירושלם ויהודה נפל כי לשונם ומעלליהם אל יהוה למרות עיני כבודו"</note>. This means: Jerusalem has collapsed and Judah has fallen, because their tongue and their works are against God, unto the rebellion of the eyes of His glory. So also He says through Jeremiah in the twelfth chapter: **I have abandoned my house, I have deserted my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies** <note>original Hebrew: "עזבתי את ביתי נטשתי את נחלתי נתתי את ידידות נפשי בכף אויביה"</note>. That is: I have left my house, I have abandoned or cast away my inheritance; I have given the beloved of my soul—or, I have given my soul out of love—into the hand of her enemies. My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has raised her voice over me, or against me. Therefore...

He supports these claims by citing the Midrash Tehillim and various scriptural warnings about the power of speech to provoke divine wrath.</summary>

...I hate her. <note>original Latin: "odi eam"</note> Thus far the tradition. From this, the proposition is clear. For since God says that out of His love He gave His soul—or Himself—it is surely not to be doubted that He gave Himself over to passion and death for their redemption. This is indicated when He says: *Into the hand of her enemies.* 

Furthermore, that God, because of the love for His people, was to give His soul—that is, Himself—is clear through the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>A Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Song of Songs</note>, that is, through the exposition of the Song of Songs. Regarding that saying in the first chapter of that book: **Tell me, you whom my soul loves** <note>original Hebrew: "הגידה לי את שאהבה נפשי"</note>, it explains it thus: "Tell me of the people whom my soul loved; namely, the people for whom I gave **my soul** <note>original Hebrew: "נפשי" (naphshi)</note>," meaning my soul, or my very self, or my person. 

Moreover, that God was to undergo death is clear through what is written in Malachi, chapter 1: **And you said, "Behold, what a weariness!" and you have snuffed at it, says the LORD of hosts** <note>original Hebrew: "ואמרתם הנה מתלאה והפחתם אתו אמר יהוה צבאות"</note>. For there it was originally written: "you have made **me** expire." But the Scribes <note>A reference to the "Tiqqune Sopherim," or Scribal Corrections, where tradition holds that early scholars changed phrases to avoid appearing disrespectful to God</note> changed it to "you have made **him** expire," as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> testifies in his gloss there. 

Likewise, in Habakkuk chapter 1: **Are you not from everlasting, O LORD my God, my Holy One? You shall not die.** <note>original Hebrew: "הלוא אתה מקדם יהוה אלהי קדושי לא נמות"</note> For it was written there in that way; however, the Scribes placed "we shall not die," as is stated in the book *Siphre* <note>An ancient legal commentary on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy</note> regarding the saying in Numbers chapter 10: "Rise up, Lord, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee." 

From these things which have been said, therefore, it is manifest that God was to suffer strikes, insults, and death. Since God [in His divine nature] cannot suffer these things, it is clearly evident that they were to be understood concerning the Messiah, who was to be both God and man. For the prophets also predicted that He would suffer all these same things.

->*That the Messiah in his passion was to be sold, reproached, beaten with whips and fists, affected by innumerable shames and insults, clothed in purple, and crowned with thorns.* **Chapter XIII.**<-

# CAPNIO,

<margin>GALATINUS</margin>**CAPNIO:** Since our Lord Jesus Christ, in His passion, was sold, reproached, despised, beaten with whips and fists, afflicted with the gravest shames and injuries, clothed in purple, and crowned with a crown of thorns; I would like to know, not without reason, whether it can be proven through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that the Messiah was to undergo these same things in His passion. 

**GALATINUS:** It certainly can. For Zechariah foretold in the 11th chapter that the Messiah—God and man—was to be sold for a cheap price, that is, thirty pieces of silver. He speaks in His [the Messiah's] person, saying: **And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said to me: "Cast it to the potter"—the magnificent price at which I was valued by them.** <note>original Hebrew: "וישקלו את שכרי שלשים כסף ויאמר יהוה אלי השליכהו אל היוצר אדר היקר אשר יקרתי מעליהם"</note> Concerning this, Amos also says in chapter 2:

**For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn it back, because they sold the righteous for silver.** <note>Amos 2:6. Original Hebrew: "על שלשה פשעי ישראל ועל ארבעה לא אשיבנו על מכרם בכסף צדיק"</note>

> i. For three crimes of Israel, and for four I will not convert, or I will not lead back, or I will not transfer it, because they have sold, or have traded the righteous one for silver.

The explanation of these words is set forth very extensively in the 24th chapter of the fourth book. That the Messiah himself was to be reproached in his passion is held in Psalm 89. Where it is said: **With which your enemies have reproached, O Lord, with which they have reproached the footsteps of your Messiah.** <note>Psalm 89:51–52. Original Hebrew: "אשר חרפו אויביך יהוה אשר חרפו עקבות משיחך"</note>

> That is: Which your enemies have reproached, O God, which they have reproached the ankles <note>The Hebrew "akvot" can mean heels, footsteps, or the "end" of something</note> of your Messiah.

Where the gloss of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential Jewish commentator</note> says: "The ankles of your Messiah," he says, means "the final days of the King Messiah." For then the final things of the Messiah were reproached, when he himself was despised by all in his passion and death. Moreover, that this exposition is correct is evident in the exposition of the book of Genesis by **Rabbi Moses Hadarshan** <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations</note>, regarding that which is said in the 39th chapter concerning Joseph, *And he fled outside*. For there it is read that Rabbi Iodan said: "David said, 'Just as I did not speak a Song until I was reproached or despised, so the children of Israel are not going to speak a Song when the King Messiah comes until he himself has been reproached, or despised, or dishonored.'" Just as it is written: **Which your enemies have reproached, O God, which they have reproached the ankles**—that is, the extremities, or the end—**of your Messiah.** Concerning the reproach of the Messiah, it is also found in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, upon that title of Psalm 17: *The words of this Song*. For it is said there: "When the Messiah comes in haste, they will not say the Song until the Messiah himself has been reproached." Just as it was said: **that your enemies have reproached, O God, that they have reproached the ankles**—that is, the final days—**of your Messiah.** Also in the *Mishnah* <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note>, that is, in the Talmud, it is written that in the "ankles"—that is, against the final days of the Messiah—impudence shall be multiplied. Indeed, that he was to be struck with whips and blows, and affected by the gravest insults, is most clear through what Isaiah said, speaking in his person in the 50th chapter: **I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to those who pluck the hair; I did not hide my face from shame and spitting.** <note>Isaiah 50:6. Original Hebrew: "גוי נתתי למכים ולחי יהוה למורטים פני לא הסתרתי מכלמות ורוק"</note>

> i. My back I gave to those striking, and my cheeks to those plucking or tearing. My face I did not cover from confusion and spit.

The Psalmist also signified that this was to happen in Psalm 129, saying: **The plowers plowed upon my back; they made their furrows long.** <note>Psalm 129:3. Original Hebrew: "על גבי חרשו חורשים האריכו למעניתם"</note>

> This is: Upon my back the plowers plowed, they prolonged their furrow.

Which the Aramaic interpreter <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> who is at hand translates thus: **Upon my body the rulers ruled, prolonging their domain.** <note>Original Aramaic: "על גושמי רדו רדוי לאריכא למורוחתהון"</note>

> i. Upon my body the plowers plowed, they prolonged their plowings.

Where the prophet, taking the past for the future in the prophetic manner, spoke in the person of the Messiah to show the infallible certainty of the future truth. Therefore, the "plowers" were going to plow upon the body of the Messiah, because the Jews were to strike it most cruelly with whips. They were also going to prolong the furrows or plowings upon him, because they were going to fill it entirely with wounds and strikes, according to that which was said in Isaiah, chapter 1: *From the sole of the foot even to the head, there is no [soundness]...*
