in him is health. The fact that he was to be dressed in purple as a mockery is also found in the exposition of the book of Genesis by **Rabbi Moses Hadarshan** <note>An 11th-century Jewish scholar from Narbonne</note>, concerning that statement in the 49th chapter of the same book: **He washes his garment in wine, and his robe in the blood of grapes.** <note>Genesis 49:11. Original Hebrew: "כבס ביין לבושו ובדם ענבים סותה"</note> This means: "He will wash his garment in wine, and his covering or clothing in the blood of grapes." For there it is read as follows: "He will wash (it says) his garment in wine." For when the Messiah comes, he is clothed in purple, beautiful to the sight, which will be similar in color to wine. It follows: "And his clothing in the blood of grapes." For the clothing of the King Messiah will be silk, red as blood, and it will be embroidered on top with other colors. And he himself will be the head of Israel. And this is what was said in the 63rd chapter of Isaiah: **Why is your garment red?** <note>Isaiah 63:2. Original Hebrew: "מדיע ארום ללבושך"</note> That is, "Why is your clothing red?" And "his clothing in the blood of grapes." Just as it was said by the same prophet in the same place: **And your garments like those of one treading in the winepress.** <note>Isaiah 63:2. Original Hebrew: "וכדידך בדורך בגת"</note> This is the tradition. In this, both the literal purple garment with which the Messiah was to be mocked, and his seamless tunic woven from the top throughout, are clearly established.

However, the words of both Isaiah and the patriarch Jacob are to be understood mystically. For when he says, "He will wash his garment in wine, and his covering in the blood of grapes," he wanted to explain the great mystery of the Messiah's passion by repeating the same sentiment with different words. For this Hebrew word **anauim** <note>Original Hebrew: ענבים</note>—that is, "of grapes"—which is contained in the second clause, by the Hebrew grammatical rule in which the letters **bumaph** <note>Original Hebrew: בומפ''ו. This refers to the "labial" consonants (B, V, M, P) which are often phonetically interchangeable in Semitic linguistics</note> (that is, one is placed for another), by changing the **beth** into a **vau**, is the same as "of the humble." <note>The author is performing a linguistic maneuver to link 'grapes' (anavim) with 'the humble' (aniim) to argue for a suffering Messiah</note> And then the sense of this text will be: "And in the blood of the humble [he will wash] his covering." This was to show that the Messiah, in his humility, would wash his covering or his garment—that is, his body—in his own blood. The words of Isaiah express this more clearly.

Furthermore, that he was to be crowned with thorns is clearly gathered from the words of the same prophet, when in the 5th chapter he says: **My beloved had a vineyard.** <note>Isaiah 5:1. Original Hebrew: "כרם היה לידידי"</note> And after a little while: **And I hoped it would produce grapes, and it produced thorns.** <note>Isaiah 5:4. Original Hebrew: "ויקו לעשות ענבים ויעש באשים"</note> In this place, although that Hebrew word **beussim** <note>Original Hebrew: באשים</note> is ambiguous, meaning both wild grapes and thorns, here it signifies thorns, not wild grapes. As the expositions of the ancients clearly indicate. And so **Rabbi Jonah** <note>Likely referring to Jonah ibn Janah, the famous medieval Hebrew grammarian</note> explains in this place, when he says, "And it produced *beussim*—that is, thorns." Just as it is said in the 31st chapter of Job: "And instead of barley, **baassa**"—that is, a thorn. <note>Job 31:40. The author relates the "stinkweed" or "noisome weed" of Job to the thorns of the Passion</note> This is suggested by the preceding clause, in which it is said: "Instead of wheat, the thistle comes forth." **Rabbi Kimhi** <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a leading medieval rabbi and grammarian</note> also affirms this, saying that *beussim* in this text of Isaiah is a type of thorn. 

Therefore, it is certain that all of this was fulfilled when, as John relates in the 19th chapter: "The soldiers, weaving a crown of thorns, placed it upon his head, and surrounded him with a purple garment." <note>John 19:2</note> From all of these things it is clear that the Messiah, in his passion, was to be sold, reproached, and despised; beaten with whips and fists; afflicted with the gravest insults and outrages; and was to be clothed in purple and crowned with thorns. These and all the other things which we have premised concerning the passion of the Messiah were announced even more expressly and distinctly by Isaiah himself.

## *That the mystery of the Messiah's passion was expressly and distinctly foretold by Isaiah. Chapter XIV.*

->CAPNIO,<-

**T**ell me, I pray, where Isaiah explicitly and distinctly mentioned the mystery of the Messiah's passion. GAL. In the fifty-third chapter. For beginning the discourse on this mystery at the end of the 52nd, he pursues it so expressly and so distinctly through the whole of the 53rd that he seems not to be a prophet foretelling things to come, but an Evangelist <note>The author suggests Isaiah's description is so vivid it reads like an eyewitness account of the Gospels</note> narrating things already done. For he says thus:

<note>original Hebrew: "הנה ישכיל עבדי..." — The following is the Hebrew text of Isaiah 52:13–53:12 translated into English</note>

Behold, my servant shall prosper, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high. Just as many were astonished at you—so marred was his appearance beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of the sons of men—so shall he sprinkle many nations. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him; for that which had not been told them they shall see, and that which they had not heard they shall understand. Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way; and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth. Yet it was the will of the Lord to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.

That is: Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted, and lifted up, and shall be very high. Just as many were astonished over you, and just as his look was despised, or wasted away from men, and his form from the sons of men. So shall he sprinkle many nations; over him kings shall shut their mouth, because they have seen what was not told to them, and they have understood or contemplated what they had not heard. Who has believed our report? And over whom, or to whom, has the arm of God been revealed? And he shall go up like a twig before him, and like a root from the dry ground. There is no beauty in him, nor any grace. And we saw him, and there was no sightly appearance, and we did not desire him. He was despised, and the last of men, a man of sorrows, and known by infirmity, and as it were with faces veiled from him, or, with a veiling of faces from him. Vile, and we did not esteem him. Truly he himself has borne our languors, and endured our sorrows. And we esteemed him as one ulcerated, struck by God, and afflicted. But he himself was wounded, or slain, on account of our faults, crushed on account of our sins. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and in his bruise, or wound, it was healed for us. All we like sheep have wandered, each one [turning] to [his own] way...

In these words, many mysteries of the Messiah himself are related. The first is that the Messiah himself, as the servant of God, according to his <margin>Sixteen mysteries.</margin> humanity, was to be more excellent than all other saints, both those in heaven and those on earth. Concerning this, the prophet says: *He shall be exalted, and lifted up, and shall be very high.* For this is explained in the book of the *Sanhedrin* <note>A major collection of Jewish law and tradition within the Talmud.</note>, in the chapter *Helec* <note>The eleventh chapter of Tractate Sanhedrin, which discusses the afterlife and the coming of the Messiah.</note>, in this way: <margin>Talmudic exposition.</margin> "He shall be exalted more than Abraham, lifted up more than Moses, and shall be very high, more than the ministering angels" <note>original Hebrew: "ירום מאברהם ונשא ממשה וגבה מאד יותר ממלאכי השרת"</note>—that is, those who minister to God. From these words, it follows that the Messiah was to be God. For since God alone exceeds the angelic nature, and the Messiah was to be higher than the angels who minister to God—who, according to the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>, are more worthy and more sublime than all others—the Jews must certainly concede, by their own scriptures, that he is God.

The second mystery concerns his exaltation on the cross, through which he was to be exalted, lifted up, and greatly elevated; for through his passion and resurrection, he was meant to draw all things to himself. Therefore it follows: *Just as many were astonished at you, and just as his appearance was despised—or wasted away by men—and his form was marred among the sons of men, so shall he sprinkle many nations,* namely with the water of <term>baptism</term> <note>The author interprets "sprinkling nations" not as a physical ritual, but as the spiritual cleansing of the world through Christian initiation.</note>. Through this, he was to lead those who would receive his law toward eternal salvation. Nor does it matter that the prophet sometimes speaks in the second person and sometimes in the third, as he does this in the prophetic manner. Therefore, the kings of the nations, wondering at him, were to shut their mouths, placing their hands over their lips. For they were to see what had not been told to them, and they were to contemplate what they had not heard. <meta>This page continues the detailed analysis of Isaiah 53, following the previous page's transcription of the prophetic text. Here, the author breaks down the prophecy into specific points to prove they refer to the life and passion of Jesus.</meta>

# BOOK

he adds, *Who has believed our report: and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?* <note>Isaiah 53:1</note> That is: Who ever believed our message, so that those to whom such a mystery was never told, nor ever revealed—namely, the manner in which God would accomplish it—should firmly believe it? The third point is that the Messiah, in his beginning, was to be a little child and would have a humble origin. When he says, *And he shall grow up as a tender plant before him, and as a root out of a dry ground.* <note>Isaiah 53:2</note> Here, both the poverty of the newborn Messiah is expressed, and the virginity of his mother giving birth. For he, on account of his poverty, was rightly to be compared at his birth to a slender and thin shoot; and his mother, on account of her virginity, is not unaptly likened to "dry ground," because she was to conceive and give birth to him having been moistened by no human seed at all. The fourth point is that in his progress he was despised, and regarded as almost nothing. Concerning which he says, *There is no form in him, nor beauty. And we saw him, and there was no sightly appearance, and we did not desire him.* For even if the text says "and we desired" affirmatively, it must nevertheless be understood negatively. For the preceding negative word <term>לא</term> (*lo*), meaning "not," as <note>original: "R. Dauid"</note> Rabbi David <note>Referring to David Kimhi, a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator known as Radak.</note> says, serves both clauses. It is as if he were saying: "And we saw him, and there was no sightly appearance, nor did we desire him." And wishing to give the reason why they did not desire him, he immediately added, *He was despised, and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity; and as one from whom faces are hidden.* As if to say: We hid our faces so as not to look at him. And this was because he was lowly. Whence we did not even esteem him. The fifth point is that he was to suffer because of our sins. Therefore he says, *Surely he has borne our infirmities, and carried our sorrows. And we esteemed him as a leper, struck by God, and afflicted.* <note>Isaiah 53:4</note> Here it is greatly to be noted that the Hebrew text has "a struck God," and not "struck by God," as our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> says. For the Hebrew text itself says <term>מוכה אלהים</term> (*Mucche Elohim*), that is, "a struck or wounded God." For if it meant "struck by God," it would say <term>מוכה מאלהים</term> (*Mucche meelohim*), with the preposition <term>מ</term> (*me*), which among the Hebrews signifies "by," "from," or "out of." It follows: *But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins.* "Discipline," that is, the correction of our peace was upon him, and in his bruise or wound—that is, through his bruise and wound—we are healed.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The sixth point is that all the righteous except for himself and his mother have strayed from the way of salvation according to the common law <note>The author likely means the "common law" of human nature or original sin, from which he exempts Jesus and Mary.</note>, and he bore the sins of all, namely as far as the punishment is concerned. Therefore he says, *All we like sheep have gone astray; every one has turned aside into his own way. And God caused the sin of us all to meet in him,* so that he might satisfy the debt for us all. The seventh point is that he endured these punishments or sorrows voluntarily and patiently for us even unto death. Therefore he says, *He was offered, and he himself was afflicted,* or "voluntary and willing," *and he shall not open his mouth. Like a lamb to the slaughter*

...shall be led to slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearers, he shall be silent, and shall not open his mouth. <note>Continuing the quote of Isaiah 53:7 from the previous page.</note> The eighth point is that although he was to suffer as a man, yet as God he was to be entirely beyond the reach of suffering. Therefore he adds, *He was taken from distress and from judgment, and who shall declare his generation?* <note>Isaiah 53:8</note> Here indeed God the Father speaks of the Messiah as a man, saying: After he has been taken away from those things which could happen to the Messiah regarding his humanity—that is, when he is considered with that human part set aside—who shall be able to declare his generation? This means: who can explain the manner and cause of his incarnation? For to no one will such power be given that they might be able to explain it fully and perfectly. And giving the reason, he adds: *Because he was cut off*—that is, he shall be cut off—*from the land of the living, for the wickedness of my people, and their sore,* or that which was upon them. This he interprets as the sore of <term>original sin</term> <note>The Christian doctrine that humanity inherits a state of sin from the first humans, Adam and Eve.</note>. For a "sore" (as physicians agree) is an old wound.

The ninth point is that just as the prophet described him as the redeemer of the faithful through the merit of his passion, so he hinted at him as the judge of the unfaithful through the power of his divinity, where he says, *He shall give the ungodly in his burial,* or in his pit. This is, according to the exposition of <note>original: "R. Ionathæ"</note> Rabbi Jonathan <note>Refers to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note>: He shall deliver the ungodly into <term>Gehenna</term> <note>A term used here for hell or a place of divine punishment.</note>, and the rich men of wealth who have acted wickedly into the death of perdition.

The tenth is that he ought to be entirely just and free from all sin, when he says, *Because he did no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth.* <note>Isaiah 53:9</note> And God willed to crush him with weakness. It is as if he were saying: Even if he will be entirely just and devoid of all sin, he is nonetheless to suffer for the sins of others.

The eleventh is that on account of the merit of his death, he would have many spiritual sons—that is, disciples—until the end of the world. And this is what he says, *If he shall lay down*—that is, because he will lay down—*his soul for sin, he shall see a seed of length of days.* <note>Isaiah 53:10</note> This is understood to refer to his faithful followers and his faith, which shall stand forever. It follows, *And the will of God shall prosper in his hand.* And the reason is because, as it is said, *From the labor*—that is, on account of the labor—*of his soul, which he himself shall see, he shall be satisfied.* <note>Isaiah 53:11</note>

The twelfth is that through the wisdom of his teaching, he was to justify many. Wherefore he adds, *In his knowledge shall my just servant justify many, and he himself shall bear their sins.*

The thirteenth is that he was to have victory against the devil and divide the spoils of the strong, because he was to deliver himself up to death. Therefore he says, *Therefore I will divide to him among many,* or I will make him share with many, *and he shall divide the spoil with the strong*—that is, the spoils. *Because he exposed* or delivered *his soul unto death*—that is, himself. <note>Isaiah 53:12</note>

The fourteenth is that he was to be *counted among the wicked* as if he were a criminal and a wrongdoer. Therefore he says, *and he was numbered with the transgressors.*

The fifteenth is that although his passion was to be sufficient for blotting out the sins of all people, it was not, however, going to blot out the sins of everyone, but only of those who would believe in him and perform penance. For that reason he adds, **And he himself [bore the sins of many]** <note>The text breaks off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

## *Refutation of the objection of the more recent Jews, who falsely interpret the words of Isaiah, using the interpretations of the ancient Talmudists. Chapter 15.*

->CAPNIO,<- <note>The character name used for the German Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin.</note>

Even if all these things are exactly as you have explained them, the more recent Jewish scholars object to us, saying that the prophet speaks there not of the Messiah (as you have explained), but rather, according to the literal sense, of the people of Israel as if of a single man. Just as it says in the 4th chapter concerning the same: *Israel is my firstborn son.* <note>Exodus 4:22</note> For this reason, nearly all the more recent writers, and especially Rabbi David <note>David Kimhi, a 13th-century grammarian and commentator.</note> and Rabbi Solomon <note>Known as Rashi, the 11th-century commentator.</note>, interpreting those same words of Isaiah as referring to the Jewish people themselves, apply everything contained in those words—namely the sicknesses, the plagues, the contempt, the shames, and others of that kind—to that same people. Therefore, you would do very well if, to convict them of their faithlessness, you would refute their false and perverse interpretation by proving through their own scriptures that those same words of the prophet can only be interpreted as referring to the Messiah. 

GALATINUS: It is indeed true that Rabbi Solomon and Rabbi David, and almost all the other more recent writers, invented this forced interpretation against the literal sense and the opinion of all the ancients, so that they might hide and obscure the mystery of the Messiah’s <term>passion</term> <note>The suffering and death of Jesus.</note>, which is clearly handed down in the aforementioned words of the prophet. But since the truth is never hidden, it is easy to convict those who speak falsely and lie. I will therefore do two things here. First, I will show that the aforementioned words of Isaiah can in no way be applied to the Jewish people existing in this most recent captivity <note>Referring to the long Diaspora following the Roman destruction of the Second Temple.</note>. Then, I will prove through scriptures that are authentic and approved among them that these same words can only be interpreted as referring to the Messiah. 

The first point <margin>The first point.</margin> is evident especially from the fact that many things contained in these same words can in no way be applied to the Jewish people. There are three in particular. The first of these is: *But he was wounded for our offenses, bruised for our sins.* <note>Isaiah 53:5</note> For although the Jewish people have been afflicted in many ways in this captivity, they do not suffer this because of the iniquities and crimes of the Gentiles. It is not as if the Gentiles themselves receive pardon and are saved by God because of the merits of the Jews suffering such things—as they say, who assert that the Gentiles would speak these words. For this is not only clearly false, since it is against divine justice (according to which God renders to each according to their works), but also against their own opinion, since almost all of them...

# BOOK EIGHT

<page-num>585</page-num>

<header>EIGHTH</header>

...with no one disagreeing, they say that the nations which now suppress and afflict the Jewish people in this captivity <note>The "captivity" refers to the Jewish Diaspora following the Roman destruction of Jerusalem.</note> will similarly be punished by God for this reason. To prove this, they bring forward the statement from the last chapter of Joel: *I will gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and will plead with them there for my people.* <note>Joel 3:2</note> Since the prophet says that through the bruising or the wound of this servant of God (of whom he speaks here) others are healed, and that God laid upon him the sin of all other men, it certainly follows that he is not speaking here of the Jewish people; for through their punishments others are not saved, but rather punished.

<margin>Second point.</margin> The second point is that when the prophet speaks of the same servant of God, he says: *Because he had done no iniquity, neither was there any deceit in his mouth.* <note>Isaiah 53:9</note> This is clearly false regarding the Jews, as is plainly evident from the facts of the matter. This is because for the most part they are all immersed in usury, iniquities, deceits, fortune-telling, sorceries, and other outrages. Furthermore, it is clearly held from the testimony of Holy Scripture that in this most recent captivity (as we have proved elsewhere) they remain only because of their own crimes. Indeed, if they were willing to perform penance for their sins, they would be redeemed immediately (as will be clear in what follows). Moreover, this is against their own exposition. For they, presupposing that they are not in this captivity except because of a great sin, or great sins, and seeking among themselves what that sin might be, or what those sins might be, different people feel differently. Nevertheless, they all agree in this: that the Jewish people are not in this captivity without sin or iniquity, nor because of the sins of other nations, but only because of their own. From this it is clearly evident that this servant of God of whom Isaiah speaks cannot be understood as the Jewish people, but the Messiah himself, who was to be entirely immune from sin.

<margin>Third point.</margin> Finally, the third point is when the prophet at last says of the same servant of God: *And he shall pray for the sinners.* <note>Isaiah 53:12</note> This can in no way be understood regarding the Jewish people existing in this captivity. For they not only do not pray for the salvation of the sinners of other nations, but rather for their destruction, and especially for the ruin and perdition of the Roman Empire and the Christian Church, thinking that after the fall of the Roman Empire and the destruction of the Church of Christ, they are soon to be liberated from this servitude and captivity, as we have shown elsewhere. From this it is manifest that this saying of the prophet—*and he shall pray for the sinners*—can in no way be verified concerning them. Therefore, from these and many other things contained in this prophecy, which can in no way fit the Jewish people existing in this captivity, it is clear and transparent that the servant of God himself of whom the prophet speaks cannot possibly be the Jewish people themselves. Moreover, that the aforementioned words of Isaiah can rightly fit no one else than the Messiah himself is clearly evident not only from the preceding points and the text itself, but also appears more clearly and evidently from the sayings of the ancient expositors. Indeed, all the ancient expositors, both those who preceded the coming of Christ and those who lived after the passion of Christ, held these same views...

...they explained the words of Isaiah as being understood only concerning the Messiah. Just as Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "R. Selomo," referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki, 1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> himself also openly testifies while explaining these same words, upon that verse, *Behold, my servant shall deal prudently*, along with the rest: he says, "Our masters affirm that this whole passage is to be understood as referring to the Messiah." This can also be seen through many others who, in various places, assert that these words were spoken concerning the Messiah. For in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>original: "R. Moysis Hadarsan," an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note>, upon that statement in the 24th chapter, <note>Genesis 24:67</note> *And Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother*: it is said word for word, "This is the King Messiah, who existed in the generation of the wicked and rejected them, and chose the holy and blessed God and His holy name, so that he might worship Him with all his heart. And he gave his heart to seeking mercies for Israel, and to fasting, and to humbling himself for them. Just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 53: *But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him.* And since the children of Israel were sinners, he shall pray for them. Just as it is said in the same chapter of Isaiah: *And with his stripes we are healed.* And for this reason, God preserves him, so that he may save Israel, and that he may exult with them in the resurrection of the dead. Just as it is said in Deuteronomy chapter 33: *Happy are you, O Israel: who is like you, a people saved by the Lord, the shield of your help?* Just as Isaiah also says in chapter 45: *Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation. You shall not be ashamed nor confounded, world without end.*" This is the tradition.

Furthermore, it is written in the book Sanhedrin, in the chapter *Helek* <note>A significant section of the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b) discussing the afterlife and the coming of the Messiah.</note>, that it was said by the house of Rabbi—that is, by the disciples of the Rabbi—that "The Languid One" <note>original: "languidus," likely reflecting the Hebrew "Chivaya" (the leper/the sick one).</note> is the name of the Messiah, according to what is said in Isaiah chapter 53: *Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows.* In the same place it is also read that the Rabbi said: "If the Messiah is among the living, he is like our holy master <note>Referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the redactor of the Mishnah.</note>. If, however, he is among the dead, he is like Daniel, the 'man of desires'." <note>A title for the prophet Daniel (Daniel 10:11), here used to denote a person of high spiritual merit.</note> Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "If the Messiah is (he says) among those who are still living, in truth he is like our holy master. For he both endured illnesses and was holy. If, however, he is among those who are already dead, behold, he was like Daniel, the 'man of desires,' who was sentenced to sufferings in the lions' den, and was holy, perfect, and a prince." However, <term>chegon</term> <note>A Hebrew/Aramaic term meaning "such as," "like," or "for example."</note>—that is, "such as"—is not taken strictly here. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. From these things it is clearly evident that there was a doubt among the ancient Jews as to whether the Messiah was living then or was dead. For it was established among them that he had already come. 

Moreover, in the same book and chapter, those words, *Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high* (as we said in the preceding chapter) are explained in this way: "Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper; he shall be exalted more than Abraham, extolled more than Moses, and raised higher than the ministering angels" <note>That is, the angels who serve God directly.</note>. From all these things it is quite clearly evident that all the words of Isaiah from that place, *Behold, my servant shall deal prudently*, up to the end of the 53rd chapter, were understood by the ancient wise men of the Jews as referring to the Messiah.

# Confirmation of the aforementioned refutation through the Aramaic paraphrase of Rabbi Jonathan on the same words of Isaiah. Chapter XVI.

->CAPNIO<-

**S**ince the Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaica," referring to Aramaic, which was often called Chaldean in this period.</note> translation of Rabbi Jonathan son of Uziel <note>Jonathan ben Uziel was a premier student of Hillel the Elder (1st century BCE/CE) and the traditional author of the Targum (Aramaic paraphrase) of the Prophets.</note>, which they call the Targum, is of such great authority among them that none of them dare to contradict it, I would like you to show—as a confirmation of this refutation—through that same Rabbi's Targum that all the aforementioned words of Isaiah cannot be understood as referring to the people of Israel, nor to any other man, but only to the Messiah himself. *GALATINUS:* It is not without reason, my dear Capnio, that you urge me to do this. For indeed, that same Rabbi in his Aramaic paraphrase explains all these same words (as you know) concerning the Messiah, just as we propose. For where the Hebrew text says, *Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high* <note>Isaiah 52:13</note>, he himself says in Aramaic: <note>original Aramaic: "הא יצלח עבדי משיחא ירום ויסגי ויתקוף לחדא"</note>. That is, *Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper, he shall be exalted, and shall increase, and shall be very strong.* But where the Hebrew text has, *So shall he sprinkle many nations; the kings shall shut their mouths at him* <note>Isaiah 52:15</note>, he says in Aramaic: <note>original Aramaic: "כן יבדר עממין סגיאין עלוהי ישתקון מלכין ישוון ידיהון על פומהון"</note>. That is, *So shall he cleanse (or choose) many nations. Because of him kings shall be silent, and they shall place their hand upon their mouth.* From this it is clear that the Hebrew word *yazah* <note>Hebrew: יזה</note> which is placed there is ambiguous (for it signifies both to open and to shorten or tighten). Here it is not taken to mean "to open" (as the author of our edition <note>A reference to the Latin Vulgate's translation of the verb.</note> took it), but for that which is "to shorten" or "to tighten." Furthermore, where the Hebrew letter says, *For that which had not been told them they have seen, and that which they had not heard they have perceived (or contemplated)*, Jonathan himself says: <note>original Aramaic: "ארי דלא אשתעיאו להון חזו ודלא שמעו וסתכלו"</note>. That is, *For those to whom it was not told concerning him have seen, and those who did not hear have contemplated.* And where it says in Hebrew, *Who has believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?* <note>Isaiah 53:1</note>, he says in Aramaic: <note>original Aramaic: "מאן הימין לבסורתנא דא ותקוף דרע גבורתיה דיהוה ברין על מאן אתגליאת"</note>. That is, *Who has believed this our announcement? And the strength of the arm of the power of the Lord, upon whom has it been thus revealed?* And where the Hebrew has, *He has no form nor comeliness*, with the rest <note>Isaiah 53:2</note>, the same man explains it in Aramaic: <note>original Aramaic: "לא חיזו חילא חזויה ולא אימתיה אימת הדיוט ויהי זיו קודשא זויה וכל דיחזיניה יסתכל ביה"</note>. That is, *His appearance shall not be a common appearance, nor his fear (or authority) the fear of a commoner <term>idiotae</term> <note>From the Greek 'idiotes,' meaning a private person or commoner without specialized knowledge or status.</note>. But his glory shall be the glory of holiness; and whoever sees him shall gaze upon him.* Because of this, it shall be for a good announcement. And where the Hebrew letter has, *And as it were faces hidden from him*, with the rest, he translated it into Aramaic thus: *Because of our sins, the face of the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah</term> was removed from us...*

<margin>Accounted <note>Aramaic: חשיבין (chashibin)</note></margin> That is: And it was as if the face of his divinity had been taken away or removed from us, who saw him and did not esteem him. Furthermore, regarding what is said in Hebrew, *Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows* <note>Isaiah 53:4</note>, he <note>Jonathan ben Uziel</note> translates it into Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldæum," referring to Aramaic</note> thus: **Then he shall pray for our sins, and our iniquities shall be forgiven for his sake.** <margin>We shall be forgiven <note>Aramaic: ישתבקון אנחנא (yishtabkun anachna)</note></margin> This means: Thus, or at that time, he himself shall make intercession for our crimes, and our sins will be forgiven us because of him. And as for what is found in the Hebrew, *The chastisement of our peace was upon him* <note>Isaiah 53:5</note>, along with the rest, he translated it into Aramaic in this way: **And in his teaching, peace shall multiply upon us, and by his worthiness of his words, our guilt** <margin>Will be forgiven us <note>Aramaic: ישתבקון לנא (yishtabkun lana)</note></margin> **shall be forgiven us.** That is: And in his doctrine, peace shall be increased over us, and in his death <note>The Latin text here reads "morte" (death), though the Aramaic "בהגינותוהי" usually implies "worthiness" or "conduct." The translator is likely emphasizing a Christological link to the Messiah's death.</note>, at his word, our crimes shall be forgiven us. Indeed, where it says in Hebrew, *All we like sheep have gone astray* <note>Isaiah 53:6</note>, with what follows, he explained it in Aramaic thus: **All of us like a flock have been scattered; each man was exiled toward his own way.** <margin>The guilt of us all for his sake <note>Aramaic: חובא כולנא בריליה (chova kulana b'reileh)</note></margin> **And from before the Lord there was a desire to spare, or forgive.** That is: We were all scattered like sheep; every person was taken captive toward his own path. And on God’s part, it was a good pleasure to spare or remit the guilt of us all because of him. And where the Hebrew text has, *He was offered, and he was afflicted*—or *voluntary*, or *willing*—*and he shall not open his mouth* <note>Isaiah 53:7</note>, he translated it into Aramaic thus: **He prayed, and he was answered, and before he opened his mouth, he received the strong ones of the nations.** <margin>The strong ones of the nations <note>Aramaic: חקימי עממיא (chakimei ammaya), literally "the wise of the nations."</note></margin> That is: He made intercession, and he himself was heard, even before he opened his mouth, being about to receive the powerful of the nations. And where it is held in Hebrew, *He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter* <note>Isaiah 53:7</note>, and so forth, he says the same in Aramaic: **Like a ram he shall be delivered to the slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearers, he shall be silent. And there will be no one who opens his mouth before him** <margin>And speak a word <note>Aramaic: ומליל מילא (u'malil mila)</note></margin> **and speaks a word.** That is: Just as a ram is delivered to the slaughter, and as a sheep before those shearing it becomes mute. And there will be no one who opens his mouth on his behalf and speaks a word. And where the Hebrew letter has, *And who shall declare his generation?* <note>Isaiah 53:8</note>, he translated it into Aramaic thus: **And the wonders that shall be done for us in his days,** <margin>Who can count? <note>Aramaic: מאן יכיל לממני (man yakil le'mne)</note></margin> **who will be able to recount?** That is: And the miracles which will happen for us in his days, who shall be able to describe them? Furthermore, where it is read in Hebrew, *He shall give the wicked in his sepulcher, and the rich in his deaths* <note>Isaiah 53:9</note>, he explained it in Aramaic thus: **And he will deliver the wicked to Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna <gloss>A place of spiritual punishment or purgation, often translated as "Hell."</gloss></note>, and the rich in possessions who acted iniquitously, into the death of perdition.** That is: And he shall hand over the ungodly to Gehenna, and those rich in wealth who acted wickedly, into the death of destruction. And where it is said in Hebrew, *And the Lord willed to bruise him in infirmity. If he shall lay down his soul for sin* <note>Isaiah 53:10</note>, and so forth, he also explained it in Aramaic thus: **And from before the Lord there was a pleasure to refine and cleanse the remnant of his people, so that their souls might be purified from guilt. They shall see the Kingdom of their Messiah; they shall multiply sons and daughters, they shall prolong their days. And those who perform the law of the Lord** <margin>Shall prosper in his pleasure <note>Aramaic: ברעותיה יצלחון (b'reuteh yitzlakhun)</note></margin> **shall prosper in his good pleasure.** That is: And on God's part, it was a good pleasure that the remnant of his people should be refined and bruised, so that their souls might be cleansed from their crimes and see the Kingdom of their Messiah. They shall multiply sons and daughters, who will prolong their days. And those who follow the law of God shall prosper in his good pleasure. Where it also says in Hebrew, *By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, and he shall bear their sins* <note>Isaiah 53:11</note>.

## That God was to be hung on a cross and affixed to a cross; and that it is the Messiah who was to die by the death of the cross. Chapter XVII.

**CAPNIO** <note>The persona of the scholar Johannes Reuchlin.</note>
Although the stubbornness of the Jews of our time is so thoroughly refuted by what you have said so far regarding the passion of the Messiah that they should no longer dare to even open their mouths, their impiety must still be more clearly exposed. They deny that our Lord Jesus was the true Messiah precisely because he was affixed to a cross—even though most of them falsely claim he was merely "hung." <note>This likely refers to the Jewish polemical work *Toledot Yeshu*, which claimed Jesus was hung from a cabbage stalk rather than a Roman cross.</note> Therefore, it is necessary that you demonstrate through their own scriptures that the Messiah, as both God and man, was to be hung on a cross and meet his end through the death of the cross.

**GALATINUS**
There are two things I must do here. First, I must prove that God himself was to be suspended and affixed to a cross. And second, that the Messiah himself was to die by the death of the cross. That God was to be suspended is found clearly enough in Deuteronomy chapter 28, where it is said: **And your lives shall be hanging before you, and you shall fear night and day, and you shall not believe in your lives.** <note>Deuteronomy 28:66. The Hebrew word for "life" used here, *chayyekha*, is plural. Galatinus exploits this grammatical plurality for his theological argument.</note> Perhaps he spoke of "lives" in the plural here because, just as the Messiah has a dual nature, so too is his life dual: namely, God and soul. These "lives" of the Messiah, which were to be hung on the cross for us, are ours. For regarding the life which is God, we read in Deuteronomy chapter 30: **For he is your life and the length of your days.** That the Messiah is also "life" has already been proven above. For the Lord Jesus himself testified to this, saying: *I am the way, the truth, and the life.* Also in the *Genesis Rabbah Ketanna* <note>The "Little Genesis Rabbah," a midrashic commentary.</note>—that is, in the lesser exposition of the book of Genesis—this truly wonderful thing I am about to say is written concerning that statement in chapter 22 of the same book: *And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it upon Isaac his son.* For it is said there: **Just as "this one" <note>Hebrew: זה (ze)</note>, that is, God who**

...who carries his cross upon his shoulder. A similar thing to this is found in the Jerusalem book of *Berachoth* <note>original: ברכות, "Blessings," a tractate of the Talmud</note> in the chapter that begins *Meemathai korin* <note>original: מאימתי קורין, "From what time do they read?"</note>. For there it is said: "And it happened, when Solomon had finished offering all this prayer and supplication to the Lord, he rose from before the altar of the Lord, where he had been kneeling on his knees, with his hands spread out toward the heavens." Rabbi Abhu said: "And his hands were spread out toward the heavens. For just as **this one** <note>original: זה (*Ze*)</note>—the one who was crucified, or extended on a cross—was standing." This is the passage there; and the word *Ze*, which is translated into Latin as "this one," refers in this context to nothing other than God. 

This is most strongly proven by what is written in the book *Menahoth* <note>original: מנחות, "Grain Offerings"</note> in the chapter beginning *Hammenahoth* <note>original: המנחות, "The Offerings"</note>. There it is said: **The Holy One, blessed be He, is called *Ze* <note>this one</note>, as it is written in Exodus chapter 15: "This (*Ze*) is my God, and I will glorify him."** This is the tradition. According to these two traditions, therefore, God was to carry the cross on his own shoulders and be affixed to that cross with his hands extended. Since God, by his own nature, cannot suffer these things, they must necessarily be understood as referring to the <term>Messiah</term> <note>The "Anointed One" promised in scripture</note>, who was to be both God and man, and was to die by the death of the cross. 

That the hands and feet of the Messiah himself were to be pierced on the cross was proclaimed by the Psalmist in Psalm 22, saying: **For dogs have surrounded me; a council of evildoers has besieged me; they have pierced <note>original: foderunt</note> my hands and my feet.** <note>The Hebrew text Galatinus cites is: כי סבבוני כלבים עדת מרעים הקפיחני כארי ידי ורגלי</note> The Scribes <note>original: *Sophrim*, referring to the early Jewish transmitters of the biblical text</note>, however, changed that word *caru* <note>כרו, "they pierced"</note> into *caari* <note>כארי, "like a lion"</note>, perverting both the scripture and the meaning at the same time. We have shown very extensively in the first book that they have done this in many other places as well. 

Nevertheless, some of our own scholars (acting out of piety and good zeal) say: "Since the Hebrew text here says 'Like a lion my hands and my feet,' the grammatical structure is simply missing a word." They believe it should be understood as: "The wicked, like a lion, have pierced, perforated, fixed, or treated my hands and my feet badly." To prove this, they bring forward the Aramaic translation <note>The Targum</note>, which reads: **Because the wicked have surrounded me, who are like many dogs; the assembly of the malignant have encircled me, biting like lions my hands and my feet.** <note>original Aramaic: מטול דאחזרו עלי רשיעי...</note> 

From this, they conclude that the Hebrews did not corrupt this passage. But to tell the truth, this argument of theirs does not please me at all. First, because in almost infinite manuscripts which the Jews now have in their hands, the word is corrupted as *caari* <note>"like a lion"</note>; yet in some very ancient ones, *caru* <note>"they pierced"</note> is still found written. Even so, the Jews do not read it as *caru* (as it is written), but as *caari*. For they say it is a case of *ketiv* <note>original: כתיב, "what is written"</note>—that it is written as *caru*—but *qere* <note>original: קרי, "what is read"</note>—that it must be read as *caari*.

...*caari* <note>original: כארי, "like a lion"</note>. This is the third method of corrupting the scripture, as was shown more extensively in the first book. Although that translation also does much against the Jews of our time (which is most noteworthy) and here, as in many other places, serves our purpose. 

Finally, it is clearly evident that it was originally written here not as <term>כארי</term> (*caari*), meaning "like a lion," but as <term>כארו</term> (*caru*), meaning "they dug" or "they pierced." This is plain not only in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan (as seen in chapter 8 of the first book) regarding the passage: "And Abraham still stood before the Lord." It is also proven by the edition of the 70 interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, who translated these words thus: *For many dogs have surrounded me, a congregation of evildoers has encircled me; they pierced my hands and my feet.* <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἐκύκλωσάν με κύνες πολλοί, συναγωγὴ πονηρευομένων περιέσχον με, ὤρυξαν χεῖράς μου καὶ πόδας μου.</note> <margin>Psalm 21</margin> <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 22:16</note>. From this it clearly appears that <term>כארו</term> (*caru*), that is "they pierced," and not <term>כארי</term> (*caari*), "like a lion," was written in this place. 

This can also be seen most strongly from that Chaldean translation which the Indians and Ethiopians use. For it reads: **ቀኖዐ፡ እደውየ፡ ወእገሪየ** <note>Transliterated: *Canauuni oyouiya uaogariya*</note>. That is: *They wounded, or they dug through my hands and my feet.* 

Therefore, David did not utter these words in his own person, as the raving younger Jews say, but in the person of the Messiah, whom he foresaw would suffer such things. This is also openly hinted at in the words that immediately follow, when it is said: **I will count all my bones, or all my detractors. They will look and stare at me; they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.** <margin>Psalm 21</margin> Since David never suffered these things, nor were they ever fulfilled in him, they must be understood as referring to the Messiah. This is especially true since it is written in the book <term>שבת</term> (*Sabbath*) <note>A tractate of the Talmud</note>, in the chapter beginning <term>במה אשה יוצאת</term> (*Bamme haissa yocza*), that is, "With what may a woman go out," that Rabbi <term>חיא</term> (Hiya) had said all the prophets prophesied only concerning the days of the Messiah. 

The ancient Talmudists also attribute that saying from Zechariah chapter 12, **And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced** <note>original Hebrew: והביטו אלי את אשר דקרו</note>, to the Messiah son of Joseph <note>In Jewish tradition, a Messiah who suffers and dies before the arrival of the victorious Messiah son of David</note>, as Rabbi David Kimhi reports in that same place. This is easily proven by what is contained in the book <term>סוכה</term> (*Succa*) <note>A Talmudic tractate regarding the Festival of Booths</note>, in the chapter **The Flute** <note>original: החליל המשנה, *Hahalil hammisla*</note>. There it is read: It is written in Zechariah chapter 12, **The land shall mourn, family by family apart.** For what purpose will this mourning be? There is a controversy there between Rabbi <term>דוסא</term> (Dossa) and the masters. For one says that the mourning will be for the Messiah son of Joseph who will be killed. And the other says that it will be over the "evil inclination" which will be slaughtered. <term>בשלמא</term> (*Bislama*), that is, "It is well for him" <note>A common Talmudic expression meaning "it makes sense according to..."</note> who said the aforementioned mourning will be over the Messiah son of Joseph. For this is what is written in Zechariah 12: *And they shall look upon me...*

...whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him as one mourns for an only son, and shall be in bitterness over him, as one who is in bitterness for his firstborn. <note>original Hebrew: את אשר דקרו וספדו עליו כמספד על היחיד והמר עליו כהמר על הבכור</note>

This is: *And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him as if mourning for an only son. And there shall be sorrow over him, just as there is usually sorrow for a firstborn.* This is the tradition. However, although the commentators leave it unexamined there, whether that Messiah is called the "son of Joseph" because he was to come from the tribe of Joseph, or from a father named Joseph, the saying of the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Teachers of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> is nevertheless understood to refer to Christ our Lord. For this reason, the Talmudists called him the "son of Joseph," because he was to have no other father on earth except a <term>putative</term> one <note>putative: commonly accepted or supposed, but not necessarily biological</note>—namely, Joseph, the spouse of his virgin mother, who, as the Evangelists record, was thought to be his father. For this reason, the glorious Virgin herself said to him in Luke chapter 2: *Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have sought you sorrowing.* Therefore, from this tradition it necessarily follows that God himself was to be wounded and pierced. For since those words—*And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced*—which the ancient Talmudists wanted to be understood as referring to the Messiah, were uttered by the prophet in the person of God, it is as if God himself were to be crucified. This could not even have been imagined unless the divinity had been <term>hypostatically united</term> <note>hypostatic union: the Christian doctrine that Christ is one person with two distinct natures, divine and human</note> with humanity in the Messiah himself. It follows, therefore, that the Messiah who was to be crucified was to be both God and man. 

Furthermore, since the pouring out of the spirit of grace upon men belongs to no one except God alone, it is certainly clear that he in whose person the prophet speaks is entirely God, saying: *And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced.* <note>original Hebrew: ושפכתי על בית דויד ועל יושב ירושלם רוח חן ותחנונים והביטו אלי את אשר דקרו</note> That is: *And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of devotion, or of prayers. And they shall look upon me whom they have transfixed, or pierced.*

<margin>Objection of the younger Jews</margin>
**CAP.** The younger Jews <note>Referring to contemporary or medieval Jewish scholars who disagreed with the Christian interpretation</note>, being unable to distort such evident testimony of the passion of God and man, say regarding this passage that "they shall look upon *him*," and not "upon *me*," is what is written among them.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
**GAL.** First, their falsehood is evident from the fact that all their ancient books (as you yourself know best) have it exactly as I have written and translated it. Secondly, it is proven through the <term>Chaldaic</term> <note>Aramaic paraphrase of the Bible, known as a Targum</note> translation of Rabbi Jonathan, which brings forth the same words in Aramaic: *And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of piety and mercies, and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced.* Wherefore the same prophet says in chapter 13: *And one shall say to him, What are these wounds in your hands? And he shall say, With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me*—that is, who *ought* to have loved me. *Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is my companion*—or my equal, or joined to me—*says the Lord of hosts. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.* <note>original Hebrew: ואמר אליו מה המכות האלה בין ידיך ואמר אשר הכיתי בית מאהבי : חרב עורי על רעי ועל גבר עמיתי נאם יהוה צבאות הך את הרעה ותפצין הצאן</note> From all of this, it stands more clearly than light that the Messiah, as God and man, was to be hung on the gallows of the cross and was to meet his end through the death of the cross.

### *Response to the objection of the Jews, who assert that Christ was not God for this reason: that on the cross he cried out that he had been forsaken by God. Chapter xviii.*

## REUCHLIN, <note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pen name of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous humanist and scholar of Hebrew.</note>

Here, the impious faithlessness of the more recent Jews opposes us. They say: "If your Christ was God, why, when he was about to die on the cross, did he cry out that he was forsaken by God, saying: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* <note>original Hebrew: אלי אלי למה עזבתני (Eli eli lama azabtani)</note> That is: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* For if he had been both God and man, that man could never have been deserted by the God to whom he was <term>hypostatically</term> <note>Hypostatic union refers to the belief in Christian theology that the divine and human natures are perfectly joined in the single person of Jesus.</note> united (as you claim). This is because, as you yourselves assert, what he once assumed, he never laid aside. Therefore, since he cried out that he was forsaken by God, he himself openly protested that he was not God."

<margin>HOOGSTRATEN</margin> <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten was a conservative theologian and inquisitor often depicted as Reuchlin’s opponent.</note> To this, Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> says that Christ sang Psalm 21 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 22.</note> on the cross, and others following it, up to that verse in Psalm 30: <note>In modern Bibles, Psalm 31:5.</note> *Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.* From this it follows that he did not say those words, *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?*, in order to show that he was truly forsaken by God, but because those words occurred in the other Psalms he was meant to recite.

<margin>GALATINO</margin> <note>Pietro Galatino, the author of this work.</note> I certainly do not contradict Jerome, but I add this one thing: that just as it was also said to the Jews in Isaiah chapter 33: <note>This quote, "Why will you die, O house of Israel?", is traditionally found in Ezekiel 18:31 or 33:11. The author may be citing a different version or simply misattributing the chapter.</note> *And why will you die, O house of Israel?*—not indeed so that he might learn this from them, but rather to salutarily rouse them to the consideration of their own perdition—so also Christ, when as a man he cried out and asked God why He had forsaken him into the hands of the Jews to be mocked, spat upon, scourged, crucified, and killed, he did so not as one who was ignorant, nor as one complaining against God or accusing Him. Instead, he did it so that he might lead the Jews who heard him to the most soul-saving consideration and faith in his passion. The words immediately following there clearly suggest this. For when the prophet, speaking in the person of the Messiah (as has been said), had said: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* <note>Hebrew: אלי אלי למה עזבתני</note>, he immediately added: *The words of my roaring are far from my salvation.* <note>original Hebrew: רחוק מישועתי דברי שאגתי (Rachoq mishuati dibre shaagati)</note> That is: *Far from my salvation are the words of my roaring.* Truly, the words of Christ’s "roaring"—by which as a man he cried out that he was forsaken by God—were, in the hearts of the Jews who desired to kill him, far from his "salvation" (the salvation by which God raised him up and lifted him into heaven while his disciples watched). Or, to put it another way: since it was said in the sixth book, according to the opinion of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of Jewish law and tradition.</note>, that our salvation is the salvation of God (because God, in saving Israel, is said to save Himself), for this reason the Messiah himself, who was to save the human race, is often called "the saved one" in place of "the savior." On that account, it can also be said quite fittingly that the "words of roaring"—that is, of Christ's lamentation—were to be "far from his salvation" (meaning the future redemption of the human race) only in regard to those who, on account of their unrepentant and obdurate...

...their obstinate hearts were not going to receive the fruit of human redemption. For this reason, he immediately added, "I thirst," <note>John 19:28</note> which is to say: "I desire the salvation of all," because I suffer for all, even if not everyone will be saved by the merit of my passion. And it seems that the <term>Chaldean interpreter</term> <note>This refers to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated the aforementioned words in this sense. For he says in Aramaic: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me, far from my redemption are the words of my lamentation.* <note>original Aramaic: אלהי אלהי מטול מה שבקתני רחיק מן פורקני מילי אכליתני (Elohi Elohi metul mah shebaqtani rahiq min purqani milli akhlitani)</note>

<margin>HOOGSTRATEN</margin> Our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible translation used by the Church at the time.</note> has it far differently than you have translated it. For it says: *God, my God, look upon me, why have you forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my sins.*

<margin>GALATINO</margin> As is clearly evident to any observer, the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>A scholarly term (*Hebraica veritas*) used by humanists like Reuchlin to argue that the original Hebrew text was more accurate than the later Greek or Latin translations.</note> is far better for the Christian faith here than our edition—whether Greek or Latin—has it. The authors of those versions, moved by I know not what spirit, removed the pronoun "my" from the beginning of the verse, added "look upon me" in the middle, and at the end, changed "the words of my roaring" into "the words of my sins." Indeed, it is discovered that they very often did these three things—namely, subtracting, adding, and changing—in many other places in Holy Scripture, both among the Greeks and the Latins.

Therefore, the excessive and false cunning of the Jews of our time can by no means conclude that he was not God simply because our Savior cried out that he was forsaken by God. Nor can they argue that we believe a God who is entirely impassible, immortal, and unchangeable was crucified, pierced with nails and a spear, and died. For we assert that the Messiah suffered all these things as both God and man—certainly not according to his divinity, but according to the nature of our mortality which he assumed. Long before us, the prophets, the other holy fathers, and the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> both confessed and believed all these things with us, as was clearly shown in the preceding sections.

For these reasons, they themselves (as seen above) not ineptly called him *El naaraz*, that is, the "Broken God," or "Crushed," or "Terrified." For *El* means God, according to the "form of God," and *naaraz* means "broken," "crushed," or "terrified" according to the "form of a servant." <note>This draws on Philippians 2:6-7, contrasting Christ's divine nature with his humble human nature.</note> According to this form, in his passion, as Mark relates in chapter 14, he began to be terrified and distressed, and was crushed by whips, beaten with fists and palms, crucified, and pierced and broken by nails and a spear.

For this reason, the <term>Psalm-writer</term> <note>Referring to King David, traditionally considered the author of the Psalms.</note>—addressing God and in a way arguing against him because of the judgment of the impious, as if God were acting against what he had promised concerning the Messiah—says in Psalm 89: *But you have rejected and cast off, you have been full of wrath with your Messiah. You have neglected the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his crown on the earth.* <note>original Hebrew: ואתה זנחת ותמאס התעברת עם משיחך : נארת ברית עבדך חללת לארץ נזרו</note> And a little later: *How long, O Lord, will you hide yourself forever? Shall your wrath burn like fire?* <note>Psalm 89:46</note> Where the <term>gloss</term> <note>A scholarly commentary or explanation.</note> of **Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>A distinguished Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator (1089–1167).</note> says: "How long (he says) will God hide—"

## *That the Messiah in his death was to be given gall and vinegar to drink, and that at his dying, darkness was to occur over the whole earth. Chapter XIX.*

### CAPNIO, <note>This is the humanist name for Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering Christian scholar of Hebrew.</note>

Since we read that Christ our Redeemer was given gall and vinegar to drink during his passion, and that darkness happened over the entire earth as he was dying, we must also prove through their own scriptures that all these things were destined to happen at the death of the Messiah, in order to further rebuke the impious and obstinate disbelief of the Jews of our time. 

<margin>GALATINO</margin> First, therefore, it should be noted what is read in the book <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>A major tractate of the Talmud dealing with judicial procedures and capital punishment.</note> in the chapter that begins, *The judgment is finished.* <note>original Hebrew: נגמר הדין (Nigmar haddin).</note> Where it is said literally: "Rabbi <term>Hasda</term> <note>Rav Hisda (d. 309 AD), a prominent Babylonian Talmudist.</note> said: One going out to be killed was given a grain of frankincense in a cup of wine to drink so that his senses would be separated from him [numbed]." Just as it is said in Proverbs chapter 31: *Give an intoxicant to the one perishing, and wine to the bitter of soul.* <note>original Hebrew: תנו שכר לאובד ויין למרי נפש (Tenu shekhar le-oved ve-yayin le-marei nafash).</note> There were in Jerusalem honorable women who would provide these things voluntarily. This is from the Talmud. 

Therefore, the Jews drank the good wine that had been sent for this purpose to the Lord Jesus Christ and the others to be crucified with him. Because of this, what had been said long before through Amos in chapter 2 was then fulfilled: *And they shall drink the wine of the condemned in the house of their God.* <note>original Hebrew: ויין ענושים ישתו בית אלהיהם (Ve-yayin anushim yishtu beit eloheihem).</note> It is as if he said: "The house of Israel will drink the wine of the condemned, and—what will be the greater crime—even the wine of their God." Nor should it seem unfitting to anyone that the prophet attributes the deed of a very few Jews to the whole "house of Israel." For not only was a huge multitude of people present there, consenting to what was being done, but there were also those of whom it is said in Matthew chapter 27: "In the same way, the chief priests also, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: He saved others, himself he cannot..."

<summary>This page discusses the Messianic interpretation of Psalm 89 and uses the Talmudic tradition of offering wine and frankincense to the condemned to explain the vinegar and gall given to Christ. Galatino argues that the Jewish leaders’ rejection and consumption of this wine fulfilled a prophecy in the book of Amos.</summary>

...save himself? If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. He trusts in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him. For we read in Joshua, chapter 7, that the Lord said to Joshua himself: *Israel has sinned, and they have transgressed my covenant which I commanded them; they have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen,* and so forth. <note>original Latin: "Peccauit Israel, & transgressi sunt pactum meum..." from Joshua 7:11. Reuchlin is explaining why the entire Jewish people are often blamed for the actions of individuals, using the biblical precedent of Achan, whose single theft brought guilt upon all Israel.</note> See how the Lord attributed to all Israel what Achan alone had perpetrated. And then that saying of the Psalm was fulfilled: <note>original Hebrew: ויתנו בברותי ראש ולצמאי ישקוני חמץ (*Veyitnu bevrauti rosh velitsmai yashkuni chametz*). This is from Psalm 69:21.</note> *And they gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.* That these things were to be understood as referring to the Messiah appears even more clearly in the *Midrash Ruth* <note>A <term>Midrash</term> is a traditional Jewish commentary or homiletic interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Book of Ruth—regarding what Boaz said in the second chapter: *Come here, and eat of the bread, and dip your morsel (or your mouthful) in the vinegar.* <note>Ruth 2:14. Reuchlin is following a traditional Messianic reading of this verse.</note> For it is said there: "It speaks of the King Messiah. *Come here*—that is, approach the Kingdom. *And eat of the bread*—this is the bread of the Kingdom. *And dip your morsel in the vinegar*—these are the passions (or the torments) of the Messiah." Concerning him, it was said in Isaiah 53: *And he was wounded (or killed) for our transgressions, and bruised for our sins.* This is the tradition. From this, it is clearly shown that the "vinegar" of Ruth signified and prefigured the passions and torments of the Messiah. How much more, therefore, must it be said that what was previously sent was in the person of the Messiah: *And they shall give me gall for my food, and in my thirst they shall give me vinegar to drink.*

This especially hints at the just retribution of the Jews, when it is immediately added in the same Psalm: <note>original Hebrew: יהי שלחנם לפניהם לפח ולשלומים למוקש תחשכנה עיניהם מראות ומתניהם תמיד המעד : שפך עליהם זעמך וחרון אפך ישיגם : תהי טירתם נשמה באהליהם אל יהי יושב (*Yehi shulchanam lifnehem lepach...*). Psalm 69:22–25.</note> That is: *Let their table become a snare before them, and what should be for their peace, let it be a stumbling block. Let their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and make their loins shake continually. Pour out your indignation upon them, and let your burning anger overtake them. Let their habitation be desolate, and let there be no dweller in their tents.* And immediately after this, it is added: <note>original Hebrew: כי אתה אשר הכית רדפו ואל מכאוב חלליך יספרו : תנה עון על עונם ואל יבאו בצדקתך : ימחו מספר חיים ועם צדיקים אל יכתבו (*Ki attah asher hikkita radafu...*). Psalm 69:26–28.</note> That is: *Because they have persecuted him whom you have smitten, and they talk of the grief (or affliction) of those you have wounded (or killed). Add iniquity to their iniquity, and let them not come into (or with) your righteousness. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous.* 

The Chaldean interpreter <note>The <term>Chaldean interpreter</term> refers to the Targum, an Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible used in synagogues.</note> translated and explained all these things in the Chaldean language <note>Aramaic</note> as follows: <note>original Aramaic: יהי פתורהון דסדרו קומיי באבלי קומיהון לקלא ונבסתהון לתקלא... To clarify these words of the <term>Psalm-writer</term> <note>Referring to King David, traditionally considered the author of the Psalms.</note>, it must be noted that in Holy Scripture a "table" is sometimes called a "kingdom." This is why in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>A traditional Jewish commentary or homiletic interpretation of the Book of Psalms.</note>, in the exposition of the 23rd Psalm, on the verse: <note>original Hebrew: תערוך לפני שלחן (*Ta’aroch lefanai shulchan*)</note> *You prepare a table before me*, it is said: "This table is the Kingdom." 

At other times, however, the whole of Divine Scripture itself, which is divided into twenty-four books, is called a "table," according to what is said in Deuteronomy, chapter 8: <note>original Hebrew: לא על הלחם לבדו יחיה האדם כי על כל מוצא פי יהוה יחיה האדם (*Lo al ha-lechem levado yichyeh ha-adam...*)</note> *Man does not live by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord does man live.* Both of these "tables" became a snare for the Jews. For because they gave the Messiah wine mixed with myrrh and vinegar mixed with gall to drink, they therefore lost both their kingdom and the true understanding of the Scriptures. 

For this reason, regarding their blindness, it is added: *Let their eyes be obscured from vision*, that is, so they may not see. Hence also the true Messiah, who should have been for them a source of peace—and is indeed called "Peace"—was made into a stumbling block for them by the righteous judgment of God. This happened because they embittered his mouth with gall and vinegar. And this is what Jeremiah says in the first chapter of his Lamentations: <note>original Hebrew: צדיק הוא יהוה כי פיהו מריתי (*Tzadik hu Adonai ki fihu mariti*)</note> *The Lord himself is righteous, for I have embittered his mouth.* <note>The author is using a specific philological argument here. Standard translations of Lamentations 1:18 read "I have rebelled against his commandment," but Galatinus argues the Hebrew root refers to bitterness.</note> 

For then Jewish wickedness embittered the mouth of God, when they placed a sponge full of vinegar and gall, fixed upon a reed, to the mouth and nose of our Lord Jesus, the true Messiah. Because of this, that saying in Ezekiel, chapter 8, was also fulfilled: <note>original Hebrew: והנם שולחים את הזמורה אל אפי (*Vehinnam sholchim et ha-zemorah el api*)</note> *And behold, they shall be sending a stench to my nose.* Explaining this, <term>Rabbi Kimhi</term> <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), also known as the Radak, a famous medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> says: "He means to say, a foul odor."

<margin>HOG.</margin>
In these places, our Scripture <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible used by the Church.</note> reads very differently than how you have translated it. For that passage in the Lamentations of Jeremiah reads: *The Lord is righteous, for I have provoked his mouth to anger.* And this one from Ezekiel reads: *And behold, they apply the branch to my nostrils.*

<margin>GAL.</margin>
In both cases, the author of our edition <note>Referring to St. Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate.</note> (if I may say so with all due respect) was too lenient toward the Jews. For the word *marithi*, which is placed in the words of Jeremiah, is derived from the verb *mara*, which properly signifies "to embitter." Therefore, *marithi* is the same as "I have embittered." Furthermore, the saying of Ezekiel has been utterly corrupted both among us and among the Hebrews, but much more among us than among them. For they have it as: *And they shall be sending a stench to their own nose.* Yet neither version...

->CAPNIO,<-

The Messiah, afflicted and humbled by fasting and affected by punishments, will return merit and reward to all. As it is said <margin>Isaiah ch. 53</margin> *And the Lord has caused the sin of all of us to meet in him.* These things are from the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>. In this same way, that supreme <term>Talmudist</term> <term>Paul</term> <note>The author refers to the Apostle Paul as a "Talmudist" to emphasize his background in Jewish law.</note> argued when, writing to the Romans in the 5th chapter, he says: *If by the offense of one many died, much more has the grace of God, and the gift in the grace of one man Jesus Christ, abounded unto many.* Moreover, the merit of the death of the Messiah is shown most especially from this, that in the same book, it is read thus: <note>original Hebrew: מחמס בני יהודה אשר שפכו דם נקי בארצם כאותה שעה ויחודה לעולם תשב ונקתי דמם לא ניקתי וכפר אדמתו עמו מניין אתה אומר שהריגו שביד אומות העולם כפרה היא להם לעולם הבא שנאמר מזמור לאסף אלהים באו גויים בנחלתך</note> That is, *Concerning the iniquity of the sons of Judah, who shed innocent blood in their land at that hour. And from where do you have it that his death, which is at the hands of the nations of the world, will pardon them in the world to come? Because it is said in the Psalm of Asaph: O God, the nations have come into your inheritance.* This is the tradition. From which it clearly appears that through the death of the Messiah, there was to be the remission of sins.

This is both from what he says, that "his land"—that is, his corpse—will pardon his people; and also because he says that his death, namely that of the Messiah, ought to pardon the nations in the world to come, that is, in the time of the Messiah. And rightly so. For the Messiah himself was going to die for the salvation of the human race, and especially for the sake of the fathers <note>The patriarchs of the Old Testament.</note> who were to be saved. This is openly shown from the commentaries of <term>R. Moses Hadarshan</term> <note>Moses the Preacher, an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic commentaries.</note> upon that <margin>Psalm 49</margin> *And he shall live further forever, and shall not see the pit <note>The author uses the word "infernum" (hell/the pit).</note>, when he sees the wise dying,* or, *as he shall see the wise dying,* as some have interpreted it. For it is said there: <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבי משה הדרשן זה הפסוק נאמר על מלך המשיח שימות כדי לפדות את האבות ואחר יחיה לנצח לא יראה שחת כמו החכמים שימותו</note> That is, *Rabbi Moses Hadarshan said: This text is spoken of the King Messiah, who will die for the sake of redeeming the fathers. And afterward he will live forever. Nor will he see the pit, in the same way as the wise who die.* 

However, that it was only through the shedding of the Messiah’s blood that the faithful were to be cleansed from sins and liberated from hell, is clear through what was said in <margin>Zechariah chapter nine,</margin> *Even you, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.* For the understanding of this saying, it should be noted that these words "you" and "your" <note>The author is highlighting that the Hebrew pronouns used here are feminine.</note>, placed here, are of the feminine gender. Therefore, it is necessary to refer them to some feminine noun that was mentioned previously. To which feminine noun they are to be referred, he shows in the same place when, shortly before these words, it is said: <note>original Hebrew: גילי מאד בת ציון הריעי בת ירושלם הנה מלכך יבוא לך צדיק ונושע הוא</note> That is, *Exult greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, daughter of Jerusalem; behold, your King comes to you, he is just and bringing salvation.*
