# BOOK EIGHT

...daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your King will come to you, just and having salvation himself. <note>Zechariah 9:9</note> Regarding this, the <term>Chaldaic translation</term> <note>Referring to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Jonathan says: *Exult greatly, O congregation of Zion; shout for joy, O congregation of Jerusalem.* <note>original: חראי לחדא כנשתא ציון גילי קהלא דירושלם</note> That is, "Exult in one, church of Zion, rejoice, church of Jerusalem." Therefore, these pronouns placed here must refer to the daughter—that is, the church—of Zion and Jerusalem when it says: *As for you also, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners out of the 
<margin>Exposition of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term>.</margin> <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), was a famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note>
pit in which there is no water.* <note>Zechariah 9:11</note> Indeed, Rabbi Solomon explains these words in this way: "As for you also, the church of Zion and Jerusalem, you shall be saved with the Messiah, just as he himself is righteous and saved. Through the blood of your covenant—that is, through the merit of the blood of the covenant which was poured out upon you at <term>Sinai</term>." Concerning this, it is said in Exodus chapter 24: *Behold the blood of the covenant, which the Lord has made.* "I have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit—that is, out of captivity." These are his words. 

When he says "out of the pit, that is, out of captivity," this cannot be understood as the pit of the Egyptian or Babylonian captivity, since both of those places abound with water, and the prophet says the pit he speaks of lacks water. Therefore, his saying must be understood as referring to the pit of <term>Gehenna</term> <note>A term often used for hell or a place of spiritual punishment.</note> in which there is no water, but rather fire and sulfur, as is clear in the prologue of <term>Echa Rabbethi</term> <note>Lamentations Rabbah, a midrashic (interpretative) commentary on the Book of Lamentations.</note>, that is, the exposition of the lamentations of Jeremiah. There it is said: "The holy and blessed God promised us that he would rescue us from Gehenna through the merit of circumcision." And where did he say this? In Zechariah, who says: *As for you also, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit in which there is no water.* This is the tradition.

However, when it says that salvation was to come through the merit of circumcision, it intended for it to be understood as through the merit of the shedding of Christ’s blood, which circumcision prefigured. For since all the patriarchs, prophets, and all the holy fathers, however holy they were, who received circumcision, descended into the underworld until the passion of Christ—as is clear in many places in the <term>Talmud</term>, and especially in the book called <term>Haghiga</term> <note>Tractate Chagigah, which deals with festival offerings and spiritual matters.</note>, in the chapter beginning *Haccol hayyabin* <note>meaning "All are obligated."</note>, as we have shown more extensively in the preceding pages—it clearly follows that we were to be liberated from the underworld not through the merit of circumcision, but through the merit of the passion of Christ, which circumcision prefigured. 

Furthermore, since neither the pardon of sins, nor satisfaction, nor consequently the salvation of souls, ought to occur except through the shedding of blood—as is clear in the book <term>Yoma</term> <note>The Talmudic tractate concerning the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur).</note>, that is, "Of the Days," in the chapter beginning *Seven days before the day of atonement*—where it is read thus word-for-word: "There is no pardon or remission of sin except through blood." Just as it is written in Leviticus chapter 17: *For the blood itself shall make satisfaction for the soul*—or *shall cause the soul to be spared.* <note>original: כי הדם הוא בנפש יכפר</note> Since salvation would not have happened except through the Messiah, as has been proven in the higher sections, it necessarily follows that God did not remit sins by the merit of circumcision, nor by the merit of the blood poured out over the sons of Israel on Mount Sinai, but only by the merit of the blood of the Messiah to be shed, which the aforementioned bloods prefigured. Without this, there never was, nor is, nor ever will be a perfect remission of sins.

He concludes that true forgiveness of sins and rescue from the "pit" of hell only occur through the blood of the Messiah.</summary>

## That the Messiah would descend to hell, and lead out all the chosen from there. Chapter XXI.

### CAPNIO,
<note>Capnio is the Latinized name of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and scholar of Hebrew.</note>

Since we believe and confess that Christ our Lord descended to the underworld after his death, and from there led out the souls of his chosen ones, it is necessary to prove through their own scriptures that the Messiah was destined to do this very thing. This is done so that the stubborn disbelief of the latter-day Jews may be more and more convinced. 

### GALATINUS,
<note>Galatinus refers to the author, Petrus Galatinus (c. 1460–1540), who presents himself as a teacher in this dialogue.</note>

That the Messiah would descend to hell and lead out all the chosen from there is evident first from what is read in the *Bereshit Rabbah*—that is, the exposition of the book of Genesis—by <term>Rabbi Moses Hadarshan</term> <note>A 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic explanations.</note>. There, concerning the saying in the 24th chapter of that same book, *And he led me into the tabernacle*, it is said word for word:

"Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said: I went with the angel of death named *Kippod* <note>original: קיפור</note> until I reached the gates of Gehenna <note>Gehenna is the Hebrew term for hell or a place of purification.</note>. I immediately sent the angel *Kippod*, who is in charge of Gehenna, to measure Gehenna from the beginning to the end, but he did not have a free hour to measure it. This was because they had just killed <term>Rabban Simeon</term> <note>Simeon ben Gamliel, a high-ranking Jewish leader and martyr.</note> the son of Gamliel. I wanted to go in, but I could not. After this, however, I went with the angel *Kippod*, and the Messiah son of David went with me, until I reached the gates of Gehenna. When the captives who were in Gehenna saw the light of the Messiah, they rejoiced to receive him, saying: 'This one will lead us out of these shadows.' Just as it is said in Hosea, chapter 13: *From the hand of hell I will redeem them, from death I will free them.* <note>original: מיד שאול אפדם ממות אגאלם</note> And so Isaiah also says in chapter 35: *And the redeemed of God shall return, and shall come (or enter) into Zion.* <note>original: ופדויי יהוה ישבון ובאו ציון</note> And the rest continues until: *And sorrow and sighing shall flee away.* <note>original: ונסו יגון ואנחה</note>" 

Now, "Zion" is not used in this place to mean anything other than the <term>Garden of Eden</term> <note>original: גן עדן (Gan Eden)</note>—that is, the garden of delight, which is Paradise. 

Thus far the tradition. And even if it seems to present a certain foolish fiction, the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> were accustomed to hand down the secrets of the Messiah only in parables. They fashioned that fiction so they might suggest the Messiah's descent to the underworld and the joy of the holy fathers existing in <term>Limbo</term> <note>In Catholic theology, Limbo was the temporary place of the souls of the righteous who died before Christ's resurrection.</note>, which they were to have because of his arrival and their liberation. This they prove excellently by the testimonies of Hosea and Isaiah. 

This same point was shown even more clearly long before the birth of Christ by that teacher of theirs whom they call <term>Our Holy Master</term> <note>original: רבנו הקדוש (Rabbenu Haccados), referring to Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishnah.</note>, in the book he called the *Revealer of Secrets* <note>original: גלי רזיא (Galei Razayya)</note>. This occurs especially in his response to the second petition of <term>Antoninus</term>, the Consul of the city of Rome <note>Rabbinic literature contains many accounts of dialogues between Rabbi Judah the Prince and a Roman Emperor "Antoninus."</note>. Among other things, this same Antoninus asked him, saying: "Since the word *man* <note>original: גבר (gheuer/geuer)</note> signifies God, what is the meaning of that text written in Lamentations, chapter 3: *I am the man seeing poverty in the rod of his indignation; he has driven me and brought me into darkness and not into light*?" <note>original: אני הגבר ראה עני בשבט עברתו : אותי נהג וילך חשך ולא אור</note> 

Our Master answered him: "This is God, holy and blessed, who says: I am the man..."

<summary>This page uses Jewish Rabbinic literature and parables to argue that the Messiah’s descent into hell to free the righteous was a prophesied event recognized by ancient Jewish scholars. It highlights the use of allegorical "fictions" by the Talmudists to convey divine mysteries like the Harrowing of Hell.</summary>

"I am the man who has seen poverty" <note>original: "uir qui uidi paupertatem"; a reference to Lamentations 3:1</note>. He drove me and led me into darkness, and not into light. Likewise, this is the Holy and Blessed God, who said: "I have decreed to descend to the lower regions to redeem the souls of the righteous, which my Father who is in heaven thrust down there with the rod of his indignation because of the sin of Adam." Also, in the same book, regarding the sixth petition of that same Antoninus, the same <term>Rabbenu HaKadosh</term> <note>Hebrew for "Our Holy Teacher," referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note> says that he found these things among others in the book of Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai <term>Mechkar HaSodot</term>, which is called <term>Investigation of the Secrets</term> <note>original: "מחקר הסודות"</note>. Upon hearing these things, Rabbi Hoshaiah began to weep and said: "Woe to them, woe to those impious, wicked, and murderous ones of Israel! For out of love for them, and so that he might forgive their sins, the Holy and Blessed God will send his holy son, who will clothe himself in human flesh. Woe to them, for because of their depraved deeds they will be rebels against this Messiah, and they will reject the words by which he will command them to be cleansed with the water of purification to purge their sins. Indeed, they will not walk in the ways pleasing to God, nor will they do his will, but moved by great wrath, they will kill him. Then his soul will descend to the lower regions, where it will remain for three days, so that he may lead out from there all the souls of the fathers and the righteous." Just as it is said in Genesis, chapter 47: <term>I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you up again</term> <note>original: "אנכי ארד עמך מצרימה ואנכי אעלך"; this is actually Genesis 46:4.</note>. And the Holy and Blessed God shall act to lead them into paradise, so that they may be joyful in the glory of God, according to that saying of Hosea, chapter 6: "After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence." All these things were said by him whom the Jews call "Our Holy Master." From all of this, it is clearly enough revealed that the Messiah—as both God and man—was to descend to hell immediately after his death and lead the souls of his chosen ones out from there.

## That the Messiah was to rise from the dead on the third day. Chapter XXII.

->CAPNIO,<-

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> **T**he Evangelists have also written that Jesus Christ our Lord rose from the dead on the third day. Therefore, you ought to show through the Hebrew scriptures that this same thing was destined to happen to the Messiah.

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> First, therefore, I will state what the ancient Talmudists felt regarding that saying in Psalm 16: <term>In righteousness I shall behold your face; I shall be satisfied when your image awakes</term> <note>original: "אני בצדק אחזה פניך אשבעה בהקיץ תמונתך". The Latin text interprets "awakes" as "rises from the dead."</note>. This means: I, in justice (or through justice), shall see your face; I shall be satisfied when your form (or figure, or image, or likeness) shall have risen. 

<margin>Talmudic explanation.</margin> It has been proven above through the writings of the Talmudists that the Messiah is the "Face of God." Furthermore, this form, figure, image, or likeness of God of which the prophet speaks here is none other than the Son of God, or the Messiah himself according to his divinity—in which the Son of God himself is like the Father—as was also shown above in the third book. And this was that figure, or image of God, which Moses saw,

As it is said in Numbers chapter 12: "And he beholds the form of the Lord" <note>original Hebrew: *u-temunat Adonai yabbit*</note>. Rabbi Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century convert to Judaism and author of the standard Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah.</note> translated this into Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldean"</note> as: "And he understands the likeness or image of the glory of the Lord." Therefore, according to this sense, the previously mentioned words of the prophet [from Psalm 17:15] can be explained: "I will see your face," meaning your Messiah. "I shall be satisfied when your form, or figure, or likeness, or image"—that is, your son—"shall rise again." 

Although they explain these things differently elsewhere, as will be discussed below when we come to speak of the general resurrection, the interpretation we have placed here is excellently confirmed in the *Bereshith Rabba Ketanna* (the Lesser Great Midrash on Genesis). This occurs in the commentary on the third chapter of that book regarding what is written of Adam: "And the Lord sent him out from the garden," or from the paradise of pleasure. For there it reads literally: "Rabbi Hamias said: Adam was sent out of paradise in this world, but in the future world <note>The *Olam Ha-Ba*, or the Messianic age/hereafter.</note> he will not be cast out." This saying of Rabbi Hamias is supported by what is written in Psalm 17 <note>In the source Latin text, this is cited as Psalm 16, following the Vulgate numbering.</note>: "I shall contemplate your face in righteousness," or through righteousness; "I shall be satisfied when your form, or figure, or image, or likeness arises." 

The Holy and Blessed God said: "In 그 hour, I will justify him"—namely, Adam—"from that sentence of condemnation." David said to the Holy and Blessed God: "And in 그 hour when he who is your likeness rises, I shall be satisfied, and in righteousness I shall contemplate or see your face." Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says: "I will contemplate your face," just as it is said in <margin>Isaiah 52</margin> "For they shall see eye to eye when the Lord returns to Zion." Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, traditionally the author of the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets.</note> translated this into Aramaic thus: "For with their eyes they shall see the power or might that God will perform when he settles his Divine Presence <note>The *Shekhinah*.</note> in Zion." 

All of this is tradition. Within these words, three very great mysteries are contained. The first is that God was going to justify Adam, who was long ago expelled from paradise, by removing the sentence brought against him. The second is that this was to happen when, according to David's prophecy, the <term>temuna</term> (form, figure, image, or likeness of God) should rise again. The third is that when he who is the likeness of God—that is, who was like God the Father according to his divinity, but was to rise according to his humanity—then David knew he was to be healed, and through righteousness would see and contemplate the face of God. Yet he did not say through *whose* righteousness he would achieve these things. Perhaps he preferred that this be spoken of later through Isaiah. For Isaiah, speaking after him about the Messiah, the Son of God, said in chapter 53 (as we showed in previous pages): "My righteous servant shall justify many, and he himself shall bear their sins." 

It can also be appropriately noted here what is written in the book of the Talmud called *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helek*: Rabbi Nahman said to Rabbi Isaac: "Who told you when <term>Bar niphli</term> (the son of the fallen) is coming?" He said to him: "Who is <term>Bar niphli</term>?" He replied: "The Messiah." He asked: "Do you call the Messiah <term>Bar niphli</term> (the fallen son)?" He answered: "Yes. Just as it is written of him in Amos chapter 9: 'On that..."

"In 그 hour, I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen" <note>original Hebrew: *Hahi akim et sukkat David ha-nofelet*; a citation from Amos 9:11</note>. That is to say, "In 그 day, I will rouse or set upright the small, dejected, or prostrated hut of David." This is the tradition. On this point, an ancient <term>Talmudist</term> <note>A scholar of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> not without reason called the Messiah *Bar niphli*, which means "the son of the fallen one." For as he proves his statement by the testimony of the prophet, the Messiah himself, as far as his body is concerned, had to be the dejected or prostrated "hut of David" in his passion and death, but in his resurrection, he was to be roused and set upright by God.

I also think it should not be passed over in silence what is read in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>An ancient Jewish commentary or "homiletic midrash" on the Book of Psalms.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding the title of Psalm 21 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 22.</note>, which is "Upon the hind of the dawn" <note>original Hebrew: *al ayelet ha-shahar*</note>. There it is said: This is what is written: "Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp; I will awake the dawn" <note>Psalm 57:8</note>. And further: "Awake in Edom," that is, among the Romans. For it is destined that you shall make the King Messiah stand before us. And what is this: "I will awake the dawn," and the "dawn does not awake me"? For since the beginning of time, the dawn has never come upon me and found me sleeping. And this is the meaning of: "I will awake the dawn." And so he says himself in Psalm 117 <note>Modern Psalm 119:62</note>: "At midnight I rise to confess to you" <note>original Hebrew: *chatzot laylah akum le-hodot lach*</note>. Thus far the tradition.

Where it must be noted that the "glory" of David was in the Messiah, as it is held in the *Midrash Tehillim*—that is, the exposition of the Psalms—regarding that verse of Psalm 16: "My heart is glad"—namely, in the words of the law—"and my glory rejoices." Rabbi <term>Abhu</term> <note>A famous 3rd-century scholar based in Caesarea.</note> said: "This refers to the King Messiah, who is to go forth from me." Just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 4: "For over all the glory shall be a protection." This refers to the Messiah. "Also my flesh shall dwell in confidence," namely, after death. Rabbi Isaac said: "He teaches by this that the maggot and the worm had no power over him." This is the tradition.

To the preceding points, it must also be added that in Psalm 16, it is written in this manner: "Therefore my heart is glad, and my glory rejoices; my flesh also shall dwell in confidence. For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you give your holy one, or your pious one, to see corruption" <note>Psalm 16:9–10; Hebrew: *Lachen shamach libbi... lo titen chasidcha lir'ot shachat*</note>. Here the prophet speaks openly of the incorruption of Christ's body and of his resurrection. Concerning this same incorruptibility of the Messiah's body, we read thus in Isaiah chapter 51: "He who is bowed down hastens to be loosed, and he shall not die in corruption, nor shall his bread fail" <note>Isaiah 51:14; Hebrew: *maher tzo’eh le-hippateach...*</note>. Here is the gloss of <term>Rabbi Kimhi</term> <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a major medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note>. He says that the word *lahmo* <note>meaning "his bread"</note> there refers only to his flesh, according to that passage in Leviticus chapter 21: "Because they offer the sacrifice of God, the bread of their God, they shall be holy" <note>Leviticus 21:21–22; Hebrew: *ki ishe Adonai lechem elohehem...*</note>.

Furthermore, that he was to rise on the third day is evident through what <term>Rabbi Moses Hadarsan</term> <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note> says in his exposition of the book of Genesis, regarding what is said in chapter 22 of that book: "On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes" <note>Genesis 22:4; Hebrew: *ba-yom ha-shelishi va-yisa Avraham et eynav*</note>. For there the same Rabbi says literally: "This is what is written in Hosea chapter 6: 'He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight, and we shall know...'" <note>Hosea 6:2; Hebrew: *yechayenu mi-yomayim ba-yom ha-shelishi yekimenu...*</note>

->### BOOK EIGHT<-

**He will revive us after two days** <note>original Hebrew: *Yehayenu mi-yomayim*; from Hosea 6:2</note>. This is: He will give us life after two days; on the third day, he will raise us up. And we shall live in his presence. And we shall know, so that we may press on to know God. For it is on the third day—a period of three days—just as it is written in Genesis chapter 42: "And Joseph said to them on the third day." Truly, on the third day of the giving of the Law, according to that passage in Exodus 19: "And it happened on the third day when morning came, there were voices and lightning." Also on the third day of the spies, as stated in Joshua 2: "And hide yourselves there for three days." Likewise on the third day of Jonah, according to that text: "Jonah was in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights." Even on the third day of those ascending from captivity, as stated in Ezra chapter 8: "And we camped there for three days." Finally, on the third day of the revival of the dead, according to that which is said in Hosea chapter 6: "He will give us life after two days; on the third day, he will raise us up. And we shall live in his presence." This refers to the King Messiah. As it is said in Psalm 80: **Lord God of hosts, restore us; let your face shine, and we shall be saved.** <note>original Hebrew: *Yhwh Elohim Tzevaot hashibenu ha'er panekha ve-nivasha*</note>. That is: "God of hosts, convert us; show your face—that is, your Messiah—and we shall be saved." This is the tradition.

In the book <term>Mechilta</term> <note>A term usually referring to a commentary on Exodus, but here cited regarding a Midrash on the Psalms.</note> concerning that verse in Psalm 30: **For a moment is in his anger, and life is in his favor.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ki rega be-appo hayyim bi-retzono*</note>. We read it written thus: **Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Moses Hadarsan (11th century), a famous scholar from Narbonne who compiled midrashic legends.</note> said: "For a moment is in his anger, and life is in his favor" is said concerning our righteous Messiah. For death and life will be in his power at any moment according to his will—to give life to others, and to receive it back for himself.** And this is immediately joined with what follows in the same Psalm: **In the evening weeping may linger, but in the morning comes a song of joy.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ba-erev yalin bekhi ve-la-boker rinnah*</note>. For when he brings death upon someone, they will weep for him, and when he restores him to life, they will sing a song. Moreover, when he himself dies, all who exalt his name will mourn over his death, and when he returns to life—that is, when he rises—they will rejoice and sing. And to this is added: "He will give us life after two days, and on the third day he will make us rise, and we shall live in his presence."

<margin>The Catholic explanation.</margin>
Therefore, the words of the prophet Hosea are to be understood according to these expositions in this way: "He will give us life"—namely, the Messiah will give us life from the death of sin—"after two days," which are the days he will lie in the tomb. "On the third day he will raise us up," specifically through the hope of the resurrection. For the resurrection of Christ was the pattern and cause of our own future general resurrection. Just as Christ rose, so we also shall rise. For this reason, Peter, that prince of the Apostles, as if wishing to explain this prophecy of Hosea, says in the first chapter of his first epistle: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." ## That the Messiah was to ascend into heaven, leading with him those whom he was to set free from hell. Chapter XXIII.

### CAPNIO
<note>Capnio is the Greek-derived nickname of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist and character in this dialogue.</note>

<margin>First testimony.</margin>
The Catholic faith firmly holds that Christ also ascended into heaven. Therefore, it must be proved through the testimonies of the Hebrew scriptures that the Messiah was to do that very thing after his resurrection. GALATINUS: We can prove this through seven principal testimonies. Of these, let the first be that which is placed in Deuteronomy chapter 32: **For I lift up my hand to the heavens.** <note>original Hebrew: "כי אשא אל שמים ידי"</note> Rabbi Onkelos <note>The famous 1st-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic (the Targum Onkelos).</note>, turning this into the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> language, explained it thus: **Because I will ordain, or prepare, the house of my divinity in heaven** <note>original Aramaic: "ארי אתקינית בשמיא בית שכינתי"</note>, and I will say, "I endure forever." Rabbi Solomon <note>Better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> also explained it this way: "I will lift my hand to the heavens, that is, to the place of my divinity." Now, the place and house of divinity is the Messiah according to his humanity. This is shown sufficiently through Isaiah in chapter 57, saying: **For thus says the high and lofty one who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite.** <note>original Hebrew: "כה אמר רם ונשא שוכן עד וקדוש שמו מרום וקדוש אשכון ואת דכא ושפל רוח להחיות רוח שפלים ולהחיות לב נדכאים"</note> Here, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "I dwell in the high and holy place, and from there I am with the contrite and lowly spirit. For I extend my divinity over him." These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. Moreover, no one is more aptly called "contrite and lowly in spirit"—that is, humble—than the Messiah. Concerning him, Isaiah says in chapter 53: **He was struck by God, and humbled. And he was wounded—or killed—for our transgressions, and crushed for our iniquities.** Therefore, Rabbi Solomon seems to have spoken in the preceding explanations like a prophet, although he did not know what he was prophesying.

<margin>Second testimony.</margin>
The second testimony is from Micah, saying this of the Messiah in chapter 2: **The breaker goes up before them; they break through and pass the gate, going out by it; and their King will pass on before them, and the Lord at their head.** <note>original Hebrew: "עלה הפרץ לפניהם פרצו ויעבורו שער ויצאו בו ויעבור מלכם לפניהם ויהוה בראשם"</note> That these words are to be understood as referring to the Messiah is clearly evident through their own writings. For in the explanation of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses ha-Darshan <note>An 11th-century preacher from Narbonne known for his midrashic commentaries.</note>, regarding that statement in chapter 40: **In my dream, behold, a vine was before me** <note>original Hebrew: "בחלומי והנה גפן לפני"</note>, it is said: "This is what is written in the Psalms..."

Also, in the *Midrash Rabbathi* <note>Referring here to the "Great Commentary" on Lamentations.</note>, in the exposition on Lamentations on the passage in chapter 1 of that book, **For my sighs are many and my heart is faint** <note>original Hebrew: "מרבית אנחותי ולבי דוי"</note>, it says: "You find that in the very same things in which Israel sinned, they were punished, and thereafter they were comforted. For they sinned in the 'head,' as it is written in Numbers 14: **Let us appoint a head and return to Egypt.** And they were punished in the 'head,' as it is written in Isaiah 1: **Every head is sick.** And they were to be comforted in the 'head,' just as it is written in Micah chapter 2: **And their King shall pass before them, and God at their head.**" That the Messiah is the "head" of Israel has been sufficiently proven through their scriptures in the preceding pages. This is also clearly seen through the words in Hosea chapter 1: **And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head.** <note>original Hebrew: "ונקבצי בני יהודה ובני ישראל יחדו ושמו להם ראש אחד"</note> Where the commentary of Rabbi Solomon says: "One head, that is, David their King." However, since Hosea prophesied in the time of King Ahaz, his words cannot be understood as referring to David the son of Jesse, since he lived long before. Therefore, they must be understood as referring to the Messiah, who (as we have shown above) is also often called "David" in Holy Scripture.

<margin>The fifth testimony.</margin>
The fifth testimony is placed in Deuteronomy chapter 33, where it is said: **There is none like the upright God, the rider of the heavens in your help, and in his majesty, the one ascending the clouds or heavens.** <note>original Hebrew: "אין כאל ישרון רכב שמים בעזרך ובגאותו שחקים"</note> Which Rabbi Onkelos <note>A famous convert to Judaism in the 1st century AD, known for his authoritative Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> translated into Aramaic in this way: **There is no God like the God of Israel, whose divinity is in the heavens as your help, and his power or strength in the heaven of heavens.** Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> also says in his gloss on the word "Rider of the heaven": "He is that God who is in your help, and in his majesty he himself is the one ascending the <term>shehakim</term>, that is, the heavens or clouds." <note>original: "שחקים" (shehakim), a Hebrew word for clouds or the upper heights of the sky.</note> It has been stated above, moreover, that the Messiah is called "the helper."

<margin>The sixth testimony.</margin>
The sixth testimony is found in Psalm 104, where it is read: **Who makes the cloud his chariot, or his riding-place, walking upon the wings of the wind; who makes his messengers spirits, and his ministers a burning fire; he founded the earth upon its base, it shall not slip for an age and beyond.** Mystically, in this passage, the "earth of Israel" refers to the apostles and other disciples of our Messiah, who, as has been proven elsewhere, were the true Israelites. The "base of the earth" is likewise the foundation of the Church. Regarding the purpose of this exposition, it is read in the <term>Midrash Kohelet</term> <note>A homiletic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes.</note> concerning that which is said in the first chapter of that same book: **A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains for an age, or for eternity.** There it is said word for word: "Rabbi Isaac said: 'This kingdom enters, and that kingdom exits, but Israel remains.' And this is the meaning of: 'the earth remains forever.'" This is supported by the scripture which says in Judges chapter 18: **And Jonathan the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan, until the day of the transmigration of the land.** Does the land itself transmigrate, or move itself? No, but these are the people of Israel, who are called "the earth." Just as it is said in Malachi chapter 3: **And all the nations will call you blessed, for you shall be a desirable land.** All this is according to tradition.

### That the Messiah was to sit at the right hand of God the Father. Chapter 23.

### CAPNIO, <note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pseudonym of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous German humanist and Hebraist who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

**Galatinus**, this too is something you must prove most clearly through their own scriptures: namely, that the Messiah was to sit at the right hand of God the Father. 

**GAL.** We can prove this through many sayings of the ancients. But we can do so especially through that same saying of the **Psalmist** <note>Referring to King David, traditionally considered the author of the Psalms.</note> which has now been cited by him whom they call <term>רבינו הקדוש</term> **Rabbenu Haccados**, that is, our holy master <note>original: "Our Holy Teacher," referring to Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>. For thus the Psalmist himself says in Hebrew in Psalm 110: <term>נאם יהוה לאדני שב לימיני</term>—that is: **The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.** 

**CAP.** Even if this most evident testimony of the Psalmist proves the proposition excellently, the more recent Jewish commentators—attempting to extinguish the light of truth—nevertheless assert that David spoke these words not about the Messiah, but about someone else. For some indeed say that he spoke these same words about Abraham, whom they claim David also called his "Lord" as a show of paternal reverence. Others, however, say that David uttered these words about the angel assigned to him for his protection. They say he called this angel his "Lord" because, since every man has one of the angels destined for his protection, an angel is rightly said to preside over the one he guards. For this reason, the angel can also rightly be called his "Lord" in a certain sense. They throw these and many other such ravings at us so that they might escape the truth. 

**GAL.** They can say such things to those who are ignorant of Hebrew letters, but not to those who are skilled in them. For such experts (as you know well) easily convict them by their own scriptures. Therefore, through the authentic and approved scriptures of their ancestors, it is most clearly shown that David spoke those words neither about Abraham, nor about the angel assigned as his guardian, nor about anyone else, but about the Messiah—both God and man—since it would be inappropriate for any mere creature to sit at the right hand of God. First, this is clear through the <term>Targum of Rabbi Jonathan</term> <note>The Targum is an ancient Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible. Jonathan ben Uzziel was a famous 1st-century scholar.</note>, that is, through his Aramaic edition, which explains these same words in Aramaic thus: <term>אמר יהוה למימריה תיב לימיני</term>, that is: **The Lord said to his Word: Sit at my right hand.** <note>The use of "Word" (Memra) in the Aramaic Targums is often interpreted by Christian authors as a reference to the Logos or the Second Person of the Trinity.</note> Some, however, say that it does not appear in the Aramaic translation as I have related it, but rather like this: <term>אמ' יהוה במימריה למיתן לי נבואה חלת דייהבית לאolphan אורייתא וימיני אורייך</term>—that is: **The Lord said in his word, or through his word, that he would give me dominion, because I sat to learn the law; wait at my right hand.** To whom I [answer] that it is true...

<summary>This page discusses the interpretation of Psalm 110:1, arguing that the phrase "Sit at my right hand" refers specifically to the Messiah rather than Abraham or a guardian angel. Galatinus uses the Aramaic Targum to support the Christian view that the Messiah is the "Word" of God who shares the divine throne.</summary>
<keywords>Psalm 110, Messiah, Right Hand of God, Johannes Reuchlin, Galatinus, Targum Jonathan, Memra, Word of God, Abraham, Guardian Angel</keywords>

...I say, in the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum, an Aramaic translation and exposition of the Hebrew Bible</note> translation of the Psalms, which the Jews now more frequently have at hand, it is exactly as they say. However, that translation is not by Jonathan, but by Rabbi Akilas, or Rabbi Joseph the Blind, who flourished nearly three hundred years after the destruction of the second temple. But the translation of Jonathan, which they themselves have not yet seen, is exactly as I have reported it. Nor should they deny it simply because they have not seen it. For Jonathan himself translated the entire Bible into Chaldean (as we have proved elsewhere), although not all of his books are currently at hand.

Next, it is proven that those words of David, **The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand,** were to be understood as referring to the Messiah, through the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary (midrash) on the Psalms.</note> regarding that verse of the second Psalm, <term>אספרה אל חק</term>—that is: **I will tell of the decree.** Where it says: <term>מספרים הם בחוקה של תורה ובחוקה של נביאים וכתובים</term>... <term>בחוקה של תורה בני בכורי ישראל</term>... <term>בחוקה של נביאים הנה ישכיל עבדי ירום ונשא</term>... <term>בכתובים נאם יהוה לאדני שב לימיני</term>. 

That is: "His mysteries—namely, those of the King Messiah—are told in the scripture of the Law, in the scripture of the Prophets, and in the Hagiographa <note>The "Holy Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible (Ketuvim).</note>. In the scripture of the Law, as in Exodus 4: **Israel is my firstborn son.** In the scripture of the Prophets, as in Isaiah 52: **Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and lifted up.** In the Hagiographa, as in Psalm 110: **The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.**" 

Furthermore, this very point is proven through the *Midrash Tehillim*—that is, through the exposition of the Psalms—regarding that verse of Psalm 18: <term>ותתן לי מגן ישעך וימינך תסעדני</term>. That is: **And you have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand shall comfort**—or sustain, or receive—**me.** For there it is said: <term>דבי יודן בשם רבי חייא אמר לעתיד לבא הקדוש ברוך הוא מושיב למלך המשיח לימינו שנאמר נאם יהוה לאדני שב לימיני</term>. 

That is: "Rabbi Yuden said in the name of Rabbi Hiyya: In the time to come, the Holy One, blessed be He, will seat the King Messiah at his right hand, as it is said in Psalm 110: **The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.**"

This same thing is also excellently suggested in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note>, when he comments on the statement in Chapter 18 of that book: **And the Lord appeared to him in the oak of Mamre.** He says: "Rabbi Barachia, in the name of Rabbi Levi, revealed"—that is, explained—"this through what is written in Psalm 18: **And you have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand shall comfort**—or receive—**me.** For in the future, the Holy One, blessed be He, will seat the Messiah at his right hand, as it is said: **The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.**" 

This is the tradition. From all these things, it is clearly shown that the aforementioned words of David are to be understood entirely as referring to the Messiah, and consequently, that the Messiah himself was to sit at the right hand of God the Father, which was to be proven.

-># EIGHTH [BOOK]<-

It must finally be proven through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that the Messiah himself ought to have done this same thing <note>referring to the sending of the Holy Spirit mentioned on the previous page</note>. *GALATINUS.* <note>The persona of Pietro Galatino, the author.</note> It is chiefly held from those things said in the forty-fourth chapter of Isaiah that the Holy Spirit was to be sent upon the apostles and other disciples of the Messiah, as well as upon those converted and baptized from the nations. For there it is read as follows:

> Fear not, my servant Jacob, and the most upright one whom I have chosen. For I will pour waters upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry land. I will pour out my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring. And they shall sprout in the midst of the hay, or grass, like willows by the watercourses. This one shall say, "I am the Lord’s." And that one shall call on the name of Jacob. And this one shall write with his hand—or his strength—to God, and shall be surnamed by the name of Israel. <note>original Hebrew: אל תירא עבדי יעקב וישרון בחרתי בו...</note>

*This means*, "Fear not, my servant Jacob, and the most upright one whom I have chosen. For I will pour waters upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry land. I will pour out my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring. And they shall sprout in the midst of the hay, or grass, like willows by the watercourses. This one shall say, 'I am the Lord’s.' And that one shall call on the name of Jacob. And this one shall write with his hand, or his strength, to God, and shall be surnamed by the name of Israel." Moreover, Rabbi Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> translated these words, "I will pour out my spirit" along with the rest, into Aramaic <note>The text uses the term "Chaldaic," which was the common Renaissance name for Aramaic.</note> in this way: 

> I will give my holy spirit upon your children, and my blessing upon your children's children, and the righteous shall be multiplied—tender and delicate—like the sprouts of grass, and like a tree sending its roots over the watercourses or streams of waters. <note>original Aramaic: אתן רוח קדשי על בניך...</note>

Furthermore, the gloss <note>a marginal or interlinear commentary</note> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> on those words of the prophet, "For I will pour water upon the thirsty," says this: "Just as I pour waters upon the thirsty, so I will pour my spirit upon your seed." Regarding the aforementioned pouring of waters upon those to be baptized, as well as the mission of the Holy Spirit, Ezekiel also makes mention in chapter 36, saying: 

> I will pour clean waters upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your filthiness. <note>original Hebrew: וזרקתי עליכם מים טהורים...</note>

And a little later: 

> And I will give my spirit in the midst of you, and I will cause you to walk in my precepts, and keep my judgments, and do them. <note>original Hebrew: ואת רוחי אתן בקרבכם...</note>

Where Rabbi Jonathan interpreted the phrase, "And I will give my spirit in the midst of you," into Aramaic as: "And I will give my holy spirit within your inward parts." Regarding the pouring out or sending of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles and other disciples of the Messiah on the day of Pentecost, it is found in Isaiah 32, speaking thus: 

> Until the spirit is poured upon us from on high, the desert will be for Carmel—or the vineyard of the Lord—and Carmel—or the Lord's vineyard—shall be reckoned as a forest. <note>original Hebrew: עד יערה עלינו רוח ממרום...</note>

Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "Until he pours the spirit upon us." This is just as it is said in Genesis 24: <term>vattear</term> <note>original: ותער</note>, that is: "And she emptied her pitcher." For the word <term>shephichah</term> <note>original: תשפיכה</note>, that is: "of pouring," is frequently used in this sense.

[He] speaks thrice concerning the spirit, according to that which is said in Zechariah chapter 12: **"And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of supplications."** <note>original Hebrew: וְשָׁפַכְתִּי עַל בֵּית דָּוִיד וְעַל יוֹשֵׁב יְרוּשָׁלַם רוּחַ חֵן וְתַחֲנוּנִים; Latin: Et effundam super domum Dauid, & super habitatores Ierusalem spiritum gratiae & deuotionum</note> It is also stated in Joel chapter 3: <note>In modern English Bibles, this is Joel 2:28-30</note> **"And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions. And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit. And I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke."** <note>original Hebrew: וְהָיָה אַחֲרֵי־כֵן אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ אֶת רוּחִי...; Latin: Et erit post hęc, Effundam spiritum meum super omnem carnem...</note> Where the gloss of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Also known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> says regarding the phrase "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh": "That is, upon everyone whose heart has become tender, like flesh." Concerning this, it is said in Ezekiel 36: "And I will give you a heart of flesh." These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. To the aforementioned points, he adds (not inaptly) what is read in the book *Tanhuma* <note>A collection of homiletic teachings on the Torah</note> concerning that which is said in Numbers chapter 15, "And you shall be holy." It is read in this way: "The Lord said to Israel, 'In this world, by the hand of the **evil inclination**'—<term>yeczer hara</term> <note>The Jewish concept of the innate impulse toward evil</note>, that is, the fuel or 'tinder' of original sin—'you are separated from my commandments. But in the future, in the days of the Messiah, I will uproot it from you.'" Just as it is said in Ezekiel 36: **"And I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh, and I will put my spirit within you."** <note>original Hebrew: וַהֲסִירוֹתִי אֶת לֵב הָאֶבֶן מִבְּשַׂרְכֶם...; Latin: Et auferā cor lapideum de carne uestra...</note> and the rest as above. This is the tradition. From these things it is clearly evident that the Holy Spirit did not come upon the obstinate Jews, nor was it poured out, because they refused to lay aside their stony heart. The faithful of Christ, however, received it abundantly for this reason: because they possessed a heart of flesh. This cannot be denied by any means, as experience is the witness. Furthermore, that the Messiah himself would send the Holy Spirit upon his disciples was most clearly predicted by **Rabbenus Haccados** <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah, whom the author claims predicted Christian truths</note>, who lived long before the birth of Christ, in the book titled **The Revealer of Secrets** <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: גַּלֵּי רָזַיָּא, Gale razeya</note>. Among other things, he responded this way to the sixth petition of Antoninus, the Consul of the city of Rome: 

"After ten days from his ascension—namely, at the completion of 50 days—he will send the Holy Spirit from the heavens upon the righteous, so that they may be confirmed in his faith. And soon he will command them to go and teach his law to all men. Just as it is said in Ezekiel 36: 'And I will put my spirit within you, and I will cause you to walk in my commandments, and you shall keep my judgments and do them.' Moreover, the figure <note>a symbolic foreshadowing</note> of these 50 days were those 50 days in which Israel killed the Paschal lamb and went out from the land of Egypt, during which the Holy and Blessed God sent the Holy Spirit upon them and gave them the holy law, so that they might be firm in his faith. As it is written in Exodus 19: 'Lo, now I will come to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear me speaking to you, and may believe you forever.'" These are the word-for-word comments of the man whom the adversaries <note>the Jews</note> themselves call **Our Holy Teacher** <note>Rabbenu Haccados</note>.

# Book Nine.
## On the eternal rejection of the Jews and on the calling and salvation of the Gentiles.

->That all of God’s promises were made to the Jews with a condition:<-
->namely, if they would receive the Messiah and obey him.<-

### Chapter 1.

**CAPNIO,** <note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pen name of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist. In this dialogue, he represents the seeker of knowledge.</note>

<margin>The erroneous opinion of the later Jews.</margin>
Since, after the unlocking of the mysteries of the Messiah—which the very outcome of events clearly shows were fully accomplished in our Lord Jesus Christ—I believe you are going to speak both of the eternal rejection <term>reprobatio: the theological concept of being cast off or rejected by God</term> of the Jews, who refused to receive the true Messiah himself, and of the calling and salvation of the Gentiles, who most devotedly clung to him. For the very order of the things to be discussed demands this. For that reason, both as a foundation for what is to be said, and also so that the just and perpetual rejection of the obstinate Jews may appear more clearly and be more easily proved, it is necessary first for you to show through their own scriptures that all God’s promises made to the Jews were made with a condition: namely, if they were going to receive the Messiah and obey him. **GALATINUS.** <note>Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540), the author, who portrays himself as the expert teacher in this dialogue.</note> In this, the more recent Jews err greatly, firmly asserting that a promise of God regarding good things—even if made to someone who falls from righteousness into unrighteousness—is never revoked by God, but is always necessarily fulfilled. But a threat of evils, even when made by God with an oath, is often revoked when repentance intervenes. To prove this, they especially bring forward the words of <margin>The false interpretation of Rabbi Solomon</margin> **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> regarding that saying of Jeremiah which he spoke to the false prophet Hananiah, when he says in the twenty-eighth chapter: **"The prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of the prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the Lord has truly sent the prophet."** <note>Jeremiah 28:9</note> Regarding this, Rabbi Solomon says thus: "Jeremiah said to Hananiah: I prophesy God’s vengeance. If what I prophesy happens, I will not be considered **שקרן** <gloss>*shaqran*, that is, a liar or deceiver</gloss>. For it repents God, the holy and blessed, over evil. But the prophet who prophesies peace, when his word comes, it will be known he is a prophet. If, however, his word does not come to pass, he is a liar."

As it is said in Numbers 23: <note>Numbers 23:19</note> *God is not like a man, that he should lie.* For so Rabbi Tanhuma <note>Rabbi Tanhuma bar Abba was a famous 4th-century Jewish scholar in the Land of Israel, known for his collections of homiletic teachings called Midrash.</note> explained this. So also says Rabbi Solomon. <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), known as Rashi, the most influential medieval Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note> From these words, the Jews infer that God’s promises of good can never be revoked. However, they believe God’s threats are very often rendered void when repentance intervenes. We, for our part, concede the latter part of their opinion: namely, that God’s threats and promises of punishment made because of sins can indeed be revoked through repentance. But the first part of their claim—that promises of peace or good things made by God can in no way be revoked—we utterly deny as false and heretical.

**CAPNIO.** I would like you to show through their own scriptures that they are lying in this matter.

**GALATINUS.** First, then, let the Jews of our time who are entangled in this error hear what they read in 1 Kings 2 <note>Now usually cited as 1 Samuel 2:27–31.</note> in this manner: *And a man of God came to Eli and said to him.* <note>original: "וייבא איש האלהים אל עלי ויאמר" (Vayavo ish ha-elohim el Eli va-yomer)</note> Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "This man of God was Elkanah." And a little later:

<margin>1 Kings 2.</margin>
*Therefore the Lord God of Israel says: I said indeed that your house and the house of your father should walk before me forever.* <note>original: "לכן נאם יהוה אלהי ישראל אמור, אמרתי ביתך ובית אביך יתהלכו לפני עד עולם" (Lachen neum YHVH Elohei Yisrael amor, amarti beitecha u-veit avicha yithalechu lefanai ad olam)</note> Which Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, to whom the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets is attributed.</note> interpreted in the Chaldean <note>A common Renaissance term for Aramaic.</note> tongue as: *They shall serve before me forever.* <note>original: "וישתמש קדמי עד עלמיא" (ve-yishtamesh kodami ad almaya)</note> And immediately thereafter follows: *And now the Lord says: Far be it from me. For those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed. Behold, the days come that I will break your arm, and the arm of your father’s house.* <note>original: "ועתה נאם יהוה חלילה לי כי מכבדי אכבד ובזי יקלו הנה ימים באים וגדעתי את זרעך ואת זרוע בית אביך" (Ve-ata neum YHVH halilah li ki mechabdai achabed u-vozai yekallu hineh yamim baim ve-gadati et zere’acha ve-et zero’a beit avicha)</note> Regarding this, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "This means the power which you have in my house, and of which you say: 'Otherwise I will take it by force.' <note>A reference to the corrupt behavior of Eli's sons in 1 Samuel 2:16.</note> Those who honor me—that is, the sons of <term>Pinhas</term> <note>original: "Pinhas" is the Hebrew name for Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron.</note> (whom our Latin edition corruptly calls Phinees), who honored me in Shittim—I will honor." And so it was done in the days of Solomon, when the house of the sanctuary was built. For then Solomon drove out Abiathar, who was from the house and family of Merari, so that he would not be the priest of the Lord, according to the word of the Lord which he spoke concerning the house of Eli. And Zadok was made High Priest, because he was of the sons of Pinhas. For so the genealogy is laid out in the book of the *Words of the Days*—that is, the first book of <term>Paralipomenon</term>, <note>Paralipomenon is the traditional name for the books of Chronicles in the Greek and Latin Bibles.</note> chapter 6. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon, in which he openly asserts things that contradict what you heard him say regarding Jeremiah. Then, I propose to them what they read in Jeremiah 18, where it is said:

<margin>Jeremiah 18.</margin>
*Cannot I do with you as this potter, house of Israel? says the Lord. Behold, as the clay is in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel. In an instant I will speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to root up, and to pull down, and to destroy it. And if that nation, against which I have spoken, shall repent of its evil, I also will repent of the evil that I thought to do to them. And in an instant I will speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it. If it shall do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, I will repent of the good that I thought to do to it.* <note>Jeremiah 18:6–10. Galatinus is using this to prove that God's promises of "good" are conditional on obedience.</note> This means: *Cannot I do with you as this potter, house of Israel?* says God. *Behold, as the clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, house of Israel.* And immediately

Immediately when I speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, that I may pluck it up, and break it down, or scatter it, or destroy it and lose it; and if that nation turns from its malice, on account of which I spoke against it, I will also repent of the evil that I thought to do to it. And soon when I speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, that I may build and plant it, and it does evil in my eyes, so that it does not hear my voice, I will also repent of the good that I had said I would do for it. <note>Jeremiah 18:7–10. The text uses these verses to show that God’s intent changes based on human response.</note> Here, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac (Rashi), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> on the word "I will repent" <note>original: "pœnitebit me"</note> says: "that is, I will think another thought." From these testimonies, therefore, it is clear enough (as I judge) that on account of a subsequent fault of the person to whom a promise of good was made, God makes that promise void and empty. For even if God is both truthful and faithful in all His words, His promise is nevertheless almost always understood as being made with a condition, even if the condition is not expressed.

This is also elegantly clear from what is said in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan (11th century), a scholar of Narbonne known for his midrashic (interpretive) compilations.</note> regarding that which is said in the 32nd chapter of the same book: *And Jacob feared greatly, and it was a distress to him.* <note>original: "ויירא מאד וייצר לו" (Vayira me’od va-yetzer lo); Genesis 32:7.</note> For there it is read word-for-word: "This is what is written in Proverbs chapter 28: *Blessed is the man who is always fearful.*" <note>original: "אשרי אדם מפחד תמיד" (Ashrei adam mefached tamid); Proverbs 28:14.</note> For such is the custom of the righteous. For the Holy One, blessed be He, made them certain and secure, and yet they feared. Thus did he who was chosen among the patriarchs, and he who was chosen among the prophets. Jacob indeed is the chosen among the fathers, of whom it is said in Psalm 135 <note>The text says Psalm 133, but this quote is from 135:4.</note>: *Since the Lord has chosen Jacob for himself.* To him the Holy One, blessed be He, had said in Genesis 31: *Return to the land of your fathers and to the place of your birth, and I will be with you.* And yet, in the end, he feared, as it is said in Genesis 32: *And Jacob feared greatly.* Why did he fear? Because he said: "Perhaps I have become defiled by something in the house of Laban." For it is written in Deuteronomy chapter 23: *And he shall see no uncleanness in you, and he shall not withdraw from you.*

Furthermore, Moses was the chosen among the prophets. As it is said in Psalm 106 <note>The text says Psalm 105.</note>: *And he said he would destroy them, had not Moses, his chosen, stood in the breach.* To him also God had said in Exodus chapter 3: *Because I will be with you.* And nevertheless, he later feared. Just as it is said in Numbers chapter 21: *And the Lord said to Moses: Do not fear him.* Which He would by no means have said unless Moses had feared. From this, therefore, it is said: *And Jacob feared greatly.* We also read there that Rabbi Hillel said: "Do not cease to gather merits, nor be secure in yourself until the day of your death." <note>Hillel the Elder was a famous Jewish leader and sage from the 1st century BCE. This quote is found in the Pirkei Avot (Ethics of the Fathers).</note> How so? In such a way that although a man may be righteous, he should nevertheless fear sin at all times, and not be secure in himself.

And so it is with David, saying in Psalm 27: *Unless I believed I would see the goodness of God in the land of the living.* <note>original: "לולא האמנתי לראות בטוב יהוה בארץ החיים" (Lule he’emanti lir’ot be-tuv Adonai be-eretz hayyim); Psalm 27:13.</note> Rabbi Joses <note>Rabbi Yose ben Halafta, a 2nd-century scholar.</note> said: "Why is it dotted over the word 'unless' <note>original: "לולא" (lule). In Hebrew manuscripts, special dots (puncta extraordinaria) appear over this word in Psalm 27:13, signaling a scribal or theological nuance.</note>?" Because David said thus before the Holy One, blessed be He: "Lord of the world, I trust in You that You are going to give a good reward to the righteous in the future; yet I do not know if I will have a portion among them or not." And behold, David was a *holy man* <note>original: "חסיד" (hassid); gloss: "holy" or "pious."</note>. For so he himself says in Psalm 86 <note>The text says Psalm 85.</note>: *Keep my soul, for I am holy.* And

# BOOK NINE

...nevertheless, he himself [Jacob] feared that sin might invalidate his merit. The masters also handed down a teaching, explaining that which is written in Exodus chapter 15: **Until your people pass over, O Lord, until this people passes over whom you have purchased.** <note>original: "עד יעבור עמך יהוה עד יעבור עם זו קנית" (Ad ya’avor amcha YHVH ad ya’avor am zu kanita); Exodus 15:16.</note> *Until your people pass over, O Lord.* This refers to the first entry, or arrival, into the land in the days of Joshua. *Until this people passes over whom you have purchased.* This refers to the second arrival in the days of Ezra. For the children of Israel were worthy for a sign or miracle to be performed during their second arrival, just as was done during the first. However, sin caused it so that no miracle was performed for them. For this reason, it did not happen. And it is for this reason that Jacob is found to have feared because of sin.

Rabbi Jacob also said: It is written in Genesis chapter 28, **And behold, I will be with you, and will keep you in all places where you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I spoke to you about.** <note>Genesis 28:15.</note> And yet it is written in Genesis chapter 32, **And Jacob feared greatly.** <note>Genesis 32:7.</note> He feared indeed lest perhaps sin had invalidated what God had said above and promised to him. All these things Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>Moshe HaDarshan (11th century), a famous scholar from Narbonne who collected ancient Jewish interpretations.</note> drew from the traditions of the ancients. 

To these should be added what is read in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec*, <note>Tractate Sanhedrin, Chapter 11 (Chelek), in the Babylonian Talmud.</note> in this manner: It is written in Exodus chapter 15, **Every disease that I put on Egypt, I will not put on you, for I am the Lord your healer.** <note>original: "כל המחלה אשר שמתי במצרים לא אשים עליך כי אני יהוה רפאך" (Kol ha-machalah asher shamti be-Mitzrayim lo asim alecha ki ani YHVH rofecha); Exodus 15:26.</note> This means: I will not place upon you every sickness or pain that I placed in Egypt, because I am God your physician. If He does not inflict the sickness, for what purpose would there be a physician? Rabbi Johanan said: This scripture is explained by itself, when it immediately says: **And he said, If you will diligently listen to the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is right in His eyes.** <note>original: "ויאמר אם שמוע תשמע לקול יהוה אלהיך והישר בעיניו תעשה" (Vayomer im shamoa tishma le-kol YHVH elohecha ve-hayashar be-einav ta’aseh); Exodus 15:26.</note> That is: "If you listen" (He says), "I will not inflict it." But if you do not listen, I will inflict every sickness upon you, even if I am your physician. This is the tradition. 

From all these things it is clearly evident that all of God's promises made to the Israelite people in the past were always <term>conditional</term> <note>Conditional: Meaning the fulfillment of the promise depends on the behavior of the recipients.</note>. That is, they were dependent on whether those to whom some good had been promised would obey Him—departing from evil and persevering in good—even if the scripture sometimes did not explicitly state such a condition. For in those cases, the condition was to be understood just as if it had been explicitly stated. Otherwise, Jacob and Moses, who feared greatly after they had received such firm security from God, could in no way be excused from the vice of unfaithfulness and lack of belief. To even dream such a thing about such holy men is a sacrilege. 

Since these things are so, it is clearer than the sun that all the promises made to the Jews concerning the Messiah and their salvation were conditional—namely, if they were to receive him and obey him as God their Savior. Therefore, the reason why the Jews were not redeemed and saved by the Messiah is none other than because they did not receive him, nor did they wish to listen; rather, they denied and killed him, according to that which was said by the Psalmist in the 81st Psalm: **But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not want me. So I let them go according to the hardness of their heart; they walked in their own counsels. If only my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways! In a moment [I would have humbled] their enemies...** <note>original: "ולא שמע עמי לקולי וישראל לא אבה לי : ואשלחהו בשרירות לבם ילכו במועצותיהם : לו עמי שומע לי ישראל בדרכי יהלכו : כמעט אויביהם" (Psalm 81:11–14 in Hebrew numbering; 81:12-15 in Latin numbering).</note>

<summary>This page argues that God's promises to the Israelites were always conditional upon their obedience, explaining why biblical figures like Jacob still felt fear despite divine promises. The author uses this logic to explain that the Jewish people missed the Messiah's redemption because they failed to fulfill the condition of receiving him.</summary>

-><note>original Hebrew: "אויביהם אכניע ועל צריהם אשיב ידי : משנאי יהוה יכחשו לו ויהי עתם לעולם" (Oiveihem akhnia ve-al tzareihem ashiv yadi: mishaneih YHVH yekhashu lo vi-yhi itam l'olam); Psalm 81:14–15.</note> I would soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries. That is: **But my people did not listen to my voice, and Israel would have none of me. So I gave them up to the stubbornness of their heart, and they walked in their own counsels. If only my people had listened to me, and Israel had walked in my ways! I would soon have subdued their enemies and turned my hand against their oppressors. Those who hate God would have denied him <note>The Hebrew "yekhashu" (יכחשו) can mean to deny, lie, or submit feigningly.</note>, and their time would have lasted forever.**

**CAP.** These things are certainly so true, and spoken so accurately and skillfully, that they cannot be refuted by any slander of the Jews. But indeed, because old habits are hard to cast off, and the Jews themselves (with Moses their father bearing witness) have always acted contentiously against God himself, much less against the truth—according to that which is said in Deuteronomy 31: <note>original Hebrew: "הן בעודני חי עמכם היום ממרים הייתם עם יהוה ואף כי אחרי מותי" (Hen be-odeni chai imakhem ha-yom mamrim heyitem im YHVH ve-af ki acharei moti); Deuteronomy 31:27.</note> **Behold, while I am still living with you today, you have been rebellious against the Lord; how much more, then, after my death?** Therefore, I do not doubt that the Jews of our time, imitating the wickedness of their fathers, will still contradict these things which you have proven so clearly through their own scriptures. They will try to show—not by reason, nor by the authority of scripture, but by the sheer <term>obstinacy of their treachery<note>Latin: "perfidiæ obstinatione." In medieval and Renaissance polemics, "perfidia" (treachery/faithlessness) was a standard technical term used by Christian writers to describe the Jewish rejection of the Christian Messiah.</note></term>—that the promises of good things must always be fulfilled, as no sin is strong enough to hinder them. Therefore, bring forward for the sake of example some promise of good made to them which, because of their sin hindering it, was not fulfilled.

**GAL.** I will bring forward, then, just one of many promises of good things made in the most certain words, which they are least able to show has been fulfilled according to the letter—namely, that of which Jeremiah speaks in chapter 33, when he says: <note>original Hebrew: "כי כה אמר יהוה לא יכרת לדוד איש ישב על כסא בית ישראל : ולכהנים הלוים לא יכרת איש מלפני מעלה עולה ומקטיר מנחה ועשה זבח כל הימים" (Ki kho amar YHVH lo yikaret le-David ish yoshev al kisse beit Yisrael: ve-la-kohanim ha-Leviyim lo yikaret ish mi-lifanai ma’aleh olah ve-maktir minkhah ve-oseh zevakh kol ha-yamim); Jeremiah 33:17–18.</note> **For thus says God: David shall not lack a man sitting upon the throne of the house of Israel. And to the Levitical priests, there shall not lack a man before me lifting up a burnt offering, and burning or smoking an oblation, and performing sacrifice, through all the days.** And shortly thereafter it follows: <note>original Hebrew: "ויהי דבר יהוה אל ירמיהו לאמור : כה אמר יהוה אם תפרו את בריתי היום ואת בריתי הלילה ולבלתי היות יומם ולילה בעתם : גם בריתי תפר את דוד עבדי מהיות לו בן מלך על כסאו ואת הלוים הכהנים משרתי : אשר לא יספר צבא השמים ולא ימד חול הים כן ארבה את זרע דוד עבדי ואת הלוים משרתי אתי" (Jeremiah 33:19–22).</note> That is: **And the word of God came to Jeremiah, saying: Thus says God: If you can break my covenant of the day and my covenant of the night, so that there should not be day and night in their seasons, then also my covenant with David my servant shall be broken, so that he should not have a son reigning upon his throne, and with the Levitical priests, my ministers. Just as the host of heaven cannot be numbered, nor the sand of the sea measured, so will I multiply the seed of David my servant, and the Levites who minister to me.** Thus it is written there. Furthermore, the gloss of <term>Rabbi Solomon<note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note></term> on that passage, **If you can break my covenant of the day and my covenant of the night**, says this: **If you are able to break the covenant which I struck...**

<summary>In this dialogue, the author argues that Jewish sinfulness can delay or invalidate divine promises, using Jeremiah's prophecy about the eternal Davidic throne and Levitical priesthood as a primary example of a promise that appears unfulfilled in a literal sense.</summary>

...for day and night, so that they may occur in their proper time. This is indeed the pact he struck with Noah and his sons when he said in Genesis chapter 8: **Day and night shall not cease.** <note>original: "Dies & nox nō quiescent"</note> Thus he spoke. Since it is therefore established that from the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the second temple until now, more than 1,440 years have already passed <note>This timeframe helps date the author’s perspective to the early 16th century, as the Second Temple was destroyed in 70 AD.</note>, in which they have had neither a King from the house of David (or from among themselves), nor a High Priest (great or small), nor any sacrifice, they certainly cannot show us by any true or even plausible reasoning that God fulfilled the letter of what he promised them through Jeremiah in the words mentioned above. For this reason, it is necessary that they concede the promises made by God to the Jews were conditional.

### That very few of the Jews were to be saved, while the rest were to be killed, destroyed, and scattered. Chapter 11.

->CAPNIO<-

**E**ven if it is easily apparent from what you have said that the promise made by God to the Jews regarding their salvation in the time of the Messiah was conditional—namely, if they were to receive the Messiah himself and obey him—it should not seem strange if the greatest part of them were not only spiritually unsaved through Christ's advent and passion, but even temporally lost and scattered. This is because they neither received the true Messiah nor wished to hear him, but rather killed him with a most shameful death. Nevertheless, so that their perfidy may be further proven, you would do something very suited to our purpose if you proved from their own scriptures that not all Jews, but only a very few, were to be saved through the Messiah.

->GAL.<-

This is demonstrated clearly, first of all, through their own tradition, which is placed in the book of the *Sanhedrin* <note>The Sanhedrin is a tractate of the Talmud dealing with law and messianic expectations.</note> at the end of the chapter *Helec* <note>Chapter 'Chelek' is famous for its discussions on the afterlife and the world to come.</note>. There it is read word for word as follows: Rabbi Shammai <note>original Hebrew: "שמאי"</note> said, "It is said in Jeremiah chapter 3: **And I will take you, one from a city and two from a family.** <note>original Hebrew: "ולקחתי אתכם אחד מעיר ושנים ממשפחה" (V’lakachti etkhem echad me-ir u-shnayim mi-mishpacha); Jeremiah 3:14.</note> And again it is said: **And I will bring you to Zion.** <note>original Hebrew: "והבאתי אתכם ציון" (V’heveti etkhem Tziyon).</note> Therefore, their departure from Egypt was measured against their entry into the land. Just as their entrance into the land consisted of two out of six hundred thousand." 

On this, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>This refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says: "The rest," he says, "died during the three days of darkness." <note>A reference to the Midrashic tradition that many Israelites were unworthy of the Exodus and died during the plague of darkness in Egypt.</note> Rabba said, "And so it shall be in the days of the Messiah." As it is said in the first chapter of Hosea: **And she shall respond there as in the days of her youth, and as in the days of her coming up from the land of Egypt.** <note>original Hebrew: "וענתה שמה כימי נעוריה וביום עלותה מארץ מצרים" (V’anata shama kimei neureiha u-vyom alota me-eretz Mitzrayim); Hosea 2:15 in modern numbering.</note> 

This is the tradition. From this it is clearly held that just as out of the six hundred thousand Jews who had departed from Egypt, none entered the promised land except for two alone, Joshua and Caleb, so also in the days of the Messiah (as the tradition proves through the prophet Hosea) there would be only two out of [six hundred thousand] <note>The Latin text here ends with "de sex," a shorthand for "de sexcentis milibus" (of six hundred thousand), referencing the ratio of survivors mentioned earlier.</note> Jews.

<summary>Galatinus argues that God's promises to the Jews were conditional on their acceptance of the Messiah, citing a Talmudic tradition from Sanhedrin to suggest that only a tiny fraction of the Jewish people (a remnant) was ever destined to be saved.</summary>

...out of six hundred thousand to be saved, as if "one from a city and two from a family" (as had been prophesied through Jeremiah) were to be taken up, while all the rest were to be utterly destroyed and scattered. Nor does the aforementioned destruction of the Jews, which took place in his days, detract from Christ in any way; rather, it provides the strongest testimony for him among all who are not ignorant of the truth, regarding how the ancient fathers of the Jews (as their own Talmud testifies) understood the words of the prophets. For we read in the book of the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The Sanhedrin is a section of the Talmud dealing with the high court and legal procedures.</note>, in the chapter that begins <term>Dine mammonoth</term> <note>original: "דיני ממונות" meaning "Monetary Laws" or "Civil Suits."</note>, that is, "judgments of riches." Since they did not wish to speak anything regarding the secrets of Holy Scripture which they had received from their father, the Rabbi said to the servant: "Give them more wine, so that they will speak." When this had been 
<margin>Tradition of the sons of Rabbi Hiyya.</margin>
done, one of them opened his mouth and said, "The son of David <note>A common title for the Messiah.</note> will not come until the two patriarchal houses of Israel fail, which are the head of the captivity that was in Babylon, and the <term>Nasi</term> <note>original: "נשיא" (Nasi) meaning "Prince" or "President" of the Sanhedrin.</note>, that is, the Prince who is in the land of Israel." Just as it is said in Isaiah 8: **And he shall be for a sanctuary and for a stone of stumbling, and for a rock of offense to both the houses of Israel, for a snare and for a ruin to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken. Bind up the testimony, and seal the law among my disciples.
