->BOOK NINE<-

...[as] was said in Daniel 7: *After this I saw in the night vision, and behold, a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful, and exceedingly strong, and it had great iron teeth; it devoured and crushed, and the rest it trampled with its feet. And it was different from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns.* <note>Daniel 7:7. In this context, the "fourth beast" is traditionally interpreted by Christians as the Roman Empire or the Church, and by Jewish commentators as the final oppressive empire before the redemption.</note> For the nations of this world are compared to beasts of this kind. Moreover, at whatever time the horns of the nations of the world are healthy, the horns of Israel will be broken. As it is said in Lamentations chapter 2: *He has broken in the wrath of his fury every horn of Israel.* All of this is from tradition. These things are placed in almost the same words in the <term>Echa Rabbethi</term> <note>original: איכה רבתי; This is the Midrash on the Book of Lamentations.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Lamentations of Jeremiah, regarding that saying in the second chapter of the same book, *He has broken in the wrath of his fury every horn of Israel.* This is the only exception: that in the tenth place, the horn of the Messiah is not positioned, but only the horn of Israel. Therefore, since in this tradition all the aforementioned horns are said to have been given to the head of Israel, and then truly taken away from them because of their fault and handed over to the nations, and since one of them was the Messiah, it follows that the Messiah has already come; and first indeed he was given to the Jews, but then (their <term>perfidy</term> <note>original: "perfidia"; here used in the historical theological sense meaning "unfaithfulness" or "rejection of faith"</note> demanding it) he was taken from them along with all the other horns, and given to the nations.

<margin>Objection of the younger Jews.</margin> ->CAPNIO<- Since the quite fraudulent wickedness of the younger Jews asserts that the beast mentioned a moment ago is our Pope and the Roman Church, from which they hope the aforementioned horns are to be taken away and restored to themselves—for that reason, you would do very well if you would explain when these horns of the Jews were given to this fourth beast, that is, to the Roman Empire, which (on account of its idolatry) was not inaptly compared to a beast.

<margin>Response.</margin> ->GALATINUS<- And so, the horn of the **Jewish Kingdom** was placed upon the head of this fourth beast when the Jewish kingdom, with the Jews themselves, was given over to the empire and power of the Romans to be possessed—indeed, to be crushed and scattered—in the times of Vespasian, Titus, and Hadrian. <note>Vespasian and Titus oversaw the destruction of the Temple in 70 AD; Hadrian suppressed the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135 AD.</note> But the horn of the **Priesthood and of the Levites** was then taken away from the Jews when [the Empire] killed their priests and Levites, and utterly destroyed the divine worship among them on account of their crimes. But in the time of **Sylvester**, the Roman Bishop, and the Emperor **Constantine**, that very horn was placed upon the head of the Romans. <note>Pope Sylvester I and Emperor Constantine the Great (4th century AD) are credited with the establishment of legal Christianity in the Roman Empire.</note> Also, the **horn of the Messiah** was then given to them when the Messiah himself was sent to them for their salvation. But it was then taken away from them when they, rejecting the Messiah himself, crucified him. Then, however, that same horn was given to the Roman Church and the rest of the faithful when the nations received the same Messiah to be worshiped. Furthermore, the **horn of Jerusalem and of the Sanctuary** was then taken from them and handed over to the Romans when the city itself and the Temple were overturned and burned by Titus. Finally, the **horn of the Law**, as far as ceremonial matters are concerned, was handed over to this beast to be destroyed when the Roman Princes prohibited the Jews from keeping the Sabbath or circumcision and other legal requirements, as will be more clearly seen in the following book. But then the same horn, as far as moral matters are concerned, was given to the Romans and other Gentiles to be kept more perfectly, when the Gentiles themselves received the law of the Lord Jesus, the true Messiah, as something divine to be observed.

<summary>This page argues that the spiritual and political "horns" (powers) of Israel were transferred to Rome and the Christian Church as a result of Israel's rejection of Jesus. It provides a historical timeline linking the Roman destruction of Jerusalem to the theological transfer of the Priesthood, the Kingdom, and the Law.</summary>

# Book Ten.

## On the institution of the new divine law which was to be established through the Messiah.

### That the Messiah was to establish a new divine law, more perfect than the old, which the Gentiles were to receive. Chapter 1.

CAPNIO,
<margin>The Jews for the most part rejected.</margin>
**I**f, therefore, the Gentiles were to receive the new law of the Messiah as divine—those Gentiles who (since the Jews for the most part were rejected on account of their perfidy <note>In this context, "perfidy" refers to the theological concept of the "unfaithfulness" or refusal of the Jewish people to recognize Jesus as the Messiah.</note>) you have already proved were to adhere to the Messiah himself. It is now not inappropriate, in order to further break the most hardened neck of the Jews themselves, to speak of the institution of that same new divine law. Therefore, you must first show by Hebrew testimonies that the Messiah himself was to establish a new divine law, more perfect than the old, and that the Gentiles were to receive it.

<margin>Jeremiah 31.</margin>
GALATINUS: Indeed, it was prophesied long ago through Jeremiah in the 31st chapter, in these words, that God would give another new law, different from that which he had given through Moses on Mount Sinai:

> <note>Jeremiah 31:31-33</note> Behold, the days come, says the Lord, and I will strike <note>original: *scindam*; the Latin reflects the Hebrew idiom *karat*, meaning to "cut" a covenant.</note> a new covenant or pact with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. Not like the pact that I struck with their fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, they who disturbed my pact, and I neglected them, says God. But this shall be the pact that I will strike with the house of Israel. After those days, says God, I will put my law in the midst of them, and I will write it upon their heart. And I will be to them as a God, and they shall be to me as a people.

Moreover, that <term>Berith</term> <note>original: ברית; a Hebrew word meaning covenant or treaty.</note>—that is, a pact or covenant—is the same as "law" in the preceding passages is clearly shown in the book <term>Mechilta</term> <note>original: מכילתא; an early Rabbinic commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Exodus.</note>. There, concerning that which is said in Exodus chapter 12, "On the tenth of this month," it is stated: "There is no <term>Berith</term> (that is, covenant or pact) except the law. Just as it is said in Deuteronomy 24 <note>The citation refers to what is now Deuteronomy 29:1 in many English Bibles, though the numbering varied in older Latin editions.</note>:
<margin>Exodus 12, chapter; Deuteronomy 24.</margin>
These are the words of the covenant which the LORD commanded Moses to strike with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which he struck with them in Horeb."

**...at Horeb.** <note>original: *B’Horeb*</note> That is, "These are the words of the covenant" <note>original: *haberith*</note>, that is, of that pact which God commanded Moses to strike <note>original: *scinderet*; the Latin reflects the Hebrew idiom *karat*, meaning to "cut" a covenant.</note> with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides that covenant <note>original: *haberith*</note> which he struck with them at Horeb. Because it was said in Isaiah, chapter 11: **To him the nations shall study** <note>original: *elav goyim yidroshu*</note>—that is, the Gentiles shall apply themselves to him. Rabbi Hanina, in the name of Rabbi **Aha**, said: "What is it that immediately follows in the same place in Isaiah: **And his rest shall be honor** <note>original: *ve-haytah menuchato kavod*</note>, or glory? Because the Holy and Blessed God will be bestowing some of the supernal glory and honor upon the King Messiah." Thus far the tradition. Moreover, in Isaiah, chapter 42, it is read: **Behold my servant, I will uphold him,** or I will lean upon him, **my chosen, in whom my soul has delighted,** or has desired, or in whom my soul or person has been well-pleased. **I have put my spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the nations.** <note>original: *Hen avdi etmokh bo bechiri ratztah nafshi natati ruchi alav mishpat la-goyim yotzi*</note> Which Rabbi Jonathan, son of Uzziel, thus explained in the Chaldaic <note>Aramaic; specifically referring to the Targum, the Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>: **Behold my servant the Messiah, I will bring him near, my chosen in whom my Word has delighted; I will put my Holy Spirit upon him, he shall reveal judgment to the nations.** <note>original: *Ha avdi Meshicha...*</note> It follows in Isaiah, chapter 42: **He shall not cry out, nor lift up his voice, nor cause his voice to be heard abroad.** <note>original: *Lo yitzak ve-lo yisa ve-lo yashmia ba-chutz kolo*</note> Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> says: "He shall bring forth judgment to the nations." Just as it was said in Micah, chapter 4: **And he shall judge among many peoples, and rebuke strong nations afar off.** <note>original: *ve-shafat beyn amim...*</note> "He shall not cry out and he shall not lift up his voice." Because there will be no need for him to shout—namely, to rebuke and persuade the Gentiles. For they themselves, of their own accord, shall come to learn. It follows in Isaiah in the same place: **A bruised reed he shall not break, and the dim** or dark **flax he shall not quench; he shall bring forth judgment unto truth.** <note>original: *Kaneh ratzutz lo yishbor u-fishtah kehah lo yekhavennah l'emet yotzi mishpat*</note>

...he shall bring forth judgment unto truth. Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: This (he says) is how Jonathan <note>Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and expansion of the Prophetic books.</note> interpreted it: **The bruised reed he shall not break, and the flickering wick** <note>original Aramaic: *shibta de-beqane re'u'ah la yitbar ve-hushika de-nebutzin*</note>—that is, those who are fragile like a broken reed, he shall not break, and the dark, or dim, or misty ones, whose light is faint, he shall not extinguish; he shall bring forth judgment according to his truth. But another scripture in Jeremiah chapter 30 says: **And I will cause him to draw near, and he shall cling, or be joined, to me.** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-hiqravtiv ve-nigash elai*</note> Behold the manner by which the angels shall lead him even into their midst! But God, holy and blessed, shall stretch out His hand and lead him to Himself. Because of this, it was said of the King Messiah, "And I will cause him to draw near, and he shall cling to me." Thus far the tradition.

By these things, therefore, it is clearly shown that Isaiah spoke in the person of the Messiah when he said in chapter 51: **Attend to me, my people; and my nation, give ear to me: for a law shall go forth from me, and I will make my judgment to rest for a light of the people, or I will make it frequent.** <note>original Hebrew: *haqshivu elai ammi u-le'ummi elai ha'azinu ki torah me-itti tetze u-mishpati le-or ammim argia* from Isaiah 51:4.</note> In this place where I have translated "my nation," the Hebrews have "my people." But it is a <term>scribal correction</term> <note>original: *ticcun sophrim*; refers to a tradition of minor emendations made to the biblical text by early scribes to preserve the dignity of God or clarify meaning.</note>, or rather a corruption by the scribes. For it was not originally written there as **my nation** <note>original: *le’ummi*</note>, but rather as **my mother** <note>original: *immi*</note>, as Rabbi Elazar ben Jose says in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim*—that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs—concerning that which is said in chapter 3 of the same book: **In the crown with which his mother crowned him.** <note>original Hebrew: *ba-atarah she-atarah lo immo*</note> Why God called the Jewish nation His "mother" was discussed in chapter 24 of the third book. Now, that this new law which the Messiah was to establish ought to go forth from Jerusalem to the Gentiles throughout the whole world is clear through Isaiah, chapter 2, saying: **For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of God from Jerusalem.** <note>original Hebrew: *ki mi-tzion tetze torah u-devar Adonai mi-yerushalayim*</note> This cannot be understood as the Law of Moses, since the Law of Moses itself did not go forth from Zion or from Jerusalem <note>The author argues that since the original Law was given at Mount Sinai, this prophecy must refer to a second, Messianic law originating in Jerusalem.</note>.

He is the one who gave the old law on Mount Sinai. He is the one who established the new law in Jerusalem. He is the one who is both the creator of the men to whom the laws were delivered, and the supreme architect of all things that are in the heavens and under the heavens. For that reason, it was both fitting and worthy that, in his own descent, he should reserve for himself greater and better things to give than those he had delivered through Moses on Mount Sinai. And this is a sufficient argument against the Jews of our age. 

For if anyone seeks a more "necessary" reason in matters of the will than the voluntary actions themselves allow, he is entirely unteachable, according to the opinion of Aristotle in the first book of the *Ethics*. <note>A reference to Aristotle’s principle that one should only seek as much precision as the subject matter allows; in theology and law, "fittingness" is often the standard rather than mathematical necessity.</note> Since this reasoning concerns voluntary actions, it is therefore quite sufficient. And this is for a twofold reason: First, so that they may make their arrival more honorable by more honorable gifts. ## That the Messiah was to institute the sacrament of baptism, by which circumcision was to be set aside. Chapter 11.

->CAPNIO,<- <note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pen name of the famous Hebraist Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

**S**ince Christ commanded the apostles—who were to proclaim the Gospel law to the nations throughout the world—that they should baptize the Gentiles, and since he handed down to them the form of baptizing, saying in the last chapter of Matthew: *Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.* And since the sacrament of <term>baptism</term> <note>From the Greek 'baptizein,' meaning to dip or immerse; here described as the 'gateway' to the Christian life.</note> is the door of the sacraments of this new and evangelical law. Therefore, both for a clearer expression of universal truth and for the greater confounding of Jewish stubbornness, it is necessary to prove through the Hebrew scriptures that the Messiah himself was to institute baptism for the remission of sins.

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> <note>Pietro Galatino, the author and primary speaker, defending Christian doctrine using Jewish sources.</note> This is first understood from the fact that Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Messiah himself in chapter 44, brought forth these words:
<margin>Hebrew: "Do not fear..."</margin>
**Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and Jeshurun whom I have chosen: for I will pour out waters upon the thirsty, and flowing streams upon the dry land; I will pour out my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring: and they shall spring up among the grass like willows by the watercourses. This one shall say, "I am the Lord's," and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob, and another shall write with his hand to the Lord, and shall be surnamed by the name of Israel.** <note>original Hebrew: *Al tira avdi Ya'akov...* from Isaiah 44:2-5. The author uses this prophecy of "pouring out water" as a prefiguration of Christian baptism.</note>

That is: *Fear not, my servant Jacob, and O most upright one, in whom or whom I have chosen. Because I will pour waters upon the thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground. I will pour my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your lineages. And they shall bud among the grass, like willows by the channels of waters. This one shall say, "I am God's." And this one shall call in the name of Jacob. And this one shall write with his hand to God, and shall be named by the name of Israel.* Now, these words, *Because I will pour waters upon the thirsty*, along with the rest, <term>Rabbi Jonathan</term> <note>Refers to Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Targum (Aramaic translation) of the Prophets.</note> translated and explained in the <term>Chaldean</term> <note>The term "Chaldean" was commonly used by Renaissance scholars to refer to the Aramaic language.</note> manner as follows:

**For as waters are given upon the thirsty land, and flowing streams upon the dry ground, so will I give my Holy Spirit upon your sons, and my blessing upon your grandsons: and the righteous shall grow, tender and delicate, like the sprouts of grass as if sending their roots over the courses of the waters. This one shall say, "I am of those who fear the Lord," and this one shall pray in the name of Jacob, and this one shall offer his sacrifice before God, and shall be called by the name of Israel.** <note>This is a translation of the Aramaic Targum provided in the text.</note>

That is, (to render it word for word): *Because just as waters are given upon the thirsty land, and floods upon the dry. So will I give my Holy Spirit upon your son, and my blessing upon the sons of your son. And the righteous shall be anointed, or multiplied, tender and delicate, like a tree that sends its roots over the stretches of waters. This one shall say, "I am of those who fear God." And this one shall pray in the name of Jacob. And this one shall offer his sacrifice before God, and shall be called by the name of Israel.* Therefore, from these words of the prophet, where he speaks openly of baptism, it is most clearly evident that by the power of baptism those converted from the Gentiles, and all Christians, were to be made children of Israel. For the confirmation of this matter, it should be noted that in the Jerusalem <term>Yoma</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the rituals of the Day of Atonement.</note> book, in the chapter that begins *Yom HaKippurim*, that is, the "Day of Atonements," it is read in this manner:

<header>### BOOK TENTH</header>

It is written in the 16th chapter of Jeremiah: <note>original: "מקוה ישראל יהוה" — Usually found in Jeremiah 17:13.</note> **The Lord is the gathering of Israel.** <note>The author plays on the dual meaning of the Hebrew word 'mikveh,' which means both 'hope' and 'a ritual bath' or 'gathering of waters.'</note> For just as a gathering of waters, or a sea of waters, cleanses those who are defiled, so shall the Holy and Blessed God be the one who cleanses Israel in the future. For He himself says in the 36th chapter of Ezekiel: <note>original: "וזרקתי עליכם מים טהורים וטהרתם מכל טומאתיכם ומכל גלוליכם אטהר אתכם"</note> **And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleanness, and from all your filthiness, or your defilements, I will cleanse you.** This is the tradition.

To understand these matters, it should be noted that in the *Bereshit Ketanna* <note>meaning 'the Lesser Genesis,' a title for certain midrashic or homiletic commentaries on the first book of the Bible.</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis, it is written regarding that statement in the 49th chapter of the same book: <note>original: "אסרי לגפן עירה ולשרקה בני אתנו"</note> **Binding his foal to the vine, and his donkey’s colt to the choice branch.** For it is said there: This is he of whom it is written in the 9th chapter of Zechariah: **And riding upon a donkey, and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey.** And he is the one who will plant all Israel like a <term>sorek</term> <note>Hebrew 'sorekah,' referring to a particularly noble or choice vine.</note>, that is, a choice branch. As it is written in the second chapter of Jeremiah: <note>original: "ואנכי נטעתיך שורק כלה זרע אמת"</note> **And I planted you as a choice vine, entirely a seed of truth.** And how shall he act? As it was said in the thirty-sixth chapter of Ezekiel: **And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleanness,** and so forth. This is the tradition.

You see how clearly it is stated here that the Messiah would be the one to sprinkle these waters of Ezekiel, and by so doing, would plant all Israel, both the literal and the spiritual, of which we spoke shortly before. For the aforementioned words of Zechariah can be understood as referring to no one else but the Messiah. For upon that which was said in the ninth chapter of the same prophet—**Behold, your King comes to you, just and having salvation**—the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac, 1040–1105), the famous medieval commentator whose work was essential for Christian Hebraists.</note> says: "It is not possible to explain this except as referring to the King Messiah."

To the aforementioned things it is also quite fittingly added what is written in the book <term>Kiddushin</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning 'Sanctifications' or betrothals.</note>, that is, of Sanctifications, in the chapter that begins <term>Assara Yohasin</term> <note>Hebrew for 'Ten Lineages,' referring to the tenth chapter of the tractate Kiddushin which discusses the genealogical standing of various families.</note>, that is, the "ten nobles." There it is written: The <term>Rabbanan</term> <note>A term for the 'Rabbis' or 'Masters' of the Talmud.</note>, that is, the masters, handed down: That the illegitimate and the children of menstruating women shall be clean in the future (these are the words of Rabbi Yose), as it is said in the 36th chapter of Ezekiel: **And I will sprinkle clean water upon you,** with the rest.

Even the water of baptism and its power were prophesied in that place where it was spoken through Zechariah in the 13th chapter: <note>original: "ביום ההוא יהיה מקור נפתח לבית דוד וליושבי ירושלם לחטאת ולנדה : והיה ביום ההוא נאם יהוה צבאות אכרית את שמות העצבים מן הארץ ולא יוכרו עוד"</note> **In that day there shall be a fountain opened to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for cleansing, and for sprinkling, or for removing. And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I will cut off the names of the idols from the land, and they shall no longer be remembered.** These words are most aptly explained in this way: "In that day," that is, in the time of the Messiah—just as we have proved the prophet is speaking of the Messiah there—there shall be a "fountain," namely of baptism; "open," that is, common to all men; for the house of David and the inhabi- <note>The text cuts off here to be continued on the next page.</note>

...and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, that is, the Church of Christ gathered from both Jews and Gentiles. This fountain is for the purpose of cleansing souls from **original sin** <note>The inherited sin believed to be passed down from Adam, which Christian theology teaches is washed away in baptism.</note> and from all other sins; and for sprinkling—that is, for washing—sinners from every stain of sin, or for distancing—that is, removing—the uncleanness of any sin whatsoever from the soul. 

When exactly this was all meant to take place is shown when the text immediately adds: **And it shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will cut off the names of the idols from the earth, and they shall be remembered no more.** <note>Quoting Zechariah 13:2.</note> Since this was not accomplished through Abraham, nor through any of the prophets, nor in their days, but was only accomplished in the days of Jesus our Messiah, through himself and his disciples and others believing in him, it is clearly evident that our Savior is the "David"—that is, the Messiah—mentioned in the previous words of Zechariah. It follows that his baptism is that fountain open to all, of which he spoke. 

The prophet also gave another very clear sign of this truth when he immediately added these words: <note>original: "וגם את הנביאים ואת רוח הטומאה אעביר מן הארץ"</note> **And also the prophets and the spirit of uncleanness I will cause to pass out of the land.** <note>Zechariah 13:2 continued.</note> Rabbi Jonathan explained this in the <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Galatinus refers to Aramaic as "Chaldean," specifically the Targum or Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> paraphrase in this way: <note>original: "ואת ית נבייא שקרא ויית רוח מסאבא אבטיל מן ארעא"</note> **And also the prophets of a lying spirit, and the unclean spirit, I will abolish from the earth.** 

If the younger Jews were to deny that this was fulfilled in the days of our Messiah, let them be reminded that before our Savior’s advent, there was such a great abundance of false prophets in the world—not only among the Gentiles, but among themselves as well. For instance, the prophet of the Lord, Elijah, said to Ahab, the King of Israel: **Gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, and the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and the four hundred prophets of the groves <note>Often associated with the goddess Asherah.</note> who eat at Jezebel's table.** Besides these, there were many other false prophets among the Jews whom Ahab later consulted as to whether he should go to Ramoth-Gilead. 

Let them also recall that before the times of our Messiah, in the days of their fathers, unclean spirits were accustomed to give oracles through idols. For as we read in the first book of Kings, chapter 1: <note>In the Vulgate, this is 4 Kings 1; in modern English Bibles, 2 Kings 1.</note> Ahaziah, King of Israel, said among other things to his messengers: **Go and inquire of <note>original: "בעל זבוב"</note> Baal-Zebub—that is, the Lord of the Flies, the god of <note>original: "עקרון"</note> Ekron—whether I shall recover from this illness.** In the 10th chapter of Zechariah, it is also said that the idols spoke fraud. 

Therefore, since in the days of the Jews and before the advent of Christ our Lord, idolatry flourished so strongly not only among the Gentiles but also among the Jews—as well as false prophets and unclean spirits, as has been shown by these few examples out of many—and since it is established that in the days of our Messiah all these things were so utterly destroyed that no proof is needed, it is undoubtedly true that whatever we concluded just a moment ago is entirely correct. 

To what has been said, I think it is appropriate to add what is read in the Babylonian book <term>Yoma</term> <note>The tractate of the Talmud concerning the rituals of the Day of Atonement.</note> (that is, the "Book of Days"), in the chapter <term>Yom Ha-Kippurim</term> (that is, the "Day of Atonements"), where it is written: Rabbi Akiba said...

He cites historical biblical examples of widespread Jewish idolatry (such as Baal-Zebub) to prove that only the Christian era succeeded in "cleansing" the world of these spirits.</summary>

# TENTH BOOK

Akiba said: "Blessed are you, Israel, before Him by whom you shall be cleansed. And who shall cleanse you? Your Father, who is in heaven." As it is said in Ezekiel chapter 36: **And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed.** And so on as above. And again in Jeremiah 17: <note>original: מקוה ישראל יהוה</note> **The Lord is the Hope of Israel.** That is: God is the Gathering or Collection of the waters of Israel. <note>The Hebrew word *mikveh* means both "hope" and a "ritual bath" or "collection of waters." Galatinus is connecting the ritual immersion bath to God Himself.</note> For just as a collection of waters cleanses the impure, so the Holy and Blessed God will cleanse Israel. This is the tradition. Since, therefore, this act is attributed to the Messiah by the ancient Jewish teachers through this authority of Ezekiel a little earlier, it necessarily follows according to their sayings that the Messiah is God, who was meant to cleanse all of Israel through the waters of baptism by the power of his Holy Spirit, as was explained above. 

That baptism was to be instituted against all sins, and especially against **original sin**, was specifically foretold through Ezekiel, saying in chapter 36: <note>original: וזרקתי עליכם מים טהורים וטהרתם מכל טמאתכם ומכל גלוליכם אטהר אתכם : ונתתי לכם לב חדש ורוח חדשה אתן בקרבכם והסרתי את לב האבן מבשרכם ונתתי ללב בשר : ואת רוחי אתן בקרבכם ועשיתי את אשר בחקי תלכו ומשפטי תשמרו ועשיתם</note> **And I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleanness, and from all your filthiness I will cleanse you. And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you. And I will make it so that you walk in my precepts, and keep my judgments, and do them.** Now, this "heart of stone" which he says must be taken away—to be succeeded by a "heart of flesh" and the Holy Spirit through grace—is understood to be **original sin**, which was to be utterly removed by God through the mediation of baptism.

Furthermore, to understand that baptism was meant to empty out <note>i.e., supersede or fulfill</note> circumcision, the saying of Rabbi Joshua must be noted above all, when in the book <term>Yevamot</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with levirate marriage and converts.</note>, meaning "of the brothers-in-law," in the chapter <term>Ha-Cholets</term> <note>Meaning "The one who has removed the shoe," referring to a specific legal ritual.</note>, he says: <note>original: מי שהוא טבול ואינו נימול הנה הוא גר כמו שהוא ונמצא באמיות</note> **He who is baptized and not circumcised, behold, he is a gher**—that is, a convert from the Gentiles to the true faith. For so we find it to be with the mothers, namely Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, and Leah, who were baptized and not circumcised. <note>Galatinus uses this rabbinic argument to show that even in Jewish tradition, ritual washing (baptism) was seen as a primary mark of conversion that could exist apart from circumcision, especially for women.</note> 

In this place it should also be known that circumcision was a figure of the shedding of Christ’s blood. He began to shed it at his own circumcision, and finally poured it all out in his Passion for the salvation of the human race. From then on, circumcision was never to be performed again, since Christ commanded baptism to be performed in its place, which deletes sins more perfectly, and which both women and men can use.

### *On the sacrament of penance, which the Messiah was to institute through vocal confession for the remission of sins. Chapter III.*

### CAPNIO,
<note>Capnio is the Latinized name for Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist, who acts as a character in this dialogue.</note>

Since the Lord instituted not only baptism, but also the sacrament of penance for the remission of sins. And rightly so. For since baptism can only be received once (for it is a sacrament that cannot be repeated), it was necessary for penance to be instituted. This was so that the sacrament of penance might come to the aid of those who happened to sin after receiving baptism. For this reason, some have not ineptly called penance "the second plank after a shipwreck." <note>A common medieval metaphor: if the "ship" of baptismal innocence is wrecked by sin, penance is the plank that saves the soul from drowning.</note> Therefore, since enough has been said regarding baptism, something must now be said from the Hebrew scriptures concerning the sacrament of penance, which the Messiah was to institute through vocal confession for the remission of sins.

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> Since we have already said enough (as I believe) in the eighth book concerning the penance which the Messiah was to preach through himself and through his disciples, and concerning its efficacy and power, it should now suffice to reveal from the scriptures of the Hebrews only those things which pertain to vocal confession. Therefore, let what is read in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>A "Midrash" is a Jewish homiletic commentary; "Tehillim" is the Hebrew name for the Book of Psalms.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Psalms—be heard first. Where, upon Psalm 100, it is said word for word: <note>original: מזמור לתודה הריעו ליהוה כל הארץ</note> **A Psalm for confession. Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.** God, holy and blessed, said: "All nations shall confess to me, and I will receive them." As it is said in Isaiah chapter 45: <note>original: כי לי תכרע כל ברך</note> **For every knee shall bow to me.** Another discourse—that is, another exposition: **A Psalm for confession.** This is what is written in Proverbs chapter 28: <note>original: מכסה פשעיו לא יצליח ומודה ועוזב ירוחם</note> **He who hides his crimes shall not prosper; but he who confesses and forsakes them shall obtain mercy.** "He who hides his crimes"—such a one was Saul, to whom it was said in 1 Samuel 15: "What then is this voice of sheep?" <note>Referring to King Saul's attempt to hide his disobedience to God's command by keeping the spoils of the Amalekites.</note> But he responded,

It is said of these: "Of the righteous, who conquer or subdue their own tinder <term>fomentum/sensuality: the 'spark' or inclination toward sin</term> and confess their acts to their fathers. For everyone who confesses his acts is worthy of the world to come." As it is said in Psalm 50: <note>original: זובח תודה יכבדנני ושם דרך אראנו בישע אלהים / "Id est, Qui sacrificat confessionem, honorabit me, & qui ponit uiam, ostendam illi in saluatione Dei"</note> **He who sacrifices a confession shall honor me, and to him who sets his way aright, I will show the salvation of God.** <note>Psalm 50:23 in the Vulgate; Psalm 51 in other traditions.</note>

Immediately, therefore, he conquered his sensuality or his impulse, and confessed. However, the Holy and Blessed God curses everyone who does not confess his works. For so we find in the case of Cain, who denied it and said in Genesis chapter 4: **Am I my brother's keeper?** Therefore he was cursed. But he who confesses and forsakes them shall obtain mercy.** This concludes the tradition. <margin>The judgment is finished</margin> <note>original: חדין / Nigmar haddin</note>—that is, the judgment has been determined. As it is said in the sixty-fifth Psalm: **"The hope of all the ends of the earth, and of the sea of those far away"**—namely, this is repentance. # BOOK TEN

### *That the Messiah was to institute a new sacrifice, in which he himself*
### *ought to be the bread and food. Chapter 4.*

## CAPNIO <note>The Latinized name for Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist, who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

**H**aving spoken of baptism and penance—insofar as it concerns vocal confession—we must now speak of the sacrament of the Eucharist. By divine power, the Messiah was to institute this in bread and wine, transubstantiating <term>transubstantiatio</term> <note>The theological doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist are changed into the literal body and blood of Christ.</note> the bread into his body and the wine into his blood. Therefore, it must first be proved through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that the Messiah himself was to institute a new sacrifice, of which he himself should be the bread and food.

GALATINUS: <note>The author, Pietro Galatino, who represents the voice of Catholic orthodoxy in the text.</note> First, it must not be overlooked that Psalm 72, which begins, *Give the King your judgment, O God*, is understood by the ancient Jewish doctors to speak entirely of the Messiah. This is shown most clearly in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>An ancient Jewish rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Psalms—where it is read regarding the title of the same Psalm, which is: לשלמה (*Lishlomo*), meaning "To Solomon," or "To the Peaceful One." For it is said there: **This is the King Messiah, of whom it was said** in the 11th chapter of Isaiah: **"A branch shall go forth from the stem of Jesse."** Although Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the famous 11th-century Jewish commentator.</note> attempts to explain this Psalm as being about King Solomon—and therefore explains those words of the same Psalm: **"The just shall sprout in his days, and abundance of peace, until the moon fails"** as: "In his days, that is, in the days of Solomon, the just shall be multiplied, and there shall be abundance of peace until the end of the world"—yet, when he reached the place where our edition <note>Referring to the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible.</note> has: *There shall be a firmament in the earth on the tops of the mountains*, but the Hebrew truth is: יהי פיסת בר (*Yehi pissath bar*), which means **There shall be a bread-cake of grain** (which is commonly called a focaccia) **or a piece of grain in the earth, on the head of the mountains**, he was unable to completely silence the truth. He produced these words against his own position, saying: **"Our masters of blessed memory explained this as a type of cake in the days of the Messiah, and they explained the whole Psalm as being about the King Messiah."** Thus he spoke.

Furthermore, how and in what manner the Messiah would be <term>פיסת בר</term> <term>Pissath bar</term>, that is, a "bread-cake of grain," according to the exposition of the wise Jewish Masters, is found in the book called <term>סיפרי</term> <term>Siphre</term> <note>An ancient rabbinic commentary on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note> among them. There, upon that passage of Deuteronomy chapter 32: *The Lord alone shall lead him, and there shall be no strange god with him*, it is said: **Another word. God, the Holy and Blessed, said: It is to come that I will seat you in rest in the world, and "there is no foreign god with him," meaning there shall not be among you people who busy themselves with worthless business... as it is said, "There shall be a handful of grain in the earth" etc., so that the wheat shall bring forth fine cakes** <note>original: גלוסקאות / gluskaot; a Greek loanword used in Hebrew for fine bread or pastries.</note> **as full as the palm of a hand, and its fruit shall rustle like Lebanon, so that the wheat will rub one against the other and drop their fine flour onto the earth, and you will come and take it—taking from it a palm-full—for your sustenance.**

According to that saying of the Psalm: **"And there shall be a cake of wheat in the earth."** For this reason, Rabbi Jonathan, the son of Uzziel <note>The reputed author of the Targum (Aramaic translation) of the Prophets.</note>, in turning this passage into Aramaic, explained it thus: <term>יהי קרבן דעיבורא בארעא</term> <note>original: *Yehei qurban de-ibura be-ar'a*</note> **"There shall be a sacrifice of grain in the land."**

...forever according to the word of Melchizedek. <note>Latin: *in æternum secundum uerbum Melchisedec*; refers to Psalm 110:4.</note> **HOGSTRATUS.** Our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> says Melchizedek *bringing forth* bread and wine. And if it cheers men, in what way does it bring joy to God? In the sacrifice that shall be made of it. Indeed, that the sacrifice of bread is never to fail is apparent from what is said in Psalm 72: "And there shall be a cake of grain in the earth, on the top of the mountains." <note>Latin: *placenta frumenti*; usually translated in modern Bibles as "an abundance of grain."</note> All these things were said by that Rabbi Iohai, who preceded Christ by many years.

->*That the Messiah, in this sacrifice, was meant to <term>transubstantiate>the change of the substance of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ</term> bread into his body, and wine into his blood. Chapter VI.*<-

### CAPNIO,

**T**he Catholic faith firmly confesses and holds that in this sacrifice, by divine power, bread is really transubstantiated into the true body of Christ, and wine into his true blood. Therefore, I would not be uninterested to know whether it can be proved through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that bread was truly and really to be transubstantiated into the body of the Messiah, and wine into his blood, in this same sacrifice. **GALATINUS.** It certainly can. For concerning the conversion of bread into the flesh of the Messiah himself, who is the true God, it is found in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan of Narbonne (11th century).</note> regarding that verse of the hundred and thirty-sixth Psalm, "Who gives bread to all flesh" <note>original Hebrew: *noten lekhem le-khol basar*</note>. Where it is said: *A well-known word is further stated: "He gives bread to all flesh." This is what is said in Psalm 34: "Taste and see, for God is good." Because the bread, which he gives to all, is his very flesh. And while the bread is tasted, it is converted into flesh.* And this is what is meant by "And see," <note>Galatinus is arguing that the "seeing" in the Psalm refers to an intellectual or spiritual recognition of the change in substance.</note>

<summary>Galatinus argues that ancient Jewish commentators, including Simeon bar Yochai and Moses ha-Darshan, foresaw that the Messiah's sacrifice would consist of bread and wine and would involve the bread becoming his literal flesh.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnio (Johann Reuchlin) and Galatinus regarding Rabbinic proofs for the Eucharist, specifically focusing on the invisible presence of the Messiah's blood under the appearance of wine.</meta>

"See, for God is good. And this will be a great wonder." These few words, if they are well examined, are understood to refer to the conversion of the bread into the body of the Messiah. Concerning his blood, however, which is daily sacrificed upon the altar—invisible to us, that is, hidden under the appearance of wine, but visible to God alone—it is written in the book *Mechilta* <note>A Rabbinic commentary (midrash) on the Book of Exodus.</note> as follows:

"And you have acted impiously against the blood of the innocent. This is what was said: *And I will see the blood* <note>original Hebrew: *ve-ra'iti et ha-dam*; Exodus 12:13</note>, which will be seen by me and not by others. These are the words of Rabbi Ishmael. And next to it is joined: *And the blood shall be a sign for you*. A sign, I say, for you, but it will not be a sign <note>The Latin text here uses *lignum* (wood/cross), likely a pun or typological reference to the wood of the cross, contrasting with *signum* (sign).</note> for others."

**CAPNIO.** I would like you to show more clearly from their scriptures this conversion of both species <note>The "two species" refers to the bread and the wine used in the rite.</note> into the body and blood of the Messiah. 

**GALATINUS.** Rabbi Cahana <note>A name referring to several Talmudic sages; here used to cite a specific mystical interpretation.</note> clearly declares this regarding both, based on what is said in Genesis chapter 49: *Binding his foal to the vine, and his ass's colt to the choice vine; he washed his garments in wine, and his clothes in the blood of grapes: His eyes shall be red with wine, and his teeth white with milk.* <note>Genesis 49:11–12, traditionally seen by Christians as a prophecy of Christ.</note> Whereupon Rabbi Cahana says: "These words, *binding his foal to the vine*, show that the sacrifice which will be made of wine will not only be transmuted <note>or changed in substance</note> into the substance of the blood of the Messiah, but will also be converted into the substance of his body." Furthermore, those words, *and his ass's colt to the choice vine*, signify that the divinity and the Son of God will be united to the 'ass,' that is, to his matter. For <term>hamor</term> <note>Hebrew for "donkey" or "ass."</note> is interpreted as "materiality." <note>A play on the Hebrew words *hamor* (donkey) and *homer* (matter/physical substance).</note> Just as an ass carries burdens and the clothes of travelers, so the King Messiah will carry upon himself the sins of the whole world. This is according to what is said in Isaiah chapter 53: *And God made the sin of us all to meet in him.* 

When it is said, *He shall wash his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes*, the same meaning is expressed in different words. For "garment" refers to matter <note>the physical body</note>. Just as it is said in Job chapter 10: *You have clothed me with skin and flesh.* And *his cloak in the blood of grapes* refers to his divinity. For just as a cloak surrounds the whole man, so God fills the entire world. 

*His eyes shall be red with wine, and his teeth white with milk.* This means: In the sacrifice which will be made of bread, notwithstanding that it is white like milk, the substance will be converted into the substance of the body of the Messiah, and there will be in that sacrifice the substance of the blood of the Messiah, red as wine. Likewise, in the sacrifice of wine, there will be the blood and the flesh of the Messiah, and the same will be in the bread. For the body of the Messiah cannot be divided. Reason demands this. For if the flesh and blood were divided, they would be distinguished from one another. But the body of the Messiah cannot be divided. As it is written in Exodus 12: *And you shall not break a bone in it.* <note>Originally referring to the Passover lamb, here applied to the Eucharist.</note> Furthermore, flesh without blood, and vice versa, are dead things. But the body of the Messiah after the resurrection...

because it will be glorified, it will live forever. and from this comes that famous saying, <note>original Hebrew: *Dovid Melekh Yisrael Chai ve'kayom*</note> **David, King of Israel, lives forever.** <note>A phrase still used in Jewish liturgy and song, here interpreted as a reference to the eternal life of the Messiah.</note> Moreover, he spoke of eyes and teeth so that the speech might become more beautiful and its deeper meaning might be concealed. This is the literal word of that Rabbi Cahana, who lived long before the birth of Christ. Furthermore, he says that the body of the Messiah will be living forever after the resurrection. This is because (as was proven more extensively above) the ancient Hebrews say that one of the names of the Messiah is **David**. They prove this primarily by the testimony of Jeremiah in the 30th chapter, saying: <note>original Hebrew: *ve-avdu et Adonai Elohehem ve-et David Malkam asher akim lahem*</note> **And they shall serve the Lord their God, and David their King, whom I will raise up for them.** Because he says "I will raise up," which is in the future tense, they say that these words of Jeremiah ought to be understood not as the historical David (who had preceded him by a long time), but as the Messiah. Wherefore Rabbi Jonathan <note>Refers to Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Targum (Aramaic translation) of the Prophets.</note> also translated them into Aramaic <note>original: *Chaldaicè*</note> in this way: <note>original Aramaic: *ve-yiflachun qadam Adonai Elohahon ve-yishtam'un le-David Meshicha Malkehon*</note> **And they shall serve before the Lord their God, and they shall obey David the Messiah, their King.** For that reason, they asserted that one of the names of the Messiah was to be **David**. Therefore, Rabbi Cahana correctly said: from this comes that secret, **David the King of Israel lives forever.**

<margin>Question.</margin> **HOG.** Our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible, the standard Bible of the Catholic Church at the time.</note> contains the words quoted from Genesis chapter 49 in a much different way. For it says: *Binding his foal to the vine, and his ass's colt, O my son, to the choice vine. He shall wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape. His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk.* From this it is clear that where Rabbi Cahana says "his city," our text has "his foal." And where he says "His eyes are redder than wine," we have "His eyes are more beautiful than wine." Furthermore, where you translated "his male donkey," our text has "his female donkey." From where does this discord arise?

<margin>Response.</margin> **GAL.** It certainly arises from the ambiguity of the words. For where the author of our edition translated "his foal," it is written as *iro* <note>original Hebrew: עירה</note> in the Hebrew. However, this word among the Hebrews signifies both "city" and "foal," depending on the diversity of the <term>vowel points</term> <note>Hebrew was originally written without vowels; the dots and dashes (points) added later determine the pronunciation and meaning.</note>. For if it is pointed with the single point called <term>hirik</term> <note>A small dot placed under a Hebrew letter representing the "i" sound.</note>, thus *iro*, it sounds the same as "his city" among us. But if it is pointed with two points, namely <term>patah</term> and <term>shva</term> <note>Vowel marks representing "a" and a neutral "e" or vocal break.</note>, in this manner—*airo*—it signifies "his foal" to them. Although before the sacred scripture was pointed, this word could have been read in either way (namely *iro* or *airo*), now it must be read as *iro* and not *airo*, for so it has been pointed. Therefore, the author of our edition should have translated it as "his city" and not "his foal." Also, regarding that which our text says, "they are more beautiful": in Hebrew it is written *hachlili* <note>original Hebrew: חכלילי</note>, which is ambiguous for both "red" and "beautiful." Here, however, it is more in harmony with the letter and the truth to say "redder" than "more beautiful." Finally, as to why our text has "his female donkey" while you say "his male donkey" was translated by me: it is because *hamor* <note>original Hebrew: חמור</note>, that is "donkey," is of common gender among the Hebrews...

<margin>Another inquiry.</margin>
That text which the same Rabbi Cahana brought forward from Exodus to prove that the body of the Messiah cannot be divided, saying: "And you shall not break the <term>substance</term> <note>Rabbinic interpretation often reads the Hebrew word for "bone" as "essence" or "substance."</note> in him." I also think that to the aforementioned things, this most noteworthy point should be added: that Rabbi Yohai <note>likely Simeon bar Yochai, a famous 2nd-century sage</note> says regarding the previously mentioned text written in Numbers chapter 28, "My offering, my bread," and so forth. He says thus: "My offering, my bread, you shall look to the fires of my sweet savor to offer to me in its time," that is, in the time of the Messiah. And you shall say to them, "The sacrifices which you ought to offer, the Lamb," with the rest. This is the sacrifice which you perform at present. However, this bread will be "of two faces." Concerning which it is written in Exodus chapter 25: <gloss>original Hebrew: לחם פנים לפני תמיד, *Lechem panim le-fanai tamid*</gloss> That is, **The bread of the faces before me always.** <note>Commonly known as the Showbread or Bread of Presence in English Bibles.</note> Now, the reason why it is called "bread of faces" is because, as Rabbi Judah says, it will be transmuted from the substance of bread—when it is sacrificed—into the substance of the body of the Messiah, who shall descend from the heavens. And he himself will be the sacrifice. Therefore it says, "You shall look to offering to me," that is, to me being offered. And it will be invisible and impalpable. The **Seat of Elijah** provides proof of this matter. And the Masters say that for this reason it is called bread of faces, because in the sacrifice itself there will be two substances: divinity and humanity. Thus says that Rabbi, who preceded Christ by many years. **HOG.**
<margin>Another inquiry.</margin>
How is the saying of Rabbi Judah understood, when he said that the **Seat of Elijah** bears witness to this matter, in order to prove that the body of the Messiah would be invisible and impalpable in the sacrifice itself? **GAL.** The teachers of the <margin>Answer.</margin> Hebrews report that God gave this prerogative to Elijah: that no circumcision should happen in which he himself did not intervene. For this reason, the Masters themselves established that whenever a circumcision was to be performed, two highly decorated seats should always be prepared. One in which the person holding the infant would sit. The other in which no one could sit, but it would remain empty, because they said that Elijah would come to sit in it. Therefore, for that reason, Rabbi Judah said that the **Seat of Elijah** provides proof for the invisible and impalpable body of the Messiah in the future sacrifice of bread and wine, lest the more recent Jews (whose lack of faith he himself foresaw) should say that the body of the Messiah is not in this sacrifice simply because it is neither seen nor felt there. Since they both believe and confess that Elijah is invisible and impalpable in that seat, and also that the same man can exist in several places at the same hour.

# CAPNIO,

<note>Capnio is the Latinized name for Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist of the Renaissance who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

**Y**ou have indeed brought forth mixed and wonderful things concerning the mysteries of this ineffable sacrifice from the scriptures of the Hebrews. It remains for you now to reveal what their ancients thought regarding its efficacy.

**GAL.** Indeed, they held quite wonderful views. For among the other signs and figures of this unspeakable sacrament handed down to the Hebrew fathers, that which is read concerning its miraculous conversion and efficacy in the Chaldean <note>Aramaic (Targumic) translation.</note> interpreter of the most holy book of Job—whoever he may have been—is not to be counted among the least of signs and figures. For he says there: 

<note>original Aramaic text: "And his three friends heard all this evil... their gardens withered, and the bread of their meal was turned into living flesh, and the wine of their drink was turned into blood... and by that merit they were delivered from the place of Gehenna."</note> 
And the three companions of Job heard all this evil that had come upon him, and when they saw that the trees in their gardens had withered, and the bread of their sustenance was turned into living flesh, and the wine of their drinking was turned into blood, then each man came from his place. And by the merit of this thing, they were delivered from the place that was designated for them in Gehenna—Eliphaz from the region of Teman, and Bildad from the province of Shuah, and Zophar from the region of Naamah—and they joined together as one to come to mourn with him and comfort him.

<margin>Behold.</margin> That is: "And the three companions of Job perceived all the evils that had happened to him." Where, specifically, they saw that the trees in their gardens had withered, and they saw the bread by which they were sustained converted into living flesh, and the wine they were about to drink converted into blood. And each one departed from his own place. And by the merit of this thing, they were delivered from descending into the place that had been assigned to them in hell <note>original: *inferno*</note>: Eliphaz from the region of Teman (which, as many agree, is an island in the Arabian Gulf); Bildad from the province of Shuah (which they believe to be part of Upper Egypt); Zophar from the region of Naamah (which is the land of Judea, which they call the Land of Promise). And they themselves met together as one, so that they might go to him—namely Job—to console him. Thus ends the quote. 

When it is said here, "And by the merit of this thing they were delivered from the place of hell," the efficacy of this sacred thing is openly suggested, by which those using it were to be delivered from the eternal death of hell. Furthermore, one must not overlook what that ancient <term>Teacher</term> of theirs—whom they call <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi*, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, that is, "Our Holy Master"—reports in the book which he calls <term>Gale razeya</term> <note>original: "The Revealer of Secrets."</note>, that is...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 667, where Galatinus is explaining the nature of the sacrifice (the Eucharist) and the requirements for the priest. He is moving from mystical interpretations to a philological analysis of the biblical text, specifically debating the translation of the Hebrew word 'lehem' in the Vulgate Bible.</meta>

<header># BOOK</header>

...how the priest’s life ought to be while performing this sacrifice, the Lord himself indicates when, speaking of the sacrifice of our own time and of the quality of the one consecrating it, he says in Leviticus chapter 21: 

<gloss>And you shall sanctify him, because he is, or will be, the one sacrificing the flesh of your God. He shall be holy to you, because I, the Lord who sanctifies you, am holy.</gloss> <note>The Hebrew text provided is Leviticus 21:8: וקדשתו כי את לחם אלהיך הוא מקריב קדש יהיה כי קדוש אני יהוה מקדשכם.</note>

**HOG.** <note>Presumably Hogstraten, a frequent interlocutor in these dialogues.</note> Our text <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> in this place says: *And he offers the loaves of proposition.* <note>The "loaves of proposition" are the Showbread of the Tabernacle.</note> Let him therefore be holy, because *I also am holy, the Lord who sanctifies you.*

**GAL.** <note>Galatinus.</note> Here our edition <note>the Vulgate translation</note> has two significant corruptions. The first is that the first clause of this text is entirely missing—namely, *And you shall sanctify him*—which could be the fault of the scribes. The second is that in the second clause, the Hebrew truth <note>the original Hebrew text</note> reads far differently. For where we have, *And he offers the loaves of proposition,* the Hebrew has: *Because he is, or will be, the one sacrificing the flesh of your God.* This agrees more closely with the truth of our faith. I cannot help but attribute this corruption to the author of our edition <note>St. Jerome</note>, since the cause of this error was nothing other than the ambiguity of a word. For this Hebrew word <term>lehem</term> <note>original: לחם</note> has many meanings. Sometimes it signifies food, sometimes bread, and sometimes flesh. As Rabbi David Kimhi says in the <term>Book of Roots</term> <note>original: *Sefer Shorashim*, a standard medieval Hebrew dictionary</note>: "The meaning of this word *lehem* encompasses everything edible." However, it is sometimes used for bread alone, as in that saying from Deuteronomy chapter 8: *Man does not live by bread alone.* <note>original: לא על הלחם לבדו יחיה האדם</note> But sometimes it refers specifically to flesh, as in Numbers chapter 28: *My sacrifice, my flesh for the fire, or for my flame.* <note>original: קרבני לחמי לאשי</note> And it is the same in Leviticus chapter 21: *He himself sacrificing the flesh of his God.* <note>original: לחם אלהיו הוא מקריב</note> So too in Job chapter 6: *They are like the sorrows of my flesh.* <note>original: המה כדוי לחמי</note> These are the words of Rabbi Kimhi.

->Therefore, where it should have been translated as 'the flesh of your God,'<-
->the author of our edition translated it as 'loaves of proposition.'<-

<summary>Galatinus argues that the Vulgate translation of Leviticus 21:8 is "corrupt" because it uses "bread" where the original Hebrew implies "flesh." He uses the scholarship of Rabbi David Kimhi to prove that the Hebrew word 'lehem' can mean flesh, thereby linking the Old Testament priesthood more directly to the Christian Eucharist.</summary>

# Book Eleven.

## On the cessation of the ancient law.

### That upon the coming of the Law of the Messiah, the Mosaical Law was to cease in all ceremonial matters. Chapter 1.

->CAPNIO,<- <note>Johannes Reuchlin, a famous German humanist and scholar of Hebrew, referred to here by his Greek-derived pen name "Capnio."</note>

**S**ince you have said much in the preceding remarks, not only regarding baptism—by which circumcision was to be rendered void—and regarding the sacrifice of bread and wine—by which all the sacrifices of the old law were to fail—but also regarding the institution of the new divine law itself, which was to be established by the Messiah, through which the entire ancient law was to pass away in regard to its ceremonies. Therefore, so that the obstinate <term>perfidy</term> <note>In this historical context, "perfidy" was a standard, albeit polemical, theological term used by Christian writers to describe the Jewish rejection of Christ as the Messiah.</note> of the more recent Jews may be even more thoroughly refuted—those who assert that the old law itself is unchangeable and will endure until the end of the world—it is now necessary for you to prove through their own scriptures that the law (upon the coming of the Messiah’s law) was intended to have an end in all its ceremonial requirements.

<margin>GALATINUS.</margin> So that with the Law of the Messiah itself, it might be observed not according to the letter, but according to the spiritual and mystical sense. That it was thus to be is most clearly shown in the <term>Midrash Coheleth</term> <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes, upon that saying in the second chapter of the same book: <gloss>I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with joy and look upon good; and behold, this too is vanity."</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: אמרתי אני בלבי לכה נא אנסכה בשמחה וראה בטוב והנה גם הוא הבל</note> For it is said there: *And look upon good*—namely, the good of the Law. *And behold, even this is vanity.* Was it not necessary for the scripture to say, "And behold, even this is joy"? Why then did it say, "Behold, it is vanity"? <margin>HEZKIYA.</margin> Rabbi Hezkiya said: "Because every law which you learn in this world is <term>vanity</term> <note>Hebrew: *habelim*</note> before the law of the world to come." <note>This suggests that the earthly, literal laws are insubstantial compared to the spiritual reality of the Messianic age.</note> Furthermore, that this "law of the world to come" is the Law of the Messiah, and the "days of the world to come" are his days, is evident from what is read in the same Midrash regarding that saying in Ecclesiastes chapter 11: <gloss>If a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all; and let him remember the days of darkness.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: אם שנים הרבה יחיה האדם בכלם ישמח ויזכר את ימי החשך</note> For there, those words are explained thus: *If a man lives many years, let him rejoice in all these*—namely, in the joy of the Law. *And let him remember the days of darkness.* These are the days of malice; how many will they be? "Behold, I make a new thing." "Now it shall sprout." "Will you not recognize it?"

By "former things," he means the **Mizraim** <gloss>Hebrew: מצרים</gloss>, that is, the Egyptian signs. By "ancient things," he means those things that were done after the departure from Egypt. "Behold, I am doing a new thing," and so forth: these refer to the events concerning **Gog** <note>In biblical tradition, Gog is a leader whose defeat signals the beginning of the Messianic era.</note> in the days of the **Messiah**. Thus far the tradition.

The Commentary <gloss>Glossa</gloss> of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> explains it this way: **Do not remember the former things**, that is, the signs and miracles which I mention to you and which I performed in Egypt; do not remember them from now on. For you shall be so devoted to this current redemption, to confessing it and praising it. It follows: **And do not care for the ancient things**, that is, do not pay attention to them, nor set your heart upon them. This is the view of **Rabbi Solomon**.

Almost the same thing as what was said in the preceding tradition is also placed in the Babylonian book **Berachoth** <gloss>Hebrew: ברכות</gloss>, that is, the book of "Blessings," at the end of the chapter titled **Meemathai korin** <gloss>Hebrew: מאימתי קורין; "From what time do we recite?"</gloss>. There it is said: It is a tradition that **Ben Zoma** said to the wise men: "And how shall they be mindful of the departure from Egypt in the days of the Messiah? Is it not already written in **Jeremiah**, in the twenty-third chapter: **Behold, the days come, says God, and they shall no longer say: 'The Lord lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt'**—along with the rest?" They answered him: Not that the departure from Egypt is to be uprooted from its place, but that the deeds of the **Kingdoms** (that is, the signs that will happen in the times of the Kingdoms) shall be the substance. And the departure from Egypt (that is, the signs of the departure from Egypt) shall be an addition to it; that is, they will behave like an "accident," which is present or absent without the destruction of the substance. And so says **Isaiah** in the forty-third chapter: **Do not remember the former things**, with the rest, as above. This is the tradition.

To this also pertains most strongly what the Lord commanded the Jews through **Moses** in the 26th chapter of **Leviticus**, saying: **And you shall cast out the old because of the new.** <gloss>Hebrew: וישן מפני חדש תוציאו</gloss> That this should be understood in this sense is held from what is read in the book called **Siphre** <note>An ancient legal commentary (midrash) on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note> regarding that passage in **Leviticus** 26, which says: **And I will look upon you, and make you fruitful, and multiply you (or make you grow), and I will establish my covenant with you; and you shall eat the old store, and you shall exclude (or expel) the old because of the new.** <gloss>Hebrew: ופניתי אליכם והפריתי אתכם והרביתי אתכם והקימותי את בריתי אתכם ואכלתם ישן נושן וישן מפני חדש תוציאו</gloss> For these things are thus explained there: "And I will look upon you" for good, "and I will make you fruitful" through physical generation. "And I will multiply you (or make you grow)" through an upright stature. "And I will establish my covenant with you." Not like the first covenant which you transgressed, as it is said in **Jeremiah** 31: **Because they themselves transgressed my covenant.** But a **new covenant** which they shall not transgress henceforth. **"And I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant..."** <note>original Hebrew: וכרתי את בית ישראל ואת בית יהודה ברית חדשה לא כברית</note> It is written in Jeremiah, chapter 31: **I will make a new covenant for the house of Israel and the house of Judah. Not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.** And regarding this he says: **And you shall eat the old store, and you shall cast out the old because of the new.** <note>Quoting Leviticus 26:10</note> This is the tradition.

Furthermore, it is clearly shown in the book **Mechilta** <note>A collection of ancient Jewish interpretations (Midrash) on the Book of Exodus</note> that the "covenant" mentioned in the preceding words is the same thing as the "law." Where it says regarding that passage in Exodus chapter 12, "On the tenth day of this month," it is stated: **There is no covenant except for the Law.** Just as it is said in Deuteronomy chapter 29: **These are the words of the covenant which God commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which he made with them in Horeb.** <note>Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, where the Ten Commandments were given.</note> Likewise elsewhere, namely in Exodus chapter 34: **And he wrote upon the tables the ten words of the covenant.** These things are in the same book, *Mechilta*. Therefore, from the preceding tradition, it is clearly held that when the New Law of the Messiah arrived, the Old Law had to cease.

Furthermore, in the book called **Eruvin** <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing primarily with Sabbath laws</note>, in the chapter beginning **Osin Passin** <note>Hebrew: עושין פסין; the name of the second chapter of the tractate Eruvin</note>, it is read that Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said: **For it is written: Keep the commandments and the statutes and the judgments which I command you today to do them.** <gloss>Hebrew: דכתיב ושמורת את המצות ואת החקים ואת המשפטים אשר אנכי מצוך היום לעשותם</gloss> **To do them today, but not to do them tomorrow.** <gloss>Hebrew: היום לעשותם ולא מחר לעשותם</gloss> This is the tradition. Therefore, "today"—that is, before the Messiah came—and "not tomorrow"—that is, not after he had already come—the ceremonial commandments <term>cæremonialia præcepta; religious rituals like dietary laws or specific sacrifices</term> were to be observed. 

From all these things, it is quite clearly evident that upon the arrival of the Messiah, who was to institute a new law, the Old Law was to cease in all its ceremonies. Since it has been very extensively proven in the preceding sections that the Messiah has already come, and that he was our Lord Jesus Christ. He did not cease to write the New Law of his Gospel into the hearts of believers—and especially his apostles and disciples—for nearly three and a half years through deeds and words. And finally, by sending the Holy Spirit, he made whatever he had written in their hearts by teaching so firm that it could be erased by no persecution and no forgetfulness. 

Therefore, it is certain that what had been prophesied long before through Jeremiah chapter 31 was then fulfilled in these words: **After those days (said God), I will put my law in their midst, and I will write it upon their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.** <gloss>Hebrew: אחרי הימים ההם נאם יהוה נתתי את תורתי בקרבם ועל לבם אכתבנה והיתי להם לאלהים והמה יהיו לי לעם</gloss> 

From all these points, it plainly follows that the Old Law has now ceased in all its ceremonies. Wherefore it is publicly evident that no one is further bound to perform circumcision <note>The physical sign of the Old Covenant</note> literally, no one is bound to keep the Sabbath and other Jewish feasts, nor to celebrate annual commemorations for their ancient miracles. For since the Messiah came and gave the New Law, the old having been cast aside, all are bound to observe the New.

### Chapter 11. How and why Christ fulfilled the Old Law.

### CAPNIO

<margin>The objection of the Jews.</margin>
The Jews oppose us on this point in many ways, wishing to prove that the ancient Law would by no means cease upon the arrival of the Messiah. They argue that because we Christians say Christ our Lord was the Messiah, and yet he himself observed that entire Law and led others to observe it by both word and deed. For he says in the fifth chapter of Matthew: **"I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them."** <note>original Latin: "Non ueni soluere legem, aut prophetas, sed adimplere."</note> And again, a little later: **"Whoever,"** he says, **"breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do so, will be called least in the Kingdom of Heaven. But whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the Kingdom of Heaven."** <note>Matthew 5:17, 19</note> Therefore, from the words and deeds of your Christ (whom you call the Messiah), it is clearly evident—they say—that the Mosaic Law does not cease at all. Wherefore, you should not say that it ought to have ceased upon his arrival.

**GALATINO.** Indeed, they speak the truth when they say that Christ fulfilled the entire Old Law. 

<margin>The response.</margin>
<margin>What the Old Law contained.</margin>
However, from this they can in no way infer that it did not cease in those aspects where it was intended to cease. So that it may be known to all how he fulfilled that Law and the Prophets, it must be noted that within the Law and the Prophets, five things were chiefly contained: namely, **Moral** laws, **Judicial** laws, **Ceremonial** laws, **Promises and Threats**, and **Sacramental** matters.

<margin>Moral laws.</margin>
The Moral laws are the ten commandments, without which salvation is impossible for adults. These are found specifically in the twentieth chapter of Exodus, where it is said: **"You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Honor your father and your mother. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor's house. You shall not covet your neighbor's wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor's."** <note>original Hebrew: לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים , על פני לא תשא את שם יהוה אלהיך לשוא : זכור את יום השבת לקדשו : כבד את אביך ואת אמך : לא תרצח : לא תנאף : לא תגנב : לא תענה ברעך עד שקר : לא תחמד בית רעך : לא תחמד אשת רעך ועבדו ואמתו ושורו וחמורו וכל אשר לרעך</note> These, however, were not meant to cease upon the arrival of the Messiah, but to be perfected. Therefore, our Savior, the true Messiah—in order to perfect them—prohibited not only the act of murder and other evil deeds, but also the intent of the heart. Saying in Matthew chapter 5: **"You have heard that it was said to the ancients: 'You shall not kill,' and 'Whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.' But I say to you, that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment,"** along with the other things that follow. For that reason, he both observed them himself and led others to observe them. Thus, in Matthew chapter 19, he says: **"If you wish** <insert>to enter into life...</insert>

Galatino responds by dividing the Law into five categories, arguing that the "Moral Law" (the Ten Commandments) was not abolished but "perfected" by Christ.</summary>
