<meta>This page continues the response of Galatino to the objection raised on the previous page regarding whether Jesus's fulfillment of the Law meant the Law should remain in force. Galatino is breaking down the different categories of the Mosaic Law—Judicial, Ceremonial, Promises, and Sacramental—to explain how each was specifically transformed or completed by the Messiah.</meta>

<page-num>674</page-num>
**BOOK ELEVEN**

<margin>Judicial Laws.</margin> ...to enter into life, keep the commandments. <note>This continues the thought from the previous page regarding the Moral Law.</note> The **Judicial Laws**, however, are those about which it is said in Deuteronomy 25: **"An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth,"** and so forth. Because these laws were incomplete, and were carried out with excessive rigor and without mercy, they were to be softened by the sweetness of mercy in the time of the Messiah. For this reason, they have now been perfectly fulfilled, since they are carried out and tempered—especially with mercy—in the court of the Church.

<margin>Ceremonial Laws</margin> The **Ceremonial Laws** were all the sacrifices and the practices surrounding them, such as circumcision, the new moons, the fringes, the phylacteries, <note>The Latin *fimbriae* refers to the ritual fringes or "tzitzit," and *phylacteria* refers to "tefillin" worn during prayer.</note> and many other things of that kind. Since these were figures of the things that were to be done in the Messiah and by the Messiah, they were intended to come to an end upon the arrival of the Messiah himself. Nevertheless, the Messiah Jesus our Lord fulfilled them perfectly: first by observing them literally until the determined time of their cessation; then, through himself and his followers, by bringing them back to their spiritual and mystical meaning.

<margin>The Promises.</margin> The **Promises** were the coming of the Messiah, the promised land, the conversion of the nations, the forgiveness of sins, and eternal salvation. These our Savior also perfectly fulfilled by taking on flesh from a Virgin, being born, performing miracles possible only for God by his own power, suffering, dying, rising again, ascending to heaven in the sight of many, and by promising far better things than the Old Law promised. Indeed, that Law promised its practitioners only temporal and earthly goods, which nevertheless symbolized spiritual and eternal ones. But our Savior and Messiah promised his worshippers the spiritual and eternal things that the Law prefigured. For he said in Matthew 19: **"Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name's sake, will receive a hundredfold, and will possess eternal life."** And again in Luke 6: **"Blessed are you poor,"** he says, **"for yours is the Kingdom of God."** For this reason, as it says in Matthew 4: **"Jesus began to preach and to say: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."**

<margin>Sacramental Signs</margin> Finally, the **Sacramental Signs** were the Passover lamb, the red heifer, <note>The "red heifer" refers to the ritual in Numbers 19 used for purification.</note> and others of this kind. These were the figure and shadow of the passion of Christ. Therefore, upon the arrival of the one whom they represented, they had to cease entirely. Christ himself fulfilled these by suffering and dying. The Evangelist <note>The "Evangelist" here refers to John (John 19:36).</note> testified to this when he said: **"These things were done so that the scripture might be fulfilled, which says: You shall not break a bone of him."** From these points, therefore, it is clear how and why Christ fulfilled the Law and the Prophets. He fulfilled the Prophets (as Chrysostom says) <note>Referring to St. John Chrysostom, an influential early Church Father and preacher.</note> by completing everything they had predicted about him. And he fulfilled the Law: first by transgressing nothing of the legal requirements, and finally by justifying through faith, which the Law itself was unable to do through the "letter." <note>A reference to the theological distinction between the "letter" of the law and the "spirit" of faith.</note> For this reason he said: **"I have not come to abolish the law, or the prophets, but to fulfill them."** From these things it is also clearly shown that although Christ fulfilled the Old Law in the manner we have described, it does not follow that the Law did not cease—in those aspects meant to cease at his coming—once he had arrived.

<summary>Galatino categorizes the Old Law into four types—Judicial, Ceremonial, Promises, and Sacramental—explaining how Christ fulfilled each by transforming their literal or temporal requirements into spiritual and eternal realities.</summary>

## Refutation of Jewish arguments. And that the Mosaic law was changeable. Chapter III.

### CAPNIO

<margin>Arguments of the more recent Jews.</margin>
<margin>First argument.</margin>
The more recent Jews, attempting to prove the stability of their law, put forward several arguments against us which you ought to resolve. This is so that their unbelief <note>original: *perfidia*; in this context, it refers to the Jewish rejection of the Christian claim that the Law has changed.</note> may be more forcefully exposed, and the truth of the Catholic faith may shine more clearly. Thus, they argue first in this way: As long as the cause of an effect remains, that effect also endures. However, the cause of the Law always remains; therefore, the entire Law shall always endure. That the cause of the Law always remains, they prove thus: The final cause <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or goal for which something exists</term> of the entire Law is the intention of leading men back to their own perfection. This intention always remains. Therefore, the entire Law will also always remain.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
Next, they argue thus: The perfection of any power is its own proper act. Of the powers of man, some are bodily and others are intellectual. Therefore, human perfection consists in both bodily and intellectual acts. The Law, being ordained toward human perfection, necessarily leads men back to these two things. From this it follows that whatever the Law intends is directed toward either the ornament of the body or the soul. But the body is truly adorned by morals, and the soul by the intellect. The literal and **tropological** <term>tropological: the moral or ethical interpretation of a text</term> interpretation of the Law demonstrates the former, while the **allegorical** and **anagogical** <term>anagogical: the spiritual or "heavenly" interpretation that points toward the afterlife</term> understanding suggests the latter. Since, therefore, in this life man always stands in need of both the ordering of morals and the understanding of the intellect, the Law, which administers all these things, must necessarily endure forever.

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
Finally, they argue thus: While the *thing figured* <note>original: *figuratum*; the reality or person symbolized by a ritual or sign.</note> stands, the *figure* <note>original: *figura*; the symbol or ritual itself.</note> stands. This is proved because, since the object of faith is uncreated truth (for nothing corruptible is the perfection of an incorruptible power, such as the intellectual soul), if anything regarding the foundations of faith was created in "figures," it is believable for this reason: because it is led back to uncreated truth as matter is to form. Therefore, while the thing figured stands, the figure stands. But the thing figured is eternal, because it is eternal truth. Therefore, the figure is also eternal. Wherefore, it follows that the Mosaic Law itself, which is full of figures, is eternal. From these points, they conclude that the Old Law is always stable, even regarding its ceremonial matters.

<margin>Refutation of the Jewish conclusion.</margin>
GAL. Certainly these arguments are quite frivolous, and like the chaff of falsehood, they are to be burned by the fire of truth. But first, I will show that their conclusion is entirely false. Then, I will respond to the arguments themselves. The conclusion by which they assert the ancient Law is always obligatory in the same rite is refuted by this reason: Whatever is received by something changeable can also be changed. This is proved by the fact that everything capable of receiving is received according to the manner of the recipient. This can be judged in individual cases and in the powers of our own soul. But the Old Law is of this kind, because it is received by man, whose nature is driven by constant change; therefore, the Law itself can also be changed.

# BOOK ELEVEN

Just as a father educates his son through different laws as he grows from an infant to a boy, then to an adolescent and a young man, so too is a human congregation led by one law when it is wise and just, and by another when it is unwise. The Jewish people, redeemed from Egyptian slavery through Moses, were unwise and wicked. The Mosaic scripture itself testifies to this many times. For this reason, many ceremonial precepts of the Law <note>original: "plurima legis præcepta cæremonialia"</note> were required more by the dullness of that people and their wicked habit of idolatry than by any perfection in them—as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204).</note> testifies in the third treatise of his book called *The Guide* <note>original: "More"; referring to the *Moreh Nevukhim* or *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>. This follows the saying of the Psalmist: *With bit and bridle bind the jaws of those who do not come near to you.* <note>Psalm 32:9.</note> Therefore, because the dullness and wicked habits of the recipient have changed—just as the age of infancy passes—it happened that the thing received, namely the Law, also changed. The Law, therefore, does not always bind with the same ritual. 

This is confirmed both by the testimony of the Law itself and by that of the ancient Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>. For the Law itself did not bind one to its observation (except for the Decalogue <term>Decalogue: The Ten Commandments</term>) except in the Promised Land, specifically while the Temple stood and the scepter of the Jews remained. Outside the Promised Land itself, it barely bound them at all. The literal text clearly shows this, saying in Deuteronomy chapter 4: *See, I have taught you ceremonies and judgments, just as the Lord my God commanded me, so that you should do them in the midst of the land which you are entering to possess.* <note>original Hebrew: "ראה למדתי אתכם חקים ומשפטים כאשר ציוני יהוה אלהי לעשות כן בקרב הארץ אשר אתם באים שמה לרשתה"</note> And a few lines later it says: *And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, even the ten words, which he wrote upon two tables of stone. And the Lord commanded me at that time to teach you the ceremonies and judgments that you ought to do in the land which you are entering to possess.* <note>original Hebrew: "ויגד לכם את בריתו אשר צוה אתכם לעשות עשרת הדברים ויכתבם על שני לחת אבנים : ואתי צוה יהוה בעת ההוא ללמד אתכם חקים ומשפטים לעשתכם אתם בארץ אשר אתם עברים שמה לרשתה"</note> 

In this passage, two things are especially worth noting. First, he specifically called the Ten Commandments "his covenant," a term more frequently used for the entire Law. This was to make it known that the intention of the whole Law consists in and depends upon these ten precepts. The Jewish Doctors suggest this even more clearly, especially Rabbi Saadia <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942), a prominent Jewish philosopher and exegete.</note> in his book *The Beliefs* <note>original: "Haemunoth"; referring to *Emunot ve-Deot* (The Book of Beliefs and Opinions).</note>. There, he teaches that all the mandates of the Law can be reduced to the ten precepts of the Decalogue. 

Second, it should be noted that he commanded these ten words to be followed simply, without adding any condition of place. This was done to show that they would never cease to be in effect. Since these ten precepts belong to **natural law** <term>natural law: a body of unchanging moral principles regarded as a basis for all human conduct</term> and are our innate participation in the eternal law, they do not vary by place or time. However, when speaking of the other mandates of the Law, he immediately added: *Which you ought to do in the land which you are entering to possess.* From this it is clearly evident that the Jews are not at all bound to them outside the Promised Land. This same sentiment is found in other places, namely in Deuteronomy chapters 5, 6, 11, and 12. Therefore...

# ELEVEN

<margin>The opinion of the Talmudists concerning the mutability of the law.</margin>
It is manifest that the law itself testifies to its own mutability according to the change of place. This same point is also proven through the sayings of the ancient Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>; and although these are many, it shall suffice to bring forward only one for the sake of brevity, namely from the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter that begins, **These are those who are strangled** <note>original: "אלו הנחנקים" (*Ellu ha-nekhnakim*)</note>. There it says: **Rabbi Johanan said: In everything, if a prophet says to you, 'Transgress the words of the Torah,' obey him, except in the case of idolatry.** <note>original: "אמר ר' יוחנן בכל אם יאמר לך הנביא עבור על דברי תורה עבור חוץ מעבודה זרה"</note> Wherefore they finally conclude that if the time requires something of the law to be changed—which they call <term>Horat Sha'ah: A temporary legal ruling</term> <note>original: "הוראת שעה" (*Horath saa*), literally "an instruction for the hour."</note>—a prophet, or even someone lesser than a prophet, provided he is considered wiser than others in his generation, can change it. And if that occasion of time should endure, then that changed part of the law shall also remain so. Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> also clearly shows this same thing in his *Book of Judges*, in the **Laws of Rebels** <note>original: "הלכות ממרים" (*Hilkoth Mamrim*)</note>, chapter 2.

<margin>The opinion of the Kabbalists regarding the giving and the cessation of the old law.</margin>
I am silent here regarding the opinion of the Kabbalists <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism.</note>, who say that the law was given because of the serpent’s venom injected into Adam, and that upon the arrival of the Messiah, this sort of venom will cease. And consequently, the law itself must cease at the arrival of the Messiah. From these points, therefore, the falsehood of the Jews' conclusion regarding the perpetual obligation of legal observance is clearly evident. Now to their arguments. Although the solution to the reasons by which they strive to prove their conclusion can easily be established from what has already been said, let us nevertheless respond to them so that the falsehood of those same reasons may appear more clearly.

<margin>Response to the arguments.</margin>
<margin>To the first.</margin>
When, therefore, they first argue in this way: "As long as the cause remains, so long remains its effect." This is conceded regarding a cause which an effect follows necessarily and of itself; and then the minor premise must be denied—namely, that the cause of the *whole* law always remains, taking the whole for each individual part. For although the chief intention of the law always remains, the same is not true of every little part of the law. For there are many things in the law which are not necessitated by the end <note>The "end" here refers to the ultimate purpose or goal of a law.</note> of themselves and by primary intention, but are either for the removal of hindrances or for the "well-being" of the system. Such are the sacrifices and many of the ceremonies. As Rabbi Moses the Egyptian also shows in the third treatise of the book *The Guide* <note>Maimonides' *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>. and according to the opinion of the Talmudists, such are the things which do not bind one to observance outside the land of promise. This could not happen if those things pertained to human salvation of themselves and by necessity.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
The second reason, which seems more particular to them, proves nothing other than that those things which pertain to knowledge and morals shall remain. And the Catholic truth does not reject this. Rather, it commands all the moral portions of the law to be kept—not because they are of the Mosaic law, but because they are of the eternal law, the inscription of which upon our minds is usually called the **Law of Nature**.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
Finally, when they argue thus: "As long as the reality being symbolized <note>original: "figuratum"</note> stands, the symbol <note>original: "figura"</note> stands. But the reality being symbolized stands forever, because it is eternal truth. Therefore, the symbol also stands forever." That indeed...

Through that which says in the thirty-third chapter of Deuteronomy: "Moses commanded us a law" <note>original: "תורה צוה לנו משה" (*Torah tzivah lanu Mosheh*)</note>. For "Torah" <note>original: "תורה"</note>, that is, the law, works out arithmetically—that is, it is written with such letters—to equal six hundred and eleven. <note>This is the practice of Gematria, where letters have numerical values.</note> For *Tau* [ת] signifies four hundred, and *Vau* [ו] six, *Resh* [ר] two hundred, and *He* [ה] five. But two others are found in the twentieth chapter of Exodus, where it is said: "There shall not be for you another God before my faces" (or "in my presence"). "Do not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness," and so forth. These two commandments we heard from the mouth of Truth, that is, of God. <note>The 611 from the word "Torah" plus the 2 commandments heard directly from God equal 613.</note> All of which together are six hundred and thirteen. But then David came and established those six hundred and thirteen commandments upon eleven. As it is said in Psalm 15: "A Psalm of David. Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? And who shall stay on your holy mountain? He who walks perfectly, and who works justice, and who speaks truth in his heart. And he did not carry [tales] upon his tongue"—that is, he did not slander. "Nor did he do evil to his friend"—that is, his companion—"and he did not bring reproach upon his neighbor." In whose eyes the rejected person is despised. Such was Hezekiah, King of Judah, who...

Namely, that you should perform the judgment of justice, love the piety of mercy, and walk honorably or secretly with your God. For the custom of the Holy and Blessed God is not like the custom of flesh and blood. Indeed, the custom of flesh and blood is that if a man shames his neighbor before many people, and afterwards comes to appease him, the neighbor says to him: "I will not be appeased by you until those people come before whom you shamed me." But God does not want a man to repent except between himself and Him alone. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon.

# BOOK [ELEVEN]

...it is written in the 2nd chapter of the same prophet: **And the righteous shall live by his faith** <note>original: "וצדיק באמונתו יחיה" (*ve-tzaddik be-emunato yikhyeh*), from Habakkuk 2:4.</note>. This means: And the just shall live by his faith. All of this is the aforementioned tradition, with the exception of the glosses of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note>. He also says at the beginning of the same tradition: "At all times, the generations have made a reduction of the commandments, making them fewer. For in the beginning there were righteous men who were powerful enough to take up the yoke of many commandments. But in the generations of those who came later, there were no longer such righteous men. Therefore, if they had come to observe all those commandments, there would have been no one who could have been justified." Thus says Rabbi Solomon. Furthermore, in the same book and place, it is read word for word as follows: **Rabbi Jose** said, "Moses established four decrees over Israel. Then four prophets came and abolished them." 

For Moses said in the 33rd chapter of Deuteronomy: **And Israel shall dwell in safety, alone, the fountain of Jacob** <note>original: "וישכן ישראל בטח בדד עין יעקב" (*Va-yishkon Yisrael betach badad ein Ya'akov*). The Latin translator renders "ein" (fountain/source) as "oculus" (eye).</note>. This means: And Israel shall dwell confidently, only the eye of Jacob. Regarding this, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "When (he asks) shall Israel dwell confidently? When they are like the 'eye' of Jacob, that is, entirely such as Jacob was." However, **Amos** came and annulled that. Just as it is said in the 7th chapter of Amos: **Lord God, be merciful, I pray; who shall stand like Jacob?** <note>original: "אדני יהוה סלח נא מי יקום יעקב" (*Adonai Elohim selach na mi yakum Ya'akov*), from Amos 7:2.</note> This means: Lord God, be favorable, I pray; who shall stand as Jacob? Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "Who could be holy, like Jacob?" Is this not enough? Because it is also written in the same place: **The Lord relented concerning this; it shall not be, said the Lord** <note>original: "נחם יהוה על זאת גם היא לא תהיה אמר יהוה" (*Nicham Adonai al zot gam hi lo tihyeh amar Adonai*), from Amos 7:3.</note>. That is: God took pity, or God repented concerning this. "Even this shall not be," said God. 

Moses also said in the twenty-eighth chapter of Deuteronomy <note>The Latin text says "trigesimo octavo" (38th), but Deuteronomy only has 34 chapters; the reference is to Deut 28:65.</note>: **And among those nations you shall find no rest** <note>original: "ובגוים ההם לא תרגיע" (*U-va-goyim ha-hem lo targia*).</note>. This means: And in those nations you will not rest. However, **Jeremiah** came and abolished that, as it is said in the thirty-first chapter of Jeremiah: **Israel went to its rest** <note>original: "הלוך להרגיעו ישראל" (*Halokh le-hargio Yisrael*), from Jeremiah 31:2.</note>. This means: Israel shall go to its rest. 

Moses also said in the chapter of Exodus <note>The text cites chapter 9, but refers to the "Fourteen Attributes" or the Decalogue found in chapters 20 and 34.</note>: **Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children** <note>original: "פקד עון אבות על בנים" (*Poked avon avot al banim*).</note>, and so on. This means: Visiting the sin of the fathers upon the sons, etc. However, **Ezekiel** came and abolished that: as it is said in the eighteenth chapter of Ezekiel: **The soul that sins, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son** <note>original: "הנפש החוטאת היא תמות בן לא ישא בעון האב ואב לא ישא בעון הבן" (*Ha-nefesh ha-chotet hi tamut ben lo yissa ba-avon ha-av ve-av lo yissa ba-avon ha-ben*), from Ezekiel 18:20.</note>. That is: The soul that has sinned, the same shall die: the son will not carry the sin of the father, and the father will not carry the sin of the son. 

Furthermore, Moses said in the twenty-sixth chapter of Leviticus: **And you shall perish among the nations** <note>original: "ואבדתם בגוים" (*Va-avadtem ba-goyim*), from Leviticus 26:38.</note>. This means: And you shall be lost among the nations. However, **Isaiah** came and abolished that, just as it is said in the twenty-seventh chapter of the same prophet: **And it shall come to pass in that day, that a great trumpet shall be blown, and those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out in the land of Egypt shall come and worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem** <note>original: "והיה ביום ההוא יתקע בשופר גדול ובאו האובדים בארץ אשור והנדחים בארץ מצרים והשתחוו ליהוה בהר הקדש בירושלם" (*Ve-haya ba-yom ha-hu yitaka be-shofar gadol u-vau ha-ovedim be-eretz Ashur ve-ha-nidachim be-eretz Mitzrayim ve-hishtachavu l'Adonai be-har ha-kodesh bi-Yerushalayim*), from Isaiah 27:13.</note>. That is: And it shall be on that day, a great trumpet shall sound, and the lost in the land of Assyria shall come, and those driven out in the land of Egypt, and they shall adore God on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

Thus far the tradition. To which must be added what is read in the **Midrash Bamidbar Sinai** <term>Midrash: an ancient rabbinic method of interpreting and explaining biblical texts, often through stories or legal analysis</term> <note>original: "במדבר סיני", meaning 'In the desert of Sinai', referring to a commentary on the Book of Numbers.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Numbers, where that which was said in the twenty-second [chapter] of Numbers is explained: **And now, if it is evil in your eyes, I will return** <note>original: "ועתה אם רע בעיניך אשובה לי" (*Ve-atah im ra be-einekha ashuvah li*), the words of Balaam to the Angel of the Lord in Numbers 22:34.</note>. This means: And now if it is bad in your eyes, I will return for myself. He said to him,

Balaam <note>The non-Israelite prophet from the Book of Numbers.</note> said to the angel: "I did not go until the Holy and Blessed God said to me: 'Rise and go with them.' And yet you tell me to return?" The angel said to him: "For such is his office, or his method." Did he not also say to Abraham in the twenty-second chapter of Genesis that he should sacrifice his son? And yet after this it is written in the same place: "And the angel of the Lord called to him and said: Do not stretch out your hand over your son." In this, it is taught that a thing or a word which He Himself has spoken, He sometimes revokes through His angel according to His will. Finally, to the preceding points must be added what is written in the book of the **Sanhedrin** <note>The Talmudic tractate dealing with the high court and legal procedures.</note>, in the chapter **These are the ones who are strangled** <note>original: "אלו הן הנחנקים" (*Ellu hen hannehenakim*), the eleventh chapter of Tractate Sanhedrin.</note>: "There is more or greater weight in the words of the scribes <note>original: "Sophrim"</note> (that is, the sages) than in the words of the Law." That is, the words of the masters possess greater authority than the Law itself. For he who says "There are no **phylacteries**" <note>original: "תפילין" (*tephillin*); small leather boxes containing Torah verses worn during prayer.</note>, thus transgressing the words of the Law, is **exempt** <note>original: "פטור" (*Patur*); not legally liable for punishment.</note>. But he who says there are five **frontlets** <note>original: "טוטפת" (*totaphoth*); another term for phylacteries.</note> (regarding which mention is made in the sixth chapter of Deuteronomy), by adding to the words of the **Scribes** <note>original: "Sophrim"</note>, he is guilty. Likewise in the **Midrash** <note>A genre of rabbinic commentary and storytelling.</note> on **These are the words** <note>original: "אלה הדברים" (*Elle haddebarim*), the Hebrew name for the book of Deuteronomy.</note>, that is, in the exposition of Deuteronomy upon that word: *You shall not deviate or turn aside from the word which they declare to you, to the right or to the left.* It is said: "Even if they show your eyes that the right is the left and the left is the right: believe them, or obey them."

<margin>GAL. Regarding what these phylacteries were.</margin>
HOG. What were these phylacteries? In the sixth chapter of Deuteronomy, it is read written thus: **And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes** <note>original: "וקשרתם לאות על ידך והיו לטטפת בין עיניך" (*U-keshartam le-ot al yadecha ve-hayu le-totaphot bein einecha*), from Deuteronomy 6:8.</note>. This means: And you shall bind those commandments as a sign upon your hands, and they shall be as **frontlets** <note>original: "totaphoth"</note>, that is, in phylacteries between your eyes. You should know, therefore, that "phylactery" is a Greek name, and it is said (as it pleases some) to come from the Greek word *phylassein* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ φυλάξειν"</note>, which is "to preserve," and the Hebrew **Torah**, which signifies "Law." From this, "phylactery" is as if it were a "preservatory of the Law." This, however, pleases me very little, since the Greek and Hebrew languages can by no means be so mixed. Therefore, I say this word is entirely Greek, and in Greek is called *phylakterion*. For they made four such "preservatories" in which the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> was placed. They would bind one on the head, where the brain of small children pulsates <note>The fontanelle or "soft spot" on an infant's head.</note>. These are called **tephillin** in the Talmud, but in Deuteronomy they are called **totaphoth**.

<margin>Conclusion of the aforementioned things.</margin>
From all these things, therefore, it clearly appears that the Mosaic Law was not only mutable, but indeed has frequently been changed. Therefore, reducing all the preceding points into a rational order, let us finally conclude: Since all things which a prophet—or even some other sage lesser than a prophet—has said should be transgressed (idolatry excepted), they must be transgressed. This has been proven through the Talmud in the preceding chapter. For this reason, David reduced the six hundred and thirteen precepts of the Law to eleven. And after him, Isaiah reduced them to six.

### Chapter V.

### CAPNIO, <note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), the famous Christian Hebraist, who used the name 'Capnio'—a Greek-inspired pun on his German name 'Rauch' (smoke)—as his persona in this dialogue.</note>

<margin>*Objections of the later Jews. The first objection regarding the law.*</margin>
**F**rom these things, the more recent Jews, inflamed with greater anger and hatred, bring forth against us testimonies of the law which seem to show the permanence of the legal ceremonies. First, they bring into the discussion that which is written in the twenty-ninth chapter of Deuteronomy: **The secret things belong to the Lord our God, and the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ha-nistarot l’Adonai Eloheinu ve-ha-niglot lanu u-le-vaneinu ad olam la’asot et kol divrei ha-torah ha-zot*</note> That is, the hidden is attributed to our God, and the things that are manifest are granted to us and our children even unto eternity, so that we may perform all the requirements of this law. From this, they infer that the entire law is to remain for eternity. Next, regarding circumcision, they bring forward what was said in the seventeenth chapter of Genesis: <margin>*The second objection regarding circumcision.*</margin> **And my covenant shall be in your flesh for an eternal covenant. And the uncircumcised male who does not circumcise the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall surely be cut off from his people.** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-hayeta veriti bi-vesarkhem li-verit olam; ve-arel zakhar asher lo yimol et besar orlato ve-nikhreta ha-nefesh ha-hi me-ameiha*</note> That is, My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting bond. And the uncircumcised male who has not circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, his soul shall certainly be cut off from his people. Regarding the Sabbath, they object to us with that which is written in the thirty-first chapter of Exodus in this manner: <margin>*The third objection regarding the Sabbath.*</margin> **And the children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, to observe the Sabbath throughout their generations as an eternal covenant; it is a sign between me and the children of Israel forever. Because in six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-shamru venei yisrael et ha-shabbat la’asot et ha-shabbat le-dorotam berit olam; beini u-vein venei yisrael ot hi le-olam ki sheshet yamim asah Adonai et ha-shamayim ve-et ha-aretz u-va-yom ha-shevi’i shavat va-yinafash*</note> That is, the children of Israel shall guard the Sabbath, to perform the Sabbath in their generations as an everlasting pact; it is a sign forever between me and the children of Israel. For in six days God made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and took breath. Furthermore, regarding the feast of Passover, they oppose us with what is written in the twelfth chapter of Exodus: <margin>*The fourth objection regarding the feast of Passover.*</margin> **And this day shall be for a memorial to you, and you shall solemnize it as a feast to the Lord throughout your generations; you shall celebrate it by an eternal law.** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-hayah ha-yom ha-zeh lakhem le-zikaron ve-hagotem oto hag l’Adonai le-dorotekhem hukat olam tehagehu*</note> That is, this day shall be a memorial for you, and you shall celebrate it as a solemnity to the Lord in your generations by an eternal law. Again, in the same place,

<margin>
Regarding the fifth objection concerning other ceremonial matters.

"And you shall observe this thing for a statute for you and your sons forever." <note>original: "ושימרתם את הדבר הזה לחק לך ולבניך עד עולם" (Exodus 12:24)</note> **This means: And keep this matter as a law, or as a precept for you, and for your sons forever.** Regarding the offering of the first fruits of the crops, the solemnity of Pentecost, the offerings and other sacrifices, and the Day of Atonement <note>The text mentions *in casulis* (in booths/little houses), likely referring to the Feast of Tabernacles which follows shortly after the Day of Atonement in the same month.</note>, as well as the "bread of proposition" (which they more correctly call "bread of faces" <note>original: *panibus facierum*. In Hebrew, *Lechem HaPanim*, usually translated as Showbread or Bread of the Presence.</note>), they bring against us that which is contained in the twenty-third chapter of Leviticus. Where it is said concerning that dwelling in booths: "You shall do no work; it shall be a perpetual law for your generations in all your dwellings." <note>original: "כל מלאכה לא תעשו חקת עולם לדורותיכם בכל מושבותיכם" (Leviticus 23:31)</note> **That is: You shall not do any work. It shall be an eternal law or precept for your generations in all your dwellings.** And again in the twenty-fourth chapter: "On the Sabbath day they shall be prepared before God continually by the children of Israel as an eternal covenant." <note>original: "ביום חשבת יערכנו לפני יהוח תמיד מאת בני ישראל ברית עולם" (Leviticus 24:8)</note> **This means: On the Sabbath day they shall be prepared before God continually by the sons of Israel as an eternal covenant.** Regarding what was said of the bread of faces (that is, of proposition), by these and similar points our most persistent Jewish opponents of this time strive to prove that the Mosaic Law, in regards to the ceremonies, was by no means intended to cease, but was to endure forever. Therefore, it is necessary for you to refute these things as best you can. GALATINUS.

<margin>
Refutation of the aforementioned objections.
</margin>
I shall do that most gladly. Regarding that from which they first conclude that the mandates of the law are to be kept forever: if they refer to the moral precepts, they indeed speak the truth. For whatever pertains to morals remains forever, and must always be observed. And in this way, the Catholic truth (as was said above) commands that the moral aspects of the law be kept, not because they are precepts of the Mosaic law, but because they are of the eternal law. However, if their argument is applied to the ceremonies, I say that then "eternal" or "everlasting" is understood to mean "perpetual," or for an "age" <note>original: *seculo*. In this context, it refers to a long but finite period or an era.</note>. For wherever we have "eternal" or "everlasting" in our edition in these places, the Hebrew text has **olam** <note>original: "עולם"</note>, which is understood there to mean "perpetual" or for an "age."

<margin>
What the Hebrew word *Olam* signifies.
</margin>
If, therefore, **olam** is understood in these same places as "perpetual," then *olam* is the same as "continuous," and something that lasts for the "age" or duration of a certain thing without interruption. For "perpetual" is properly the same as "continuous." According to that line of Ovid: *"Bring down a perpetual song to my times."* <note>A quote from the opening of Ovid's *Metamorphoses*: "ad mea perpetuum deducite tempora carmen."</note> From this we speak of a "perpetual oration," which is continuous and without interruption. Hence a "perpetual Consul," a "perpetual Censor," or a "perpetual Emperor" is so named because he remained as Censor, Consul, or Emperor always and continually as long as he lived. Yet when he died, another was substituted. In this way circumcision, and so also the other ceremonies, were given to the Jews to be kept as a covenant *olam*—that is, perpetual—meaning: always and continually, for as long as they were meant to be kept, and no further. If, however, *olam* is understood as an "age," then *olam* does not imply eternity, but a determined time. To prove this, I shall first bring forward what was said of Samuel by his mother Hannah, in the first [chapter] of the first book of Kings... <note>In the Vulgate, the books of Samuel are called 1 and 2 Kings. The text here refers to 1 Samuel 1:22, where Hannah says Samuel will appear before the Lord and stay there "forever" (*olam*), which meant for his lifetime.</note>

In the first chapter <note>1 Samuel 1:22</note> it is spoken thus: **"And I will bring him, and he shall appear before the face of the Lord, and he shall dwell there forever."** <note>original Hebrew: והביאתיו ונראה את פני יהוה וישב שם עד עולם</note> That is: "And I will bring him, and he shall appear in the sight of God, and he shall remain there *leolam*," which means "for an age." Regarding this, the commentary of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), the famous commentator known as Rashi.</note> says: "that is, until the age of the Levites." This is just as it is said in the eighth chapter of Numbers: **"And from the age of fifty years, the business of serving shall cease, and he shall serve no more."** <note>original Hebrew: ומבן חמשים שנה ישוב מצבא העבודה ולא יעבד עוד</note> This means: "And from a son of fifty years, the work of serving shall cease, and he shall not serve further." And thus all the days of Samuel were fifty-two years. <note>The author uses this to show that Samuel's "forever" in the Temple actually had a numerical limit.</note>

Next, it is particularly noteworthy that in the Midrash **"These are the words"** <note>original: אלה הדברים (*Elle hadebarim*). This refers to *Deuteronomy Rabbah*, a collection of homiletic interpretations on the book of Deuteronomy.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the book of Deuteronomy—it is read concerning what is said in the fifteenth chapter of that same book: **"And you shall take an awl and put it through his ear and into the door, and he shall be your servant for an age."** <note>original Hebrew: ולקחת את המרצע ונתת באזנו ובדלת והיה לך עבד עולם</note> This means: "And you shall take an awl, and you shall put it in his ear, and in the door, and he shall be to you a servant *olam*," meaning "of an age." For there, "age" is said to mean all the days of the age of the Master until the Jubilee <note>A special year of release occurring every fifty years in the Hebrew calendar, when slaves were freed and land was returned to its original owners.</note>, even if the servant had been bought thirty or forty years before the Jubilee. Thus far the Midrash, or exposition. From this it is clear that in this place *olam* (an age)—for which our translator <note>The Latin Vulgate translator.</note> used "eternal"—is a single year, or even less, depending on whether the master of that servant might die sooner or later.

Moreover, Rabbi Solomon, in his commentary on those same words, proves it this way: "And he shall be your servant *olam*," that is, for an age. He says: "It is possible for this to be just as the hearing of it shows," which is written in the twenty-fifth chapter of Leviticus: **"And each of you shall return to his possession, and each to his family shall return."** <note>original Hebrew: ושבתם איש אל אחזתו ואיש אל משפחתו תשבו</note> This means: "And you shall return, each man to his own possession, and everyone shall return to his family." Behold, from this you are taught that this *olam* is nothing other than the age of the Jubilee. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon.

This is also confirmed in the book *Kiddushin* <note>term: *Kiddushin* (Sanctifications/Betrothals) — a volume of the Talmud dealing with marriage and the legal status of persons.</note>. When it is said there among other things: "What is that which is written in the twenty-first chapter of Exodus: **'And his master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him forever'**?" <note>original Hebrew: ורצע אדניו את אזנו במרצע ועבדו לעולם</note> This means: "And his Lord shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him *leolam*," that is, for an age. Until which age? Until the age of the Jubilee, or until the death of his master. Just as it is written above: "And he shall serve *him*." Therefore, he shall not serve his master's son. This is the tradition.

The same is also clear through Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval grammarian and commentator (1160–1235).</note>, speaking thus in the book *Serafim* <note>note: This likely refers to *Sefer Hashorashim* (The Book of Roots), Kimhi's Hebrew dictionary.</note>: "It is written in the twenty-first chapter of Exodus: 'And he shall serve him *leolam*,' that is, for an age. It means to say: 'on all days until the Jubilee'." Likewise, that which is written in the twenty-second chapter of Proverbs: **"Do not remove the ancient boundary which your fathers have made."** <note>original Hebrew: אל תסג גבול עולם אשר עשו אבותיך</note> This means: "Do not push back, or do not postpone the boundary *olam*," meaning "of many days," which your fathers made. Likewise in the second chapter of Jeremiah: **"For from long ago I have broken your yoke."** <note>original Hebrew: כי מעולם שברתי עלך</note> That is: "Since *meolam*," meaning "from a long time ago," you have broken your yoke. And in Psalm 119: **"Forever I will not forget your precepts."** <note>original Hebrew: לעולם לא אשכח פקודיך</note> This means: "In an age I will not forget your commands." It means to say *leolam*, or "for an age"—that is, in all the days of my life I will not forget your commands. These are the words of Rabbi Kimhi. From all these things, therefore, it is manifest that this word *olam* signifies neither eternity nor everlastingness, but...

<summary>This page analyzes the Hebrew word "olam" to argue that it often refers to a finite period, such as the time until a Jubilee or a person's lifespan, rather than literal eternity. This philological argument is used to suggest that biblical laws described as "forever" were not necessarily intended to be permanent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological argument from the previous section, where the author demonstrates that the Hebrew word "olam"—frequently translated as "eternal"—often refers to a finite historical period rather than infinite time.</meta>

<page-num>689</page-num>

<header>BOOK ELEVENTH</header>

...but an age, and a determined time, and sometimes a very small one, as has already been shown. From this it is clear that the author of our edition, both the Greek and the Latin <note>This refers to the Septuagint and the Vulgate Bible translations.</note>, as well as any other translators who have rendered this word <term>olam</term> <note>original: עולם (*olam*). Usually meaning "age" or "world," but often translated as "forever."</note> as "eternal" or "everlasting" where the Divine Scripture speaks of circumcision, the Sabbath, the priestly garments, or other ceremonies, have interpreted it far differently than the truth of the matter holds. Because of this, several people have fallen into the Jewish error and been irrevocably led away from the Christian faith, as it happened that they heard or read of an "eternal covenant" or an "everlasting statute" regarding circumcision and other ceremonies.

But what "eternal" or "everlasting" truly means among the Hebrews, Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, a preeminent medieval Jewish grammarian and exegete.</note> declares most excellently in his *Book of Roots* <note>original: *Seraffim*, an OCR error for *Shorashim* (the Hebrew word for "roots"). This refers to Kimhi’s famous Hebrew dictionary and grammar.</note>, when he says: It is written in Psalm 84, **"They will praise you *selah*."** <note>original Hebrew: יהללוך סלה</note> That is: "They will praise you forever." For they explained this word <term>selah</term> <note>original: סלה (*selah*)</note> as <term>had</term> <note>original: עד (*ad*), meaning "until" or "forever."</note>, which is to say, "unto eternity." 

So also in the words of our Masters, the tradition from the house of Rabbi Elazar is that every place in which the words <term>Nezah</term> <note>original: נצח (*netzach*), meaning "endurance" or "eternity."</note>, <term>Sela</term>, or <term>Vahed</term> <note>original: ועד (*va'ed*), meaning "and ever."</note> are placed, there is no interruption, but it signifies "for an age" and "for ages of ages." For *Nezah* is as it is written in Isaiah chapter 57: **"And I will not be angry unto *Nezah*."** <note>original Hebrew: ולא לנצח אקציף</note> This is: "And I will not be angry unto eternity," or "I will not foam with rage forever." 

Truly *Sela* is as it is written in Psalm 48: **"He will establish her even unto the age, *selah*."** <note>original Hebrew: יכוננה עד עולם סלה</note> This is: "He will rectify, or compose, or ordain her even unto the age *selah*," which means "unto the everlasting age," or "always." 

And *Vaed* is as it is written in Exodus 15: **"The Lord shall reign for an age and *vaed*."** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה ימלוך לעולם ועד</note> This is: "God shall reign for the age *vaed*," that is, "into eternity" or "everlasting." 

Thus says Rabbi Kimhi. Since, therefore, none of these specific words are placed in the Law where mention is made of circumcision, the Sabbath, sacrifices, and other ceremonies—but only <term>olam</term>, as has been seen—it is openly and beyond doubt manifest that those ceremonies were not to be kept literally for eternity, but for a determined time, namely up until the coming of the Messiah. Especially since, while they were "not good" according to the letter, they were meant to be kept only spiritually in the days of the Messiah.

### That all ceremonial precepts of the old law were "not good," 
### yet not evil. Chapter VI.

## CAPNIO,

<note>Capnio is the scholarly Greek nickname for Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

Since the ceremonial mandates of the Mosaic law were given by God, I wonder that you have called them "not good."

**GAL.** <note>Galatinus (Pietro Colonna Galatino, c. 1460–1540), the author of the work, defending his theological positions.</note> I called the Jewish ceremonies "precepts that are not good" for this reason: because God himself called them so, when in Ezekiel chapter 20 he spoke thus: **"I gave them statutes that were not good, and judgments in which they would not live. And I polluted them in their own gifts, in the passing over of everything that opens the womb, so that I might destroy them, so that they might know that I am the Lord."** <note>original Hebrew: אני נתתי להם חקים לא טובים ומשפטים לא יחיו בהם : ואטמא אותם במתנותם בהעביר כל פטר רחם למען אשימם למען אשר ידעו אשר אני יהוה</note> That is: "I gave them precepts that were not good, and judgments in which they shall not live. And I polluted them in their offerings, in the transferring or passing over of everything opening the womb, because of their sins, or so that..."

...that I might desolate them. So that they might know that I am God. Here the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), known as Rashi, the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> explains that word **so that I might desolate them** <note>original Hebrew: למען אשימם (*Lemaan ashimem*)</note>, that is, so that I might desolate and destroy them. For **I will desolate them** <note>original Hebrew: אשימם (*Ashimem*)</note> is a word of desolation, meaning "signifying desolation." Therefore, anyone who explained this through a word for "sin," saying "on account of their sins," is in error. For the letter *Aleph* which is found there is not from the root of the word. "So that they may know," or "so that they might know, that I am God." That is, when I shall have brought evils upon them. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. If, therefore, God Himself called the ceremonial precepts which He gave to the Jews "not good," it should not seem a wonder to you, nor to anyone else, if I have also called them such.

<term>CAPITO</term> <note>An interlocutor in the dialogue, likely representing a student or a specific historical figure like Wolfgang Capito.</note>: For what reason, then, were they called "not good"?

<term>GALATINUS</term> <note>The author, Pietro Galatino, speaking as the authority in the dialogue.</note>: Because through them men were not justified. For they were shadows, prefiguring the grace by which we are now justified. Yet they are not to be called "evil," since they were commanded by God and were appropriate for the time and the persons. And for that reason, perhaps, God did not call them "evil," but only "not good"—that is, not of such a kind that men would become good and righteous through them. For this reason, Abraham and all the other fathers were held liable and guilty before God, to the point that, despite sacrifices and other ceremonies, they descended into hell <note>Refers to the *Limbus Patrum* (Limbo of the Fathers), where the righteous of the Old Testament were said to wait until Christ's resurrection.</note>, as we have proved sufficiently and abundantly in the preceding sections.

Hence, not without reason, Isaiah said in the 40th chapter: **And Lebanon is not enough to burn, nor its beasts enough for a burnt offering.** <note>original Hebrew: וללבנון אין די בער וחיותו אין די עולה</note> Which the gloss of Rabbi Solomon explains thus: that is, it is not enough to satisfy for the sins of the nations. Moreover, "Lebanon" is understood as nothing other than the Temple, as is clearly evident in the <term>Midrash</term> <note>A genre of rabbinic literature containing interpretations or expansions of Biblical texts.</note> on the **Song of Songs** <note>original Hebrew: שיר השירים (*Shir ha-Shirim*)</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Canticle of Canticles. Where it is said, concerning that passage in the 7th chapter of the same book: **Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.** <note>original Hebrew: אפך כמגדל הלבנון</note> This means the House of the Sanctuary. For just as this nose is placed at the height of a man, so the House of the Lord—that is, the Temple—was placed at the height of the world. When, therefore, it is said, "Like the tower of Lebanon," Lebanon means nothing other than the House of the Sanctuary. Just as it is said in Deuteronomy, chapter 3: **This good mountain and Lebanon.** <note>original Hebrew: ההר הטוב הזה והלבנון</note> This is the tradition.

Therefore Lebanon—that is, the Temple—just as it was not sufficient with all its burnt offerings and sacrifices to satisfy for the sins of the nations according to Rabbi Solomon’s exposition, so it was not enough to satisfy for the sins of the Jews. Since all men, both the good and the bad, even if in different ways, descended into hell. This is also excellently proved by what is written in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarshan <note>An 11th-century preacher and commentator from Narbonne known for using aggadic (narrative) traditions.</note>, when it says concerning the 27th chapter of that book: **And it came to pass when Isaac was old.** <note>original Hebrew: ויהי כי זקן יצחק</note> It is read there: Rabbi Nahmia said, "Tribulations are more beloved by God than sacrifices. For sacrifices come from a man's wealth, but tribulations come from his very body." As it is said in the second chapter of Job: **Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul.** <note>original Hebrew: עור בעד עור וכל אשר לאיש יתן בעד נפשו</note>

### *That circumcision in the time of the Messiah was to be observed not carnally, but spiritually. Chapter VII.*

->**CAPNIO**<- <note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous humanist and Hebraist, who appears here as a character in the dialogue.</note>

<margin>GALATIANS</margin>
**S**o that the obstinacy <note>original: "perfidia," often used in a polemical sense to mean "unbelief" or "lack of faith" regarding the Jewish rejection of Christian claims.</note> of the Jews may be more and more refuted, it must now be proven through their own scriptures that in the days of their Messiah, their ceremonies were to be observed spiritually. In the *Midrash* <note>An ancient commentary on Hebrew scripture.</note> on *Shir ha-Shirim*, that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs, regarding the statement in the second chapter of that same book: <note>original Hebrew: ענה דודי ואמר לי</note> That is, "My beloved answered and said to me." ...and with the house of Judah a new covenant, that is, a new law. Thus far the tradition.

From which it clearly follows that just as there are four foreskins, so there are also

four types of circumcisions. Three of these—namely of the ear, of the mouth, and of the heart—are spiritual, and are always necessary for everyone. The fourth type, however, because it is bodily and is a shadow or figure <note>A "shadow" (umbra) or "figure" (figura) is a common theological term for an Old Testament practice that prefigures a New Testament reality.</note> of the others, has become not only useless since the coming of our Messiah (the Master of spiritual precepts), but indeed is exceedingly perilous for all who perform it. For it is a sign not of the faithful, as it once was, but of the unfaithful, and of those whom God has rejected.

is interpreted. Wherefore, it signified not only the rest of the Messiah in the sepulcher on the seventh day, but also that seventh rest which those who have spiritually kept the Sabbath—abstaining from every vice and sin—will have in the seventh age of the world after the general resurrection.

<margin>How the Sabbath is interpreted and what it prefigured.</margin>
Regarding this everlasting Sabbath, it is found in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Psalms.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that verse of Psalm 89 <note>Psalm 90:15 in modern numbering.</note>: <term>Make us glad according to the days you have afflicted us</term> <note>original Hebrew: שמחנו כימות עניתני (*Samcheinu ki-mot innitanu*)</note>. That is, "Make us joyful for the days, or according to the days, in which you have afflicted us." For so it is said there: *According to the days in which you have afflicted us:* namely, by Babylon, by Greece, and by the Romans, and in the days of the Messiah. And how many are the days of the Messiah? Rabbi Joshua <note>Rabbi Joshua ben Levi, a prominent 3rd-century scholar.</note> said: They are two thousand years. Just as it is said here, "According to the days you have humbled us," that is, according to two days. For one day of the Holy and Blessed God is a thousand years, according to what is said in the same Psalm: <term>For a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday</term> <note>original Hebrew: כי אלף שנים בעיניך כיום אתמול (*Ki elef shanim be-einecha ke-yom etmol*). Psalm 90:4.</note>. That is, "Because a thousand years in your eyes are as the day of yesterday." The Masters also said: According to the future, the day of the Messiah will be one. For the Holy and Blessed God in the future will make for him one day, of which it is said in Zechariah, chapter 14: <term>And it shall be one day, and it is known to the Lord; not day nor night. and it shall be, at the time of evening there shall be light</term> <note>original Hebrew: והיה יום־אחד הוא יודע ליהוה לא־יום ולא־לילה והיה לעת־ערב יהיה־אור (*Ve-hayah yom-echad hu yivvada l’Adonai, lo-yom ve-lo-laylah; ve-hayah l’et-erev yihyeh-or*). Zechariah 14:7.</note>. This day is the <term>world to come</term> <note>The "Olam Ha-Ba," referring to the messianic age or the afterlife.</note> and the bringing of the dead to life. And this is the light which the Holy and Blessed God reserved for the righteous at the beginning of the world—namely, that of which it is said in Genesis 1: *And he saw the light itself, that it was good.* And again it is said of it in Psalm 36: *Because with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light.* Furthermore, Isaiah says in the last chapter: <term>And it shall be from month to month, and from Sabbath to Sabbath</term> <note>original Hebrew: והיה מדי־חדש בחדשו ומדי שבת בשבתו (*Ve-hayah middei-chodesh be-chodsho u-middei shabbat be-shabbato*). Isaiah 66:23.</note>. That is, "And their seed shall be from the sufficiency of the month in its month, and from the sufficiency of the Sabbath in its Sabbath." That Sabbath is the world to come, which is entirely Sabbath—that is, rest. Thus far the tradition. From which the proposition is clear. 

But for the understanding of the words of Isaiah, which this tradition very appropriately brings forward at the end, it must be noted: That "month" in Hebrew is called <term>hodes</term> <note>original Hebrew: חדש (*chodesh*)</note>, and it is used among them for the perfection of all days in which the moon completes its course. For the Jews calculate times by the moon and not by the sun. Therefore, "month" is used for *perfection*, but "Sabbath" for *rest*. Thus, according to the aforementioned tradition, these words of Isaiah are to be explained: *And their seed shall be*—that is, the spiritual children of the apostles and holy teachers—*from the sufficiency of the month*—that is, from the sufficiency of the perfection of the present life—*in its month*—that is, in the perfection of their glory in the future. So also the aforesaid seed, *from the sufficiency of the Sabbath*—that is, from the sufficiency of rest and the ceasing from vices and sins in this life—*shall be in its Sabbath*—that is, in its everlasting rest in the life of the world to come, which will be entirely Sabbath, that is, rest, as the aforementioned tradition says. In accordance with its intention, we have explained the words of Isaiah.

It interprets Isaiah 66 as a prophecy of spiritual perfection and eternal rest achieved through the Messiah.</summary>

## Solution to the objections of the Jews, by which they attempt to show that the sabbath ought to be observed literally by Christians and by all others, not only by the Jews. Chapter IX.

---

### CAPNIO, <note>The persona of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and Hebraist.</note>

<margin>
<unclear>...</unclear>
<unclear>...</unclear>
<unclear>...</unclear>
</margin>

<margin>
Jewish objections regarding the observation of the sabbath.
</margin>
**T**he impious perfidy of the Jews of our age opposes us in many ways in this matter, wishing to prove with every effort that the sabbath must be observed literally by right, not only by the Jews themselves, but also by us Christians, and by all others of whatever sect they may be.

<margin>
First objection.
</margin>
And first indeed, they argue because its observation is numbered among the ten moral commandments. For it is the third in order among the commandments of the Decalogue <note>In the numbering system common in the medieval West, the commandment to keep the Sabbath was often counted as the third, combining the prohibition of other gods and graven images into the first.</note>, as the Lord himself said in Exodus chapter 20: <gloss>Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: זכור את יום השבת לקדשו (*Zakhor et yom ha-shabbat le-kadsho*)</note>. Therefore, since the commandments of the Decalogue must be observed by everyone, because they are of natural law,

<margin>
Second objection.
</margin>
it clearly follows that the sabbath ought to be observed by all. Secondly, because the sabbath regards the benefit of creation, which is common to all people. For on the sabbath God rested from all the work which He had performed; therefore He sanctified it and blessed it. For this reason, when He commanded it to be sanctified, as if assigning a reason, He immediately added: *Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant nor your female servant, your cattle, nor the stranger who is within your gates. For in six days God made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the sabbath day and sanctified it.* Since, therefore, everyone is obligated to God by reason of creation, it follows that all are held to the observation of the sabbath.

<margin>
Third objection.
</margin>
Thirdly and finally, because a natural example leads everyone to this: the <term>Sabbatic River</term> <note>Also known as the Sambatyon, a legendary river in Jewish mythology that flows violently with stones during the week but stops on the Sabbath.</note>, which (as they say) flows rapidly through the whole week,

<margin>
The fable of the Sabbatic river.
</margin>
dragging stones along, but on the sabbath it rests. Whence it is read in <term>Bereshith Ketanna</term> <note>Literally "The Minor Genesis," referring to a Midrashic commentary on the Book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis, upon that saying in the second chapter of the same book: <gloss>And He blessed the seventh day.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: ויברך את יום השביעי (*Va-yevarekh et yom ha-shvi'i*)</note>. There it is said that the lord <term>Rufus the Roman</term> <note>Likely Quintus Tineius Rufus, the Roman governor of Judea during the Bar Kokhba revolt.</note> questioned <term>Rabbi Akiba</term> <note>A foundational tannaic sage of the late 1st and early 2nd centuries.</note>, and said to him: "What is the difference between this day and other days?" Rabbi Akiba answered him, saying: "And what is the difference between this man and other men?" Rufus said to him: "What have I said to you, and what have you said to me?" He answered him: "You indeed said to me: In what does the sabbath differ from all other days? But I said to you: In what does Rufus excel all other men?" Just as, therefore, a King exceeds all others because of his glory, so also God wished this day to be honored above the others. Rufus said to him: "How will you make me know this?" The Rabbi answered: "The Sabbatic River shows this, which drags stones through the whole week, and rests on the sabbath." By these arguments, therefore, the more recent Jews attempt to prove that the sabbath not only should never cease...

...[not only by the Jews] themselves, but also that it must always be observed by everyone. Although these reasons are of little weight, you should first refute them to further confound the obstinacy of those who lean on such a fragile and ruinous foundation. Next, it is necessary to show through their own scriptures that even among them the Sabbath itself has been dissolved. GAL. <note>Likely Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540), a Franciscan friar and Hebraist known for his work "De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis," which uses Jewish sources to argue for Christian truths.</note> I will indeed strive with every effort to satisfy your wishes. 

<margin>Response to the first objection.</margin>
To their first reason, therefore, I say briefly: the commandment regarding the observation of the Sabbath was partly moral and partly ceremonial. It was moral in insofar as it commanded that men ought to be free at some time for divine matters. According to that passage in Psalm 45: <gloss>Be still and know that I am God.</gloss> <note>original: "Cessate & cognoscite, quia ego sum Deus"; this is Psalm 46:10 in modern English Bibles, but Psalm 45:11 in the Vulgate.</note> And according to this, it was numbered among the moral commandments of the Decalogue. But it was ceremonial regarding the specific designation of the seventh day; and according to this, it was counted among the commandments of the Decalogue, but among other ceremonial laws. Hence it is that we find the Sabbath to have been dissolved many times in the Old Testament. This would by no means have happened if it were numbered among the commandments of the Decalogue specifically regarding the observance of the seventh day, since it is never permitted to loosen those [moral] laws at any time, because they are part of <term>natural law<gloss>Universal moral principles viewed as inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</gloss></term>. Hence also our Lord Jesus, the true Messiah, after he reached thirty years of age, is read to have dissolved the Sabbath itself several times in regard to this part. For on that day he both healed the sick—giving them the power to carry their beds—and he permitted his hungry disciples to pluck and rub ears of grain.

<margin>To the second objection.</margin>
To the second reason, I say: just as the Sabbath looks back to the benefit of Creation, so the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note> displays the benefit of Redemption. For just as God completed the work of creation on the Sabbath, so on the Lord’s Day He perfected the work of redemption through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. For Christ himself (as the Apostle says) died for our justification and rose for our glory. <note>A paraphrase of Romans 4:25.</note> Since, therefore, in everyone's opinion the work of redemption is greater than the work of creation—for in creation indeed God spoke and the world was made, as the <term>Talmudists<gloss>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</gloss></term> say; but in redemption, as those same ones say, it was necessary for God himself not only to speak, but also to do and to suffer many things, as we have proved most extensively from their own sayings in the eighth book—therefore the Sabbath, in regards to its ceremonial aspect, had to be changed into the Lord’s Day by the same one who instituted it. This day looks to the benefit of both creation and redemption. For on that day the world took its beginning, and through the resurrection of the Lord, death received its destruction and life took its beginning.

<margin>To the third objection regarding the Sabbatic River.</margin>
Finally, to the third objection, I respond by turning that Jewish fiction of the Sabbatic River against them. For just as that fictitious river was a sign for observing the Sabbath—since it would flow by dragging stones throughout the whole week and rest on the Sabbaths, as they fabulate—so also it is now an effective argument against them for *not* observing the Sabbath. Since there is nowhere under heaven now a river that rests more on Sabbaths than [on other days].

...rest on other days. For merchants travel across the whole world, and just as they bring medicinal goods and various pigments from the farthest lands, they would also tell each other if this were true; they would not keep silent about the name of the province where a river of this kind was, when Jews inquired of them. 
<margin><unclear>it is related in</unclear> book 7, chapter 35</margin>
In fact, Josephus, in the book titled *The Jewish War*, relates where that river was. To avoid further delay, I will relate his own words. For he says in Book 7, Chapter 35: 
"Prince Titus indeed remained for some time at Beirut, just as we said. Then, returning from there..." And further down: "He sees on the journey a river most worthy of knowledge. It flows between Arcas and Raphaneae, cities of the kingdom of Agrippa. It has a certain unique wonder. For though, when it flows, it is abundant and not slow in its course, nevertheless, after six days have passed, it fails from its springs and offers a dry place to be seen. Then, as if no change had been made, it rises again on the seventh day. It is well established that it always observes this order. From which it is also called 'Sabbatic,' named after the sacred seventh day of the Jews." These are the words of Josephus. Pliny also mentions this river in Book 31 of his *Natural History*, chapter 2, saying: "In Judea, a river dries up every Sabbath." <note>Note the discrepancy: Josephus describes a river that only flows on the Sabbath, whereas Pliny describes a river that stops flowing on the Sabbath. Galatinus uses this inconsistency to undermine the argument.</note> Therefore the Jews would say it is not a fiction, but the truth, that there was a river of this kind, since both Josephus and Pliny mention it and assign the place where it was.

<margin>GAL.</margin> 
I admit that a river of that kind existed then. Now, however, there is no one who says they have seen it themselves, or reports it has been seen by anyone else. Therefore, to say that such a river exists now is rightly judged to be both a fiction and a lie. 
<margin><unclear>... manifest</unclear></margin>
Neither Josephus nor Pliny say that it rested on the Sabbath, as these people [the Jews] assert. Rather, one records that it failed, the other that it was accustomed to be dried up on the Sabbaths. From which the future failure and dryness of the Sabbath was portended, because from that day forward it was no longer to be venerated. <note>Galatinus argues that the river's intermittent nature was a divine sign that the Sabbath's ritual status was temporary and would eventually "dry up" or cease to be required.</note> From these things, therefore, the solution to the Jewish arguments is clear, by which they strive to prove that the Sabbath must be literally observed by everyone. Their opinion is best refuted even by their own ancient writers. 

For it is read among them in the **Perush** <note>original: "פרוש"; Hebrew for "interpretation" or "gloss."</note>, that is, in the gloss on that passage of Exodus: **See that the Lord has given you the Sabbath.** <note>original: "ראו כי יהוה נתן לכם את השבת"; Exodus 16:29.</note> That is, "See, because God has given you the Sabbath." And what does "given you the Sabbath" mean? Because he gave it to *you*, namely the Jews, and not to the nations of the world. In the book also named **Beitzah** <note>original: "ביצה"; Hebrew for "Egg," a tractate of the Talmud concerning laws of festivals.</note>, that is, *The Egg*, in the chapter **Yom Tov** <note>original: "יום טוב"; Hebrew for "Good Day," a common term for a holy day.</note>, that is, *The Good Day*, it is said: "Rabbi Jochanan said: Every commandment that the Holy and Blessed God gave to Israel, He gave to them publicly, except for the Sabbath, which He gave to them in secret. As it is said in Exodus 31: **Between Me and the children of Israel.**" <note>original: "ביני ובין בני ישראל"; Exodus 31:17.</note> If this is so, the **Goim** <note>original: "גוים"; Hebrew for "nations" or "Gentiles."</note>, that is, the nations, are not bound to the Sabbath. This is the tradition. From these things, the falsehood of the aforementioned conclusion of the Jews is clearly evident.

...was dissolved at the beginning of the world. For where our edition has Genesis chapter 2: "And God completed his works on the sixth day, which he had made," the Hebrew truth <note>original: "Hebraica veritas"; a term used by scholars like Jerome to refer to the authentic Hebrew text of the Bible.</note> has it thus: *And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made* <note>original Hebrew: "ויכל אלהים ביום השביעי מלאכתו אשר עשה" (Vayechal Elohim bayom hashvi'i melachto asher asah)</note>. Where we, both Greeks and Latins (except for St. Jerome), say in our edition that God perfected the work of creation on the sixth day, the Hebrew letter reports that God did this on the seventh day. From this, therefore, the Jews—who boast of the leisure of the Sabbath—are greatly constrained. For even then, in the beginning, the Sabbath itself was dissolved, while God worked on the Sabbath, completing His works in it, and blessing the day itself because He completed the universe within it.

**HOG.** From where, then, did our people (except for St. Jerome, who, as you say, translated this place well) take the cause of their error, so that they put the sixth day instead of the seventh?

**GAL.** From the 70 interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, who translated this passage as can be seen in their edition. This is also clearly shown in the *Bereshit Zuta* <note>original: "Bereffith זוטא ketanna"; a "Small" or minor Midrashic exposition on the Book of Genesis.</note> regarding this same passage. For it is said there: "And this is one of the words which the wise men changed for King Ptolemy." For King Ptolemy questioned the elders, saying: "In how many days did the Holy and Blessed God create His world?" They said to him: "In six. As in Genesis 2: And God completed His work on the sixth day." So it says there. I say further, that neither Abraham, nor Isaac, nor Jacob observed the Sabbath, and yet they were righteous. That Abraham himself did not observe it is held in the *Bereshit Zuta* on that passage in chapter 2 of the same book, "And God blessed the seventh day." Where it is read: "Rabbi Johanan said: The observation of the Sabbath is not written concerning Abraham."

**CAP.** A Jew might perhaps say here that the commandment concerning the sanctification of the Sabbath had not yet been given.
<margin>An objection of the younger Jews.</margin> Therefore, Abraham did not observe it, since no one was held to observe it before the commandment.

**GAL.** From this, at least, it is inferred that the worship of the Sabbath is not part of the natural law. For since the natural law is inscribed on the mind of everyone, it has obligated all men capable of reason to its observation ever since the beginning of the world. Nevertheless, I will show through their own scriptures that even after the commandment for the sanctification of the Sabbath was given, the Sabbath itself was dissolved by them many times. Therefore, so that I say nothing of this myself, I will only report those things which their own scriptures narrate. First, then, one must hear what is read among them in the book *Sifre* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary (Midrash) on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note> regarding that passage in Numbers 9: "And they performed the Passover in the first..." and so on. For there it is said: "They did not perform it except for that one time." Rabbi Elazar said: It is held in Exodus 16: *The people rested on the seventh day* <note>original Hebrew: "וישבתו העם ביום השביעי" (Vayishbetu ha-am bayom hashvi'i)</note>. Through this he teaches that in all the 40 years in which the children of Israel were in the desert, they only observed the very first Sabbath. Just as the prophet Amos himself says in the fifth chapter: *Did you offer sacrifices and offerings to me in the desert for forty years, O house of Israel?* <note>original Hebrew: "הזיבחים ומנחת הגשתם לי במדבר ארבעים שנה בית ישראל" (Ha-zeva-chim u-minchah higashtem li bammidbar arba’im shanah beit Yisrael)</note>. In the chapter that begins, "And the people who went up from the Jordan," regarding what is said in the 6th chapter of Joshua, "On the seventh day," with the rest, it is written thus: Rabbi Joses said, "It was the Sabbath day when the battle in Jericho took place." Also in the *Bereshit Ketanna* <gloss>meaning the Minor or Small Exposition of the book of Genesis</gloss>, regarding the 17th chapter of that same book, on the verse "All the men of his house," it is said: "We find that Jericho was not captured except on the Sabbath." Rabbi Rahmon said: "This is what is written in the 6th chapter of Joshua, <note>original Hebrew: וביום השביעי תסבו את העיר שבע פעמים (V'bayom hashvi'i tasobu et ha'ir sheva pe'amim)</note> which is: *And on the seventh day you shall circle the city seven times.*" Furthermore, in the book called *Rosh Hashanah* <gloss>meaning the Head of the Year</gloss>, in the chapter *Arba Rashe Shanim* <gloss>meaning the four heads of years</gloss>, it is read: "For two months they dissolved the Sabbath: for Nisan <gloss>meaning March</gloss> and for Tishri <gloss>meaning September</gloss>." For in those months they sent messengers out into Syria, and there they bought necessary things. Moreover, when the House of the Sanctuary <note>The Temple in Jerusalem.</note> stood in its established state, they also dissolved the Sabbath during all months because of the preparations for those things which were necessary for the sacrifices. Also in the book called *Sabbath* <note>The Talmudic tractate *Shabbat*.</note>, it says: "Because Rabbi Simeon said: 'For a living child of one day they dissolve the Sabbath; but for King David the King, being dead, they do not dissolve the Sabbath.'" <note>A legal principle in the Talmud: saving a life, even that of an infant, overrides Sabbath laws, while the honors for a dead king do not.</note> In the *Midrash*—that is, in the later exposition of the book of Numbers—regarding the 15th chapter of that same book, "Send for yourself men," it is said: "For a messenger of a commandment, it is permitted to depart on whatever day he wishes." For what reason? "Because he is a messenger of a commandment. And a messenger of a commandment excludes the Sabbath." From all these things, therefore, it clearly stands that the Sabbath was frequently dissolved among the Jews.
