->*That even the sacrifices of the Jews in the time of the Messiah were to be kept only spiritually.*<-
->Chapter IX.<-

### CAPNIO, <note>The scholarly nickname for Johannes Reuchlin.</note>

**N**ow we must speak concerning the sacrifices of the Old Law, whether in the days of the Messiah they were to be kept only spiritually. GALATINUS: They were indeed, as is clearly shown through their own scriptures. For in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Midrash on the Psalms.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Psalms—regarding that verse of Psalm 56, <note>original Hebrew: עלי אלהים נדריך אשלם תודות (Alai Elohim nedarecha, ashalem todot)</note> which is: *Upon me, O God, are your vows; I will pay confessions (or praises),* it is read that Rabbi Pinhas said in the name of Rabbi Levi, and Rabbi Johanan in the name of Rabbi Menahem: "All prayers will be abolished in the future, but confession (or praise) will not be abolished forever." For it is written in the 12th chapter of Nehemiah: "And two confessions <note>Usually translated as "choirs" or "thanksgiving companies."</note> shall stand in the house of the Lord." One in the place of prayer, and the other in the place of sacrifice. This is the tradition. With this, that Davidic saying of Psalm 51 greatly agrees: <note>original Hebrew: אדני שפתי תפתח ופי יגיד תהלתך : כי לא תחפוץ זבח ואתנה עולה לא תרצה : זבחי אלהים רוח נשברה לב נשבר ונדכה אלהים לא תבוז (Adonai sefatai tiftach...)</note> which is: *O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall announce your praise. ...a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise. <note>Psalm 51:17. This completes the sentence started on the previous page.</note> Hence it is read in the book *Succa* <gloss>meaning of the booths or Tabernacles</gloss>, in the chapter *Sota hamegale ishto* <note>original Hebrew: שוטה המגלה אשתו (Shoteh ha-megaleh ishto). This refers to a section in the Talmudic tractate Sotah regarding the "foolishness" of certain behaviors.</note>, which means: "A fool despises his wife." On this, Rabbi Joshua the son of Levi said: "Come and see how great are the humble. In the time when the House of the Sanctuary <note>The Temple in Jerusalem</note> stood, a man would offer a <term>burnt offering</term> <gloss>original Latin: holocaustum</gloss>, and the reward for that offering was in his hand. If he offered a grain offering, the reward for that offering was in his hand. But regarding him whose conscience is humble, the Scripture considers it as if he had offered all possible sacrifices." This is according to that saying: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit." Nor is this all, but even his prayer is not rejected, according to what follows: "A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise." Also in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Nigmar haddin* <note>original Hebrew: נגמר הדין. Meaning "The judgment is finished."</note>, it is said: What Rabbi Joshua the son of Levi said, "For everyone who slaughters his 'tinder' <note>The 'tinder' or 'fomentation' of sin, referring to the evil impulse.</note>, or his <term>concupiscence</term> <gloss>strong desire or lust</gloss>, and confesses it, the Scripture regards him no differently than if he had honored God in two worlds. One of these is the present world, the other is the world to come." This is according to that saying of the Psalm: "He who offers a sacrifice of confession shall honor me." <note>Psalm 50:23.</note>

For the declaration of these things, it must be noted that if they consider with reason the things they used to sacrifice, they would find that some of them signified vices and the mortification of vices. Others, however, signified virtues and good morals, or the passion of Christ. For the firstborn of the sheep, the lambs, which Abel began to offer to the Lord, as well as the Paschal lamb, prefigured the passion of the Messiah and his immolation for the sins of men. But the he-goats and she-goats and certain other things designated nothing but vices and sins, and the mortification of the flesh through <term>penitence</term> <gloss>the act of repenting for sins</gloss>. For in the he-goat and she-goat was signified the stinking and lustful petulance of every sinner, full of shameful words. And similarly, in the bull was pride; in the calf, lasciviousness; in the kid and the sparrow, clamor and inconstancy. Indeed, when these vices are slaughtered and destroyed through confession and penitence, they are sacrifices acceptable and most pleasing to God himself, which were prefigured in those ancient sacrifices (as we have said). 

However, the sacrifices which pre-signified virtues and good morals were the sheep, the lamb, the ox, the ram, the turtle-dove, the young pigeon, and others of that kind. For in the sheep was signified simplicity and gentleness; in the lamb, innocence; in the ox, fruitful preaching; in the ram, useful and mild leadership. In the turtle-dove—which, having lost its mate, never couples with another—chastity was prefigured; and in the doves, which lack gall <note>A common medieval belief that doves had no gall bladder and thus were free of bitterness or malice.</note> and fly in flocks, charity was prefigured. From the aforementioned things, therefore, it is clear what kind of sacrifices God now desires. Especially since in the 6th chapter of Hosea, he himself says: <note>original Hebrew: כי חסד חפצתי ולא זבח ודעת אלהים מעלות (Ki chesed chafatzti v'lo zavach, v'da'at Elohim me'olot)</note> That is: "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings." Finally, that he wished the aforementioned spiritual sacrifices to be offered to him by the Gentiles who were to receive the Messiah, and not by the Jews (the faithless Jews themselves having been rejected), is clearly shown from what is said in the first chapter of Malachi: <note>original Hebrew: אין לי חפץ בכם אמר יהוה צבאות ומנחה לא ארצה מידכם : כי ממזרח שמש עד מבואו גדול שמי בגוים ובכל מקום מקטור (Ein li chefetz bachem amar Adonai Tzevaot u'minchah lo ertzeh mi-yedchem: ki mi-mizrach shemesh ad mevo'o gadol shemi ba-goyim u've-chol makom muktar)</note> <note>This verse from Malachi 1:10-11 translates to: "I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, neither will I accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to its going down my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered..."</note>

From all of which it clearly appears that the Jewish sacrifices formerly commanded through Moses were intended to be observed spiritually in the time of the Messiah.

### *That all things which according to the old law were unclean, ought to be clean in the time of the Messiah, and pig’s flesh could be lawfully eaten. Chapter XII.*

# CAPNIO,

<margin>GAL.</margin>
**S**ince the younger among the Jews, when they see us either eating pig’s flesh or eating other things which according to the ancient law were unclean and illicit, immediately argue with and accuse us. Therefore, it must be proven through their own scriptures: that all things which they considered unclean and illicit in the old law ought to have been clean and licit in the time of the Messiah. This also is best proven by their own testimonies. For it is read in this way in the exposition of the book of Genesis by **Rabbi Moses Hadarsan** <note>An 11th-century scholar known for his Midrashic compilations.</note>, upon that saying in the 41st chapter of the same book: "And it happened at the end of two full years, and Pharaoh dreamed." <note>original Hebrew: ויהי מקץ שנתים ימים ופרעה חלם. Genesis 41:1.</note> This is: After the end of two years of days,

And Pharaoh dreamed. This is what the Scripture says in Psalm 146: <note>original Hebrew: יהוה מתיר אסורים (YHVH mattir asurim)</note> "The Lord releases the bound." That is, God will be the one loosening prohibitions. <note>The author is playing on the Hebrew word "asur," which can mean both "imprisoned" and "forbidden."</note> For every beast which is considered unclean in this world, the Holy and Blessed God will make clean in the world to come—that is, in the time of the Messiah.

How were all things clean at first for the sons of Noah? As it is said in Genesis 9: <note>original Hebrew: כל רמש אשר הוא חי לכם יהיה לאכלה כירק עשב נתתי לכם את כל</note> "And everything that moves and lives shall be food for you; as the green herb, I have given you everything." Just as, therefore, the herb was clean to all, and as the animals and beasts were clean to the sons of Noah, so also in the future age—that is, in the days of the Messiah—He Himself will be loosening whatever He prohibited.

And why did He prohibit them in this world? So that He might see who would receive His words. And what is it that Psalm 145 says? "God is <term>mattir</term> <gloss>loosening or releasing</gloss>"—that is, loosening prohibitions? There is no greater prohibition than <term>niddah</term> <gloss>the ritual impurity of a menstruating woman</gloss>, which God prohibited. And yet in the future age—that is, the time of the Messiah—He Himself will release it. For thus He Himself says in Zechariah chapter 13: <note>original Hebrew: וגם את הנביאים ואת רוח הטמא אעביר מן הארץ</note> "And I will also remove the prophets and the spirit of uncleanness from the land." Now, there is no "uncleanness" except that of the menstruating woman. <note>This reflects a specific Rabbinic interpretation that equates "the spirit of uncleanness" primarily with these purity laws.</note> And so He says in Leviticus chapter 18: "And you shall not approach a woman in the uncleanness of her menstruation."

And there are those who say that even the <term>service of the bed</term> <gloss>marital relations</gloss> will be prohibited at certain times in the future. But know this for yourself: that on the day when the Holy and Blessed God was revealed upon Mount Sinai, He prohibited the service of the bed for three days. As it is said in Exodus 19: <note>original Hebrew: היו נכנים לשלשת ימים אל תגשו אל אשה</note> "Be ready for the third day; do not approach a woman." Why this? Because on the third day the Lord will descend upon Mount Sinai. If, therefore, on the one day that the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, He prohibited it to them for three days, in the world to come—that is, in the days of the Messiah when the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>the Divine Presence</gloss> <note>original: fechina. A Latinization of the Hebrew term for God's indwelling presence.</note> will be among them, it will not be entirely the same.

But what will it be? Furthermore, that which is said in the same Psalm: "God will release the <term>asurim</term> <gloss>the bound or imprisoned</gloss>"—according to another sense, namely the captives of hell and the captives of death.

Thus far the tradition. Which is to be held as no less than prophecy, since it speaks so clearly. It also fits perfectly with what is written in Deuteronomy 12 in this manner: <note>original Hebrew: הטמא והטהור יאכלנו כצבי וכאיל הטמא והטהור יחדו יאכלנו רק חזק לבלתי אכל הדם כי הדם הוא הנפש ולא תאכל הנפש עם הבשר</note> "The unclean and the clean alike shall eat it. Only be sure that the blood is not eaten. For the blood itself is the soul, and the soul shall not be eaten with the flesh."

**Rabbi Judah** said on this passage: It announces that the children of Israel were mixing flesh with blood before the giving of the Law. It follows: "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh." This refers to eating a limb from a living animal. <note>This refers to one of the "Seven Laws of Noah" which forbids cruelty to animals.</note>

Thus it says there. Although our Jews of the present time say that "unclean" in these places refers to a blind, weak, or lame animal, and things of this sort which were "unclean" for sacrifice. Nevertheless, according to the aforementioned tradition of the ancients, it is to be understood regarding *all* unclean things, which indeed in the days of the Messiah were to become clean for eating.

This was to denote that it would lawfully "return" to being used for human consumption. From the foregoing, it is most clearly established that no one is held to the observance of the ceremonial commandments. This is especially true since it was said previously that the Old Law was to fade away in the presence of the Law of the Messiah, and it was no longer fitting for there to be any memory of the signs or miracles of Egypt and the departure from Egypt. Rather, the entire Law itself was to be reduced to a "newness"—that is, to a spiritual sense. Therefore, by God’s permission, it happened that the observance of the Law itself was prohibited to the Jews by the Romans, although it was later restored to them through the devil.

# On the second coming of the Messiah, and on the things to happen then.

## *That the second coming of the Messiah will be near the end of the world. Chapter 1.*

CAPNIO <note>The character "Capnio" represents the famous Christian Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin.</note>,
**S**ince you have revealed in the preceding books so many and such great secrets regarding the first coming of the Messiah—which until now lay hidden in the Talmud and other books of the Hebrews—it is now truly fitting; indeed, it is necessary, in order to further shatter the stubborn <term>perfidiam</term> <note>In this 16th-century context, "perfidia" refers to "unbelief" or "lack of faith" rather than "treachery" in the modern sense.</note> of the Jews of our age, that those things which lie hidden in the Talmud and their other volumes concerning his second coming also be made known. Therefore, it must first be proven through their own scriptures that the second coming of the Messiah will take place near the end of the world—not for redeeming (as the Jews themselves falsely believe), but for judging. **GAL.** <note>The character "Galatinus" represents the author, Pietro Galatino, a Franciscan friar.</note> Indeed, the wretched Jews wait and wait for the coming of the Messiah, coming not to judge, but (as you say) to redeem them. However, they are certainly very much mistaken. For all the prophecies by which they expect him to come foretell not his first, but his second coming; such as that of Daniel, which predicted he would come in the clouds of heaven (as was shown elsewhere in the 7th chapter). That prophecy of Joel in the 3rd chapter, in which—according to the opinion of all commentators—the coming of the Messiah is described, also speaks of his second coming. It calls that time <gloss>יום יהוה הגדול והנורא</gloss> <note>original: *yom Yehovah ha-gadol ve-ha-nora*</note>, that is, "the great and terrible day of the Lord." This is a phrase that the prophets only ever use to refer to the Day of Judgment. And what he adds a little later, saying: <gloss>וקבצתי את כל הגוים והורדתים אל עמק יהושפט ונשפטתי עמם</gloss> <note>Joel 3:2</note>, which is, "And I will gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I will plead with them there." This too is understood only as referring to the Day of Judgment. Likewise, that which is said in the last chapter of Malachi: <gloss>הנה אנכי שלח לכם את אליהו הנביא לפני בוא יום יהוה הגדול והנורא</gloss> <note>Malachi 4:5</note>, that is, "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the Lord." This cannot be understood as anything except the second coming of the Messiah. Furthermore, the ancient Talmudists clearly assert that the second coming of the Messiah will be at the end of the world. For in *Bereshith Rabba Ketanna* <note>A midrashic commentary on Genesis; *ketanna* means "small" or "lesser."</note>, that is in...

It must be proven through the sayings of the ancient Talmudists that both a general resurrection of the dead (which the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect known in antiquity for denying the resurrection of the dead and the existence of spirits.</note> deny) will occur, and that the dead themselves will be raised through the Messiah—a point which the younger Jews dare to claim is false. GAL. You urge me here, my dear Capnio <note>Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist, often called by his Greek-derived name "Capnio."</note>, to show through the ancient Jewish scriptures that there will be a general resurrection of the dead and that it will be accomplished through the Messiah. The first point is evident not only through the testimonies of sacred scripture, but also through the sayings of the Talmudists. For instance, that statement from Psalm 17: **"I, in justice, shall see your face; I shall be satisfied when your form awakes."** <note>original Hebrew: אני בצדק אחזה פניך אשבעה בהקיץ תמונתך (Psalm 17:15). Indeed, Rabbi Abraham says: "This vision is not of the eye, but of the intellect. And no one sees these words unless they have learned the wisdom of the soul." But Rabbi Solomon says in his gloss: "**I shall see your face**, just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 52: 'Because they shall see eye to eye.' **I shall be satisfied when your form awakes** (or figure, or image, or likeness)—that is, when the dead awake from their sleep."

Also in the book *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient commentary on the Psalms.</note>, regarding that verse of Psalm 78: **"And he remembered that they were but flesh; a spirit that goes and does not return."** <note>original Hebrew: ויזכר כי בשר המה רוח הולך ולא ישוב (Psalm 78:39)</note> It is read thus: "Some have dared to say that the dead will not live, because it is said: 'A spirit that goes and does not return.' However, this refers to the *yetzer hara* <term>the evil inclination (literally: the evil formation or "fomes")</term>, which goes with a man at the hour of death, but does not return with him at the hour when the dead shall rise."

Furthermore, in the book *Elle Haddevarim Rabbah* (that is, in the commentaries on the book of Deuteronomy), it says:

> Rabbi Simai says: Of all creatures that were created from heaven, their soul and their body belong to heaven. And all that were created from the earth, their soul and their body belong to the earth. Therefore, if a man fulfills the Law and does the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is surely counted among the number of the higher creatures, as it is written: *I said, You are gods, etc.* But if he does not fulfill the Law nor the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is counted among the number of the lower creatures, as it is written: *But you shall die like Adam.* And so Rabbi Simai used to say: There is no portion of the Torah that does not contain the resurrection of the dead, but we lack the power to interpret it, as it is written: *He shall call to the heavens from above, etc.* **He shall call to the heavens from above**—this refers to the soul; **and to the earth, that he may judge his people**—this refers to the body. Who is judged with him? And how do we know this refers only to the resurrection of the dead? As it is said: *Come from the four winds, O spirit... for there I will call upon the name of the Lord.* And we find that Moses did not mention the name of the Place <note>A common Jewish epithet for God (HaMakom).</note> until after twenty-one words. From whom did he learn this? From the ministering angels, who do not mention the Name until after three "Holies," as it is written: *And one called to another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Hosts.*

This means: Rabbi Simai said, "For all creatures that were created from heaven, the soul and body belong to heaven. But for creatures created from the earth, the soul and body belong to the earth. If, therefore, a man observes the law and the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is made without doubt of the number of the heavenly creatures. As it is written: *I said, You are gods.* But if he does not observe the law and the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is made of the number of the lower creatures. As it is written: *Indeed, just like Adam...*"

### That after the general resurrection all men will speak in one idiom of language, and what that shall be. Chapter III.

## CAPNIO,
<note>Capnio is the Greek-style pseudonym of the author, Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and scholar of Hebrew.</note>

**S**ephaniah the prophet, speaking of the coming of the Messiah for judgment—which will occur after the general resurrection—says that a refined lip <note>original: "labium electum," a translation of the Hebrew *shaphah berurah*, meaning a pure or clear language.</note> is to be turned toward all men and they are to be led back to it. For he says thus in the third chapter: **"Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, until the day of my rising for the witness; for my judgment is to gather the nations, to assemble the kingdoms, to pour upon them my indignation and all the fierce anger of my nose. For all the earth shall be devoured by the fire of my jealousy. For then I will turn to the peoples a pure lip, so that they may all call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder."** <note>original Hebrew: "לכן חכו לי נאם יהוה... כי אז אהפך אל עמים שפה ברורה לקרא כלם בשם יהוה לעבדו שכם אחד". Reuchlin interprets "my rising" (*kumi*) specifically as the day of the Messiah's resurrection.</note> This is: "Wait for me," says God, "on the day of my resurrection in the future. Because it is my judgment to gather the nations and collect the kingdoms, to pour out my indignation upon them and all the anger of my nose. For in the fire of my zeal the entire earth shall be devoured. For then I will turn toward the peoples a refined lip, so that they may all call upon the name of God and worship him with one shoulder." Thus says the prophet. Where the Midrash <note>A Jewish homiletic commentary or "gloss" on the biblical text.</note> (that is, the explanation) says: "With one shoulder" means "as one part." Just as it is said in Genesis, chapter 48: **"And I have given to you one shoulder,"** <note>original Hebrew: "ואני נתתי לך שכם אחד" (*Va-ani natati lecha shechem echad*). In the biblical context, Jacob is giving Joseph an extra "portion" or "ridge of land" (*shechem*), but the Midrash interprets it here as unity of purpose.</note> that is, "I have given you one part." When the prophet therefore speaks with the voice of God, saying, "I will turn toward the peoples a refined lip," what is understood by this "refined lip"? And what is this tongue that the Lord chose for the invoking of his name and for the worship of himself by all nations with "one shoulder" (that is, as one part)? GALATINUS: In this matter, various people say various things.

<margin>The opinion of the Greeks.</margin>
For some say that this refined lip is the Greek language, which the Lord chose so that his name might be invoked in it and he might be worshipped through it. For the New Testament (except for the Gospel of Matthew) was written entirely in the Greek language, and the entire primitive church was founded in the Greek tongue. The name of the "Christians" itself is the greatest evidence of this thing. For <term>Christos</term> <note>original: χρισòς. The Greek word for "the Anointed One."</note>, from which the "Christians" are named, is a Greek name. Not only this, but also the very names of the dignities and offices that pertain to the Christian religion and concern the worship of God are almost all Greek: such as Church (*Ecclesia*), Pope (*Papa*), Patriarch, Archbishop, Bishop (*Episcopus*), Priest (*Presbyter*), Deacon, Subdeacon, Acolyte, cleric, layman, and others of that kind. For this reason, they say the Greek language was chosen by God so that his name might be invoked everywhere through the world in it, and he himself might be worshipped by all. Whence the Messiah himself, the Son of God, is called "Christ" by all nations even to this day by a Greek name.

<margin>The opinion of the Latins.</margin>

BOOK TWELVE

...these other nations both call upon the name of the Lord and worship God himself. Therefore, in the aforementioned words of the prophet, the Lord specifically said he would turn this "chosen lip" <note>original Latin: *labium electum*, a translation of the Hebrew *shaphah berurah* from Zephaniah 3:9, meaning a pure or clear language.</note> not to everyone universally, but to "the peoples." For not all peoples who confess Christ call upon the name of the Lord or worship him in the Latin language—the tongue chosen by God—but only some. 

This is expressed more clearly by what follows: when it is said, **"With one shoulder."** Has this not also been plainly fulfilled? For whoever calls upon the name of the Lord in the Latin or Roman language, they all call upon him under the "shoulder" and authority of one Supreme Pontiff. From him they undergo canonical punishments, and from him they obtain the benefit of absolution from both those punishments and their sins. And they worship God according to his laws and statutes, performing divine service and fulfilling sacred offices according to the rite of the Roman Church—which is the Mistress and Teacher of all churches—and according to the decrees of the Roman Pontiff, who is the Vicar of Christ and acts in God's stead.

The Talmudists <note>Jewish scholars and commentators on the Talmud.</note>, however, assert that this "chosen lip" is the Hebrew language. They argue that God chose it above all others: in it he spoke to the patriarchs and gave his Law. For this reason, he willed that the Law itself, and nearly all the secrets revealed to the prophets, be written in that language. Hence they call it by the specific name "Holy." <margin>451</margin> Because of these things, they say that according to the prophetic prediction, the Lord will turn the "chosen lip" to the peoples to call upon his name and to worship him "with one shoulder" when all the nations to be saved through the Messiah will praise God in the Hebrew language "with one shoulder"—that is, under the one Kingdom of the Messiah himself. 

This will be fulfilled among the chosen after the general resurrection. For just as before the division of languages at the Tower of Babel the whole earth was of "one lip," so in the general resurrection all men will speak one language, namely Hebrew, which the first parents spoke in Paradise and which all the chosen would have spoken in the state of innocence if those first parents had remained in the grace of God. And this opinion is indeed more consistent with the literal text. For in these same words the prophet is speaking not of the first coming of the Messiah, but of the second, specifically when he will come to judge. 

This is even more clearly evident through the Targum of Rabbi Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and interpretive paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, who translated and explained these very words of the prophet into Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> thus: <term>בכן סברי לממרי אמר יהוה ליום אתגלויותי</term> <note>original Aramaic: "Therefore wait for my word, says the Lord, for the day of my revelation."</note> That is: **"Therefore expect my word, says God, on the day of my manifestation for judgment."** And below: <term>ארי באשת פורענותי יסופון בל רשיעי ארעא</term> <note>original Aramaic: "For in the fire of my retribution all the wicked of the earth shall be consumed."</note> That is: **"For in the fire of my vengeance all the wicked of the earth shall be consumed."** Since the Messiah is the Word of God (as we have shown in previous sections), it is manifest that the Messiah himself will come at the end of the world to judge. From this it is clearly evident that

### *That the general judgment will be carried out by the Messiah, who is to judge in a glorious human form. Chapter 5.*

->CAPNIO,<-
<note>Capnio is the Greek-style nickname for the famous German humanist Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522).</note>

**T**he entire Church of Christians confesses and believes without doubt that Christ our Lord will be the judge of the living and the dead, and that he will come in a glorious human form to judge. Therefore, so that the <term>perfidy</term> <note>In this historical context, "perfidy" was a common but harsh polemical term used by Christian writers to describe the Jewish refusal to accept Jesus as the Messiah.</note> of the younger Jews may be further convinced, you ought to prove through their own scriptures that the Messiah will perform the universal judgment at the end of the world, and that he will come to judge in a glorious human form. 

GALATINUS: That a universal judgment must indeed be performed by the Messiah at the end of the world is most evident through what is read in the ancient *Bereshith Rabbah* <note>original: "Beresthith Rabba," a classical collection of Jewish homilies and interpretations on the Book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis. For there, regarding that passage in the 49th chapter of the same book, *Until Shiloh comes* <note>Genesis 49:10, a verse traditionally interpreted by both Jews and Christians as referring to the Messiah.</note>, it is said: "This is the Messiah. And to him the peoples shall gather. Because he himself will be judging the whole world." 

And this is what is written in the fourth chapter of Micah: **"And he shall judge between many peoples, and shall reprove strong nations."** <note>original Hebrew: "ושפט בין עמים רבים והוכיח לגוים עצמים"</note> 

And it is also said in the 11th chapter of Isaiah <note>The text mistakenly cites chapter 9, but the quote is from Isaiah 11:4.</note>: **"And he shall judge the poor in justice, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth. And he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the impious."** <note>original Hebrew: "ושפט בצדק דלים והוכיח במישור לענוי ארץ והכה ארץ בשבט פיו וברוח שפתיו ימית רשע"</note> All this is tradition. 

Moreover, that he is to judge in a glorious human form is found in the seventh chapter of Daniel, where he says: **"I saw in the night vision, and behold, with the clouds of heaven, one like a son of man was coming, and he reached even to the Ancient of Days, and they brought him before him. And he gave him power, and honor, and a Kingdom. And all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His power is an eternal power, which shall not pass away, and his Kingdom is one that shall not be destroyed."** <note>original Aramaic: "חזה הוית בחזוי ליליא וארו עם ענני שמיא כבר אנש אתה הוה ועד עתיק יומיא מטה וקדמוהי הקרבוהי וליה יהב שלטן ויקר ומלכו וכל עממיא אמיא ולשניא לה יפלחון שלטנה שלטן עלם די לא יעדה ומלכותה דילא תתחבל"</note> 

Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A significant 12th-century Spanish Jewish commentator and philosopher.</note>, commenting on this passage in Daniel, says that Rabbi Joshua stated that this "one like a son of man" is the Messiah; and he says he spoke most excellently. Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> also confirms this, saying in a <gloss>gloss</gloss> upon that word, "one like a son of man," that he is the King Messiah. 

That Daniel is speaking of the second coming of the Messiah in the aforementioned words is clear most of all from the fact that in the first coming, he was to come with humility and poverty, as was made very plain in the preceding sections. But in the second, he is to come with majesty and glory, as the words of Daniel themselves openly suggest. The preceding and following parts of the same chapter also clearly show this. For to the words mentioned above, he prefixed...

Just as it is said in Deuteronomy chapter 32: **"Is he not your father, your possessor?"** This means: Is he not your father, your possessor, or your buyer? All these things are tradition. From all these it clearly appears that the Messiah, God and man, will perform the universal judgment at the end of the world, and will come to judge in human form with glory and majesty.

This is the tradition. From these things it is clearly evident that the Messiah himself shall be the eternal reward and prize of the righteous. This opinion of the Talmudists is confirmed also by that saying in Genesis, chapter 15: <note>original Hebrew: "אל תירא אברם..."</note> *Fear not, Abram: I am your shield, and your reward shall be very great.* For this reason, He himself said in the tenth chapter of John: *I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved, and he shall go in and go out, and find pasture.* Namely, he shall find the pasture of eternal blessedness in me (understand) within and without. Within, through the clear vision of divinity and perfect enjoyment; without, through the contemplation of His glorious humanity. And this is what He meant by, *And he shall go in and go out.*

# BOOK TWELFTH

<margin>ff 2</margin>

...from the foundation of your disputation (with the help of divine aid) I have excerpted and collected into these twelve books, as if into bundles. I have done this so that from them it might be easily perceived what should be thought concerning the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, which was the subject of intense debate and censorship during the Renaissance.</note>, about which there has been such long-standing debate between you. Indeed, in another work—which is divided into six distinct books according to the distinction of the articles of <term>Hogostratus</term> <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican inquisitor and a leading opponent of Johannes Reuchlin in the "Battle of the Books" over Hebrew literature.</note>, and which I hope soon (God favoring) to bring into the light—a most ample space for disputing will be given to you. Thus, once those articles have been skillfully discussed and the reasons of each of you diligently heard, the truth itself which you seek with such zeal may appear more clearly determined.

Now, however, I would ask this of you: if anything in this work seems to you to have been stated by me less than correctly, please reveal it to me in a friendly manner. For since only a year and a half was granted to me to complete such a great work—for which (to tell the truth) a man’s entire lifetime would hardly have been enough—I fear greatly that on account of excessive haste, it may have happened that I said many things otherwise than was proper. Therefore, I am prepared, by the judgment of wise friends, to amend all things poorly stated by me and, where necessary, to retract them.

**HOGOSTRATUS:** The things you have said in this work, <term>Galatinus</term> <note>Pietro Colonna Galatino (1460–1540), the author of this text, a Franciscan friar who sought to use the Kabbalah and Jewish texts to prove Christian doctrines.</note>, all seem to me to be well-stated, except for one.

**GALATINUS:** Tell me, pray, what is that one thing?

**HOGOSTRATUS:** That in many instances you have not observed the common manner of writing and pronouncing. For indeed, you have produced some names written with aspiration <note>The addition of the "h" sound (the letter 'H').</note> which usually reject it, while others you have pronounced and written far differently than established usage has maintained.

**GALATINUS:** Which ones are those, I ask you to explain?

**HOGOSTRATUS:** Those which you have reported written with aspiration, contrary to the accustomed manner of writing, are many indeed, but especially these: **Heua** <note>Eve</note>, **Habel** <note>Abel</note>, **Hanna** <note>Hannah</note>, **Johannes** <note>John</note>, **Halleluia**. 

Furthermore, those which you have pronounced and written contrary to the law of our orthography <note>Traditional Latin spelling rules used in the Church.</note>—though they are also many—these among others seem to be the primary ones: **Hanoch**, **Methuselas**, **Noas**, **Peres**, **Moses**, **Jehosuas**, **Pinhas**, **Semuel**, **Selomo**, **Sealthiel**, **Jehoiakim**, **Hoseas**, **Bathseba**, **Eliseba**, **Amora**. 

Yet these are commonly written and pronounced by our people as: **Enoch**, **Mathusalem**, **Noe**, **Phares**, **Moyses**, **Josue**, **Phinees**, **Samuel**, **Salomon**, **Salathiel**, **Joakim**, **Osee**, **Bersabea**, **Elizabeth**, **Gomorra**. On account of this, I have no doubt that you will be criticized by many.

**GALATINUS:** Regarding those who you think will criticize me for this, I ask and beseech them not to be willing to accuse me before they hear the reason why I did it. For that reason, I would wish both you and them to know that the author of our edition <note>Referring to St. Jerome, the traditional translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note>, imitating the Greek edition <note>The Septuagint, the early Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, translated many things into a different sense that utterly abhorred the Hebrew truth. In the same way, he also translated almost infinite names corruptly and depravedly. Since these are not Greek but Hebrew names, we ought to follow the Hebrews in them, and not the Greeks. And this is especially true in those names where a variation in the letters results in a variation of meaning; such are the ones I have taken care to correct in this work above others. Therefore, whatever names are written with the letter **he** or **heth** among the Hebrews, I have written with aspiration...

-># BOOK<-

<margin>First rule.</margin>
...should be written among us. For I do not agree with the opinion of those who, comparing the Hebrew letters <term>Heth</term> <note>The eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ח), representing a "rough" or guttural "h" sound.</note> and <term>He</term> <note>The fifth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ה), representing a softer "h" sound.</note> to the <term>prosodies</term> <note>In this context, the marks used in Greek to indicate breathing or aspiration.</note> of the Greeks—namely <term>dasia</term> <note>A rough breathing mark in Greek.</note> and <term>psili</term> <note>A smooth breathing mark in Greek.</note>—claim that only those words occurring with a *Heth* among the Hebrews ought to be written with an aspiration (the letter "h") among us. This is partly because in Hebrew words (as I have said), the <term>orthography</term> <note>The conventional system of spelling.</note> of the Hebrews, not the Greeks, must be observed—at least as far as our letters allow. It is also because, even if *Heth* is a strong aspiration and *He* is a light one, both letters function as an aspiration among them. For that reason, wherever either a *Heth* or a *He* is placed among them, an aspiration must be placed in the same spot among us, except at the end of words, since our aspiration can never be final, except in certain <term>interjections</term> <note>Short exclamations like "Ah!" or "Oh!"</note>. Therefore, those who write *Heua* (Eve), *Habel* (Abel), *Hanna* (Hannah), *Iohannes* (John), and *Halleluia* without an "h" err significantly, since these are usually written among the Hebrews with either a *Heth* or a *He*. For *Heua* is indeed written with a *Heth* among them, thus *hauah* <note>original: חוה</note>, since it is derived from the verb *haia* <note>original: חיה</note>, which signifies "to live," with the letter *iod* changed into a *uau*. Hence *Heua* (as Holy Scripture testifies) is interpreted as "the mother of the living." *Hanna* is also written with a *Heth*, thus *Hannah* <note>original: חנה</note>, as they come from the noun *hen* <note>original: חן</note>, which is the same as "grace." *Ioannes* likewise is written with a *Heth* among them, thus *Iohanan* <note>original: יוחנן</note>. For it is composed from the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter divine name of God, YHWH; here specifically referring to the short form "Yah" (יה).</note> name of God, which is *Iah*, and from the noun *hen*, which is "grace." Therefore, *Ioannes* is interpreted as "the grace of God." *Habel*, however, is written with a *He* among them; for it descends from the verb *habal* <note>original: הבל</note>, which is the same as "he vanished." *Hallelu ia* is similarly written with a *He*, in this manner: *hallelu iah* <note>original: הללויה</note>, for there are two words. The first is *hallelu*, which is in the imperative mood and the second person plural of this verb *hillel*, meaning "he praised." The second is *iah*, which is one of the divine names and signifies God or the Lord. Thence comes *hallelu ia*, which is translated into our language as "praise God" or "praise the Lord." From the aforementioned, therefore, it is clearly evident that not only these, but indeed all other words which are found written with either a *Heth* or a *He* among the Hebrews, must be written with an aspiration among us. For in these, and in all remaining Hebrew words, the Hebrew manner of both writing and pronouncing must always be preserved by us (as far as can be done with our letters).

<margin>Second rule.</margin>
Otherwise, the same word would not retain the exact same meaning among us as it has among them. Hence it is—to bring forward only a few examples from the many you yourself have cited—that we ought to write and pronounce not *Henoch* but *Hanoch*, not *Mathusalem* but *Methuselas* with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, not *Noe* but *Noas*, not *Phares* but *Peres*, not *Moyses* but *Moses*, not *Iosue* but *Iehofuas* with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, not *Phinees* but *Pinhas*, not *Samuel* but *Semuel*, not *Salomon* but *Selomo*, not *Salathiel* but *Sealthiel*, not *Ioakim* but *Iehoiakim*, not *Osee* but *Hoseas* with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, not *Bersabee* but *Bathseba* also with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, not *Elisabeth* but *Elisheba* likewise with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, not *Gomorra* but *Amora*. For this is how the Hebrews both write and...

<summary>This page outlines two linguistic rules for transliterating Hebrew into Latin, focusing on the necessity of the letter 'h' to represent Hebrew aspirations and arguing for a more phonetically accurate spelling of biblical names to preserve their original meanings.</summary>
<keywords>Heth, He, aspiration, orthography, transliteration, Tetragrammaton, etymology, biblical names, Hebrew grammar</keywords>

-># BOOK TWELVE<-

<margin>Third rule.</margin>
...they may write and pronounce. However, it is permissible that these letters—<term>He</term> <note>ה</note>, <term>Heth</term> <note>ח</note>, and <term>Ain</term> <note>ע</note>—when they are final in these as in other masculine names, are very frequently changed by us into the letter "s" for the sake of a better <term>hiatus</term> <note>An opening or gap between two vowel sounds, which can sound awkward in Latin.</note>. Nevertheless, this change brings no change to the meaning. For I shall bring forward only two examples of each of these letters: among the Hebrews, **משה** (*Moseh*) and **ישעיה** (*Iesaiah*) end in *He*; **נח** (*Noah*) and **משיח** (*Massiah*) in *Heth*; and **יהושע** (*Iehosua*) and **מושיע** (*Mossia*) in *Ain*. Yet these and others of this kind are very often accustomed to end in the letter "s" among us without any variation in meaning. Examples include *Moses*; *Isaias* or *Esaias* (for it can be said both ways); *Noas*; *Messias*; *Iohosuas*; and *Mossias*, which is translated as "Savior."

<margin>Fourth rule: **עזרא**</margin>
The same thing often happens in proper names of the masculine gender ending in <term>Aleph</term> <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, א.</note>. For example, **עזרא** *Ezra* becomes *Ezras*; **שלמא** *Salma* (although it is sometimes found written with a *He*) becomes *Salmas*, who was the son of Nahshon and was also called *Salmon*, just as we read him named in the genealogy of our Savior in Matthew.

<margin>Fifth rule.</margin>
Furthermore, to those names which end in <term>Iod</term> <note>The letter י.</note> preceded by a <term>Patha</term> or <term>Camez</term> <note>Hebrew vowel markings: Patah (a short "a") and Qamets (a long "a").</note>, we add the syllable "-us," while the *Iod* and the preceding *Patha* or *Camez* are changed into a long "e" or the "æ" diphthong. For example: **חגי** *Haggai* becomes *Haggeus*; **מרדכי** *Mordochai* becomes *Mordocheus*; **זכאי** *Zaccai* becomes *Zacchæus*.

<margin>Sixth rule.</margin>
In most other cases, however, the ending "-us" is joined to our final letter in such a way that a single syllable is formed from them; meanwhile, the <term>acute accent</term> <note>The emphasis or stress placed on a syllable.</note> which among them was on the last syllable remains on the <term>penultimate</term> <note>The second-to-last syllable.</note> among us. For example, **יעקב** *Iaakob* becomes *Iacobus*, and **יוסף** *Ioseph* becomes *Iosephus*. And this indeed happens when we wish to bring those names into the <term>declensions</term> <note>The inflectional categories of nouns in Latin grammar.</note> of our own names. 

Since these things are so, no one, <term>Hogostratus</term> <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, a conservative theologian and opponent of Hebrew studies who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note> (as you might think), ought to criticize me, and no one ought to accuse or argue against me because I have not preserved the customary way of writing and pronouncing in the aforementioned cases and many others. For I did not do this out of ignorance or rash presumption, but so that I might correct those things and render them better. Nevertheless, I by no means deny that many things said in this work could have been said more elegantly and ornately, had it not been necessary to use a humbler style and more well-known, common words. This was done, first, so that the mysteries of the Christian faith found in Hebrew volumes might become better known to all. Second, it was so that there might be a more faithful interpretation of Hebrew words; for since I wished to translate them word for word, I was hardly able to maintain the <term>congruity</term> <note>The grammatical harmony or proper flow.</note> of the Latin language in some instances.

**CAP.** <note>Capnio, the Latinized name for Johann Reuchlin, the famous humanist and Hebrew scholar.</note> I indeed, Galatino (to speak from the heart), judge that whatever you have said, you have said so well and so elegantly that I think no one could have spoken better or more elegantly, especially in such a short time. You certainly would not have been able to do this unless you had been inspired by the Holy Spirit. Just as He once pronounced the mysteries of the Messiah through the prophets, that same Spirit now explains those same mysteries more clearly through you. From this, it is openly shown how useful, how profitable, and how conducive it is to the Christian commonwealth [to have] a Christian theologian...

<summary>Galatino details the linguistic rules for converting Hebrew names into Latin, explaining why he adds suffixes like "-us" or changes endings to "s" to suit Latin grammar. He defends his literal translation style against critics like Hoogstraten, claiming it is necessary to preserve the divine mysteries found in the Hebrew text.</summary>

<header>BOOK XII.</header>

...[it is clear] that you are not ignorant of Hebrew letters, from which you have so precisely extracted so many secrets of Catholic truth. By these, not only is the stubborn defiance of the Jews of our time so thoroughly defeated that they dare not even gape further, but also the truth of the orthodox faith is most strongly confirmed, and many—nearly infinite—passages of the Holy Scripture of the Old Testament, which are considered corrupted among the Greeks and Latins either by the fault of writers or the length of time, are corrected exactly according to our faith. For all these things, the whole Christian religion owes you very much.

**GALATINUS.** Although you, my dear Capnio <note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew. "Capnio" is a Greek translation of his German name, which relates to "smoke."</note>, say these things ingenuously out of your great kindness toward me (just as you feel), I, however, since I am not entirely unaware or unmindful of my own resources, leave and submit everything I have said in this work to the judgment and determination of the Apostolic See and the most holy Roman Church. And indeed, I do so in such a way that whatever is said poorly or ineptly may be attributed to my ignorance. Truly, let what is written erroneously be imputed to the scribe <term>amanuensis</term> <note>A person employed to write or type what another dictates or to copy manuscripts.</note>; for men of this kind are often accustomed to pervert, spoil, and corrupt almost everything written correctly to such an extent that their errors can hardly be corrected at all. But let whatever is good be attributed to Almighty God, from whom all the best things proceed. To whom be praise, honor, and—

**THE WORK IS COMPLETED**, *by the help of divine grace, concerning the Secrets of Catholic Truth, recently extracted from Jewish manuscripts and dedicated to the Most Invincible Maximilian, Emperor and ever August <note>Maximilian I (1459–1519), Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, at Bari, in the year of the Virgin's birth 1516, on the day before the Nones of September <note>September 4, 1516.</note>: in the fourth year of the Pontificate of our Most Holy Lord Leo X: during the reign of the Most Serene Rulers of both Hesperias <note>A poetic term for the West, here referring to the Spanish kingdoms of Castile and Aragon, as well as Naples and Sicily.</note>, Joanna <note>Joanna "the Mad" of Castile.</note> and her son Charles <note>The future Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note>, cultivator and foster-child of all virtues: under the auspices of the Most Reverend Lord Lorenzo Pucci, Cardinal Priest of the Most Holy Roman Church of the title of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs: with the favor of the most illustrious Isabella of Aragon, Duchess of Milan and Bari.*

### Sequence of sheets.
<note>Known as a register, this list helped the bookbinder verify that all sections of the book were present and in the correct order before sewing them together.</note>

->*All are <term>ternions</term>, except for yy*<-
<note>original: "Omnes terniones" — A ternion is a quire consisting of three folded sheets of paper, which creates six leaves or twelve pages.</note>
->*which is a <term>duernion</term>.*<-
<note>original: "qui est duernio" — A duernion is a quire consisting of two folded sheets, creating four leaves or eight pages.</note>

--- Page 671 ---
<meta>This page represents the final leaf of the volume printed in 1550. In Renaissance bookmaking, the very last page was often left blank or used to display the printer's personal emblem (the printer's mark), serving as a final "signature" for the publishing house.</meta>

<note>The text visible at the top and bottom of this page is mirrored "show-through" from the previous page and is not intended to be read here.</note>

->[Central Woodcut Illustration]<-

<note>This intricate woodcut is the printer's mark of Johannes Herwagen of Basel. It features a <term>herm</term>—a type of statue consisting of a head or torso atop a square pillar—with three faces. This "Triple Hermes" likely represents Prudence looking into the past, present, and future, or perhaps the "Hermathena" (a fusion of Hermes and Athena) symbolizing the union of eloquence and wisdom. The figure holds a <term>caduceus</term>, the traditional winged staff of the messenger god Mercury, which is entwined by two serpents and serves as a symbol of peace, trade, and negotiation. The pedestal is decorated with a lion's mask and floral swags, grounding the symbolic figure in a classical landscape.</note>

<summary>This final page displays the printer's mark of Johannes Herwagen, featuring a symbolic three-faced herm holding a caduceus. It serves as the visual signature of the Basel publishing house that produced this edition of Galatino and Reuchlin's works.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Herwagen, printer's mark, Basel, woodcut, herm, caduceus, Renaissance symbolism, 1550 edition</keywords>

--- Page 675 ---
<meta>This page represents the interior marbled endpaper or the inside cover of the binding, following the blank flyleaves at the conclusion of the 1550 edition.</meta>

[This page features a decorative marbled pattern.]

<note>The image displays a classic example of historical <term>marbled paper</term>, a decorative technique used by bookbinders to adorn the interior covers (pastedowns) and <term>endpapers</term> of a volume. This specific pattern, featuring swirling shades of green, black, and earth tones, was created by floating pigments on a liquid surface, manipulating them with combs or styluses, and then dipping the paper to "lift" the design. This was often used in the 17th through 19th centuries to reinforce bindings and hide the structural elements of the book’s spine and boards.</note>
